title: How £100 vanishes in minutes: inside the ‘slot farms’ targeted in the budget | Gambling | The Guardian
description: John Healey has hit adult gaming centres with 25% tax. Undercover footage shows how they lure customers
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: John Healey has hit adult gaming centres with 25% tax. Undercover footage shows how they lure customers
Content: AGCs and bookmakers line a Peterborough street, some open 24 hours a dayGamblingHow £100 vanishes in minutes: inside the ‘slot farms’ targeted in the budgetJohn Healey has hit adult gaming centres with 25% tax. Undercover footage shows how they lure customersRob DaviesThu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe last of five £20 notes disappears into the slot machine as The Verve’s Bittersweet Symphony plays over the shop’s sound system.That’s it, £100 gone in the space of about five minutes, swallowed up by one of the many “slot farms” that dominate the shopping streets ofPeterborough.All that’s left to show for it is a free KitKat, one of the incentives staff use to tempt customers into staying a little longer and losing a little more.It’s lunchtime on a Thursday and dozens of glassy-eyed hopefuls are having the same experience, feeding in what little cash they have and cursing as it disappears.The same pattern is repeated across the country. Gamblers in Great Britain lost £2.7bn on slot machines last year, nearly double the annual budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, which oversees the sector.In his inaugural budget this week, the chancellor, John Healey, took direct aim at slot machines by raising “machine games duty”, the tax levied on them, from 20% to 25%. This, he said, would bring in nearly £150m a year, “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.But what is the reality of Britain’s booming slot machine industry and why is it in the government’s crosshairs?What are slot machines?The most popular machines in the UK are so-called category B3 terminals. They allow you to stake £2 every 2.5 seconds for a jackpot of up to £500. A £2 maximum stake may not sound like a lot but losses can stack up quickly. In this test, £100 is gone in just five minutes.How £100 disappears in five minutes on high-speed B3 terminal machineThat’s one reason why each machine earns £40,000 a year on average, more than the median pay of a British worker. Slot machines are found in bookmakers, casinos and bingo halls but the venues that really pack them are adult gaming centres (AGCs), sometimes known as slot farms.How are AGCs making their money?They’re on pretty much every British high street,disproportionately in poorer areas. On some, such as this stretch in Peterborough, almost every shop is a bookmaker or an AGC.By far the two biggest AGC operators are Admiral, which is owned by an Austrian billionaire, and Merkur, owned by a German billionaire. Both havetargeted the UK for growthin recent years.Why are AGCs controversial?AGCs have their critics, including Andy Burnham, who has accused them of “targeting some of the most vulnerablein our communities”. Notable examples include when Merkur was fined £100,000 in 2025, after the Guardian revealed it had allowed an older woman with terminal cancer torack up huge lossesover two spells lasting 16 hours.As well as the potential for rapid losses, the machines are associated with higher rates of problem gambling than products such as sports betting. Critics also point to practices apparently designed to keep punters playing and losing. For a start, the majority of venues are open 24 hours a day,while the Guardian has previously revealed that staff are paidbonuses linked to customers’ losses, undermining their incentive to intervene to prevent problem gambling.Comfy armchairs, immersive screens, and staff serving snacks keep punters relaxedShops are increasingly offering a new breed of super slot machine, featuring a comfy armchair and a highly-immersive, 65-inch screen. Staff will offer drinks and snacks to keep punters playing, there are regular prize draws and “free spin” offers, and you can make cash withdrawals from your bank without leaving the shop.Punters will sometimes play more than one machine simultaneously. Admiral has introduced a two-machine limit, which it says is designed to reduce harmful gambling.Many are open under bingo licences, which may sound more benign to local authority planning committees. In practice, most have one bingo machine that is rarely used, if ever.Bingo machines are not in working order and are rarely usedCan you win?On a one-off basis, it’s possible to win up to £500. In tests across several AGC venues, the Guardian occasionally won some money, which will be donated to charity. But the machines have a fixed “return to player”, meaning that regular slot machine players will always lose. That’s why slots are a good target for a tax raid, and a valuable cash cow for companies, which like predictable sources of income. It’s also why gambling harm experts think they’re dangerous.Will the budget tax raid change things?Bookmakers say it will cost them money, leading to shop closures. Entain, which owns Ladbrokes, expects a £25m hit. But shares in the three listed slot machine operators – Entain, the William Hill owner Evoke and the Grosvenor Casinos owner Rank Group – rose sharply after the budget. Relieved investors had feared Healey would opt for a 40% rate.AGCs were singled out by the chancellor, who said they and vape shops would be excluded from business rates relief, costing them a combined £10m. But AGCs appear well-placed to thrive anyway because of their low overheads and 24-hour opening. For the slot farms, it’s business as usual.What do the slots companies say?Neither Admiral nor Merkur responded to a request for comment. Bacta, the slot machine trade body, said its members’ venues were “among the safest places to gamble, with experienced staff on hand to identify problems and provide support to customers”.“Player protection is central to our approach, and machines in AGCs are designed with inbuilt tools to encourage safe play, facilitate self-exclusion and help prevent problem gambling,” it said.“Games in these venues are low-stake – costing as little as 10p a spin – and these businesses have been a longstanding part of the high street for decades, providing low-stake entertainment, local jobs and a boost to local economies. AGCs tend to open on high streets where there is already footfall, alongside other hospitality and leisure venues, and where planning and licensing permissions allow.“Our members operate within one of the most tightly regulated licensing regimes in the world. Venues are regularly inspected, must comply with strict conditions, and can have licences refused or revoked where licensing objectives are at risk.”Explore more on these topicsGamblingBudget 2026PeterboroughfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The tabloids that used Thomas Markle to attack Meghan should now reflect. I bet they won’t | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: The Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday plundered Meghan’s estranged father for clicks. But soul searching or remorse would be institutionally impossible, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday plundered Meghan’s estranged father for clicks. But soul searching or remorse would be institutionally impossible, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: The Duchess of Sussex in Melbourne, Australia, in April.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/APView image in fullscreenThe Duchess of Sussex in Melbourne, Australia, in April.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/APOpinionAssociated NewspapersThe tabloids that used Thomas Markle to attack Meghan should now reflect. I bet they won’tZoe WilliamsThe Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday plundered Meghan’s estranged father for clicks. But soul searching or remorse would be institutionally impossibleThu 29 Oct 2026 10.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTShareAs theallegations mountagainst Thomas Markle Sr, his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, has released a statement describing her deep distress, and saying her priority is the protection of children. Is this the point at which Thomas Markle will cease to be an acceptable source for the Sussex character attacks that have become a tabloid staple? The Daily Mail and its sister paper, the Mail on Sunday, have been utterly brazen in their cultivation of the embittered Thomas Snr, using him as a weapon against his daughter since she first married into the royal family. Now, they’ll cut loose from him and describe the charges laid against him with the same outrage as everyone else. It would be institutionally impossible for them to discuss or reflect on their prior relationship with Markle without admitting a long-range and vindictive grudge against his daughter.View image in fullscreenFront page of the Mail on Sunday from 7 December 2025.Photograph: The Mail on SundayMarkle denies all allegations against him. His son, Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Markle Jr,described in a video for the Sunthe material he claims to have found on his father’s spare mobile phone, after Markle Sr had gone back to the US to have his leg amputated. Markle Jr was in the Philippines, where both men had moved in 2025. He said the material included “the most horrific video of a very young Asian girl … couldn’t have been more than 10 years old”. He almost threw up; he almost dropped the phone. His immediate fear was for what else he might be inadvertently in possession of. “I’m on the hook for this, now,” he said.As he made contact with the FBI, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children and the Pennsylvania state police, he reportedly found more and more material: “the most obscene, disgusting, lowest-of-the-low images … thousands and thousands of them.” He said he started to question every aspect of his family history, all the times his father had hastily snapped shut his laptop, “all the locked rooms in all the houses we’ve ever lived in”.Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. In 2019, she was passed a letter alleging that he had sexually abused a child, which she sayshad been sent to the Metropolitan police. The Met took no action on that letter and it has been reportedthat they subsequently misplaced it– whether that’s because they could believe no ill of Thomas Markle, or simply because they lose things, is unknown.But until now, the Daily Mail and the Mail on Sunday’s trust in Markle Sr and solidarity with him have been without question.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow did Mail on Sunday’s US editor become ‘rock solid friend’ of Meghan’s father?Read moreIn 2018, he handed the Mail on Sunday a five-page letter that his daughter had written to him after her wedding, which he had declined to attend, citing health reasons. Meghansuccessfully sued Associated Newspapersfor printing part of the letter, though “printing” doesn’t really encompass the torrent of coverage and insinuation they wrung from its contents. It was the start of a relationship between the newspaper and the now alleged sex offender that was so close by last year that when Thomas Markle learned about his amputation, thefirst person he toldwas Caroline Graham, the Mail on Sunday’s US editor (and previously a biographer of Queen Camilla). In photos of the pair together, the emotions are almost laughably legible: Markle looks pugnacious and triumphant, like the guy who’s managed to get public opinion on speed dial. Graham looks serene and also victorious, the first reporter on to Goose Green in the tabloids’ favourite war.View image in fullscreenFront page of the Daily Mail from 26 October 2026.Photograph: Daily MailA free press is essential and sometimes it is scabrous. But is this what a free press is for? To groom an estranged parent or other former intimate of someone in public life in order to undermine the latter person’s credibility and standing, seems sadistic. That’s a large word, particularly in the context of the allegations against Thomas Markle, and I use it advisedly. One of the hideous things about family estrangement is the feeling that everyone involved has had their character besmirched. The accused fight back with counter-claims. Nobody’s probity survives unscathed (although most of us could tell that Meghan’s father was exploiting her lovelessly for attention, and probably cash, long before these charges surfaced).A political or media enemy plundering that dynamic for an easy win, for clicks, for a vendetta, does not even have the fog of emotionality as a defence. Everybody recoils from it. When the Republican gubernatorial candidate in Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy, made an attack adfeaturing his opponent’s mothercalling her daughter, Amy Acton, a liar, most people didn’t know the history. They didn’t know that Donna Arthur had lost custody of her children decades previously, after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted on charges of child rape. People could nevertheless see how low it was to air a view that was poisonous by definition under the fig leaf of hearing from both sides.Ramaswamy lost a major endorsement and had venue cancellationswithin a day of that attack ad. What the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday would have to lose to even reflect on their allegiances in this episode is impossible to guess.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Exploding heads, mutant aliens and bursting chests: horror’s greatest special effects – ranked! | Movies | The Guardian
description: From the beheading in The Omen to the attic scene in The Birds, here’s a countdown of the genre’s most iconic moments – in glorious, old-school pre-CGI style
Author: Anne Billson
Headline: From the beheading in The Omen to the attic scene in The Birds, here’s a countdown of the genre’s most iconic moments – in glorious, old-school pre-CGI style
Content: Legendary … The ExorcistPhotograph: Warner Bros./AllstarView image in fullscreenLegendary … The ExorcistPhotograph: Warner Bros./AllstarRankedMoviesExploding heads, mutant aliens and bursting chests: horror’s greatest special effects – ranked!From the beheading in The Omen to the attic scene in The Birds, here’s a countdown of the genre’s most iconic moments – in glorious, old-school pre-CGI styleAnne BillsonThu 29 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 18.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Ring (1998)Towards the end of the 20th century, when film-makers’ overreliance on CGI was increasingly making special effects less special, it took the old-school practical approach of Japanese film-maker Hideo Nakata to make one’s hair stand on end. Just when you think the cursed VHS tape has claimed its last victim, Sadako’s vengeful ghost emerges from the well, comes closer … and climbs out of the television screen.19. The Phantom Carriage (1921)The Swedish director Victor Sjöström makes extensive use of double exposure – all done in-camera because optical printing had yet to be developed – to depict Death’s soul-collecting carriage in this folk-horror classic. Sjöström also plays the dissolute antihero, condemned to be the spectral vehicle’s driver unless he can mend his ways.18. The Student of Prague (1926)Henrik Galeen’s expressionist variation on the Faust legend reunites the stars of The Cabinet of Dr Caligari: Conrad Veidt plays the student who makes a deal with the devil (Werner Krauss), who steals his reflection. This evil doppelganger runs amok until Veidt confronts it in a split-screen climax.View image in fullscreenVampire Count Orlok (Max Schreck) being destroyed by sunlight.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty Images17. Nosferatu (1922)FW Murnau commandeers a variety of in-camera effects for this vampire masterpiece. Flipped negatives, sped-up action and stop-motion add to theunheimlichambience until, exposed to the sun’s rays, cadaverous Count Orlok (Max Schreck) vanishes in a puff of smoke.16. Dawn of the Dead (1978)Raise a glass to Jim Krut, who died in August but who will forever be remembered as “Helicopter Zombie” in George A Romero’s undead classic. Thanks to the magic of splatter makeup maestro Tom Savini, he shambles into frame – and gets the top of his head sliced off by a spinning rotor.15. Tetsuo: The Iron Man (1989)Shinya Tsukamoto burst on to the body horror scene with a no-budget semi-experimental cyberpunk nightmare in which a Japanese salaryman’s body parts gradually turn to metal through a combination of juddery time-lapse, stop motion and jump-cutting, all set to a clanging soundtrack. Finally, his penis turns into a giant drill and destroys a coffee table.View image in fullscreenOld school … RingPhotograph: TCD/Prod.DB/Alamy14. The Invisible Man (1933)James Whale’s adaptation of HG Wells’s novel owes much to the sardonic tones of Claude Rains, whose face is only briefly glimpsed in his Hollywood debut. John P Fulton’s special effects show the actor unwrapping bandages from his head to reveal – nothing!13. Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1931)Fredric March won the best actor Oscar for his performance in this violent, sexy pre-code adaptation of Robert Louis Stevenson’s novella. It would be 38 years before the director, Rouben Mamoulian, revealed how they achieved the groundbreaking onscreen transformation of Jekyll into Hyde: Wally Westmore’s makeup combined with coloured filters over the lens.12. Eyes Without a Face (1960)A surgeon kidnaps young women and – in explicit black and white – slices their faces off with a scalpel in an attempt to restore the beauty of his disfigured daughter. Georges Franju’s eerie arthouse horror was dismissed on its release, but is now hailed as an influential masterpiece.View image in fullscreenInfluential … Eyes Without a FacePhotograph: Cinetext/Allstar Collection/The Criterion Collection/Allstar11. The Exorcist (1973)The pea-coloured puke popularised the term “projectile vomiting”, and the deleted “spider-walk” became legendary before its restitution. But the signature effect in William Friedkin’s film is Linda Blair’s 360-degree head rotation, an effect at once ludicrous and horrifying, thanks to Dick Smith and Marcel Vercoutere’s lifesize animatronic dummy.10. The Birds (1963)The climbing frame, the schoolchildren, the gas station are impeccable set pieces, but the attack on Tippi Hedren in the attic is particularly terrifying. Much of the impact was achieved by editing, but some birds were attached to her clothes by nylon threads, and one of the beaks nearly took her eye out. The scene took seven days to shoot; Hedren described it as “the worst week of my life”.9. Eraserhead (1977)David Lynch’s first full-length feature is set in an industrial hellscape, where Jack Nance, he of the tumbleweed hair-do, ends up having to look after a chittering mutant baby. The creature, designed by Lynch himself, was reportedly made from an embalmed calf foetus with added working parts, and was ceremonially buried in a secret location after production wrapped.8. The Omen (1976)Graphic decapitation goes mainstream in a special effect supervised by John Richardson. Photographer Keith Jennings (David Warner) stoops to retrieve the Daggers of Megiddo, the only weapons effective against Damien the Antichrist – and is beheaded by a sheet of glass sliding off a runaway truck. Warner reportedly kept the severed head until his divorce, when his ex-wife claimed custody of it.View image in fullscreenPosh partygoers meld into each other in Society.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/Alamy7. The Howling (1981)Joe Dante’s werewolf satire, co-written by John Sayles, shows Robert Picardo (AKA Star Trek’s holographic doctor) saying “I’m gonna give you a piece of my mind” and offering a bit of his own brain to a horrified Dee Wallace before pulsating air bladders transform him into a beast before our very eyes. Take a bow, Rob Bottin, making his solo special effects debut.6. The Fury (1978)John Cassavetes, darling of American indie cinema, found Brian De Palma’s film “degrading”, but his villain’s comeuppance is so satisfying you wish Rick Baker’s effects could have been retroactively applied to the same actor’s character in Rosemary’s Baby as well. One of the psychic teenagers the scumbag has been trying to control zaps him with her full telekinetic force and kaboom! He explodes!5. Society (1989)Brian Yuzna’s body-horror satire unmasks the upper classes as shapeshifting entities who literally feed off the proletariat. The film climaxes with an orgiastic “shunt” in which posh partygoers merge into an orifice-invading mass not unlikeSalvador Dalí’s Great Masturbator, surreal effects courtesy of Screaming Mad George.4. Scanners (1981)There is no shortage of mind-boggling effects in the early films of David Cronenberg, but his sci-fi thriller about warring psychics provides one of the most memorable. One telepath’s demonstration of his ability is hijacked by a more powerful scanner (Michael Ironside) who makes his head explode. Dick Smith and Chris Walas packed a plaster skull with “leftover burgers”, then blasted it with an out-of-frame shotgun.3. An American Werewolf in London (1981)Rick Baker won the inaugural best makeup Oscar for his work on John Landis’s horror-comedy (with a budget three times that of The Howling). As Sam Cooke’s Blue Moon plays on the radio, David Naughton stares aghast at his hand turning into a werewolf’s paw. As his skeleton painfully reconfigures itself, his shrieks of agony turn into a howl.View image in fullscreenShocking … the cast didn’t know a critter would emerge from John Hurt’s chest.Photograph: Collection Christophel/Alamy2. Alien (1979)The rest of the cast knew something was about to happen, but didn’t know precisely what, so when a critter erupts out of John Hurt’s chest, their shock is almost as extreme as the audience’s. For the money shot, Hurt’s torso was replaced by a mechanical one packed with compressed air and animal entrails, with puppeteers hiding beneath the table. Director Ridley Scott designed the creature, Roger Dicken constructed it and sci-fi cinema would never be the same again.1. The Thing (1982)View image in fullscreenHorrifying .. The Thing.Photograph: Universal Pictures/AllstarA shapeshifting alien infiltrates a US research station in the Antarctic, sporadically erupting into displays of special effects that have yet to be equalled. Take another bow, Rob Bottin, who riffs on elements of human and animal anatomy in surreal sculptures that are simultaneously repulsive and beautiful. In one of the highlights, a geologist’s head separates from his body, sprouts spider-legs and tries to scuttle away. Palmer the pothead (David Clennon) says what we’ve all been thinking: “You’ve gotta be fucking kidding.”Explore more on these topicsFilmRankedHorror filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My sister-in-law is nearly 40 but cannot handle losing at board games. What can I do? | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: A game is not a moral exemption to your usual self. Sometimes the best way to puncture ‘it’s just a game’ is to show people that you’re judging them in reality
Author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
Headline: A game is not a moral exemption to your usual self. Sometimes the best way to puncture ‘it’s just a game’ is to show people that you’re judging them in reality
Content: When it comes to behaviour during board games, ‘as with all things, if you want her to know you’d prefer she stopped this, you have to endure the discomfort of her learning how you feel’, writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Painting: The Dispute at Cards by Jan Steen.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenWhen it comes to behaviour during board games, ‘as with all things, if you want her to know you’d prefer she stopped this, you have to endure the discomfort of her learning how you feel’, writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Painting: The Dispute at Cards by Jan Steen.Photograph: AlamyLeading questionsAustralian lifestyleMy sister-in-law is nearly 40 but cannot handle losing at board games. What can I do?A game is not a moral exemption to your usual self. Sometimes the best way to puncture ‘it’s just a game’ is to show people that you’re judging them in realityRead moreLeading questionsEleanor Gordon-SmithThu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 19.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy sister-in-law is nearly 40 but cannot handle losing at board games. No matter how high or low the stakes, she has to win. When she doesn’t, she becomes explosive with rage, and often upends the game, sweeps dice off the table, or storms off in a rage. She is otherwise a normal and lovely person, with whom I get on very well. Seeing this side of her makes me deeply uncomfortable and it feels really childish and inappropriate. Will she behave that way with me if I say or do something she doesn’t like?I think in an effort to smooth the tension, my husband’s family always laughs and teases her about her reaction. It’s like her “special little characteristic” that everyone pretends to love. I wish there was a way to address it but everyone seems to just sweep it under the rug. My husband is aware of how I feel about this.Recently, she’s started dating a new partner, who is absolutely lovely. When she has a big reaction after board games I can also sense him tensing up, so I know this is affecting more than just me. Ultimately, I’m worried for my sister-in-law that if she continues this behaviour, and the family continues to indulge it, she will suffer personal and professional consequences. I also don’t enjoy being around the dynamic, and think it is likely we’ll spend less time with her as a result. What can I do?A financially comfortable friend has set up a GoFundMe for vet bills. Is this socially acceptable? | Leading questionsRead moreEleanor says:I know someone who ended a relationship because their partner too gleefully teamed up with an ex to lie in a game of wink murder. I know someone who decided not to have kids with their then partner because, when he played with kids, he got a kick out of really scaring them. I know someone whose friendship never recovered after one shouted the c-word in a card game.Often it’s in the fictional that we most see the real.It’s not that the way you behave in a game is a straightforward guide to the kind of person you are. The whole reason games are fun is that that isn’t true. Games let you experiment with being a different kind of person; they let youexplore different kinds of agency. They are fun and absorbing precisely because youfocus on a single goal or way of reasoning. A game is a vacation from the rules and goals of normal life, and an excursion into new ones.But games aren’t meant to be a moral exemption to your usual self. They’re meant to let you play with and develop your usual self by putting it in unusual circumstances. Treating games as a forum for exorcising the worst parts of yourself with the petulant excuse “it’s just a game” misunderstands the whole enterprise.So what can you do about your sister in law doing exactly that?You’re astute to notice that the family going along with it doesn’t help. And you’re astute to notice that their laughter might be a bid to make things less awkward – not a sign that they actually enjoy it. Like how we laugh after an off-colour comment, hoping to social magic it into counting as a joke. They might hope that if they applaud, make this “her thing”, that transforms her behaviour into a fun bit – not just an adult having a tantrum.Their approach might make things less awkward, but it doesn’t give the disruptive personevidence of how disruptive they are. As always, the more you paper over the cracks someone’s created, the less you can be surprised when they don’t notice them.Sometimes the best way to puncture “it’s just a game” is to show people that you’re judging them in reality.You don’t have to say “don’t do that” or “why are you so mad” while they’re heated. (In fact, if it’s a real anger management thing, it’s better not to). You can just let your sincere attitude show in a moment they presumed would be structured by the fiction. A long look without a smile or a laugh. Silence. A hint of the ick it’s giving you in real life. In the same way that laughing along is a bid to turn a tantrum into a joke, reacting as you would in other circumstances can be a bid to separate her behaviour from the game.Awkward, yes; socially costly, yes. But as with all things, if you want her to know you’d prefer she stopped this, you have to endure the discomfort of her learning how you feel.The boyfriend who lied in wink murder, the man who scared the kids and the friend who shouted in the card game didn’t realise that the way they acted in games would affect how people saw them in real life until it was too late. A long look across the table now – or even a quiet word from a relative once she’s calmed down – is a much kinder way for her to find out.The reader’s letter has been edited.Ask Eleanor a questionShare your questionTell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions.
