title: Puddlesuits, movie nights and daytime baths: how to survive rainy days with small kids | Activities for children | The Guardian
description: Wet weather dampening your plans? From screen-free stories and craft kits to waterproof gear, here’s how to keep little ones – and grownups – entertained
Author: Rose Stokes
Headline: Wet weather dampening your plans? From screen-free stories and craft kits to waterproof gear, here’s how to keep little ones – and grownups – entertained
Content: Sofa, so good: the classic den is forever a favourite for keeping children entertained at home.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSofa, so good: the classic den is forever a favourite for keeping children entertained at home.Photograph: Getty ImagesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterActivities for childrenPuddlesuits, movie nights and daytime baths: how to survive rainy days with small kidsWet weather dampening your plans? From screen-free stories and craft kits to waterproof gear, here’s how to keep little ones – and grownups – entertainedThe best gifts for kids by ageRose StokesThu 29 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJump to:The best indoor rainy-day activities for kidsActivities on the cheap or even for freeBraving the weather: the best wet-weather clothing for kidsBefore becoming a mum, I never appreciated quite how complicated getting out the front door would be with kids in tow. But in my four and a half years of parenting two small people, I can confidently say it’s nothing compared with the challenge of a day spent inside when outside is off-limits. Whether because of endless rain or illnesses you don’t want to pass on, I panic at the thought of filling the hours spent indoors.Being outside is profoundly helpful for my mental health, and it comes with its own built-in entertainment for small children: a bus ride becomes a sensory experience, a trip to the doctor’s an opportunity to pick up role-play ideas.But what to do when leaving the house really isn’t possible? Over the years, I have developed a list of ideas for keeping my children (and me) sane indoors, and the productsthat have helped us muddle through (and dare I say, enjoy) those days. I’ve also recommended some gear to help you brave the wet weather.How have you been keeping the kids – and yourself – entertained during the rainy days? Let us know by emailing us atthefilter@theguardian.comThe best indoor rainy-day activities for kidsPlay tentAn unexpectedly popular item in our house came from one of the kids’ many generous aunties and uncles: a play tent. My initial thoughts? “How big! How intrusive! How unnecessary!” How wrong I was.Kids of all ages seem to gravitate towards it – perhaps owing to the illusion of privacy it offers (as well as being a very non-obvious place to scarper when playing hide-and-seek, wink wink). When ours was played with so much and broke beyond repair, I didn’t think twice about replacing it with this lovely, bright Djeco one. We chose it because of its colourful design, but I’d also seen one at a play cafe from the same brand and admired how sturdy it was. It’s a great place for us all to get cosy and read, and somewhere for my four-year-old to take a minute when his little brother is destroying his beautiful Magna-Tiles creations.View image in fullscreenDjeco multicoloured play tent£55.25 at Baby Mori£59.99 at VertbaudetSuitable for:3+Magna-TilesThat brings me nicely to Magna-Tiles. Parents seem to enjoy these almost as much as their kids do, and they’re popular with older children too. We don’t have it, but I just know this Rail Racers set would be an absolute hit in this house. There are imitation brands, but we invested in the official Magna-Tiles, which have lasted really well and endured being lobbed around by our toddler – who may or may not end up being a bowler in later life, given how much he likes to throw. Friends with cheaper knock-offs say you get what you pay for in this case.View image in fullscreenMagna-TilesRailRacers set£40 at ArgosSuitable for:3+This random car toyLook, I don’t really understand why, but my children were given this car toy by another auntie for Christmas last year, and every single child who has crossed the threshold of our house since then, big and small, has been obsessed with it. Not only does it play really earwormy songs, which they love, but it has a roller beneath a screen that shows a road unfolding in front of you as you “drive” with the steering wheel. You can also just push it around like any other toy car.So many friends have gone on to buy one too, but sorry in advance for the noise of the songs and for the fact it is, essentially, a big lump of plastic.View image in fullscreenSteering wheel car toy£29.89 at AmazonSuitable for:3+Craft kitsOur kids have a higgledy-piggledy medley of millions of different craft bits and pieces that their mother has bought for herself, used once and discarded. A visit to a craft shop such as Hobbycraft is probably the cheapest option for this, but there are a few nice premade kits out there too, like the Djeco one below. Another wildly popular craft activity in our house – also from a clever auntie – is this foil sticker set from Galt. It’s easy to use with minimal mess, so it ticks all my boxes.View image in fullscreenDjeco animal houses craft pack£25.50 at Baby MoriSuitable for:3+View image in fullscreenGalt foil set£7 at Hobbycraft£7 at AmazonSuitable for:6+Toy subscriptionBefore I became a mum, I used to say I would be vigilant in rotating toys to maintain interest (putting some into storage and bringing others out from time to time), then I actually became a mum and, well, that never happened. But then I discovered Lovevery.At first, I was a bit confused about why our kids might need new toys every few months, but after a few boxes, the value became evident. Those who sign up get a new set of toys (often sustainably made) every two to three months that are focused at their current age. It’s not cheap, but we’ve bought one or two boxes over the years or asked family to (as well as being sent some samples as press gifts in the past). There are favourites in every kit that have been thrown into the routine toy circulation, and saving them for a time stuck indoors has been a total salvation when I’m low on ideas.The toys are good quality, often wooden, and a one-off box makes a great present for grandparents to give when they’re looking for new ideas. The newborn Looker play kit is especially valuable, chiefly owing to the wooden mobile I hung above the changing table, which helped entertain them while I was committing the grave offence of cleaning their bottoms.View image in fullscreenThe Lookerplaykit£80 per kit on subscription at Lovevery£93.85 for one kit at AmazonSuitable for:0+Pikler triangleWhen our eldest was given one of these as a toddler, I struggled to see the value. But then came baby number two: a future rock-climbing tornado who makes it his business to scale any piece of furniture that crosses his path. Pikler triangles can be added to with other products to make little indoor climbing frames, and ours has a slide, which our toddler spends his life climbing up and throwing himself down, especially on days when the park is off limits.View image in fullscreenTPToysclimbingtriangle£69.99 at John Lewis£62.32 at AmazonSuitable for:1+PuzzlesWe have a wide array ofRavensburgerpuzzles, gifted by a very keen nanna. The brand makes a wide range of puzzles for different ages, so it’s worth investing in a couple. Hits in our house include the Hey Duggee one for younger kids and the current obsession: Spidey & His Amazing Friends (Ghost Spider specifically – IYKYK).View image in fullscreenHey Duggee puzzle£11.99 at RavensburgerSuitable for:2+View image in fullscreenSpidey&HisAmazingFriends puzzle£4.99 at Ravensburger£4.99 at AmazonSuitable for:3+Ice-cream shopNo imagination-based toy has been more used in our house than this ice-cream shop, made mostly of wood, by American brand Melissa & Doug. My friend’s children, seven and nine, still won’t part with theirs, which in my book is the sign of a good toy.View image in fullscreenMelissa& Doug Scoop and Serveice-creamcounter£39.99 at John Lewis£34.99 at AmazonSuitable for:3+Portable race trackI have seen these Speed Track car-racing tracks pop up in living rooms and birthday parties, with little kids, teenagers and even adults getting in on the action. It works with most small car toys you probably already own, and it’s easy to roll up and put away.View image in fullscreenSpeedTrack, 4 metres (without cars)£27.99 at Speed Track£27.99 at AmazonSuitable for:3+Play sofaA relatively new phenomenon, “play sofas” (modular sofas that can be rearranged to spark kids’ imagination) are fast becoming a go-to for parents of active children. Ours is from the Irish brand Baby Elegance, and has become a castle, a train, a spaceship, a cave, a house, a shop and many other things, all in the first few months. It has a foam core covered in hard-wearing corduroy fabric and doubles as a very comfortable bed for fans of what I like to call lying-down parenting (favoured by those with early-rising offspring, who have difficulties sitting up or who may have just had one too many the night before).View image in fullscreenBaby Elegance play sofa£213 at Baby EleganceSuitable for:1+ (with adult supervision)skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStepping stonesI first came across Stapelstein stepping stones at a local play cafe, and initially had no idea what the appeal was. Doubly so when I found out the price. Nonetheless, I have been blown away by just how many hours of fun my two have had playing with them, especially when friends come over. They’re made from high-density foamed plastic, making them lightweight and easy to pick up, but sturdy enough to support up to 180kg in weight, so they’re perfect for stacking, climbing on, using as hats or making seats from.They are great for mobility and practising balance, and they spark my kids’ imagination like nothing else I’ve seen. Visiting older kids have been just as obsessed with these, suggesting it may be a toy for the long haul, too.View image in fullscreenStapelstein stepping stones£154.95 at the Kid Collective£154.95 at ScandibornSuitable for:1+ (with adult supervision)Audio playerThe Yoto player is a screen-free audio player that’s a reliable all-rounder for both my kids. We listen to stories and songs, and grandparents and other relatives have recorded their own cards of them reading stories or singing for the kids to listen to. Cards can be targeted to a specific age, too. Our two-year-old loves the nursery rhymes and our four-year-old listens to stories, and both get a real kick out of “being in control” of the content, without realising that it’s actually their father and me who oversee it all. The smartphone app means we can stop and start playback from our phones, and we have recently discovered the software is available on Android Auto, meaning we can listen to our cards when in the car.View image in fullscreenYotoplayerFrom £64.99 at Yoto£65 at ArgosSuitable for:3+A movie projectorBad weather always leaves me jealous of friends who have projectors ready to turn their living rooms into home cinemas. A friend recommended this Samsung one, and it’s on my “if we ever have spare money” list.View image in fullscreenSamsung Freestyle 2£399 at John Lewis£349 at AmazonNintendo SwitchFriends with older kids rave about the Nintendo Switch their families got for Christmas. It can be played alone or as a family, with plenty of games for everyone. In their case, the console is kept in the living room, and children can swap TV time for console time on weekends.Mario KartandJust Danceare good for getting the whole family together.The Switch 2 is the latest, but the original Switch has a huge library of games and is now cheaper thanks to the arrival of its successor.View image in fullscreenNintendo Switch 2£389.99 at Argos£384.99 at AmazonSuitable for:3+View image in fullscreenNintendo Switch (first generation)£248 at John Lewis£259.99 at ArgosSuitable for:3+Activities on the cheap or even for freeHomemade playdoughI bought this fairly extensivecolour palette of food dyesfrom Amazon, and the kids love being able to pick which shade they will play with that day. I use thisrecipe, but there are loads out there. One thing to be aware of is these playdoughs are more likely to stain than the shop-bought stuff, so are best limited to the kitchen.A daytime bathWhen all else fails, I chuck my kids into the bath and let them have an extended play session they wouldn’t ordinarily have in the evening. If I’m feeling generous, I throw in aMunchkin ColourMixbath bomb, which my kids adore, even if the yellow shade does often make me think they may have had an accident.Costume playI found a pile of costumes in my kids’ sizes onVintedfor days when we just need a little extra inspiration. I spent about £6 and got a huge range for whoever they feel like being on that particular day.A denA timeless classic that is still a favourite for a reason. All you need is some chairs and bed sheets. For extra pizzazz, I sometimes add fairy lights, but this is not at all necessary.Active gamesWe also often play the floor is lava (with the very annoying song you can find on Spotify), hide-and-seek or Bluey-style “keepy uppy” with a balloon and accompanying soundtrack music.Braving the weather: the best wet-weather clothing for kidsView image in fullscreenSplish, splash, having a blast … but good waterproofs are essential.Photograph: onebluelight/Getty ImagesGood-quality waterproofsWe live in the rainy south-west, so to have a fighting chance of leaving the house between November and April, good waterproofs for the kids are a must. For smaller ones, many friends have recommended these Muddy Puddles suitswith a removable warm inner layer for adapting them to fluctuating temperatures.For older kids, I love shell trousers because they really do keep kids dry. I am a huge Mini Rodini fan and, though they are expensive, their sizes span 1.5 to 2 years generally, so on average, can be worn for two winters. I also know many fans of Polarn O Pyret, which offers more reasonably priced options for toddlers through to 12-year-olds.View image in fullscreenMuddy Puddles Scampsuit£95 at John Lewis£95 at Muddy PuddlesView image in fullscreenMini Rodiniwaterprooftrousers£82 at Mini Rodini£82 at SmallableView image in fullscreenPolarn O Pyret shell trousersFrom £40 at Polarn O PyretWellies and warm socksA good pair of wellies is essential, and my kids have always liked their colour-changing ones from Grass & Air. Put their little tootsies in some merino wool socks like these from Polarn O Pyret and job’s a good’un.One final tip I must add is not to buy fur-lined wellies. I know they look cute, but trust me, they get wet quickly, and then your kid is essentially walking around in soggy socks.View image in fullscreenGrass & Airwellies£27 at Mountain Warehouse£27 at AmazonView image in fullscreenMerinowoolsocksFrom £11.20 at Polarn O PyretView image in fullscreenDon’t buy anything until you’ve read the Filter, the Guardian’s home for truly independent product reviews and recommendations. Whether you’re after rigorous tests or shopping inspiration, affordable gifts or advice on how to make your belongings last longer, we’re here to help you make smarter, more sustainable choices.The Filter is packed with trustworthy buying advice on everything from coffee machines to hiking boots, mascara to secateurs. So visit us today and start buying better and smarter, and wasting less.Explore the FilterFor more, read thebest wellies for everyoneand thebest umbrellasRose Stokes is a Bath-basedjournalistwho balances writing about women’s health and parenting two small humansExplore more on these topicsActivities for childrenThe FilterToysHomesInteriorsGadgetsFamilyHobbiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Flávio Bolsonaro’s defeat is a major blow to Trump and his orange wave | Brazil | The Guardian
description: The far-right candidate was supposed to claim the presidency, but Brazilian voters had other ideas
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: The far-right candidate was supposed to claim the presidency, but Brazilian voters had other ideas
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro during a press conference in Brasília, Brazil, on 25 October.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro during a press conference in Brasília, Brazil, on 25 October.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBrazilFlávio Bolsonaro’s defeat is a major blow to Trump and his orange waveThe far-right candidate was supposed to claim the presidency, but Brazilian voters had other ideasTom Phillipsin São PauloThu 29 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForDonald Trump, Brazil’s presidential election was meant to represent the crest of the “orange wave” – a three-year surge of rightwing triumphs that has reshaped Latin American politics in the US president’s tangerine-hued image.The far-right candidate,Flávio Bolsonaro, was supposed to claim the presidency on Sunday, bringing the region’s biggest democracy and economy into Trump’s orbit, after similar victories in Argentina,Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Honduras, Ecuador and Peru – not to mention the capture of Venezuela’s government after the country was invaded in January.But Brazilian voters had other ideas, turning out in huge numbers to vote against the pro-Trump populist and return the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to power. On Tuesday, as Lula celebrated his 81st birthday to the sound of samba in Brasília, Bolsonaro fled to Miami on a private jet.“This is a significant blow, indisputably, to Trump’s regional strategy,” Benjamin Gedan, the director of the Stimson Center’s Latin America programme, said of Bolsonaro’s defeat.“[Trump] was perceived to be steamrolling over South America, having invaded Venezuela and seen close allies win elections in Argentina and Chile, in Bolivia and Colombia. That momentum had given the impression that he could determine political outcomes throughout Latin America – and he clearly enjoyed it,” added Gedan, a former White House South America adviser.View image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, during a press conference following the runoff election, in São Paulo, Brazil, on 25 October.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images“This is a region where he was really perceived to have a successful foreign policy, and this just flies in the face of that image.”The US setback was celebrated in China, whose rapidly growing influence in Latin America Trump has been trying to combat with his so-called “Donroe doctrine” of regional domination. “[Lula has] effectively thwarted Trump’s strategy for the region … Trump failed to bring Brazil, the largest nation in South America, under his sway,” Hu Xijin, a prominent Beijing propagandist, enthused on X.Trump has responded to his ally’s failure by halfheartedly querying the election, which Lula won by 4.3m votes.“I think the election was really strange … It’s so terrible to see,” he told reporters. “But I wasn’t involved,” Trump added, despitea months-long campaign of economic and diplomatic pressureapparently designed to boost Bolsonaro.Despite Trump’s decision to offer shelter to Bolsonaro – who is facing several criminal investigations in Brazil – many observers suspect the US president is unlikely to pick a major fight with Lula over his rightwing ally’s plight.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro steps off a plane after arriving at the Miami-Opa locka executive airport in Miami, Floria, on 28 October.Photograph: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP/Getty Images“One of Trump’s good qualities - and I mean this sincerely, even though it sounds ironic – is that he can smell a loser, and he wants to be around winners,” said Michael Paarlberg, a former Latin America adviser to Bernie Sanders.Lula supporters celebrate shock election victory – in picturesRead morePaarlberg noted how Trump got along with leftist “winners” including Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum; New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani – and even Lula himself. “I like Lula, I get along with him very well,” Trump said this week.“He will certainly favour his ideological co-partisans,” Paarlberg said of Trump, “but if the stink of loserdom starts to waft over them, he will drop them.”The “stink of loserdom” certainly wafted over Bolsonaro as he fled into Argentina on Tuesday and caught a private jet to Florida, wherehe briefly declared himself Brazil’s “true president-elect”before apparently changing his mind.Brazilian social networks filled with memes mocking the far-right politician who, only hours earlier, had vowed to stay in Brazil to lead opposition to Lula.One particularly scathing internet joke featured a photo of Bolsonaro and a parody of his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan, which was “God, Homeland, and Family.” “Goodbye, Homeland and Family,” it said.Speaking at his birthday party, Lula said: “This is what the Bolsonaro family is like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US.”View image in fullscreenThe front page of a newspaper displays the victory of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in São Paulo, Brazil, on 26 October.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesLula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, claimed Bolsonaro’s movement – which was founded by his jailed father, former president Jair Bolsonaro – was dead in the water after Sunday’s defeat, although the losing candidate secured 59.8m votes.“I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Amorim said, recalling how the movement had lost two successive elections to Lula, in 2022 and 2026.Amorim predicted a more reasonable conservative movement would replace Bolsonaro’s “extremist” one and called his loss “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying right wing”.Under Lula, Amorim indicated Brazil would not join Trump’s controversial Shield of theAmericas“counter-cartel coalition” – as Bolsonaro had planned to do.But Amorim also signalled that Lula would pursue pragmatic ties with Washington. “[Trump] has a certain level of pragmatism. They know Brazil isn’t just any old country. So I think we’ll seek to have proper, balanced relations without failing to defend our interests, but without being needlessly hostile, as we’ve always tried to do,” he said, recalling Lula’s good rapport with George W Bush.Amorim attributed Trump’s questioning of Brazil’s election to “incorrect things” that “rightwing radicals from the state department” had put on his desk.On Monday, Trump’s former chief strategist, Steve Bannon, urged Trump and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, to sever diplomatic and trade relations and “shut down everything with Brazil” as a result of the election supposedly being “stolen up in your face”.Paarlberg said Trump’s remarks – criticizing the election, but emphasising his fondness for Lula – suggested he would not take Bannon’s advice.“I read that as: ‘I will give you [Bolsonaro] moral support, but nothing else,’” Paarlberg said. “He certainly wasn’t saying: ‘I’m going to call for further tariffs, or further visa sanctions or any further actual measures to try to punish the Lula government.’”Gedan was unsure about Trump’s next move. “Anything’s possible, and I’m certain he has no idea how he’s going to approach it either,” he said.But Gedan believed Trump and Lula could patch things up – perhaps striking a deal involving Brazil’s massive critical mineral reserves – despite Trump’s hopes of a “glorious return” for the Bolsonaros being dashed.“There’s actually quite a bit of space for a positive relationship, if Trump does not decide to explode US-Brazil relations,”he said. “I think you absolutely could see Trump finding a way to admire Lula’s political skills.”Explore more on these topicsBrazilDonald TrumpFlávio BolsonaroUS foreign policyUS politicsAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Patrick Stewart, Star Trek actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86 | Patrick Stewart | The Guardian
description: Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men actor died at his home after ‘a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia’
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men actor died at his home after ‘a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia’
Content: Patrick Stewart, who has died aged 86, played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Treak: the Next Generation and Charles Xavier in X-Men.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPatrick Stewart, who has died aged 86, played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Treak: the Next Generation and Charles Xavier in X-Men.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The GuardianPatrick StewartPatrick Stewart, Star Trek actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men actor died at his home after ‘a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia’Patrick Stewart – a life in picturesPatrick Stewart dies aged 86 – latest updatesAdrian HortonandBenjamin LeeThu 29 Oct 2026 17.02 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatrick Stewart, the acclaimed British stage and screen actor renowned for both Shakespeare and sci-fi, has died. He was 86.The Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men star died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”, said Kelly Bush Novak, his longtime spokesperson, tothe Hollywood Reporter.Patrick Stewart – a life in picturesRead more“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” she wrote. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”With his authoritative baritone voice and commanding visage, Stewart was already a staple of the British stage by the late 1980s when, at 47, he was cast as a graying Capt Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: the Next Generation, the first live-action spin-off of the groundbreaking 1960s TV series. Over seven seasons onboard the Starship Enterprise, Stewart’s even-keeled performance and steely directives – “engage!” and “make it so” – turned him into a global star.View image in fullscreenPatrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1990.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesStewart reprised his role in four feature film spin-offs – Star Trek Generations (1994), Star Trek: First Contact (1996), Star Trek: Insurrection (1998) and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002) – as well as the TV series Star Trek: Picard, which ran from 2020 until 2023.His longtime friend, fellow Shakespearean actor and X-Men co-star Ian McKellenwrote on social media: “Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.”Fellow Star Trek actor William Shatner paid tribute on social media. “From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did,” hewrote. “Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.”‘On stage, I could escape’: Sir Patrick Stewart on childhood trauma and acting successRead moreGeorge Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the original series, also wrote about Stewart on Bluesky. “He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity,” heposted. “Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.”His other most well-known role was playing Prof Charles Xavier in the X-Men series. The actor had found work hard to obtain after feeling typecast as a result of his Star Trek role but had been intrigued by working with director Bryan Singer for 2000’s X-Men.He went on to play the role in seven films and will be seen reprising the role in this December’s Avengers: Doomsday.View image in fullscreenPatrick Stewart as Charles Xavier in X-Men 2.Photograph: Marvel/AllstarHis X-Men co-star Hugh Jackmansharedon Instagram: “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”Marvel chief Kevin Feige has paid tribute in a statement calling him “brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas … Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor. It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.”Stewart’s other film roles included the gay comedy Jeffrey, romantic thriller Conspiracy Theory, violent horror Green Room and voice roles in Ted, Gnomeo & Juliet and, most recently, The Sheep Detectives.View image in fullscreenPatrick Stewart and Ian Holm on stage in The Iceman Cometh.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyBorn on 13 July 1940 in the small industrial village of Mirfield, England, Stewart was the youngest of three sons born to Alfred Stewart, a British military veteran turned semiskilled laborer, and Gladys Stewart, a weaver at a textile factory. His childhood, in a small house with no running hot water, was marred by alcoholism and domestic violence, a situation he later described, in anarticlefor the Guardian from 2009, as “barely tolerable”.He found respite in acting, first in school – he was 12 when an English teacher assigned him the part of Shylock in Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice – and then local drama groups. “I managed to find my own refuge in acting,” he wrote. “The stage was a far safer place for me than anything I had to live through at home – it offered escape. I could be someone else, in another place, in another time.”After graduating from secondary school at 15, he worked as a local reporter and furniture salesman before a local arts council provided the funding to attend the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theater School, where he enrolled in 1957, at 17. Having shed his Yorkshire accent, he took his first professional theater role two years later, and in 1966 joined the Royal Shakespeare Company. During his 16 years with the company, Stewart developed a reputation as one of the finest thespians of his era and a representative of Shakespeare to new audiences; it was while conducting master classes on Shakespeare in LA, at the invitation of a friend, that he first caught the eye of a TV casting director for Star Trek.Stewart made his Broadway debut in 1971 in Peter Brook’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and appeared again 20 years later in a solo production of A Christmas Carol. The holiday season show, which he revived in 1992, 1994 and 2001, received a Drama Desk award.View image in fullscreenDavid Tennant as Hamlet and Patrick Stewart as Claudius, in a Royal Shakespeare Company production of Hamlet.Photograph: Robbie Jack/Corbis/Getty ImagesOver the course of his career, Stewart embodied many of Shakespeare’s signature roles, including Macbeth, Othello, Prospero, Shylock and Mark Antony. He was the recipient of two Laurence Olivier awards – in 1979, for Antony and Cleopatra, and in 2009 for Hamlet – as well as a Grammy in 1996 for a spoken word children’s album Prokofiev: Peter and the Wolf. He was also nominated for a Tony and four Emmys.His final major stage role was in 2016, when he appeared as Hirst in Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land at London’s Wyndham Theatre. In 2023, he released his memoir called Making It So.Stewart was a vocal fan of Huddersfield Town FC since he was a child and was seen cheering them on most recently in 2024.In a Facebook postfrom the official team, he was called “a titan of his craft and a legend and hero to millions worldwide”.Stewart was married three times: to theater choreographer Sheila Falconer, from 1966 until 1990 and with whom he had two children, fellow actors Daniel and Sophie; to Star Trek producer Wendy Neuss from 2000 until 2003; and to jazz musician Sunny Ozell from 2013 until his death. His friend and occasional collaborator Ian McKellen, with whom Stewart starred in two Broadway productions in 2013, officiated his final wedding after a rehearsal.“I think I’ve been in denial about my life for a very long time,” he said to the Guardian ina 2023 interview. “I never really took on board how successful I had become. Even today I sometimes think, ‘You’re a lucky son of a bitch, Patrick,’ when something unexpected or good happens to me.”Explore more on these topicsPatrick StewartStar TrekTelevisionUS televisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Healey backs away from cutting welfare cost amid warnings of public finance shortfall | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Experts round on chancellor over ‘scattergun’ budget, saying he ducked big tax and spending decisions
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Experts round on chancellor over ‘scattergun’ budget, saying he ducked big tax and spending decisions
Content: Disabled people and supporters protest against cuts to welfare benefits in Westminster in June.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDisabled people and supporters protest against cuts to welfare benefits in Westminster in June.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesBudget 2026Healey backs away from cutting welfare cost amid warnings of public finance shortfallExperts round on chancellor over ‘scattergun’ budget, saying he ducked big tax and spending decisionsHeather Stewart,Rowena Mason,Richard PartingtonandPhillip InmanThu 29 Oct 2026 16.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 18.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.Experts rounded on Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget on Thursday, with the Institute for Fiscal Studies saying he hadleft himself a mountain to climbby ducking big tax and spending decisions.In a damning analysis, the IFS said Healey would need to have set aside an additional £28bn a year, to offset the impact of inflation on future spending plans and hit the target of spending 3% of GDP in defence by 2030.Instead Helen Miller, the IFS director, said Healey had opened the way to “a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments” – including real-term budget cuts.“Public service spending plans look extremely tight. They don’t look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver,” she said, adding that meant Healey could face “another season of damaging speculation about tax rises”.The welfare bill will not be part of the spending review, which focuses on departmental budgets. But in a bid to underline his determination to balance the books, the chancellor pointed to plans for reform, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We have to bring the benefits bill down.”He had earlier appeared to say cuts would be made in this parliament, when asked if there would be a reduction in the bill before the next election. “There will be. There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Healey. “We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progress to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.”Budget 2026: what it means for your wallet, your mortgage and your payRead moreHowever, Treasury officials clarified that he had not meant to give a timeline and Healey later told Channel 4: “It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.”Instead, he pointed to forthcoming reviews from Alan Milburn on employment support for young people, and from Stephen Timms on disability benefits.Milburn is expected to recommend additional spending upfront, aimed at bringing down costs over the longer term by helping more young people into employment.The Office forBudgetResponsibility has said total welfare spending will grow from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030 – with about half of that being spent on pensioners and a quarter on sickness and disability benefits. The overall forecast spending has risen by £8bn since March.With a tough global economic backdrop, Healey has said the single biggest driver of better prospects for the UK would be an end to the Iran and Ukraine wars.But in his interviews, Healey appeared to take a more cautious view than the prime minister on the potential for growth from rejoining Europe or the single market. Asked by LBC if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU or the single market, Healey replied: “Well, I don’t actually accept that. Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union. The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient.”Asked later by Channel 4 if he, like Andy Burnham, hoped for the UK to re-enter the bloc in his lifetime, Healey said: “I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.”The chancellor put measures to ease the cost of living at the heart of his first budget, including a £100 winter cost of living payment for most households. However, critics lined up on Thursday to accuse him of taking a “scattergun” approach – and of not hitting Britain’s banks hard enough to fund the package.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Resolution Foundation thinktank said Healey had failed to target energy support to the households that need it most ahead of a difficult winter, with bills expected to rise sharply in January and the Bank of England to raise interest rates next week.Ruth Curtice, Resolution’s chief executive, said: “Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain.“Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.”John Healey faces questions over budget leak that moved bank share pricesRead morePaul Nowak, the TUC’s general secretary, has strongly advocated for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support. He said he welcomed Healey’s approach, but would be pushing for him to go further.The chancellor has doubled the surcharge banks pay on their profits from 3% to 6% for 15 months. Novak said: “It was right to tax banks to help people with their energy bills, but I think banks could have been asked to pay a fairer share. He’s going to review it in 15 months. We’re going to be looking as part of that review – if banks are still making windfall profits – for him to extend and increase the bank tax.”As well as casting doubt on whether Healey’s future spending plans are realistic, the IFS said the £15bn headroom, or buffer, he has left himself against Labour’s fiscal rules could easily be eroded by higher than expected energy costs.The chancellor allowed the buffer to absorb some of the impact of the Iran war, which has driven up the government’s cost of borrowing. At the time of the spring statement, Rachel Reeves had built up headroom of £24bn.Miller said that was a “reasonable” decision to make, but “a lower buffer leaves the chancellor more exposed to future bad news”.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyInstitute for Fiscal StudiesThinktanksBudgetTax and spendingWelfarenewsShareReuse this content

title: Netanyahu accused of smearing Arab voters to hold on to power | Benjamin Netanyahu | The Guardian
description: Prime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majority
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Prime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majority
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu gesturing to supporters on election night. He has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.Photograph: Jalaa Marey/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu gesturing to supporters on election night. He has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.Photograph: Jalaa Marey/AFP/Getty ImagesBenjamin NetanyahuNetanyahu accused of smearing Arab voters to hold on to powerPrime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majorityJulian Borgerin JerusalemThu 29 Oct 2026 19.14 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics to cling to power, after he claimed that Arab Israeli parties had used foreign backing to “steal” Tuesday’s election, in which the prime minister’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority.Netanyahu and his allies called on the internal security service, Shin Bet, to investigate alleged vote buying and other irregularities in Palestinian communities inIsrael, supposedly funded by foreign money.Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the main opposition bloc, accused the prime minister and his Likud party of trying to derail the election results.“It’s already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election,” Eisenkot said in a video message.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot at an election night rally in Tel Aviv after the first exit polls were announced.Photograph: Noam Galai/Getty ImagesThe prime minister’s allegations were quickly disowned by a range of government officials, including police officers and members of the election committee. Netanyahu was also rebuked by the president for “tarnishing an entire community”.On Wednesday night, the prime ministerposted a statement by Likud online, which described the claimed violations as “an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of rightwing rule”.Tuesday’s elections led to Netanyahu’s far-right coalition losing its majority after four years in power. The main Jewish opposition bloc also fell short, however, leaving two Arab Israeli parties, the Joint List and Ra’am,holding the balance of power.Final results released early on Friday local time showed the pro-Netanyahu bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset and Eisenkot’s bloc taking 48 seats. Joint List and Ra’am won the remaining 19 seats, a historic high for the Arab Israeli community, which makes up about a fifth of Israel’s population.The prime minister’s attack appeared aimed at stopping the Jewish and Arab opposition from voting together in the new Knesset to oust the incumbent speaker, Amir Ohana, a Likud politician and former Shin Bet official, and advancing their own legislation.The Likud statement posted by Netanyahu on X said: “It is clear that no Zionist party should cooperate with Ra’am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker through votes bought for cash, and form a government that is dangerous to Israel.”View image in fullscreenAmir Ohana (centre) applauding Donald Trump alongside Isaac Herzog (right) before the US president spoke in the Knesset in October 2025.Photograph: Getty ImagesOpposition leaders lambasted the claims of Netanyahu, 77, who has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List leader, accused the prime minister of incitement. “Netanyahu was defeated at the ballot box,” Jabareen said, adding that he “refuses to come to terms with the fact that the Arab public voted and decided”.Eisenkot said any investigation should be conducted “without fear or favour,” and with “the utmost caution”, but insisted it could not be used as a reason to delay the convening of the newly elected Knesset, due to be sworn in within 14 days of the election.The acting director general of the central elections committee, Dean Livneh, said there appeared to be no basis for the claims. Police officials quoted across the Israeli press said the allegations were groundless, adding that voting had been relatively trouble-free.View image in fullscreenYousef Jabareen casting his ballot in the Arab-Israeli town of Umm al-Fahm.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesThe president, Isaac Herzog, called for political leaders to “avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy”.It was not specified in Likud statements, but press reports said Qatar was the foreign power alleged to have funded vote-buying and voter mobilisation. Majed al-Ansari, an adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said its government “categorically” denied any involvement in the elections.The record turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship) appeared to be driven by outrage at routine discrimination and fear that it could become far worse if extremist and openly racist members of the government, such as the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, secured another term in office.On Thursday, Ben-Gvir called for the arrest of Arab party leaders, and Smotrich demanded they be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation.View image in fullscreenElection campaign posters in Nazareth.Photograph: Adri Salido/Anadolu/Getty ImagesVoting in Nazareth, the biggest majority-Palestinian town in Israel, was brisk on Tuesday, with few signs of irregularities, other than apparent ploys by the government and coalition parties to suppress the Arab vote.Some packets of ballots sent to Nazareth polling stations were in Hebrew alone, rather than in Hebrew and Arabic. Election workers said that monitors sent by far-right parties had attempted procedural ploys to slow down voting but had been largely unsuccessful.The leaders of the Joint List and the Zionist “Change” bloc have ruled out a formal coalition, but officials from both have discussed thepossibility of tactical votingin the Knesset to unseat Ohana, the speaker, and to pass some consensus legislation.One proposed bill would establish a commission of inquiry into the security failures that helped lead to the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, something Netanyahu has blocked over the past two years.Ahmad Tibi, a party leader on the Joint List, said Netanyahu was trying to subvert the election results by trying to sabotage a common front between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties.View image in fullscreenAhmad Tibi casting his vote.Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told the Reuters news agency.Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who is a partner in the “Change” bloc, pointed out the irony of Netanyahu denouncing Qatar for election meddling while the Israeli leader’s own political advisers are beingaccused of taking Qatari moneyfor promoting the Gulf monarchy’s image.“This morning, suddenly, when it serves his interests, Netanyahu remembered Qatar and is using it to sow chaos and undermine public confidence in the democratic process,” Bennett wrote on X.Explore more on these topicsBenjamin NetanyahuIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Female Lib Dem MP accuses Nigel Farage of shoving her in parliament  | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Caroline Voaden says Reform UK leader grabbed her by the arm and tried to push past her in incident in May
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Caroline Voaden says Reform UK leader grabbed her by the arm and tried to push past her in incident in May
Content: Caroline Voaden said the incident happened after Nigel Farage told her to let him past and she said he should ‘wait his turn like everyone else’.Composite: House of Commons; Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenCaroline Voaden said the incident happened after Nigel Farage told her to let him past and she said he should ‘wait his turn like everyone else’.Composite: House of Commons; Stefan Rousseau/PANigel FarageFemale Lib Dem MP accuses Nigel Farage of shoving her in parliamentCaroline Voaden says Reform UK leader grabbed her by the arm and tried to push past her in incident in MayRowena MasonandPeter WalkerThu 29 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 10.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA female Liberal Democrat MP has accusedNigel Farageof shoving her aside at the state opening of parliament after which one of her male colleagues intervened.Caroline Voaden gave her account of the incident in May this year after Farage revealed on Wednesday that there had been a “physical altercation” in parliament which meant he had decided to avoid the budget.Voaden told the Guardian: “He was trying to get out of the chamber and instead of just asking if he could go past, he said: ‘Let me past’. I turned round and said: ‘No, you can wait your turn like everyone else’. He grabbed me by the arm or the shoulder, pushed me to one side and tried to push past me. One of my colleagues tried to stop him because he thought I was going to fall down the stairs. And then we all shuffled down.“Quite deliberately, he grabbed me by the arm from behind and pushed me to one side so that I fell into a colleague or the wall on the other side. I was really taken aback and really angry because I think you just don’t behave like that in any workplace, let alone the chamber of the House of Commons. It was rude. It was nasty.”Voaden said she had complained to the serjeant at arms who she believed had written to Farage asking him to apologise. She also raised it with the speaker. “Nothing ever came of it,” she said.View image in fullscreenCaroline Voaden speaking in parliament.Photograph: House of CommonsAReform UKsource said it was “not true at all, it was the Lib Dem MPs being aggressive towards Nigel. This is typical Lib Dem dishonesty in an attempt to stay relevant.”The male Lib Dem MP who intervened is understood to be Max Wilkinson, with sources saying he put a hand on Farage’s shoulder, “fairly gently” grabbed him and said he could not do that to another MP.Reform sources also suggested a video from the Commons showed her account was wrong, but the Lib Dems said the incident took place before the footage started.The row erupted after the Reform leader said he had skipped John Healey’s budget speech in the Commons on Wednesday because his seat reservation had been moved and he decided to give it a “wide berth” in order to “avoid conflict” in the chamber.He claimed he had been involved in a “physical altercation” with another MP on the day of the state opening of parliament in May.It later emerged his reservation had been removed by Commons staff as it did not have the proper date stamp.Nigel Farage skips budget in Commons over seating ‘altercation’ concernsRead moreDaisy Cooper, the Lib Dem deputy leader, told Sky News on Thursday morning that her party’s MPs were involved in the May incident mentioned by Farage.She said: “My understanding – I didn’t see it, I wasn’t there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that.“I didn’t see it, I didn’t witness what happened, but that was several months ago.“And let’s be really clear: it’s Reform UK that had a problem at their conference with bundling female journalists and members out of their hall. So, we’ll take no lessons from them on this.”Afterwards, Voadenpostedon social media in response to Farage’s claim that he was at risk of “another physical altercation”: “We both know that’s not true Nigel don’t we?“I’m still waiting for the apology you were required to write to me … Though I won’t hold my breath.”When asked for a response to the accusations, Robert Jenrick, Reform’s shadow chancellor, said: “You know what? I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates.“The thing about Reform politicians is, yeah, we love parliament, the institution of parliament. I go there every day. I speak in parliament. I represent my constituents.“But I’m much more interested about, actually, the issues, trying to change this country, getting out and about outside of the bubble. And I’m not interested in even responding, dignifying the nonsense that Daisy Cooper is talking about there.”Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageLiberal DemocratsReform UKBudgetnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spain begins mourning period as search continues for train crash victims | Spain | The Guardian
description: Emergency services, drones and dog unit continue to comb carriages as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Emergency services, drones and dog unit continue to comb carriages as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples
Content: Seville residents hold five minutes’ silence for the crash victims at Santa Justa train station in Seville.Photograph: Marcelo del Pozo/ReutersView image in fullscreenSeville residents hold five minutes’ silence for the crash victims at Santa Justa train station in Seville.Photograph: Marcelo del Pozo/ReutersSpainSpain begins mourning period as search continues for train crash victimsEmergency services, drones and dog unit continue to comb carriages as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samplesHow did the Spain train crash happen and what will investigators be asking?Sam JonesandAshifa Kassamin MadridThu 29 Oct 2026 13.59 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 01.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpain began three days of mourning on Thursday for at least 69 people who died in a high-speed rail collision, as hospitals continued to treat dozens of injured passengers and train drivers went on strike to urge more investment in railway safety.The trains – one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo – were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.Spain’s foreign ministry said 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, adding that one had been killed and at least seven injured.10:20Survivors shell-shocked after deadly Spain train crash - The LatestThe crash came 10 months after 46people were killedand dozens more injured when two trains – one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s large, modern high-speed rail network. The transport minister, Óscar Puente, said rear-end collisions such as Wednesday’s were “highly unlikely”, and suggested the accident could have been caused by human error under “inexplicable” circumstances.View image in fullscreenIryo employees in Madrid embrace after observing a minute’s silence for the victims of the train crash.Photograph: Bernat Armangué/APEmergency services combed the wreckage through the night for more victims, using cranes to hoist pieces of mangled metal. At daybreak, police once again launched drones to survey the crash site.Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on Thursday morning that rescue teams did not think they would find any more bodies in one damaged carriage that was ‌still overturned, but added that body parts had been found that would need to be identified.“Yesterday we experienced a catastrophe that without a doubt has left all of Spain in shock,” said García-Page. He confirmed that 50 of the people who had been taken to hospitals in the region were still being treated.View image in fullscreenThe crash scene on Wednesday.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesThe prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, speaking during a visit to the emergency command centre in the city of Toledo, said the authorities were doing all they could to establish the cause of the crash and prevent another rail tragedy.“I’d like to let all Spaniards know that every institution that is part of the state – from the smallest municipality to the government of Spain – is working day and night, not only to provide a response to the families of the victims, but also, of course, to uncover every last detail of this tragedy and to strengthen safety measures so that something like this never happens again.”King Felipe, who visited a hospital in Toledo where some of the injured were being treated, said Spain had “once again suffered an extremely harsh blow” and called for lessons to be learned.“There is obviously an ongoing investigation, which should establish how and why this tragedy happened,” he said on Thursday. “Measures will need to be looked at and adopted so that this doesn’t happen again.”View image in fullscreenWorld Central Kitchen delivers meals to emergency services and security forces at the scene of the train collision.Photograph: Angeles Visdomine/EPAMeanwhile, Spanish train drivers went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety. The crash was Europe’s deadliest train accident sincea derailment in Santiago de Compostelain north-west Spain that killed 80 people in 2013.“We will continue demanding the necessary measures to make this sector safe again ... It must have all the safety systems required to maintain the quality standards we have always had,” said Diego Martín of the train drivers’ union Semaf. “We cannot tolerate, under any circumstances, this type of incident happening again.”‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in SpainRead moreThe Guardia Civil police force has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid. The force said 64 people had been reported missing by relatives by Thursday morning.A school in Urda, which lies about 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, has been turned into an information centre where relatives can inquire about loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who had arrived, some of them in tears.Carmen García, a Red Cross psychologist, said “long and hard hours” lay ahead and that “every person will manage it in their own way”. She added: “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated.”1:31Spain in mourning after fatal rail crash, says Spanish prime minister - videoJosé Miguel Fernández, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to the victims’ families.“It is important for relatives to find their loved ones, even if they have died, because the grieving process is quicker when you have been able to say goodbye at that final moment,” he told Onda Cero radio.Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail networkRead moreSurvivors have spoken of being thrown from their seats by the impact of the crash, and of trying to help the injured in the immediate aftermath.Among the first victims to be named was José Manuel Chacón, a 31-year-old Guardia Civil officer. The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues.Also among those killed was Fátima Báñez, a former labour minister for the conservative People’s party (PP), who had gone on to chair the social and corporate responsibility arm of Spain’s ⁠employers’ association.The PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.With Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsSpainEuropeTrain crashesRail transportEmergency servicesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Met refers itself to police watchdog over Meghan warning letter | Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex | The Guardian
description: Move comes as Philippines police investigate alleged child sexual abuse images reportedly found at Thomas Markle Sr’s former home
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Move comes as Philippines police investigate alleged child sexual abuse images reportedly found at Thomas Markle Sr’s former home
Content: A letter was sent to the Met ‘to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex’.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA/APView image in fullscreenA letter was sent to the Met ‘to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex’.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA/APMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMet refers itself to police watchdog over Meghan warning letterMove comes as Philippines police investigate alleged child sexual abuse images reportedly found at Thomas Markle Sr’s former homeVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentThu 29 Oct 2026 15.55 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheMetropolitan policehas referred itself to the police watchdog over potential errors in its handling of a 2019 letter warning of dangers to the security of the Duchess of Sussex posed by her father.The letter made allegations about Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, who is facing claims of child sexual abuse images offending linked to thePhilippines, which he denies.It was allegedly written by his former wife and the Met says the letter was passed seven years ago to the private office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who were then both working royals.The Guardian understands that the long letter made claims about Markle’s activities in the US, the Philippines and Thailand.The Met said it did not investigate as the allegations related to potential unlawful activity overseas.The key problem for the Met is its admission that it did not share the letter with law enforcement agencies overseas, and that issue has been referred to the police watchdog, the Independent Office forPoliceConduct.The Guardian understands the Met is now sending details of the letter to the FBI in the US and law enforcement in the Philippines, where Markle lived until May, as well as Thai counterparts.Markle, now in the US, has admitted paying for sex but denies possessing material that would be illegal.On Saturday Jonvic Remulla, the Philippine interior minister,told the Guardian that all signs point to Marklebeing a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” and that a full forensic investigation will give a “definitive picture”.Officials and investigators in the Philippines are examining digital images alleged to belong to the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, and alleged to have been found at his former home in the south-east Asian country.Meghan’s half-brother, also called Thomas, reported to Philippine authorities last week the alleged discovery of child sexual abuse images.The allegations about the letter and alleged Met failings surfaced publicly a week ago. The Met has been unable to find its own copy of the letter making the claims, alleged to have been written by Markle’s former wife.Met Commander Adam Slonecki, who leads its Protection Command, said the letter had been sent in 2019 to the Fixated Threats Assessment Centre: “The author of the letter suggested they were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.“The letter was assessed and subsequently passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”Slonecki added: “A voluntary referral has been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.”The Met cannot find a copy of the 2019 warning letter in its systems, and asked the Duchess of Sussex to send the copy she had to assist Britain’s biggest force to better understand its decision making seven years ago, which she did.An IOPC spokesperson said: “We have received a voluntary conduct referral from the Met police, which relates to the handling of a letter it received in 2019 involving allegations of offending. We are now assessing the referral before deciding what further action may be required.”Possible options include the police watchdog independently investigating or sending the matter back for the Met to investigate.The scale of embarrassment for the Met will depend on whether investigators in the Philippines assess that the allegations relating to child sexual abuse images have any credence.Explore more on these topicsMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMetropolitan policePolicePhilippinesMonarchyLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manosphere and online misogyny should be treated as public health issues, say UK experts | Men's health | The Guardian
description: Report calls for an effort to tackle harms in similar way to obesity and smoking, and stresses need to ‘offer boys something better’
Author: Tobi Thomas
Headline: Report calls for an effort to tackle harms in similar way to obesity and smoking, and stresses need to ‘offer boys something better’
Content: ‘Men’s problems are framed [in the manosphere] as the result of feminism rather than structural conditions,’ the report says.Photograph: miniseries/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Men’s problems are framed [in the manosphere] as the result of feminism rather than structural conditions,’ the report says.Photograph: miniseries/Getty ImagesMen's healthManosphere and online misogyny should be treated as public health issues, say UK expertsReport calls for an effort to tackle harms in similar way to obesity and smoking, and stresses need to ‘offer boys something better’Tobi ThomasHealth and inequalities correspondentThu 29 Oct 2026 19.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe manosphere and online misogyny should be treated by the government as a public health issue, in the same way as obesity or smoking, experts have said.Writing in the Lancet, the authors of a new report argue that a coordinated response is needed, involving governments, schools, health services and community organisations, similar to the public-health response to tobacco use and ultra-processed food.“Men’s problems are framed [in the manosphere] as the result of feminism rather than structural conditions, and masculine identity is commodified through products and paid content that normalise and reinforce health-harming and performance-oriented masculinities,” the authors write.The report defines the manosphere as “a diffuse commercial ecosystem and loose collection of online communities united by shared beliefs about masculinity, misogyny and male victimisation”.It goes on to outline how the manosphere has evolved into a highly lucrative online industry that makes money by promoting “the most extreme expressions of misogyny and aggrieved masculinity”.Prof Kent Buse, a co-author of the paper and co-founder of the social justice thinktank Global 50/50, said: “This is a business model, not a fringe. Outrage and grievance are good for business, so the system rewards the most extreme content. Expect the playbook that served tobacco so well: blame the individual, and call regulation an attack on freedom. Public health has a tested toolkit for commercial harms and we should use it.”He added: “Boys and men are not the problem. The problem is the conditions that leave them isolated and without a secure future, and the companies that profit from their anger and insecurity.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK government to give £15m to anti-misogyny fund amid ‘manosphere’ concernsRead moreThe authors also point to growing disengagement from education among boys around the world, as well as loneliness, money worries and social exclusion, which can leave young men searching for a sense of belonging. These problems, they say, can make them more vulnerable to online communities that offer simple explanations for their difficulties and often encourage them to blame women and feminism.Prof Sarah Hawkes, the report’s other author, said: “The manosphere offers boys and young men belonging, identity and an explanation for why life feels hard.“Those needs are real. A response that only removes the manosphere, without offering something credible in its place, will fail. We need to offer boys something better, not just tell them what to avoid.”Mark Brooks, the policy and communications director at the Centre for Policy Research on Men and Boys, welcomed the report’s position that it was a public health issue and that men, boys, women and girls were all victims of this content.“Far too often, the manosphere discussion has positioned all men and boys as a problem and not taken into account the broader economic, educational and cultural challenges that drive their engagement,” he said.“Not all men and boys engage with this content equally. We are currently working on research to identify who is most at risk.”Explore more on these topicsMen's healthYoung peopleViolence against women and girlsInternet safetyMenSocial mediaOnline abusenewsShareReuse this content

title: More prisoners recalled to jail than released in England and Wales | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Ministry of Justice figures show recalls rose 27% in year to June despite emergency measures to ease overcrowding
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Ministry of Justice figures show recalls rose 27% in year to June despite emergency measures to ease overcrowding
Content: More than 52,000 recalls to prison were recorded in England and Wales in the year to June, a rise of 27% on the previous 12 months.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenMore than 52,000 recalls to prison were recorded in England and Wales in the year to June, a rise of 27% on the previous 12 months.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAPrisons and probationMore prisoners recalled to jail than released in England and WalesMinistry of Justice figures show recalls rose 27% in year to June despite emergency measures to ease overcrowdingRajeev SyalHome affairs editorThu 29 Oct 2026 14.55 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore people were recalled to jails inEnglandand Wales in the first half of this year than were released, despite government efforts to reduce the prison population, according to figures released on Thursday.Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data shows that 12,338 people were recalled to custody between the beginning of April and the end of June, while 12,278 people were released. It continues a trend set between January and March, when 13,193 people were returned to prison and 12,977 released.A total of 52,716 prisoners were put back behind bars in the year to June after breaching the terms of their licence – 27% up on the previous 12-month total.The high recall rate is a key contributor to the prison capacity crisis and helped to prompt early release schemes earlier this month.The MoJ figures also show 79,274 inmates were freed early from prison between September 2024 and June 2026 under emergency measures brought in by the government to try to tackle the overcrowding crisis.The move, known as the SDS40 early release scheme, cut the proportion of sentences some prisoners must serve in England andWalesfrom 50% to 40%. It is one of several policy changes that are likely to have contributed to the rise in recalls, the MoJ said.The emergency measures were replaced with a permanent scheme for early releases from 1 October under the Sentencing Act 2026.The Howard League for Penal Reform said the “alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse”, as it called on the government to find a “lasting solution” to the overcrowding crisis.Rob Preece, the head of communications at the Howard League, said: “The prison system is under enormous pressure, with chronic overcrowding, staff shortages and awful conditions that make it close to impossible to rehabilitate people effectively. Imposing ever longer sentences has led us to this crisis, but the alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse.”Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said the number of recalls must be urgently addressed to avoid prison spaces being filled up again by people sent back to jail.“A significant proportion of those released immediately go back to chaotic lives involving addiction, mental health problems and homelessness. Without adequate support and stable accommodation in place as soon as they step outside the gate, it is very difficult to break the revolving cycle of going back into prison too many are caught up in,” he said.The MoJ said it was “vital those who break the rules can be hauled back to prison”. The department said the rise in recalls amid SDS40 releases was also likely to have been influenced by policy changes that result in most offenders being taken back into custody for 56 days before being released again – known as a fixed-term recall – instead of being held until the end of their sentence.Incidents of self-harm and violence have remained high as pressure on the prison system has grown. Safety in custody statistics showed that 360 people in prison died in the 12 months to the end of September 2026, including 66 people who died in circumstances recorded as “self-inflicted”.Prisons recorded 68,231 incidents of self-harm in the 12 months to the end of June 2026, at a rate of one every eight minutes. Self-harm incidents fell by 12% in men’s prisons and fell by 3.8% in women’s prisons.A separate dataset showed that the number of serious offenders on probation who were charged with a serious further offence had increased for the third successive year, to a record number.Of 281 serious offenders charged, 119 were registered sexual offenders, 128 were murderers, and four were terrorists or posed a terror risk, according to figures on multi-agency public protection arrangements.Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content
