title: Behind the scenes at the scream park: fear, fainting, clowns – and ‘code brown’ | Theme parks | The Guardian
description: At Norfolk’s ‘premier scare attraction’ there are ghouls, chainsaws, satanic cults and a haunted hospital. But what goes on behind the scenes?
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: At Norfolk’s ‘premier scare attraction’ there are ghouls, chainsaws, satanic cults and a haunted hospital. But what goes on behind the scenes?
Content: ‘I remember being absolutely terrified’ … a performer at PrimEvil. Photograph: Ali Smith/The GuardianAt Norfolk’s ‘premier scare attraction’ there are ghouls, chainsaws, satanic cults and a haunted hospital. But what goes on behind the scenes?ByElle Hunt. Photographs and video by Ali SmithThu 29 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘We always say to the scare actors, you’re going to think the boys will be the worst. They are not.” Backstage at PrimEvil, billed as “Norfolk’s premier scare attraction”, park director Ben Francis is sharing the advice he gives each year to his new crop of performers, before they set out to give punters the fright of their lives – or at least their Saturday night. As Francis covers each demographic, he ticks them off on his fingers. Teenage boys “scream like banshees, and run in packs”. Teenage girls tend towards being unimpressed: “Do your scare and move on, because theywillget nasty.” And mixed groups? “There will be an alpha and he’ll be wearing a North Face top.” Francis’s advice is to not waste time. “He will not react to anything … Aim for the weaker one at the back.”This is part of the workplace induction at PrimEvil, one of many immersive “scream parks” that pop up across the UK in the lead up toHalloween. For about £40 a ticket, groups of all ages spend the night roaming themed attractions and being terrorised by actors and special effects. Though the risks are minimal, the spikes in heart rate are very real.For Francis and the rest of the team, PrimEvil is months in the making. The nightly production involves more than 100 actors and dozens of crew, spread across six themed attractions, each drawing from familiar horror tropes – the scary clowns at the Circus of Terror, the cannibalistic trailer-dwellers over at Route 666, the satanic cult of The Offering. The winding routes are designed to disorient you with strobe lights, smoke machines, mirrored walls, hidden doors, false exits and unstable floors. But it’s down to the performers to bring the nightmare to life.View image in fullscreen‘It’s the best form of therapy and you get paid to do it’ … park director Ben Francis“I think people who don’t know what to expect think it’s just a nice little walk round, where you see the odd actor, they have a chat with you, then you carry on,” says Francis. “Actually, what the industry does now is completely immerse you in the theme of this world for 10 minutes.”PrimEvil is the special Halloween event of ROARR!, a dinosaur-themed adventure park a half-hour drive from central Norwich. That family-friendly attraction remains open in the day during PrimEvil’s run. Now, coming up to 5pm, an hour before the gates open, the transition from theme park to scream park is under way.It’s Saturday, the second night of PrimEvil’s nearly two-week run. Yesterday, 1,400 people spent the evening here, despite steady drizzle; the same number are expected later.Clowns, nurses and creepy twins scare visitors at PrimEvil scare parkAt PrimEvil HQ, a purpose-built warehouse, actors start flooding in for wardrobe and makeup. For our interview, Francis and I hole up in the laundry room, out of their way. Still, we’re intermittently interrupted by performers, partway through changing into costume, looking for plastic gloves or spray-on blood. Francis himself is in high demand, not just as PrimEvil’s boss of operations but also as an old hand. This is the 17th year he’s been involved, having attended the very first event in 2009. Though there were UK scare attractions then – notably Tulleys Shocktoberfest, now 30 years old, and Fright Night at Thorpe Park – they were still fringe.View image in fullscreenPark life … a performer at PrimEvil takes a break from scaring puntersFrancis didn’t know what to expect, he says. “I remember being absolutely terrified.” The following year, he applied to be an actor, and discovered a passion for scaring people. It’s not as sinister as it sounds, he insists. “It’s the best form of therapy, and you get paid to do it.” Francis was cast as a clown, “apart from one year where I was a hillbilly”. He found venting in character to be effective stress relief from his day job in the charities sector. “You shout at people, and they love it.” One evening in 2016, Francis arrived at PrimEvil in a foul mood after a board meeting had left him feeling disillusioned about his purpose. Martin Goymour, ROARR!’s founder and managing director, offered him a job. Both were in costume at the time, Francis confirms. “I was a clown, and he was in lederhosen.”View image in fullscreenA familiar sight … Martin Goymour, ROARR!’s founder and managing director, dressed as SkullmoreGoymour joins us in the laundry room now, looking for face paint. We met earlier, at ROARR!’s offices across the park; I don’t immediately recognise him in his brocade suit and top hat, his face white and bloody. To PrimEvil regulars, Goymour is a familiar sight as “Skullmore”, the dark Victorian ringmaster, sweeping the park on his Segway.Goymour was inspired to start PrimEvil in the mid-00s, after visiting Hollywood and one of Universal Studios’ legendary Halloween Horror events. The first PrimEvil, in 2009, was a single maze, built within the steel frame of ROARR!’s office building, after construction was paused by the recession. The idea was to draw a new crowd to the park after dark, and “have some fun” themselves. It was half a decade before the event broke even.Now PrimEvil attracts 20,000 visitors annually (Tulleys, the largest in Europe, boasts 150,000), while most theme parks stage spooky-season events. Their popularity has grown alongside the mainstreaming of Halloween and horror in the UK, driving up the standard. There is even a trade show, ScareCON, and industry awards, the SCARs; PrimEvilwon the top prizein 2024.View image in fullscreen‘We say to the actors you can’t all be jump scares. You can be someone who just stands and stares …’Francis and Goymour tweak the attractions every year and regularly travel to the US to scope out new tech and props. There, a single scare attraction can grossnearly $1m per season, though that’s offset by mounting costs. Goymour told me he spent “quite a bit” on “gory bodies” last year – about £10,000. According to IT manager Richard Colsell, responsible for the technical aspects of PrimEvil, the innovation is focused on electronic control systems. These trigger features such as animatronics or lighting changes; increasingly, the industry is using AI to read and respond to visitors in real-time, and even track their gaze.Wherever possible, Colsell prefers to leave control in the hands of the actors. “Sometimes less is more.” With each performance typically lasting less than 30 seconds (then repeated for hours), theatrical chops are less important than dynamic range across the cast. “We say to the actors, ‘You can’t all be jump scares,’” Francis says. “That’s what gets the reaction, and the adrenaline – but actually, you can be a creeper scare, a stalker, someone who just stands and stares …”View image in fullscreen‘More than once, catching someone’s eye, I’m startled by their red or white irises’This year PrimEvil received an unprecedented 230 applications for about 132 paid spots. They were selected at a group audition, starting with a dance-off, then testing their improv skills. “The more of a prat you feel, the better you will be coming across,” says Francis. A self-avowed control freak, this year he “granted the gift” of assessment to his six team leaders, one for each attraction, who could also call dibs on performers. One man in his 70s was sought after by all six. “I had to shake a dice,” says Francis. The man wound up in Mayhem Manor, the haunted residential hospital where guests are chased by doctors and nurses wanting to violently uncover their “inner beauty”.View image in fullscreenA performer prepares for the night aheadThere are strict rules in place to protect actors and visitors, chiefly: no touching. Older women on a girls’ night can struggle with that one, says Francis. “They can get very touchy-feely.” Contracted security patrol the park for disruptive or intoxicated visitors. Performers are likewise instructed “no rude, lewd or crude” behaviour. People do strike out in terror, but actors are taught to distinguish between dodgy reflexes and ill intentions – and to watch visitors’ hands, which can suddenly spring up.Still, accidents happen. “We have had code browns,” says Francis, though “not as often as you might think”. He estimates there are two each year, with more “code yellows”, though he assumes both are underreported. “Sometimes we’ll lend them trousers from our wardrobe, if they come and tell us.” Last night there were four panic attacks (about average, Francis says) plus two girls who fainted, and another who broke her finger. “She fell over while running away.” Most often, the on-site welfare team assists those wanting some quiet time-out.View image in fullscreen‘My boyfriend kept jumping while watching Insidious, while I was literally taking notes’ … Courteney Dunn, head of makeup at PrimEvilAs Francis and I talk, actors emerge from the wardrobe transformed. A young man has traded his trackies for a boilersuit; there’s an increasing number of nuns. Francis admits to feeling a little wistful. “I used to love being a scare actor.” When he took the job at PrimEvil, nearly 10 years ago, he was “adamant” he wouldn’t give up performing. Now, due to the demands of his job as park director across ROARR!, he’s had to quit the Circus. His costume is still stored in wardrobe. From a wall lined with grotesque masks, Francis pulls down one with demonic arched eyebrows and crazed red curls, and introduces me to Lofty the clown: his longtime alter ego. “No one’s allowed to touch my clown costume,” he says, fingering the satin sleeve. He declines to don it for a photo – soon, it will be showtime.Across the hall, the makeup team is finishing up the final few actors with brisk efficiency. Kara Field is applying brown and purple shadows to a Route 666 cannibal, to create sunken-looking eyes. “If you do it wrong, they look like drag queens,” she warns. Taped to the mirrors are print-outs with guide images and keywords for each attraction. This year the clowns’ makeup is monochrome for greater impact under the Circus’ UV lights. “We decided to go a lot darker, with more depth, shadows and contours,” says Courteney Dunn, 28, head of makeup and props.View image in fullscreen‘Less nightmare, more fever dream’Most of Dunn’s team of eight makeup artists are “obsessed” with horror. Watching the new Insidious film with her partner, “he kept jumping, while all I was doing was looking at the makeup, literally taking notes.” Where possible, makeup artists work with the actors’ style: unnatural hair colours or facial piercings might suit workers at the toxic Werehouse 51, but not the plague-time nuns of The Crypt. Dunn appraises me: “I feel like I could put you in Route 666.”With 20 minutes before the gates open, actors are applying finishing touches to their looks, bloodying blond wigs or blackening their teeth. The scene is less nightmare than fever dream. There’s a nun, texting intently; two pilgrims at the sink, filling up their vapour-powered torches; a clown juggling a can of Monster, a vape and a sausage roll. More than once, catching someone’s eye, I’m startled by their red or white irises.An estimated 50% of this year’s cast are returning, motivated by the experience as much as the work. “It’s a good way to make money, but it’s also really fun,” says Mia McConnell, 19, hanging out the front of the warehouse, vaping with friends. A shop worker by day, tonight McConnell is a mutant nurse. “The best way to scare people is to hide in the smoke. They don’t see you coming.” Sometimes the shock is mutual. Last night a trainee drama teacher (who requests anonymity) came face to face with some of her pupils, “super-excited to see Miss outside school,” she tells me, wincing beneath her bloody head bandages. Yesterday’s costume offered less coverage. “If I’d looked like this, I’d have been fine.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s a good way to make money, but it’s also really fun’ … Mia McConnell in costumeA slowly clanging bell gathers everyone to the front of PrimEvil HQ for Goymour’s pre-curtain pep talk. In character as Skullmore, he greets his “children of the fright” and urges them to “speak up, entertain” – and stick to their assigned spots. Then, after a team chant of “PrimEvil”, the horde is released into the park, grabbing a fortifying Mars bar from the box Francis is shaking.Scarlett Morris, 23, a barista and musician, is playing a ditzy sheriff at Route 666. In ordinary life, Morris tells me, she can be self-conscious and never leaves the house without makeup. “PrimEvil is the place to go to leave everything behind … it’s good for your confidence, dressing up and doing something you’d never do in real life.”That might also explain the draw for punters. Research into “recreational fear”suggests it’snot just thrill-seeking but also a form of play, offering people a safe way to engage with difficult emotions.A 2025 studyfound that groups who went to a haunted house attraction reported feeling closer to each other, the “collective storytelling” solidifying their bonds.View image in fullscreenNeville Everett wields his chainsawFor some actors it seems akin to a calling. This is Neville Everett’s 10th PrimEvil, and at the moment his only gig. “I’m a man of leisure,” he says, eyes mischievous beneath his evil-clown makeup. Everett sticks largely to the same playbook, loitering by the Circus’s exit and jumping out just when people think they’re safe. “Then I chase them,” he says. Usually he has a chainsaw going.He struggles to articulate the precise appeal. “It’s just something I like doing … You get rid of your frustrations on people.”Watching Everett in action, however, this sells him short: his dance with the public seems both conscious and two-way. A group of teenage girls literally plead for his attention (“Hi! Hi! Shalom!”), squealing in delight when he duly revs his chainsaw. When a pair of boys pass by, studiedly aloof and above the game, Everett calls their bluff and ignores them; they can’t hide their disappointment.View image in fullscreenBringing the nightmare to life …Judging by the screams coming from the nearby Werehouse 51 and the whacks reverberating along the corrugated-iron walls, PrimEvil is in full flow. In the now-quiet warehouse HQ, Francis settles in for the late evening, keeping things ticking over until the gates close at 11pm, and beyond. One of his tasks is doing “constant” loads of laundry, washing and drying the black bags that go over visitors’ heads for The Offering.For all the hard work that goes into designing a frightening night out, ultimately it’s all about the visitors’ imaginations, Francis says. A sign hangs in his office, gifted to him by Goymour: “The biggest fear is the fear of the unknown.”Explore more on these topicsTheme parksHalloweenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ​‘He buckled. I could hear his bass ringing out ...’ The luminous rise and tragic end of US alt heroes Morphine | Music | The Guardian
description: ​Fronted by Mark Sandman​,​ the group brought enigmatic, elegant rock to post-grunge America. As lost demos surface, those closest to Sandman remember a man who grabbed on to life’s joys
Author: Stevie Chick
Headline: ​Fronted by Mark Sandman​,​ the group brought enigmatic, elegant rock to post-grunge America. As lost demos surface, those closest to Sandman remember a man who grabbed on to life’s joys
Content: ‘A guy who lived nine lives.’ … Mark Sandman in Morphine.Photograph: Martin Beddall/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A guy who lived nine lives.’ … Mark Sandman in Morphine.Photograph: Martin Beddall/AlamyMusic​‘He buckled. I could hear his bass ringing out ...’ The luminous rise and tragic end of US alt heroes Morphine​Fronted by Mark Sandman​,​ the group brought enigmatic, elegant rock to post-grunge America. As lost demos surface, those closest to Sandman remember a man who grabbed on to life’s joysStevie ChickThu 29 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s early 1998, and at Fort Apache recording studio in Massachusetts, Mark Sandman, the suave frontman of Morphine, is nearing breaking point. Morphine’s four enigmatic and blackly humorous albums have won critical acclaim and, lately, unexpected commercial success considering their uncompromising creative vision. After the excesses of grunge, Sandman considered their idiosyncratic blend of sophisticated storytelling, prowling slide-bass and Dana Colley’s atmospheric saxophone a kind of “palate cleanser”.In 1997 Morphine had signed to DreamWorks Records, founded by industry bigwigs David Geffen and Mo Ostin. Now, working on Morphine’s first LP for his new paymasters – a batch of songs finally seeing release almost three decades later – Sandman was consumed by doubt over their direction. “For the first time, Morphine were trying to please someone other than just ourselves,” remembers Colley.View image in fullscreenRootsy … The pre-Morphine band Treat Her Right in 1989, from left: Jim Fitting, Dave Champagne, Billy Conway and Mark Sandman.Photograph: Jim Steinfeldt/Getty Images“DreamWorks wanted to make the ‘big Morphine record’,” says Paul Q Kolderie, who had produced all of Morphine’s albums and was overseeing the sessions. “But the label didn’t know what they wanted. And Mark didn’t know what he wanted. He wasn’t happy.”The pressure built until DreamWorks ho-hummed over the latest demos, and Sandman had “a particularly bad fight” with Kolderie, ditching the producer and Fort Apache. Soon, he would write and self-produce a whole new batch of songs, later released as Morphine’s fifth album, The Night. But by the time it hit the shelves in February 2000, Sandman was dead.Though only 46 when he died, Sandman was “a guy who lived nine lives”, says Kolderie. “This wasnothis first go-round – he was an old soul.” His partner, Sabine Hrechdakian, says Sandman “was not someone who liked to dwell on the past”.No Reason, a 1989 track by his rootsy pre-Morphine vehicle Treat Her Right, saw him indulge in uncharacteristic autobiography. Describing foundational real-life losses and near-death experiences, Sandman concluded: “There’s no reason in this life / someone lives and someone dies.”View image in fullscreenA rebel … Sandman live in 1994.Photograph: Marie Le MaufRaised in a middle-class home in Massachusetts, Sandman was a rebel whose parents were “lovely people, but they just didn’t understand their bohemian, rule-breaking son”, says Hrechdakian. At 18 he left for Alaska where he worked as a fisher. His travels ended after an early brush with death: having contracted kidney-damaging intestinal problems, Sandman flew home for urgent treatment and recuperation.He returned at a dark time for his family. His youngest brother Roger, who had cerebral palsy, had died in 1978; 16 months later, his brother Jon died after falling from a window at a party. Sandman was distraught, and while he would rarely discuss it, Hrechdakian says these losses acted as “a call to action, to live the life he wanted and pursue it with determination. Mark knew how temporary life was.”double quotation markMy theory is, somewhere inside he knew he was not wellKolderie met Sandman in the early 80s, on Boston’s music scene. “Mark had agreattime. He was completely nocturnal – all he wanted was to hang out and make music with friends.” Sandman also worked in construction and catering, and drove a cab, until – in another near-death experience – he was stabbed in the chest by muggers and left for dead.His next close shave set Morphine in motion. Treat Her Right were splitting up, Sandman having realised he needed to “be the leader and have a band that followedhisvision”, Kolderie says. As Sandman drove home after a farewell show, a car crashed into his Chevrolet Corvair. He ended up in hospital but won a $20,000 settlement and quit work to focus on his next project. “His material suddenly got much better,” says Kolderie, “marrying introspective, thoughtful songwriting to these cool grooves.”Colley had befriended Sandman when his previous band supported Treat Her Right. “Mark invited me to his loft because he had this one-string bass he’d been working with,” says Colley. “We jammed, and it was like a lightbulb went on for Mark. We got a drummer, Jerome Deupree, and immediately started recording Morphine’s debut album.”View image in fullscreenIneffable cool … Morphine’s Sandman (left), Conway and Colley (right) in 1995.Photograph: Bob Berg/Getty ImagesMorphine arrived fully formed on their debut, 1992’s Good, calling their sound “low rock”. Sandman’s murmured voice injected his beat poetics, noirish intrigue and blackly comedic stories with ineffable cool. It seduced everyone who heard it – like Rykodisc president Don Rose, who signed Morphine for their second album, 1993’s Cure for Pain. Aftertheir debut appearance on Late Night with Conan O’Brien, Colley says, “every show we played sold out, until our very last gig,” while Morphine’s music added sulphurous mystery to movies including Get Shorty and Wild Things, plusan early episode of Sex and the City. Being some years older than the typical indie-rocker – Sandman was 40 when Cure for Pain dropped – the success hardly went to their heads. “We weren’t throwing televisions out of hotel windows,” says Colley. “We loved what we were doing, and didn’t take it for granted.”Sandman, meanwhile, had just met the love of his life. “He saw me one night and Cupid drew his arrow,” Hrechdakian laughs. Fourteen years younger than Sandman, she bartended at Boston venue the Middle East, where he “would make puppy-dog eyes at me. He was lovestruck,verydriven; he pursued me for months. I wasn’t playing hard to get, I just didn’t feel an immediate … ” She tails off. But one night Hrechdakian heard Sandman singing No Reason in her living room. “I don’t know if it was hearing his vulnerability, but I was like, ‘Oh myGod– I think I’m in love with this man.’”Much of their early relationship would be conducted via fax machine: Sandman was always touring, Hrechdakian pursuing her master’s in environmental studies. “We could not have lived more opposite lives. But in 1997 I decided, ‘this sucks’, and moved in with him.” They shared Sandman’s loft, where he had built his studio, Hi-N-Dry. “That was his cocoon.”He began work on Morphine’s fifth album in an experimental mood. Deupree, who had left during the Cure for Pain sessions due to an injury, returned to play alongside his replacement, Billy Conway. The new material was strong, but the label’s lack of enthusiasm got under Sandman’s skin. His mood continued to plummet after they relocated to Fort Apache, where Kolderie had recorded Radiohead’s Pablo Honey and Hole’s Live Through This. “He would zone out during sessions,” says Kolderie. “His health did not seem good. People would ask me, ‘Is Mark OK? He looks grey.’ He was the heaviest smoker I ever knew. And it took its toll.”After splitting from Fort Apache, Sandman returned to the loft and self-produced The Night, Morphine’s fifth album, expanding the lineup to include more bass, violin and cello. “My theory is, somewhere inside he knew he was not well,” says Hrechdakian. “The Night is an album of him saying goodbye.”View image in fullscreen‘Oh myGod– I think I’m in love with this man.’ … Hrechdakian on Sandman.Photograph: Mark SandmanSandman signed off The Night in summer 1999 and Morphine readied for dates in Europe. Two weeks before the tour, however, Sandman suffered what Hrechdakian realises now was “the warning”: a minor heart attack. “His arm went numb. The colour drained from his face. I said, ‘Please let’s go to the emergency room’. He refused. So what did I do? I went to fucking Blockbuster to get videos and a pint of ice-cream.”Morphine arrived in Europe in July during a debilitating heatwave. At the first show in Lisbon, Colley remembers “the air coming through my instrument into my lungs felt like a furnace”. The second date was at a festival near Rome. The heat remained intense, but Colley remembers “a beautiful evening, shining faces looking back at us. Seven songs in, we were playing Super Sex and Mark buckled at the knee and fell down. I could hear his bass ringing out, and put my horns down and ran to him. They took him to the emergency room down the street, but he was already gone.”View image in fullscreenSandman in 1994 in his native Massachusetts.Photograph: MediaMedium/AlamyAfter Sandman’s death, Colley “wasn’t sure I’d ever play again”. Over the years since, however, he’s kept Sandman’s music alive via various live projects. Sandman’s estate fell into the control of his father, who “didn’t have any idea what to do with it,” says Kolderie. “He was an ornery cuss. Nike would try to license Morphine songs for an ad and he’d say, ‘Nah, that’s not enough money.’” A posthumous box set of unreleased material, Sandbox, was stymied by an ultimately unsuccessful lawsuit from Rykodisc that nonetheless smothered momentum.Hrechdakian and Morphine’s manager, Deborah Klein, took over the estate after Sandman’s father died, and Hrechdakian began sorting through a huge storage space of Sandman’s artwork, music and correspondence. She contacted Kolderie for help preserving the tapes and realised that the 1998 loft demos that preceded the Fort Apache sessions were a goldmine. “There’s a looseness,” Hrechdakian says. Those excellent recordings are now set to be released (with new sax parts from Colley) as Cocoon. “You can hear him laughing, his fingers on the strings … I sobbed for a while, listening to it.”Everyone involved with the project calls it a “healing” experience. Hrechdakian says she “didn’t fully understand the depth of his love for me until after he was gone. Putting Cocoon together feels like a love story, like we’re communicating across time and space. It’s like Mark has come back to life for everyone who hears it, and he has for me as well.”Cocoon is released via Partisan on 4 DecemberThis article was updated on 29 October to correct details in Sandman’s biography: his brand of car, where he worked as a fisher, and where Hrechdakian heard him play No Reason.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents? | Technology | The Guardian
description: Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workers
Author: Arielle Pardes
Headline: Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workers
Content: In the San Francisco tech scene, agents have quickly become a new status symbol.Photograph: Romilly Lockyer/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIn the San Francisco tech scene, agents have quickly become a new status symbol.Photograph: Romilly Lockyer/Getty ImagesReworkedTechnologyWhat is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workersSupported byAbout this contentArielle PardesThu 29 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn an average workday, Dhruv Amin chats with dozens of colleagues to get things done at hisAIstartup Anything. He might ask Gwen, his executive assistant, to schedule a meeting, then troubleshoot a technical problem with Cody, his coding partner. Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. If the office runs out of snacks, he sends a Slack message to Justin, the office manager charged with stocking the kitchen.But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. At Anything, there are 15 human employees and roughly 150 agents – a ratio that Amin believes will soon be the norm.“I think in a year, every company will have more AI co-workers than human co-workers,” he said.In the San Francisco tech scene, agents have quickly become a new status symbol, showing that a company can do more with less, several startup employees said. It’s common for workers to brag about how well their agents can handle common office drudgery like answering emails or help with essential business operations such as giving sales pitches.I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu ShashankaRead moreBut agents are also creating tension. They are alienating customers and colleagues who seek human interaction, eliminating roles and forcing employees to become overnight managers of the bots that often make mistakes.While startup techies such as Amin are some of the early adopters, corporate America may not be far behind. About 40% of large organizations used AI agents in some capacity between May 2025 and June 2026, up from 27% the year before, according toMcKinsey’s State of AI Global Survey. Companies also expect to scale back their workforce by 10% to 15% over the next few years as they delegate more work to AI, a recentreportfrom Boston Consulting Group found. In the present moment, companies are not seeing major productivity gains from AI,MIT research shows.Agents are a ‘status symbol’A wave of startups and big tech companies are fueling the push toward AI agents, selling companies on automated co-workers.There’s Viktor, a company that lets companies create their own “AI chief of staff”, and Lindy, which makes customizable agents for sales, customer support or admin work. OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Claude Cowork and Microsoft’s Scout can each integrate with thousands of other tools to handle projects after employees leave for the day.Each of these products promises companies the tantalizing dream of cranking out new co-workers, who never clock out, complain or cause human resource problems. Delegating to an agent is also cheaper than hiring a human, making a large ratio of agents to humans a point of pride among startups.“That’s the status symbol,” said Rafael López Muñoz, chief of staff at Wordware, a San Francisco-based startup that makes AI tools. Outsourcing parts of the job to agents is “an extreme time saver”.Experts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the companyRead moreLindy, for example, used to have almost 50 employees. Now, after laying off one-third of its staff, the company says it has about 20 and has filled many of its open roles with AI agents instead. It’s still hiring people for some positions.“People are constrained by having two hands and 24 hours in a day,” said Haneen Azhar, Lindy’s senior growth marketing manager. “Now, that constraint has gone away, because your one laptop screen can be divided into 16 different agents that are running in parallel. These tools make you feel so powerful.”Azhar says she has outsourced a long list of tasks to agents, from managing her calendar to testing how well customers respond to different marketing taglines to generating brand images. She worries about her role in eliminating jobs as she offloads work to agents. Azhar says that Lindy’s agents now handle product announcements, social media posts and marketing videos, work that used to be handled by about 100 people in its creator program, for example.She also worries about how the shift will affect the next generation of workers. “If I was trying to get my foot in the door right now, I’d be worse off than I was a year ago,” she said.In some cases, agents have stepped in to cover for missing staff. Jay Blumenfield runs a production company in Los Angeles that creates vertical microdramas – short, scripted series meant to be viewed on your phone. The production schedules are tight, and so are budgets. So when he had to fire an assistant director on a recent shoot, he decided to try using an AI agent instead of hiring a replacement at the last minute.Blumenfield uploaded the script and prompted the agent to do everything the assistant director would have done. The agent produced the schedule, call sheet and day’s script, and then sent the materials to the cast and crew. The result? Everyone got their work done.“It would have been an unmitigated disaster, but this kind of saved us,” he said.Now, Blumenfield and his partner, Tony Marsh, run the company alone with a suite of agents. “We don’t even have an assistant anymore,” he said.AI agents handle everything from reading scripts, running social media and planning travel. He created an agent called Shirley to act as his chief of staff, and another that scouts and books locations needed for upcoming shoots. Normally, he would have to hire two to three people to work on these tasks for two or three weeks, he said. Now, it happens within hours.Still, it does feel a little taboo to use so many agents instead of hiring people, Blumenfield said. But the economics of filmmaking had changed enough that he felt he simply didn’t have a choice. By using agents, he can afford to make the microdramas that star actual people – at least, for now.“The game in Hollywood is that you’re not allowed to talk about using AI,” he said, reflecting industry fears that it could end creative work. “I don’t want it to replace people. But we should be honest about how it is helping us.”Rising tensionSeveral workers who regularly rely on agents are adamant that the tech can’t replace the human workforce entirely. But agents are changing the kinds of skills and workers needed to manage them. Agents can code, making routine programming skills less valuable, but they still require humans to prompt them thoughtfully and judge the results. They also require a fair amount of oversight.López Muñoz said that after he let AI agents run his startup’s recruiting, he spent most of his time undoing agents’ mistakes, such as mixing up candidates with similar names or hallucinating parts of a résumé.“The qualities we’re looking for are changing,” Azhar said about new hires, adding that he now prioritizes the ability to coordinate and delegate over years of experience.Tarek Abillama, founder of River, which makes an AI agent for sales calls, said workers now are required to constantly check AI’s work and give it feedback.“We all became managers,” Abillama said. “We have to be great at multitasking, because now you’re running six agents who are doing different tasks.” Abillama’s first agent, a clone of himself, gave sales demos of River’s product. Later, he replaced it with an agent called Liv, a female persona that researches customers and their companies, demos the product and handles the sale process in any language, at any time of day.Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling backRead moreEven though River tells customers that Liv is an AI agent, Abillama said people seem to anthropomorphize the experience. He’s seen transcripts from calls with Liv where customers appear to flirt with it. Customers have also tried to push the agent to go off-script and get bigger discounts.Founder Brooke Hopkins said while her San Francisco-based AI voice startup Coval uses agents to speed up tasks, she views the tech as tools, not colleagues. She’s also banned her company from using agents to communicate with customers, suggesting that it’s lazy and sends the wrong message.“I can immediately look at an email and know whether or not it was written by AI,” she said. “If I get an email and it feels like a human, then I usually will read it.”The loss of human interaction has become a point of tension, Hopkins said. Using an agent to handle a company’s sales demos or recruiting process might save time, but at what cost?Duncan McClure, who evaluates AI models as a contractor, said he had recently been hounded with emails and phone calls from AI agents seeking to hire him.“The message it sends is that we don’t care enough to actually put in any effort,” he said, adding that he was turned off from working with those employers. Recruiters may save hours by using agents, “but it’s my time that they’re wasting”.Though AI can automate the time-consuming and costly parts of people’s jobs, that doesn’t always mean working less, several startup employees said. Amin, for example, said he gets more done with agents. Still, he hasn’t stopped working on weekends.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)ChatbotsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Middlemarch review – World’s Greatest Novel hurtles from deathbed panto to jolting marital tragedy | Stage | The Guardian
description: This RSC staging of the sprawling middle England masterpiece has humour, compassion – and even George Eliot herself as a character
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: This RSC staging of the sprawling middle England masterpiece has humour, compassion – and even George Eliot herself as a character
Content: Each scene shakes you … Rory Alexander as Will Ladislaw and Nia Towle as Dorothea in Middlemarch.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenEach scene shakes you … Rory Alexander as Will Ladislaw and Nia Towle as Dorothea in Middlemarch.Photograph: Johan PerssonStageReviewMiddlemarch review – World’s Greatest Novel hurtles from deathbed panto to jolting marital tragedySwan theatre, Stratford-Upon-AvonThis RSC staging of the sprawling middle England masterpiece has humour, compassion – and even George Eliot herself as a characterArifa AkbarThu 29 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 18.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs there a literary achievement greater than George Eliot’s stonking masterpiece?Not according to a Guardian poll,toppedby this sprawling, contemplative and profound book about marriage, moral goodness, debt, death, God and everything in between. So how do you adapt its nonpareil greatness for the stage without flattening the moral, philosophical and psychological complexities?Andrew Davies had a go at it with his watchable enough 1994 television costume drama, retelling Eliot’s story about provincial life, in six parts. Ameresix-parts, you might say, for a novel that is about 900 pages. While its timeline only spans three years in the life of a fictional Midlands town, it juggles multiple storylines and perspectives, weaves the local with the big socio-political backdrops of its age and follows the trajectories of characters with such detail that it becomes hard to replicate in another form.Now theRoyal Shakespeare Companyhas had a go at a stage adaptation, divided into two parts and totalling almost six hours of viewing (including the intervals). Again, you might say, a mere six hours, particularly in relation to the compressions of Part One. Jeremy Herrin’s production at first seems to sacrifice character study and emotional connection for plot and pace, although it hits all the beats of a pleasing costume drama, is easy on the eye, full of incident and with an understated visual beauty that suits the town of Middlemarch perfectly. Grace Smart’s supple set design contains ecclesiastical touches in the vaulted ceiling and back window, alluding to Eliot’s exploration of divinity. The stage is often lit by candles, perhaps to gesture at Eliot’s famed passage about the candle and pier-glass, which is quoted at the outset of the show. But there is so much incident to get through that you do not get much more than momentary philosophical reflection or inner outpourings before the next flick of the proverbial page.View image in fullscreenPantomime entertainment … Peter Forbes and John Hodgkinson.Photograph: Johan PerssonLike the book, the beginning focuses on the marriage of the young, devout Dorothea (Nia Towle), who sees wedlock as a means of higher learning, but does not quite make you feel enough. Her failed suitor, Sir James Chettam (Gunnar Cauthery), remains featureless, as does her sister, Celia (Lizzie Annis; why is she dressed in the same shockingly unfashionable frock throughout?). Outsider-artist Will Ladislaw (Rory Alexander), meanwhile, is barely there, appearing in brief spotlight as little more than a motif. Beyond the parish of Lowick, the drama of the Vincy family ticks over: Fred’s (Ebenezer Gyau) feckless ways with money, his tenderness for Mary Garth (also Annis), along with the budding romance between Rosamond (Emma McDonald) and the town’s ambitious new doctor, Tertius Lydgate (Andrew Richardson). It is Dorothea’s scholarly and sour husband, Casaubon (Ian Drysdale), who serves as the highlight in Part One, happy to marry a much younger woman but disdainful in the face of marital intimacy.Eliot’s book has sometimes been seen as a satire of middle England, and Nina Raine’s script leans into humour, tipping into a bumptious broadness, which verges on pantomime entertainment in scenes featuring Peter Featherstone (Peter Forbes) on his deathbed, his hands gripped around his money box. He is played like a provincial Scrooge, his greedy family comprising a tableaux of other Dickensian types around him in the inheritance wrangles.Raine treads a fine line between faithfulness and invention, keeping many of Eliot’s lines but turning the omniscient narrator into a character (Amanda Root). It becomes clear that this is Eliot herself, not only watching over her story but listening to characters divulge anxieties or yearning, and sometimes interrupting them, mid-scene. It is a very inventive way to get around delivering a backstory without clumsy exposition, but it feels too much like a device.View image in fullscreenTreading a fine line between faithfulness and invention … Middlemarch.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe author Tom McCarthy recently argued that Middlemarch has been middlebrowed and “heritage-industried to death,” in a podcast for London Review of Books, and this production runs the risk of doing the same by the end of this first half. But then the heavens open and it seems, for a book so preoccupied with divinity, that Eliot herself has descended to touch it with her greatness. Part Two finds its footing and doesn’t take one wrong step: the humour working brilliantly in occasional flecks, the drama leading with emotion, thought and the everyday tragedy of marital disappointment. The piano music, by Nathan Feeney, which sounded so mannered, now seems emotionally integrated. Characters come fiercely, painfully, to life. Dorothea, now a widow, carries great depths. The marriage between debt-worn Lydgate and his starkly withdrawn wife, Rosamond, is heartbreaking. Take away the 19th-century costumes and their marital friction would feel utterly contemporary. Each scene shakes you, each performer excels.The interaction between these characters and the narrator takes on a lovely, tender texture, too. She challenges or soothes them in their worst moments, like a mother would. Eliot’s narration excels in its sustained compassion for the most fallen of characters and Raine’s script does the same. You feel for Casaubon with his writerly paralysis over his unwritten magnum opus, The Key to All Mythologies (the narrator, Eliot, voices her own sympathies), and you even feel for the rapacious Nicholas Bulstrode (John Hodgkinson), for his inability to do good.Marriage is a “noose,” warns Dorothea’s uncle at the start, but there is a return to the “marriage plot” in Eliot’s work, however much she is said to have upturned it. The romance between Ladislaw and Dorothea is heady, intense and also – to invoke the words of Virginia Woolf – very “grownup”. You want happiness for them, for her. You believe in this second go at it.AtSwan theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, until 16 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreGeorge EliotRoyal Shakespeare CompanyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My hands are shaking’ - what it’s like to be an expert witness - video |  | The Guardian
description: As one of the world’s leading forensic anthropologists, Dame Sue Black has acted as an expert witness in a myriad of high-profile criminal cases. Her work has taken her from the lab to active war zones and the aftermath of natural disasters to identify victims’ bodies. Speaking to Ian Sample, the professor explains why standing up in front of a judge and jury has been one of the more terrifying parts of her career, the reputational risk of presenting evidence in court and what the future of forensic science could look like

title: Fake film deals and emails from top agents: who is behind the explosion in literary scams?  | Scams | The Guardian
description: Writers are being bombarded daily with invitations from fake book groups and offers to publicise their work. For the scamming industry, aspiring authors can be a soft touch
Author: Snigdha Poonam
Headline: Writers are being bombarded daily with invitations from fake book groups and offers to publicise their work. For the scamming industry, aspiring authors can be a soft touch
Content: Illustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian DesignThe long readScamsFake film deals and emails from top agents: who is behind the explosion in literary scams?Writers are being bombarded daily with invitations from fake book groups and offers to publicise their work. For the scamming industry, aspiring authors can be a soft touchThis piece first appeared inthe DialSnigdha PoonamThu 29 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTShare‘Hello Professor Snigdha Poonam,” the email began. I read that again. Nobody has ever called me “professor” for the obvious reason that I am not a professor. Bracing myself, I read on. The email was from Timothy Firth, organiser of a Seattle-based life-drawing community with 1,943 members that regularly has “thoughtful discussions inspired by creative works”. A recent inspiration was my first book,Dreamers: How Young Indians Are Changing Their World. The group wanted to discuss it, the email said, at one of its upcoming meetups. Attendees would be encouraged to post reviews on Goodreads and Amazon after.I looked up CAM Life Drawing and found an events page and an Instagram account. The latter had some photos of Timothy Firth – white, male – as well as testimonials from members who said he worked “day and night to create more community space”. Something told me this wasn’t the man who had reached out to me.Why would a hyperlocal life-drawing community in Seattle be interested in a nonfiction book about the shifting aspirations of young people in India’s small towns? The book was published seven years ago. What did they want from me?I accepted the invitation. The next email had a slick poster promoting the Zoom event, with the book cover as the backdrop and blurbs from the Economist and other publications. My attention was drawn to something more intriguing: a request for a “contribution fee”, with no amount specified. It would cover promotion, coordination and administration. But, oddly, this email didn’t come from Timothy. Signing off this time was Stephen – “Organiser, Community Improv LA”, which was another group in another city. According to the improv community’s Facebook group, Stephen is indeed the name of the organiser. However, Stephen had written to me using Timothy’s email address. To add to the chaos, Stephen/Timothy had also left what I suspect was an AI prompt in the email, which included the line: “MAKE IT MORE PROFESSIONAL.”This was undoubtedly a scam. Genuine book clubs don’t ask for money from authors. But who was behind it?Had these individuals actually read my work, they would have wanted to stay away from me. I have spent the last 10 years reporting on transnational fraud. My first book, Dreamers, closed with a chapter on fake call centres in India; my second, Scamlands, travelled to other low-income countries in Asia to portray an invisible empire that thrives on inequality, technological change and the erosion of trust.Along the way, I met and interviewed the scammers whose labour keeps this empire running. For some, fraud was a route to upward mobility; for others, an act of revenge against the privileged.Though I have formally emerged from this underworld, I can never delete a scam email without wanting to know more.I agreed to pay the book club – but after rather than before the event. After clarifying that “Stephen” was a typing error, “Timothy” sent me a Google Meet link for the book discussion. I joined the meeting to find about 20 people already in there: Alexander, Andrew, Mira, Rajnish, another Alexander, and several others. Timothy was also there and so was Stephen. None of them had their cameras on. Going by the profile pictures they used, most of them appeared to be white.Then the questions began.“Professor, what was your inspiration for writing Dreamers?”“Professor, what did you learn while reporting from Indian small towns?”“Professor, what surprised you?”While the questions may have been AI-generated, the voices seemed human. They did not always align with their pictures. Timothy seemed to be a woman, not a man, judging by the voice. Who were these people? They left only one clue. All these ostensibly white people, men and women, spoke with a west African accent.I am not the only author to have found myself stuck in a Zoom book club with fake readers. Countless writers with published books have been receiving invitations from reading communities that start to unravel after a basic Google search.As often happens with scams, most invitations sound too good to be true – thousands of members, incredible Goodreads clout and, at times, something even more alluring for an author: a deep understanding of their book.Many authors spot red flags from the first email onward, but not all.One author who engaged with a book-club impersonator was told a $100 (£75) contribution for the online event would cover snacks for the participants; she withdrew without asking how they would partake of the snacks while on Zoom. Novelist Marsh Rose, playing along, exchanged 29 emails with the Chicago LGBTQ Book Club. “The individuals whose voices I heard on the Zoom didn’t seem to be speaking from Chicago. They all sounded like my friend in Nigeria,”she wrotein a blog post for WritersWeekly.com, an online resource for authors that offers writing opportunities and industry news.Writers are also being bombarded with offers to publish our next book, market our book, handle social media for us, represent us as agents and get us book-to-movie deals with Netflix and Paramount. Every major publisher, agent, editor, author union and literary award executive is at risk of being impersonated.The money requested often seems small. “Amounts reported to me range from $55 to $350. In one case, the scammer offered three ‘spotlight packages’ – basic, essential and premium – for between $100 and $200,” Victoria Strauss, co-founder of Writer Beware, an anti-scam watchdog, wrote in a blog post. Often, the paper trail leads to Nigerian third parties holding bank accounts in the US. Author Jon Cockspaid $478.65 to one “Mary Brown,” who claimed a wide network of book clubs across the US, the UK and Australia, only to later notice the name Dayo Oguntuase listed as the recipient on the PayPal statement.View image in fullscreenA handout photo issued by the US National Crime Agency of a suspected scam centre in Accra, Ghana.Photograph: NCA/PAThe Writers’ Guild of Great Britain (WGGB) reports “an explosion” in the number of members seeking advice about unusually enticing offers in recent months. “Even the most vigilant of writers are understandably falling prey to these scams,” WGGB’s general secretary, Ellie Piers,said in a statementcommenting on new guidance, co-issued with the Society of Authors in May, to help authors protect themselves against scammers. “Our advisory team receives at least a dozen reports of scams each week,” Anna Ganley, chief executive of the Society of Authors, said in her own statement, tracing the spike to the emergence of generative AI. The US Authors Guildsays it hearsfrom authors who have been scammed, or nearly scammed, every day. Angela Hoy, the founder of WritersWeekly.com, told me she is in touch with “authors all day long, every day, thinking they got an offer from one of the top five publishers in New York or thinking they’ve been contacted by a famous literary agent”.A prominent trendsetter was the PageTurner scam, named after a fictitious US-registered publishing company that operated between 2017 and 2024. Call centre staff in Cebu, the Philippines, claimed PageTurner was an intermediary between authors and literary agents, film studios and streaming services and persuaded authors to pay so-called taxes, transaction fees and other costs before their books could be published or adapted.The scale of the operation became clear after US authorities launched an investigation into the business. According to the Department of Justice, more than 800 authors were defrauded of upwards of $48m (£36m). Writer Beware received hundreds of complaints about PageTurner. One author reportedly lost more than $600,000 (£450,000). The prosecutors found that at least $42m in proceeds were laundered through accounts in the Philippines. One defendant pleaded guilty in May of this year, while three others are awaiting trial.Judging by the surge in both the number and range of baits used on authors over the past couple of years, the scams seem to be launched from multiple territories. Anyone who has researched publishing would know most authors don’t have bundles of cash lying around. So why are the scammers coming after us?Hoy, who has dealt with thousands of writers at WritersWeekly.com, puts it down to ego. Brian Whiddon, the site’s managing editor, elaborated: “Not every author is a narcissist, but they all want to be recognised. That’s exactly what these scammers are targeting. They have identified a very, very lucrative niche.”Writers are waiting “for somebody to read their writing”, Hoy added. She argued that is why many writers believe the praise scammers heap on them. AI makes many of the compliments sound nuanced and personalised. Elderly authors are particularly vulnerable. As Hoy explained, a significant number of people who have a book in them leave off the writing until they have retired. Something else also kicks into the picture at this life stage: a sizable retirement fund. Scammers know American people have worked their whole lives and have retirement accounts, Hoy said.Some authors are so hell-bent on signing up for the deals the scammers promise that they disregard Hoy’s counsel. Others come to Hoy when it’s too late. She has said one of the writers in her community paid more than $100,000 for a fake book-to-movie deal.“I’ve actually used some of the verbiage from these emails talking about how fantastic my book is in my advertising,” authorDonna Strong commentedin the Goodreads discussion forum Readers Group Scams.Even as a new category of literary scamsemerges every few days, authors have very little information about the people behind them.In August, Danny de Hek, a New Zealand-based scam buster, forwarded me an Excel spreadsheet he received from a scammer in Karachi,Pakistan, with permission from the sender. Titled “LinkedIn Outreach 2026”, it has monthly data on targeted authors from March until August. One sheet has 403 names, each neatly labelled: new author, cookbook author, religious author, investigative author, poetry author, New York Times bestselling author and so on. Most are based in the US; the rest are in Canada, Australia or Europe.It’s an incredibly detailed document, with columns for the name of the person who found the profile, the person who first reached out, the service the author needs (website development, illustrator, social media visibility), the department handling the author, meeting links shared with the author. In a few cases, the document also lists the outcome of the outreach.“Paid $1,200 UP FRONT.”“Not willing to pay, has been scammed before.”“Meeting booked Wed 12 Aug, 10pm PKT, number confirmed, deep trust-built relationship, ready to invest, needs custom package built around limited budget and multi-project scope.”Some of the details only make sense if you know the context. 10pm PKT would mean 10am on the US west coast and 1pm in the east. Danny told me that most of the people working on this scam are Pakistani, yet the names of the callers are all American-sounding – Ashley, Jocelyn, Megan – probably to fool the authors into thinking they are Americans working for US-based companies and groups.Scam recipients often find the emails they receive haphazard and random. But the modern scam industry is a highly organised system modelled on the global corporate setup, with clearly laid out deliverables, salaries, incentives and reporting structures. Even though the schemes are mind-boggling in range, the young people joining these “companies” are given the same targets: Americans on top, followed by gullible foreigners in other western countries. I spent several years reporting from India on its massive scam call-centre network, which employs hundreds of thousands of educated young people trying to beat the dim economic prospects offered by the domestic labour market. Similar Excel spreadsheets are used to organise schemes where Indian scammers in Delhi or Kolkata impersonate Microsoft tech support, the Internal Revenue Service or even the Federal Bureau of Investigation.View image in fullscreenScam buster Danny de Hek at home in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 2022.Photograph: Tatsiana Chypsanava/The New York Times/Redux/eyevineDe Hek, who exposes transnational scams on his blog and YouTube channel with relentless zeal, told me Pakistan’s fake companies offering literary services operate in a similar fashion to India’s scam call centres. The majority of them maintain physical offices in Karachi and Lahore and employ people aged 20 to 24. Upon joining, the young employees typically get assigned to a unit, each designed around a specific literary swindle. While entry-level employees may only be tasked with outreach, the more experienced ones are entrusted with building long-term relationships aimed at selling multiple “packages” to clients over months and sometimes years.The most profitable service targets authors lurking outside the notoriously gatekept realm of traditional publishing. Rather than through a cold call or email, the scammers lure them through websites offering self-publishing or vanity publishing.Scam companies in Pakistan trap writers by impersonating known publishing houses and paying thousands of dollars to influence search results on Google. As a result, someone with a finished manuscript who searches online may find sites such as penguinwriters.com or amazonglobalpublishers.com before any legitimate self-publishing platform. Unlike traditional publishing websites, these feature open calls for new writers. WritersWeekly.com estimates there are at least 3,000 such sites. The biggest tell: a chat box pops up in the bottom right of all fake publishing websites as soon as the page opens, followed by a message from someone with an American-sounding name (such as Mark Anderson or Jessica Parker) and a white person’s face: “How can I help you today?” “Talk to a live agent, not a bot!” claims a ticker. And that much is absolutely true: the person messaging you is a scammer whose shift is dictated by the waking hours in your time zone.None of the five major trade publishers has sued alleged impersonators. The only recorded instance involves Amazon, which took nearly 20 individuals and associated companies to court in California for falsely claiming affiliation with AmazonPublishingand Kindle Direct Publishing to deceive authors. Amazon won $36.4m (£27m) in February 2025.M L Stark, a Danish self-published author of several psychological thrillers, is one of the rare victims who has met – and confronted – her scammer in person. Last year, she flew to Thailand to meet with Ethan Williams, a man she believed had become her longtime editor at an LA-based self-publishing house affiliated with Amazon – and a close friend. By this time, she had been talking to him over Zoom and email for more than a year and paid his company about $100,000 for different author services, from editing and cover design to coverage in the New York Times and the Los Angeles Times.View image in fullscreen‘I had paid $10,000 for that.’ M L Stark beneath a billboard advertising one of her novels in New York’s Times Square.Photograph: M L StarkWhile most of the services she paid for never materialised, the company did follow through on some. They signed her up on IngramSpark, a self-publishing platform, which enabled her to release two books, and Amazon, which made the books available on the platform. Most notably, in 2024, one of her titles was displayed on a digital billboard in Times Square.“I had paid $10,000 for that,” she told me. Only later, she told me, did she come to see these deliveries as strategic concessions, held back for moments when a long-term client reached the end of her tether. “Each time, it happened when I told them, after months of them stalling, that I wanted my money back.”The scammers’ last pitch was a Netflix adaptation that they claimed the film-makers wanted to shoot in Thailand – an important setting in her upcoming book, a thriller based on her own life. Stark and Williams were meeting in Thailand to scout locations.He had told her he was a British citizen, half English and half Arab; as a light-skinned Pakistani, his story was plausible. “He is an artist, he knew how to play the role,” she said. Still, she asked him to show an ID. He produced one that looked clearly faked. “I demanded he show me his passport,” she said. That exposed his real name and citizenship. He came clean. “He said, ‘Yeah, this has been a scam from the beginning. Even Peter is using a fake name; even Ronald is using a fake name. Everybody in the company that you have talked to is a scammer. It’s a huge scam operation, and we are not based in Los Angeles. We are based in Karachi.’” She is still processing her shock.I clicked on a random website from a list of known scam sites; it happened to be impersonating Red Rock, a real literary agency based in London whose authors have been published by major publishers such as Hurst, which published my first book in the UK. Bold promises greeted me on the homepage.“Get seen on Times Square.”“Bring your book and brand on Broadway.”“Join our authors making their mark in Manhattan.”A chat window opened, and someone with the username “Rae Donnaelly” asked how she could help. I told her I had an idea for a book. She asked for my contact, then called me on WhatsApp from a US number. She spoke like a South Asian imitating an American accent, something I could easily recognise because I’m South Asian myself, and we’ve all tried it at one point or another.I told her the truth: I was writing an article about author-baiting scams, and I was hoping she could tell me about her experience working for a fake publishing house.She told me she wasn’t “authorised” to talk about the company she works for, and she refused to tell me her real name. But she had no qualms spilling the beans on her ex-employer.Rae has a law degree but found it difficult to find a job in law after university. Her first job after graduating was at a fake publishing company in Karachi. “I started working for a company which was a scam – a guaranteed scam – and I didn’t know it when I started off with them. I was an intern trying to learn how the system really works; what the pros and cons are.”It took Rae only a few days to figure out the company’s business model: proxy sales. They would tell the author they would get them a guaranteed sale order for 1,000 copies, or something like that, making “fake commitments”. The scam rarely stopped there. After a client signed up for developmental editing, they would be offered a discount on book-cover design, and once they paid for that, the scammer would dangle social media management. “It could start off from as little as $400- $500, and it could go up to the skies, like $10,000, $15,000.”As with all scams, those executing the con learned how easily people can be manipulated if you know what they desired. “You could see how the human brain works. It’s actually scary when you think about it,” Rae admitted.She believes Americans make easy scam targets. “People in the US are very nice, they’re very good-hearted people. They trust you. Whatever you’re saying, they trust you. That’s the problem.”At times, the clients only noticed they had been scammed after they had paid all the way up to a Times Square display and Broadway adaptation. “When the authors did not see results, they would either reverse the charge on their card or accuse us of being scamsters,” Rae recalled.According to Talal Choudhary, an Islamabad-based tech journalist, there are about 1,000 Pakistani companies running scam sites. “One company runs as many as 25 websites. I personally know a company that had about 200 employees, just offering services to writers.”These companies are “very, very profitable”, he said. “From one client, you can make $60,000.”In Pakistan, Choudhary told me, the workforce of the author-baiting scams is largely made up of high-school and university graduates. They earn an average salary of about 50,000 Pakistani rupees (£136) a month. For high performers, there is commission. For every sale worth $1,000, they might get a 10-20% commission, he said, upselling until the author backs out.According to Rae, any guilt the scammers felt was cancelled out by the increasingly skewed conversion rate between the American dollar and Pakistani rupee. “Generally, the mentality was: when you’re making income in dollars, you have a stable life, you have sustainability. So that’s what they did. They just ripped people off.”I have heard multiple versions of this statement since I first reported on the rise of organised transnational fraud. Earlier this year, Hoy received a message on Facebook from a Nigerian man who offered to market her latest novel. Convinced he was part of the suspected author-scam network, she made him an offer of her own: write an article for Writersweekly.com about how the company he worked for scams Americans while being based overseas.But he wrote it using AI, which is against the site’s submission rules. He also ignored the brief. Instead, he chose to highlight, as Hoy recalls, “how it’s so hard for people in Africa and therefore it’s OK to scam Americans because all of us are rich over here”.Salil Mahmood, who asked that I change his name, is another self-described ex-scammer from Karachi. He reached out to me after hearing from Danny de Hek about the article I was writing. Compared with some of the more outrageous deals his seniors offered their clients, his job, as an entry-level recruit, was low-key. He cold-emailed published authors with a proposal to create their official pages on Wikipedia and have those approved. However, many of the pages he created – largely based on information provided by the authors – failed verification because the citations he supplied were fabricated. “The pages would remain active for a while and then disappear.” The authors never got their money back.Ransomware hunters: the self-taught tech geniuses fighting cybercrimeRead moreWhile he only worked there for a few months, he said the setup was highly aspirational for those who wanted to make serious money. “The bosses would show us pictures of their lifestyles: mansions, fast cars, parties and lots of alcohol. If you met your targets, they would have a rented car drive you around.” But in keeping with the nature of such enterprises, failure was not an option. “If an employee did not meet the target, they and their families were threatened with violence,” he said.Rae left the company she had been working for after a disagreement with her manager less than a year into the job. But rather than go back on the job market, she and a few friends started a new company that, as she described, provides American authors with tailored services.She insisted her company did not defraud its clients. I could have asked her why, if it was a genuine publishing house in Pakistan, it gave clients the impression that it was based in the US; why the website featured books it had not published; or why the individuals who popped up in the chat boxes used fake, American-sounding names, including her. But I left it at that. I could sense she wanted me to believe she had nothing to do with the scammers. She even pointed out that her religion does not allow her to earn money from fraud.“You can look out for us at the next Frankfurt book fair,” she said. I told her I would.I still get emails from Timothy Firth – the impersonator – reminding me to send my voluntary contribution in gratitude for the book club discussion. The person writing to me as Timothy probably knows it is not coming. I have a feeling the scammers know I am on to them because of how the meeting ended. After running through all the questions they had prepared, the moderator asked if I had any final comments.I asked if any of them had thoughts to share about the last chapter in my book. Reported from fake call centres in Delhi, I explained, it is the story of ambitious young people being drawn into an underworld of scams and fraud.Nobody spoke for a while. Then I saw Timothy unmute herself.“It is happening all over the world,” she said, “including in Africa.”That’s all she had to say.Published in The Dial asThe Lucrative World of Literary ScamsListen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.Explore more on these topicsScamsThe long readSelf-publishingPublishingPakistanAfricaSouth and central AsiaShare

title: The ‘breathing space budget’ – breathing space for the government, that is | John Crace | The Guardian
description: John Healey aced the morning-after media round because his Martin Lewis measures left nothing to challenge him on
Author: John Crace
Headline: John Healey aced the morning-after media round because his Martin Lewis measures left nothing to challenge him on
Content: It was sighs of relief all round for John and Andy after the chancellor’s budget of small things.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt was sighs of relief all round for John and Andy after the chancellor’s budget of small things.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesThe politics sketchBudget 2026The ‘breathing space budget’ – breathing space for the government, that isJohn CraceJohn Healey aced the morning-after media round because his Martin Lewis measures left nothing to challenge him onThu 29 Oct 2026 12.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTShareMaybe it had been one of the greatest acts of political genius after all. The day after the budget is usually the moment when things start to fall apart. When clued-up journalists and economists have had a chance to go through all the fine points the chancellor would rather everyone had missed. The forecasts that suggest everything is predicated on a wing and a prayer. The hidden unfunded tax cuts. The greater-than-expected spending commitments.But on Thursday morning Andy Burnham and John Healey could afford themselves a sigh of relief. All had gone about as well as they could have hoped. It turns out that when youdon’t make any massive tax or spending commitments, there isn’t a great deal to unravel. All there had been was a raft of small-scale interventions designed to help people with their personal finances. Call itthe Martin Lewis budget. In fact, Healey and Lewis now seem unable to get through the day without spending some time with each other. They certainly can’t stop talking about one another. It’s becoming unhealthily co-dependent. The gods of small things.It had been billed as the “breathing space” budget. A budget to help get everyone through the coming year more or less alive. No hiding under tables or breaking open the emergency supplies of baked beans. Apocalypse averted. But the breathing space might just as well have been for the government. Difficult decisions delayed. Hope that we all wake up in 52 weeks’ time and the world looks like a less frightening place. And even if it doesn’t, it will always have had a year’s grace. A chance for the Tories and Reform to implode. You can always hope.Come the traditional morning-after interview with the chancellor on the Today programme, the presenter Nick Robinson seemed uncharacteristically subdued. Normally he’s a terrier on occasions like these. There’s never been a budget that Nick wouldn’t have been able to do far better himself. But this one? This one was something you might find on the consumer affairs programme, You and Yours. And the BBC was in the process of axing that.So the 20 minutes passed with little fuss. More a softball back and forth. Healey started with his usual infectious brand of pessimism. He was born to be the bearer of bad news. The poster boy for assisted dying. Everything was absolutely terrible. He wasn’t quite sure why anyone was still bothering with anything. If it had been up to him he would have ended the interview before it had started. There was nothing to say. Other than that, given the chance, he wouldn’t have started from here. Brexit, the pandemic, Ukraine, Iran, energy prices. The world was screwed. Britain was screwed. Lie back and prepare for the worst 10 years of your already miserable life.Nick tried to find a reason to believe. Couldn’t the chancellor have made just a little more effort? Having a plan to have a plan wasn’t the usual budget fare. Healey, AKA Dr Death, shrugged. It was one up on having a plan to not have a plan. By now Robbo was audibly struggling. How could he put it politely? In the third year of a government with a 160-seat majority, surely Healey could have been a little more ambitious. This wasn’t exactly the big transformation that had been promised.10:59Bills, banks, ‘breathing space’: what was in Burnham’s first budget? - The LatestCould he even say if he would bring down the benefits bill? Apparently he could. “There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Dr Death. Cue panic stations in the Treasury. Within seconds of Healey opening his mouth, dozens of government spinners were on the phones to every journalist to tell them they hadn’t heard what they had just heard. There had been collective false consciousness. When Healey had said that he would be bringing down a benefits bill that everyone agreed was too high and that the country could not afford, what he had really meant to say was that he would not be bringing down the benefits bill that he had no idea how to pay for. Fag packets gratefully received. That was about as close to news as we got.Maybe it was just that while Healey was having one of his better days, Robinson was having one of his worse ones. Because he had also sounded uninterested in his interview with Andrew Griffith an hour earlier. An exercise in box-ticking rather than revelation because the shadow chancellor never has anything useful to add on the day after. Sure enough, Griffith insisted that he would have done everything differently while never going into the details of how. At which point, Robbo opened half an eye and observed that if it was really that easy, how come the Tories hadn’t fixed it when in office?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs this play-safe budget a sign that the prime minister is planning an early election? | Larry ElliottRead moreIndeed, Nick continued, it could be argued thatLabourhad been left to clear up the mess the Tories created. “I’ve never shied away from saying that the Tories have a chequered record,” Griffith said defensively. Er, I’m not sure that’s entirely true, Andrew. Your usual line is that history started in 2024 and that everything is the Labour government’s fault.That just left time for Robinson to remind the shadow chancellor that he had been part of the Treasury team that had defended the Liz Truss mini-budget even as it was being shredded. “I will never publish plans without saying where the money is coming from,” said Griffith, before announcing £30bn of planned tax cuts without specifying which benefits he would cut to pay for them. Fair to say, he’s not a man who seems to learn from experience. Once in the Truss image, always in the Truss image.The final piece of the Thursday jigsaw was the verdict from the Institute for Fiscal Studies. In the past this has been enough to completely destroy the reputation of some chancellors. I could never look at George Osborne in quite the same way after the IFS had rubbished one of his budgets. It’s one thing to be thought of as an economic quarter-wit. What’s really devastating is to have it proved.Helen Miller, the IFS director, looked a bit knackered. She and her team had been up most of the night, going through both the budget and the OBR figures line by line, searching for the fatal flaw. And she was gutted to announce that there actually wasn’t one. There was as little in the budget as had first appeared. She announced that she was grumpy about some measures. Disappointed in others. Another was cack-handed. The tax system had been made more complicated, not less. Yet, all in all, these were minor gripes.“This chancellor is hoping that things get better without actually needing to do anything,” Miller said in conclusion. I don’t think that’s right. Healey never travels in hope. Like the rest of us, he’s pretty confident everything is going to be worse in a year’s time. But he had got himself some breathing space.On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of theGuardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026.
