title: Hold your nose: a £1.25bn subsidy for rich Rolls-Royce’s new engine had to happen | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: The chancellor’s budget giveaway is, unfortunately, a reflection of how life works in the global aerospace business
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: The chancellor’s budget giveaway is, unfortunately, a reflection of how life works in the global aerospace business
Content: Andy Burnham gets up close to a Rolls-Royce Trent 500 engine during a visit to its factory in Derby on Thursday.Photograph: Darren Staples/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham gets up close to a Rolls-Royce Trent 500 engine during a visit to its factory in Derby on Thursday.Photograph: Darren Staples/PANils Pratley on financeRolls-RoyceHold your nose: a £1.25bn subsidy for rich Rolls-Royce’s new engine had to happenNils PratleyThe chancellor’s budget giveaway is, unfortunately, a reflection of how life works in the global aerospace businessThu 29 Oct 2026 14.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.35 EDTShareIt wasn’t a “nothing”budgetfor engine-maker Rolls-Royce. The company was handed £1.25bn from public coffers to part-fund the development of a next-generation engine for single-aisle commercial planes.The chancellor buried this giveaway in two short sentences in the stodgy middle of his speech, presumably because it would look too much like a case of corporate welfare just after he had grumbled about the £14bn extra we’ll be paying in debt interest this year.And it’s not as if Rolls is on its uppers. The pride of Derby is the UK’smost radically improved major company of the past few years. It sits in fifth spot in the FTSE 100 index, sporting a market value of £105bn, and has enough spare cash tospend up to £9bn on share buy-backsthis year.But there had been an air of inevitability about this subsidy ever since the company’s chief executive, Tufan Erginbilgiç, talked earlier this year about howhe would “appreciate” financial support from the governmentin developing the UltraFan engine. Appreciate? What he meant is that other governments would cough up if the UK didn’t.That, unfortunately, is how life works in the global aerospace business. Subsidies are a down payment on the jobs and factories that can follow. Germany, reeling from the woes of its carmakers, would love to have a bigger slice of the hi-tech UltraFan action (and has a role in the gearboxes anyway). The US aerospace industry is a study in how generous defence contracts subsidise civil operations. Healey couldn’t ignore those facts of aerospace life.Budget 2026: key points at a glanceRead moreWhat’s more, one can see how the possible long-term return on the £1.25bn could turn out very well. “The single biggest opportunity in aerospace over the next 50 years is to secure a UK engine position on next generation narrow body programmes,” saidthe government’s strategy document for advanced manufacturing. Aircraft engines are high-value products. About 80% would be exported, doing wonders for the national balance of payments. Projections of “tens of thousands of highly skilled jobs” eventually are credible.The big “if” is that Rolls hasn’t yet got a slot on a narrow-body programme. The company exited that market a couple of decades ago; its civil aircraft side currently only supplies engines to the smaller wide-body long-haul market. Rolls needs to get on to either the Airbus or Boeing narrow-body programmes, and success or failure won’t be known until some time around 2030.Thus the government is only contributing to a joint 10-year £2.5bn research and development programme, including a “demonstrator” engine to show off the gas turbine tech. There will be spillover benefits for defence capability but, ultimately, UltraFan needs to be on a civil project. It is a big bet – and Rolls, even if it wins, will need a corporate partner at a later stage.The point, though, is that the UK government had to get behind the UK runner in this race. One trusts the guarantees on UK jobs and investment, beyond the 3,300 roles supported initially, will be written in triplicate in the final agreement. That must be a fundamental condition of support on this scale.But this is an occasion to hold your nose. Rolls is plainly not a corporate pauper but, yes, it is justifiable to shove £1.25bn its way. Andy Burnham’s “reindustrialisation” talk would otherwise ring very hollow.Explore more on these topicsRolls-RoyceNils Pratley on financeBudget 2026BudgetJohn HealeycommentShareReuse this content

title: If British Library reading rooms become ‘co-working spaces’, what, exactly, is a national library for? | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: The plan to generate revenue from areas currently used by the public is causing bitter dispute, and raises fundamental questions, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: The plan to generate revenue from areas currently used by the public is causing bitter dispute, and raises fundamental questions, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesOpinionBritish LibraryIf British Library reading rooms become ‘co-working spaces’, what, exactly, is a national library for?Andy BeckettThe plan to generate revenue from areas currently used by the public is causing bitter dispute, and raises fundamental questionsThu 29 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTShareIn a crowded country that is short of public money, any expansive public building that seems underused in any way is vulnerable. Professional critics of state spending can claim taxpayers’ money is being wasted. Managers of the building who are under financial pressure can argue it needs to be used more intensely, perhaps that some spaces should be commercialised and offered for rent. The original open, uncommodified, egalitarian quality of the building can be steadily sliced away.The British Library in London is in danger of that fate. A huge brick battleship moored on the Euston Road since 1997, itclaims to bethe largest public building constructed in the UK in the 20th century. Its both forbidding and exhilarating exterior conceals 11 unusually elegant and comfortable reading rooms and one of the world’s most extensive print and digital collections, free to use for anyone who is over 18. Last week, these readers received an email with the subject line, “Transforming your Library”. Next summer, the library would “begin work on repurposing our [three] Science and Social Sciences Reading Rooms to become a flexible workspace … available for hire by workers and businesses for co-working, collaboration and meetings”. The reason given for removing more than a quarter of the library’s much-loved research space was “ensuring we generate the necessary revenue to keep our core services free”.The library has a currentannual budgetof about £170m – a third the size of my local London hospital’s – 84% of which comes from the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. The rest is from donations, investments and “charitable and other trading activities”, such as the private parties and ticketed exhibitions already frequently held in the sweeping interior connecting its reading rooms. Even with these multiple income streams, the library’s financial reserves are perilously low – according to its latest accounts – thanks to inflation and austerity, which meanits state fundinghas in real terms declined to two-thirds of what it was in 2010, and also adevastating cyber-attackin 2023, from which the library has still not fully recovered.Despite this troubled context, and in some ways because of it, the library’s drastic reading room reduction plan has provoked “outrage” from staff, say the Prospect and Public and Commercial Services (PCS) unions that represent them. Reading room staff understandably fear for their jobs, but also for the building’s fundamental purpose, which wasset out by lawin 1972 – an indication of how hard the complex was to conceive and build – as “the establishment for the United Kingdom of a national library”. Staff are now “the most furious I’ve ever seen them about anything”, says a union source. A strike over the reading room plan, followingone last yearover low pay, could begin as soon as December.Behind this potentially explosive dispute – not least because many well-connected authors, academics and journalists use the library – lurks a big question. In a digital age of decentralised study and dispersed online resources, what is a national library for?During the quarter of a century I’ve been regularly using the library, usually the reading rooms that are now under threat, its hierarchy has been trying to answer that existential question by steadily, not always harmoniously, widening the building’s user base and functions. Reading room passes have been transformed from a rationed credential for a few thousand people with supposedly serious research intentions – though some always ended up snoring at their desks – to something provided in minutes to everyone from elderly amateur family historians to undergraduates, particularly when dissertation deadlines pile up in early summer.Meanwhile, the library’s lobbies, landings, hallways and outdoor terraces have been lined with hundreds of chairs and tables and turned into study areas, meeting places, cafes and locations for loud laptop video conversations. These are all heavily used: a sign of good, free spaces lacking elsewhere. A “family station” inside the entrance offers play materials, art supplies and reading corners for young children. What Karl Marx, who researched for years in the reading room of the British Museum, precursor to theBritish Library, would have made of the latter’s invitation this Halloween to “pop in for spooky crafts” and “enjoy a fang-tastic time” is an intriguing question.I generally like the contrast between the library’s studious and boisterous sides: an antidote to the solitary obsessiveness of research and writing. But there are also tensions between the library’s diverging uses, which its management prefers not to acknowledge – and which the proposed changes would almost certainly worsen. Modern life is noisy, especially in London, and the semi-silence of the long, wood-lined reading rooms, with pages softly turning, keyboards pattering, books being slid on and off shelves, and the odd murmured conversation, is precious and addictive, as the constant influx of new young readers makes obvious. First thing in the morning and last thing in the evening, the rooms are half empty. That will probably be used to argue that fewer are needed. But a half-empty place can be an aid to crucial thinking and concentration. And if the reading rooms become fewer and therefore fuller, then users from outside London, whose taxes also pay for this national library, are less likely to be able to get there in time to grab a desk. In the busiest periods, they already sometimes run out.The library is straining to cope with its daily crowds. On bad mornings, the entrance queue lasts over half an hour. The toilets are increasingly often out of order. The free lockers are wearing out, partly because of use by travellers from the many stations nearby. And across the reading rooms, a mysterious hissing has been spreading for months, like a kettle that never boils. The library says it is coming from a failing pneumatic ventilation system, and “there is no quick solution”. The library is starting to get old.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 2032, a towering extension, blander than the original building, is due to open. It is already noisily under construction. Last year, Rebecca Lawrence, then the library’s chief executive, who resigned during the strike, said the extension would “open up the Library even further … [for] future generations of visitors, learners, researchers and budding entrepreneurs”. It will not contain new reading rooms. If you find that ominous, you are not alone.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBritish LibraryOpinionLibrariescommentShareReuse this content

title: A simple pub sign led me down a very disturbing rabbit hole | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: The cleanliness, or otherwise, of a pub’s pipes has never bothered me before. But that was before I read about the potential yeast, bacteria and mould ...
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: The cleanliness, or otherwise, of a pub’s pipes has never bothered me before. But that was before I read about the potential yeast, bacteria and mould ...
Content: Should they tell us they don’t sneeze on the food, too?Photograph: Courtesy of Adrian ChilesView image in fullscreenShould they tell us they don’t sneeze on the food, too?Photograph: Courtesy of Adrian ChilesOpinionBeerA simple pub sign led me down a very disturbing rabbit holeAdrian ChilesThe cleanliness, or otherwise, of a pub’s pipes has never bothered me before. But that was before I read about the potential yeast, bacteria and mould ...Thu 29 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.49 EDTShareThere’s a pub near me with an eye-catching sign outside. I’ve driven past it many times, and it always gives me pause for a little idle thought. On the sign there is a loud and proud notice that in this pub they clean their lines every week.There’s a lot going on with this simple sign. First and foremost, in a long life of pub observance, I don’t recall ever reading such a boast adorning any other establishment. What’s going on here? Surely it’s not the case that this pub, and only this pub, is so scrupulous about the cleanliness of its lines. (By lines, I assume they refer to the pipes that convey the beer from the kegs or casks to the pump and into the glass.)Surely all pubs have a weekly flush-through? In which case, this sign is clever, but daft, making a virtue of a norm. Like a restaurant stating its chefs don’t sneeze on the food, or an airline assuring us that the planes’ wings are checked before every flight.From Bentley Pauncefoot to Yetts O’Muckhart, I’m obsessed with Britain’s weirdly named villages | Adrian ChilesRead moreAlways on the lookout for a fresh source of worry, I’ve been down a rabbit hole on the subject of beer line issues, and I’ve come up smelling not very nice. There’s a lot going on in those pipes – an awful lot if you’re not careful. Potentially, it’s hell in there. Living wild yeast and bacteria attaching itself to the interior of the tubes; mould around the taps and connectors; sticky protein residue left behind by the grain; and something called beerstone, a stubborn mineral scale that bonds to the plastic lining. Ye gods, it’s enough to put you off your beer.I’m going to pop into this pub and suggest they clean daily instead of weekly. And as for every other pub I frequent, before I shout up a pint I’ll henceforth be asking for details of their line-cleaning regime. I may carry a hazmat suit to have a poke around in the cellar myself. You can’t be too careful.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Is this play-safe budget a sign that the prime minister is planning an early election? | Larry Elliott | The Guardian
description: There’s no real strategy behind this hotchpotch of measures. Andy Burnham may be parking the big decisions until he has a true mandate, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Author: Larry Elliott
Headline: There’s no real strategy behind this hotchpotch of measures. Andy Burnham may be parking the big decisions until he has a true mandate, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Content: John Healey and Andy Burnham visit the Abbey community centre in Westminster following the budget announcement on Wednesday.Photograph: Richard Pohle/ReutersView image in fullscreenJohn Healey and Andy Burnham visit the Abbey community centre in Westminster following the budget announcement on Wednesday.Photograph: Richard Pohle/ReutersOpinionBudget 2026Is this play-safe budget a sign that the prime minister is planning an early election?Larry ElliottThere’s no real strategy behind this hotchpotch of measures. Andy Burnham may be parking the big decisions until he has a true mandateThu 29 Oct 2026 08.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTShareGreat hopes were invested in Andy Burnham when he became prime minister in July. Hewent bigon the failings of 40 years of neoliberalism, emphasised the need for Britain to start making things again and promisedgrowth in every postcode.Back in the summer, John Healey’s first budget was seen as an opportunity to start delivering on these ambitions, but it has been clear for some time that it wouldn’t do so. The road to the New Jerusalem – judging by the chancellor’s “breathing space” package – will be a slow and arduous one. Healey has taken what he inherited from Rachel Reeves and performed some minor tweaks. Not so much a revolution as continuity Keir Starmer.As has been the hallmark of Burnham’s first 100 days in Downing Street, there was plenty of activity in the budget but the slew of measures – almost 100 in all – was a hotchpotch and had no real semblance of a strategy being fleshed out. Not many budgets linger long in the memory and it is unlikely that Healey’s will break with this tradition.In essence, it has bought Healey and Burnham some time. For the moment they can argue that the budget was just part one of a three-stage process, to be followed by the government’s 10-year-plan and next year’s spending review. They need to use that time wisely or the glitzy PR will cease to impress.There are, of course, reasons why the chancellor played it safe. Energy prices have rocketed since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February. Theconsequent higher inflationhas resulted in higher interest rates for mortgages, business loans and government borrowing.Optimism about an early resolution to the war is fast fading. Indeed, the prospect of anintensification of the conflictafter next week’s US midterm elections has led to a fresh surge in the cost of crude oil and gas in the past couple of weeks. The modest help provided in the budget to reduce energy bills will be dwarfed by the expected price increases in January. A tough winter lies ahead.As the dust settles, a number of conclusions can be drawn. One is that Britain remains – as Burnhamonce put it– in hock to the bond markets. Healey may well have wanted to come up with a more generous energy support package, but was constrained by the fear that the financial markets would cut up rough. Ever since Liz Truss’s mini budget in 2022, governments have lived in fear of another sell off in government bonds. Healey is like a contestant in Strictly Come Dancing – he knows that the markets always have the casting vote.To be fair to the chancellor, he borrowed £20bn more to invest ininfrastructure spending, using the flexibility in meeting the government’s rules for the public finances provided by Reeves. That was welcome and – at first glance – didn’t appear to unsettle the markets.Whether Healey’s array of minor fixes to help with cost of living pressures is enough to keep voters sweet is another matter. The economy has so far showed impressive resilience in the face of the energy shock caused by events in the Middle East, but that strength has been concentrated in the financial and business sectors of the economy, with growth in artificial intelligence particularly striking. Consumer-facing sectors – such as hospitality and housing – have been much weaker, with the mostrecent reporton consumer confidence showing the sharpest monthly fall since the Brexit referendum in 2016.That’s hardly surprising given the fact that taxes as a share of national income are on course next year to be at their highest ever level, and that spending power is being eroded by rising fuel and energy costs. In itslatest reporton the economy, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimates that living standards will fall next year and by 2030-31 will be only 2% higher than they were before the Covid pandemic. A lost decade in other words.It is against this unpropitious backdrop that many pundits – particularly in the City – have seen the lack of meat in the budget not as an indication that the government is dithering, but as a sign that Burnham is preparing the groundfor an early general election. On this reading, all the big decisions – on social care, relations with the EU, and defence – have been parked until the prime minister has his own mandate.The case for holding a snap poll is not just that voters seem to have taken to Burnham, although he is certainly enjoying a honeymoon period. It is also that Labour is currently benefiting from the lack of a single challenger on the right as the Conservatives and Reform slug it out, and from the problems facing both the Greens and the Liberal Democrats on the left. The polls show Labourin the lead.Even so, an early election would be a colossal risk for a party with a commanding majority and two and a half years of the current parliament still to run. The OBR thinks the economy will grow more slowly in 2027 than in 2026, while living standards will actually fall before picking up in 2028 as the energy shock abates. Next week’s anticipated rise in interest rates from the Bank of England may not be the last. The prime minister is arguably at the peak of his popularity.Burnham has repeatedly said that he has no plans to go to the country early, which if true will be a relief to the many Labour MPs who would almost certainly lose their seats, even now that the polls are looking more favourable. But if that is his intention, he will need to get a move on – because now is as good as it is going to get.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLarry Elliott is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBudget 2026OpinionBudgetAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyEnergy billsHousehold billsEconomic growth (GDP)commentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s plea – ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’ – deserves to backfire | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: With his poll numbers tanking and his behavior getting odder, the remark seems more appealing to himself than to voters
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: With his poll numbers tanking and his behavior getting odder, the remark seems more appealing to himself than to voters
Content: ‘“Pretend I’m on the ballot” has become a regular rallying cry as Trump tries to fend off a Democratic “blue wave” in Congress.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘“Pretend I’m on the ballot” has become a regular rallying cry as Trump tries to fend off a Democratic “blue wave” in Congress.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Trump’s plea – ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’ – deserves to backfireMargaret SullivanWith his poll numbers tanking and his behavior getting odder, the remark seems more appealing to himself than to votersThu 29 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTShareAs he criss-crosses the nation, stumping for Republican candidates,Donald Trumpkeeps asking voters to use their imaginations.“In this election, I’m asking you to pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just pretend,” heurgedat a Kansas rally as he campaigned for the incumbent senator Roger Marshall and gubernatorial challenger Ty Masterson last month.“Pretend I’m on the ballot” has become a regular rallying cry as Trump tries to fend off a Democratic “blue wave” in Congress.But will it work? That seems increasingly unlikely.Given his own lack of popularity and weird behavior, it’s an egotistical notion – more appealing to himself than to voters.After all, his approval ratings are in the basement. Gas pricesare higher, on average, than at any time during the Biden years. People feel like they need to float a loan before heading to the supermarket.Donald Trump has been a disaster for rural America | Steven GreenhouseRead moreIn that Kansas rally, he referred to the opposition as “Dumocrats”, which is typical of the level of presidential discourse to which the nation has become accustomed.In his rallies, he appears “increasingly detached from reality”, as one campaignanalysisin the Independent put it, as he “vacillates between topics to the point where his remarks border on the nonsensical and he ends every appearance by awkwardly dancing to the Village People’s well-known gay anthem YMCA”.Stranger still, as the Guardian’s Adam Gabbattreportedrecently, Trumphas been offering “unsolicited and increasingly unhinged assessments of men’s bodies” over the past few weeks.“I examined his ass,” the president said in Kentucky, speaking about Republican senator Jon Husted. “And then I looked at his shoulders … I looked at his jawline … I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I’m still recovering.”Trump has also been – to put it mildly – stretching the truth on the campaign trail, sometimes merely misleading in his remarks, sometimes straight-up lying.For example, he promised a North Carolina rally that gas and oil prices would tumble soon and he claimed: “I had it down to the lowest level in years,” apparently speaking about the price of filling up a gas tank at the pump. APolitiFact examinationdisputed this, noting that when Trump took office at the beginning of last year, the average gas price was $3.23 a gallon, but by late September of this year, it was $4.61.But it’s not just what he says at rallies that may backfire on the candidates he hopes to help.Much of what’s happened in Trump’s second term is working against Republican candidates. That includes the widespread self-dealing that, as the historian Garrett Graffwroterecently, “is so endemic and so obvious that it has broken through to voters”.It’s also his misguided war, his rants on social media, his disparagement of longtime allies, including Canada. It’s also his obvious plan to declare the election rigged should it not go his way.If Democrats win big, will they learn the right lessons from their victory? | Jan-Werner MuellerRead more“Even Maga die-hards and GOP allies in Congress have grown weary of his erratic behavior,” as the Wall Street Journal’s Jason Rileynoted.And Democrats, including Barack Obama, are only too happy to campaign by associating Republican candidates with Trump.These midterm elections, Obama told a crowd in Ohio, “is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration. It’s the circuit breaker in the system.”That blast of sanity and good sense seems far more likely to resonate with potential voters than Trump’s unhinged rants and dangerous threats.Pretend he’s on the ballot?Maybe that’s effective with Trump’s remaining cult-like base. And maybe itwillbring some of those loyalists out to vote next week if they had been thinking of sitting out this election.But more likely, the imagined association with Trump will serve to remind most voters that Trump’s malfeasance must be rebuked and rejected. Certainly not encouraged.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionDonald TrumpUS politicsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: My phone thinks my boyfriend is my ‘best friend’. It’s not alone | Patrick Lenton | The Guardian
description: Being in a same-sex relationship can make you weirdly invisible. Queer identity shouldn’t be treated as abnormal
Author: Patrick Lenton
Headline: Being in a same-sex relationship can make you weirdly invisible. Queer identity shouldn’t be treated as abnormal
Content: ‘It seems as though we have a Goldilocks problem with queer relationship visibility: there’s too much visibility or there’s not enough.’Photograph: Vanessa Nunes/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It seems as though we have a Goldilocks problem with queer relationship visibility: there’s too much visibility or there’s not enough.’Photograph: Vanessa Nunes/AlamyOpinionLGBTQ+ rightsMy phone thinks my boyfriend is my ‘best friend’. It’s not alonePatrick LentonBeing in a same-sex relationship can make you weirdly invisible. Queer identity shouldn’t be treated as abnormalThu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 20.15 EDTShareMy boyfriend and I invented a game on our recent trip toItaly. We called it “invisible gays”, which might have been an attempt at some kind of word play around “gays” and “gaze” – but I was on holiday and feeling lazy, so I didn’t push it.The game began when one night he took me out to a little trattoria to celebrate my birthday. It was a warm night, and fairy lights were entangled in the fragrant blooming flowers over our heads, and we drank good wine and ate bowls of perfect pasta, and there was candlelight, and it was so romantic I wouldn’t have blinked if two dogs had started smooching over a strand of spaghetti. Che bello!We were one of four tables, all couples of various ages looking at each other with disgusting wet amorous eyes. During the evening a man selling roses approached the other tables. One young guy even bought one, presenting the blossom with a flourish to his girlfriend, earning applause from other patrons and a round of toothy photos. Caught up in the moment, my partner pulled out his wallet to buy a rose for me too, despite my wildly insincere protestations – but the rose man didn’t even clock us as a couple and wandered off into the night.Puppy love: why asking my boyfriend to coparent Basil the greyhound was the most important proposal of all | Patrick LentonRead moreI briefly wondered if it was because my outfit wasn’t chic enough for Rome. Then I realised we were the only couple who weren’t the societal default setting of a man and a woman, having instead made the dire mistake of being two beautiful men dining together. I wonder if he thought we were some kind of complicated interracial brothers?This continued all around Italy, with more than seven episodes of being passed over at romantic tourist traps marked on our scorecard. When I organised a fancy dinner for my boyfriend’s birthday weeks later, one of the servers said I was a “good friend” for doing so.I’m used to the way that being in a same-sex couple can make you hyper visible or put a homophobic spotlight on you, so that it feels like every time you kiss in public it’s like Frodo putting on the One Ring, drawing the attention of the Dark Lord and his screeching Nazgûl. I’m used to muttered comments from people you walk by on the streets when you’re holding hands, or of making out with a tall guy outside a bar after our first date only for a car full of men to stop and yell slurs at us. I’m used to holding the hand of a boyfriend as we were chased down the backstreets of Newtown late at night by three silent men.I’ve also dated enough women to know that there’s a contrast – no woman I’ve ever dated has flinched away from a kiss on the cheek and whispered: “Maybe not in public.” I’ve had men I’ve dated comment on how “openly affectionate” I am, because I haven’t had to learn to self-censor my public love languages. Women I date usually just comment on how clean my legs are and how many Gilmore Girls references I make.Obviously being hyper visible and therefore at risk of overt and violent homophobia is worse than not being able to buy an overpriced street flower. Over the past year in Australia,hate crimes against gay and bisexual menhave been making headlines. As someone who has suffered a hate crime or two, I can confirm that dealing with this should be the authorities’ priority instead of cracking down on the rose men of Rome.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Patrick LentonBut with the 10-year anniversary of the marriage equality win coming up next year, it’s worth looking at all the ways being in a same-sex relationship can still make you weirdly invisible. It’s another argument for why Mardi Gras, pride flags andIdahobit daysin schools are still so necessary – because, when love between queer people goes unseen, it makes it seem as though it isn’t “normal”. And when queer identity is treated as abnormal, it fertilises the ground necessary to justify violence against queer people.We all know the little “collections” of photos and videos our smartphones occasionally create. This can be anything from “Your trip in Italy 2026” to “Furry pals throughout the years”. It’s been a source of constant amusement to me that it sorts all the photos of my boyfriend and me into a collection called “best friends”. These are photos of two men kissing and, without oversharing, sometimes photos of two men doing things even more intimate than kissing (kayaking).It shows you that homosexual invisibility is so hardwired into aspects of society that a phone short-circuits and decides that two men in love are just good bros. I’ve never had any of the women I’ve dated put into a folder called “best friends”. In fact, none of the women who are my actual best friends have made it into those folders either. My dog does get filed there, which, when its alongside my boyfriend, feels a little like one of those slippery slope arguments made by the Australian Christian Lobby during the plebiscite.It seems as though we have a Goldilocks problem with queer relationship visibility: there’s too much visibility or there’s not enough. Make up your mind!Not only do I simply want to express my love for my boyfriend publicly and without risk of violence, and for it to be recognised for what it is; I also don’t want my sexuality to be the only thing that people notice me for. I want to be noticed for my abnormally good looks and sex appeal.Patrick Lenton is a writer. His latest novel isIn Spite of YouExplore more on these topicsLGBTQ+ rightsOpinionRelationshipsItaly holidaysItalyMarriage equalitycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on a changing Brexit debate: Kemi Badenoch is trapped in denial | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The prime minister’s ambitions might be ambiguous, but unlike the Conservative leader, he is following voters and the facts
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The prime minister’s ambitions might be ambiguous, but unlike the Conservative leader, he is following voters and the facts
Content: Kemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons, 28 October 2026.Photograph: House of Commons/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons, 28 October 2026.Photograph: House of Commons/PAOpinionBrexitThe Guardian view on a changing Brexit debate: Kemi Badenoch is trapped in denialEditorialThe prime minister’s ambitions might be ambiguous, but unlike the Conservative leader, he is following voters and the factsThu 29 Oct 2026 14.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.55 EDTShareBritish politics is still polarised around Brexit, although 10 years on from the referendum, the terms of debate are very different. Or they should be. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has moved discussions of European solidarity from the realm of abstraction to a matter of urgent defence partnership. Donald Trump’s presidency in the US, marked by scorn for European democracies andindulgence of Vladimir Putin, has undermined confidence that Britain can rely on any “special relationship” with Washington.Under these circumstances, it would be absurd to deny that a reappraisal of Brexit is in order. The prime minister acknowledged this inhis speechat the Labour party conference last month, calling for a national conversation about the future relationship with every option, including rejoining, on the table. The Eurosceptic opposition are having none of it. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, accuses the government of stirring division by raising the European question. She told MPs this week that Labour should thank the Tories for the Brexit deal they negotiated.The Tories and Reform UK like to remind Andy Burnham of comments he made whencampaigning in Makerfieldearlier this year for the seat that became his launchpad to reach No 10. Mr Burnham said that rerunning the old Brexit arguments was “the last thing we should do right now”. That can be made consistent with his current position in the sense that an exact rerun of the 2016 debate would indeed be pointless, which is why something different, more future-facing, is being proposed instead. Mr Burnham’s critics see that as sleight of hand to conceal a flagrant change of line. But the distinction between relitigating outdated arguments and engaging with present realities is a vital one.The Tory position, shared with Reform, contains no audit of Britain’s foreign and economic policy interests. It is based on ideology and fear of confronting the facts that such an evaluation reveals.Brexithas made Britain poorer and diminished its influence on the world stage. The public know this all too well, as evidenced by opinion polls indicating majority support for a closer EU relationship.Mrs Badenoch’s position is also disingenuous, givenher commitmentto pull Britain out of the European convention on human rights. That would pointlessly reopen some of the most fissile Brexit arguments because of the ECHR’s codification in the Good Friday agreement for Northern Ireland.A phenomenon that Mrs Badenoch and Mr Burnham have observed, but respond to differently, is that voters have no desire for a return to the poisonous political atmosphere of the immediate post-referendum period. The Tory leader uses that aversion to justify her lack of a strategic concept for Britain’s future relationship with its continental neighbours. The prime minister’s approach is to sound ecumenical, saying that he aspires to national consensus on the best way forward, whilesounding vagueabout his personal preferences.That ambiguity has given the opposition cause to accuse the prime minister of conspiring to undo Brexit, but it has alsodissolvedsome of the taboo around discussion of much closer models of reintegration with the EU, which is a necessary condition for a healthier fact-based debate. That isn’t a conversation the Conservatives want to have, but for the prime minister to share in their denial would be, as he has said, adereliction of duty.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on online harms: Ofcom is failing at its job | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Expressions of disappointment are not an adequate response to the concerning lack of safety improvements for children on social media
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Expressions of disappointment are not an adequate response to the concerning lack of safety improvements for children on social media
Content: A poster on a bus shelter in London. ‘The proportion of children viewing harmful content has stayed the same despite a raft of measures in the Online Safety Act designed to protect them.’Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA poster on a bus shelter in London. ‘The proportion of children viewing harmful content has stayed the same despite a raft of measures in the Online Safety Act designed to protect them.’Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesOpinionInternet safetyThe Guardian view on online harms: Ofcom is failing at its jobEditorialExpressions of disappointment are not an adequate response to the concerning lack of safety improvements for children on social mediaThu 29 Oct 2026 14.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.55 EDTShareOne thing is clear following last week’s report from the media regulator, Ofcom: the mammoth task of protecting children from online harms has barely begun. Campaigners said that they were dismayed but not surprised that the proportion ofchildren viewing harmful contenthas stayed the same despite a raft of measures in the Online Safety Act designed to protect them. Research showed that high-priority material including pornography and self-harm, as well as a broader category covering bullying, abuse and the promotion of violence, continued to be encountered regularly in the nine months after new safety duties came into force.The regulator found that personalised feeds were the main way that such content was presented, and noted that such feeds show different material to boys and girls. Suicide and self-harm content were more commonly seen by girls and children with special educational needs or disabilities. In a grim irony, Ofcom’s report appeared one day after acoroner in Norfolkruled that suicide imagery viewed on TikTok “may have played a significant part” in the decision by a 14-year-old girl to take her own life in May.This is a deeply concerning situation. Significant resources went into the UK’s online safety bill on the understanding that, after two decades during which tech companies had been granted extraordinary freedom over the terms of their engagement with citizens, democratic control was being reasserted. Silicon Valley’s reckless disregard of children’s safety and wellbeing convinced the public, and then parliament, that action was needed. Yet three years after the bill passed, Meta, TikTok and X are all engaged inlegal challenges against Ofcomand appear to believe that their interests should trump the law.View image in fullscreenLisa Nandy.Photograph: Martin Dalton/ShutterstockAndy Burnham’s government needs a step change in how it treats big tech, which currently differs little from its predecessor. Lisa Nandy held on to her job as secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport; a ban on social media accounts for under-16s is due to come into force in spring 2027. Ministers want the UK to take a tougher approach than Australia, apioneerin preventing online harm, and are looking at proposalsrequiringphoto ID for teens to access sites.But the new age limit and other safety rules can only work if the regulator is capable of enforcing them. Andthe Ofcom reportwas not encouraging. Inevidence to MPsabout the lack of a “safety culture” at social media companies, Ofcom’s chief executive, Melanie Dawes, sounded far too tentative. Whistleblowers have been making similar points more forcefully for years.The Online Safety Act was never meant to be a once-and-for-all law. The pace of technological change – above all, the rise of AI – madefurther legislationinevitable. But searching questions must be asked about a situation in which a new law has led to no benefits at all for the user group – children – that it was designed to protect. As the Guardian has argued previously, ministers should haveimposed a duty of careand made businesses accountable for improvements, rather than simply obliging them to follow a code.Accountability remains too easily evaded at the top of tech. Executives should face a greater risk of criminal penalties for serious failings. Expressions of disappointment are no substitute for action. Regulators and ministers have the powers to secure change. They need to demonstrate an appetite for using them.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I pooh-poohed Latin until won over by Winnie in translation | Languages | The Guardian
description: Letter: Virginia Orrey recalls how her Latin teacher grabbed the class’s attention with Alexander Lenard’s Winnie Ille Pu
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Virginia Orrey recalls how her Latin teacher grabbed the class’s attention with Alexander Lenard’s Winnie Ille Pu
Content: A still from the 2017 filmGoodbye Christopher Robin, describing AA Milne’s creation of Winnie-the-Pooh.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyView image in fullscreenA still from the 2017 filmGoodbye Christopher Robin, describing AA Milne’s creation of Winnie-the-Pooh.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyLanguagesLettersI pooh-poohed Latin until won over by Winnie in translationVirginia Orreyrecalls how her Latin teacher grabbed the class’s attention in 1973 with Alexander Lenard’s Winnie Ille PuThu 29 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareAs a callow 17-year-old in 1973, I and one other classmate had the distinction of being the only pupils in the sixth form at our grammar school to study Latin as an additional O-level alongside our A-levels.Our – in retrospect very young, newly qualified – teacher was at her wits’ end to engage us in the joys of verbs that are passive in form but active in meaning, and the class was more often than not 50% empty.However, in what can only have been a moment of divine inspiration, she brought in two copies of Alexander Lenard’s Winnie Ille Pu, a Latin translation of AA Milne’s timeless book (Letters, 23 October). Our attention was grabbed – and lifelong. Job done.Virginia OrreyCowes, Isle of WightHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Save Hammersmith Bridge – but keep it free of cars | Transport policy | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Simon Jenkins’s article on the west London crossing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Simon Jenkins’s article on the west London crossing
Content: Hammersmith Bridge has been closed to motor vehicles since April 2019.Photograph: Gibson Blanc/AlamyView image in fullscreenHammersmith Bridge has been closed to motor vehicles since April 2019.Photograph: Gibson Blanc/AlamyTransport policyLettersSave Hammersmith Bridge – but keep it free of carsReaders respond to Simon Jenkins’s article on the west London crossingThu 29 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTShareSimon Jenkins is a great defender of our national heritage, having produced many books on the subject and frequently written in the Guardian against aggressive modern architectural horrors. How shocking, then, to find him arguing for the replacement of Hammersmith Bridge simply to provide for yet more cars on the roads (Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t, 23 October). He claims that the principal cause of congestion is “London’s epidemic of roadworks”, when actually it’s the fact that there are just too many cars trying to use a road network that isn’t designed for them.Furthermore, he says that, in its present state, the bridge “merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross it” – and yet between 12,000 and 15,000 people use it every day. Reopening it to motor traffic (and increasingly heavy cars have massively contributed to the current state of degradation of the bridge) would bring little benefit. Well over half the households in Hammersmith and Fulham don’t have access to a car, and there are very good public transport links in the area; there is even a well-thought-out plan put forward by the Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit group to run driverless electric “pod” vehicles to provide for those who are unable to walk across Hammersmith Bridge.And quite apart from the huge difficulty involved in enabling the tearing down of a Grade II* listed structure (where’s our doughty defender of national heritage now?), there is no effective business case for replacing it at enormous cost to provide for yet more cars, when for both environmental and health reasons (particularly because of the pollution they cause), the whole emphasis should be on reducing our reliance on cars. If only someone in authority would summon up the courage to tackle the motoring lobby.Dr RichardCarterPutney, LondonSimon Jenkins is right to castigate the different London authorities that have failed to replace Hammersmith Bridge over a period of seven years. No other capital city in Europe would allow such a prolonged truncation of a major transport artery, preventing vehicles from crossing the river. London is not a unitary authority and its mayor does not have the powers of his peers in other capitals to raise the finance to pay for the cost of a new bridge. The lack of joined-up thinking appears to be baked in to the planning processes of the different relevant authorities.This sorry state of affairs in south-west London has led to permanent traffic chaos along the Upper Richmond Road and the hell that is Putney High Street during rush hour. Were it not for the British obsession for so-called “heritage” projects, we could have had a temporary bridge capable of carrying traffic years ago. Instead citizens are obliged to walk or pedal their way across a wonky bridge in order to get to the other side for the sake of a misplaced nostalgia for Victorian engineering feats.Julian HeddyEast Sheen, LondonThe outdated photograph published with Simon Jenkins’s off-beam article on Hammersmith Bridge suggests decrepitude, when the reality is quite different. Thanks to £55m of investment by Hammersmith and Fulham council, this iconic, Grade II* listed bridge has found a successful new purpose as an active travel crossing, with 15,000 people a day walking and wheeling across its reopened main carriageway.I know of no “growing body of opinion” calling for its replacement. On the contrary, the settled local preference has moved to build on this success with a proposal to introduce a fleet of lightweight, autonomous electric shuttles to fill the public transport gap to ensure all residents can cross comfortably and safely. Community-led Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit is working with Ohmio UK and partners to deliver this vision.Traffic on neighbouring bridges and the wider road network is down compared with before the bridge closed to motor vehicles, while Barnes’s local economy is booming, aided by the ebike revolution.There is no credible business case for spending hundreds of millions bringing back polluting, dangerous and exclusionary through traffic. With the mayor targeting a 27% reduction in car traffic by 2030, the priority must be to build on this success, not undo it.Charles CampionChair, Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light TransitView image in fullscreenThe Millennium Bridge, which opened in 2001.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PASimon Jenkins is a respected commentator on London’s heritage and built environment, with a deep understanding of the costs of maintaining historic infrastructure. We share his commitment to London’s bridges, but not his views on how the City Bridge Foundation’s charitable funds should be used.We maintain five Thames bridges: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium and Blackfriars, spanning centuries of engineering history. Their upkeep requires sustained investment and commitment, demonstrated by our current £15m Blackfriars Bridge refurbishment, repairing more than 2,000 cast-iron balusters and repainting the entire structure.Our endowment exists to meet these responsibilities in perpetuity. It is not a general fund for London’s infrastructure, nor is its value a measure of money freely available to spend.Alongside maintaining and supporting our bridges, where there are funds available, we make grants to charities tackling inequality and disadvantage across London. These funds are made for charitable purposes and governed by the legal and regulatory arrangements that apply to our work. They cannot simply be redirected to pay for the restoration or replacement of a bridge outside our remit.We recognise the importance of London’s bridges to the people who rely on them every day, but other Thames crossings are the responsibility of other organisations. We share knowledge and experience with those responsible through industry groups.For nearly 900 years, the legacy of Bridge House Estates has helped keep London’s bridges standing while supporting charitable work across the city. We are proud of this legacy and the charity partners working alongside us to build a fairer London.Paul MartinelliChairman, City Bridge FoundationExplore more on these topicsTransport policyTransportArchitectureMotoring (Technology)Motoring (Money)HeritagelettersShareReuse this content

title: Donald Trump’s male gaze | Psychology | The Guardian
description: Letter: The US president’s commentary on the beauty and brawn of various political figures is not without historical precedent, writes Randy Fair
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: The US president’s commentary on the beauty and brawn of various political figures is not without historical precedent, writes Randy Fair
Content: Detail of a Nazi poster (We Prepare Our Body and Soul), from the mid-1930s.Photograph: Glasshouse Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenDetail of a Nazi poster (We Prepare Our Body and Soul), from the mid-1930s.Photograph: Glasshouse Images/AlamyPsychologyLettersDonald Trump’s male gazeThe US president’s commentary on the beauty and brawn of various political figures is not without historical precedent, writesRandy FairThu 29 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareAdam Gabbatt’s analysis explores the seemingly odd statements that Donald Trump has made recently regarding the male anatomy of his political friends and foes (What’s up with Trump’s unhinged fixation on male candidates’ bodies?, 23 October).These statements may seem strange, but they are not without historical precedent. The Nazis, paradoxically, feared same-sex desire while also obsessing over a hypermasculine form as the highest possible aesthetic. We have also seen this obsession in other far-right figures – notably Vladimir Putin, whose shirtless photos are used to send a strongman message. Luckily, Trump has so far spared us those images of himself, except in AI form.Randy FairWilton Manors, Florida, USHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Emergency stockpiles are a luxury that not everyone can afford | Emergency planning | The Guardian
description: Letters: Keira Callaghan says being prepared should be a public health measure, not a privilege, and Chris Rotheram is experiencing prescription anxiety. Plus five more letters in response to the Be Ready campaign
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Keira Callaghan says being prepared should be a public health measure, not a privilege, and Chris Rotheram is experiencing prescription anxiety. Plus five more letters in response to the Be Ready campaign
Content: ‘Perhaps local councils could create a stockpile hub where those in need could access the recommended supplies, free of charge.’Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreen‘Perhaps local councils could create a stockpile hub where those in need could access the recommended supplies, free of charge.’Photograph: GettyEmergency planningLettersEmergency stockpiles are a luxury that not everyone can affordKeira Callaghansaysbeing prepared should be a public health measure, not a privilege, andChris Rotheramis experiencing prescription anxiety. Plus five more letters in response to the Be Ready campaignThu 29 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareThe Be Ready campaign may offer sensible advice in principle (Every Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advises, 22 October), but as a midwife working in Tower Hamlets, one of the poorest boroughs in London, I can see first-hand that its practical recommendations risk excluding precisely those families who are already most vulnerable.For families living in a single room in a shared house, storing nine litres of water per person alongside three days’ worth of essential supplies may simply be unrealistic. When families are already struggling with the cost of food, heating and everyday necessities, buying additional emergency provisions may also be financially impossible.Perhaps local councils could create a stockpile hub where those in need could access the recommended supplies, free of charge. Being prepared should be a public health measure, not a privilege reserved for those who can afford it.Keira CallaghanLondonWhile it flies in the face ofjust-in-timeprinciples, I think the initiative to improve resilience is sensible in the current situation (Andy Burnham says he has emergency stockpile of beans, soup and Twiglets, 23 October). However, due to health issues, I rely on a monthly repeat prescription of several life-preserving medications. It used to be normal practice to request a new prescription when I opened the last box, but now the policy at my GP surgery appears to be that they will not issue a new prescription until a week before I need them.The pharmacy then requires up to a week to process the prescription, meaning that my medications are always dispensed at the last minute. Localised shortages and periodic mistakes have caused me problems in the past, and I suffer from prescription anxiety every month. This policy is also incompatible with the latest government advice to stockpile essential medication. When the inevitable catastrophe strikes, I will find myself without my essential medication, and I doubt that 75 tins of beans and a packet of Twiglets will be much consolation.Chris RotheramThornton-Cleveleys, LancashireThe government is urging us to stock up enough supplies to survive for 72 hours. People might be wondering if it is time to dust off their copies ofProtect and Survivefrom the 1980s. That document advised us to ready ourselves for nuclear war by preparing a bucket of sand for a toilet, and laying in some jigsaws to keep the kiddies amused. I feel pretty sanguine that such precautions won’t be needed today, because here in Hexham, where there used to be a nuclear bunker (for the use of officialdom, not for us, of course), there is now a McDonald’s. So, just keep calm and carry on.Caroline WestgateHexham, NorthumberlandYou tell us the new government guidance for stocking up on supplies to survive for three days in an emergency, but nowhere does the advice tackle effluent. If we need three litres of bottled drinking water per person per day, the assumption is that mains water is not available.Could the government please provide advice on where and how we will be expected to do our ablutions in a sanitary way when the toilets will not flush? We do not all have the luxury of a garden in which we can dig a hole. Some of us live in a block of flats, and dealing with three days’ worth of shit is something that needs planning.Peter SlessengerReading, BerkshireWe are beginning to see the elements of a Labour survival kit.Andy Burnhamhas gone for Twiglets, while John Healey is carrying a bottle of HP Sauce (Harold Wilson’s gravy). To complete it a flask of tea is required (Tony Benn).Keith FlettTottenham, LondonRegarding Wes Streeting’s advice to stock up on essential food items in the event of food shortages and power cuts, can he please now advise on how to heat up tins of beans, soup, peas, etc when the electricity/gas is off?Jane KilsbyCountesthorpe, LeicestershireCall me a cynic, but might the government’s call to stock up on emergency supplies have been an attempt to increase economic activity before the budget?Pete BibbySheffieldHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Pleaseemailus your letter and it will be considered for publication in ourletterssection.Explore more on these topicsEmergency planningAndy BurnhamWes StreetingJohn HealeyFoodWaterLabourlettersShareReuse this content

title: Everton ease past Newcastle to set up Fleetwood trip after Grealish is dropped | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Everton beat Newcastle 3-1 with goals by James Garner, Hayden Hackney and Thierno Barry to set up a Carabao Cup quarter-final with Fleetwood Town
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Everton beat Newcastle 3-1 with goals by James Garner, Hayden Hackney and Thierno Barry to set up a Carabao Cup quarter-final with Fleetwood Town
Content: Thierno Barry enjoys putting the finishing touch to Everton’s win after scoring their third goal.Photograph: Jon Super/ReutersView image in fullscreenThierno Barry enjoys putting the finishing touch to Everton’s win after scoring their third goal.Photograph: Jon Super/ReutersCarabao CupEverton ease past Newcastle to set up Fleetwood trip after Grealish is droppedAndy Hunterat Hill Dickinson StadiumThu 29 Oct 2026 18.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 19.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe biggest night in Everton’s season started with a big call from David Moyes and demanded a big performance from his players.With the exception of Jack Grealish, they did not let him down. A quarter-final at Fleetwood Town is their prize after a clinical, committed display shattered Newcastle’s hopes of lifting the Carabao Cup for a second time in three seasons.Newcastle dominated spells of the fourth round tie and the stats – registering 28 shots to Everton’s 11, although only nine visiting attempts were on target – but individual defensive errors and an ineffective attack proved a ruinous combination. Matthias Jaissle denied his team are a soft touch, despite persuasive evidence to the contrary, yet called Newcastle “naive” and the defeat, in front of almost 8,000 of their fans, “shocking”. Andy Burnham was among the many Evertonians in attendance grateful for Newcastle’s generosity.Everton 3-1 Newcastle: Carabao Cup fourth round – liveRead moreJames Garner, with his first goal of the season, Hayden Hackney, with his first goal for the club, and Thierno Barry were on target to take Everton into the last eight of a competition they have never won. Jordan Pickford was in commanding form against his old adversaries while Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall ran the show from midfield. But it was the absent Grealish who dominated the buildup after Everton announced he had been dropped for disciplinary reasons.Grealish is understood to have missed training on Monday without permission. Despite the importance of the fixture and the limited options at his disposal, and the playmaker’s subsequent return to training, Moyes demonstrated that no player is bigger than the club by banishing the 31-year-old from the game. The Everton manager later claimed it was “a club decision” but it was taken by him and the chief executive, Angus Kinnear. Ultimately, and no doubt to Grealish’s great relief, he was not missed.Newcastle dominated the opening 20 minutes to the extent that a two-goal interval lead for Everton would have seemed inconceivable. Pickford saved an early header from Harvey Barnes, who then turned provider to set up Jacob Ramsey for a shot that was blocked superbly by Vitalii Mykolenko. Fabian Schär also tested Pickford from distance, leaving the England international raging at the lack of protection in front of him. He could not fault his defenders’ willingness to put their bodies on the line, however.View image in fullscreenHayden Hackney scores Everton’s second goal against Newcastle.Photograph: Aidan Hunter/Action Plus/ShutterstockEverton gradually turned the contest around. Putting an end to ineffective long balls up to Barry, when he was marked by Dan Burn, helped their cause, although it was a long clearance from Pickford that led to the breakthrough. Amar Dedic looked to retrieve the goalkeeper’s punt but was harried out of possession by Tyrique George. The ball broke to Hackney, who squared inside for Garner to find the far corner of Lukas Hornicek’s goal. “The first goal, it’s no risk, clear it,” said a dismayed Jaissle. “But we concede out of nothing. The first, second and third goals were the same with individual mistakes. We need to be more efficient and learn fast.”Pickford came in for his customary Sunderland stick from the Newcastle support. He responded in the best way possible; with a hand in a second goal that deflated the sizeable away section. The Everton keeper reacted sharply to launch a quick throw towards Dewsbury-Hall in the centre circle. Dewsbury-Hall spun away from Burn before embarking on a determined run that was halted by a trip from behind by Ramsey. The referee, Farai Hallam, played an excellent advantage as the ball broke to Barry. Newcastle appeared to pause, waiting for the free-kick, and were punished when Barry clipped over a cross for Hackney to volley home from close range.A triple half-time substitution from Jaissle was an unmistakable sign of discontent with Newcastle’s ineffective display at both ends of the pitch.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideCarabao Cup quarter-final drawShowFleetwood v EvertonManchester City v Bradford CityCrystal Palace v SunderlandLiverpool v BournemouthTies will take place during the week commencing 14 DecemberWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.There was more menace from the visitors in the second half with the substitute Yoane Wissa having an early chance from Joe Willock’s chip and Dedic’s shot looping over off Hackney’s heel. But with Pickford standing firm and saving smartly from Lewis Hall, Anthony Elanga and Ramsey, and Wissa almost hitting the corner flag with one decent chance, Newcastle’s failure to make their pressure count continued.The visitors were punished when Everton made the game safe in devastating style. Garner, a growing influence, intercepted a pass from Dedic and released Dewsbury-Hall behind a static Newcastle defence. The midfielder took Burn out of the equation with a perfect pass across to Barry, who had time to control and place a fine finish beyond Hornicek.Burn finally broke Everton’s resistance with a late header from an Elanga cross. A melee involving the goalscorer, Pickford, James Tarkowski and Joelinton broke out as they fought over the ball – all four were booked – but there would be no miraculous escape for Newcastle. It is Everton who march on to face the Cod Army.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupEvertonNewcastle Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: George Russell determined not to let disappointing F1 season define career | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: George Russell has insisted he will not let his difficult Formula One season define his career and still has plenty of time to win the world championship
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: George Russell has insisted he will not let his difficult Formula One season define his career and still has plenty of time to win the world championship
Content: George Russell has been outdriven by his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli this season.Photograph: Daniel Cárdenas/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeorge Russell has been outdriven by his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli this season.Photograph: Daniel Cárdenas/Anadolu/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026George Russell determined not to let disappointing F1 season define career28-year-old still believes he will win world title one dayKimi Antonelli misses media duties with ‘viral illness’Giles Richardsin Mexico CityThu 29 Oct 2026 18.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 19.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorge Russell has insisted he will not let his difficult Formula One season define his career and believes he still has plenty of years left to come back and win the world championship.Russell has been outdriven by his 20-year-old Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli in a bruising season for the British driver. Antonelli isset to win the titleand become F1’s youngest world champion at this weekend’s Mexican Grand Prix if he finishes in ninth place or above.Wolff hails Antonelli’s US Grand Prix demolition as the Italian’s ‘best race yet’Read moreHe has taken nine wins thus far to Russell’s three, with the British driver struggling for consistency in adapting to the demands of the energy management required by the new cars which, alongside the tyres in use this year, does not suit the 28-year-old’s driving style.Russell has delivered some impeccable weekends, including commanding victories in Austria and Baku, but more often than not has been left baffled as to why he cannot make the car work to the same effect as Antonelli, a process which he conceded had been hard to deal with.“I’ve probably learned more about myself this year than I would have liked to, in all honesty,” he said at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.“You know, the highs and lows you go through in sport are immense and that’s because we all care so much for what we’re doing.“But I remind myself I’m 28 years old. I see Lewis [Hamilton] still competing extremely well at 41 and Fernando [Alonso] at 45. Lewis won the majority of his titles in his thirties and this year is absolutely not going to define my career as a whole.”Russell has suffered with no little bad luck this season but has offered praise to Antonelli, admitting the Italian has been the better driver and is thoroughly deserving of taking his first title in only his second season in F1.The British driver had opened the season strongly witha win at the Australian GPbut was then battered as Antonelli took five wins in a row and the lead of the championship which he has not relinquished since. However, Russell maintained he would learn from the experience to return stronger in 2027.“It’s not going to break me. If anything, it’s going to make me stronger,” he said. “I’ve been pretty proud of my resilience and how I’ve sort of bounced back from very tough moments.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli is set to win the title this weekend although he was absent on Thursday due to illness.Photograph: Jason Pohuski/BMR/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock“Through my lowest points of this season, I’ve generally bounced back really, really strong and then I had another bad race after the good one. So, maybe it’s something I need to analyse as well because I always perform best after my worst races. Maybe it’s just a coincidence, maybe there’s something in it.“I don’t think any athlete, no matter how great, has every single year of their career performing at their highest level. Unfortunately, this year for me has come at maybe the time when I needed it most. By no means the end of my journey, I have still got a good 12 to 15 years left in me.”Russell is in a tight battle for second place in the championship, just one point ahead of Hamilton and six in front of Red Bull’s Max Verstappen.Antonelli did not take part in media duties on Thursday as the team said he was unwell with a “viral illness”. He was given leave by the FIA to not take part, as the team noted, as “a precaution to give him the chance to rest ahead of the weekend”. He is expected to be in the car for free practice on Friday.The Cadillac team also withdrew Valtteri Bottas from his media duties on Thursday in Mexico, noting that he was “unwell” and subsequently that “the team has taken the decision to allow him a day of rest, to support his recovery”.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Mercedes GPFormula OneGeorge RussellKimi AntonelliMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Carrick keeps Fernandes as captain and says he needs no assurances on United future | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick has said he will not strip Bruno Fernandes of the Manchester United captaincy and is not surprised to have kept his job as the head coach
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Michael Carrick has said he will not strip Bruno Fernandes of the Manchester United captaincy and is not surprised to have kept his job as the head coach
Content: Michael Carrick said: ‘I care about what the supporters think. I care about what it feels like in the stadium.’Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick said: ‘I care about what the supporters think. I care about what it feels like in the stadium.’Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedCarrick keeps Fernandes as captain and says he needs no assurances on United futureCarrick says he is not surprised to still be head coachHe describes Fernandes as ‘important’ for the squadWill UnwinThu 29 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick has said he will not strip Bruno Fernandes of the Manchester United captaincy after dropping him for thedefeat by Bournemouthand that he is not surprised to have kept his job as the head coach.Carrick and Fernandesheld talksthis week after the Portuguesecriticised the tacticsin the loss to Como, resulting in the midfielder being an unused substitute on Sunday. Harry Maguire took the armband but will not retain it for Saturday’s game at Chelsea, with Carrick saying “there is no decision to be made” and praising Fernandes.Howe, Nagelsmann, Pochettino: can anyone end Manchester United’s doom loop?Read more“He’s an important player for this group,” he said. “He has been and he will be. Between us, we’ve got to make a difference and we’ve got to push things in a good direction. He’s fully committed to this football club, he’s fully committed to making things better. It doesn’t change for me. He’s the one that’s kind of led the team so well for many a game and many a year, and he’ll continue to do that.”Carrick’s future remains unclear but he has beengiven a chanceto turn around United’s form. The hierarchy held talks over whether to stick with Carrick at the start of the week after eight games without a win, including a wait of more than two months for a Premier League victory. There is keen interest inEddie Howe or Julian Nagelsmannas potential replacements.“I don’t need any assurances from anyone,” Carrick said. “I totally get the position, I understand the job, I understand the responsibilities, I understand what comes with that.”Asked whether he was surprised still to be in charge, Carrick said: “No, I am here to do my job. I am here to do the best for the team, and I am desperate to make us better and improve things, so I’m not surprised, no.”The United supporters cheered Carrick off after the Bournemouth game, turning their anger on the players, who were booed at Old Trafford. “I care about what the supporters think,” Carrick said. “I care about what it feels like in the stadium, and them travelling for games, to come and see us and support us.“I care about what we give them, and what we offer them, and what they see. I genuinely don’t take any notice of anything else. I know this job, I know what it brings, I know what we need to do really to be better. I don’t need anyone else to tell me anything else.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnited will be without the striker Benjamin Sesko until the new year because of a shin injury but Carrick was boosted by Kobbie Mainoo’s return to training this week.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarricknewsShareReuse this content

title: PSG claim late point after Shaw penalty to hit Manchester City’s WCL top-four hopes | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Tara Elimbi Gilbert’s late equaliser came moments after Khadija Shaw scored a penalty as Manchester City drew their third league phase game in a row
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Tara Elimbi Gilbert’s late equaliser came moments after Khadija Shaw scored a penalty as Manchester City drew their third league phase game in a row
Content: Tara Elimbi Gilbert is embraced by her PSG teammates after scoring a late equaliser.Photograph: Morgan Harlow/Uefa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTara Elimbi Gilbert is embraced by her PSG teammates after scoring a late equaliser.Photograph: Morgan Harlow/Uefa/Getty ImagesWomen's Champions LeaguePSG claim late point after Shaw penalty to hit Manchester City’s WCL top-four hopesTom Garryat the Joie StadiumThu 29 Oct 2026 18.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 19.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou cannot miss half a dozen big chances at Women’s Champions League level and expect to get away with it. That is the harsh lesson Manchester City learnt on Thursday against Paris Saint-Germain, who extended the English champions’ wait for their first win in Europe this season by striking late to secure a point at a disappointed Joie Stadium.City’s third draw from three Champions League games so far this season really ought to have been a victory. Instead, their hopes of a top-four spot and with it automatic qualification for the quarter-finals are looking increasingly slim.Manchester City 1-1 Paris Saint-Germain: Women’s Champions League – as it happenedRead moreThey thought they had won the game through Khadija “Bunny” Shaw’s 85th-minute penalty, but conceding sparked PSG into life and they snatched a point with a scrappy equaliser three minutes later as their substitute Tara Elimbi Gilbert found the net from close range.How, therefore, should we look upon City’s season? Are they the team that is unbeaten in all competitions? Or the team without a win in Europe? Both ring true, and although they are still likely to progress to the knockout stages, they will have been hugely frustrated with their profligacy.“There are a lot of things in this game we are pleased with. The result is not what we wanted, of course. Maybe we should kill the game earlier,” the City manager, Andrée Jeglertz, reflected. “Annoying is not the right word but it’s a little bit a feeling of ‘argh’. We deserved more, I think, but that’s how it is in the Champions League. When you dominate games and you don’t score, the opponent will take their chances and that’s what they did.”View image in fullscreenKhadija Shaw converts her penalty to give Manchester City the lead.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PADrawsaway to Bayern Munichand athome against Real Madridin their first two games were certainly not poor results, against strong opposition and with theoretically kinder fixtures to come, so there was no need to panic, but City’s 11th-placed position in the table, only one above the final qualification spot, before kick-off will nonetheless have looked a little concerning to some of their supporters. They ended the night 10th.Jeglertz was positive about their chances: “We got drawn against six teams and we have played the three toughest of them, I think, so now we have three games that we have the opportunity, again, to get the points we need to qualify for the next round. So that’s our goal and nothing has changed.”Nonetheless, this latest draw was a blow. PSG sought to frustrate City in the first half, and succeeded after riding out an early storm. Shaw’s header dropped wide at the far post from Aoba Fujino’s third-minute cross, as the home side made a bright start but were unable to score while on top. Shaw fizzed a low strike narrowly wide 11 minutes later after terrific play from Lauren Hemp.
