City controlled possession but did not test the PSG goalkeeper, Oliwia Peda, until the second half.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideRoundup: Barcelona stay perfect, Juventus win again, Paris FC and Häcken drawShowBarcelonalaid down another marker in their defence of the Women’s Champions League with an 8-0 win thrashing of the Danish champions,HB Køge.A Caroline Graham Hansen penalty and a goal from Ewa Pajor, who finished second in the Ballon d'Or behind her recently departed teammate Alexia Putellas, had the holders in command by half-time in Denmark. Esmee Brugts, Patri Guijarro, Clara Serrajordi, Kika Nazareth and Clàudia Pina, who grabbed a brace, all scored in the second half to complete the rout.Barcelona, who won the women's club award at the Ballon d'Or to go with Pere Romeu's coach of the year prize,  remain top of the league phase with three wins from three by an aggregate score of 19-2, while despite the heavy defeat Køge remain in the playoff places.Juventusstruck twice late on to get the better ofAustria Vienna4-1. Goals by Matilde Pavan and Alba Redondo put Juve seemingly in control before Lotta Cordes reduced the deficit with 12 minutes left, but Kysha Sylla and Júlia Bartel struck in the final nine minutes. This second straight away win puts Juventus fifth, a point off the last automatic quarter-final qualification spot, while Austria Vienna sit 15th and two points off the playoffs.Paris FCandHäckenshared the spoils in the French capital after Anna Anvegard scored in the fourth minute of stoppage time to cancel out Evelyne Viens’ early opener and grab the Swedish champions their first point in Europe this season. They and Paris FC both remain outside the playoff spots.Photograph: Sebastian Elias Uth/Ritzau Scanpix DenmarkWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.This tricky game came in a testing week for City, sandwiched between last Sunday’s Manchester derby – wherethey dropped points for the first timethis season after conceding a late equaliser – and this Sunday’s mouthwatering game away to in-form London City Lionesses and theirBallon d’Or winner, Alexia Putellas, who sit just one place and three points behind them in the WSL. Nobody in sky blue could afford to think about that game yet, though – PSG were no pushovers.Straight after the restart, Fujino went close as she latched onto Kerstin Casparij’s clever ball and shot over from a tight angle. Fujino, a livewire throughout the night, also saw a shot blocked by Thiniba Samoura, as the hosts began to ask tougher questions. Soon they were creating chance after chance.Shaw’s powerful low shot was turned behind by Peda. From the resulting corner, curled in expertly by Alex Greenwood, Shaw had a free header but was unable to connect. Mary Fowler then scuffed wide as frustrations began to mount. Shaw headed wide again moments later.Surely the WSL’s top goalscorer was not going to fire a blank? Indeed not. She finally broke the deadlock after winning a spot-kick, brought down by Griedge Mbock Bathy, and then fired her penalty low to the keeper’s right. But that triggered PSG to attack with vigour for the first time in the match and they were soon level, bursting the City bubble.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueManchester City WomenParis Saint-Germain WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Premiership makes first UK move to remove Saturday 3pm broadcast blackout | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The Scottish Premiership has made the first move in a likely attempt by the UK’s domestic leagues to remove the Saturday afternoon broadcast blackout
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The Scottish Premiership has made the first move in a likely attempt by the UK’s domestic leagues to remove the Saturday afternoon broadcast blackout
Content: The Scottish Premiership is aiming to broadcast all matches from its next rights cycle from 2029.Photograph: Vagelis Georgariou/Action Plus/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Scottish Premiership is aiming to broadcast all matches from its next rights cycle from 2029.Photograph: Vagelis Georgariou/Action Plus/ShutterstockSoccerScottish Premiership makes first UK move to remove Saturday 3pm broadcast blackoutLeague to invite bids to televise all games from 2029UK leagues expected to coordinate move to end blackoutMatt HughesThu 29 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 16.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheScottish Premiershiphas made the first move in what is expected to be a coordinated attempt from the UK’s domestic leagues to remove the Saturday afternoon broadcast blackout by inviting bids to televise all of its matches in the next rights cycle from 2029.A tender document issued by the Scottish Professional Football League (SPFL) last week is understood to have given broadcasters an option to bid for live rights to all matches, including games kicking off at 3pm on Saturdays, the domestic broadcast of which is currently prohibited under Article 48 of Uefa’s statutes.The Guardian revealed last year that the Premier League and English Football League wereeager for the blackout to be liftedbecause they have concluded that selling more matches to broadcasters is the best way to raise revenues, a view that also appears to have taken hold in Scotland.The SPFL’s invitation to tender, first reported bySports Business, is understood to give bidders the flexibility to bid on the basis of the blocked hours governed by Article 48 not being in place.A source with knowledge of the tender said it appeared increasingly unlikely that the four British Football Associations would apply blocked hours in their territories after 2029.UK broadcasters are prevented from showing live football between 2.45pm and 5.15pm on Saturdays when 50% of games in the top two divisions take place during that period, a provision that means 3pm kick-offs can be broadcast on FA Cup weekends and on weekend bank holidays over Christmas.The UK is the last country in Europe to invoke Article 48, which allows associations to stipulate a period during which matches cannot be televised live in their territory.While the English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish FAs are responsible for applying Article 48, they will be guided by the wishes of the clubs.UK broadcasters can currently show up to 270 Premier League matches, 1,059 EFL games and 82 from the Scottish Premiership, amounting to 35% of fixtures across the season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Premier League chief executive, Richard Masters, said in August the subject of lifting Article 48 was a live discussion. “We’ve got to take that decision at some point in the future about whether things are going to change,” he told TalkSport. “It’s not a decision for now. It’s a decision we’ve got to make before the next set of domestic processes that the EFL and the Premier League are going to do. I’d say in about 18 months’ time we’ll come back to that decision about whether Article 48 should remain or not.”Explore more on these topicsFootballScottish PremiershipSports rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Duckett and Dawson steer England to victory over Sri Lanka in tri-series farewell | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Ben Duckett scored 167 and Liam Dawson took four wickets as England secured a consolation victory over Sri Lanka in the tri-series
Author: Taha Hashim
Headline: Ben Duckett scored 167 and Liam Dawson took four wickets as England secured a consolation victory over Sri Lanka in the tri-series
Content: England's Liam Dawson celebrates the wicket of Sri Lanka's Avishka Fernando.Photograph: KM Chaudary/APView image in fullscreenEngland's Liam Dawson celebrates the wicket of Sri Lanka's Avishka Fernando.Photograph: KM Chaudary/APCricketDuckett and Dawson steer England to victory over Sri Lanka in tri-series farewellDuckett hits superb 167 as England make 386 in LahoreDawson takes four wickets to deny Sri Lankan chaseTaha HashimThu 29 Oct 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 18.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot this time. Sri Lanka threateneda repeat of Rawalpindi, and a target of 387 in Lahore was within reach. Pavan Rathnayake was the thorn again with another century but, unlike his captain Harry Brook’s last week, Ben Duckett’s epic was not in vain. The left-hander struck 167 before Liam Dawson took four wickets, setting up a consolation 55-run victory for England.England beat Sri Lanka by 55 runs but fail to make final: men’s cricket tri-series one-day international – as it happenedRead moreSri Lanka had already booked their place in Saturday’s tri-series final against Pakistan but looked ready to take this dead rubber, too. With 87 runs required from the last 10 overs, and Rathnayake’s low hands working their magic, the game looked theirs.But England’s attack kept calm and Dawson, back for his final over, nabbed Rathnayake for 118 as the last five wickets fell in a rush. The win rounded off a bizarre tour for England who lost two seemingly unloseable games. Here, they were grateful for their left-arm spinner’s steel in another run-fest. Four for 49 in a 700-plus game is a special return.“I wasn’t getting nervy,” said Brook. “We had a clear plan and a lot of clarity at the top of the mark with the bowlers. The lads have learned a hell of a lot from that game we played a couple of days ago. To finish the game off like we did there was an exceptional effort.”Duckett was the leading man in the first half. He struggled in the 430 game, way off his best with a scratchy 29 while everyone else teed off. Move forward a week and he has two more ODI tons,105 in the low-scorer against Pakistanfollowed by a career-best. With Tom Banton punching his way to his fifth 50-plus score in six innings, the first-wicket stand was worth 163 from 25 overs. England now have a healthy problem: where does Jacob Bethell, back next month in Australia, fit into the picture? Banton taking the gloves could be an option if England want to keep this opening partnership intact, with Bethell going to the middle order.Banton will undoubtedly be peeved that he failed to turn three half-centuries in the series into at least one helmet-raising moment. He fell for 74 when his footwork went missing, dragging a Dasun Shanaka delivery on to the stumps. But Duckett, in love with Lahore, was on for the big one. He reached his third ODI hundred on this ground off 89 deliveries, and the southpaw swung freely from there, his next 50 taking only 29 balls. Middling his pull shots, Duckett eventually tired, though only after he had gone pasthis 165 against Australiaat this venue last year.View image in fullscreenBen Duckett plays a shot on his way to a rapid-fire 167 in Lahore.Photograph: Arif Ali/AFP/Getty ImagesBrook promoted himself to No 3 as England pushed towards another gargantuan total, but an errant scoop limited him to 44. Will Jacks, Jordan Cox and Sam Curran kept England moving at pace but Brook’s dismissal still felt significant, the moment that eliminated the chance of another 400. Asitha Fernando, armed with his tailing yorker, helped limit the damage with figures of two for 63, but England still made their way to the highest-ever ODI total at the Gaddafi Stadium. Joe Root was not even required.Sri Lanka had no reason to be daunted, even with an early dismissal: Sonny Baker dropped Avishka Fernando at deep fine leg but went through Kamindu Mendis not long after. Kusal Mendis’s bat split in half early on when facing Gus Atkinson, but the replacement blade worked just fine.England looked short with the ball having left out Adil Rashid once again, and Henry Crocombe was barely called upon in his second ODI. At 177 for two off 26 overs, Sri Lanka were more than well-placed on a dewy pitch.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBrook called for Root’s off-spin, a move that felt desperate but quickly worked. Kusal edged down the leg-side on 89, into the gloves of Cox, and Dawson had Shanaka leg-before three overs later after a successful review.Spin was tightening things from both ends, but Root’s third over was expensive as Janith Liyanage thumped over the on-side. Curran was handled comfortably, his moon ball punished, and Jacks was too short as Rathnayake made up for a patient start.Nonetheless, England rediscovered some composure as the game closed in. Baker had been expensive against Kusal but he prompted the removal of Liyanage on 27. Crocombe had bowled only two overs when Brook called him in for the 43rd, and Sahan Arachchige launched the newbie into the hands of the captain at long-on.Curran’s tricks began to work too, setting up the run-out of Dunith Wellalage, and Dawson returned for one final over, getting Rathnayake to lob an edge to short fine leg. Next up for England: Australia.Explore more on these topicsCricketEngland cricket teamSri Lanka cricket teammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Inter and Milan unveil plans for new shared stadium to replace San Siro | Milan | The Guardian
description: Internazionale and Milan have revealed more details about their 71,500-seat stadium which will replace San Siro as their shared home
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Internazionale and Milan have revealed more details about their 71,500-seat stadium which will replace San Siro as their shared home
Content: An image of the planned new stadium, designed by Norman Foster and David Manica, which will be built on the San Siro site.Photograph: Foster + PartnersView image in fullscreenAn image of the planned new stadium, designed by Norman Foster and David Manica, which will be built on the San Siro site.Photograph: Foster + PartnersMilanInter and Milan unveil plans for new shared stadium to replace San SiroGenerali Stadium will have 71,500-seat capacityInter fans protest the plans outside gala eventAgence France-PresseThu 29 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 18.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInternazionale and Milan have unveiled plans for their new Generali Stadium, which will replace the shared San Siro venue from the 2031-32 season.The stadium, sponsored by Generali – Italy’s largest insurance company – will have a capacity of 71,500 seats and is expected to cost the two clubs €1.2 billion (£1bn). The plans were revealed at a gala event at Milan’s Castello Sforzesco on Thursday – but some fans in attendance voiced their opposition to San Siro being demolished.Alessandro Costacurta: ‘San Siro is an icon – it’s incredibly beautiful but it’s not functional’Read moreShortly before the briefing began, a group of Inter fans walked into the courtyard of the castle and unfurled a banner reading “you will never extinguish the lights at San Siro,” and chanting “hands off San Siro.” Work on the new stadium is set to begin in 2028, on the site of the existing 75,000-capacity venue.The Generali Stadium will be shaped “low in the body, and rises up at either end” behind the goals, architect Norman Foster said. David Manica, a stadium specialist who collaborated with Foster on the project, added that the steep-sided design aims to bring fans as close to the pitch as possible.“The most important thing that we realised when we designed this project is that San Siro is a feeling,” Manica said. “It’s more than a building, it’s a feeling … we brought all the seats as close as possible to the field. They could not be any closer, it’ll actually feel as though you’re sitting on the grass.”View image in fullscreenAn artist’s impression of a concourse inside the planned 71,500-capacity arena.Photograph: Foster + PartnersThe stadium will also be capable of hosting NFL international games, rugby matches and concerts. Milan and Inter paid €197 million (£165m) to acquire the current San Siro stadium and its adjacent parking arenas. The current ground will be largely demolished once construction work nears completion.Also known as the Giuseppe Meazza Stadium, San Siro opened in 1926 and is the largest sports stadium in Italy. It is considered to be one of European football’s most iconic venues, but requires extensive modernisation despite undergoing a number of renovations during its lifespan.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Generali Stadium could be used as a venue for Euro 2032, which is being jointly hosted by Italy and Turkey. Foster and Manica previously worked together on the new Wembley Stadium, while the architect’s Foster + Partners firm also designed the plans for Manchester United’s proposed new 100,000-capacity home.Additional reporting from Associated PressExplore more on these topicsMilanInternazionaleSerie AEuropean club footballArchitecturenewsShareReuse this content

title: Uefa close to selecting candidate to run against Infantino in Fifa election | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: Uefa and its allies are close to identifying a candidate to run against Gianni Infantino in the Fifa election and could approve the challenger next week
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Uefa and its allies are close to identifying a candidate to run against Gianni Infantino in the Fifa election and could approve the challenger next week
Content: Gianni Infantino has embarked on an international effort to recover his position after the Fifa Forward Enterprise scandal.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino has embarked on an international effort to recover his position after the Fifa Forward Enterprise scandal.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersGianni InfantinoUefa close to selecting candidate to run against Infantino in Fifa electionChallenger’s identity could be approved by next weekArsène Wenger not thought to have entered reckoningExclusive byNick AmesandMatt HughesThu 29 Oct 2026 14.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 16.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUefa and its allies are close to identifying a candidate to run againstGianni Infantinoin the Fifa election and could select the challenger as early as next week.The clock is ticking on efforts to oppose Infantino in March, with candidates required to confirm they are standing by 18 November, but there is growing confidence those attempts are nearing a successful resolution. Discussions with potential nominees have gained momentum despite recent setbacks that included a U-turn by the Asian Football Confederation president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa,who surprisingly endorsed Infantino’spush for a fourth term.Should an opponent’s identity be confirmed, it will be presented to Uefa’s executive committee and in an online meeting of the confederation’s FA heads. There remains an appetite to leave any announcement until as close to the deadline as possible, largely to head off the possibility of a “dirty tricks” campaign byFifaagainst the proposed candidate, but some sources believe the relevant meetings may be called in the next seven days.Although Arsène Wenger has been among the high-profile names mooted, and is highly favoured as a potential unity candidate in some European football circles, the former Arsenal manager is not believed to have seriously entered the reckoning. Wenger, Fifa’s chief of global football development, could be found at the Fifa Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan this week extolling the virtues of his employer’s new tournament.Anyone confirming their desire to stand will have to tackle severe doubts about the prospects of defeating Infantino, who has embarkedon an international effortto recover his position in recent weeks after being heavily damaged by the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scandal. They would need to add a substantial number of votes from Asia, Concacaf and Africa to the European bloc, which itself may not be taken for granted in a secret ballot, to reach the 106 required.There has been growing cynicism in some corners about the prospects of unseating Infantino in an election, one argument being that a more effective strategy would be a mass boycott or abstention from the vote in Rabat. A view exists that this would isolate Infantino, who has never hidden the fact that his organisation is dependent on Europe for vast amounts of its revenue. Now he finds it in a form of administrative paralysis. The 2029 men’s Club World Cup, currently without a host, is among the events stuck in a deep freeze with little progress being made on its shape or location.View image in fullscreenAleksander Ceferin is a strong critic of Gianni Infantino’s actions.Photograph: Mark Pain/AlamyBut there remains a determination to face down Infantino in March, with some close to the process pointing out that events may have turned further against the Fifa president by then. Infantino faces the spectre of Uefa’s application to four courts in the US for the release of documents pertainingto the failed FFE scheme, with a view to lodging a criminal complaint in Switzerland alleging financial mismanagement. Fifa has accused Uefa of “harassment” and “misinformation” and denied wrongdoing by Infantino.A preliminary ruling is expected in the coming weeks, although the prospect of Fifa appealing against any decision that goes against it means the process may be extended. ShouldUefamake significant progress with the case, any election or candidature process may come to feel inconsequential.Fifa has until Monday, a deadline set by Uefa, to respond to 42 questions regarding its governance and decision making. Those include issues surrounding FFE, the Fifa peace prize and the suspension ofFolarin Balogun’s banat the World Cup. The Guardian understands Uefa is yet to receive any response. Infantino said last week that Fifa would “answer all the questions posed, to the extent that the process allows and to the best of our ability”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe US midterms, which will be held on Tuesday, may provide further hope for Infantino’s opponents. In July Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, launched an investigation into links between Infantino, Fifa and the Trump administration. He asked Infantino to provide relevant documents and sit for a transcribed interview, although that is yet to take place. Should the Democrats flip the House, currently controlled by the Republicans, his quest may receive fresh impetus.Regardless, the period before 18 November feels critical for Uefa and its president, Aleksander Ceferin. The Slovene has driven a hardline approach against Fifa’s leadership, which he restated in his “Emperor’s New Clothes” polemic against Infantino at the general assembly of European Football Clubs in Copenhagen last month. Fielding a viable candidate would go a long way towards underlining its credibility.A repeat of Uefa’s climbdown on the eve of the Under-20 Women’s World Cup, when it withdrew its threat to boycott the competition, would prove damaging. The extensive autumn charm offensive launched by Infantino has included visits to Latvia, Czechia and Azerbaijan.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoUefaFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win | Brazil | The Guardian
description: The trouncing of the far right provides a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: The trouncing of the far right provides a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France
Content: Lula’s win brought rapturous supporters on to the streets at home and inspired activists abroad.Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPAView image in fullscreenLula’s win brought rapturous supporters on to the streets at home and inspired activists abroad.Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPABrazilAnalysisBrazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s winJonathan WattsThe trouncing of the far right provides a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and FranceThu 29 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTShareThank you,Brazil, for demonstrating how the far right can be trounced while protection for the Amazon is strengthened. In a world where nature and democracy appeared to be bleeding out in tandem, voters and forest defenders in this global south powerhouse have shown it is possible to staunch the flow. This should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France.Lula miraculously beat the Brazilian far right and Donald Trump. But have no doubt: the region is still in peril | Jordana TimmermanRead moreThe astonishing comeback victory ofLuiz Inácio Lula da Silvain Sunday’s presidential runoff against his extreme right challenger Flavío Bolsonaro has brought oceans of rapturous supporters on to the streets, while also thrilling conservationists, climate activists and social justice campaigners across the world.Coming just weeks after the Lula administration announced arecord fallin Amazon and Cerrado destruction, they hope Brazil can now go on to achieve its target of zerodeforestation by 2030and continue to support a global transition away from fossil fuels. That would provide a huge boost to flagging global efforts to stabilise the climate and protect degraded ecosystems. It would also set a remarkable example of leadership by the global south.Big battles lie ahead. In the Amazon region itself, far-right members of Bolsonaro’s party have won the governorships of seven of the nine states and a large number of municipal mayorships. Brazil’s congress is now dominated by agribusiness and mining interests that have set the political agenda in recent years, and will push hard to allow more extractivist industries in indigenous lands, expand road-building, privatise rivers, weaken environmental protections and possibly attempt to impeach the president.In the regional sphere, Lula, alone among the leaders of main South American nations in not aligning with Donald Trump’s so-called Shield of the Americas, will face pressure from Washington to channel critical minerals and other natural resources to the US, rather than selling to China or Europe, or leaving them in the ground. And, on the planetary level, Brazil faces the threat of accelerating global heating, which is pushing the Amazon ever closer to the point of no return.View image in fullscreenIndigenous activists protesting at last year’s Cop30 summit in Brazil.Photograph: André Penner/APSo although Sunday’s result will hopefully provide a little breathing space for the Amazon and other crucially important biomes, the joy and hope that Brazil has gifted the world will quickly fade unless it inspires political change in other countries. In that sense, the biggest environmental impact of Lula’s victory may be the lessons it provides for campaigners elsewhere. Here are some initial takeaways:Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote loomsRead more1 Politics matter. There is no higher environmental priority than defeating the far right, which is a Trojan horse for extractivist – and often criminal – groups to capture states and erode protections for people, democracy and the environment. Just look at the59.5% surge of Amazon deforestationunder the 2019-2022 term of Jair Bolsonaro – the highest level of any four-year presidency in Brazil. Compare that with the 71.2% fall during the Lula administration. Over the past year, forest loss was 3,335 sq km, the lowest level since the start of satellite measurements in 1988. And Lula is not, by any means, an environmentalist. He has approved several destructive projects himself, but he is a people person who listens to the voice of social movements.2Don’t give up. Lula was largely written off by the markets and some polls after his first-round defeat. No first-round loser had ever previously come back to win the runoff. Lula was able to do so by securing an extra 10m votes over three weeks. The energy for this came from the streets and the forests. Social movements organised giant rallies in cities. In the Amazon, indigenous, riverine and quilombola groups travelled by hours – sometimes days – to reach polling stations by boats or buses.View image in fullscreenPro-Lula supporters rally in Copacabana after Lula’s first-round defeat.Photograph: Bob Karp/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock3Mobilise a campaign army. The first round of Lula’s campaign had been stodgy, old-fashioned and defensive – three traits that are also often applicable to environmental campaigns. This was transformed during the runoff, when federal deputy André Janones launched a “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp group that used humorous memes, live streams and algorithmic outreach to seize digital territory that had long been dominated by the right. By voting day, this army had 10m “soldiers”, about 8% of the electorate. Volunteers devoted hours posting stories and spreading messages across social media, speeding up the Lula campaign’s response time and emotional impact. Everyone was instructed not to share or respond to posts by the opposition camp.4Go on the offensive against US tech giants.Lula’s campaign accused Meta, which runs the Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram social media platforms, of political favouritism towards Bolsonaro in its algorithms and AI tools. Meta denied bias but acknowledged technical failures. Brazil’s electoral court ordered corrective action. Among the most popular chants of Lula supporters was “Hey Meta, vai tomar no cu!” (Hey Meta, take it up the arse!). Many on the left have blamed US social media platforms for spreading rightwing disinformation and fearmongering, causing recent electoral defeats inColombia, Chile and Peru. Lula made clear that would not be allowed in Brazil: “We had to overcome foreign interference through digital platforms, which we will have to regulate. We cannot have a monstrously large corporation earning millions and billions paying no taxes to this country and trying to steer our election results.”View image in fullscreenA Lula supporter holds up a mask of Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg at a protest over alleged electoral interference outside the firm’s São Paulo headquarters.Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty Images5Reclaim the flag. Brazil’s green, yellow and blue national colours had been associated with Bolsonaro’s movement in previous elections. This time, Lula seized it back by posing in a national football team strip while his “army” launched a campaign called “The green and yellow is ours”. Before voting day, millions of people across Brazil and the world – from Indigenous leaders in the Amazon to Hollywood celebrities and European football stars – flooded social networks with images of themselves in Brazil colours making an L (for Lula) sign with their thumb and little finger extended.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro arriving in Florida after losing to Lula.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images6Increase social spending. Amazon protection may have galvanised conservationists, but the far greater motivations for many Lula voters were record low unemployment, robust wage growth, a 15% increase in “bolsa familia” poverty relief payments and a promise to raise the minimum wage. The importance of combining social justice with climate and nature action is widely recognised by Brazilian environmental groups. Without it, elections are lost and protests can erupt in the streets – as the world learned from France during the violentgilets jaunes(yellow vests)demonstrations of 2018.7Defend sovereignty, democracy and sustainability. Lula and his army called out the interlinked threats posed by the Bolsonaro family’s fealty to Donald Trump (now doubly confirmed by Flávio’s post-election flight to the US). They highlighted the interlinked threats posed by the obsequience to Trump, Bolsonaro’s desire to change the constitution and his promise to open up exploration of the Amazon and other biomes. This reflects a global phenomenon. Now that seven of theplanetary boundariesessential for the flourishing of life have been breached, more and more people are affected by business activities that make the situation worse by destabilising the climate, damaging ecosystems and polluting the air, soil and rivers. This makes it harder for extractive companies to secure a social mandate so they become more inclined to either break the law or support extreme politics that override democracy.The former environment minister Marina Silva pulled these threads together during the victory celebrations, saying Brazil had come together against these threats: “Long live the people who emerged from every corner of Brazil to sow hope for a future that is socially just, sovereign, democratic and sustainable.”Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action. Now it needs others to follow.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmazon rainforestEnvironmental activismDeforestationLand rightsTrees and forestsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand’s wife tells court he is ‘amazingly attentive husband’ | UK news | The Guardian
description: Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand says couple previously split up over his promiscuity
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand says couple previously split up over his promiscuity
Content: Russell and Laura Brand arrive at Southwark crown court on Thursday.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreenRussell and Laura Brand arrive at Southwark crown court on Thursday.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersUK newsRussell Brand’s wife tells court he is ‘amazingly attentive husband’Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand says couple previously split up over his promiscuityEmine SinmazThu 29 Oct 2026 09.12 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand’s wife has told a court that they previously split up over his promiscuity but that he was a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband”.Giving evidence at her husband’s rape trial, Laura Brand, 39, said they fell in love after meeting in 2006 but that the comedian found monogamy difficult.“I wasn’t interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people,” she said.Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.Giving evidence at Southwark crown court on Wednesday, Laura told the court she met Brand at the Edinburgh festival in 2006 after his show Shame, which was “very, very, very funny”, “extremely entertaining” and sexually explicit.She said they met in the foyer of the Assembly Rooms, where Brand complimented her friend, who had a boyfriend. Laura recalled: “And he said to me: ‘But tell me you don’t have a boyfriend,’ and I said: ‘No, I don’t.’”Laura recalled that Brand contacted her the next day and they had oral sex. Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked: “Did he want to have penetrative sex?” to which Laura replied: “I didn’t want to, but I don’t remember it even being a topic. I didn’t intend to and I don’t remember him asking.”They began dating in September 2006 and Brand “absolutely” respected her wishes sexually, Laura said. Describing his treatment of her, she said: “Very caring, totally at my pace. I was not experienced, I had only had one partner before Russell and I felt entirely cared for, and looked after by Russell.”But the court heard their relationship broke down over his cheating. Winter asked: “Did you become aware shortly thereafter that he was promiscuous and engaging in sexual activity with others?” Laura replied: “I was aware when I met him that he liked women and I was aware towards the latter part of that year that he was engaging with other women, yes.”Laura said the couple split up in February 2007 because of his infidelity. “I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous. We talked about it. I did find that difficult,” she said.Laura said she was “heartbroken” after the breakup but that the pair resumed contact as friends in summer 2007. She said she became friendly again with Brand when his marriage to the US pop star Katy Perry ended, and that they restarted their relationship in 2015, married two years later, and now have three children together.When asked if she was aware of Brand’s promiscuity during their time apart, Laura said: “I was very aware of it and I would read about it regularly in the papers and he also told me; we talked about it.”Both the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, and the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, objected when Winter asked Laura what her view was “as to the truth” of the criminal allegations her husband faces.“She’s not here as an expert witness,” the judge said.Winter then asked Laura to describe Brand, to which she replied: “Russell, my husband, is caring, he’s kind, he’s a wonderful father to our children, he’s an amazingly attentive husband.“He’s got an eye for detail I’ve never known before. The way he treats me is to really know me, I feel very seen by him, in a way I’ve never experienced before. I love him very much.”She continued: “We have a very frank, honest and clear relationship and marriage. It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest.”In cross-examination, Karmy-Jones noted that Laura had been present throughout most of the trial and had taken notes. She also challenged Laura about how much contact she had had with Brand after their break up in 2007.Laura said she had spoken to Brand after his marriage to Perry ended. “He called me after his marriage and gifted me meditation for me and my boyfriend at the time,” she said.Brand nodded and smiled as Laura insisted that while they had not had a sexual relationship in the years before they got back together in 2015, they had spent time together by going to the theatre and watching TV box sets.The prosecutor said that in 2017, shortly after the couple had their first child, Brand was a guest on the US talkshow, The Wendy Williams Show. She said the comedian had said of his relationship with Laura: “When we went out with each other we loved each other very much but I was in a phase where I thought the world was an amusement park made out of orgasms.”Laura replied: “I’m not denying he said that. I probably didn’t watch it.”Earlier, statements from two of Brand’s ex-girlfriends were read to the court, as they gave good accounts of his character. They also said he had cheated on them and they had supported him financially.Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Visit Norway makes shithouses ‘great again’ after Trump insult | Norway | The Guardian
description: Tourist board responds with toilet humour after US president’s ‘shithouse country’ jibe over failure to win Nobel peace prize
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Tourist board responds with toilet humour after US president’s ‘shithouse country’ jibe over failure to win Nobel peace prize
Content: A still from Visit Norway’s list of great toilets.Photograph: Visit NorwayView image in fullscreenA still from Visit Norway’s list of great toilets.Photograph: Visit NorwayNorwayVisit Norway makes shithouses ‘great again’ after Trump insultTourist board responds with toilet humour after US president’s ‘shithouse country’ jibe over failure to win Nobel peace prizeJon HenleyEurope correspondentThu 29 Oct 2026 13.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome might find it decidedly incommodious to be dumped on byDonald Trumpas a “shithouse country”. Not the Norwegian tourist board, which chose instead to lift the lid on some of the nation’s loveliest lavatories.“Are these the world’s best shit houses?” askedVisit Norway on its website, days after the US president vented his fury once more over failing to win the Nobel peace prize by describing Norway as a “shithouse country” at a rally on Sunday.“Norway makes shit houses great again!” the agency continued above pictures of some of the country’s most striking public conveniences, adding: “These toilets are worth a visit, both when you really have to go – and when you don’t.”View image in fullscreenAt Ostasteidn in Ryfylke, the restroom is designed so that moss will start to grow on the outer walls, like camouflage.Photograph: Vist NorwayTrump delivered his tirade at a rally in Michigan days before the US midterm elections. “Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a shithouse country, actually,” he declared, using a term he has previously applied to Haiti, ​Libya, Somalia and Yemen.He added that he would welcome migrants from some countries but not Norway, “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize”. Earlier this month,Trump denouncedthe decision to award the prize to Navi Pillay, a former ⁠international criminal court judge.“This is an indelible stain on the ‌country ⁠of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” he said. “I never heard of this person. The ⁠Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited … And we will ​not forget, Norway.”Along 18 designated scenic routes around Norway, Visit Norway said, leading architects had been tasked with transforming the humble wayside privy into an attraction in its own right. Several have since won international architecture awards.View image in fullscreenA toilet at Allmannajuvet in Sauda, Norway.Photograph: Andreas Solbakken/Vist NorwayThe agency pictured a series of designer public conveniences, many of them architecturally striking and all offering breathtaking vistas overlooking fjords, beside rushing rivers and foaming waterfalls, and at stunning scenic viewpoints.They “invite you to take your time and enjoy the scenery, even if you don’t have any business to take care of”, Visit Norway said, highlighting – among others – the restrooms at the Stegastein viewpoint in the Sognefjord region of western Norway.This particular comfort station, the tourist board noted with uninhibited pride, had been ranked amongthe 10 best public toilets in the worldby DesignCurial, the online architecture, design and interiors magazine.Combining clean, minimalist lines with the fjord’s rugged and brooding landscape, the loos are famous for their large, black-tinted glass windows, which allow visitors a sweeping view from the throne while remaining invisible from the outside.View image in fullscreenThe ‘golden toilet’ at Ersfjordstranda in Senja.Photograph: Hugo Fagermo/Foto: Hugo FagermoIt also highlighted the unique, wave-shaped Ureddplassen loo on the wild coast of Helgeland, the southernmost district of northern Norway, hailed by several international publications as the most scenic restroom in the world.Also featured are the solar-powered modernist bog at the Utsikten viewpoint, the “Instagram-worthy” Tungeneset loo (“looks pretty good underneath the northern lights”), and the world-famous triangular “golden toilet” on Senja island.Jens Kjeldsen, a rhetoric professor at the University of Bergen, said that under the circumstances, Visit Norway’s response was well judged. “It’s like the bully in kindergarten,”he told NRK public television. “If you get too serious, the bully wins.”View image in fullscreenUredd Rest Area (Ureddplassen) on the Helgeland coast.Photograph: Steinar Skaar/Steinar Skaar, Statens vegvesenEvgenia Egorova, a senior consultant at Visit Norway, told the broadcaster the response to its social media fightback had been immense. “The world needs a little laugh,” she said. “We thought: let’s meet them with kindness, and a little humour.”Visit Norway said it had more stylish loos in the pipeline, including a forest-inspired latrine using dried wood from more than 60 trees. “Get ready for the pit stop of your life,” it urged, before signing off with a cheery: “Toodeloo!”The Nobel peace prize is famously not awarded by the nation or even the government of Norway, but by the Nobel prize committee, which operates independently – something Trump “knows very well”, the foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said. “We have reminded him of that, in case anyone is wondering.”View image in fullscreenThe toilet at Eggum in Lofoten is built as an amphitheatre underneath the ruins of a German radar station.Photograph: Jarle Wæhler (jw), TuristvegExplore more on these topicsNorwayDonald TrumpTrump administrationNobel peace prizeEuropeShareReuse this content

title: Sara won a prized place to study medicine in Glasgow. Why is the Home Office blocking her? | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: After fleeing an abusive father, the Taliban and an enforced marriage, Sara got a place to study medicine at the University of Glasgow. So why has her visa been blocked?
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: After fleeing an abusive father, the Taliban and an enforced marriage, Sara got a place to study medicine at the University of Glasgow. So why has her visa been blocked?
Content: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood.Composite: Guardian Design; Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock; Wahidullah Kakar/APView image in fullscreenHome Secretary Shabana Mahmood.Composite: Guardian Design; Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock; Wahidullah Kakar/APImmigration and asylumSara won a prized place to study medicine in Glasgow. Why is the Home Office blocking her?She fought every obstacle in Afghanistan to pursue her dream of becoming a doctor – fleeing her abusive father and the Taliban. But this talented, tenacious student has now been denied a visa, for contradictory reasons, three timesDiane TaylorThu 29 Oct 2026 14.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the last decade, Sara (not her real name), 25, has dreamed of becoming a doctor. She secured a highly sought after place to study medicine at Kabul University in February 2021, but in a matter of months theTalibanreturned to power and imposed a ban on women studying for degrees. Sara had been searching for other options. Then the University of Glasgow offered her a lifeline.Her visa application was made just days before the Home Office introduced avisa brakein March 2026 for students from Afghanistan, Sudan, Myanmar and Cameroon. Her teachers consider her to be an exceptionally able and dedicated student, she had secured funding and the university was waiting to welcome her on to a gateway course at its school of medicine, dentistry and nursing – a route to a full degree course to become a doctor. So why have the UK’s home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, and her officials gone to such extraordinary lengths to bar her?View image in fullscreen‘Challenge after challenge’ … Sara still wants a career in medicine.Photograph: Supplied imageSara says her life has been “challenge after challenge”. She survived a suicide bomb attack on her school, swerved her father’s attempts to force her into early marriage, as well as the omnipresent Taliban who patrol Kabul’s streets. Then she made a nail-biting escape from her country and avoided capture by police in Pakistan who were searching for her. But it is the UK’sHome Office, which champions women’s rights, that has inflicted the deadliest blow.Sara grew up in a poor household in Kabul in the period before the Taliban regained power. Against the wishes of her violent father, who wanted to see her follow the traditional path of teenage marriage and a life of enforced domesticity in service to a husband, she fought to continue her education, encouraged to aim high by inspirational female teachers at her single-sex school.“The community I come from is a particularly traditional one,” she says. “Even among my relatives I couldn’t find any girl who has been educated. While boys were free, my mum, who has always supported me, was told by relatives that rather than pursuing an education I needed to go somewhere where I could be taught to cook. After a relative’s daughter got married I was told I was next in line.”But at school, she saw that life could be different. “I was about seven years old when one of my teachers first encouraged us girls,” she says. “Later, my physics teacher was also very supportive. She said that we would face challenges but should never give up in pursuing our dreams.”View image in fullscreenTaliban soldiers in Mazar-e-Sharif, 2023.Photograph: EPASara says that she is still in contact with some of the girls she was at school with, who were similarly inspired by their female teachers. Some of them are now flying high in other countries, having been granted full university scholarships.But there were others whose ambitions were thwarted. “I can still see the face of one 15-year-old girl who was like a supportive older sister to me at school. She wanted to continue her education but she was full of tears when she came to school one day and told us her family was forcing her to leave school and get married.”When Sara was 15, a much-loved uncle died after his heart disease was misdiagnosed. At that moment, she vowed to become a doctor. “My uncle was such a kind soul. He always supported me when my father was being harsh. ‘It’s OK. Whatever your father is doing, I’m with you,’ he used to say to me.”Sara always put everything into her studies at school, getting marks close to 100% in her tests and exams. Along with her love of science, she speaks multiple languages. She is Hazara and along with Hazaragi speaks Dari, Pashto, Urdu, English, as well as some Spanish and Arabic.Somehow, despite her father’s disapproval, she continued her studies and attended an educational centre to prepare for Afghanistan’s university entrance exam, the Kankor, so she could secure a place at Kabul University to begin her medical studies. In October 2020, it was targeted by a Taliban suicide bomb attack. She was feeling unwell that day so did not go to school. Many of her friends were killed.Against the odds, in February 2021,she passed her exam, secured her place at the Kabul University’s medical school, and was overjoyed – until she and other women at the university had their right to study brutally terminated when the Taliban came to power in August 2021.Devastated, but undeterred from pursuing her dream, she began volunteering at medical clinics in Kabul, taken there and back by clinical staff who supported her, ducking down and hiding in the car when they approached Taliban checkpoints. When Taliban members came to the clinic for treatment, she was bundled into the staff room to hide until they had left. She continued her medical studies at home, begging friends who were studying to send her PDFs of medical textbooks because she couldn’t afford to buy them. She devoured the medical bible Gray’s Anatomy.Despite the Taliban obstacle, she was determined to keep studying any way she could. “I was at the clinic one day in 2023. I wasn’t allowed to perform medical procedures on patients but wanted to learn as much as I could. I asked a friend to teach me how to do sutures and then practised the technique on a banana. The head surgeon came in and asked what we were doing, saw how enthusiastic I was and allowed me to observe an operation.”By 2024, life at home with her father was becoming increasingly violent and dangerous and the pressure on Sara to marry was increasing. “The situation was deteriorating so much that we had to find a way to get out,” she says.Sara hoped she could pursue her medical studies in Pakistan, so before she left Afghanistan she went to the medical school in Kabul to try to get her course records to prove that she had started a medical degree. “Taliban guards wouldn’t let me through the front gate and were very abusive to me so I couldn’t get them,” she says.View image in fullscreenAn Afghan student walks in front of the Kabul University in 2022.Photograph: Ali Khara/ReutersSara was later able to get a reference from one of her lecturers at the university which described her as a “highly dedicated and capable student.”“She demonstrated strong academic performance, critical thinking and a deep passion for medicine. She is a resilient, compassionate and motivated individual,” the lecturer said.Sara, her mother, her siblings and other relatives had to leave Afghanistan in a hurry when things reached crisis point with her father. “I could only pack a few clothes,” she says. “But I took my white medical coat with me, hoping that even if I was unable to continue my medical studies in Afghanistan, I would be able to qualify to be a doctor somewhere else.”The family managed to get together the money to escape to Pakistan by plane. Their cover story was that Sara’s mother needed urgent medical treatment. Their male escort was Sara’s brother-in-law. At Kabul Airport, they were stopped by the Taliban and taken into a room for questioning.“We arrived at the airport at 12.30pm for a 2pm flight. We were questioned in that room until 1.50pm. My hands were shaking so much. I didn’t think they would let us go. They wanted to know why my father was not accompanying us to Pakistan. When they finally released us at 1.50pm, we all had to run to make it on to the plane before it took off. When we sat on the plane my mum said to us; ‘Our life is full of challenges. If we overcome one, another one comes.’”Life in Pakistan was not much better. The family overstayed their visa because they had nowhere else to run to and Sara was unable to continue her medical studies. “Sometimes the police came to look for us at the place where we were staying. I hid in the kitchen cupboard when they knocked on our door so they wouldn’t find me,” she says.A London-based English teacher, Jane Conway, became another lifeline. She taught English to refugee students and became involved in a group called Save AfghanWomen. After the Taliban regained power, Conway helped with online English classes for women no longer able to physically study in Afghanistan, and got to know Sara and other members of her family who she supported as they continued their higher education.It was Conway who found that the University of Glasgow had a gateway course for female students from Afghanistan who wanted to pursue a degree in medicine, and helped her apply. “It was teacher Jane who found this option for me,” says Sara.She applied for the scheme and was accepted after finding, with Conway’s help, sources of funding to support her with bursaries to cover fees and living expenses. Hope was restored. All she needed now was for the Home Office to grant her a visa to take up the course in Glasgow. She thought that after everything she had been through this would be the easy bit. But three rejections citing contradictory reasons followed.She was told in one rejection that the Home Office was satisfied she had appropriate funds in place to support her study in the UK although they deemed her not to be a genuine student. She cried and cried at that accusation, after all the years of doing everything possible to pursue her medical studies. “I would like to ask the home secretary what is her definition of a ‘genuine student?’ I wish I had the opportunity to visit her in person and ask her this question face to face, eye to eye.”View image in fullscreenWomen chant slogans and hold placards during a women’s rights protest in Kabul, 2021.Photograph: Bülent Kılıç/AFP/Getty ImagesThen, in another refusal, they said she didn’t have suitable funds in place, but accepted she was a genuine student.Sara underwent a phone interview with a Home Office official. “The interview was very tough. It lasted about an hour and a half and the man asked me lots of questions about my mother, my father, my background. After the interview he told me to keep checking my email and I was hopeful I was going to be granted a visa.”But once again her hopes were dashed. She is now pursuing a degree in accounting and finance in another country, undisclosed for safety reasons, because it is more affordable than a medical course. “I don’t have any other option,” she says.In London, Conway despairs about the inconsistent decision making by the Home Office. “Sara is a good and wonderful person who wants to do good in the world,” she says. “It would seem that the Home Office is so obsessive in its target seeking that it has become blinded to exceptional cases like Sara’s, denying the UK of the benefits that such motivated and talented people could bring.“In spite of all the obstacles Sara encountered pursuing her dream to become a doctor, she never gave up. Then, when that wonderful new door of opportunity was opened up to her by the University of Glasgow, instead of walking through it with hope and excitement, it is our British Home Office that unequivocally slams the door shut in her path. I feel a deep shame that the government is cutting off a life-changing opportunity for a truly exceptional person, who has already been persecuted in her own country simply for being a woman.”double quotation markMy goal is to inspire other Afghan girls to pursue education and overcome the obstacles in their livesOn 28 September, Mahmood delighted the audience at the Labour party conference by announcing she was reactivating a refugee resettlement route, albeit a small one, highlighting Afghan women and girls as one of the groups who would benefit. Itlater emergedthat there will be significant restrictions to the scheme for some eligible nationalities (it is only open to Palestinian refugees who have already escaped Gaza and are registered as refugees with the UN, for instance), while the much larger refugee family reunion schemeremains suspendedafter more than a year.Sara refuses to give up on her dream of qualifying to become a doctor. She tries to keep up with the latest scientific developments in medicine.View image in fullscreenAfghan amputees at a hospital in Jalalabad, Afghanistan.Photograph: Noorullah Shirzada/AFP/Getty Images“In Afghanistan, so many people don’t have arms or legs because of all the fighting,” she says. “If I can qualify as a doctor I would like to help people in my country. My ambition is to become a cardiac surgeon because as far as I know there are no female cardiac surgeons in Afghanistan and I would like to be the first.” If she achieves this, she says, “my goal is to use my experiences to inspire other Afghan girls to pursue education and overcome the obstacles in their lives”.If she can’t ever return to her country, she wants to work with Doctors Without Borders. “They work with people in difficult-to-reach places. I believe that people in those places deserve to have a good doctor to treat them. From my perspective, doctors are superheroes. They are the best for people. Whatever happens, I will always keep my white coat with me. It is the history of my struggle.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeAfghanistanTalibanWomenAccess to universityMedicinefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why jet lag throws even foraging seabirds off course | Science | The Guardian
description: Oxford study shows Manx shearwaters lose direction when their body clocks get out of sync
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Oxford study shows Manx shearwaters lose direction when their body clocks get out of sync
Content: Manx shearwaters spend most of their lives at sea and navigate using the sun.Photograph: George Reszeter/AlamyView image in fullscreenManx shearwaters spend most of their lives at sea and navigate using the sun.Photograph: George Reszeter/AlamyScienceWhy jet lag throws even foraging seabirds off courseOxford study shows Manx shearwaters lose direction when their body clocks get out of syncHanad AhmedThu 29 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 16.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeabirds returning from foraging trips can be thrown hundreds of miles off course by a form of jet lag that arises when their body clocks get out of sync with local time, researchers say.Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.The impact was limited on adult shearwaters because the birds were able to correct their bearings in flight. At most, the birds veered off course by about 15 degrees. After correcting their course, this added only an estimated 3 miles to a 600-mile journey.But less experienced birds were likely to have a tougher time, the study found, with first-time foragers at risk of flying off course by hundreds of miles.Most studies on birds’ biological clocks have been conducted under laboratory conditions but Dr Patrick Lewin, a behavioural and sensory ecologist at theUniversity of Oxford, set out to investigate wild birds with the help of his colleagues.Their analysis of 20 years of GPS tracking data revealed a clear effect when the Manx shearwaters flew east across lines of longitude as they returned home, leading their clocks to run up to an hour or so behind local time. “The bird’s internal clock can be subject to a jet lag phenomenon, manifesting as birds flying off course,” Lewin said.Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. Because the sun moves across the sky as the Earth rotates, reading its position correctly relies on the birds adjusting their heading relative to the sun, using their body clock to keep track of the time of day. Sunset and sunrise keep the bird’s body clock in sync, helping them adjust to changes in local time.Writing inScience, Lewin said the mismatch between local time and the birds’ internal clocks could make them drift off course when the sun lay farther around the sky than expected. Surprisingly, the errors remained when birds followed the coastline, where landmarks could have guided them, further supporting the idea that the sun plays a central role in anchoring their sense of direction.“For adult shearwaters, this lag has very limited impact on their overall journey, with errors adding a calculated 5km to a 1,000km journey,” Lewin said. “However, for first-time migrant birds, such orientation shifts due to sun compass errors could result in deviations of hundreds of kilometres as they lack a map sense to help reorient them when they lose their way.”Prof Richard Holland of Bangor University, who was not involved in the study, said it was a significant finding: “It seems to confirm in wild animals what more controlled experimental studies have shown: reliance on the sun compass for animals that move during the day, even when it is not accurate.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionManx shearwaters spend most of their lives far out at sea. They cover enormous distances but return each year to islands off the west coast of the UK to breed in burrows.“It’s not clear from the study what the consequences of these errors are, since the birds return to their colony and the errors are small,” Holland said. “Nonetheless, it highlights the importance of understanding the role of biological rhythms across multiple contexts in animal behaviour, as more and more we are starting to realise just how important these are for numerous biological functions.”Explore more on these topicsScienceAnimal behaviourWildlifeBirdsMarine lifeUniversity of OxfordnewsShareReuse this content

title: A new wave of electric ferries is here in the US. Some even fly | US news | The Guardian
description: Replacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air quality
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Replacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air quality
Content: An electric ferry in New York.Photograph: Climate CentralView image in fullscreenAn electric ferry in New York.Photograph: Climate CentralThe alternativesUS newsA new wave of electric ferries is here in the US. Some even flyReplacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air qualityBen Tracy of Climate CentralThu 29 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCutting through New York Harbor in the shadow of the Statue of Liberty, the small white boat we were riding on caught the attention of passengers aboard a nearby sightseeing ferry.“It’s quite a curiosity at the moment,” Eric Laakmann, the chief executive and co-founder of Vessev, said.His company builds fully electric hydrofoil boats. These vessels use underwater “wings” to lift their hulls above the surface as they pick up speed. By raising the boat out of the water, the design dramatically reduces drag, one of the biggest obstacles to making boats more energy-efficient.“We’re picking up speed. We’re going for a takeoff,” Laakmann said as the boat rapidly accelerated.The hydrofoils lifted the hull about a foot and a half above the water. Almost immediately, the ride transformed. The familiar slap of the boat pushing through waves became a smooth, almost airborne glide.How hydrofoils make electric boats ‘viable’The hydrofoil effect is more than a novelty. Water creates significant resistance, and overcoming it takes energy. Electrifying boats is a challenge because batteries are heavy, and that extra weight increases the power needed to move the vessel. Hydrofoils may offer a solution. By lifting much of the hull out of the water, they reduce drag, allowing a vessel to move more efficiently.“We substantially reduce the drag that you feel and that’s really what makes electrification viable,” Laakmann said.Vessev says its hydrofoil design cuts drag by about 66%. That greater efficiency allows the boats to carry smaller battery packs, reducing both weight and cost.But efficiency is only part of the equation. Making a boat electric is not simply a matter of replacing a diesel engine with a motor and battery. Operators must also consider how far a vessel needs to travel, how many passengers it carries, how quickly it must recharge, and how much weight it can accommodate.From novelty to everyday transportVessev operates passenger services in New Zealand and is expanding to Australia. In the US, its first service is planned for Lake Tahoe. Laakmann sees a future in which electric vessels become a routine part of public transportation, rather than a niche attraction.“More like subways, more like buses, more like Ubers, more like taxis but on the water,” he said.Waterways can connect communities and move passengers without adding more vehicles to crowded roads. When powered by increasingly clean electricity, electric ferries can also cut the pollution associated with diesel engines.Transportation remains the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States, according to federal environmental data. Road vehicles account for much of that pollution, but ships and other watercraft also burn fossil fuels. Replacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air quality around busy waterfronts.Vessev is not alone in pursuing the technology. In Stockholm, commuters are already riding electric hydrofoil ferries built by the Swedish company Candela. The company says its design can reduce energy use by as much as 80% compared with conventional vessels of a similar type. Norway has ordered 20 of its electric hydrofoil boats for coastal service.For ferry operators, the attraction is not simply environmental. More efficient designs and advances in battery technology are opening up routes for electric boats that might once have been impractical. There is also the potential for lower operating costs as fuel prices soar.“I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Laakmann said.San Francisco prepares to plug inIn San Francisco, the city’s largest ferry operator carries about 3.5 million passengers a year, according to Seamus Murphy, who leads the agency. The network serves a region shaped by water, with commuters relying on boats to cross the bay and reach the city.“We have a lot of waterfront,” Murphy said.Yet the fleet runs entirely on fossil fuels. All 18 vessels in the system are powered by diesel. That is set to change as the agency prepares to add four battery-powered ferries over the next two years. It is part of an electric overhaul worth about half a billion dollars that also includes charging infrastructure at docks.Unlike a car that can be plugged in at home overnight, a ferry may need to complete repeated trips on a fixed timetable. Its batteries must provide enough energy for the route, while shore-side chargers deliver enough power during the time the vessel spends at the terminal.Making that work requires more than the right boat. Operators must coordinate vessel range, timetables and charging capacity to keep passengers moving without disrupting service. San Francisco won’t initially be using hydrofoil boats, but the agency says its new vessels will make it the first ferry operator in the United States to run high-speed, all-electric ferries.The economics of going electricFor transit agencies, climate goals alone rarely justify a major fleet overhaul. The numbers have to add up.Battery-powered ferries generally require a larger initial investment in vessels and charging equipment. But electric motors can be more efficient than diesel engines, and operators may save money over time on fuel and maintenance. Murphy said rising diesel costs and improvements in battery technology strengthened the case for making the switch.“You make the upfront investment at the beginning and then you save over time and at the end of the day you’re going to have lower costs in the long term,” he said.The financial case depends a lot on the route. Batteries remain heavy and expensive, charging infrastructure can be costly, and not every route is suited to a fully electric vessel. Long distances, tight schedules and limited opportunities to recharge can all complicate the transition.The shift could create opportunities well beyond the water. For San Francisco’s expansion, the boats and their batteries are being built in the United States. This could create opportunities for domestic manufacturing jobs.For Murphy, the transition is a chance to cut pollution while helping develop new business for shipbuilders and battery manufacturers.“These jobs are going to get created in other countries and we have an ability to create them here if we manage this in the right way,” Murphy said. “We don’t want to be left behind,” he added.Climate Centralis an independent group of scientists and communicators who research and report the facts about our changing climate and how it affects people’s lives.Explore more on these topicsUS newsThe alternativesElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsGreenhouse gas emissionsFerry travelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Queen of Spain butterfly invades Britain – but will it become native? | Butterflies | The Guardian
description: This year thousands of the golden-coloured butterfly have arrived in Britain in what one expert calls ‘a bold attempt at colonisation’
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: This year thousands of the golden-coloured butterfly have arrived in Britain in what one expert calls ‘a bold attempt at colonisation’
Content: The Queen of Spain could finally conquer Britain once and for all.Photograph: imageBROKER/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Queen of Spain could finally conquer Britain once and for all.Photograph: imageBROKER/AlamyButterflywatchButterfliesQueen of Spain butterfly invades Britain – but will it become native?This year thousands of the golden-coloured butterfly have arrived in Britain in what one expert calls ‘a bold attempt at colonisation’Patrick BarkhamThu 29 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Queen of Spain has invaded. The enigmatic British visits of this gorgeous golden-coloured butterfly with distinctively shaped, squared-off hindwings have been recorded by lepidopterists for four centuries. Usually there are barely a handful of sightings each summer of a butterfly that is widespread across continental Europe.This year, thousands have flown in, some from France and Spain that have reached the south coast, and others from the Netherlands, which have fluttered into East Anglia.These migrants have bred, and British-born offspring have emerged this autumn. Last week, hundreds were spotted at East Tilbury and Linford beside the Thames in Essex.“It’s a bold attempt at the colonisation of the UK,” says butterfly expert Neil Hulme. “The numbers that have poured into the UK has been phenomenal.”Will the Queen of Spain become Britain’s 61st native species? It has probably only successfully overwintered here twice in the last 30 years, at Minsmere in Suffolk in the 1990s, and close to Chichester around 2010.But Hulme is certain that so many arrivals will mean some butterflies will be seen in Britain again next spring. “That’s not necessarily the same as a permanent establishment, but it could gain a foothold with regular top-ups from continental Europe,” he says.Butterfly-lovers can plant wild and field pansies – its caterpillar’s preferred food plant – to hopefully help this regal arrival conquer Britain once and for all.Explore more on these topicsButterfliesButterflywatchInsectsAnimalsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Eight of England’s nine water companies still failing on environment, report finds | Water industry | The Guardian
description: Angela Eagle tells industry ‘people are sick of excuses’ as pollution levels remain high despite billions in investment
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: Angela Eagle tells industry ‘people are sick of excuses’ as pollution levels remain high despite billions in investment
Content: Thames Water’s Mogden sewage treatment works in west London. The company had the most pollution incidents among providers in England.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenThames Water’s Mogden sewage treatment works in west London. The company had the most pollution incidents among providers in England.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersWater industryEight of England’s nine water companies still failing on environment, report findsAngela Eagle tells industry ‘people are sick of excuses’ as pollution levels remain high despite billions in investmentDamien GayleThu 29 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAngela Eagle, the environment secretary, has summoned water industry bosses to Whitehall after a report found that the environmental performance of the big companies has worsened despite investment.“People are sick of excuses,” Dame Angela said, after theEnvironment Agencyjoined the Drinking Water Inspectorate, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat for a joint report that rated eight of the nine water companies in England as “poor” or “requiring improvement”.There were 74 serious pollution incidents, the category that causes significant harm to the environment, the report said. That was just one fewer than the previous year, despite billions of pounds of investment, bans on bosses’ bonuses and a public outcry. The watchdog’s environmental performance assessment ratings of water companies added up to 16 “stars” out of a possible 36, a fall from 19 the previous year, and the lowest score since the process began.View image in fullscreenAngela Eagle, the environment secretary, said the public were sick of excuses from the water industry.Photograph: Zeynep Demir Aslim/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockChanges could be imposed on the industry, Eagle warned: “Water companies have let the public down time and time again, and today’s report is further proof that root-and-branch reform cannot wait.”The UK is one of only two countries in the world where the provision of water is fully privatised. The other is Chile, where water privatisation was imposed in the 1980s by a military dictatorship.Overall, there were 2,666 pollution incidents in England in 2025 – a 40% increase on 2016, the EA said. Thames Water had the most, followed by Anglian Water, United Utilities, Yorkshire Water and Southern Water.How might Andy Burnham tackle Thames Water debacle?Read moreThe Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Eagle was preparing to take “further action”, with “tougher consequences” for executives at failing companies.Defra said it would “set out a clear set of improvement actions”, such as “tackling leakage”, “reductions in pollution incidents” and “improving customer satisfaction”. Rules that took effect last year would block bonuses for executives at companies receiving a one-star rating.Environmental campaigners called for stronger action. “This is a system that rewards shareholders and creditors while our rivers, wildlife and bill payers lose out,” said James Wallace, the chief executive of River Action.Thames Water, the worst offender, ought to go into special administration immediately, he said. “Ministers must end the failed privatisation experiment, review alternative models including public ownership, and give regulators the power to make polluters pay not the public.”The four agencies have pooled their data in a joint report for the first time – a step towards combining currently fragmented regulatory responsibilities under a single watchdog. But Richard Benwell, the chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said a new regulator “must be more than a merger of existing institutions”.UK government to make unprecedented intervention in setting of water billsRead more“It needs a clear legal duty to restore nature, strong environmental targets and the powers and resources to enforce the law across the water industry, industrial agriculture, and chemical companies,” he said.Water UK, the industry trade body, said: “Today’s report shows the lowest level of leakage in history, as well as other areas of good performance.
