However, the fact remains that the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough.“While more than half of all pollution incidents last year were caused by blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies, there is clearly more work to do.“It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth and end sewage entering rivers and seas.”Explore more on these topicsWater industryEnvironment AgencyPollutionAngela EagleLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: HMRC puts 200 billionaires on UK tax crackdown hitlist | The super-rich | The Guardian
description: ‘Compliance managers’ to have discussions with authority’s wealthiest customers in attempt to raise tax revenues
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: ‘Compliance managers’ to have discussions with authority’s wealthiest customers in attempt to raise tax revenues
Content: HMRC is aiming to pin down the complex tax affairs of billionaires required to pay tax in the UK.Photograph: Rosemary Roberts/AlamyView image in fullscreenHMRC is aiming to pin down the complex tax affairs of billionaires required to pay tax in the UK.Photograph: Rosemary Roberts/AlamyThe super-richHMRC puts 200 billionaires on UK tax crackdown hitlist‘Compliance managers’ to have discussions with authority’s wealthiest customers in attempt to raise tax revenuesBusiness live – latest updatesKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentThu 29 Oct 2026 08.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 17.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s tax authority is assigning dedicated “customer compliance managers” to more than 200 billionaires as part of a crackdown meant to raise £500m for the public purse.HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) said it had for the first time compiled a list of billionaires who are required to pay tax in the UK, regardless of whether they formally live in the country, to tackle a “wealthy tax gap” caused by those who do not pay what they ought.In an announcement after Wednesday’s budget, the authoritysaid it was allocatinga customer compliance manager (CCM) to each billionaire with a UK tax footprint, whose complex tax affairs are often hard for HMRC to manage.“Billionaires can present a particular example of this, with affairs often spanning multiple taxes, entities and jurisdictions and a greater need for early and coordinated engagement,” HMRC said.It said the managers would offer voluntary discussions to each billionaire before they filed their taxes, to “help build a shared understanding of the customers’ UK tax affairs and make subsequent engagement more focused and proportionate”.The authority also plans to start deploying new tech to monitor wealthy individuals –defined asthose with income of more than £200,000 or assets over £2m in any of the last three years – involving “advanced analytics, automated triggers and artificial intelligence (AI) to identify emerging risks earlier and target compliance activity where it will have greatest impact”.It is part of wider efforts to tacklethe wealthy tax gap, whereby rich people are failing to pay what they should if all of their assets were disclosed to the tax authority. The wealthy tax gap for 2024-25 was estimated to be worth £3.6bn, equivalent to 6% of thetotal tax gapacross the UK’s entire tax-paying population.The tax authority said its actions would contribute at least £500m towards a larger commitment to raise £10bn of additional tax revenues by 2030.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHMRC was grilled in July last year by MPson the parliamentary public accounts committee over its lack of understanding of tax compliance by about 1.3 million wealthy taxpayers.Adam Craggs, the head of tax, investigations and financial crime at the law firm RPC, said anyone with more than £200,000 of annual income, or net assets above £2m, should now “reflect on how clearly they understand and can evidence their UK tax position and their interaction with HMRC”.Explore more on these topicsThe super-richHMRCTax and spendingTaxnewsShareReuse this content

title: Angry Labour MPs urge leadership not to overrule energy secretary on Rosebank | Oil | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Backbenchers voice alarm over ‘intolerable position’ faced by Miatta Fahnbulleh over oilfield decision
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Exclusive: Backbenchers voice alarm over ‘intolerable position’ faced by Miatta Fahnbulleh over oilfield decision
Content: The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, and the chancellor, John Healey, during a visit last week to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/TreasuryView image in fullscreenThe energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, and the chancellor, John Healey, during a visit last week to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/TreasuryOilAngry Labour MPs urge leadership not to overrule energy secretary on RosebankExclusive: Backbenchers voice alarm over ‘intolerable position’ faced by Miatta Fahnbulleh over oilfield decisionJessica Elgot,Kiran Stacey,Pippa CrerarandFiona HarveyThu 29 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFuriousLabourMPs have been lobbying the prime minister and chancellor not to overrule the energy secretary should she decide to block the Rosebank oilfield.MPs say they are alarmed at the cabinet splits that have emerged over the issue after sourcestold the Guardianthat Miatta Fahnbulleh was minded to refuse environmental permission for the field.Sources close to the chancellor, John Healey, have since made it clear he is in favour of the scheme, while some in government believe the prime minister,Andy Burnham, also wants it to go ahead.Backbenchers worried about the environmental impact of the project are now urging their whips and Downing Street not to allow other ministers to intervene in Fahnbulleh’s decision.Catherine Fookes, a Labour member of the energy select committee, said: “Approving Rosebank will blow a hole in our green credentials. A group of us is making it clear to leadership that this should be Miatta’s decision and I hope they listen.Climate damage would obliterate any economic benefits of new North Sea fields, analysis showsRead more“Labour MPs are really, really concerned about it – it would go against the thrust of our manifesto.”Another MP said: “If Healey pushes through Rosebank, there will be blood. It’s economically shortsighted as well as politically explosive – they aren’t listening at all to the discomfort on the backbenches.”Another commented: “Lots of us have raised this. I think the position Miatta has been put in by these briefings is intolerable.” Concerns are understood to also have been raised with Healey directly in budget meetings with MPs.Fahnbulleh’s parliamentary aides have circulated a memo to MPs insisting she would have the final say on the proposals, after a number of MPs contacted them to raise concerns that she would be overruled.“No decision has been made on Rosebank,” the memo said. “The energy secretary will consider all relevant factors in a case before reaching a decision.“The energy secretary is the only decision maker and will consider all relevant factors as part of the quasi-judicial process. No other cabinet member or minister has any role in this decision and does not see the advice on it,” it added.Map showing location of Rosebank oilfieldBurnham has promised to take a “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil drilling, calling the Jackdaw gasfield, which the government approved last week, “a bridge to the future”.The prime minister insists the decision over Rosebank will be for Fahnbulleh alone to make.But he prompted speculation about his support for the project on Wednesday, when he told the Commons: “Use of our reserves can support and accelerate a clean energy future, and that was very much the logic behind the decision that the government announced on Jackdaw last week.”Many in government believe Fahnbullehcan approvethe bigger Rosebank scheme without breaching the UK’s carbon commitments, in part because most of its oil would be exported.The Guardian also revealed on Tuesday that the Treasury hadalready factored in tax revenuesfrom the scheme, which are expected to hit about £500m by the end of this parliament.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTreasury officials said on Wednesday the money had been included in forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) since 2019, and that doing so would not prevent the energy secretary from blocking it.The OBR said inits budget forecaston Wednesday: “The projection includes production from currently producing fields (including Jackdaw), and the North Sea Transition Authority’s estimate of production from development of new fields, which includes Rosebank, and from future discoveries.“The forecast annual pace of decline [in oil and gas production] would be around 14% a year if there were no production from any new fields.”The memo from Fahnbulleh’s aides added that decisions to score Rosebank as part of the forecast would be a decision for the OBR.Burnham in danger of sleepwalking into climate disaster, say campaignersRead moreHowever, some Labour MPs believe the Treasury has been using aggressive tactics to strong-arm the energy department, with one describing the approach of No 11 as “macho bullshit”.Clive Lewis, another Labour MP, said: “You cannot claim global climate leadership while approving new oilfields simply because you’ve already pencilled in the tax receipts. Tax ‘receipts’, as I understand it, that will be the operator’s estimate and not actual Treasury revenue.”Analysis by Uplift, a campaign group, found that on the government’s and industry’s estimates, the tax take from Rosebank would probably be limited and could be outweighed by the tax breaks and incentives likely to be offered for the development and decommissioning of the fields.Areeba Hamid, a co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, said: “Any tax revenues from this far-off field in a rapidly declining basin don’t just leave our public services at the hostage of future oil prices, they also leave taxpayers on the hook for the costs of decommissioning for decades to come. The truth is that approving new oil drilling in the North Sea will only add to the costs of climate impacts, costs not fully factored into forecasts such as those from the OBR. Any economist should be able to see that.”MPs said there would be a significant parliamentary rebellion on Rosebank, unlike Jackdaw, where they were prepared to accept the argument to allow gas to be extracted for domestic consumption.Fookes said: “The case was made for Jackdaw to some degree and we remained quite quiet over that. Rosebank, however, is a different issue.”Explore more on these topicsOilEnvironment policyLabourGreenhouse gas emissionsFossil fuelsMiatta FahnbullehEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: UK social media ban may lock out more than 100,000 teenagers without ID | Social media ban | The Guardian
description: Watchdog says under-16 ban may affect older teenagers without passport or licence, and that ‘motivated children’ will skirt restrictions
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Watchdog says under-16 ban may affect older teenagers without passport or licence, and that ‘motivated children’ will skirt restrictions
Content: The ban is set to come into force next spring.Photograph: Peter Cripps/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe ban is set to come into force next spring.Photograph: Peter Cripps/AlamySocial media banUK social media ban may lock out more than 100,000 teenagers without IDWatchdog says under-16 ban may affect older teenagers without passport or licence, and that ‘motivated children’ will skirt restrictionsDan MilmoGlobal technology editorThu 29 Oct 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 16.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 100,000 British teenagers risk being locked out of social media if they do not have a passport or driving licence when an under-16 ban is introduced next year.Ofcom, the UK’s online watchdog, said about 150,000 16- to 17-year-olds do not own a passport or driving licence, which are likely to be needed to access age-restricted platforms.The Australia-style ban on under-16s accessing social media services, including Instagram, TikTok andYouTube, is due to come into force next spring.Online safety laws have failed to protect children in UK, Ofcom admitsRead moreThe head of Ofcom, Melanie Dawes, said “motivated children” would seek to bypass the restrictions,as has happened in Australia.On Thursday, Ofcom published an assessment of age verification measures that could underpin the ban, outlining four “highly effective” methods: checking a person’s official ID against a live selfie, a bank verifying an account holder’s age, an official digital ID service like the Young Scot card, or estimating someone’s age via a selfie.However, the watchdog said a form of official ID would probably be needed as a “backstop” for other methods, such as facial age estimation, which could be inaccurate by several years. Ofcom said a cohort of 16- to 17-year-olds could miss out as a result.“This means that people without a form of photo ID will likely need to take steps to obtain one to access age-restricted services,” the regulator said.View image in fullscreenFacial age estimation can be inaccurate by several years.Photograph: Gemth/Getty ImagesMore than nine out of 10 Britons over 16 have passports or driving licences.Facial age estimation has been a popular measure for enforcing over-18 access to pornographic websites in the UK, which have beensubject to stringent age checks since last year, indicating that this method will be used by social media plaforms as well.The UK government has not confirmed which platforms will be affected by the ban but it is expected to cover the same sites as in Australia. Those are: Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit,Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube.In March, Australia’s eSafety commissioner said a “substantial proportion” of under-16s had flouted the ban since it was imposed in December last year. A survey of 900 Australian parents found 31% said their children still had one or more social media accounts after the ban, compared with 49% before the laws.Ofcom’s chief executive acknowledged the risk of evasion and said the ban would be a “huge cultural shift for the UK”.“We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk,” said Dawes. “This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play.”The government is expected to introduce regulations confirming the ban by the end of the year, with Ofcom also opening a consultation on the best age verification methods before issuing official guidance on which measures to adopt.Explore more on these topicsSocial media banSocial mediaOfcomTikTokYouTubeTwitchRedditnewsShareReuse this content

title: Finland launches criminal investigation into Google’s clearing of forest for datacentre site | Finland | The Guardian
description: Authorities allege company may have breached Finnish environmental laws by forgoing required impact assessment
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Authorities allege company may have breached Finnish environmental laws by forgoing required impact assessment
Content: An aerial view of the site where Google’s datacentre is set to be built in Muhos.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the site where Google’s datacentre is set to be built in Muhos.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesFinlandFinland launches criminal investigation into Google’s clearing of forest for datacentre siteAuthorities allege company may have breached Finnish environmental laws by forgoing required impact assessment‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentreJon HenleyThu 29 Oct 2026 10.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinnish ⁠police have launched a criminal investigation into possible breaches ⁠of the country’s environmental ⁠laws ​at the site of a planned Google datacentre in rural northernFinland.Authorities allege that Tuike Finland, a Google subsidiary,cleared and drained 330 hectares (815 acres) of forestat the planned site in Muhos before environmental impact assessments required by Finnish law had been completed.View image in fullscreenIn the northern Finnish town of Muhos, the forest has already been cut down on land acquired by Google, with excavators now clearing the ground and rumbling trucks shuttling back and forth to the construction area located next to major power lines.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesLike other Nordic countries, Finland is attractive to tech companies seeking to build datacentres because of its relative geopolitical stability and abundance of land, but also because its cool climate should allow them to cut energy costs.“Based on preliminary information, there have been ambiguities and ‌shortcomings in the drainage and water management at the construction site of Tuike Finland ​Oy’s datacentre project,” Finnish police said in a statement on Thursday.“The criminal investigation will examine, among other things, circumstances related to these issues,” they added.Finnish authorities are considering applications for a total of 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, including a €13bn (£11bn) artificial intelligence infrastructure project byGooglethat the US company has called its largest ‌investment in Europe.MapEarlier this month Finnish authorities ordered Google to suspend work at two sites – Muhos and Otanmäki, about 100km to the south-east – after the company failed to complete environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land.The Supervisory ⁠Agency, which oversees environmental permits and assessments, told Google to halt “preparatory ​measures altering the environment”. Campaigners estimate 250,000 trees have been felled at Muhos and 150,000 at Otanmäki.View image in fullscreenGoogle’s clearcut area of about 200 hectares (500 acres) in Otanmäki, Finland.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianGoogle’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, has apologised for the forest clearings, but argued that the company had acted according to “the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time”.The Finnish government has encouraged the projects. In September, when Google’s plans were announced, the prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a “top priority” and the deal would “deliver lasting benefits”.But the revelations over Google’s alleged misconduct have sparked a national debate over what datacentre deals mean for communities, the environment and energy prices. The issue could impact parliamentary elections due in April.More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and compensation for environmental damage. Experts say datacentres bring a limited number of local jobs, and benefits on a national level are minimal.“Really, for Finland, there are no benefits,” said Jussi Kangasharju, professor of computer science at University of Helsinki. “They are international companies serving international customers.Datacentresultimately have little benefit for others except the datacentre operator.”Explore more on these topicsFinlandDatacentresEuropeGoogleTrees and forestsDeforestationLogging and land-clearingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hong Kong’s leader apologises for residential fire that killed 168 people | World news | The Guardian
description: Blaze was world’s deadliest residential fire since 1980, but some survivors and bereaved families say justice has yet to be served
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Blaze was world’s deadliest residential fire since 1980, but some survivors and bereaved families say justice has yet to be served
Content: The Wang Fuk Court residential estate in Hong Kong's Tai Po district as fire took hold on 26 November 2025.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Wang Fuk Court residential estate in Hong Kong's Tai Po district as fire took hold on 26 November 2025.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesWorld newsHong Kong’s leader apologises for residential fire that killed 168 peopleBlaze was world’s deadliest residential fire since 1980, but some survivors and bereaved families say justice has yet to be servedGuardian reporterThu 29 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHong Kong’s leader has apologised for government shortcomings that contributed to a fire that killed 168 people in the city last year, a rare sign of public contrition that nevertheless failed to impress some victims’ families.The chief executive, John Lee, and seven other officials bowed in apology at the release of a report that pointed to “decades of failure” by government bodies.Four departments “should bear part of the responsibility” for the high casualties, the report said. So far one official, housing secretary Winnie Ho, has resigned.Last November,a small fire probably started by a cigarette grew into an infernothat enveloped seven of the eight towers in Wang Fuk Court, a housing complex that was shrouded in bamboo scaffolding and netting for renovations.Former residents and victims’ families have been waiting to see how the government will address who is to blame for the ignored warnings, substandard building materials and disabled fire alarms that made the fire the world’s deadliest in a residential building since 1980.How the Hong Kong fire unfolded – visual guideRead moreAuthorities have filed charges, includingmanslaughter, against seven individuals and two companiesover their roles in the fire. At least 35 people have been arrested.The independent report released on Thursday found the “main culprits” of the fire were private contractors but also accused officials of “lax enforcement”.Had the four departments better recognised the risks and acted accordingly, “there was a real possibility that the misconduct of the private-sector parties and the fire hazards in WF Court could have been rectified or removed before the fire”, it said.Lee said a three-month investigation would now begin into the government’s role.“I am deeply saddened. I would like to apologise to the affected residents and the general public,” Lee said on Thursday, adding that housing minister Ho should “bear political responsibility”.But Yip Ka-kui, who lost his wife and home in the fire, told reporters he did not consider the government’s acceptance of accountability adequate. “All the secretaries for the departments named should step down,” he said, according to AFP news agency. “Administrative responsibility falls short” and political accountability even more so, Yip added.Phyllis Lo, whose mother died in the fire, told AP news agency that progress had been made but that justice had yet to be served.She added the officials’ apology was late, though it was better than nothing.Hong Kong’s government has previously been accused by critics of being more concerned with clamping down on criticism than addressing the causes of the disaster.Ashes and memories: one family’s return to the site of Hong Kong’s worst fire in decadesRead moreSince a national security law was imposed on the city in 2020 by Beijing, the city’s once vibrant civil society groups and political opposition have been all but quashed.In the weeks after the fire, authorities warned against crimes that “exploit the tragedy” and reportedly arrested at least three people for sedition.China’s national security agency in Hong Kong also summoned international media representatives, saying they had smeared the government in their reports on the fire.On Thursday Lee promised that “similar incidents will never be allowed to happen again”.Some observers had called for a more legally powerful inquiry commission to be set up, rather than the judge-led independent review committee that compiled Thursday’s report.Lee told reporters that authorities had proposed “systematic reforms”, including criminalising bid-rigging and overhauling the complaints system.The report stated: “The fire has been put out, but the reform has only just begun.”Explore more on these topicsWorld newsHong KongAsia PacificHong Kong apartment firesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hegseth reportedly fires high-ranking army strategist over alleged leaks | US military | The Guardian
description: Pentagon says it has referred leak case to justice department for criminal investigation
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Pentagon says it has referred leak case to justice department for criminal investigation
Content: Brett Sylvia, then a brigadier general, speaks at a combined arms rehearsal at Konotop, Poland, in 2020.Photograph: Spc. Javan Johnson/Training Support Activity EuropeView image in fullscreenBrett Sylvia, then a brigadier general, speaks at a combined arms rehearsal at Konotop, Poland, in 2020.Photograph: Spc. Javan Johnson/Training Support Activity EuropeUS militaryHegseth reportedly fires high-ranking army strategist over alleged leaksPentagon says it has referred leak case to justice department for criminal investigationMarina DunbarThu 29 Oct 2026 18.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US defense secretary,Pete Hegseth, has reportedly dismissed Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, a high-ranking army strategist serving on the Pentagon’s joint staff, following allegations that he disclosed classified information to the public.The Pentagon announced on Thursday that it had referred an alleged information leak case for criminal investigation, maintaining that the removal of the senior general was essential “to protect sensitive information”, theWashington Postreported.Sylvia had served as the director for strategy, plans and policy on the joint staff.Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell acknowledged the dismissal in astatementon social media, though he did not mention Sylvia by name.Democratic senator says Hegseth trying to hide costs of Iran war from US publicRead more“Following an extensive Air Force OSI investigation, the Department took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information,” Parnell wrote. “To protect the integrity of the investigation, no further comment will be made regarding the individual or the circumstances of this action.”“This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action,” he added.A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said in a statement that it “has ongoing investigations related to possible leaks of classified information”.“We work closely with our government partners, which includes the Department of War,” the spokesperson added, using the Trump administration’s name for the Pentagon.Sylvia’s removal represents one of the most significant actions so far in Hegseth’s extensive campaign to identify officials suspected of sharing information with journalists, as theunpopularUS war on Iran moves into its ninth month.In July, Hegseth ​announced that the Pentagon and the US Department of Justice hadcreated a joint taskforce“​to identify and ​prosecute” what he called the “unauthorized disclosure ​of sensitive” information to the press.Last year, Hegseth implemented new restrictions governing media access that prompted legal concerns from press organizations.Dozens of journalists surrendered their press badges rather than agree to the new media policies, which have been subject to legal challenges.A senior Pentagon official toldReutersthat Sylvia failed three separate polygraph tests, in which he was asked whether he had disclosed classified material.“The extent of his leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security. Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second,” the official said, according to Reuters.However, a colleague of Sylvia told the Washington Post that the general had consistently rejected accusations that he leaked classified information, while also acknowledging that he had previously communicated with members of the press.In August, three journalistsfiredby the Pentagon from the US government-funded news outlet Stars and Stripes sued the department in federal court, arguing their dismissals were illegal and violated their first amendment rights to free speech.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryPete HegsethnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spy | Nvidia | The Guardian
description: Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
Content: Jensen Huang gives a keynote address at the Nvidia Berlin GPU technology conference on 21 October 2026 in Berlin, Germany.Photograph: Sean Gallup/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJensen Huang gives a keynote address at the Nvidia Berlin GPU technology conference on 21 October 2026 in Berlin, Germany.Photograph: Sean Gallup/Getty ImagesNvidiaNvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spyJensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to ChinaJohana BhuiyanThu 29 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 17.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS intelligence agencies believe theNvidiachief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to anew reportby the New York Times.Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips toChina, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenarioRead moreIn the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips toChinaas a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.Explore more on these topicsNvidiaChinaEspionageAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Polymarket temporarily suspends trading on international platform due to security incident | Polymarket | The Guardian
description: Security incident linked to performance-monitoring tool spurred platform to halt trading for about an hour
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Security incident linked to performance-monitoring tool spurred platform to halt trading for about an hour
Content: Polymarket said it referred the incident to a law enforcement agency in the United Kingdom.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolymarket said it referred the incident to a law enforcement agency in the United Kingdom.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesPolymarketPolymarket temporarily suspends trading on international platform due to security incidentSecurity incident linked to performance-monitoring tool spurred platform to halt trading for about an hourAssociated PressThu 29 Oct 2026 19.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolymarket temporarily halted trading on its international platform on Thursday because of a security incident that compromised a third-party provider, the company said.Trading was paused for about an hour and resumed on Thursday afternoon. The company has promised to fully reimburse any affected traders.Prediction markets surge in US as public health advocates call for support to combat gamblingRead moreThe prediction market platform said it halted trading “out of an abundance of caution” after identifying and fixing the issue affecting its international platform.“We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company posted on X once trading had resumed.Polymarket said it referred the incident to a law enforcement agency in the United Kingdom.Reports have linked the source of the incident to DebugBear, a UK-based company offering website performance-monitoring tools.DebugBear’s own website was unavailable on Thursday afternoon and the company posted on X that it was “impacted by an ongoing security incident”. It also advised clients who were using one of its products to remove the embed code from their websites. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.It was not immediately clear to what extent traders using the popular prediction market platform were affected, or the breadth of the impact. The company said anyone who was affected “will be made whole”.Explore more on these topicsPolymarketPrediction marketsGamblingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Google owner Alphabet loses $500bn in market value after profit disappoints Wall Street  | Technology | The Guardian
description: Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn, well short of expectations, though revenue rose to $127.6bn
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn, well short of expectations, though revenue rose to $127.6bn
Content: Google logo is displayed at its headquarters in New York City.Photograph: Aleksandra Michalska/ReutersView image in fullscreenGoogle logo is displayed at its headquarters in New York City.Photograph: Aleksandra Michalska/ReutersTechnologyGoogle owner Alphabet loses $500bn in market value after profit disappoints Wall StreetNet profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn, well short of expectations, though revenue rose to $127.6bnAgence France-PresseThu 29 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShares in the Google parentAlphabetfell double digits Wednesday evening into Thursday trading, erasing hundreds of billions of dollars in stock market value from the $4tn tech giant.The company had reported lower-than-expected profit and a slowdown in its advertising business while it maintained big spending on AI.Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn in the July-to-September period, or $2.12 a share, well short of expectations by analysts surveyed by FactSet.Alphabet booked an $8.7bn loss on its equity investments, which it attributed to its stake in SpaceX, the Elon Musk-led company where shares have struggled since going public in June.‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentreRead moreRevenue, however, rose 25% to an enormous $127.6bn. The figure was slightly below the roughly $128bn analysts had forecast.Advertising revenue grew 11% to $82bn, short of expectations. Revenue from Google’s search business, still the company’s largest source of income, rose 12% to $63.4bn, slowing from 17% growth in the previous quarter.YouTube, now the most-watched content provider on American TV screens, saw advertising revenue grow 9% to $11.2bn, down from 13% growth in the previous quarter. YouTube Music and Premium passed 150 million subscribers worldwide, including trials.Google Cloud, which rents computing power and AI tools to businesses, saw revenue jump 103% to $30.7bn, ahead of analyst expectations.The company said sales of its in-house AI chips, known as TPUs, contributed significantly to that growth. Operating income for the unit tripled to $11.1bn.Google is also selling its TPU chips to outside companies, in a growing challenge to market leader Nvidia. OpenAI reportedly plans to buy some of the chips.Alphabet’s “Other Bets” division, which includes the robotaxi company Waymo, posted revenue of $372m and an operating loss of $2bn.Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides a week across 15 US metropolitan areas and aims to reach 1m weekly rides by the end of the year.Alphabet spent $51.4bn on capital expenditures during the quarter, mostly on datacenters and AI chips, more than double the $24bn a year earlier.Its latest forecast for capex spending is between $195bn to $205bn in spending for 2026.The company said it would continue to increase capex spending significantly in 2027.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I would broadly think of all of this as a long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise,” Sundar Pichai, the Google CEO, told analysts of the company’s investment splurge.The company’s spending, which included a fine paid to the European Union, outstripped the cash generated by Alphabet’s businesses for a second straight quarter, leaving a $9.1bn gap.During the quarter Alphabet raised $28.7bn by selling bonds and $12.4bn by issuing new shares to help pay for its AI ambitions.Google has stepped up the pace of its AI releases since a delay to a flagship model in July raised questions about whether it was falling behind rivals OpenAI and Anthropic.It launched Gemini 4 at the end of September and later released a version focused on cybersecurity.The Gemini app has reached 1bn users. Google’s AI models now process nearly 32bn tokens, or units of text, per minute, more than four times the level of a year ago, the company said.Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is also one of Google’s largest cloud customers. It has committed to using up to one million Google AI chips.In September, a US judge declined to order Google to sell off parts of its advertising technology business, imposing restrictions on how it operates instead.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyGoogleAlphabetQuarterly resultsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The beautiful, shocking work of artist Hoda Afshar: ‘I don’t take freedom of speech for granted’ | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Afshar’s experiences as a young woman in Iran have shaped her artistic career in Australia, focusing her eye on the humanity within inhumane systems
Author: Dee Jefferson
Headline: Afshar’s experiences as a young woman in Iran have shaped her artistic career in Australia, focusing her eye on the humanity within inhumane systems
Content: Iranian Australian artist Hoda Afshar: ‘What I care about is human life and human dignity.’Photograph: Adam Ferguson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIranian Australian artist Hoda Afshar: ‘What I care about is human life and human dignity.’Photograph: Adam Ferguson/The GuardianArt and designInterviewThe beautiful, shocking work of artist Hoda Afshar: ‘I don’t take freedom of speech for granted’Dee JeffersonAfshar’s experiences as a young woman in Iran have shaped her artistic career in Australia, focusing her eye on the humanity within inhumane systemsGet our weekend culture and lifestyle emailThu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 17.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Hoda Afshar was a teenager, coming of age in theocratic and authoritarianIranin the 1990s, she and her friends were repeatedly arrested and physically punished by the “morality police”, for wearing their hijabs incorrectly in public and for attending underground parties. “They used to put a few of us in small solitary confinement cells together for a night or two, it was very common for my generation to experience that,” she says.“We are part of thenasl-e sukhteh, or ‘burned generation’; the generation born after the 1979 revolution, who had to pay the price for many of the transformations and changes that happened.”These formative experiences left the artist with an ongoing sensitivity to injustice, and an interest in incarceration, marginalisation and state violence. They have also amplified her appreciation of the rights and freedoms she now enjoys as a citizen of Australia, where she migrated in 2007, then as a lapsed photojournalist and emerging artist. “I grew up under a system that didn’t give me freedom of speech, or equal rights as a woman, so I don’t take it for granted,” she says.View image in fullscreenHoda Afshar: ‘Iran’s struggles and our movements are often hijacked and used for other political purposes and ends.’Photograph: Adam Ferguson/The GuardianBut it has also made her more sensitive to Australia’s human rights and social justice failures: “Australia claims beautiful values. It is the country of a ‘fair go’, that wants everything equal for everybody. But rights are not distributed equally.”“From the beginning, I was very excited to be able to critique authority; to be a responsible citizen in a society where we can fight for change,” she adds.This combination of lived experience and strongly held values has resulted in some of the most vivid, urgent and achingly beautiful works ofAustralian artseen in the last decade – several of which are brought together in a/part, her new exhibition at the University of Melbourne’s Buxton ContemporaryThe show brings together three projects that deal with what she calls “states of exception”, a term coined by the Italian political theorist Giorgio Agamben for “sites where the laws that are applied to normal citizens don’t apply or can be broken,” Afshar says.View image in fullscreenAfshar’s Code Black/Riot on display at Buxton Contemporary, the University of Melbourne.Photograph: Christian CapurroFor each project, she has created video and photographic portraits that foreground the humanity of her subjects, while interrogating the narratives that underpin each state of exception; the ways of depicting a marginalised person or group that make it possible to accept their disenfranchisement.Sign up for the fun stuff with our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morningBest known among these works isRemain, the 2018 work Afshar made with the Kurdish Iranian journalist and author Behrouz Boochani and a group of refugee men detained on Manus Island as part of Australia’s offshore immigration detention system. Shot on a tiny island near Manus, the two-channel video marries the beguilingly beautiful aesthetic of the tropical paradise with poetry, Kurdish song and personal testimony to express the humanity of its subjects – and the depth of their suffering.“The intention was to create a new visual language that can impact people about this issue, because we have become absolutely immune to images of suffering from the refugee crisis,” Afshar told me back when Remain debuted in 2018. Almost a decade later, it is her most exhibited work in Australia and abroad.View image in fullscreenA still from Remain, 2018.Photograph: Courtesy of Hoda Afshar and Milani GalleryCode Black/Riot, showing at Buxton for the first time since its debut at theSydney Biennalein March, is an immersive video installation and series of portraits focusing on Indigenous youth in detention shot in far north Queensland.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSaved for SundayEase your Sunday scaries with the best of Guardian Australia’s culture and lifestyle journalism.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I must continue until I die’: inside the fight to bring Iran’s thriving art scene to the worldRead moreCreated with Boochani and Kuku Yalandji/Waanji/Yidinji/Gugu Yimithirr artist Vernon Ah Kee, the video features former detainees and staff from a youth detention centre, talking about living and working within a dehumanising system.The former staff talk about the rainbow-coloured system of “codes” used to identify security and safety issues, and the practice of “night mode”, in which children are locked in their cells, in pitch dark, for days at a time. The children describe beatings from guards, solitary confinement, and a seemingly endless cycle of arrests, incarceration and probation.To protect the identities of her young subjects, Afshar shot them in tight closeup, focusing on bodies and the lower halves of faces, highlighting the tension in the children’s bodies and mouths as they share harrowing experiences.View image in fullscreenUntitled #03 from Code Black/Riot, 2025.Photograph: Christian CapurroThe studio-based interviews are intercut with footage of the young people: navigating Cairns at night amid revelling locals and tourists, floating in rivers and waterholes, perching in trees and bouncing on trampolines.“It was very important not to depict them as broken,” Afshar says of the children; theirphotographic portraitsshow them in playful and defiant poses, using hands, flowers, face paint and clothing to obscure their faces.As in Remain, beauty is juxtaposed with violence; the humanity of the narrators is contrasted with the inhumanity of the systems they are trapped in.Her 2021 projectAgonistes, spotlighting prominent Australian whistleblowers such as theformer Australian army lawyer David McBride, explores a different “state of exception”: government employees who breach confidentiality agreements to speak up about witnessing wrongdoing, and are prosecuted and imprisoned as a result.View image in fullscreenThe Agonistes series at Buxton Contemporary explores whistleblowers: ‘They lose everything because they believe in the values that the society claims to have,’ Afshar says.Photograph: Christian Capurro“These people all made a sacrifice; they had to choose between the law and the public, and they chose the public, believing that if the public knows what is happening, things will change,” says Afshar. “They lose everything because they believe in the values that the society claims to have.”A fourth work, Shafaq, premiering in a/part, is more personal. Made during a camping trip on Larrakia country in the Northern Territory in July, it reflects her anxiety as the US resumed bombing Iran’s south, where her family lives. Shafaq is “a conversation across distance to my family members”, she says.The last year has been difficult, with career highs marred by grief and anxiety over the bombing of her homeland. “Seeing places that you grew up in being demolished like that, it’s like part of your body and identity is being erased by it too. It’s a kind of pain I didn’t know till that moment,” she says.View image in fullscreenHoda Afshar in her studio: ‘For me, it’s not about east or west, right or left.’Photograph: Adam Ferguson/The GuardianThe way Iran has been portrayed internationally has left her sceptical of documentary modes of storytelling. “Our struggles and our movements are often hijacked and used for other political purposes and ends,” she says. “I wanted to rethink what documentary means, to allow for interpretation; to never present an image with concrete messaging or didacticism.”The end goal of her art, she says, is to bring people together. “For me, it’s not about east or west, right or left, or these binaries that keep us endlessly separated and fighting with each other. I don’t belong to anyone’s camps … What I care about is human life and human dignity.”Hoda Afshar’s a/partis on at Buxton Contemporary, the University of Melbourne, until 24 April 2027. Entry is freeExplore more on these topicsArt and designPhotographyAustralian artIranMiddle East and north AfricaVideo artinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mega mega mega, going back to Romford! How an outer London suburb became a metropolis for 90s dance music | Dance music | The Guardian
description: When 17-year-0ld Danny Donelly got a bank loan to open a record shop and sell dancefloor-filling electronic music, he little knew how he would help revolutionise his town and dance music at large
Author: Tim Burrows
Headline: When 17-year-0ld Danny Donelly got a bank loan to open a record shop and sell dancefloor-filling electronic music, he little knew how he would help revolutionise his town and dance music at large
Content: ‘It was like a youth club’ … Boogie Times Records in Romford.Photograph: Danny DonnellyView image in fullscreen‘It was like a youth club’ … Boogie Times Records in Romford.Photograph: Danny DonnellyDance musicMega mega mega, going back to Romford! How an outer London suburb became a metropolis for 90s dance musicWhen 17-year-0ld Danny Donelly got a bank loan to open a record shop and sell dancefloor-filling electronic music, he little knew how he would help revolutionise his town and dance music at largeTim BurrowsThu 29 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 07.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early 1990s, the suburban town of Romford was known for three things. It was the home of the world’s best snooker player, Steve Davis. It was where people placed bets at Romford dog track, over a dinner of chicken in a basket. And for those in the know, it was where the UK’s best underground dance music was bought and sold.That pedigree was immortalised by Romford’s most famous musical act, Underworld, with frontman Karl Hyde shouting the words “mega mega mega, going back to Romford” at the climax of 1995’s Born Slippy. Those words now form the title of a new exhibition in the town,Mega Mega: Romford’s Suburban Sound Revolution, which charts how this unglamorous but party-spirited backwater became an upstart rival to great dance music cities such as Manchester or Detroit.View image in fullscreenBought with a bank loan … Boogie Times Records, pictured in the 90s.Photograph: westhamdan/Danny BreaksThe scene’s key hub was the record shop Boogie Times, opened in 1989 by Danny Donnelly with a bank loan secured shortly before his 18th birthday. He was born in Stratford, east London, but when he was five his parents moved out to Romford, an oldEssexmarket town that had effectively become a suburb of London as the capital sprawled outwards after the second world war.View image in fullscreenThe Donnellys’ old shop at 18 Abbey Lane, Stratford in 2006.Photograph: © Vici MacDonaldDonnelly’s dad commuted back to Stratford to run the family corner shop, while young Danny inherited his entrepreneurial streak. “I was already buying and selling records at school,” he says. He loved rare groove, where hard-to-find jazz, funk and R&B records were selected for the quality of their breakbeats. At 14, he bought huge speakers for his bedroom, which he later used to put on parties around east London: “You’d hire someone’s flat, charge at the door and it would be treated like a club for the event.”Boogie Times opened just as house music and ecstasy found their way into post-industrial spaces and farmers’ fields, building demand for rave tunes on vinyl. The location of Donnelly’s dad’s shop in Stratford was similarly fortuitous: east London pirate station Fantasy FM launched in the block next door in 1989. “They would come downstairs and get a cup of tea and a sandwich after they had done their show,” says Donnelly. His dad got chatting to future drum’n’bass legend DJ Hype, who soon paid a visit to Boogie Times with another artist, DJ Krome. “Krome said: ‘Your mum makes the best cheese and onion sandwich.’” After being switched on to hardcore rave, Donnelly endeavoured to supply some of the freshest vinyl to a burgeoning local clientele.View image in fullscreenA visiting legend … DJ Hype in Boogie Times Records 1990s dance music record shop in Romford, Essex,Photograph: Danny DonnellyRomford and the wider borough of Havering already housed parties by people such as the polymath producer and promoter Mark Ryder – who later became a star in the UK garage era as Mark “Ruff” Ryder – but Romford was still best known for dancing to pop music on a Saturday night with your glad rags on.Tony Grimley, another local DJ inspired by his first rave, was asked to run a night at Romford’s biggest nightclub, Hollywood. He named it Culture Shock to describe the way the music landed there. “It was a party venue: a very Sharon and Tracy, 80s place,” says Grimley. Instead of tame disco and “erection section” slow dances, suddenly there were exciting new electronic DJs such as Andrew Weatherall, Danny Rampling and Underworld’s Darren Emerson. The local crowd didn’t like hard techno, Grimley says, “but that happy, high-energy sort of house music [such as] Danny Rampling … every time we booked Danny, we reached capacity.”View image in fullscreenMaking music themselves … Danny Donnelly leans on his Jeep with Boogie Times manager and Suburban Base Records artist Winston Run Tings.Photograph: Danny DonnellySimon Duggins AKA Uncle Dugs, DJ and former station manager of pirate-turned-legit radio station Rinse FM, went to his first rave after he noticed a circus big top on the side of the A13 when his dad was driving him to football training at Leyton Orient. “I walked into that rave a budding professional footballer,” says Duggins. “I walked out wanting to be [rave DJ] Slipmatt.” Duggins had already been nervously stepping into Boogie Times on a packed Saturday when he was still at school. “Someone would walk in, and then the whisper would go round the shop:That’s DJ Hype. You can’t even believe that you’re in the same space as these people.”View image in fullscreenGarage music? … Suburban Base’s first recording studio, built in Danny Donnelly’s parents’ garage.Photograph: westhamdan/Danny BreaksRomford was also surrounded by pirate radio stations such as Conflict FM in Rainham, and Force FM, which operated above a nearby sweet shop. “Pirate radio, the community around record stores and flyering was the analogue version of the internet,” says Donnelly. He broadened that community by creating his own record label, Suburban Base, brainstorming its name in the office above the shop on the day of the Rumbelows Football League cup final on 21 April 1991. It was a canny way to surpass dance music’s supply-chain gatekeepers by making the music themselves. “We were trying to compete with more established dance music shops in central London that were getting exclusives, stuff that we couldn’t get hold of,” says Donnelly. So he used Suburban Base to press small runs of records, “that we could keep exclusive to our shop for at least the first few weeks. People had to come to us.”The name Suburban Base accurately described Romford’s outsider status in a scene defined by the inner city: away from more credible tracks in London, sometimes Essex artists veered into full-on cheese such as the kids-TV-samplingSesame’s Treetby Loughton locals Smart E’s. Released by Suburban Base, it reached No 2 in the UK singles chart in July 1992. Donnelly says the track was seen by some on the scene as selling out, but adds: “It was hugely popular amongst rave DJs before it crossed over.” And it does have an innocence that chimed with the family vibe of the Boogie Times shop, which was “like a youth club in a way, with loads of people hanging around listening to music”, says Rachel Wallace, a key member of the Boogie Times tribe. She dated Donnelly and recorded her first tracks for the label in a studio in his parents’ garage, including the relentless and evocatively 90s tuneTell Me Why.View image in fullscreenKey member of the Boogie Times tribe … Rachel Wallace in 1992.Photograph: Suburban Bass RecordsSuburban Base helped to propel the dance scene as breakbeats got faster and more intricate, the bass got bigger and rounder, and ragga MCs became more prevalent. This new sound became known as jungle, showcased on hot Suburban Base dancefloor fillers such as RIP by Remarc. DJ Rap, AKA Charissa Saverio, was living in nearby Walthamstow and put jungle tracks out on Suburban Base, and found the scene unusually welcoming. “You saw Black people and white people together for the first time,” she says. “You walked in [to a jungle night] as a girl, and you weren’t harassed by a bunch of men; you could wear what you want, you didn’t have to look sexy, you could just be you.”Suburban Base Brazil … DJ Marky Mark enters the roster.Photograph: Courtesy Danny DonnellyAs the 90s progressed, Suburban Base became the first independent UK rave label to open up an office in the US, on the corner of Hollywood and Vine in Los Angeles in 1994. It expanded into Brazil, wheredrum’n’bass took off in a big way. Donnelly discovered a DJ working in a São Paulo record shop called Marky Mark, who became DJ Marky, and whose track LK became one of drum’n’bass’s biggest UK hits. “If you travel to Brazil now, particularly São Paulo, and you’re wearing a Suburban Base shirt, someone will come up to you,” Donnelly says.Boogie Times carried on into the 2000s after a record seller from the other side of the river in Gravesend decided to buy it off Donnelly, who had already stepped back from Suburban Base to focus on compiling huge-selling CD compilation series such as Pure Garage and Euphoria.View image in fullscreenSuburban Base on tour … Danny Breaks, MC Special A and Dave Nodz on stage in Orlando Florida 1992.Photograph: Danny DonnellyDuggins, meanwhile, had soundproofed an old primary school building in nearby Dagenham to house Rinse FM, and was putting on nights in Romford to showcase garage-era acts that pre-empted the incoming grime explosion, such as DJ EZ, Masterstepz and Pay as U Go Cartel. EZ would return to Romford to put on what might be the town’s most famous clubbing event:Todd Edwards at Time & Envy on New Year’s Day 2003, in which the US DJ and producer, whose style had so influenced UK garage, stared out at his adoring (and very male) crowd with a mixture of shock, fear and delight – scenes that still frequently go viral on social media.Murder on the dancefloor: are phones, drugs and chatter killing off dancing?Read moreTime & Envy was rebranded a few times before it closed for good in 2024, and the empty venue will now host the Mega Mega exhibition, including a replica of a 90s recording studio with original equipment from Suburban Base, and a pirate station recreated using original transmitters, aerials and the turntables from Boogie Times. “Young people now are so interested in those kind of analogue and early digital forms of music making,” says Katherine Green, the show’s curator.Like his old man might have done on a quiet day in the shop, Donnelly is finally taking stock. “I definitely played my part in the global expansion of the scene,” he reflects, but adds a warning that it wasn’t all parties and glamour. “It just comes from the ethos of doing things in a professional way,” he says. “Creating a label identity – and putting barcodes on the records.”Mega Mega: Romford’s Suburban Sound Revolutionruns from 29 October to 20 December at Atik, Romford. See You Down Raquels: Clubbing and Commune-ing in Essex, edited by Tim Burrows, isavailable to buy here.Explore more on these topicsDance musicClub cultureElectronic musicEssexfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Elke Sommer, prolific German star of A Shot in the Dark and And Then There Were None, dies aged 85 | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Berlin-born performer had a gift for languages that took her to Hollywood, landing roles alongside Peter Sellers, Dick Van Dyke and Paul Newman
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The Berlin-born performer had a gift for languages that took her to Hollywood, landing roles alongside Peter Sellers, Dick Van Dyke and Paul Newman
Content: Bombshell image … Elke Sommer.Photograph: Kobal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBombshell image … Elke Sommer.Photograph: Kobal/ShutterstockMoviesElke Sommer, prolific German star of A Shot in the Dark and And Then There Were None, dies aged 85The Berlin-born performer had a gift for languages that took her to Hollywood, landing roles alongside Peter Sellers, Dick Van Dyke and Paul NewmanAndrew PulverThu 29 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElke Sommer, the prolific German star of the Pink Panther film A Shot in the Dark, early 70s Agatha Christie adaptation And Then there Were None, and British sex comedy Carry on Behind, has died aged 85.Bild magazine reportedthat Sommer died in Los Angeles of heart failure.German-born Sommer, whose best-known film roles were in the 1960s and 70s, was one of the wave of European performers who crossed over to Hollywood and English-language cinema with considerable success, following the postwar emergence of European new wave cinema. Sommer was one of the few German actors to make waves at the time, as Hollywood made much of her bombshell image.View image in fullscreenHollywood breakthrough … Elke Sommer with Paul Newman in The Prize.Photograph: Moviestore/ShutterstockBorn Elke Schletz in 1940 in Berlin, the daughter of a Protestant pastor, she was evacuated with her family to Bavaria during the war. Intending to work as an interpreter, she was spotted by celebrated Italian director Vittorio De Sica after winning a beauty contest on a trip to Italy in 1958, and subsequently offered roles in a string of Italian comedy films. She crossed back into more serious work with the West German drama The Death Ship, opposite Horst Buchholz (who would go on to appear in cowboy classic The Magnificent Seven).With her gift for languages, Sommer made her first film in English, the 1961 British comedy Don’t Bother to Knock, opposite Richard Todd, and was billed as one of the “six most exciting women in the world” alongside Melina Mercouri, Jeanne Moreau and Romy Schneider in Carl Foreman’s 1963 war fable, The Victors. Sommer’s Hollywood breakthrough arrived in the same year, with The Prize; she was cast as Paul Newman’s lover in an adaptation of Irving Wallace’s hit novel, for which she was a joint winner of a most promising newcomer Golden Globe.View image in fullscreenLeaning into her ‘sexpot’ image … with Peter Sellers in A Shot in the Dark.Photograph: Moviestore/ShutterstockSommer’s Hollywood career then took off with A Shot in the Dark, in which she leaned heavily into her “sexpot” image as a maid suspected of a series of murders in the sequel to The Pink Panther, starring Peter Sellers. Following its success, Sommer appeared in a string of high profile Hollywood films, including The Art of Love with James Garner and Dick Van Dyke, The Oscar with Stephen Boyd, and the Bob Hope comedy Boy, Did I Get a Wrong Number! In 1968, she achieved leading actor status with The Wicked Dreams of Paula Schultz, a comedy about an East German athlete who pole-vaults over the Berlin Wall.In the 1970s, Sommer appeared in two cult horror films by Mario Bava, Baron Blood and Lisa and the Devil, and sex comedies Percy and Percy’s Progress for British director Ralph Thomas. She followed these with two high-profile British films: as secretary Vera Clyde in And Then There Were None in 1974, adapted from Christie’s hit novel, and a year later, Carry on Behind, the 27th in the Carry On series.View image in fullscreenIn Mario Bava’s cult horror Lisa and the Devil.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockAfter another Sellers film, The Prisoner of Zenda, and Ralph Thomas’s heist film A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square, Sommer scaled back her screen appearances and concentrated on painting. In the mid-1980s, she also became embroiled in a long-running feud with Zsa Zsa Gabor after they appeared together on TV show Circus of the Stars;Sommer was ultimately awarded $3.3min damages for defamation.Sommer was married twice, to writer Joe Hyams from 1964 until 1981, and hotelier Wolf Walther from 1993 until his death in 2026.Explore more on these topicsFilmGermanyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Wicker review – Olivia Colman finds the perfect lover in intriguing folk-horror romance | Movies | The Guardian
description: Colman stars as a depressed and bullied fisherwoman in medieval England. Fortunately, Peter Dinklage’s basketmaker delivers the answer to her dreams – an Alexander Skarsgård made of wicker
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Colman stars as a depressed and bullied fisherwoman in medieval England. Fortunately, Peter Dinklage’s basketmaker delivers the answer to her dreams – an Alexander Skarsgård made of wicker
Content: True love … Olivia Colman as the fisherwoman and Alexander Skarsgård as her wicker husband in Wicker.Photograph: Black Bear/PAView image in fullscreenTrue love … Olivia Colman as the fisherwoman and Alexander Skarsgård as her wicker husband in Wicker.Photograph: Black Bear/PAMoviesReviewWicker review – Olivia Colman finds the perfect lover in intriguing folk-horror romanceColman stars as a depressed and bullied fisherwoman in medieval England. Fortunately, Peter Dinklage’s basketmaker delivers the answer to her dreams – an Alexander Skarsgård made of wickerPeter BradshawThu 29 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe spirit of mystery author Shirley Jackson is interestingly revived in this peculiar folk-horror romance, adapted from a 2006 story called The Wicker Husband by British writer Ursula Wills. It’s almost funny but not exactly, and almost disturbing but not exactly, occupying a strange and intriguing Venn-diagram overlap between macabre horror and sentimentality. Yet devotees of bucolic British screen-scariness will note that it is, after all, about a wicker man.The scene is a fabular medieval-effect village that could be in central Europe or England, where there are bizarre patriarchal rituals, like the placing of metal collars on new brides. A depressed middle-aged fisherwoman (fiercely and naturalistically played by Olivia Colman) lives alone in a remote cottage and regularly brings her unappetising tench and gudgeon to market, where she is mocked and bullied by the nasty, closed-minded locals, including Richard E Grant as a lazy and incompetent doctor. Chief among her tormentors is the spiteful tailor’s wife, an elegant, sharp-faced woman played byElizabeth Debicki.But the fisherwoman, showing a good deal more imagination than everyone else, boldly approaches the Basketmaker (a droll performance from Peter Dinklage) and commissions him to make a wicker husband for her; this wicker hunk, magicked up in a secret workshop, is played byAlexander Skarsgård. His soulful eyes look out attractively from that weird wicker face.This new husband turns out to be an amazing catch: attentive, sensitive, non-toxically masculine, a wicker man of few words, great at fixing things in the cottage as he creaks self-effacingly around the place. (This is just as well as it’s still Colman who is earning a living for them both.) And above all, he is a wonderful lover; we don’t see his wicker genitals but there is evidently no problem with abrasion discomfort. (A movie more conventionally aware of comedy might have felt the need to explain this away a little more.)Instantly, the fisherwoman’s domestic bliss triggers poisonous envy among the sex-starved villagers, especially that noisome tailor’s wife. And it leads to an almost disquieting (and certainly amusing) climax of dismay.Wicker is out on 23 October in the US, on 30 October in the UK and 5 November in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmPeriod and historical filmsDrama filmsOlivia ColmanAlexander SkarsgårdScience fiction and fantasy filmsRomance filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Mosquito Bowl review – Netflix mixes football, war and cliches in slick by-the-numbers saga | War films | The Guardian
description: Peter Berg’s handsomely made second world war drama about a football game before the battle of Okinawa is stirring but filled with eye-rolling dialogue
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Peter Berg’s handsomely made second world war drama about a football game before the battle of Okinawa is stirring but filled with eye-rolling dialogue
Content: Nicholas Galitzine and Ray Nicholson in The Mosquito Bowl.Photograph: Kane Skennar/Netflix ©2026View image in fullscreenNicholas Galitzine and Ray Nicholson in The Mosquito Bowl.Photograph: Kane Skennar/Netflix ©2026War filmsReviewThe Mosquito Bowl review – Netflix mixes football, war and cliches in slick by-the-numbers sagaPeter Berg’s handsomely made second world war drama about a football game before the battle of Okinawa is stirring but filled with eye-rolling dialogueAdrian HortonThu 29 Oct 2026 13.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForgive me, but it is difficult not to be a little cynical about The Mosquito Bowl, Peter Berg’s grimly serious action feature situated (and marketed during many an NFL game) at the intersection of two predominant male interests: football and the second world war. Though both are certainly rich topics for cinema, and though I have been a fan of many a football/war story – most especially Berg’s NBC seriesFriday Night Lights– it is, let’s say, a tricky time for movies filled with dubiously nostalgic patriotism and masculinity. The trailer practically drips with a borderline parodic virility: a cadre of handsome up-and-coming male actors streaked with dirt; a group of men “trained for glory” and “called to war”, triumphantly hoisting aloft footballs, beer and guns to ponderous music.Wicker review – Olivia Colman finds the perfect lover in intriguing folk-horror romanceRead moreBut Berg is a capable and battle-tested director who knows his way around both a clock-ticking thriller (Deepwater Horizon,Lone Survivor) and the football field. So while The Mosquito Bowl, adapted forNetflixby Berg and Mark L Smith from anonfiction bookby Buzz Bissinger, fulfills its promise of American male pablum – there is many a clunky monologue about honor and duty and the “white buzz” of adrenaline – it also delivers on competently made, absorbing action sequences. (In huge news for Friday Night Lights fans, the football scenes here are once again scored by Explosions in the Sky.) Both in sport and in war, Berg has a knack for grace within visual cacophony and chaos; graphic sequences in battle and from the 1944 Christmas Eve pickup game at Guadalcanal that gives the film its name suggest, far more than its anvil-heavy dialogue, the connections between the gridiron and the battlefield, how the fleetness and camaraderie of sport can be wielded for survival and killing. There is a stomach-churning catharsis in experiencing, as inSam Mendes’s 1917orAlex Garland’s Warfare, the real-time brutality and capriciousness of war.That is, if you can stomach the rest of it. Every sepia-toned off-field scene, with the boys being boys or with their token supportive girlfriends, is liable to prompt an eye roll, such as when the Wisconsin Badger Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård) quotes Jack London’s The Call of the Wild from memory. Or when a shirtless Anthony “Touchdown Tony” Butkovich (Ray Nicholson, who inherited his father’s wild eyes but less of the magnetism), proclaims that “New York City’s the biggest goddamn bull I known of, and I intend to ride the hell out of it” in a sweaty locker room. Or when John “Mac” McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine) waxes poetic about how playing football “feels like magic” in a romantic bathtub scene with his girlfriend (Ella Newton) – who, of course, can only compare such flow-state nirvana to the feeling she gets when she has sex with him. Or when Dave Schreiner (Jeremy Allen White lookalike Tom Francis), the most grounded of this quartet, simmers when confronted by a college rival at marines registration.These are scant character details for a real group of college football stars who traded professional glory for the US marines and the Pacific theater after the attack on Pearl Harbor (relayed, as in several other historical sequences, by a scattershot montage of archival footage). But The Mosquito Bowl doesn’t have much more to say than that about its central quartet: they love football, their girlfriends and their country. They have bigger dreams but naively head to war anyway. The cliche of careless, precious youth about to be squandered – gestured by an impromptu football game in the snow – is rote, if still baseline moving, because obviously no 24-year-old brimming with life should die. (And you know that some of our strapping boys will.)And for what? From basic training, to Tarawa, to camp at Guadalcanal, to the deadly assault atOkinawa, sergeants and soldiers offer their own blunt reasons to fight the Japanese, most laced with racism toward Asian people that ranges from casual to menacing (our heroes, at least, are violently put off by fellow marines hawking “Jap teeth”). One could argue – I have to assume, given that the film ends with a title card acknowledging not only the Japanese civilians slain at Okinawa but the 75m global deaths from the entire conflict, that the film-makers would argue – that such inclusion is merely period accuracy, a way to represent how US soldiers rationalize their role. But it’s hard to separate what is merely telling the story as these marines experienced it – the Japanese a faceless, mystifying “other” prone to murder-suicide – and what is American propaganda. The elegiac music for US victories, the planting of American flags and the prolonged, gut-twisting sequences of marine suffering and death, sit uneasily with the unnamed anguish of the many Japanese, soldier and civilian.As with every war movie, there are a thousand possibly better or more challenging war movies existing at the margins of this one. But this one, firmly for the marines, is what we got. Berg at times cuts to a wide shot of the Earth, the whizzing of bullets giving way to the silence of space, in a ham-fisted suggestion of war’s futility. It’s of little comfort, when the heat of battle is the reason to watch.The Mosquito Bowl is in cinemas on 30 October and onNetflixon 25 NovemberExplore more on these topicsWar filmsSecond world warNetflixAction and adventure filmsSport filmsFilm adaptationsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nocturne review – Stephen Graham is TV’s most evil serial killer … and it’s impossible to stop watching him  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The star plays a sadistic murderer still pulling the strings from behind bars. With his high-pitched giggles and fatal whispers, it is a perfectly terrifying show for Halloween
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The star plays a sadistic murderer still pulling the strings from behind bars. With his high-pitched giggles and fatal whispers, it is a perfectly terrifying show for Halloween
Content: Stephen Graham in a scene from Nocturne.Photograph: Dennis P Mong Jr/Apple TVView image in fullscreenStephen Graham in a scene from Nocturne.Photograph: Dennis P Mong Jr/Apple TVTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewNocturne review – Stephen Graham is TV’s most evil serial killer … and it’s impossible to stop watching himThe star plays a sadistic murderer still pulling the strings from behind bars.  With his high-pitched giggles and fatal whispers, it is a perfectly terrifying show for HalloweenLucy ManganThu 29 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has taken a while, but I think the torch may finally have passed from Anthony Hopkins as the screen’s most profoundly unsettling and instantly-absorbed-by-the-cultural-imagination serial killer. From Hannibal’s hitherto unfailing hands it has been thrown toStephen Graham, who plays multiple murderer Jurek Walter in the new 10-part psychological thriller Nocturne.Walter, who draws out the deaths of his victims in order to torture their families as much as the individuals themselves, is incarcerated for life in the bowels of Riverside psychiatric hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He passes the time by doing push-ups, stashing contraband behind his toilet bowl for as-yet-unspecified purposes, and driving fellow inmates to suicide by whispering to them through the pipes. Graham – muscle-bound, preternaturally still and occasionally emitting a high-pitched giggle – is mesmerising and utterly terrifying.He soon has his hooks into his new nurse, Karl (Rory Culkin), who is too young, inexperienced and tender-hearted to heed the staff’s warnings about the manipulative monster in the basement. Walter has a way, as one former nurse notes, of making you feel sorry for him – “a man who buried people alive”. Soon Walter has Karl offering up personal information and carrying illicit messages to his supposed lawyer.View image in fullscreenHoodwinked … Rory Culkin in Nocturne.Photograph: Apple TVIn addition to the murders he was convicted for, Walter is also suspected of abducting and killing two children, Michael and Felicia Frost, though their bodies were never found. When Michael (Landon Valentin) stumbles out of the woods after three years, the man who was in charge of the Frost case, Jonah Lynn, comes out of voluntary retirement to work out if and how he was wrong, and where Felicia might be. Lynn (Liev Schreiber) is still grieving for the wife and son he lost in an accident and the partner who killed himself. The question of whether these many sorrows threaten to make him reckless in pursuit of the truth or merely relentless is one of the many uncertainties that will come to infuse the story.His late partner’s child, Saga (Zazie Beetz), is an FBI agent who has become a surrogate daughter to Lynn. Which is why he is not best pleased when, as the police begin to suspect that Walter has smuggled out a note telling an accomplice to release Michael, she insists that the best way for them to find out more is for her to go undercover as a patient at the facility.In she goes, parlaying her experience with a long-institutionalised mother into something useful – palming pills, fighting off assaults from other staff members and behaving badly enough to get herself sent down to the basement and become Walter’s neighbour. Can you pretend to be criminally insane without jeopardising your own sanity? Can you instigate a relationship with someone who lives to unearth weaknesses in others and exploit them without getting suckered in?
