Can you exist within a dehumanising system and keep your sense of self, let alone a professional self, intact? More uncertainties and ambiguities gather.‘I felt like I was a made man’: Stephen Graham on working with his childhood heroesRead moreNocturne is adapted, by Rowan Joffé, from two volumes of the Joona Linna series by Lars Kepler (the nom de plume of husband-and-wife team Alexander Ahndoril and Alexandra Coelho Ahndoril). As with most Scandi noir, their books are slow burns, and so too is Nocturne, though the series’ focus is narrower – there is less space given to the impact of Walter’s crimes on the community and more to his present influence on those around him.This means that certain roles are underdeveloped, despite some beautiful work from the cast (particularly veteran character actors Bill Camp as the harrowed police chief and Chrissy Metz as the children’s mother). They do, however, give glimpses of how the series might have been strengthened by a little more emphasis on the trail of suffering caused rather than just its execution; if perhaps a few twists and revelations had been cleared for emotional delineation and investment instead. There is a slight but growing sense as the series wears on that it is just a bit less impressive than it was shaping up to be, a little more hollow than it thinks.Then Graham appears again and the adrenaline that floods your system in the presence of his radiant evil pushes all rational thoughts from your mind, and you are captivated once more. It is the perfect watch for Halloween, especially for those of us who are always more horrified by the menace that stalks the earth in all-too-human form than by anything they say the supernatural can throw at us.Nocturne streams on Apple TV from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionStephen GrahamThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Big Moon: Forever review – the hell of hearing loss inspires a defiantly hopeful pop-disco marvel | Music | The Guardian
description: After frontperson Juliette Jackson lost half her hearing, she wrote sad songs and felt frustrated. So she pivoted, writing herself a happy ending. The results are joyfully convincing
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: After frontperson Juliette Jackson lost half her hearing, she wrote sad songs and felt frustrated. So she pivoted, writing herself a happy ending. The results are joyfully convincing
Content: ‘An extra frisson’ … Celia Archer, Juliette Jackson (in red), Soph Nathan and Fern Ford of the Big Moon.Photograph: Melanie LehmannView image in fullscreen‘An extra frisson’ … Celia Archer, Juliette Jackson (in red), Soph Nathan and Fern Ford of the Big Moon.Photograph: Melanie LehmannMusicReviewThe Big Moon: Forever review – the hell of hearing loss inspires a defiantly hopeful pop-disco marvel(Fiction)After frontperson Juliette Jackson lost half her hearing, she wrote sad songs and felt frustrated. So she pivoted, writing herself a happy ending. The results are joyfully convincingDave SimpsonThu 29 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the outside, it looks as if things have gone swimmingly for the Big Moon. Fronted by Juliette Jackson, a former waitress who dreamed big, they have been active for 12 years, a success in itself in these days, notching up four albums including this latest. They have enjoyed a Mercury nomination (for 2017 debut Love in the 4th Dimension), decent chart positions, good-sized gigs and streaming figures in the hundreds of thousands, or millions in the case of 2019 single Your Light.View image in fullscreenThe Big Moon: Forever.Delve beneath the surface, however, and things haven’t always been so sunny. After their debut’s ramshackle wide-eyed pop, second album Walking Like We Do detailed the travails of contemporary womanhood, and Your Light found Jackson bemoaning her generation’s lot with a weary resignation: “We were promised the world, but so was everyone else”. 2022’s Here Is Everything was conceived during Covid and processed Jackson’s life-changing experience of becoming a mother, including the disorienting experience of lack of sleep. Tricky stuff, if nothing that made Jackson’s concerns much different from vast swathes of the population.Forever, though, has a much more troubling backdrop. In 2024, the singer was diagnosed with a cholesteatoma – a destructive cyst inside the middle ear that requires surgical removal. It caused her to lose most of her hearing on one side, which would be an alarming and unbalancing experience for anyone, never mind someone whose life and livelihood centres so much on sound. As she admits: “It was pretty much existential, because writing songs is my job and my identity.” When she was even able to think about writing songs, she understandably found herself writing material so throughly miserable she didn’t like it. At which point she did a complete volte face, and began writing songs not just to cheer herself up but actively imagining “a happy ending that didn’t exist yet”.The Big Moon: Gravity – videoThere are historical precedents for such a sudden pivot from agony to ecstasy. One thinks of New Order throwing off the bleakness of Ian Curtis’s death, and their grand but morose debut Movement, to blissfully reconfigure for Temptation and Power, Corruption and Lies; the Cure’s mid-80s pop rush after years of magnificently anguished albums, or Bon Iver’s move from the melancholy For Emma, Forever Ago, recorded in an isolated log cabin, to the lush, more celebratory Bon Iver, Bon Iver. Here, Jackson’s personal shift results in a collection of joyous, uplifting, ethereally classy pop-disco tunes that have an extra frisson because they have come about through sadness. Shimmery opener Gravity clings to the simple joy of picking up your child from nursery, an unlikely but effective launchpad for a rapturous pop song with shades of Dreaming-era Blondie.Three Things celebrates youth and pop (“My whole life imminent / I remember living inside the songs on the radio”), the wistful undercurrent carefully smothered in bouncy, MGMT-style keyboard riffs and juddering sequencers straight out of new wave and disco. The universally relatable Fun imagines a life beyond constraints – “I’ll slip away and take my brain on holiday” – the dreamily summery sounds recalling Haim and, appropriately, Madonna circa Holiday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I’d rather live through something publicly than escape it privately’: Jack Antonoff on survivor’s guilt and still singing love songs after his breakupRead moreIf Jackson’s lyrics have a recurring theme, it’s of relishing – rather than fearing – life’s transience. Delicate harmonies, Fleetwood Mac production gloss and Soph Nathan’s big guitar twangs power recent single F.O.R.E.V.E.R, a rather poetic song about grabbing moments and milestones while we can, because “some day the ocean will include the drinks that we spill / And rain that used to be red wine will fall on this hill”. The yearning, classic 60s pop-tinged Can I Get a Reading Please picks up the theme: “Life’s not long, regret is though / Can you tell me something I don’t know?” The slightly country Sounds gets even darker – “I’m going to lose something very dear to me, if not now eventually” – but such shadows are more than banished by the overall musical sunniness and loveliness.The Bananarama-ish I See You, Honey seems to celebrate the comfort of being loved (“There’s no need to say ‘I love you’, it’s everywhere to me”). Other songs celebrate the power of determination as Jackson is “pushing through” obstacles in Speed Bump or insisting “I can give a good life / As long as I’m still on my feet” during Sounds. The album’s sense of finding joy in sometimes difficult circumstances crystallises on the wonderfully titled You Remind Me That I’m Dying (And That It’s Good to Be Alive), those words providing what may well be this year’s most bittersweet euphoric chorus. “Happy endings that don’t exist yet” or not, the song is an absolute banger, which suggests Jackson and her band really do have a lot to smile about.This week Dave listened toNell Davies – Never Ever EverI caught this Penzance-based DIY singer-guitarist’s ace set in Leeds. She tours by train and sounds, wonderfully, like an effervescent, witty, one-woman Buzzcocks.Alexis Petridis is awayExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bram Stoker’s Dracula audiobook review – cinematic horror with an A-list cast | Bram Stoker | The Guardian
description: Jonathan Bailey, Ella Purnell, Aimee-Lou Wood, Maggie Gyllenhaal and more bring shock and gore to an immersive retelling with real bite
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: Jonathan Bailey, Ella Purnell, Aimee-Lou Wood, Maggie Gyllenhaal and more bring shock and gore to an immersive retelling with real bite
Content: Gothic garlic-wielding … Maggie Gyllenhaal.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/Getty Images for NetflixView image in fullscreenGothic garlic-wielding … Maggie Gyllenhaal.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/Getty Images for NetflixAudiobook of the weekBram StokerReviewBram Stoker’s Dracula audiobook review – cinematic horror with an A-list castJonathan Bailey, Ella Purnell, Aimee-Lou Wood, Maggie Gyllenhaal and more bring shock and gore to an immersive retelling with real biteFiona SturgesThu 29 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo we really need another retelling of Bram Stoker’s fabled horror novel, which has already yielded multiple films, plays and radio dramas? Perhaps not, but this new audio version of Dracula, directed by Mary Lambert and adapted by Robyn Aherne, justifies its existence with an unusually star-studded cast, a streamlined story and an immersive and frequently nightmarish sound palette.Bridgerton’s Jonathan Bailey is smooth and charismatic as the eponymous count who invites a young solicitor, Jonathan Harker (Louis Partridge), to his castle in Transylvania to assist him with the sale of a property. There, Harker becomes increasingly uneasy as he glimpses the count’s diabolical powers and realises that he is, in fact, a prisoner.Meanwhile, there are strange goings-on in Whitby, England, where Jonathan’s fiancee Mina (Ella Purnell) is visiting her friend Lucy (Aimee Lou Wood). Shortly after a Russian ship is found wrecked on the shore with its captain murdered and its crew nowhere to be seen, Lucy has an unusual encounter in a graveyard that leaves her with puncture wounds on her throat and prone to night terrors. David Jonsson plays the doctor who tends to Lucy, while Maggie Gyllenhaal is brilliantly cast as garlic-wielding vampire hunter Van Helsing.This adaptation comes with a haunting score by Ilan Eshkeri and cinematic sound that plunges the listener into Dracula’s castle with its disembodied voices and echoing corridors (this is a series best heard via headphones). It doesn’t shrink from the shock and gore, either, even though the blood-sucking scenes are done sparingly and without a hint of camp.Available via Audible Originals, 5hr 57minFurther listeningA Rebel and a TraitorRory Carroll, HarperCollins, 11hr 24minThe Killing Thatcher author trawls through letters, police reports and declassified government documents to tell the story of Sir Roger Casement, the British diplomat who became an Irish nationalist and fierce critic of British imperialism. title: Britten: Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings album review – Wilson explores British music’s highway and byways | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The Sinfonia and John Wilson bring warmth and sparkle to works by Ireland, Walton and Goosens; rising star tenor Laurence Kilsby and Christopher Parkes are expressive soloists in the Britten Serenade
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The Sinfonia and John Wilson bring warmth and sparkle to works by Ireland, Walton and Goosens; rising star tenor Laurence Kilsby and Christopher Parkes are expressive soloists in the Britten Serenade
Content: Seriously impressive … tenor Laurence Kilsby.Photograph: Benjamin ReasonView image in fullscreenSeriously impressive … tenor Laurence Kilsby.Photograph: Benjamin ReasonClassical musicReviewBritten: Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings album review – Wilson explores British music’s highway and bywaysSinfonia of London/Wilson/Kilsby/Parkes(Chandos)The Sinfonia and John Wilson bring warmth and sparkle to works by Ireland, Walton and Goosens; rising star tenor Laurence Kilsby and Christopher Parkes are expressive soloists in the Britten SerenadeClive PagetThu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 10.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is John Wilson and the Sinfonia of London’s third album exploring British music for strings and, like its predecessors, showcases lesser-known repertoire alongside an acknowledged masterpiece. In this case, the byways include music by Ireland, Walton and Goossens with Britten’s Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings as centrepiece.View image in fullscreenBritten: Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings album cover.Written with the country on the brink of war, Ireland’s Concertino Pastorale comes with a baked-in nostalgia for an imagined rural idyll. Wilson gets to the troubled heart of the matter with a brooding Eclogue and poignant Threnody before finding release in the upbeat Toccata. The Sinfonia of London string sound displays a tremendous warmth in Chandos’ spacious recording, especially evident in Goossens’ lyrical nature poem, By the Tarn.Walton’s Sonata for String Orchestra, a late work from 1971, is a mix of honey and vinegar with an affecting central Lento. The counterpoint comes up polished and gleaming in the sparkling Presto and a syncopated finale.Laurence Kilsby and Christopher Parkes are the soloists in an expressive performance of the Britten. Like the young Peter Pears, Kilsby has a light, supple tenor that floats through Cotton’s dusk-infused Pastoral and Keats’ Sonnet and lends brilliance to Tennyson’s Nocturne and Jonson’s Hymn. Parkes, for his part, is sure-footed and sonorous. Horn and orchestra slightly overpower the voice at the terrifying climax of the Lyke-Wake Dirge. Nevertheless, this is a seriously impressive and subtly inflected account by Kilsby, a rapidly rising star.Listen onSpotifyExplore more on these topicsClassical musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Mad Lover review – eccentric charm and baroque brilliance as duo move from Eccles to Indiana Jones | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Part of the London Festival of Baroque Music, lutenist Thomas Dunford and violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte’s concert struck a balance between freewheeling music-making and precise virtuosity
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Part of the London Festival of Baroque Music, lutenist Thomas Dunford and violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte’s concert struck a balance between freewheeling music-making and precise virtuosity
Content: ‘Freewheeling’ … violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte and lutenist Thomas Dunford.Photograph: Sophie OliverView image in fullscreen‘Freewheeling’ … violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte and lutenist Thomas Dunford.Photograph: Sophie OliverClassical musicReviewThe Mad Lover review – eccentric charm and baroque brilliance as duo move from Eccles to Indiana JonesSmith Square Hall, LondonPart of the London Festival of Baroque Music, lutenist Thomas Dunford and violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte’s concert struck a balance between freewheeling music-making and precise virtuosityErica JealThu 29 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Mad Lover was a 1616 play with incidental music by the English composer John Eccles. But, as the lutenist Thomas Dunford explained, we didn’t really need to know that: he and the violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte just liked the title. You can imagine it fitting many more programmes this duo might play together in the future – as they surely should, judging by the amount of fun they were having here.The two recorded this 75-minute programme of music by Eccles and his 17th-century contemporaries back in 2020, but this performance of it was their first in London. It was part of the week-long London Festival of Baroque Music – the last before a two-year break while the festival’s venue, Smith Square Hall, is refurbished – and struck a balance between freewheeling music-making and precise virtuosity.The hall was set up with a low platform in the centre, the audience on all four sides. The musicians walked in playing, the neck of Dunford’s lute swinging over our heads, Langlois de Swarte’s violin tone muscular yet sweet. An Eccles Aire gave way to a sonata by Daniel Purcell, then to an improvisation from Dunford, one of many: sometimes authentically baroque, sometimes expressing a more modern melancholy. Dunford also played the troll, throwing in snippets of Indiana Jones or Radiohead to make his colleague laugh.One of Dunford’s reveries morphed into the familiar repeating harmonies of La Folia, the 12-bar blues of the baroque period, here in a piece by the obscure London composer Nicola Matteis. The Fantasia in A minor by his son, Nicola Matteis Jr, was a web of chords delicately seesawing back and forth across the strings, and should be every violinist’s next encore. In Matteis Sr’s C Major Suite, one of Dunford’s lute strings unfurled, but he worked around it so skilfully that you could barely tell.Finally, Dunford persuaded an unusually willing audience to sing, thus providing harmonies first for a Henry Eccles piece drawing on a tavern song, then for a mystery encore based on JS Bach: the Beatles’ Blackbird, a song that can’t help being beautiful, and a fitting sign off given this concert’s eccentric charm.TheLondon Festival of Baroque Musiccontinues until Saturday. The Mad Lover is available onHarmonia Mundi.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Are You With Me Now? by Hanif Kureishi review – a novelist unleashed | Hanif Kureishi | The Guardian
description: The constraints of Kureishi’s life after a devastating accident infuse his writing with a new and thrilling immediacy
Author: Melissa Denes
Headline: The constraints of Kureishi’s life after a devastating accident infuse his writing with a new and thrilling immediacy
Content: Hanif Kureshi.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHanif Kureshi.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianBook of the dayHanif KureishiAre You With Me Now? by Hanif Kureishi review – a novelist unleashedThe constraints of Kureishi’s life after a devastating accident infuse his writing with a new and thrilling immediacyMelissa DenesThu 29 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome months after returning home, after a grim year in hospitals in Rome and London,Hanif Kureishibegins to rebel. Not against his family, or the physical reality of beingtetraplegic(and how could he?), but the liberal homogeneity of Shepherd’s Bush. He gets a diamond stud in his left ear at Westfield shopping centre, a piercing that enraged his father when he was 17. He sends off for a Maga cap and wears both to the farmers’ market, hoping for vitriol but getting nothing. “These quiescent scumbags only cared about themselves and their shopping,” he grumbles. “Being a fascist is far less thrilling than I imagined.”Kureishi’s “re-punking” after decades in the metropolitan elite remains an ongoing project, just one response to his paralysis after a fall on Boxing Day 2022. His memoirShatteredwas written in the long shock of that severance from a former life, which left him with no movement in his hands or legs, “a Beckettian chattering mouth”.But Kureishi’s mind remains intact, even unleashed: free from the pull of a phone (he can’t scroll), he is funny, nostalgic, profound, petty and never sentimental, not even about the family he relies on. His latest collection of essays, co-written with his son Carlo, takes its title from a song he used to listen to while driving in Italy, his partner Isabella at the wheel while he smoked a fat joint. (It’s also a question his iPad asks him in Shattered – “Are you still there?” – when paralysis leaves him unable to hit refresh.) Now, Carlo is always with him as he dictates, each chapter the product of a conversation between 10am and 1pm. The book has a more outward-looking feel – less stunned, less homesick, sometimes transcribed as a dialogue.double quotation markThere are great, gossipy digressions on taking acid with Billy Idol, a schoolmate, and his friendship with David BowieThese back-and-forths have a distinctive energy. An argument over what to write becomes a disquisition on art versus politics, Kureishi wanting to reflect on beauty, Carlo insisting that the only subject is Gaza. An experiment with a sex chatbot hits a wall of shared embarrassment. Carlo convinces his father of AI’s usefulness – but their collaboration is the perfect illustration of its limits: here are two humans with a long history of navigating each other’s weaknesses with love.Where to start with: Hanif KureishiRead moreThere are great, gossipy digressions on taking acid with Billy Idol, a schoolmate, and Kureishi’sfriendship with David Bowie. Bowie would call at 2am with an urgent question about serial killers, when Kureishi was “a new father of twins, dressed in only my underpants”. Dennis Hopper, Kureishi’s co-juror at the 1992 Venice film festival, was a disappointing square. Isabelle Huppert was a “sweet and intelligent” ally as jury president at Cannes 2009, “a frantic, crazy party that you could never leave”. He misses it all, but these memories push the horrors of the spinal injuries ward – the patient crawling across the floor at 2am, the bodies removed at dawn – that bit further away.Meanwhile, Kureishi has a house full of strangers, a drama he plays as comedy and farce. There are the carers fighting in the kitchen, and the nice woman who tells him “I really don’t like penises” as she washes his. Someone always has a finger up his arse. He and Carlo are working on a movie about his accident: who will play them, they wonder? But life is mostly a thousand small humiliations: in the park, an acquaintance pats him on the head.Kureishi revels in a new kind of writing – the essays were originally drafted as Substack posts – discursive, energised by a readership that writes back. His best novels have a clear-eyed quality that can border on cruelty – the famous “fucks for which a person would have their partner and children drown” in the autobiographical novel Intimacy. Here, that deep attention to his own ego expands to the world around him and becomes fiercely illuminating. What a thrill it is to be here, he writes from the edge of the abyss, as well as frustrating and often boring.The book ends with his marriage to Isabella, Elton John pulling up in a cherry-red Bentley. Kureishi is rawdogging life, he tells his son Sachin, in the gen Z sense of doing it without distraction: “I am compelled to be present”. Sex is difficult, but desire – for everything – remains. This exhilarating book looks death and decay in the face and asks: is that all you’ve got?Are You With Me Now? by Hanif Kureishi with Carlo Kureishi is published by Hamish Hamilton (£20). title: Night Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head trip | Games | The Guardian
description: You take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbing
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: You take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbing
Content: Unsettling … Night Plane.Photograph: Liquid StaticView image in fullscreenUnsettling … Night Plane.Photograph: Liquid StaticGamesReviewNight Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head tripLiquid Static Studio; PCYou take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbingKeith StuartThu 29 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 07.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was always something creepy about the job-simulator genre. All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop.Now, we have Night Plane, in which you take on the role of a flight attendant on a jumbo jet to hell. It all starts kind of normally. You turn up for the first day of your new job, meet your colleagues, then take your spot at the departure gate, checking in customers and being careful to root out anyone with invalid tickets. Once on the plane, you roll your trolley down the aisle, serving booze and inedible meals, and occasionally dealing with passenger complaints. Then the plane crashes and, frankly, it all goes downhill from there.View image in fullscreenWeird existential horror … Night Plane.Photograph: Liquid StaticAre you dead? Are you in purgatory? And what was that weird creature someone spotted on the wing just before the engines blew up? All you know is, you’re back at the airport, checking in customers again, only this time, some of them are demons disguised as humans and you’re the one who has to sort the people from the people-eaters.Rendered in glitchy low poly visuals, Night Plane is another indie horror game that mimics the technical limits of the original PlayStation era to unsettle the player (see also Crow Country and Fear the Spotlight). The passengers already scare you with their boxy heads and expressionless faces, so when ghostly figures start walking across the aisle and disappearing, you’re already drowning in the uncanny valley. As the game goes on, the dialogue gets weirder, and then just turns into stutters and noises, the lights in the cabin flicker, luggage lockers open and close and rattle, and weird noises follow you. There are elements of the backrooms as well as Japanese onryō movies, as you warp between the plane and the airport, finding yourself trapped in endless passenger lounges and baggage claim areas, being pursued by heaven knows what.It’s all overlaid with a droll sense of humour, so you tend to be laughing to yourself moments before a jump scare jolts you out of your seat. At the outset, New Zealand-based developer Liquid Static Studio cleverly lures you into thinking this is a daft horror spoof, and it kind of is, but its use of nightmarish imagery – from piles of dead rats in the janitor’s room to a recurring image of your burning plane’s wreckage strewn across a remote wilderness – is genuinely disturbing and rife with sick imaginative details.Horror is increasingly the genre through which games dissect and examine themselves and their conventions, and Night Plane is a clever, absorbing example. You can “complete” the game in four or five hours, but subsequent playthroughs will reveal new sub-quests and endings, and priced at less than a tenner, it’s a steal. Even if you never set foot onboard this plane again, it gives you a fascinating budget flight into weird existential horror – and you’ll never take your cabin crew for granted again.Night Plane is available nowExplore more on these topicsGamesPCRetro gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Sea review – Jennifer Saunders takes fussing over buying curtains to Shakespearean levels | Stage | The Guardian
description: Edward Bond’s play about consumerism and the strength of humans in dark times is hugely enlivened by Saunders and her tight-lipped pomposity
Author: Holly O'Mahony
Headline: Edward Bond’s play about consumerism and the strength of humans in dark times is hugely enlivened by Saunders and her tight-lipped pomposity
Content: ‘Consumerism as a distraction from the pain and absurdity of life’ … Jennifer Saunders and Lucy Briers in the draper’s shop.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreen‘Consumerism as a distraction from the pain and absurdity of life’ … Jennifer Saunders and Lucy Briers in the draper’s shop.Photograph: Marc BrennerStageReviewThe Sea review – Jennifer Saunders takes fussing over buying curtains to Shakespearean levelsTheatre Royal BathEdward Bond’s play about consumerism and the strength of humans in dark times is hugely enlivened by Saunders and her tight-lipped pomposityHolly O'MahonyThu 29 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen describing his own play, the late playwright Edward Bond said he wanted The Sea to deal with tragedy, be a comedy and end with people being as honest and open as they could. Jonathan Munby’s production – the first major revival in almost 20 years – begins by offering its audience a view that would ordinarily be obscured: we’re plunged underwater to where the seafaring Colin (Elliot Goodhill) hangs suspended from a rope, fighting for his life, as the waves of Luke Halls’ impressive videography engulf him.It’s a fitting opening sequence for a play that subsequently demands its audience look beneath the surface to find meaning in seemingly trivial interactions. It’s jarring when, come the following scene, we’re flung into a draper’s shop, where Jennifer Saunders’ avaricious, egotistical Mrs Rafi is fussing over curtain material. But Bond understood consumerism as a distraction from the pain and absurdity of life. Similarly, his characters sing their hymns ever louder when there’s gunfire in the distance. They also stage an annual play to raise money for their seaside village’s coastguards, while maintaining distance from any trouble their beneficiaries face on the ground.View image in fullscreenDressed in black … Saunders and the rest of the cast in the Bond revival.Photograph: Marc BrennerSaunders brings tight-lipped pomposity to the imperious Mrs Rafi, though her early snobbishness mellows into something more mischievous towards the end. Her character’s late speech on her disappointment in, but dependency on, others rivals Shakespeare’s Jaques in its melancholy wisdom. Meanwhile, the reclusive Evens (an enigmatic Lloyd Hutchinson) seems like a stray Beckett character with his musing on striving to find faith amid the seeming meaninglessness of it all. The play’s setting in 1907 affords these characters a listlessness that, we imagine, could well give way to a carpe diem spirit were they to live through the first world war.Bond also wanted his play to capture the strength of human beings. Though the death of Colin – “for whom the future seemed all brightness” – initially leaves his fellow sailor Willy (Sean Delaney) and fiancee Rose (Holly Godliman) with a loss of purpose, in closing on a half-spoken thought between them, it ultimately ends on a note of hope.AtTheatre Royal Bath, until 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreJennifer SaundersTheatre Royal BathreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sarah Howe wins Forward poetry prize for best collection | Poetry | The Guardian
description: Howe’s ‘exceptional’ Foretokens took the main £10,000 award, while Nur Turkmani, Tara Bergin and Biff Smith swept up the remaining categories
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Howe’s ‘exceptional’ Foretokens took the main £10,000 award, while Nur Turkmani, Tara Bergin and Biff Smith swept up the remaining categories
Content: ‘A quite brilliant return’ … Sarah Howe.Photograph: Marc LixenbergView image in fullscreen‘A quite brilliant return’ … Sarah Howe.Photograph: Marc LixenbergPoetrySarah Howe wins Forward poetry prize for best collectionHowe’s ‘exceptional’ Foretokens took the main £10,000 award, while Nur Turkmani, Tara Bergin and Biff Smith swept up the remaining categoriesEmma LoffhagenThu 29 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarah Howe has won the Forward prize for best collection, one of the UK’s most prestigious poetry awards, for Foretokens, a collection that explores new parenthood, the death of her father and her mother’s early life in Hong Kong.Howe was announced as the winner during a ceremony hosted by Joelle Taylor at London’s Southbank Centre on Saturday evening, and will receive £10,000.Howe was born in Hong Kong to an English father and a Chinese mother. Foretokens, her second collection, comes a decade afterLoop of Jadebecame thefirst debut to win the TS Eliot prize. Foretokens was also shortlisted for the 2025 TS Eliot prize.Reviewing Foretokensfor the Guardian,Rishi Dastidar called it “a quite brilliant return”, praising Howe’s “keen, probing intelligence”. “Taking on the biggest of subjects – genetics, time’s relativity, becoming a parent – as well as re-examining her mother’s occluded history in Hong Kong, there is now an anger in Howe’s tonal range, which brings a pleasing sharpness to her investigations,” he wrote.View image in fullscreenThe 2026 Forward prize winners, Nur Turkmani, Sarah Howe, Biff Smith and Tara Bergin.Photograph: Forward prizeThe Forward prizes’ co-executive director, Mónica Parle, described Foretokens as “an exceptional collection” that “can emerge after 10 years in the making and still bear distinct relevance to our time”.The prize also recognised three other winners. Nur Turkmani, a Lisbon-based poet who grew up in Beirut, won the £5,000 Jerwood prize for best first collection for October, which was also shortlisted for this year’s PEN Heaney prize. The poems were mostly written in Beirut during a period when “there were protests, wildfires, economic collapse, a port explosion and an ongoing war”, Turkmani said, “and writing became a way of seeing, understanding and continuing”. It is the first nomination and first win for her publisher, the independent Hajar Press.The Dublin-born poet Tara Bergin, who teaches creative writing at Newcastle University, won the Forward prize for best single poem in written form for The Fear, first published in the Irish literary magazine the Stinging Fly. “Many years ago I devised a poetry writing class called ‘Fear Poetry’,” she said. “I got so interested in the whole idea I had to try it myself.”The Scottish singer-songwriter Biff Smith, who won both the Scottish and World Poetry Slam Championships last year, received the prize for best single poem in the performance category for Dumbarton East, recorded at the Scottish performance night Loud Poets. Smith wrote the poem on a train: “So much of life is spent in transit, I feel an urge to make that time count – do some knitting, learn Italian or whatever (maybe even write a poem).” Bergin and Smith each received £1,000.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis year’s judges were the novelist Sarah Moss, who chaired the panel, alongside Romalyn Ante, WN Herbert, Michael Mullen and Yomi Ṣode. “In months when the world could easily seem darker every week, it was consoling to be called back into poems and collections and performances day after day,” said Moss, “not because poetry is any kind of panacea but because poets give us words, images and metaphors for what matters in interesting times.”The Forward prizes were established in 1992 and have recognised some of the biggest names in poetry, including Seamus Heaney, Ted Hughes and Claudia Rankine. Last year,the best collection prize was sharedfor the first time in its history, between Vidyan Ravinthiran for Avidyā and Karen Solie for Wellwater.Explore more on these topicsPoetryForward prize for poetryAwards and prizesSarah HowenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comeback  | Music | The Guardian
description: As John Lewis reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players, music fans share their reasons for ditching streaming
Author: Alfie Packham
Headline: As John Lewis reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players, music fans share their reasons for ditching streaming
Content: Young people select and listen to CDs in a music shop in Munich.Photograph: Sueddeutsche Zeitung Photo/AlamyView image in fullscreenYoung people select and listen to CDs in a music shop in Munich.Photograph: Sueddeutsche Zeitung Photo/AlamyMusic‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comebackAs John Lewis reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players, music fans share their reasons for ditching streamingAlfie PackhamThu 29 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCDs appear to behaving a resurgence. John Lewis said searches for CD players are up 96% since July, whileanother reporton trends in music and film this year found that CD sales are up 16%.With this in mind, we asked music fans why they favour discs over other formats, and if it is a new preference or a lifetime habit.‘I have well over 10,000 CDs’View image in fullscreenAndrew Wales says his wife is very considerate about his CD collection.View image in fullscreenMore of Wales’s CD collection.Andrew Wales, 67, from London, owns “well over 10,000” CDs. “My wife’s very considerate,” he says over the phone. “There’s quite a few in this room where I’m speaking.” They have also spilt into the next bedroom and into the corridor.“I don’t need Spotify,” says Wales. “The fact is, I like listening to music and I have always preferred owning it in a physical form. The [size of the] CD format allows me to own the number I own despite living in a two-bedroom flat and not a country mansion, so that’s another bonus.”Much of the classical music Wales buys and listens to is available only on CD. “I bought my first CD in 1991 – John Scofield, Meant to Be – around the same time that I bought my first CD player. LPs were becoming increasingly shoddy, both in terms of pressing and presentation, and their limitations meant that often or not songs or tracks were included on the CD release, but not on LP. There are still cases where that happens today.”That said, Wales also owns “about 2,000 LPs”, “a few hundred cassettes” and an increasing number of Blu-rays. “I’m not always wedded to a single format.”‘After having a baby, our records were too bulky and inconvenient’View image in fullscreenGabriela Crowley with her daughter and her CD player.Unlike Wales, Gabriela Crowley, 32, from San Jose, California, started listening to CDs only over the last year. “Growing up, my parents had a tonne of them,” she says. “My dad played them in the car and everywhere. And then he got an iPod. By the time I was like 18, everything had started to shift away from physical media.”‘I don’t give a damn what people think any more!’ Jimmy Webb on his wild days – and writing hits for Dolly, Glen and FrankRead moreHer return to physical records started with the vinyl trend a few years ago. “I met my husband, who also had a large record collection, and we enjoyed that hobby together for a while. But after having a baby, we found we really weren’t listening to our records much any more – they were too bulky and inconvenient. My father-in-law gave us one of his old CD players and now we use that every day.”A CD collection helps with the “paradox of choice” that streaming brings, she says. “Instead of being paralysed by the endless options, you become more intimately familiar with what you have. I find it a much more satisfying way to engage with music. Plus, no autoplay or AI-generated playlists are being forced on me.”‘I buy CDs directly from the bands’View image in fullscreenNeil Cumming has several hundred CDs from classical to folk, rock and blues.“I bought my first CD in 1988 and have been collecting ever since,” says Neil Cumming, 53, from Gloucester. “I have several hundred of them. Everything from classical, folk, rock, blues …”Cumming buys CDs mostly to support musicians. “I like a lot of small indie and folk bands, who are not making a lot of money. I buy CDs directly from them when I can, which means they get a bigger share of my money than they would if I streamed their music.“And it means I own the CD for ever,” he says. “Streaming means you are basically renting the music, and it can disappear from the streaming sites. I enjoy the ritual of selecting a CD and putting it in the machine – it is a nicer experience than just pressing play on an app.”Not that he’s anti-streaming. “It’s quite good for trying music before you buy CDs or finding new acts. But in the evening, with a mug of tea or a glass of whisky, I find the experience of a CD more satisfying.”‘The antithesis of scrolling’View image in fullscreenAsha Varadharajan says the patience required in listening to a whole CD makes songs memorable.“I am drawn to the narrative and aesthetic arc of an album,” says Asha Varadharajan, 65, from Toronto. “It’s the antithesis of scrolling. I’ve never been a fan of music as white noise in the background, unless I’m boogying while vacuuming.”Varadharajan has owned her CD player since 1999, “which allows me to listen to five CDs at a time in any order I choose, building my own narrative arc as I listen.“I’m grateful to friends who introduced me to artists I may never have listened to,” she says. “The patience and persistence required in listening to a CD makes songs memorable. Streaming makes music ephemeral. I think algorithms make everything predictable, but everybody’s taste is kind of random.”It helps that CDs are hard to damage, she says. “I’m a klutz and was terrified of scratching albums as a child because I never could place the needle accurately without my hand shaking.”View image in fullscreenVaradharajan’s CD player allows her to listen to five CDs at a time ‘in any order I choose’.‘They give me something tactile and tangible’Ed, 63, from London, bought his first CDs in 1986 – “Genesis, Invisible Touch, and Level 42, World Machine, if you must know” – and has “never stopped”, he says. “But my interest in the format has waxed and waned.“When they first came out, CDs were very much positioned as: they’ll last for ever, you can drill holes in them, you can put jam on them and they still play. But I got put off CDs because they sounded too bright and shiny compared to vinyl.”But over the past two years, Ed has bought more CDs owing to their “almost throwaway prices against the excessive costs of vinyl”. Having music on CD “gives me something tactile and tangible”, Ed says. “A good digital source is now every bit as engaging as a good record player.”Explore more on these topicsMusicRetail industryMusic industryPop and rockMusic streamingCollectingVinylfeaturesShareReuse this content
