title: What an eight-hour power cut taught me about food stockpiling | Food | The Guardian
description: After government advice to stockpile, how do you prepare for an emergency? A deep pantry might be the answer
Author: Morwenna Ferrier
Headline: After government advice to stockpile, how do you prepare for an emergency? A deep pantry might be the answer
Content: Stock up … you can slowly fill your pantry for times of need.Photograph: Noel Bennett/AlamyView image in fullscreenStock up … you can slowly fill your pantry for times of need.Photograph: Noel Bennett/AlamyFeastFoodWhat an eight-hour power cut taught me about food stockpilingBlue cheese and sardines can only get you so far. What you need in an emergency is a deep pantrySign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastMorwenna FerrierThu 29 Oct 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 08.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m writing this from the North Sea coast, where I’m in a semi-enforced lockdown at my in-laws’ house. It’s only temporary. Like most of the UK, storms Austen and Boelo hit us in quick succession, and we’ve been in and out of power cuts ever since. We were in the kitchen when the first storm hit and we slipped into an eight-hour power cut.Of course we didn’t know it would be eight hours at the time, so you can only imagine the panic-raid lunch of all the things we worried might go off: blue cheese and cold chicken on semi-defrosted bread; fridge-cold stewed apple with warming yoghurt; and, finally, a thumb of goat’s cheese with some dark chocolate that I found in my bag. Once the rain stopped, we headed to a pub seemingly untouched by this so-called “weather bomb” and had chips. All in all, a fairly civilised array of picky bits, though I appreciate goat’s cheese and chocolate isn’t for everyone, which is why I ate them in the bathroom.I’d already been wondering about the timing ofthe government’s Be Ready campaignlast week, which urged us to keep enough supplies to manage for 72 hours. Maybe it wasn’t just about tapping into our autumnal urge to pickle and preserve, after all. It was only once the power went off that I actually bothered to read the National Resilience Checklist before the wifi went, too. For three days, it recommends three litres of water per person per day, as well as enough non-perishable food (tinned meat, fish and vegetables, dried fruit and nuts) to get you through.With the next few days in mind, I did a quick inventory of my in-laws’ store cupboard. And while I enjoy capers, white marzipan, sardines, dried dates and cannellini beans in their own way, 72 hours suddenly felt like a lifetime. Spotting a pouch of Merchant Gourmet Spanish-style grains, I briefly flirted with the idea of hiding it in another cupboard for leverage, before accepting that might be a bad vibe. Had we been at home, it would have been coconut milk, Jaffa cakes and various seeds.View image in fullscreenNo cooking required … Meera Sodha’s vegan chickpea, tomato and cucumber salad.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianDespite government advice, I had planned to avoid Tesco, assuming it would be overrun by panicked locals and denuded shelves. There’s a logic to panic shopping in times of panic, but we’re not there yet, guys! If we start rapidly changing our buying habits, we risk dismantling an already precarious system that can adapt only so much. The so-called doom boom – the surge in doomsday prepping – will make things only worse; one person’s stockpile is another person’s shortage. It’s worth remembering that local community resilience matters much more than any fancy bunker planning.Still, fear can be powerful, which is probably why I’ve made a list of things we should add to our next few shops. I’m aiming for a more “deep-pantry” method: buyingtwo or three extra items a week max, and only what we’d want to eat tomorrow. There is something strangely relaxing about pulling together a no-cook dinner from a more prudent shopping excursion, particularly with all-year salads. Meera Sodha’sno-cook chickpea and tomato saladis a winner at mine even if there’s no power cut. I love the idea of Harumi Kurihara’sHijiki seaweed saladbecause I have most of the ingredients, and in retrospect I probably could have made Anna Berrill’ssardine and celery saladthis week. Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’s recipe forsardine and red onion saladtakes five minutes to cobble together.Other than that, if I learned anything from those eight long hours out here, it’s the following: sweetened condensed milk can be both a pudding and a coffee whitener; got kids? Get UHT milk for cereal; most prepper-friendly meals tend to come from canned food, but think about pouches, too; think first in, first out, and place new food at the back of the cupboard or fridge, so you eat the older stuff first; think about food not as an add-on but as the whole meal (canned smoked mussels go well with canned white beans, say); and, finally, if youreallywant chips, make sure you have a cooking stove, and consider planting potatoes. They are weirdly easy to grow.My week in foodView image in fullscreenScarce … cornichons are perfect in a variety of sandwiches.Photograph: imageBROKER/AlamySandwich saint|It’s been over six months since Pret stopped selling its only good sandwich, the jambon beurre,due to a possible cornichon shortage. I’ve spent almost all that time perfecting my own version using ingredients from Lidl. Then, the other week, I got a tip-off that chef Pascal Wiedemann atPompettein Oxford makes the best version, not least because every single element – baguette, ham, cornichons, butter, dijon mustard – is made in-house. It takes him three days from start to finish, and they sell it every day! I’m particularly excited by the ham, which comes from the Tamworth pigs at nearbyPaddock Farm. I’m off to Oxford next week, so will report back.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFlying solo|I’m very much married with children, but have been vicariously enjoyingEli Davies’ The Spinster Cookbook. Memoirs and recipes always make the best reading, though don’t buy this if you want only recipes – the first one, about drinking vodka and “fancified” toast, doesn’t land for about 70 pages. It’s more of a manifesto for single women that follows Davies’ relationship to cooking and domesticity as a single woman in a family-size world. Imagine Katharine Whitehorn scarfing Kettle Chips over the sink, and you’re halfway there.TV dinners|I have become quietly fascinated by the contestants’ eating habits onThe Traitors. The way they balance plates of lasagne and chopped salad on their laps. The sheer quantity of toast and juice consumed at breakfast – and why no one touches the pastries (according to previous contestants,they’re stale). I did a deep dive on Reddit to find out what’s in those jars in the kitchen, and can confirm: Skittles, dried apricots, dates and Haribo gummies.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: The rise and fall of mid-century modern: how millennials fell out of love with their favourite look | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Once coveted for its clean lines and timeless design, the functional furniture is no longer seen as cool. Anyone for cottagecore and chrome?
Author: Sarah Phillips
Headline: Once coveted for its clean lines and timeless design, the functional furniture is no longer seen as cool. Anyone for cottagecore and chrome?
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design; Dorling Kindersley; David McGlynn; Jordan Lye/Getty Images; Mnmlc; Goddard New Era; Alene Photographs; Yaroslav Litun; Sergey Skleznev/Alamy/View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design; Dorling Kindersley; David McGlynn; Jordan Lye/Getty Images; Mnmlc; Goddard New Era; Alene Photographs; Yaroslav Litun; Sergey Skleznev/Alamy/Life and styleThe rise and fall of mid-century modern: how millennials fell out of love with their favourite lookOnce coveted for its clean lines and timeless design, the functional furniture is no longer seen as cool. Anyone for cottagecore and chrome?Sarah PhillipsThu 29 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Idefinitely don’t think it is cringe,” says Laura Budds, a vintage furniture dealer based in Norfolk. “But I do think we have reached the peak, and we’re on the descent.” Budds is talking about mid-century modern furniture, which has recently come under fire from younger generations for being – like so many things, includingtrainer socksandhigh-waisted jeans– a deeply millennial aesthetic. As the Wall Street Journaldeclared: “Midcentury modern design has met the fate of pumpkin spice lattes, cocktails in mason jars, no-show socks, leggings and other aspects of millennial culture: it has become cringey.”Budds, 44, is resigned to the fact that she is a “mid-century millennial”. She’s even made a career out of it: she sells furniture and vintage clothes atWilliams & Parfitt, a modern antiques centre in Wymondham, Norfolk. But she says she has had to diversify in recent years to cater to changing tastes among younger customers, who are moving away from the “wall-to-wall mid-century” look beloved by the generation above them. She says of gen Z: “I don’t think they are so bound by the eras or designers – they just buy what they like. They aren’t afraid of older antiques and will have a bit of whimsy or taxidermy.”The term “mid-century modern” was originally coined to refer to architecture and design that became popular from the 1940s to the 1970s, largely in the US, Brazil and Europe. Famed for its clean lines and simplicity, the style had visual forebears in the Bauhaus movement and classic Scandinavian design, along with the philosophy of beautiful yet functional furniture for the masses that spread to the US, UK and beyond in the postwar era. British-made items include Ercol and Robin Day chairs and G Plan teak sideboards, all of which are still coveted. (Anglepoise’s timeless industrial lighting, too, was associated with the aesthetic.)View image in fullscreenLaura Budds, in a Wassily armchair by Marcel Breuer, for Knoll.Photograph: Supplied imageThe book Mid-Century Modern: Furniture of the 1950s, written by Cara Greenberg and published in 1984, is often seen as being responsible for popularising the phrase. Today, she says, the term has “become meaningless, applied to everything from museum-quality material to made-in-China repros on eBay”.Greenberg lives in Brooklyn, New York. Her first mid-century purchase was an Eames plywood lounge chair bought at a street market in NYC in the 1970s, which she still owns. These days, she is more interested in a comfy sofa: “not a mid-century modern speciality”, she says, given the aesthetic’s tendency for furniture to be fairly upright and firm, often designed with polite conversation in mind rather than slouching and scrolling.But, Greenberg says, she will still defend the best of it “as the most innovative and stylish furniture America ever came up with”: Charles and Ray Eames, the husband and wife duo who revolutionised design with multipurpose chairs; George Nelson’s industrial looks for the furniture company Herman Miller; Eero Saarinen’s Tulip chair for Knoll. Since then, she says, “there have been many cycles of revival, including the reissue and mass marketing of ‘best of’ classics by the original companies in the 1990s”.Affordability has always been a cornerstone of mid-century design. “The philosophy of modernism and mid-century design, when it first started, was accessibility,” says Keith Stephenson, who lives in Camberwell, south-east London with his partner, Mark Hampshire. Together they run the design and homewares companyMini Modernsand co-authored the 2019 book Mid-Century Modern Living: The Mini Moderns Guide to Pattern and Style. “It was never supposed to be an elitist thing,” he says. “It was about bringing good design at a good price to as many people as possible. Reaching more people with good design is never a bad thing.”View image in fullscreenClassic no longer? An Eames lounge chair and ottoman.Photograph: Nikreates/AlamyIt is also ideal for smaller spaces, which is one of the reasons Hampshire thinks it has “endured many a cycle of trends” to become “the endlessly go-to period of design”. The postwar period was “the first time that designers considered function and aesthetics together – so furniture was designed to solve a specific problem as well as to fulfil a function. The results of this level of considered design have, in many cases, proved hard to beat, thus becoming the template for subsequent designs.”He gives an example: “If you look at a classic mid-century style sofa, it is on legs, so you can see the floor underneath it – and that makes a place feel much bigger, because you can read the room around the piece of furniture. There’s room to breathe. All of those things are classic interior design tricks to make a place look and feel more spacious.”Mid-century modern’s design quality and price point made it irresistible to millennials who were starting to live independently in the 2010s. It fitted with the vintage aesthetic of the time and there were still bargains to be found. Even as late as 2019, says Budd, “you could find sideboards at auction for £50. Now you’re lucky to get one for less than £300-£400.” A lot of British mid-century modern has been shipped abroad in recent years, to Europe and as far as Japan, where consumers have cottoned on to British brands such as Ercol, G Plan and McIntosh. This has pushed prices up and “made it a bit too elitist. Only certain people can afford the really good quality stuff now,” says Budd.View image in fullscreenIrresistible … a showroom full of mid-century modern wares.Photograph: Elena Rostunova/AlamyThe interior designerNatasha Landershas lived in her home in Walthamstow, east London, for 26 years. Her mid-century bookcase cost £30 when she bought it, and her £50 coffee table would now sell for £200. “It’s not as accessible as it was when I first started collecting,” she says. Still, she’s reluctant to write off the whole aesthetic just because it has been widely used. “Good design doesn’t have to become bad design because it is popular,” says Landers. “There is something slightly snobbish about deciding something is no longer cool simply because more people can enjoy it. What I do have a problem with is when everyone’s houses look the same.”The proliferation of millennial style on the go-to interior design sources Pinterest and Instagram has inevitably meant that the high street and large webstores have capitalised on the trend. New furniture clearly inspired by classic mid-century modern pieces can now be found everywhere from Marks & Spencer and Dunelm to H&M and Temu.“That craze for buying a full set of mid-century tables, sofas and lighting is definitely gone,” saysCarina Harford, an interior designer from west London. “It had a paint-by-numbers experience to it that might have felt safe to its devotees but began to feel too commonplace.” The climate impact of “fast furniture” is also a consideration. “The imitation mid-century furniture that was coming out a lot in the last five or so years really irked me,” says Harford. “Stop buying new things if you don’t need them.”View image in fullscreenSpace-age surface … a G Plan Astro coffee table.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesIt is this desire to avoid having identikit homes that is fuelling the mid-century modern cringe. “I really don’t want to have the same things as everyone else,” says Sheree Millington, a copywriter based in Margate, who is renovating her Victorian terrace. Lucy Hayes, a writer and director in east London, agrees. “I like a mix of styles and ages, and things that don’t feel rooted to a particular decade or era. I want my home to feel like it exists now rather than as a time capsule.”Millington thinks a more quintessentially English style is coming back in, “whether that is cottagecore, or more like an English townhouse, with lots of mismatched things, more pattern, more print”. She is noticing chrome – a staple of 1990s homeware that has since fallen out of favour – becoming more popular again, too.Harford’s home is kitted out with secondhand treasures spanning many different eras and styles: “It’s all just sort of mushed together, and I think it works.” Most of it was bought from auctions and cost about £100 or less. Highlights include a Victorian fold-out card table (bought for £110), lighting from a shuttered billiards hall (£40), a 1940s Anglo-Indian table (£30) and a set of 1980s stools (£90 for four). Although bidding can seem more complicated than buying new online for next day delivery, you quickly get the hang of it, she says, and the result is, “something much more special and unique”.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleDesignInteriorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Despite the teething issues, Dyson’s Camerajet toothbrush packs in a lot of clever tech – but is it worth £420? | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: Dyson’s first electric toothbrush watches you brush and flosses for you, but there are far cheaper ways to get an effective clean
Author: Alan Martin
Headline: Dyson’s first electric toothbrush watches you brush and flosses for you, but there are far cheaper ways to get an effective clean
Content: Camera ready: Dyson’s pricey brush peeks inside your mouth and fires water jets between your teeth.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCamera ready: Dyson’s pricey brush peeks inside your mouth and fires water jets between your teeth.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterHealth & wellbeingReviewDespite the teething issues, Dyson’s Camerajet toothbrush packs in a lot of clever tech – but is it worth £420?Dyson’s first electric toothbrush watches you brush and flosses for you, but there are far cheaper ways to get an effective cleanThe best electric toothbrushes for every budgetAlan MartinThu 29 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenDyson announced it was entering the toothbrush market, the world responded almost as one: “Four hundred and twenty pounds? For a toothbrush!?”No, it wasn’t a stray decimal point – or if it was, Dyson is doubling down and leaning into the mistake. Unlike high-end brushes from Oral-B or Philips Sonicare, where the “recommended” in “recommended retail price” is doing a heroic amount of heavy lifting given the frequent discounts, the Dyson CameraJet will actually set you back £419.99.The CameraJet is an electric toothbrushanda water flosser, so if you were being charitable – or merely looking for a way to justify the cost to yourself – you could call this two for the price of one on thebest electric toothbrushesandwater flossers.There’s a lot of clever technology here, and Dyson’s commitment to doing something different should be applauded, even if it’s just to give your hands something to do besides reaching for your credit card.Note that the brush has had some bad post-launch publicity with multiple online accounts of the pricey purchase failing within weeks. This led to the CameraJet vanishing from virtual store shelves for a time, withDyson blaminga “single component issue affecting a small number of early batches”.I had no such issues with my review unit, and the brush is now back in stock everywhere. Nonetheless, it’s worth remembering that the more intricate moving parts in a product, the more opportunities for breakage.View at DysonView at John LewisHow I testedView image in fullscreenGood vibrations? Reviewer Alan testing the hand and mouth feel of the Dyson CameraJet.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianI’ve become something of a pro toothbrusher in the past two years, having tested dozens of models for our list of thebest electric toothbrushes. Theprocess isn’t a big secret: it just involves brushing to an obsessive degree while observing several factors, including how it feels in the hand and mouth, how easy it is to use, how portable it is and how clean your teeth feel afterwards. It’s a similar story for flossers, with the water tank capacity measured too.There are also objective details you can assess, such as power and battery life. Because the last thing you want is to wait for your brush to charge when you just want to go to bed.Dyson CameraJet: what you need to knowView image in fullscreen‘The camera means you can watch a live stream from the inside of your mouth on the Dyson app.’Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianView at DysonView at John LewisDyson isn’t the first manufacturer to combine an electric toothbrush and water flosser into one product – Irecently testedthe Soocas Neos II, which I deemed a “a jack of two trades, but a master of none” – but this is the first one I’ve used that does both jobs well enough to warrant a recommendation.There are a few reasons for this. The handle is a normal width for an electric toothbrush, rather than distended to hold the water. Unlike regular cordless flossers, where you have to awkwardly refill the reservoir by hand, here a dock tops it up with a single button press.The main advantage, though, is the camera. The 100,000-pixel macro-lens camera sits inside a hollowed-out section of the brush head and captures 28 images of your mouth every second, which Dyson’s machine-learning algorithm uses to identify gaps between teeth. When it finds one, a blast of water or mouthwash is automatically fired into the gap. This camera also means you can watch a live stream from the inside of your mouth on the Dyson app, should you have exhausted the contents of Netflix.The 12.5ml tank is described as “anti-gravity”, meaning the diaphragm pump and pressure chamber adapt to how you’re holding the brush, ensuring that it always has liquid to dispense. This is a big plus over other water flossers, where the “straw in a cup” system often misses the dregs when holding it at the angle required for hard-to-reach places.The jet, Dyson says, is also different from those fired by other water flossers. Working with the National University of Singapore, which helped develop a proxy plaque (a lab stand-in for real dental plaque), the company claims to have found that traditional “needle-type” jets merely punctured a hole in the sticky surface, rather than removing it. Dyson instead opts for a conical shape that it says “sweeps and removes plaque at once”, while being gentler to gums and enamel.So the expense is justified via R&D and clever technology. Note that the high price of entry doesn’t end with the brush itself, as you need bespokereplacement headsto work with the camera, and these cost £25 for two (though your first pair come in the box). The brush heads have an RFID (radio-frequency identification) tag that enables the toothbrush to monitor how often the head has been used and let you know when it needs replacing.Dyson CameraJet specificationsType:variable sonic oscillationModes:three cleaning modes and three brushing intensities (plus water jet)Power:58,000 movements a minutePressure sensor:yesBattery life:up to 10 daysApp:yesWarranty:two years, with 12 months for the brush head cover (registration required if you buy at a third-party retailer)Replacement head cost:£25 for twoWhat we loveView image in fullscreenPlaque, camera, action: the toothbrush’s camera is designed for closeup work.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianWhile the words “camera” and “bathroom” usually shouldn’t be found in proximity to one another, it’s pretty harmless here. It can’t be manually turned off, but no images or video are saved.According to Dyson, “the camera is only active during live viewing or auto-jetting. No images are recorded or stored on the product or in the cloud”. And, even if they could be, the lens isn’t designed for selfies; it only works up close. I mean, can you really tell much about my house from this picture?When used on your teeth, it’s an eye-opening experience, giving you the kind of private screening usually reserved for dental professionals. And, while the dentist has given my teeth a professional signoff in recent trips, seeing a closeup of the discoloration that comes from 40-plus years of chewing is an incentive not to cut any more dental hygiene corners.Intentions are one thing, and actions are quite another. We all know that we’re supposed to floss daily, but how many of us do? Even with water flossers for convenience, it’s too easy to skip it when you’re at the sink.The beauty of the Dyson CameraJet is that it makes that choice for you, and my teeth and gums undoubtedly felt the benefit. Because the jets fire automatically, flossing becomes a part of the brushing process. The result? My smile felt and looked healthier without any extra effort.That’s in part down to the dock, which is a marvellous innovation. As well as charging the toothbrush, the 200ml tank at the back offers a one-touch refill of the CameraJet’s 12.5ml reservoir –put your toothbrush in the dock, hold the button and the reservoir will refill. While you’ll still need to top up the main tank every few weeks, the refill system is significantly more convenient than all other cordless flossers I’ve tested, which either require you to unscrew a tank or awkwardly pour mouthwash or water through a small refilling hole. Crucially, this ensures flossing isn’t an easily skippable step. Dysonrecommendsusing its own low-foaming mouthwash to fill the tank, but you don’t have to.View image in fullscreenPort of call: the CameraJet in its dock, which charges it, and features a 200ml tank.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianThe battery life of 10 days may sound low to some, but it’s important to remember it’s powering a light and camera, as well as the usual motor, even if it is still disappointing to see the battery life dropping 5% as you explore your mouth with the camera. Ultimately, it’s a non-issue with the aforementioned dock: you’re unlikely to ever find yourself out of battery if using it as intended.The performance itself is good too, leaving my mouth feeling squeaky clean. Whether that’s down to the added jets or the fact that it defaults to three minutes rather than the usual two is open to debate, but the cleanliness factor puts it close to the top of the list of thebest electric toothbrushesI’ve tried (though I still find theLaifen Wave Proslightly more effective at defuzzing stickier areas after an evening on the cider). The brush rotates 58,000 times a minute, and the mouthwash distribution via the jet leaves a dentist-fresh feeling when everything works as planned …What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenHole again? Could a blocked camera beneath the bristles be causing the auto-firing issues?Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianThat cliffhanger of a last sentence was a giveaway to my first criticism: the jets don’t always automatically fire (though you can activate one manually at the press of a button if you feel an area is neglected). Through trial and error, I’ve concluded that the most common reason for the jets to take an unwelcome breather is that the camera is blocked, so it can’t see teeth.I believe this is because of toothpaste foaming up in use. When I’ve connected to the live-stream camera, the experience reminds me of trying to see out of the window when going through a carwash. And when it gets too foamy, the jets stop working until you spit out some toothpaste or have your tongue moonlight as a kind of windscreen wiper for the camera. It’s a messy experience, and your bathroom mirror won’t thank you.For this reason, it’s recommended you’re choosier with your toothpaste.Dyson sells its own recommended low-foam paste and mouthwashthat I was able to try, and this significantly improves the experience. With my regular foamy toothpaste, the app reported the jets were usually firing between 25 and 50 times per three-minute session (and on some occasions dropping to single digits). With non-foaming toothpaste and regular spitting, it settled on a fairly reliable 70 to 80.A cynic would point out that this is convenient for Dyson, diverting users from cheaper brands to its own consumables (from £8.49 for 75ml toothpaste; £8.49 for 400ml mouth rinse) for the long haul – you can even subscribe on the website. You can buy non-foaming toothpaste that isn’t Dyson-branded, but it’s not easily found in supermarkets, taking away a little of the hard-won convenience. I also tried Suri’slow-foam toothpastewith it, which worked reasonably well.View image in fullscreenRead all about it: the CameraJet’s manual is essential for decoding its operation.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianThe CameraJet is confusing to use at first, too, which somewhat eats into those convenience credentials. Having reviewed a lot of toothbrushes, I can usually get away with skipping the instructions and getting straight into testing. I quickly learned that wasn’t an option here, and I’ve found myself constantly revisiting the manual to remind myself of the buttons and decode the occasional sounds it makes.One such sound is a warning that you’re brushing incorrectly. Typically with electric toothbrushes, you hover over the tooth and move slowly along, but the Dyson CameraJet requires you to make small oval shapes as you progress. But even when I’ve been following this advice, I’ve been told off for overscrubbing. This makes me think the CameraJet’s either overzealous, or its instructions aren’t clear enough.The good news is that this can be overcome with the use of Dyson’s app to guide you through proceedings. This will tell you when the camera is blocked, and also keep a tally of its water jets, warning you if you’re moving too fast. The app is optional and can be ignored once you’ve got the swing of things, but what can’t be so easily brushed away is the size of the kit. The brush is already on the tall side at 273mm, but the dock takes this even further with a height of 315mm.Nominally, this can be used as a travel case by slipping on a clear plastic cover, but it’s pushing the definition of portable, and will not easily slip into carry-on luggage without clever organisation. Yes, you can take it without the dock and just use the bundled pogo-pin charging cable, but it’s a less elegant solution than the Suri Pro 2.0’s charging travel case, which by my measure is a svelte 241.3 x 31.75 x 31.75mm.More philosophically, while the Dyson CameraJet has made my mouth feel very clean, I wonder if it could lead buyers into a false sense of security with their dental health. The convenience is great, but it leaves you to rely on the camera to detect every gap and fire accurately and at the right time, which isn’t guaranteed. The jets fire so fast that I’d defy anybody to tell the difference between mouthwash hitting the target between teeth and misfiring nearby. With a regular water flosser, the nozzle forces you to hit every gap, even if it is an added hassle, and while there’s a manual flossing mode, without the camera AI, it feels hit and miss.Beyond that, from speaking to dental professionals in the past, the jury is still out on whether water flossing is as effective as using interdental brushes. Sam Jethwa, president of the British Academy of Cosmetic Dentistry, compares flossing to cleaning an algae-covered boat. “Get a hosepipe to try to get it off, it’s not going to do anything,” he told me, arguing that you need “mechanical movement” alongside water to make an impact. So, while my teeth did feel far better than just using an electric toothbrush alone, I’m not sure this is quite the one-stop solution Dyson would like it to be.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenIt’s a brush head-to-head: the Dyson CameraJet and our highly rated flosser, the Waterpik Ultra Professional.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianAll of which brings us to the price: £419.99. Without wanting to state the obvious, that’s a huge amount of money, even taking into account that this is a 2-in-1 device. You could buy our top-rated toothbrush (theLaifen Wave Pro) and flosser (theWaterpik Ultra Professional) for under £200, or both our bargain picks (theOdonta PowerPlusandOperan Cordless Oral Irrigator) for just over £50. And that’s probably what you should do.SustainabilityWhileDyson publishes its own sustainability magazine, there’s as yet nothing about toothbrushes in it. Nor is there any mention on the product page of the Dyson CameraJet’s green credentials.Perhaps this is doing the company a minor disservice, because as well as the RFID tag in the brush heads informing you when they need changing, the company also does more than most in terms of spare parts. Although currently all listed as out of stock, you can buy areplacement battery,dock and reservoir cap, andanti-gravity tank, should any of yours give up on you outside the two-year warranty period. Awhole new refill dock can also be bought.All that’s good, but notably Dyson doesn’t currently offer a recycling programme for its brush heads, as rivals such as Suri and Ordo do.Dyson CameraJet: should I buy it?View image in fullscreen‘It offers a solid clean, and … makes flossing something you can virtually forget about.’Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianDespite its eventful launch, you can’t deny that the Dyson CameraJet is an impressive bit of tech, proving that there’s a surprising amount of room to innovate in the world of toothbrushing. In my weeks of testing, I found that it offers a solid clean, and the fact it makes flossing something you can virtually forget about is a godsend to those of us who often find ourselves skipping that all-important step. While it’s easy to be cynical about the price, it’s doing a lot of clever things, and I would be surprised if we didn’t see a range of imitators launching over the next few years.But clearly, it’s far from perfect, given how easy it is to block the camera, and its substantial travel-unfriendliness.More importantly, considering you can buy our top-rated toothbrush and flosser for a combined £182.10, is paying more than double what you need for some added convenience sensible? Unless your money-to-sense ratio is extremely off-kilter, probably not.View at DysonView at John LewisDyson CameraJet vs …Waterpik Ultra ProfessionalView image in fullscreen£89.99 at Waterpik£82.11 at AmazonYour brush doesn’t need to contain built-in water flossing, with plenty of stand-alone models to choose from. They’re mostly wireless, but if you’ve got the counter space and a bathroom shaver socket, you can’t beat the Waterpik Ultra Professional corded model, my favourite overall from testing.You don’t have to worry about keeping a battery charged, nor are you constantly topping up the water tank because of the built-in 650ml reservoir. On top of that, the nozzle is easier to aim and manoeuvre as it doesn’t have the bulky reservoir built into the handle. The only downside is you can’t easily take it on your travels, where floss or disposable interdental picks will have to sub in.For more, read our guide to thebest water flossersSoocas Neos IIView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£99.99 at Soocas£84.99 at AmazonIf you’re dead set on a two-in-one device but don’t have Dyson money, the Soocas Neos II fits the bill. It also has a built-in water tank, with water-flossing jets fired manually via a small hole in the toothbrush head. It does, however, feel like a jack of all trades and master of none, and I feel you’re better off buying independent devices instead.Lining up the water flosser between teeth is tricky as it doesn’t have tapered tips to direct the jet, nor a camera system like Dyson’s to identify the gaps for you. As a toothbrush, it falls short of the best, in part because the water tank makes the handle bulky. Nonetheless, it does save space overall, and at just under a third of the price of the Dyson CameraJet, it’s worth a look.Laifen Wave ProView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£119.99 at Currys£99.99 at AmazonOur current favourite electric toothbrush is the Laifen Wave Pro. While most brushes make you choose between sonic vibration and physically oscillating heads, the Laifen Wave Pro includes both, with speeds of up to 66,000 vibrations per minute for the former, and a neck that twists left and right up to 60 degrees for the latter.The result is not only an impeccable clean, but something that can truly be customised to your tastes. The accompanying app lets you adjust vibration intensity, oscillation range and speed from scores between 1 and 10, giving you more than 1,000 possible combinations to ensure it’s just right. There’s no water flossing as there is with the Dyson, but for pure brushing, it can’t be beaten – and it’s about a quarter of the price.Suri Pro 2.0View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£105 at Suri£109 at BootsThe need to change the heads on electric toothbrushes makes them environmentally problematic. But Suri has put sustainability at the centre of its design, and while it’s not perfect, it’s one of the strongest options on the market, thanks to its use of plant-based heads (made from cornstarch, with castor oil bristles) that can be sent back to Suri free of charge for recycling.The Suri Pro 2.0 is a big improvement over the original, with less fragile chargers and a pressure sensor built in. It’s not the most powerful brush in town, but if sustainability is your number-one priority, it’s one of the best options (there’s also the cheaperSuri Core 1.0, of course).Read my fullSuri Pro 2.0 reviewFor more:The best electric toothbrushes for every budgetHow to make your toothbrush last longer – and keep it out of landfillSuri Core 1.0 electric toothbrush review: this new budget model is still sustainable – and the one I’d buyExplore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingThe FilterGadgetsBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu – recipe | Italian food and drink | The Guardian
description: A historical adventure deep in the very heart of pasta country in southern Italy unexpectedly unearths a sauce dish with roots in Senegal
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: A historical adventure deep in the very heart of pasta country in southern Italy unexpectedly unearths a sauce dish with roots in Senegal
Content: Rachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkRachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu – recipeA historical adventure deep in the very heart of pasta country in southern Italy unexpectedly unearths a sauce with roots in SenegalRachel RoddyThu 29 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 30 kilometres south of Naples, the town of Gragnano is surrounded by the Monti Lattari mountain range – the limestone backbone of the Sorrento peninsula. Historically, a series of natural springs fed into a larger stream called Vernotico, which flowed down the mountainside, passing through what was at the time the small village of Gragnano.The natural slope of the terrain was fortuitous, because it allowed for the construction of a sequence of mills, which started in around 1263. During a visit to Gragnano last month, local historian Giuseppe Di Massa explained how it all worked; how gravity drove the flow of water from one mill to the next, in order to power vertical millstones – a system created for the inconsistent flow. The valley, with its clever water system, became known as the valley of the mills; its role milling grain, which arrived at the nearby port of Castellammare di Stabia, a vital operation to Naples and surrounding towns.The activity of the 30 mills peaked during the 18th century, but another industry was growing, one that harnessed another natural aspect of the town: its climate. The temperature, humidity and sea breeze were ideal conditions for drying pasta.Often in strings hung over wooden frames, pasta was dried in the streets of Gragnano, then moved inside when necessary; the skill of the pasta makers and their ability to harness the weather every bit as important as the weather itself. And the industry grew. According to the city of Gragnano website, by 1859 there were 81 pasta factories, requiring ever increasing amounts of hard durum wheat for their pasta, while the mills produced soft wheat. The mills ceased operations in the 1950s, and were largely abandoned until renovation projects turned some of them into small museums.What has continued to grow in Gragnano, though, is the tradition and art of pasta making; now with its own Indicazione Geografica Protetta, which protects its quality (provenance of wheat, how it is extruded, how long it is dried) and connection with the region. These days, 23 producers – from tiny to vast, 15 of which make up a consortium – make more than 100,000 tonnes of pasta annually in carefully controlled conditions – conditions very different from the open streets, but requiring just as much skill. I returned to Rome with bags of pasta from seven different makers – Di Martino, Faella, Garofolo, Liguori, Afeltra, Antiche Tradizioni di Gragnano, Ducato di alfalfi – all of which pleased me with their nutty scent, porous texture and resilience in the pan.I also came back from Gragnano with a recipe devised for the town’s Mondopasta festival this year by chef Astou Ndiaye. Born in Dakar and now living with her family in Milan, Ndiaye’s cooking draws both on her heritage and her home. For her beautiful Senegalese ragu, the meat (I used lamb) is marinated in an aromatic blend of vegetables, coriander and cloves before being braised for a stew soft enough to be pasta sauce. I usedcandele(hollow tubes) made by Garfalo, which I broke into short lengths. It’s a dish that sums up the spirit of pasta di Gragnano, I think; rooted in both Gragnano and Dakar, and at home anywhere.Pasta with Senegalese-inspired lamb raguServes41 stickcelery,trimmed1 small red pepper,trimmed, deseeded and cut into strips1 shallot,peeled1 small bunchcoriander2garlic cloves,peeled3 clovesSalt600g boned lamb shoulder,cubedOlive oil1 large onion,peeled and diced1 tsp paprika1 tsp garam masala400-500g pasta(broken candele, maccheroni, mezze maniche)Working in a food processor, pulse the celery, red pepper, shallot, coriander, garlic, cloves and a pinch of salt into a rough mixture. Put half the mixture into a bowl, add the meat, then toss so all the chunks are coated. Cover and leave to sit for two to 24 hours (if it’s three hours or more, put it in the fridge).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWorking in a large, heavy-based pan, warm four teaspoons of olive oil. Working in batches, brown the marinated meat, then lift out on to a plate.Add the diced onions to the empty pan, along with the remaining blended mixture and marinade, paprika and garam masala, and stir well, adding more water if it seems too dry. Add the meat, stir again, then add 300ml water. Bring to a simmer, then cover for two hours. By the end of cooking, the meat should be extremely tender and falling apart in just a little thick gravy.In a separate pot, cook the pasta in salted boiling water according to the packet instructions. Meanwhile, put half of the ragu into the bottom of a warm serving bowl. Lift the cooked, drained pasta on top, toss, adding more ragu as needed, then toss again.Explore more on these topicsItalian food and drinkA kitchen in RomePastaFoodWest African food and drinkMain courseMeatVegetablesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The high drama of volcanic wines | Wine | The Guardian
description: Is it a taste or just a feeling? Not to get woo-woo, but ashy landscapes give wines an energy
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Is it a taste or just a feeling? Not to get woo-woo, but ashy landscapes give wines an energy
Content: Volcanic landscapes impose particular demands on vines.Photograph: Dirk Renckhoff/AlamyView image in fullscreenVolcanic landscapes impose particular demands on vines.Photograph: Dirk Renckhoff/AlamyWineThe high drama of volcanic winesVines on volcanic soil are hard to grow and their grapes are hard-won, but it all combines to produce wines with a very particular sense of placeMina HollandThu 29 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGood stories need jeopardy. TakeThe Princess Bride, one of my favourite films, which I recently introduced to my mildly terrified children. It’s a cult love story of high peril: Westley, believed dead, sets out to win back Buttercup (forced into marriage with another) on a quest involving pirates, duels, torture, a miracle and a battle of wits over a goblet of poisoned wine. There is struggle, magic and, ultimately, emotional reward. You’ll need to stay with me here: volcanic vines, too, tend to have a rocky journey, albeit with happy results for the drinker.My ears perk up at the term “volcanic wine”, despite being less a style than a geological category. Volcanic soils take many forms – ash, basalt, obsidian, pumice, tuff – and interact with climate, altitude, water availability, grape variety and farming to produce wines with a very particular sense of place. Often, they have little in common with each other; a deep, rich nerello mascalese from Mount Etna’s north side bears little comparison to a light, leathery listán negro from Tenerife, say. And yet I’m sure thereissomething – perhaps it’s more a feeling than a taste – that I get from wines from volcanic terroirs. “It’s a hard thing to get across,” agrees importer Nic Rizzi ofModal Wines, “but they do have an extra tension.”Tension is the word. Volcanic landscapes impose particular demands: on Etna, for instance, the vines’ roots have to negotiate thin, stony soil formed from lava flows and ashfall; on Santorini, vines grow in loose pumice, ash and volcanic sand, with little rainfall and fierce winds; while in the Canary Islands, the vines can grow in deep layers of black ash. These are difficult landscapes to farm, but, as we know, a rocky journey does make for a good story.Rizzi imports wines made byVictoria Torres Pecisfrom La Palma in the Canaries, a place with “a majestic and wild energy”. There are black ash soils, vineyards above the cloud layer at 1,200m and ancient vines trained low to the ground to protect them from high winds. Farming here is labour-intensive; there are heatwaves and drought, and in 2021 a volcano erupted during harvest. “It takes a certain kind of person to put themselves through that pain and graft,” Rizzi says, “and that struggle comes through in the wine.” (Torres’ Las Machuqueras in today’s pick is a unicorn wine that sings deliciously of struggle.)Not to get too woo-woo about it, but, for me, volcanic wines share an energy. Legends have been built around volcanoes; they hold a mystical place in our imaginations. But, in very real terms, wines from these terroirs are deeply complex – saline, herbal, savoury and mineral – with a sense of tension that keeps you coming back. Like all interesting characters, their charisma is hard won.Volcanic wines that give you bang for your buckM&S Etna Rosato£14 Ocado, 12%. From high, lava-terraced vineyards comes this deeply hued, mineral rosé that goes with everythingBodega Volcanes Carménère 2024£12.50 Majestic, 14%. Energetic autumn red from one of Chile’s 3,000 volcanoes – expect dark fruit and umami.De Falco Fiordilava Falanghina del Vesuvio 2024£16 The Wine Society, 13%. The name means “flower of lava”, though it’s not floral, but rather a softly mineral falanghina from the slopes of Vesuvius.Rampazzi Bianco Andrea Occhipinti 2025£23.50 Sip Wines, 12%. Savoury and subtly smoky Tuscan beauty from above Europe’s oldest volcanic lake.Cave Verdier-LogelVolcanique Gamay Rouge 2024£20 Sourcing Table, 13.5%. At once juicy and peppery, this great-value Loire gamay hails from the volcanic basalt soils of the Massif Central foothills.Victoria Torres Pecis Las Machuqueras 2016/19£55 Modal Wines, 12.5%. Pricey, yes, but black ash soils, very old vines, harsh conditions and tiny yields combine to create a deeply textured and salty wineExplore more on these topicsWineFoodItalian food and drinkFrench food and drinkSpanish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content
