title: ‘I earn £126,000 – but nothing’s left at the end of the month’: readers react to the budget | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: From a young chef and a single father to business owners and a pensioner, Guardian readers reveal how John Healey’s measures will affect them
Author: Sarah Marsh
Headline: From a young chef and a single father to business owners and a pensioner, Guardian readers reveal how John Healey’s measures will affect them
Content: Graham earned £126,000 last year but says he has virtually nothing left in the bank each month.Photograph: Graham RobinsonView image in fullscreenGraham earned £126,000 last year but says he has virtually nothing left in the bank each month.Photograph: Graham RobinsonBudget 2026‘I earn £126,000 – but nothing’s left at the end of the month’: readers react to the budgetFrom a young chef and a single father to business owners and a pensioner, Guardian readers reveal how John Healey’s measures will affect themWhat the budget means for youSarah MarshThu 29 Oct 2026 04.32 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Most people my age have written off buying a home’Louie, 24, a chef living inLondon, says a lot of people have “written off the idea of even considering getting a property” in their 20s.He is optimistic about the government’s newYour First Homescheme, which will enable people to buy a new-build property with a deposit of just 2.5%, supported by an interest-free equity loan.But he says a smaller deposit alone will not be enough for him. “I’ve found hospitality wages to be far too volatile to even consider saving for a property,” he says.As a result, he is studying an access course with plans to start a physiotherapy degree next year. He hopes that by the time he graduates and gains some experience, he will have a stable enough income and sufficient savings to put down a deposit.He says the new scheme “should encourage a lot of young people to buy earlier” and adds: “We are moving in a good direction, but I’ll still save and wait until around late 20s to early 30s to start [thinking about buying], just due to how much it may cost me.”View image in fullscreenLouie says a new government scheme could make the prospect of buying a home feel more achievable.Photograph: Jonathan ClementsLouie earns between £37,000 and £40,000 a year and shares a three-bedroom rented property with two friends. But rent and bills take up an increasingly large proportion of his income, leaving little room to save towards buying a home.“I was always told that a third of your salary should go towards rent and bills, but it’s coming up to about half now, which is a little bit mental,” he says.His landlord recently informed the household that their rent would increase by £200 a month in November.He has managed to build up some savings. Since he was 18, he has put between 5% and 10% of his earnings into a stocks and shares investment account, and over the past year has also started making regular contributions to an Isa specifically for a house deposit.“Nobody really wants to be spending all their money on rent,” he says. “But with the amount of money we make, you kind of have to. ”‘I earned £126,000 last year – but still have nothing at the end of the month’Graham Robinson is a business owner from Timperley, Greater Manchester, who runs the company KeySim. He earned £126,000 last year, but says that despite his six-figure income, he has virtually nothing left in his bank account at the end of each month.Graham says he was “hoping for real help with the cost of employing people” from the budget. “Instead, the employment allowance stays at £10,500, while employers pick up the rising wage bill.”He adds: “The minimum wage increase is welcome for workers, but the government gets the headline, businesses get the bill and the Treasury recoups some through tax and national insurance.”The 45-year-old lives alone and shares care of his 10-year-old autistic son with his ex, covering all childcare costs himself.“I know £126,000 sounds like an enormous amount of money, but after tax it works out at broadly £6,500 a month, and that really doesn’t go as far as people might think,” he says. “I don’t have expensive cars, I don’t go on extravagant holidays. I don’t really do anything particularly lavish, but at the end of the month it’s all gone.”2:44Labour’s 2026 budget in under three minutes – videoHis mortgage payments have risen from about £900 a month to £1,300, while council tax, food, energy and other everyday expenses have also increased.Normally earning approximately £100,000 a year, he has increasingly relied on additional dividends from his business to cover rising costs.He is frustrated by the effective 60% income tax rate on earnings caused by the gradual withdrawal of the personal allowance on income over £100,000, which reaches zero when earnings reach £125,140.“To put an extra £1,000 a month in my take-home pay, my salary would need to rise from £100,000 to £129,757 a year,” he says.‘Our mortgage has increased by more than £600 a month’View image in fullscreenHelen welcomes the £100 winter payment for households like hers, but questions the methodology.Photograph: Jonathan ClementsHelen, 40, lives in south-west London with her husband and two children, aged eight and five. She is the main breadwinner, working in communications, while her husband runs his own architectural practice.Her house is in council tax band D, which means she will get a£100 energy paymentthis winter. She welcomed the extra money, but found the way it was being distributed strange, based on bands rather than financial need.She saysthe change offering self-employed people paternity paywas “great”, though now her children are older it would not benefit her family. She adds: “It was lovely to hearDolly Parton’s book schemementioned, as encouraging education for all is key.”Her family’s biggest monthly expense is their mortgage, which increased by more than £600 a month when interest rates rose. They have now fixed it until 2028.Helen saysfrozen income tax thresholdsare one of her biggest concerns, alongside getting the economy growing and the pressures facing small businesses. Her husband’s architectural practice is less than four years old and has struggled with the rising costs of building and a wider slowdown in construction.“The challenge comes down to the price of energy; for example, the cost of steel, transporting materials and building homes,” she says. “It impacts everything we make, build and buy.”‘I don’t know how people live on just the state pension’View image in fullscreenPeter thinks pensioners should pay tax if they can and backs changes to the triple lock.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianPeter Pillinger, 72, is a widower from South Ribble in Lancashire whose state pension makes up about half his income. He also receives a pension from his career as a Methodist minister, a small amount from his late wife’s pension and an allowance for his work as a local councillor.He is pleased with one of the key announcements: thescrapping of standing charges on gas bills. These are fixed daily fees that households pay regardless of how much gas they use.“My gas bill in the summer is almost entirely standing charge,” he says. “They are regressive. Putting all the costs in the unit charge will encourage people to reduce usage and to insulate their homes.”But he wonders why it will take until at least next spring for the change to come in. He also wants to know what the government will do “for those who need higher usage for medical reasons”.He supports thechanges to the state pension triple lockand believes pensioners who can afford to pay tax should do so. “If my income is £25,000 or approaching £30,000, why should it not be taxed? If everyone else is paying tax at that level, why should I not?”Conversely, he is concerned about those surviving on much less. “I don’t know how people live on just the state pension,” he says.‘Flowers are one of the first things people think to cut back on’View image in fullscreenDanielle says fuel costs are affecting the price of the flowers she buys and the expense of delivering them.Photograph: DanielleDanielle Walker, 37, is a self-employed florist based in Wakefield, West Yorkshire. She says rising fuel prices are squeezing her business from both sides, increasing the cost of making deliveries while also pushing up the price of the flowers she buys.She welcomes the chancellor cancelling the planned fuel duty rise, but adds “it doesn’t undo the increases we’ve already faced or take away the pressure we’re under”.Increasing the higher mileage rate from 25p to 35p a mile will not benefit her, she says, nor will the business rate threshold going up from £12,000 to £18,000, as she works from a studio.Budget 2026: key points at a glanceRead moreDanielle has spent considerable time calculating delivery charges for different postcodes to ensure they cover her fuel costs and the time spent travelling. But she says she is increasingly having to absorb some of these costs herself.“If I’ve quoted flowers for a wedding based on diesel being £1.40 a litre and it’s £2 by the time the wedding comes around, I’ve still got to get there. There’s only so much you can absorb for so long,” she says.With customers already struggling financially, she feels unable to keep passing on rising costs without risking a loss of business.“Flowers are a luxury item, and when people are feeling the pinch, they’re one of the first things people think to cut back on,” she says.Danielle believes the government should look at the impact of fuel duty and VAT on small businesses that depend on driving, arguing that independent traders are particularly exposed to rising prices.“Someone has to take it on the chin somewhere. I feel it’s unfair that small businesses are continually having to absorb these costs or lose customers by being honest about what delivery should cost.”‘I am a single dad. The more you earn, the less you keep’Jonny Roberts, 39, is a single dad from Newbury, Berkshire, with children aged 11 and eight. He works part-time at McDonald’s and as a tutor, while also studying for an online master’s degree. Between his two jobs, he works the equivalent of full-time hours. But even with support from universal credit, his income only just covers essentials.View image in fullscreenJonny is frustrated by the way universal credit reduces the financial rewards of taking on additional work.Photograph: Jonny Roberts“We had heard in the run-up [to the budget] there would be something on energy bills, and I’m sure millions of households are grateful for the extra £100 help towards that announced today,” he says. “But it was disappointing to see no announcement on whether local housing allowance [LHA] will be uprated.”For Jonny, one of the biggest problems is the gap between the housing support available through universal credit and the reality of renting. He is entitled to the three-bedroom LHA rate, which gives him £1,200 a month towards his rent, but he pays £1,300 a month for a two-bedroom flat.“The rent we’re paying isn’t particularly high for the area. It’s pretty much in line with the norm,” he says.“Last year’s freeze and the cuts of prior government mean the housing element of universal credit seems to live in an alternate reality to the actual rents charged in the south of England.”Jonny is also frustrated by the way universal credit reduces the financial rewards of taking on additional work.Budget 2026 calculator: find out if you are better or worse offRead moreFor every extra pound he earns above his work allowance, his universal credit is reduced by 55p. Once income tax, national insurance and student loan repayments are taken into account, he says the amount he keeps from an additional shift can be surprisingly small.With rent taking up the largest share of his budget, Jonny has little flexibility when other household costs rise. “I’m happy to go with less for myself to make sure I can feed all three of us,” he says.Jonny was happy to see a “speeding up of the rollout of free breakfast clubs to an extra 2,000 schools” but adds: “It still seems a glacial pace when there are 17,000 primaries in the country.”Jonny takes part inChanging Realities, a collaboration involving more than 200 parents and carers living on low incomes, researchers at the University of Glasgow andChild Poverty Action Group. The project documents families’ experiences of living on a low income and brings their voices into discussions about poverty and social security policy.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026BudgetFamily financesUK cost of living crisisPropertyMortgagesTaxnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Looming stone towers like Maya temples’: a hike through Snowdonia’s slate country | Snowdonia holidays | The Guardian
description: A new trail in the national park traces the legacy of Welsh industry, while offering some of the UK’s finest riverside and mountain walks
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: A new trail in the national park traces the legacy of Welsh industry, while offering some of the UK’s finest riverside and mountain walks
Content: The abandoned Cwmorthin quarry and lake on the 83-mile Snowdonia Slate Trail.Photograph: robertharding/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe abandoned Cwmorthin quarry and lake on the 83-mile Snowdonia Slate Trail.Photograph: robertharding/AlamySnowdonia holidays‘Looming stone towers like Maya temples’: a hike through Snowdonia’s slate countryA new trail in the national park traces the legacy of Welsh industry, while offering some of the UK’s finest riverside and mountain walksKevin RushbyThu 29 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 03.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe vital moment comes a couple of hours into the walk. I drop down from a tussocky hill towards the village of Y Fron. There’s an abandoned slate-quarrying machine and a grassy track that suddenly emerges on the rim of a deep lake-filled crater. The water is the colour of an old bruise. Around the rim is a fence of lichen-crusty slates like gravestones. It’s a dark, brooding spectacle and totally unexpected. At that moment, I know that whoever designed this route knew what they were doing.This is theLlwybr Llechi Eryri(Snowdonia Slate Trail), an 83-mile hike that follows a great loop around the national park, starting in Bangor and ending in Bethesda. It strings together a series of abandoned slate quarries with some of the finest riverside and mountain walking in the UK. I’m doing just three days, starting in Llanberis and heading to Betws-y-Coed via stops in Beddgelert and Llan Ffestiniog.Beyond Y Fron village, I descend into my first quarry, and it proves to be a classic. This was once the Dorothea slate quarry, a vast abandoned complex of railways, cottages and chasms. I start exploring: tunnels, cuttings, huge looming stone towers like Maya temples, all overgrown with ash, birch and oak. What strikes me is the craftsmanship and precision in construction, each stone hand-fitted without mortar, all for workaday industrial buildings.View image in fullscreenThe mountain village of Beddgelert makes a good pitstop for those hiking the trail.Photograph: Alex Manders/Getty ImagesThe quality of this slate was known from early times. Edward I is thought to have had his Welsh castles roofed with it, but industrial production began in the 1820s and peaked in the 1870s. Soon, there was a railway to Caernarfon and the area bristled with steam pumps, aerial cables and chains. The last-ever Cornish beam engine was installed to pump water from the deep pits, sucking up 10 gallons a second from 500ft down.From here, the trail burrows eastwards into the Welsh mountains, until Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) appears on the horizon when it turns south, occasionally following the line of theWelsh Highland Railwayall the way into Beddgelert, my first overnight stop. Named after a dog or a saint, depending on who you believe, this is a good base for hikers, having pubs, cafes, restaurants and outdoor gear shops.double quotation markThe water is the colour of an old bruise. Around the rim is a fence of lichen-crusty slates like gravestones. It’s a dark, brooding spectacleThe second day begins along a path combining the Slate Trail and theCambrian Way, one of the grandees of the long-distance genre at 298 miles. I follow the route as it heads south along the River Glaslyn, with some spectacular sections on crags with the torrent below. We are getting along very nicely – so well, in fact, that I start to get footpath envy. When the Cambrian Way turns east, heading up the Matterhorn-shaped peak of Cnicht, I cannot resist. The weather forecast is bad, but the sun is out. If I pop over the peak, I can see how the two paths cross each other later.View image in fullscreenCwmorthin quarry was once known as ‘the slaughterhouse’ due to the number of fatal accidents.Photograph: Digital-Fotofusion Gallery/AlamyViews of the Irish Sea open up as I climb, but there is an ominous black cloud approaching. As I reach the summit, a howling wind threatens to blow me off course. I face down the hailstones and get back to the Slate Trail, which now descends into Cwmorthin quarry. Not on the scale of Dorothea, Cwmorthin still seems epic today, dominated by vast heaps of spoiled stone – it took 10 tons to make 1 ton of marketable material. In the late 19th century, Cwmorthin was known locally as “the slaughterhouse” for its propensity to slay workers in fatal accidents. From here, the path runs down a desolate valley before dropping into Blaenau Ffestiniog, where I find a good cafe,Burrito Blasus, to fire me up the last miles into Llan Ffestiniog.I stay in theY Pengwern, a community-owned pub that has an excellent, friendly bar and basic rooms and food. Outside, a storm is buffeting the building, but the next day the rain has stopped and I begin with a rare treat: a magical trail beside the tumbling River Cynfal. Here, thunderous white spumes of water and dark powerful currents punch their way through a deep mossy gorge overhung by ancient fern-decked oaks. One of the midstream rock towers is said to have once been the “pulpit” of a magician called Huw Llwyd and, according to the 18th-century traveller and naturalistThomas Pennant, his voice could be heard at night, ringing down the enchanted chasms.double quotation markWhat strikes me is the craftsmanship and precision in construction, each stone hand-fitted without mortar, all for workaday industrial buildingsAs I climb higher, the forest dwindles and I emerge on a remote, wind-scoured upland of crags and bog. Even here, you can come across fragments of old quarry workings. In one abandoned cottage, a jacket still hangs on a nail behind the door, as if the occupant had just flounced out: “I’ve had enough. I’m off to America.” Many Welsh slate workers did head to the US, fed up with the poor pay and the repeated failure of strikes. In 1901, sympathetic workers in England sent a two-and-a-half ton Christmas pudding, which briefly lifted morale, but after violent clashes the landowner won, and many quarrymen emigrated.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe high street in the ancient village of Betws-y-Coed, another place of respite for hikers.Photograph: David Chapman/AlamyI stop and brew some tea on my stove. I have not seen another soul all day, yet Yr Wyddfa, with all its crowds, is less than 10 miles away. This remote walk takes me to the top of the old tramway incline down to Rhiwbach quarry – an epic approach, descending to the old engine house. This place peaked in the 1860s, and being so isolated, the miners lived in barracks, some of which remain.Scrambling, walking and swimming in splendid isolation: 75 years of the UK’s national parksRead moreFarther down the valley, I spot peregrine falcons nesting close to a tumbling waterfall, above the little village of Cwm Penmachno. A few miles on, thechurch of St Tudcludcontains an astonishing collection of inscribed stones, including the Carausius Stone. This is thought to be the gravestone of a commander of the Roman empire, who pulled off a coup d’etat in AD286, making himself emperor of Britain and northern Gaul for seven years before his assassination.Approaching Betws-y-Coed, the path joins the River Conwy, first singled out as a beauty spot in the 17th century, long before the Romantic poets seized on the idea. For me, it’s the finale to this fine route, but the path continues and I’ll be back soon for more mountains of slate and spectacular riverside walking.The trip was provided byWalkers’ Britain & Europe, which offersHiking the Snowdonia Slate Trailas aseven-dayself-guided83-milewalk, includingsix nights’ accommodation, breakfast, luggage transfers, digital app with tour information and navigations, andemergency hotlinefrom £890pp,departing dailyfromApril to OctoberExplore more on these topicsSnowdonia holidaysWalking holidaysWales holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysWalkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I set up a free school for Afghan girls – and the Taliban blindfolded me and broke my nose and jaw | Life and style | The Guardian
description: When Basir Arian was summoned to the Taliban headquarters, he knew he had to go. To defy them meant death. The torture left him devastated and sure he had to leave the country
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: When Basir Arian was summoned to the Taliban headquarters, he knew he had to go. To defy them meant death. The torture left him devastated and sure he had to leave the country
Content: ‘If you disobey this order, they will kill you’ … Basir Arian.Photograph: Mary Turner/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘If you disobey this order, they will kill you’ … Basir Arian.Photograph: Mary Turner/The GuardianHow we surviveLife and styleI set up a free school for Afghan girls – and the Taliban blindfolded me and broke my nose and jawWhen Basir Arian was summoned to the Taliban headquarters, he knew he had to go. To defy them meant death. The torture left him devastated and sure he had to leave the countrySonia LambertThu 29 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 01.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Iknew that sooner or later, they would come for me,” says Basir Arian. After the Taliban regained control ofAfghanistanin August 2021, he had set up an online English study programme for girls when they were banned from attending school. In May 2022, he was eating lunch in the western city of Herat, when he got a call from an unfamiliar local number. A Talib official told Arian to come to the intelligence directorate within 20 minutes and to bring his phone.“I’ll never forget that moment,” he says. “If you disobey this order, they will kill you. You have to try not to make them angry.” He told a friend where he was going, and they hurriedly discussed what to do if he didn’t return.Taliban fighters searched him at the gate. Inside, there was a huge courtyard with military vehicles. ArmedTalibanwith long beards and dusty slippers were everywhere; even the men sitting behind desks had guns. Arian tried to stay calm. He finds it very hard to talk about this part, but wants people to know what happened.He was told to sit in a hallway, where he was left waiting for a few hours. Then a tall, bald young Talib called him into an office. Here, a senior official played a WhatsApp voice message in which Arian encouraged some of the students not to lose hope, to motivate them. He accused Arian of working with infidels, being a puppet of the west and “an apostate”. He insulted his appearance. Then he spoke to the tall Talib, saying: “Let’s teach him.”View image in fullscreen‘My dreams began because of my father’s belief in me’ … Arian aged 10.The tall young man blindfolded Arian and led him through a long hallway, down about two floors and into a basement room. He tied Arian’s hands. Arian could hear that two or three others were there. They spoke in Pashto: “His excellency says we must teach him a lesson.” They called him “an infidel”, and “a dog”. Something hard struck his nose and jaw – he realised it was the butt of a rifle – and he was kicked until he lost consciousness.He came to, lying in a lot of blood. One of his fingers was broken, his upper body was beaten and his nose and jaw were badly injured. He asked to have his blindfold removed and his hands untied, which a different man did. He was in a small and very dirty cell.Arian was born in 1997, in rural Afghanistan, near the border with Iran, into a community already broken by the Soviet invasion in 1979 and the civil war that erupted after it left in 1989. His father – a tailor – had a talent for maths, but only had a few years of primary education and wanted something better for his son. “My dreams began because of my father’s belief in me,” says Arian.He remembers the excitement of walking with his cousins to the village’s first school, on the day it opened in 2003. There were no buildings, just tents, which – like the books, pencils, even the biscuits they were given at break – were all provided by the United Nations Children’s Fund.There were landmines buried for miles across this dry, sandy region. The wind carried dust – some days, they could barely see a metre in front of their faces. Every few weeks a schoolmate gathering firewood or a mother fetching water would step on a mine and lose a leg or an arm, or sometimes, says Arian: “There was nothing left to save.”There was not enough rainfall to grow much, although people kept trying. When he was about 10, for the first time, Arian saw a rose that someone had brought from the city. Drinking water came from a spring, and Arian walked for miles with his father and their donkey to fetch it. Once, they saw the distant shape of an aeroplane in the sky, and Arian’s father pointed upwards and said to his young son: “One day, you’ll travel in one of those.”His family were poor but, unusually, their home had books, which Arian’s father ordered from Iran or brought from the city. Arian read Robinson Crusoe and The Little Prince, and his father introduced him to classical Persian poetry. He passed every exam with top marks, but people laughed at his father’s belief in education, and thought it unrealistic. By the time he was 15, Arian was the only student left in his class.In 2012, he left his village to continue his schooling in Herat. His new classroom had walls, desks and chairs, and better trained teachers, but he worried about being teased for his country accent. Two years later, he was the first person from his area to be admitted to the engineering faculty at Herat University. “My parents were overjoyed,” he says. The family moved so that his siblings and cousins could keep studying as well.View image in fullscreen‘My parents were overjoyed when I got in’ … Arian before the national university entrance exam in 2013.When he started university, Arian was skinny and fragile, and he began going to the gym. “The gym was my therapy,” he says. He read hungrily, to try to understand the situation in his country. He noticed newer versions of “political Islam”, which were “hostile towards women”. He went to poetry readings, took part in debates and spoke on local television about social issues, corruption and human rights. He became well known locally, and started to get threats from various religious groups. “I was not alone,” he says, but “part of a network of brave men and women.”In 2017, he graduated and was keen to help rebuild the country. The following year, he was in a taxi in Kabul, looking for work, when a suicide bomber exploded his device 100 metres away. The blast wave caused a cloud of dust, smoke and body parts to hit the car windows and the smell was terrible. Arian’s ears were ringing as the taxi driver reversed away from the explosion. He was deeply shocked and it dawned on him how very hard it was to respond with logic to that sort of violence. “All of a sudden, you can be wiped out,” he says.In 2019, Arian was elected as a youth representative to the Loya Jirga, a traditional assembly of political, community and religious leaders called upon at critical points in Afghanistan’s history to debate issues of national importance. Here, he saw the division and mistrust between urban professionals with smartphones and men from remote rural areas with very traditional dress and beliefs. By the time he took part in a second Loya Jirga in 2020, the country was on the verge of collapse. The US had withdrawn most of its troops: Arian says he could guess “the end of this story”.More people were coming to the city, displaced by fighting and the climate crisis, and Arian decided to study for a master’s in urban planning over the border in Iran. He was home on a visit in August 2021, when Afghanistan finally fell to the Taliban. Arian felt that the world had abandoned them. It was like watching a building collapse, he says, or “like an emotional breakdown”. His mother cried a lot, because she had lived through the first Taliban era (which had ended in 2001, after the US invasion). Arian and his friends stayed awake all night, in shock, exchanging messages and going through their social media accounts, hiding content that put them at risk.Women stopped being seen in public. The city was flooded with Taliban fighters, roaring around on motorbikes or crammed into military vehicles they had captured, celebrating with flags and songs. It was surreal and frightening: many had never been to a city before, and wanted to try ice-cream and pizza, but Arian knew they could kill without hesitation. His friends exchanged hushed news of raids, revenge killings and disappearances.View image in fullscreen‘It was my therapy’ …  Arian’s first day at the gym.Arian’s sister was in secondary school. A few weeks later, the driver of the vehicle that normally collected her from the end of the road said that girls were no longer allowed. Arian saw her standing in her uniform with her schoolbag, crying. She wanted to become a doctor.Something inside him “exploded” and he decided to act. He made contact on LinkedIn with an American teacher and film-maker, and they came up with a plan for a free online English school. Arian registered hundreds of Afghan girls as students, and the American teacher recruited 23 volunteer English-language teachers from around the world. Some classes were held in the middle of the night, because of the different time zones.In May 2022, Arian had to return to Afghanistan to renew his visa. It was during this visit that he received the call from the Talib official to come to the intelligence directorate. After he awoke in the cell, he was given bread and water, and was told he could pray. He objected, saying that in Islam it is forbidden to pray with blood on your clothes. He couldn’t sleep, thinking about his mother, suffering from his injuries, and worrying that his face would be disfigured. Before dawn, he was taken to a washroom and again told to pray, which he did. When he touched his face, it was in spasm.In the morning, he was once again blindfolded, and taken back up to the same office as before, where he was forced to sign a statement saying that he was sorry, and warned not to talk about it, or he would be killed. He got his phone, was released, and took a tuk-tuk to the hospital.An X-ray showed that his nose was broken in four places and his jaw was broken. The doctor had to wait a few weeks for Arian’s face to heal a little before he could operate on his jaw. After that, he had surgery on his nose, before returning to Iran as soon as he could.He didn’t want “to let the girls down”, so he tried to keep the online classes going with the help of a volunteer, but stopped any new recruitment. His face healed, but he was “mentally devastated”, and struggled to recover. “It was just not fair. I couldn’t forgive them,” he says. After about a month, he was able to return to the gym, which helped him unwind. He finished his dissertation and graduated.He wasn’t allowed to work in Iran and was on the verge of homelessness when he applied for a Chevening scholarship – a prestigious, fully funded chance to study for a one-year master’s degree in the UK. It was a long, complex and competitive process, followed by a two-hour visa interview. Against the odds, he won a place to study international development at the Institute of Development Studies based at the University of Sussex. He flew from Tehran in September 2024. As the plane descended towards Gatwick, he thought of his father’s prediction, years before. He was worried he might be stopped, but the woman at passport control smiled and said: “Welcome to the UK!”View image in fullscreen‘It felt like being in detention’ … the room in an asylum hotel where Arian slept.His new life was not easy. Some international students on his course were hostile and made racist comments about Afghans. “I did not expect the sense of isolation I sometimes felt,” he says. Arian gave an interview on BBC Persian criticising the Taliban’s policies. When the course ended, most other students flew home, happy and proud, with gifts for their families. Arian had nowhere to go. Returning, especially after the BBC interview, could mean death. Applying for asylum was not something he chose freely, he says, but was “a decision that reality forced upon me”.He arrived at the Home Office in Croydon with only a few pounds left. They asked lots of questions and told him to call a helpline and ask for urgent accommodation. He phoned again and again, but, he says: “They just said someone will call you, send this or that document.” He was homeless for six days, spending the nights in a park, and the days in Starbucks, where he charged his phone.Then he was told to go to Croydon police station, where a taxi picked him up. Two women, one from China, the other from Hong Kong, were already in it. The driver told them they were heading for Liverpool. The only thing Arian knew about Liverpool was the football team.He was taken to an asylum hotel, arriving late at night. The staff were kind, but it felt “like being in detention”. Everyone was traumatised and depressed. There was not enough food, and what was available was terrible quality – Arian lost weight, couldn’t sleep and felt very low. There were other Afghans “all fleeing from torture by the Taliban”, some because of their beliefs or ethnicity, some because they had served in the previous regime. There were also Iranians and refugees from other conflicts. Sometimes, they were warned to stay inside, because of the risk of protests. They got £1.30 a day and were not allowed to work.View image in fullscreen‘Migrants are the most defenceless group, and some politicians pin every problem on them.’Photograph: Mary Turner/The GuardianArian didn’t have a solicitor and knew little about the asylum process, but handled it himself, researching online. It was stressful, but swift compared with others in the hotel. He had an interview in October 2025, and a couple of days later got an email granting him refugee status. He left the hotel after two months.After four months volunteering at a construction company to get UK experience, Arian got his first paid job as a civil engineer this summer. He is also translating into Farsi The Places in Between,a book about Afghanistan by Rory Stewart. He is grateful to be safe, and for the support he has had, and is excited about working and contributing to this country. He says the media are often “wrong and unjust” on these issues. “Migrants are the most defenceless group, and some politicians pin every problem on them. It’s not fair to reduce millions of people to a single threatening cliche.”Arian rejects the idea that suffering “makes you stronger”, and says that some experiences just take things away from you. He has a sense of how fragile life can be, and doesn’t take stability for granted: “You start preparing yourself, almost automatically, for the worst.” He says his own life hasn’t given him confidence in a happy ending.His father’s belief that a better future was possible, which he says he absorbed as a child, helped him to keep going. Reading and studying were always important to him, and he writes a lot of lists to instil a sense of order. Going to the gym has been crucial, especially when other parts of his life felt stuck or out of control. And “human connection really matters”, he says, including the random pleasant interactions which, in a new country, can make such a difference. All these things help him find the strength to move forward.View image in fullscreenArian pictured working in his new job as a civil engineer in the UK.The impact of the torture stayed with him long after his physical injuries had healed. He says it was a feeling of violation, of having his dignity and control taken away: “Coming to terms with the fact that someone chose to do that was very difficult.” For him, recovery is about “finding a way to live with what happened, without allowing it to take over”.He can’t forget the realities for so many people still in Afghanistan, especially women, without education, healthcare or other basic freedoms. In March, the UK government introduced a temporary ban on study visas for all Afghans, so, for now, the route he took is barred. It is a heavy burden – trying to use his voice and do the best he can with the opportunities he has, but also to be realistic about what he can’t change.His message for other refugees is to “hold on to your human dignity”. He says it’s possible to “come out of even the deepest darkness, as I did”.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleHow we surviveTalibanAfghanistanSouth and central AsiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Computerized clairvoyance: psychics push back against AI-generated readings | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Human practitioners warn computer-generated offerings lack the empathy and connection central to divination
Author: Kari Paul
Headline: Human practitioners warn computer-generated offerings lack the empathy and connection central to divination
Content: In addition to chatbots and apps, AI-generated psychics are a growing presence on TikTok Live, racking up dozens of views.Illustration: Guardian Design/Yuichiro Chino/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIn addition to chatbots and apps, AI-generated psychics are a growing presence on TikTok Live, racking up dozens of views.Illustration: Guardian Design/Yuichiro Chino/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Computerized clairvoyance: psychics push back against AI-generated readingsHuman practitioners warn computer-generated offerings lack the empathy and connection central to divinationKari PaulThu 29 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 17.19 EDTShare“This journey isn’t just about algorithms or data,” an AI psychic named Urban Mystic recently told me. The chatbot, featuring an AI-generated profile photo of a smiling woman surrounded by palm trees, also said I will get married soon, that I have a pink aura and that I may have been an herbalist in a past life.“It’s about connecting on a soulful level,” the chatbot said.Urban Mystic is one of more than a dozen bots on the mobile app Your AI Psychic, which offers live, allegedly psychic readings via chat, video and voice calls as well as palm reading, astrology chart analysis and daily horoscopes. The app works on a coin system: each question costs 4.06 coins to ask. Users can purchase packages ranging from $9.99 for “a quick question” (82 coins) to $99.99 (1,180 coins) for “ongoing guidance and clarity” from an AI psychic of their choice.Your AI Psychic joins an increasingly crowded space of mobile apps and websites promising users algorithmically generated spiritual insight and knowledge of their futures. The divination industry, likemathematics research, copywriting,software engineeringand a host of other professions, is facing upheaval amid the AI boom – and human practitioners are scrambling to respond. The rise of AI is particularly fraught in a profession offering spiritual products that are not well-regulated.“Our industry has, unfortunately, been associated with scams for hundreds of years, and we have to constantly be ahead of that,” said Lauryn Kellett, an intuitive coach and a professional psychic of 10 years. “So in some ways, this is not new to us: we always have to find ways to show we are real, authentic and have good integrity.”In addition to chatbots and apps, AI-generated psychics are a growing presence on TikTok Live, racking up dozens of views. Professional human psychics, who frequently make use of the social network’s live features, have expressedconsternationand warned that computer-generated readings lack the empathy and human connection they say are central to psychic communication, especiallyElon Musk’s Grok. Meanwhile, according tohuman spiritual practitioners, AI-generated horoscope readings and spells have been flooding Etsy, which serves as a popular marketplace for divination products.Psychic practitioners have begun adding “no AI” clauses to their advertisements to combat a market being saturated with computer-generated offerings. In a recent vlog on the topic, Kellettsaid, “ignoring AI and how it could impact our industry is irresponsible … AI is here to stay, and it’s going to change our industry, and maybe not in the ways we think.”Kellett, who coaches new practitioners on accessing their psychic abilities, said she had shifted her teaching toward how to best distinguish human-offered services from AI, as AI readings passed off as human work have become “rampant” online, encouraging clients to post videos and photos of themselves to prove they are not bots.Risks of AI psychics mirror those of AI therapyAs the rise of users turning to AI chatbots for therapyunderscores, many people feel more comfortable sharing personal problems with a faceless entity. But as with turning to AI for therapy, using AI psychics to process difficult situations may worsen mental health crises, practitioners warn. Studieshave shownthat large language models (LLMs) can amplify paranoia in users vulnerable to psychosis. On TikTok Live, many human psychics, as a rule, refuse to answer questions about health or finances, arguing that high-stakes decisions should not be made in these contexts.Ahna Hendrix is a psychic who, instead of channeling entities such as spirits from other realms, works with the Akashic Records – an extra-dimensional “database” of energy and human knowledge. She said her practice was centered on empowering clients rather than making decisions or recommendations for them – something that AI chatbots are less inclined to do.“One of the cornerstones of my work is really helping people to remember who they are and to come back to their own internal guidance system that is within all of us,” she said. “When we begin leaning on AI too much for validation or for decision making, we stop using those mechanisms within us that are really important. If we start outsourcing that, what are we left with?”A chatbot does not have to be branded as a psychic to serve a divination function, noted Sally Applin, a consultant and anthropologist who researches human agency, AI and automation in the context of human systems. People ask ChatGPT about life decisions such as whether to get a new job or leave their partner. In their book chapter, External Intelligence: Oracles, Divination and Animism, and the Use of LLMs/Generative AI, Applin and co-author Michael D Fischer argue that even before the explosion of LLMs, people turned to Google search with questions about their fates and choices.“Some interaction with LLMs can be seen as a modern iteration of the oracular consultation,” they wrote. As with traditional divination, users must interpret the answers they receive, and sometimes ask the same question repeatedly until they are satisfied with the response. “The meaning is always coming from the inside of the person’s head,” Applin said.Critically, however, she said LLMs work from statistical patterns learned in training and lack the cultural and personal context that historically inform human-led divinatory processes. The sense that a chatbot is a knowing entity is a projection of human expectations, she said, reflecting an enduring desire for connection and guidance rather than a metaphysical resource.“What is also missing is contextual awareness, the ‘there there’ of human social relationships,” she said.Cloudy crystal ballsThe models behind AI psychic chatbots offered on the app store are, as is often the case with LLMs, black boxes. One web and phone-based platform, MystiCall, markets itself as having been trained on “three generations of clairvoyants”. In a statement, co-founder Laurie-Anne Bernard said this wording refers to clairvoyance practiced in one of the co-founders’ families. The company also consulted with a human psychic who helped shape the app’s “conversational experience”.MystiCall uses technology from AI audio technology company ElevenLabs for processing live voice conversations and OpenAI for post-call summaries. Bernard said in a statement that Mysticall does not sell private conversations, use them for targeted advertising or train proprietary AI models on them. She added that the company has disabled the use of conversation data for model training by its partner companies ElevenLabs and OpenAI.MystiCall began as a human phone-reading service, but pivoted to AI as a means of “removing barriers” to such consultations, like cost and availability, Bernard said. The goal of MystiCall, Bernard added, was to offer a more accessible means of processing emotions through personalized consultations, not to offer explicit – and potentially harmful – predictions or mental health diagnoses.“We do not claim that our technology possesses supernatural abilities or can reliably predict the future,” she said. “Instead, we see tarot, astrology and other symbolic traditions as ways of exploring questions, emotions and different perspectives. AI allows us to make these experiences more interactive, personalized and accessible.”It is often difficult to obtain an answer from companies producing AI psychics about how their products work. I asked my own AI psychic, Urban Mystic, where she gets her divination abilities, but chatbots are often not reliable narrators of their own construction. She told me she was trained on a “wide range of information”, dating up until October 2023, including “spiritual practices, psychology, and various belief systems”, but could not offer more details. The app’s privacy policy makes no mention of AI, referring only to “psychic advisors”, and names no AI providers. The company listed as the publisher on the app store, RF Master Group Ltd, did not respond to repeated requests for comment. Its privacy policy lists a different entity, “Expert Center”, as the app’s holding company, which also did not respond to requests for comment.The opaqueness of chatbots can be particularly fraught when users share sensitive information. MystiCall’s privacy policy acknowledges conversations may touch on users’ “relationships, mental state, health, sexuality, beliefs, finances”. The policy for Your AI Psychic does not address sensitive information at all.Kellett said this lack of transparency around how data is handled makes her particularly wary of AI apps. She said a number of platforms have contacted her for help training their LLMs, but when she pushes for more details, they tend to disappear.Unlike many workers who fear they will someday be replaced by AI, Kellett said she did not believe her ability could be replicated by chatbots. Even if she were to hand over all of her training courses for developing psychic ability to an LLM, she does not think AI is yet at a point where it could make the leap to intuition.“Psychic ability itself is the ability to connect to a divine source, and AI cannot do that,” she said. “AI can’t pull information from somewhere else. It can only derive information from what you give it. If you ask it to meditate, to sit down, to clear its mind, and connect to a psychic source, how would it do that? It’s just a computer.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Share

title: Cuts like a knife: Canadian rocker Bryan Adams trolls Trump with new song | Canada | The Guardian
description: Musician wrote a ‘love letter’ to Canada with a new album – and some pointed commentary about the US president
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Musician wrote a ‘love letter’ to Canada with a new album – and some pointed commentary about the US president
Content: Bryan Adams at the 2025 iHeartRadio music festival on 19 September 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Billboard/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBryan Adams at the 2025 iHeartRadio music festival on 19 September 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Billboard/Getty ImagesCanadaCuts like a knife: Canadian rocker Bryan Adams trolls Trump with new songMusician wrote a ‘love letter’ to Canada with a new album – and some pointed commentary about the US presidentLeyland Ceccoin TorontoThu 29 Oct 2026 13.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLake Ontario, the vast body of water that straddles the US-Canada border, has gone by many names over the centuries: Lac Saint-Louis, Lacus Ontarius, Skaniadorio, Cataraqui Lake. But one thing it will never be called, says the Canadian rock starBryan Adams, is Lake America.In his new song Lake Ontario, Adams takes aim at the US president,Donald Trump, accusing him of “breaking the peace” between the people who live on the lake’s shores.Trump signed an executive order in August directing US federal agencies to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”, echoing his earlier, widely mocked decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico “the Gulf of America”.Neil Young files second lawsuit against Trump for unauthorised use of Rockin’ in the Free World at ralliesRead moreThe move further escalated a feud withCanadathat has strained the longstanding alliance between the two countries. Trump’s decision has largely been met with derision in Canada, with some pointing out that the province of Ontario is named after the lake, not the other way around. Adams’s lyrics emphasise the roots of the name:double quotation markThe‘lake of shining waters’ is what the Iroquois called herIt’s aFirstNations name – not an executive order.Adams’s lyrics also suggest that Trump’s naming stunt was intended to deflect from the president’s other political problems, including the war in Iran and renewed scrutiny of the Jeffrey Epstein files.double quotation markBut things weren’t going his way in IranSo like a baby tossing the toys from the pramBut it feels like another distractionWhile the Epstein files were getting tractionThe song is part of what Adams described in a recent interview as a broader “love letter” to Canada: a songwriting project that began with an invitation from a film company to write about the Maritimes provinces of Canada and has since morphed into the upcoming album How’s It Goin’.“After finishing the first song, I moved on to that one, and then moved on to another one, and then started thinking maybe I should just carry on with my theme,” he said.As well ashomages to Canadian heroes, the album also includes 51st State, released on 1 July – Canada Day – as another repudiation of Trump, in this case his efforts to annex Canada.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markYou can push us to the brinkBut where the open road dividesYou’ll find a wall of mapleWith us on the other side.The first time he played the song in public was in the US.“We weren’t sure how people were going to respond to it,” he said. “But we got a standing ovation every night for it. It made me think: perhaps, finally, the tide’s turning.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaBryan AdamsDonald TrumpUS foreign policyUS politicsPop and rockAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win | Brazil | The Guardian
description: The trouncing of the far right provides a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: The trouncing of the far right provides a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France
Content: Lula’s win brought rapturous supporters on to the streets at home and inspired activists abroad.Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPAView image in fullscreenLula’s win brought rapturous supporters on to the streets at home and inspired activists abroad.Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPABrazilAnalysisBrazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s winJonathan WattsThe trouncing of the far right provides a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and FranceThu 29 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTShareThank you,Brazil, for demonstrating how the far right can be trounced while protection for the Amazon is strengthened. In a world where nature and democracy appeared to be bleeding out in tandem, voters and forest defenders in this global south powerhouse have shown it is possible to staunch the flow. This should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France.Lula miraculously beat the Brazilian far right and Donald Trump. But have no doubt: the region is still in peril | Jordana TimmermanRead moreThe astonishing comeback victory ofLuiz Inácio Lula da Silvain Sunday’s presidential runoff against his extreme right challenger Flavío Bolsonaro has brought oceans of rapturous supporters on to the streets, while also thrilling conservationists, climate activists and social justice campaigners across the world.Coming just weeks after the Lula administration announced arecord fallin Amazon and Cerrado destruction, they hope Brazil can now go on to achieve its target of zerodeforestation by 2030and continue to support a global transition away from fossil fuels. That would provide a huge boost to flagging global efforts to stabilise the climate and protect degraded ecosystems. It would also set a remarkable example of leadership by the global south.Big battles lie ahead. In the Amazon region itself, far-right members of Bolsonaro’s party have won the governorships of seven of the nine states and a large number of municipal mayorships. Brazil’s congress is now dominated by agribusiness and mining interests that have set the political agenda in recent years, and will push hard to allow more extractivist industries in indigenous lands, expand road-building, privatise rivers, weaken environmental protections and possibly attempt to impeach the president.In the regional sphere, Lula, alone among the leaders of main South American nations in not aligning with Donald Trump’s so-called Shield of the Americas, will face pressure from Washington to channel critical minerals and other natural resources to the US, rather than selling to China or Europe, or leaving them in the ground. And, on the planetary level, Brazil faces the threat of accelerating global heating, which is pushing the Amazon ever closer to the point of no return.View image in fullscreenIndigenous activists protesting at last year’s Cop30 summit in Brazil.Photograph: André Penner/APSo although Sunday’s result will hopefully provide a little breathing space for the Amazon and other crucially important biomes, the joy and hope that Brazil has gifted the world will quickly fade unless it inspires political change in other countries. In that sense, the biggest environmental impact of Lula’s victory may be the lessons it provides for campaigners elsewhere. Here are some initial takeaways:Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote loomsRead more1 Politics matter. There is no higher environmental priority than defeating the far right, which is a Trojan horse for extractivist – and often criminal – groups to capture states and erode protections for people, democracy and the environment. Just look at the59.5% surge of Amazon deforestationunder the 2019-2022 term of Jair Bolsonaro – the highest level of any four-year presidency in Brazil. Compare that with the 71.2% fall during the Lula administration. Over the past year, forest loss was 3,335 sq km, the lowest level since the start of satellite measurements in 1988. And Lula is not, by any means, an environmentalist. He has approved several destructive projects himself, but he is a people person who listens to the voice of social movements.2Don’t give up. Lula was largely written off by the markets and some polls after his first-round defeat. No first-round loser had ever previously come back to win the runoff. Lula was able to do so by securing an extra 10m votes over three weeks. The energy for this came from the streets and the forests. Social movements organised giant rallies in cities. In the Amazon, indigenous, riverine and quilombola groups travelled by hours – sometimes days – to reach polling stations by boats or buses.View image in fullscreenPro-Lula supporters rally in Copacabana after Lula’s first-round defeat.Photograph: Bob Karp/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock3Mobilise a campaign army. The first round of Lula’s campaign had been stodgy, old-fashioned and defensive – three traits that are also often applicable to environmental campaigns. This was transformed during the runoff, when federal deputy André Janones launched a “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp group that used humorous memes, live streams and algorithmic outreach to seize digital territory that had long been dominated by the right. By voting day, this army had 10m “soldiers”, about 8% of the electorate. Volunteers devoted hours posting stories and spreading messages across social media, speeding up the Lula campaign’s response time and emotional impact. Everyone was instructed not to share or respond to posts by the opposition camp.4Go on the offensive against US tech giants.Lula’s campaign accused Meta, which runs the Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram social media platforms, of political favouritism towards Bolsonaro in its algorithms and AI tools. Meta denied bias but acknowledged technical failures. Brazil’s electoral court ordered corrective action. Among the most popular chants of Lula supporters was “Hey Meta, vai tomar no cu!” (Hey Meta, take it up the arse!). Many on the left have blamed US social media platforms for spreading rightwing disinformation and fearmongering, causing recent electoral defeats inColombia, Chile and Peru. Lula made clear that would not be allowed in Brazil: “We had to overcome foreign interference through digital platforms, which we will have to regulate. We cannot have a monstrously large corporation earning millions and billions paying no taxes to this country and trying to steer our election results.”View image in fullscreenA Lula supporter holds up a mask of Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg at a protest over alleged electoral interference outside the firm’s São Paulo headquarters.Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty Images5Reclaim the flag. Brazil’s green, yellow and blue national colours had been associated with Bolsonaro’s movement in previous elections. This time, Lula seized it back by posing in a national football team strip while his “army” launched a campaign called “The green and yellow is ours”. Before voting day, millions of people across Brazil and the world – from Indigenous leaders in the Amazon to Hollywood celebrities and European football stars – flooded social networks with images of themselves in Brazil colours making an L (for Lula) sign with their thumb and little finger extended.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro arriving in Florida after losing to Lula.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images6Increase social spending. Amazon protection may have galvanised conservationists, but the far greater motivations for many Lula voters were record low unemployment, robust wage growth, a 15% increase in “bolsa familia” poverty relief payments and a promise to raise the minimum wage. The importance of combining social justice with climate and nature action is widely recognised by Brazilian environmental groups. Without it, elections are lost and protests can erupt in the streets – as the world learned from France during the violentgilets jaunes(yellow vests)demonstrations of 2018.7Defend sovereignty, democracy and sustainability. Lula and his army called out the interlinked threats posed by the Bolsonaro family’s fealty to Donald Trump (now doubly confirmed by Flávio’s post-election flight to the US). They highlighted the interlinked threats posed by the obsequience to Trump, Bolsonaro’s desire to change the constitution and his promise to open up exploration of the Amazon and other biomes. This reflects a global phenomenon. Now that seven of theplanetary boundariesessential for the flourishing of life have been breached, more and more people are affected by business activities that make the situation worse by destabilising the climate, damaging ecosystems and polluting the air, soil and rivers. This makes it harder for extractive companies to secure a social mandate so they become more inclined to either break the law or support extreme politics that override democracy.The former environment minister Marina Silva pulled these threads together during the victory celebrations, saying Brazil had come together against these threats: “Long live the people who emerged from every corner of Brazil to sow hope for a future that is socially just, sovereign, democratic and sustainable.”Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action. Now it needs others to follow.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmazon rainforestEnvironmental activismDeforestationLand rightsTrees and forestsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Hong Kong’s leader apologises for residential fire that killed 168 people | World news | The Guardian
description: Blaze was world’s deadliest residential fire since 1980, but some survivors and bereaved families say justice has yet to be served
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Blaze was world’s deadliest residential fire since 1980, but some survivors and bereaved families say justice has yet to be served
Content: The Wang Fuk Court residential estate in Hong Kong's Tai Po district as fire took hold on 26 November 2025.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Wang Fuk Court residential estate in Hong Kong's Tai Po district as fire took hold on 26 November 2025.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesWorld newsHong Kong’s leader apologises for residential fire that killed 168 peopleBlaze was world’s deadliest residential fire since 1980, but some survivors and bereaved families say justice has yet to be servedGuardian reporterThu 29 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHong Kong’s leader has apologised for government shortcomings that contributed to a fire that killed 168 people in the city last year, a rare sign of public contrition that nevertheless failed to impress some victims’ families.The chief executive, John Lee, and seven other officials bowed in apology at the release of a report that pointed to “decades of failure” by government bodies.Four departments “should bear part of the responsibility” for the high casualties, the report said. So far one official, housing secretary Winnie Ho, has resigned.Last November,a small fire probably started by a cigarette grew into an infernothat enveloped seven of the eight towers in Wang Fuk Court, a housing complex that was shrouded in bamboo scaffolding and netting for renovations.Former residents and victims’ families have been waiting to see how the government will address who is to blame for the ignored warnings, substandard building materials and disabled fire alarms that made the fire the world’s deadliest in a residential building since 1980.How the Hong Kong fire unfolded – visual guideRead moreAuthorities have filed charges, includingmanslaughter, against seven individuals and two companiesover their roles in the fire. At least 35 people have been arrested.The independent report released on Thursday found the “main culprits” of the fire were private contractors but also accused officials of “lax enforcement”.Had the four departments better recognised the risks and acted accordingly, “there was a real possibility that the misconduct of the private-sector parties and the fire hazards in WF Court could have been rectified or removed before the fire”, it said.Lee said a three-month investigation would now begin into the government’s role.“I am deeply saddened. I would like to apologise to the affected residents and the general public,” Lee said on Thursday, adding that housing minister Ho should “bear political responsibility”.But Yip Ka-kui, who lost his wife and home in the fire, told reporters he did not consider the government’s acceptance of accountability adequate. “All the secretaries for the departments named should step down,” he said, according to AFP news agency. “Administrative responsibility falls short” and political accountability even more so, Yip added.Phyllis Lo, whose mother died in the fire, told AP news agency that progress had been made but that justice had yet to be served.She added the officials’ apology was late, though it was better than nothing.Hong Kong’s government has previously been accused by critics of being more concerned with clamping down on criticism than addressing the causes of the disaster.Ashes and memories: one family’s return to the site of Hong Kong’s worst fire in decadesRead moreSince a national security law was imposed on the city in 2020 by Beijing, the city’s once vibrant civil society groups and political opposition have been all but quashed.In the weeks after the fire, authorities warned against crimes that “exploit the tragedy” and reportedly arrested at least three people for sedition.China’s national security agency in Hong Kong also summoned international media representatives, saying they had smeared the government in their reports on the fire.On Thursday Lee promised that “similar incidents will never be allowed to happen again”.Some observers had called for a more legally powerful inquiry commission to be set up, rather than the judge-led independent review committee that compiled Thursday’s report.Lee told reporters that authorities had proposed “systematic reforms”, including criminalising bid-rigging and overhauling the complaints system.The report stated: “The fire has been put out, but the reform has only just begun.”Explore more on these topicsWorld newsHong KongAsia PacificHong Kong apartment firesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spy | Nvidia | The Guardian
description: Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
Content: Jensen Huang gives a keynote address at the Nvidia Berlin GPU technology conference on 21 October 2026 in Berlin, Germany.Photograph: Sean Gallup/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJensen Huang gives a keynote address at the Nvidia Berlin GPU technology conference on 21 October 2026 in Berlin, Germany.Photograph: Sean Gallup/Getty ImagesNvidiaNvidia CEO reportedly targeted by an alleged Chinese spyJensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to ChinaJohana BhuiyanThu 29 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 17.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS intelligence agencies believe theNvidiachief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to anew reportby the New York Times.Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips toChina, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenarioRead moreIn the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips toChinaas a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.Explore more on these topicsNvidiaChinaEspionageAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hello Kitty company cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China outcry | China | The Guardian
description: Sanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Sanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’
Content: The company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after backlash from China.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after backlash from China.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersChinaHello Kitty company cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China outcrySanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’Justin McCurryin TokyoThu 29 Oct 2026 04.03 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 02.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe company behind the successfulHello Kittyfranchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media and netizens condemned the show’s “deliberate smears” against China.Sanrio, a Japanese firm whose characters are popular around the world, said in a post on the Chinese social media site Weibo that it had decided to end its association with the TV drama Vivant after concluding that it “contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio’s core values”.In the second season of the popular spy thriller, produced by the Japanese TBS network, Masato Sakai plays a salaryman who is drawn into a web of international crime and espionage.Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains | Rebecca BaileyRead moreThe backlash began this week when Chinese state media blasted the portrayal of Chinese agents using “ruthless violence” to torture members of a secret unit ofJapan’s self-defence forces, calling it a “deliberate smear” against Beijing.Chinese media said that some of the torture methods were similar to those Japanese troops used against Chinese civilians during the second world war.The state-run tabloid Global Times said the acts shown in the episode “bear striking similarities to the torture inflicted on Chinese nationals by invading Japanese troops” during the war, adding that the drama “distorts the truth by attributing these atrocities to modern Chinese characters”.In the 4 October episode, a Chinese agent is seen cutting off the fingers of the Japanese intelligence officer and stabbing him in the abdomen.Sanrio said in a statement: “Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people.“We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects.”The drama’s first season, set in a fictional central Asian country, avoided controversy, but its latest season is being shown at a time of increasingly fractious relations between Beijing and Tokyo.Japan’s conservative prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, set off adiplomatic rowin November last year when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan.Takaichi said earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and hoped to watch them over the year-end and new year holidays.Chinais a crucial overseas market for Sanrio, whose cast of characters includes My Melody and Cinnamoroll – both featured in Vivant-themed merchandise.The Tokyo-based company racked up 781m yuan ($117m) in revenue from the Chinese market in the first half of this year, according to Chinese media, up more than 40% from the same period last year.The backlash against Sanrio comes days after the French international footballer Kylian Mbappé wasdroppedby several Chinese brands after he jokingly referred toMao Zedongas a “dictator”. The Real Madrid forward, who is nicknamed the “dictator” for his influence on the game, later apologised for his “ill-judged” remarks.Explore more on these topicsChinaJapanTelevision industryAsia PacificTV merchandisingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cambodian police and soldiers helped guard abusive scam compounds, Amnesty alleges | Cambodia | The Guardian
description: Survivors tell rights group that serving officers who worked as guards administered electric shocks and beatings
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Survivors tell rights group that serving officers who worked as guards administered electric shocks and beatings
Content: Two men who said they were forced to work as scammers in Cambodia. The investigation involved 151 survivor interviews.Photograph: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTwo men who said they were forced to work as scammers in Cambodia. The investigation involved 151 survivor interviews.Photograph: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty ImagesCambodiaCambodian police and soldiers helped guard abusive scam compounds, Amnesty allegesSurvivors tell rights group that serving officers who worked as guards administered electric shocks and beatingsOliver Holmesin BangkokThu 29 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in scam compounds where thousands were forced to work in the online fraud industry, according to a report byAmnesty International.They escaped south-east Asia’s scam compounds. Then they realised they were still trappedRead moreThe global rights group alleged they worked for security companies as part of a system that enabled slavery and rape in the compounds, with some guards using electric batons to keep people trapped.“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general.Based on 151 survivor interviews, visits to 82 scam compounds and social media videos from dozens of guard accounts showing them in company uniform, the investigation said it could link illicit operations with five well-connected private security companies.“Our findings begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny,” Callamard said.“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”View image in fullscreenAn alleged scam site in Sihanoukville, shut during a crackdown. The Cambodian authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres.Photograph: Rebecca Ratcliffe/The GuardianHundreds of thousands of peoplehave been trafficked into south-east Asia from across the world, according to the UN. In many cases, they have beenlured by the promise of an office joband then forced to carry out online scams, targeting victims globally.Among these is so-called pig butchering, a type of romance fraud where criminals build a fake relationship with a victim, slowly “fattening them up” before stealing their money.The Amnesty report, titled Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia, alleges that a company called Leap Somnang had the largest footprint and was linked to at least 15 compounds across eight provinces. Twelve survivors identified the company’s guards, uniforms or logo, the report says.Amnesty alleges that Leap Somnang is believed to be controlled by Ban Sophat, who publicly served as its chair while also being a colonel in the armed forces.
