It provided photos it claimed showed him alongside Leap Somnang guards at two scamming compounds.View image in fullscreenVacated online scam centres in Cambodia.Photograph: Ismail Kaplan/Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe rights group quoted a letter from Ban Sophat denying holding any ownership, director or management role in Leap Somnang, stating that he had “served as an adviser to the company owner”.“The fact that I may appear in a photograph taken at a particular location does not mean that I have knowledge of, or involvement in, the activities or operations conducted there,” it cited him as saying.Trafficked, beaten and raped: raids reveal scale of abuse of women in Asia’s cyberscam centresRead moreScam site survivors have described guards administering electric shocks and beatings, detaining people in “dark rooms” and standing guard while compound managers raped women.Amnesty said it had identified more than 20 members of the military and police who were seen to have an active presence at the compounds, including working openly as guards.With annual lossesestimated at about $100bn– a sum that outstrips the GDP of several countries in the region – international pressure has grown on countries such as Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar to crack down. Thereare signsthat some parts of the industry are moving to South Asia.In July 2025, Cambodia launched its largest-ever crackdown on scam operations, promising to wipe out the criminal networks. Authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres, and Amnesty said the industry there was now “dormant”.View image in fullscreenLeftover belongings lie scattered in a room inside a closed compound in Takeo province, Cambodia.Photograph: Roun Ry/Reuters“Even if scamming compounds are dormant, our findings clearly show that the infrastructure of impunity has not been dismantled,” Callamard said. “Cambodia will not have ended this abusive industry until it has held to account those who staffed, managed, financed and protected this abusive system.”Fake rooms, props and a script to lure victims: inside an abandoned Cambodia scam centreRead moreAmnesty said it presented its findings to Cambodian authorities, and cited a response from the ministry of interior stating that it had, as part of its ongoing crackdowns, already disciplined 77 police officers, prosecuted six private security guards for using stun batons illegally and detained 17 military, police, and civil officials for colluding with criminals.Authorities had sent 3,477 suspects to court, the letter says, citing a policy of “no tolerance, no exemption, and no retreat” to ensure Cambodia did not become a “haven or operating base for transnational criminal networks”.Amnesty said it did not receive a response from Leap Somnang.The Guardian has contacted Cambodia’s interior ministry, Ban Sophat and Leap Somnang for comment.Explore more on these topicsCambodiaAmnesty InternationalOrganised crimeHuman rightsAsia PacificScamsConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Outcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video game | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Bereaved families have urged the publisher of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove a clip from the game that shows a figure performing CPR and bodies lying in the street
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Bereaved families have urged the publisher of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove a clip from the game that shows a figure performing CPR and bodies lying in the street
Content: People queue for a pop-up ‘Korean alley’ experience in Shoreditch,  London, earlier this month before the release of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. There have been calls to remove clips of the real 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the game.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPeople queue for a pop-up ‘Korean alley’ experience in Shoreditch,  London, earlier this month before the release of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. There have been calls to remove clips of the real 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the game.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockSouth KoreaOutcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video gameBereaved families have urged the publisher of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove a clip from the game that shows a figure performing CPR and bodies lying in the streetRaphael Rashidin SeoulThu 29 Oct 2026 00.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 20.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly2022 Seoul crowd crushfrom the latest instalment of the video game.The clips, which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments ofCall of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion.One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher.A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster.“We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the bereaved families’ council and a coalition of civic groups said in a joint statement on Wednesday, demanding that the footage be removed.‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weaponRead moreThey said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise.View image in fullscreenA screengrab from the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 game released by Activision, which is made up of real news broadcast footage from Getty showing paramedics performing CPR during the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush.Composite: Youtube/ActivisionActivision, the game’s publisher, said that “in developing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, we approached the subject matter with care and respect. The game’s opening cinematic utilizes some real world news coverage to establish the game’s fictional narrative.”“It is not intended to reference or trivialize the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form.”The demand comes as the country marks the fourthanniversary of the crush on Thursday.Players in South Korea identified the clip after the game’s release, and Korean broadcasters have compared itside by side with footagefilmed on the nightof the crowd crush.The Korean Game Users Association called for an apology and for the footage to be replaced.Modern Warfare 4 follows a South Korean marine private fighting a North Korean invasion through recognisable Korean streets.The title had already become a political talking point before its release, with conservative politicians urging president Lee Jae Myung – who is pursuing a more conciliatory approach towards North Korea – to play the game to understand what they described as the threat from Pyongyang.It topped South Korea’s sales chart on Steam, the leading PC gaming platform, within days of its release.Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaSeoul crowd crushCall of DutyGamesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: More than half of Victorian lawyers use AI – but only a quarter have cut client fees as a result | Australian law | The Guardian
description: Research finds 55% of lawyers are using AI in legal practices, up from 37% last year, though efficiency gains aren’t as high as expected
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Research finds 55% of lawyers are using AI in legal practices, up from 37% last year, though efficiency gains aren’t as high as expected
Content: Lawyers say clients who use chatbots are adding to their workload, forcing them to correct errors made by AI.Photograph: Posed by models; Jacob Wackerhausen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLawyers say clients who use chatbots are adding to their workload, forcing them to correct errors made by AI.Photograph: Posed by models; Jacob Wackerhausen/Getty ImagesAustralian lawMore than half of Victorian lawyers use AI – but only a quarter have cut client fees as a resultResearch finds 55% of lawyers are using AI in legal practices, up from 37% last year, though efficiency gains aren’t as high as expectedGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterThu 29 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 20.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than half of Victoria’s lawyers have reported using AI in their work, according to a new study, but just over a quarter say they have reduced fees as a result of efficiency gains.They also say clients seeking advice from chatbots have added to their workload, forcing them to correct errors made by AI.The 2026 census of 2,221 of the state’s lawyers, conducted by the Victorian Legal Services Board and Commissioner’s legal services research centre, found a big increase in lawyers using AI in their practices, rising from 37% to 55% in the last year.‘Emotional intimacy’ from AI chatbots would be banned under Australia’s digital duty of care lawsRead moreWhile the 2025 report found AI use was highest among those under 30 years of age, in 2026 this disparity had largely disappeared, although usage remained low for those aged 60 and over.AI use was most common in trade practices (85%), banking and finance (78%) and information technology and telecommunications (78%), while it was used much less in criminal law (29%), family law (45%) and administrative law (46%).While there are AI tools designed specifically for legal services, 79% of lawyers reported using consumer chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot. Legal-specific tools alone were used by 22% of respondents.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe increased use in AI has not translated to a reduction in fees for most, the survey found, with just 26% of lawyers responding that their use of AI had resulted in lower client fees.Reduced fees were more likely to be reported by those working for business clients (34%) compared with individual fee-paying clients (23%).Some reported AI had enabled them to take on work that would have previously been uneconomical (18%).The principal researcher and report co-author, Dr Georgie Rychner, said fee reductions in corporate and big firms could be attributed to the fact clients in those settings were repeat users of legal services.“They have a high level of legal capability,” she said. “They also are perhaps using AI in their own work, so they have a better understanding and are able to advocate for lower prices … whereas we’re not seeing that as much in the community legal system sector.”Rychner said the efficiency gains of using AI were not as high as expected, but that in 2025 the survey found 89% of practitioners said they had taken steps to verify the accuracy of AI output, which might have negated the gains.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 2026 there had been a rise in clients using AI for their own legal research, she said, with 46% of lawyers reporting their clients were arriving with inaccurate or misleading information, and 41% presenting AI-generated documents that required correction.Nearly half of lawyers said there was an increase in time and effort required if their clients used AI, compared with 19% who said it led to a reduction in time and effort.“What we are hearing is that clients are more frequently arriving with misleading or inaccurate information about their legal problems, more so than they’re arriving with a better understanding of legal problems,” she said, adding that more research was needed to understand client perspectives.Courts and legal practitioner bodies across Australia have been grappling with the rise in AI use among lawyers and the public since 2023.A Victorian lawyer last yearwas the first in the country to face sanctionsfor false citations discovered, being stripped of his ability to practise as a principal lawyer. Investigations were also launched by regulatory bodies inWestern AustraliaandNew South Walesin similar cases.The federal court in Aprilissued new rulesaround using generative AI, while the chief justice of the high court, Stephen Gageler, saidlast year the use of AI-generated contentin legal cases had reached an “unsustainable phase”.Explore more on these topicsAustralian lawAI (artificial intelligence)BusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Study of 100,000 Australians seeks causes of mental health disorders and early onset cancer | Health | The Guardian
description: Sax Institute is recruiting for 18 and Up, an intergenerational study of wellbeing and ageing that follows its landmark 45 and Up study
Author: Jack Larkin
Headline: Sax Institute is recruiting for 18 and Up, an intergenerational study of wellbeing and ageing that follows its landmark 45 and Up study
Content: Participants in the 18 and Up study will be asked about health, lifestyle, social circumstances and background.Photograph: Rawpixel/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenParticipants in the 18 and Up study will be asked about health, lifestyle, social circumstances and background.Photograph: Rawpixel/Getty Images/iStockphotoHealthStudy of 100,000 Australians seeks causes of mental health disorders and early onset cancerSax Institute is recruiting for 18 and Up, an intergenerational study of wellbeing and ageing that follows its landmark 45 and Up studyGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJack LarkinThu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleResearchers hope to better understand the drivers of major health challenges facing younger people, such as mental illness and rising cancer rates, through the recruitment of 100,000 people for Australia’s largest intergenerational study of wellbeing and ageing.The independent and not-for-profit research institute the Sax Institute on Thursday launched the 18 and Up study, which will follow the health of those aged 18 to 45 throughout their lives.Two decades ago, the institute started 45 and Up, nowthe largest population-based cohort study in the southern hemisphere, with more than 267,000 taking part ranging in age from 45 to older than 100.Since then, participants have been repeatedly surveyed and their responses linked to other datasets, leading to significant discoveriesabout smoking,dementia preventionanddifferences in cardiovascular outcomesbetween men and women.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email18 and Up’s scientific director, Adjunct Prof Justine Gatt, said there was a lack of long-term data for younger generations, with existing studies often only giving researchers information from a snapshot in time.“Almost two in five young Australians aged 16 to 24 experienced a mental disorder in the past year, and that number has been rising,” Gatt, a neuroscientist and mental health researcher said. “Yet we still lack the long-term evidence needed to understand why.”Australia’s bowel cancer rates are world’s highest for under-50s. Scientists wonder if the gut microbiome is to blameRead moreSuicide is the leading cause of death among Australians aged 15 to 44, and researchers have said there is an urgent need tounderstand and address driving factorsto improve prevention efforts and mental health treatments.Children and grandchildren of 45 and Up participants will be invited to participate, which Gatt said will help researchers understand how health is influenced by a complex mix of family history, lived experiences and social conditions, and how these factors interact across generations.The chief executive of the Sax Institute, Dr Martin McNamara, said along with mental health, questions around cancer will also be an important part of the initial round of surveys.View image in fullscreen‘It’s important we follow people over time … so that we can figure out ways to fix and re-organise our health and care systems,’ says Sax Institute CEO Dr Martin McNamara.Photograph: SAX InstituteSince 2000,there has been an increase in early-onset cancers– defined as those diagnosed beyond adolescence but before the age of 50 – in Australia and other parts of the world. Thisincludes bowel, thyroid, breastand other cancers.While scientists think increased screening, changing lifestyles and different exposures to risk factors in early life and young adulthood may all be factors, there have been calls forurgent researchto better understand these and other influences.Participants will be asked about health, lifestyle, social circumstances and background and, with consent, this information will be linked to other health records, such as cancer registries and Medicare.“It’s important we follow people over time … so that we can figure out ways to fix and re-organise our health and care systems,” McNamara said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We’ll have a really good picture of their lives, the things that are important to them, their education, their employment, where they live.”The study will evolve with participants to receive age-relevant questions, and emerging health conditions or pandemics will be factored in. It is being funded by a $4.5m NationalHealthand Medical Research Council grant, with recruitment beginning in November.A professor of epidemiology and public health at the Australia National University, Emily Banks, is a former scientific director at the Sax Institute who used 45 and Up study datato reveal in 2025that smoking-related illnesses kill 66 Australians every day – more than previously thought.Banks said large-scale cohort studies are powerful as they give researchers a window into the population and help detail what people are exposed to during their lives. She said the 45 and Up data has become an important collaborative resource.Ithas been used by more than 800 researchers worldwide.“We’ve had hundreds of researchers using the data. We also have around 10% of the population of New South Wales in that age [45+] group in the study,” she said.“Some of the biggest advances in health have come from using this kind of information.”In Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14 and atMensLineon 1300 789 978.Explore more on these topicsHealthMental healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Seven oil tankers carrying 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel sail towards US | US news | The Guardian
description: Tankers, tracked by Greenpeace, are first phase of Trump-Putin deal – but there is uncertainty over whether they will unload
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Tankers, tracked by Greenpeace, are first phase of Trump-Putin deal – but there is uncertainty over whether they will unload
Content: A file photograph of the PVT Azura, one of the vessels being tracked by Greenpeace and said to be carrying Russian diesel to the US.Photograph: Martin Witte/AlamyView image in fullscreenA file photograph of the PVT Azura, one of the vessels being tracked by Greenpeace and said to be carrying Russian diesel to the US.Photograph: Martin Witte/AlamyUS newsSeven oil tankers carrying 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel sail towards USTankers, tracked by Greenpeace, are first phase of Trump-Putin deal – but there is uncertainty over whether they will unloadDan SabbaghDefence and security editorThu 29 Oct 2026 15.04 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven oil tankers carrying an estimated 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel are now sailing towards the US, though it is uncertain if the vessels will be able to unload amid a political row about the legality of the shipments.The transport,tracked by the pressure group Greenpeace, is the first phase of acontentious supply dealnegotiated between presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin earlier this month, reversing years of sanctions on Russia oil.Previous reports had counted three tankers that had departed Russian oil terminals in the Baltic Sea, but using a range of sources, including shipping tracking websites, Greenpeace believes its monitoring exercise is the most complete yet.Shaun Burnie, an energy specialist with GreenpeaceUkraine, argued that now the location of the tankers could be plotted on a map, the shipments should be halted by Congress or local authorities in the US.“Instead of rewarding Russia for its vile war against Ukraine, there needs to be more punitive sanctions against Russia,” he said. “These shipments can be stopped”.Map showing the course of tankers carrying Russian dieselOne of the seven tankers, Taurus, is relatively close to the US, but at the time the map was first published, five of the others were close to the UK, and three were sailing through or into the English Channel.In Ukraine, 14 people were reported killed on Thursday morning when a Russian drone struck a crowded train platform in the central city of Dnipro. Five others were reported killed in daytime strikes in two other cities, Chernihiv and Kremenchuk.Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway company, said a high speed jet-powered drone had struck as a commuter train was preparing to depart Dnipro’s main station. Bodies lay scattered after the relatively unusual daytime attack, which took place at around 11am.Putin agreed to supply the US with 1.8m tonnes of diesel in a surprise deal announced on 9 October, starting with 300,000 tonnes immediately. Trump announced a six-month waiver on existing sanctions to allow the shipments to proceed.Russia had been hit by waves of economic sanctions from the US, EU, UK and other leading western economies since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. But this autumn, Trump has altered course and tried to work more closely with Putin, even though Russia has not stopped attacking its neighbour.View image in fullscreenEmergency workers at the scene of a purported Russian drone attack on Dnipro’s main station on Thursday.Photograph: ReutersUkraine war briefing: Oleshky truce holding and demining under way to enable humanitarian corridor, Kyiv saysRead moreEarlier this week, a group of US lawmakers, led by a handful of Democratic senators, warned banks and port authorities that they could face congressional investigations and other legal action if they handled the Russian diesel.Mikie Sherrill, the Democratic governor of New Jersey, said she was looking at how to prevent the diesel from being unloaded, if an attempt was made to do so in her state. She described the deal as “corrupt and illegal”.There have been reports that the White House has been trying to encourage US firms to take the oil, though it is not clear buyers are forthcoming, given the legal risks so close to next Tuesday’s midterm elections.Trump’s popularity has waned as fuel prices in the US have soared since he attacked Iran in the spring. Polling suggests a high likelihood that control of the House of Representatives could pass to the Democrats in the elections, while the battle over the Senate is considered too close to call.The US president had argued that the Russia deal would help lower diesel prices, though the price per gallon has risen from $6.28 at the time the agreement was announced to $6.33, according to the American Automobile Association.Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, denounced the agreement because the money raised would help the Kremlin fund the ongoing war. “Backroom deals” gave Putin more chances on the battlefield, he said.The Kremlin has been trying to keep information about the latest oil exports secret. A presidential decree from the end of September restricted the publication of information about oil exports in an effort to evade international sanctions.Explore more on these topicsUS newsOilRussiaDonald TrumpVladimir PutinCommoditiesUkrainenewsShareReuse this content

title: Spain begins mourning period as search continues for train crash victims | Spain | The Guardian
description: Emergency services, drones and dog unit continue to comb carriages as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Emergency services, drones and dog unit continue to comb carriages as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples
Content: Seville residents hold five minutes’ silence for the crash victims at Santa Justa train station in Seville.Photograph: Marcelo del Pozo/ReutersView image in fullscreenSeville residents hold five minutes’ silence for the crash victims at Santa Justa train station in Seville.Photograph: Marcelo del Pozo/ReutersSpainSpain begins mourning period as search continues for train crash victimsEmergency services, drones and dog unit continue to comb carriages as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samplesHow did the Spain train crash happen and what will investigators be asking?Sam JonesandAshifa Kassamin MadridThu 29 Oct 2026 13.59 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 01.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpain began three days of mourning on Thursday for at least 69 people who died in a high-speed rail collision, as hospitals continued to treat dozens of injured passengers and train drivers went on strike to urge more investment in railway safety.The trains – one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo – were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.Spain’s foreign ministry said 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, adding that one had been killed and at least seven injured.10:20Survivors shell-shocked after deadly Spain train crash - The LatestThe crash came 10 months after 46people were killedand dozens more injured when two trains – one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s large, modern high-speed rail network. The transport minister, Óscar Puente, said rear-end collisions such as Wednesday’s were “highly unlikely”, and suggested the accident could have been caused by human error under “inexplicable” circumstances.View image in fullscreenIryo employees in Madrid embrace after observing a minute’s silence for the victims of the train crash.Photograph: Bernat Armangué/APEmergency services combed the wreckage through the night for more victims, using cranes to hoist pieces of mangled metal. At daybreak, police once again launched drones to survey the crash site.Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on Thursday morning that rescue teams did not think they would find any more bodies in one damaged carriage that was ‌still overturned, but added that body parts had been found that would need to be identified.“Yesterday we experienced a catastrophe that without a doubt has left all of Spain in shock,” said García-Page. He confirmed that 50 of the people who had been taken to hospitals in the region were still being treated.View image in fullscreenThe crash scene on Wednesday.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesThe prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, speaking during a visit to the emergency command centre in the city of Toledo, said the authorities were doing all they could to establish the cause of the crash and prevent another rail tragedy.“I’d like to let all Spaniards know that every institution that is part of the state – from the smallest municipality to the government of Spain – is working day and night, not only to provide a response to the families of the victims, but also, of course, to uncover every last detail of this tragedy and to strengthen safety measures so that something like this never happens again.”King Felipe, who visited a hospital in Toledo where some of the injured were being treated, said Spain had “once again suffered an extremely harsh blow” and called for lessons to be learned.“There is obviously an ongoing investigation, which should establish how and why this tragedy happened,” he said on Thursday. “Measures will need to be looked at and adopted so that this doesn’t happen again.”View image in fullscreenWorld Central Kitchen delivers meals to emergency services and security forces at the scene of the train collision.Photograph: Angeles Visdomine/EPAMeanwhile, Spanish train drivers went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety. The crash was Europe’s deadliest train accident sincea derailment in Santiago de Compostelain north-west Spain that killed 80 people in 2013.“We will continue demanding the necessary measures to make this sector safe again ... It must have all the safety systems required to maintain the quality standards we have always had,” said Diego Martín of the train drivers’ union Semaf. “We cannot tolerate, under any circumstances, this type of incident happening again.”‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in SpainRead moreThe Guardia Civil police force has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid. The force said 64 people had been reported missing by relatives by Thursday morning.A school in Urda, which lies about 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, has been turned into an information centre where relatives can inquire about loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who had arrived, some of them in tears.Carmen García, a Red Cross psychologist, said “long and hard hours” lay ahead and that “every person will manage it in their own way”. She added: “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated.”1:31Spain in mourning after fatal rail crash, says Spanish prime minister - videoJosé Miguel Fernández, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to the victims’ families.“It is important for relatives to find their loved ones, even if they have died, because the grieving process is quicker when you have been able to say goodbye at that final moment,” he told Onda Cero radio.Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail networkRead moreSurvivors have spoken of being thrown from their seats by the impact of the crash, and of trying to help the injured in the immediate aftermath.Among the first victims to be named was José Manuel Chacón, a 31-year-old Guardia Civil officer. The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues.Also among those killed was Fátima Báñez, a former labour minister for the conservative People’s party (PP), who had gone on to chair the social and corporate responsibility arm of Spain’s ⁠employers’ association.The PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.With Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsSpainEuropeTrain crashesRail transportEmergency servicesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Elke Sommer, prolific German star of A Shot in the Dark and And Then There Were None, dies aged 85 | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Berlin-born performer had a gift for languages that took her to Hollywood, landing roles alongside Peter Sellers, Dick Van Dyke and Paul Newman
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The Berlin-born performer had a gift for languages that took her to Hollywood, landing roles alongside Peter Sellers, Dick Van Dyke and Paul Newman
Content: Bombshell image … Elke Sommer.Photograph: Kobal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBombshell image … Elke Sommer.Photograph: Kobal/ShutterstockMoviesElke Sommer, prolific German star of A Shot in the Dark and And Then There Were None, dies aged 85The Berlin-born performer had a gift for languages that took her to Hollywood, landing roles alongside Peter Sellers, Dick Van Dyke and Paul NewmanAndrew PulverThu 29 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElke Sommer, the prolific German star of the Pink Panther film A Shot in the Dark, early 70s Agatha Christie adaptation And Then there Were None, and British sex comedy Carry on Behind, has died aged 85.Bild magazine reportedthat Sommer died in Los Angeles of heart failure.German-born Sommer, whose best-known film roles were in the 1960s and 70s, was one of the wave of European performers who crossed over to Hollywood and English-language cinema with considerable success, following the postwar emergence of European new wave cinema. Sommer was one of the few German actors to make waves at the time, as Hollywood made much of her bombshell image.View image in fullscreenHollywood breakthrough … Elke Sommer with Paul Newman in The Prize.Photograph: Moviestore/ShutterstockBorn Elke Schletz in 1940 in Berlin, the daughter of a Protestant pastor, she was evacuated with her family to Bavaria during the war. Intending to work as an interpreter, she was spotted by celebrated Italian director Vittorio De Sica after winning a beauty contest on a trip to Italy in 1958, and subsequently offered roles in a string of Italian comedy films. She crossed back into more serious work with the West German drama The Death Ship, opposite Horst Buchholz (who would go on to appear in cowboy classic The Magnificent Seven).With her gift for languages, Sommer made her first film in English, the 1961 British comedy Don’t Bother to Knock, opposite Richard Todd, and was billed as one of the “six most exciting women in the world” alongside Melina Mercouri, Jeanne Moreau and Romy Schneider in Carl Foreman’s 1963 war fable, The Victors. Sommer’s Hollywood breakthrough arrived in the same year, with The Prize; she was cast as Paul Newman’s lover in an adaptation of Irving Wallace’s hit novel, for which she was a joint winner of a most promising newcomer Golden Globe.View image in fullscreenLeaning into her ‘sexpot’ image … with Peter Sellers in A Shot in the Dark.Photograph: Moviestore/ShutterstockSommer’s Hollywood career then took off with A Shot in the Dark, in which she leaned heavily into her “sexpot” image as a maid suspected of a series of murders in the sequel to The Pink Panther, starring Peter Sellers. Following its success, Sommer appeared in a string of high profile Hollywood films, including The Art of Love with James Garner and Dick Van Dyke, The Oscar with Stephen Boyd, and the Bob Hope comedy Boy, Did I Get a Wrong Number! In 1968, she achieved leading actor status with The Wicked Dreams of Paula Schultz, a comedy about an East German athlete who pole-vaults over the Berlin Wall.In the 1970s, Sommer appeared in two cult horror films by Mario Bava, Baron Blood and Lisa and the Devil, and sex comedies Percy and Percy’s Progress for British director Ralph Thomas. She followed these with two high-profile British films: as secretary Vera Clyde in And Then There Were None in 1974, adapted from Christie’s hit novel, and a year later, Carry on Behind, the 27th in the Carry On series.View image in fullscreenIn Mario Bava’s cult horror Lisa and the Devil.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockAfter another Sellers film, The Prisoner of Zenda, and Ralph Thomas’s heist film A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square, Sommer scaled back her screen appearances and concentrated on painting. In the mid-1980s, she also became embroiled in a long-running feud with Zsa Zsa Gabor after they appeared together on TV show Circus of the Stars;Sommer was ultimately awarded $3.3min damages for defamation.Sommer was married twice, to writer Joe Hyams from 1964 until 1981, and hotelier Wolf Walther from 1993 until his death in 2026.Explore more on these topicsFilmGermanyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s central bank chief, Christine Lagarde, steps down for ‘freedom of speech’ | Christine Lagarde | The Guardian
description: Possible candidate to run World Economic Forum departs ECB nine months early, saying she wants to speak her mind about world affairs
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Possible candidate to run World Economic Forum departs ECB nine months early, saying she wants to speak her mind about world affairs
Content: In a video message on social media, Lagarde said it had been a ‘great pride and huge privilege’ to serve at the ECB.Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/ReutersView image in fullscreenIn a video message on social media, Lagarde said it had been a ‘great pride and huge privilege’ to serve at the ECB.Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/ReutersChristine LagardeEurope’s central bank chief, Christine Lagarde, steps down for ‘freedom of speech’Possible candidate to run World Economic Forum departs ECB nine months early, saying she wants to speak her mind about world affairsPhillip InmanandGraeme WeardenThu 29 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 06.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”.Ending months of speculation about her future at theEuropean Central Bank, Lagarde said she would quit her role as president in March rather than October next year because the rules of neutrality that governed her job prevented her from influencing debate about financial and economics affairs.She spoke at the end of a press conference to explain the ECB’s decision to hold interest rates – maintaining its key deposit rate at 2.5% – despite inflation climbing to 3.8% last month, its highest since September 2023.Lagarde said: “I ‌want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom ‌to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters.”The former managing director of the International Monetary Fund has been tipped as a candidate to take over the running of the World Economic Forum, which holds its annual meeting in Davos each January. The WEF founder, Klaus Schwab,stepped down last yearafter being accused of financial and ethical misconduct, which he denies.Lagarde’s early departure fires the starting gun on the race to replace her as ECB chief, at a time when the eurozone is struggling with weak growth and above-target inflation. Potential candidates include the former Dutch central bank president Klaas Knot, the Spanish banker Pablo Hernández de Cos, the German central bank president, Joachim Nagel, and Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank.The European Council made up of EU heads of stateappoints the head of the ECB, which sets monetary policy across the eurozone.There has been speculation that Lagarde, a former finance minister ofFrance, has been encouraged to quit early by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, so her successor can be appointed before the possibility of a far-right or far-left presidential candidate being elected to the Élysée Palace. Lagarde will also be able to participate in next April’s elections.She noted that ECB officials were bound by strict rules on not appearing partisan. “We have an obligation of neutrality; we comment on the situation with the focus on monetary policy,” Lagarde said, adding that the mandate was “the price we pay for being independent”.Lagarde said she no longer ‌felt comfortable staying silent on broader global issues. “I’m interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation,” she ​said, without elaborating.Drawing on more than two decades in international economic and financial roles, she said she had more to contribute. “There are things that I can say – whether people will listen or not is another story. But I feel that I ⁠should say those things and I cannot do so in my current ​position.”To reassure markets and staff ​that her early departure would not disrupt the central bank’s operations, she added: “A process ​has already started ‌to identify my ​successor.” She said ​there were “plenty of excellent candidates.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMacron said on Thursday ⁠that the ​succession at the ECB must ⁠be prepared in “an orderly ​and ‌balanced way” ‌with European partners, and also expressed his deep gratitude to Lagarde for her action ‌during her tenure.Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank, said: “TheEuropean Unionis trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that rightwing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027.“Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Élysée Palace. He is a long-term political adversary of Le Pen.”Lagardejoined the ECBin late 2019, shortly beforethe start of the Covid pandemic. During her tenure the central bank has also faced the economic consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war, Donald Trump’s trade war and his war in the Middle East.Lagarde was wearing two plasters on her face in her video message, which she said was because of “a small surgery earlier in the week”. She added: “Follow doctors’ orders and get your skin checked regularly.”Explore more on these topicsChristine LagardeEuropean Central BankEuropeEuropean UnionEuropean monetary unionEconomicsEurozonenewsShareReuse this content

title: Finland launches criminal investigation into Google’s clearing of forest for datacentre site | Finland | The Guardian
description: Authorities allege company may have breached Finnish environmental laws by forgoing required impact assessment
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Authorities allege company may have breached Finnish environmental laws by forgoing required impact assessment
Content: An aerial view of the site where Google’s datacentre is set to be built in Muhos.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the site where Google’s datacentre is set to be built in Muhos.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesFinlandFinland launches criminal investigation into Google’s clearing of forest for datacentre siteAuthorities allege company may have breached Finnish environmental laws by forgoing required impact assessment‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentreJon HenleyThu 29 Oct 2026 10.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinnish ⁠police have launched a criminal investigation into possible breaches ⁠of the country’s environmental ⁠laws ​at the site of a planned Google datacentre in rural northernFinland.Authorities allege that Tuike Finland, a Google subsidiary,cleared and drained 330 hectares (815 acres) of forestat the planned site in Muhos before environmental impact assessments required by Finnish law had been completed.View image in fullscreenIn the northern Finnish town of Muhos, the forest has already been cut down on land acquired by Google, with excavators now clearing the ground and rumbling trucks shuttling back and forth to the construction area located next to major power lines.Photograph: Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP/Getty ImagesLike other Nordic countries, Finland is attractive to tech companies seeking to build datacentres because of its relative geopolitical stability and abundance of land, but also because its cool climate should allow them to cut energy costs.“Based on preliminary information, there have been ambiguities and ‌shortcomings in the drainage and water management at the construction site of Tuike Finland ​Oy’s datacentre project,” Finnish police said in a statement on Thursday.“The criminal investigation will examine, among other things, circumstances related to these issues,” they added.Finnish authorities are considering applications for a total of 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, including a €13bn (£11bn) artificial intelligence infrastructure project byGooglethat the US company has called its largest ‌investment in Europe.MapEarlier this month Finnish authorities ordered Google to suspend work at two sites – Muhos and Otanmäki, about 100km to the south-east – after the company failed to complete environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land.The Supervisory ⁠Agency, which oversees environmental permits and assessments, told Google to halt “preparatory ​measures altering the environment”. Campaigners estimate 250,000 trees have been felled at Muhos and 150,000 at Otanmäki.View image in fullscreenGoogle’s clearcut area of about 200 hectares (500 acres) in Otanmäki, Finland.Photograph: Jarno Artika/The GuardianGoogle’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, has apologised for the forest clearings, but argued that the company had acted according to “the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time”.The Finnish government has encouraged the projects. In September, when Google’s plans were announced, the prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a “top priority” and the deal would “deliver lasting benefits”.But the revelations over Google’s alleged misconduct have sparked a national debate over what datacentre deals mean for communities, the environment and energy prices. The issue could impact parliamentary elections due in April.More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and compensation for environmental damage. Experts say datacentres bring a limited number of local jobs, and benefits on a national level are minimal.“Really, for Finland, there are no benefits,” said Jussi Kangasharju, professor of computer science at University of Helsinki. “They are international companies serving international customers.Datacentresultimately have little benefit for others except the datacentre operator.”Explore more on these topicsFinlandDatacentresEuropeGoogleTrees and forestsDeforestationLogging and land-clearingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Netanyahu accused of smearing Arab voters to hold on to power | Benjamin Netanyahu | The Guardian
description: Prime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majority
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Prime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majority
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu gesturing to supporters on election night. He has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.Photograph: Jalaa Marey/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu gesturing to supporters on election night. He has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.Photograph: Jalaa Marey/AFP/Getty ImagesBenjamin NetanyahuNetanyahu accused of smearing Arab voters to hold on to powerPrime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majorityJulian Borgerin JerusalemThu 29 Oct 2026 19.14 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics to cling to power, after he claimed that Arab Israeli parties had used foreign backing to “steal” Tuesday’s election, in which the prime minister’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority.Netanyahu and his allies called on the internal security service, Shin Bet, to investigate alleged vote buying and other irregularities in Palestinian communities inIsrael, supposedly funded by foreign money.Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the main opposition bloc, accused the prime minister and his Likud party of trying to derail the election results.“It’s already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election,” Eisenkot said in a video message.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot at an election night rally in Tel Aviv after the first exit polls were announced.Photograph: Noam Galai/Getty ImagesThe prime minister’s allegations were quickly disowned by a range of government officials, including police officers and members of the election committee. Netanyahu was also rebuked by the president for “tarnishing an entire community”.On Wednesday night, the prime ministerposted a statement by Likud online, which described the claimed violations as “an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of rightwing rule”.Tuesday’s elections led to Netanyahu’s far-right coalition losing its majority after four years in power. The main Jewish opposition bloc also fell short, however, leaving two Arab Israeli parties, the Joint List and Ra’am,holding the balance of power.Final results released early on Friday local time showed the pro-Netanyahu bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset and Eisenkot’s bloc taking 48 seats. Joint List and Ra’am won the remaining 19 seats, a historic high for the Arab Israeli community, which makes up about a fifth of Israel’s population.The prime minister’s attack appeared aimed at stopping the Jewish and Arab opposition from voting together in the new Knesset to oust the incumbent speaker, Amir Ohana, a Likud politician and former Shin Bet official, and advancing their own legislation.The Likud statement posted by Netanyahu on X said: “It is clear that no Zionist party should cooperate with Ra’am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker through votes bought for cash, and form a government that is dangerous to Israel.”View image in fullscreenAmir Ohana (centre) applauding Donald Trump alongside Isaac Herzog (right) before the US president spoke in the Knesset in October 2025.Photograph: Getty ImagesOpposition leaders lambasted the claims of Netanyahu, 77, who has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List leader, accused the prime minister of incitement. “Netanyahu was defeated at the ballot box,” Jabareen said, adding that he “refuses to come to terms with the fact that the Arab public voted and decided”.Eisenkot said any investigation should be conducted “without fear or favour,” and with “the utmost caution”, but insisted it could not be used as a reason to delay the convening of the newly elected Knesset, due to be sworn in within 14 days of the election.The acting director general of the central elections committee, Dean Livneh, said there appeared to be no basis for the claims. Police officials quoted across the Israeli press said the allegations were groundless, adding that voting had been relatively trouble-free.View image in fullscreenYousef Jabareen casting his ballot in the Arab-Israeli town of Umm al-Fahm.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesThe president, Isaac Herzog, called for political leaders to “avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy”.It was not specified in Likud statements, but press reports said Qatar was the foreign power alleged to have funded vote-buying and voter mobilisation. Majed al-Ansari, an adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said its government “categorically” denied any involvement in the elections.The record turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship) appeared to be driven by outrage at routine discrimination and fear that it could become far worse if extremist and openly racist members of the government, such as the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, secured another term in office.On Thursday, Ben-Gvir called for the arrest of Arab party leaders, and Smotrich demanded they be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation.View image in fullscreenElection campaign posters in Nazareth.Photograph: Adri Salido/Anadolu/Getty ImagesVoting in Nazareth, the biggest majority-Palestinian town in Israel, was brisk on Tuesday, with few signs of irregularities, other than apparent ploys by the government and coalition parties to suppress the Arab vote.Some packets of ballots sent to Nazareth polling stations were in Hebrew alone, rather than in Hebrew and Arabic. Election workers said that monitors sent by far-right parties had attempted procedural ploys to slow down voting but had been largely unsuccessful.The leaders of the Joint List and the Zionist “Change” bloc have ruled out a formal coalition, but officials from both have discussed thepossibility of tactical votingin the Knesset to unseat Ohana, the speaker, and to pass some consensus legislation.One proposed bill would establish a commission of inquiry into the security failures that helped lead to the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, something Netanyahu has blocked over the past two years.Ahmad Tibi, a party leader on the Joint List, said Netanyahu was trying to subvert the election results by trying to sabotage a common front between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties.View image in fullscreenAhmad Tibi casting his vote.Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told the Reuters news agency.Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who is a partner in the “Change” bloc, pointed out the irony of Netanyahu denouncing Qatar for election meddling while the Israeli leader’s own political advisers are beingaccused of taking Qatari moneyfor promoting the Gulf monarchy’s image.“This morning, suddenly, when it serves his interests, Netanyahu remembered Qatar and is using it to sow chaos and undermine public confidence in the democratic process,” Bennett wrote on X.Explore more on these topicsBenjamin NetanyahuIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: JD Vance letter may offer last chance to avert fresh conflict between US and Iran | Iran | The Guardian
description: US vice-president writes to top Iranian security official in sign Washington has not abandoned diplomacy
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: US vice-president writes to top Iranian security official in sign Washington has not abandoned diplomacy
Content: JD Vance is a relatively trusted US figure in Iran, though doubts remain about the power he wields in Washington.Photograph: Evan Vucci/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreenJD Vance is a relatively trusted US figure in Iran, though doubts remain about the power he wields in Washington.Photograph: Evan Vucci/Pool Reuters/APIranJD Vance letter may offer last chance to avert fresh conflict between US and IranUS vice-president writes to top Iranian security official in sign Washington has not abandoned diplomacyPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorThu 29 Oct 2026 15.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHopes of averting a major new conflagration between Iran and the US soon after Tuesday’s midterm elections could rest on Iran’s response to a personal letter from the US vice-president,JD Vance, offering to restart diplomacy.The letter, written after predominantly Qatari mediation, was sent to the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei on Sunday. It requires Tehran to agree to make commitments on its nuclear programme at the start of a process that would lead to the opening of the strait of Hormuz within seven days in return for US sanctions relief.A reply is imminent, but Iran is reluctant to give upfront and irreversible commitments on its nuclear programme, such as exporting its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country, if the compensatory US steps, such as lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports, are reversible.Some form of third-party guarantee that both sides will adhere to their commitments has been discussed, with China often mentioned as the only country of sufficient status to underwrite it.The return of Vance, a sceptic about the war, to the negotiations is significant and a sign the US has not abandoned diplomacy.View image in fullscreenAn anti-US mural in Tehran.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAOne Democratic senator briefed on the targets the US military had identified in Iran said the plan for a renewed attack was “insane” and would lead to “the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law”.In a sign of Iran’s reluctance to meet US demands about sequencing, its chief negotiator, Mohammad Ghalibaf, wrote on X: “Iran’s conditions have been repeatedly and clearly stated to the mediators. The carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran. Progress can only be achieved once Iran’s seven conditions have been agreed upon.”Those conditions include lifting sanctions, ending asset freezes and ending the war on all fronts, a phrase that requires an Israeli ceasefire in Lebanon.The US wants front-loaded, specific commitments about the removal of Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium. Tehran is reluctant to give up its bargaining leverage, and is also resistant to the return of UN nuclear inspectors for fear they might provide the US with intelligence on the whereabouts and state of the stockpile.It has proposed blending the stockpile down so it is no longer usable to make a nuclear weapon.The Vance letter was sent to Rezaei rather than Ghalibaf or the foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, because Washington judged that decision-making power rests with those closest to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. In practice, Iran tries to reach decisions through consensus at the highest level of government in a six strong committee.View image in fullscreenThe secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei.Photograph: Mohammed Salem/ReutersGhalibaf and Rezaei met the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, last week to discuss the risk of a new war. Khamenei has said he would like an end to the current state of neither war nor peace. Iran has well-laid plans ready to strike back against US interests in the region, by hitting desalination plants, internet cables and electricity grids across the Gulf.For a third US attack in two years to have any rationale, or prospect of inducing Iran’s capitulation, the plan would require the US, probably in conjunction with a caretaker government in Israel, to mount attacks on previously off-limits targets. Europe would not join the attacks, but the views of the Gulf states, the chief targets of Iran reprisals, would be key.The Connecticut senator Chris Murphy told a briefing at the Middle East Institute: “I did get a fairly detailed conversation about what the war plan would be … I will just say this their plan is insane. It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law.“There has been open reporting as to the civilian infrastructure we may be targeting … I think the plan they have developed will lead, in my judgment, to a prolongment [sic] and escalation of this war that will be devastating to our security interest.”Although Tehran trusts Vance marginally more than most White House politicians and envoys, the Iranian high command is still suspicious about his status after he negotiated a 14-point memorandum of understanding which then fell apart when other members of the US administration took charge of its implementation.That led to unilateral US steps to reopen the strait of Hormuz that Iran said contravened the terms of the agreement. Trump also came to detest it because it delayed the start of nuclear talks for as long as 60 days.In an offer made by Tehran on the margins of the UN general assembly recently, it proposed foreshortening the timeframe before nuclear talks started, saying they could start withinsix or seven days of the US restoring the sanctions waiver on its oil exports and the reopening of the strait of Hormuz.Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policyTrump administrationJD VanceMiddle East and north AfricaUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Netanyahu bloc loses majority as most ballots counted – as it happened | Israel | The Guardian
description: This live blog is now closed
Author: Jonathan Yerushalmy
Headline: This live blog is now closed
Content: 15.15 EDTClosing summaryThis live blog is now closed – you can read the latest news on the electionshere.You can also read thisanalysis from our Middle East correspondent, Emma Graham-Harrison, who has outlined the options available to Benjamin Netanyahu in the light of Tuesday’s election results.Israel’s future hangs in the balance as it has become clear that Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his governing majority. Hispolitical fate now dependson whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common frontwith Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s historic elections. Indeed, Gadi Eisenkot and his allies face a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s bloc, has told Israeli media that he will meet with three leaders tomorrow for coalition talks.According to the Times of Israel, they will be Eisenkot, the leading opposition candidate and chair of the Yashar party, and Yair Lapid, the number-two in the opposition B’Yachad party. This would mark the official start of coalition talks, and Golan has been the only opposition leader so far backing working with the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel.Israel’sCentral Elections Committeesaid it had received the Likud party’s complaint alleging that Arab parties had compromised election integrity and would examine the claims as part of its routine post-election review.Netanyahu’s party responded to partial election results showing Arab-led partiescould play a king-making role in forming a new governmentby accusing them – without evidence – of “stealing” the election and demanding that the police and Shin Bet security service investigate the allegations.UNrights chief Volker Turk has said that he hopes the next Israeli government will“change course massively” and respect international law. “The message is: don’t continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that’s what we have frankly seen in the current environment,” Turk told reporters in New York. He added: “Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them, and I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively.”ShareUpdated at20.24 EDT

title: Manosphere and online misogyny should be treated as public health issues, say UK experts | Men's health | The Guardian
description: Report calls for an effort to tackle harms in similar way to obesity and smoking, and stresses need to ‘offer boys something better’
Author: Tobi Thomas
Headline: Report calls for an effort to tackle harms in similar way to obesity and smoking, and stresses need to ‘offer boys something better’
Content: ‘Men’s problems are framed [in the manosphere] as the result of feminism rather than structural conditions,’ the report says.Photograph: miniseries/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Men’s problems are framed [in the manosphere] as the result of feminism rather than structural conditions,’ the report says.Photograph: miniseries/Getty ImagesMen's healthManosphere and online misogyny should be treated as public health issues, say UK expertsReport calls for an effort to tackle harms in similar way to obesity and smoking, and stresses need to ‘offer boys something better’Tobi ThomasHealth and inequalities correspondentThu 29 Oct 2026 19.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe manosphere and online misogyny should be treated by the government as a public health issue, in the same way as obesity or smoking, experts have said.Writing in the Lancet, the authors of a new report argue that a coordinated response is needed, involving governments, schools, health services and community organisations, similar to the public-health response to tobacco use and ultra-processed food.“Men’s problems are framed [in the manosphere] as the result of feminism rather than structural conditions, and masculine identity is commodified through products and paid content that normalise and reinforce health-harming and performance-oriented masculinities,” the authors write.The report defines the manosphere as “a diffuse commercial ecosystem and loose collection of online communities united by shared beliefs about masculinity, misogyny and male victimisation”.It goes on to outline how the manosphere has evolved into a highly lucrative online industry that makes money by promoting “the most extreme expressions of misogyny and aggrieved masculinity”.Prof Kent Buse, a co-author of the paper and co-founder of the social justice thinktank Global 50/50, said: “This is a business model, not a fringe. Outrage and grievance are good for business, so the system rewards the most extreme content. Expect the playbook that served tobacco so well: blame the individual, and call regulation an attack on freedom. Public health has a tested toolkit for commercial harms and we should use it.”He added: “Boys and men are not the problem. The problem is the conditions that leave them isolated and without a secure future, and the companies that profit from their anger and insecurity.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK government to give £15m to anti-misogyny fund amid ‘manosphere’ concernsRead moreThe authors also point to growing disengagement from education among boys around the world, as well as loneliness, money worries and social exclusion, which can leave young men searching for a sense of belonging. These problems, they say, can make them more vulnerable to online communities that offer simple explanations for their difficulties and often encourage them to blame women and feminism.Prof Sarah Hawkes, the report’s other author, said: “The manosphere offers boys and young men belonging, identity and an explanation for why life feels hard.“Those needs are real. A response that only removes the manosphere, without offering something credible in its place, will fail. We need to offer boys something better, not just tell them what to avoid.”Mark Brooks, the policy and communications director at the Centre for Policy Research on Men and Boys, welcomed the report’s position that it was a public health issue and that men, boys, women and girls were all victims of this content.“Far too often, the manosphere discussion has positioned all men and boys as a problem and not taken into account the broader economic, educational and cultural challenges that drive their engagement,” he said.“Not all men and boys engage with this content equally. We are currently working on research to identify who is most at risk.”Explore more on these topicsMen's healthYoung peopleViolence against women and girlsInternet safetyMenSocial mediaOnline abusenewsShareReuse this content

title: Polymarket temporarily suspends trading on international platform due to security incident | Polymarket | The Guardian
description: Security incident linked to performance-monitoring tool spurred platform to halt trading for about an hour
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Security incident linked to performance-monitoring tool spurred platform to halt trading for about an hour
Content: Polymarket said it referred the incident to a law enforcement agency in the United Kingdom.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolymarket said it referred the incident to a law enforcement agency in the United Kingdom.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesPolymarketPolymarket temporarily suspends trading on international platform due to security incidentSecurity incident linked to performance-monitoring tool spurred platform to halt trading for about an hourAssociated PressThu 29 Oct 2026 19.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolymarket temporarily halted trading on its international platform on Thursday because of a security incident that compromised a third-party provider, the company said.Trading was paused for about an hour and resumed on Thursday afternoon. The company has promised to fully reimburse any affected traders.Prediction markets surge in US as public health advocates call for support to combat gamblingRead moreThe prediction market platform said it halted trading “out of an abundance of caution” after identifying and fixing the issue affecting its international platform.“We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders,” the company posted on X once trading had resumed.Polymarket said it referred the incident to a law enforcement agency in the United Kingdom.Reports have linked the source of the incident to DebugBear, a UK-based company offering website performance-monitoring tools.DebugBear’s own website was unavailable on Thursday afternoon and the company posted on X that it was “impacted by an ongoing security incident”. It also advised clients who were using one of its products to remove the embed code from their websites. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.It was not immediately clear to what extent traders using the popular prediction market platform were affected, or the breadth of the impact. The company said anyone who was affected “will be made whole”.Explore more on these topicsPolymarketPrediction marketsGamblingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Patrick Stewart, Star Trek actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86 | Patrick Stewart | The Guardian
description: Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men actor died at his home after ‘a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia’
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men actor died at his home after ‘a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia’
Content: Patrick Stewart, who has died aged 86, played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Treak: the Next Generation and Charles Xavier in X-Men.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPatrick Stewart, who has died aged 86, played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Treak: the Next Generation and Charles Xavier in X-Men.Photograph: Philip Cheung/The GuardianPatrick StewartPatrick Stewart, Star Trek actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men actor died at his home after ‘a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia’Patrick Stewart – a life in picturesPatrick Stewart dies aged 86 – latest updatesAdrian HortonandBenjamin LeeThu 29 Oct 2026 17.02 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatrick Stewart, the acclaimed British stage and screen actor renowned for both Shakespeare and sci-fi, has died. He was 86.The Star Trek: the Next Generation and X-Men star died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”, said Kelly Bush Novak, his longtime spokesperson, tothe Hollywood Reporter.Patrick Stewart – a life in picturesRead more“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” she wrote. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”With his authoritative baritone voice and commanding visage, Stewart was already a staple of the British stage by the late 1980s when, at 47, he was cast as a graying Capt Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: the Next Generation, the first live-action spin-off of the groundbreaking 1960s TV series. Over seven seasons onboard the Starship Enterprise, Stewart’s even-keeled performance and steely directives – “engage!” and “make it so” – turned him into a global star.View image in fullscreenPatrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1990.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesStewart reprised his role in four feature film spin-offs – Star Trek Generations (1994), Star Trek: First Contact (1996), Star Trek: Insurrection (1998) and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002) – as well as the TV series Star Trek: Picard, which ran from 2020 until 2023.His longtime friend, fellow Shakespearean actor and X-Men co-star Ian McKellenwrote on social media: “Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.”Fellow Star Trek actor William Shatner paid tribute on social media. “From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did,” hewrote. “Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.”‘On stage, I could escape’: Sir Patrick Stewart on childhood trauma and acting successRead moreGeorge Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the original series, also wrote about Stewart on Bluesky. “He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity,” heposted. “Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.”His other most well-known role was playing Prof Charles Xavier in the X-Men series. The actor had found work hard to obtain after feeling typecast as a result of his Star Trek role but had been intrigued by working with director Bryan Singer for 2000’s X-Men.He went on to play the role in seven films and will be seen reprising the role in this December’s Avengers: Doomsday.View image in fullscreenPatrick Stewart as Charles Xavier in X-Men 2.Photograph: Marvel/AllstarHis X-Men co-star Hugh Jackmansharedon Instagram: “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”Marvel chief Kevin Feige has paid tribute in a statement calling him “brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas … Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor. It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.”Stewart’s other film roles included the gay comedy Jeffrey, romantic thriller Conspiracy Theory, violent horror Green Room and voice roles in Ted, Gnomeo & Juliet and, most recently, The Sheep Detectives.View image in fullscreenPatrick Stewart and Ian Holm on stage in The Iceman Cometh.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyBorn on 13 July 1940 in the small industrial village of Mirfield, England, Stewart was the youngest of three sons born to Alfred Stewart, a British military veteran turned semiskilled laborer, and Gladys Stewart, a weaver at a textile factory. His childhood, in a small house with no running hot water, was marred by alcoholism and domestic violence, a situation he later described, in anarticlefor the Guardian from 2009, as “barely tolerable”.He found respite in acting, first in school – he was 12 when an English teacher assigned him the part of Shylock in Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice – and then local drama groups. “I managed to find my own refuge in acting,” he wrote. “The stage was a far safer place for me than anything I had to live through at home – it offered escape. I could be someone else, in another place, in another time.”After graduating from secondary school at 15, he worked as a local reporter and furniture salesman before a local arts council provided the funding to attend the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theater School, where he enrolled in 1957, at 17. Having shed his Yorkshire accent, he took his first professional theater role two years later, and in 1966 joined the Royal Shakespeare Company. During his 16 years with the company, Stewart developed a reputation as one of the finest thespians of his era and a representative of Shakespeare to new audiences; it was while conducting master classes on Shakespeare in LA, at the invitation of a friend, that he first caught the eye of a TV casting director for Star Trek.Stewart made his Broadway debut in 1971 in Peter Brook’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and appeared again 20 years later in a solo production of A Christmas Carol. The holiday season show, which he revived in 1992, 1994 and 2001, received a Drama Desk award.View image in fullscreenDavid Tennant as Hamlet and Patrick Stewart as Claudius, in a Royal Shakespeare Company production of Hamlet.Photograph: Robbie Jack/Corbis/Getty ImagesOver the course of his career, Stewart embodied many of Shakespeare’s signature roles, including Macbeth, Othello, Prospero, Shylock and Mark Antony. He was the recipient of two Laurence Olivier awards – in 1979, for Antony and Cleopatra, and in 2009 for Hamlet – as well as a Grammy in 1996 for a spoken word children’s album Prokofiev: Peter and the Wolf. He was also nominated for a Tony and four Emmys.His final major stage role was in 2016, when he appeared as Hirst in Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land at London’s Wyndham Theatre. In 2023, he released his memoir called Making It So.Stewart was a vocal fan of Huddersfield Town FC since he was a child and was seen cheering them on most recently in 2024.In a Facebook postfrom the official team, he was called “a titan of his craft and a legend and hero to millions worldwide”.Stewart was married three times: to theater choreographer Sheila Falconer, from 1966 until 1990 and with whom he had two children, fellow actors Daniel and Sophie; to Star Trek producer Wendy Neuss from 2000 until 2003; and to jazz musician Sunny Ozell from 2013 until his death.
