His friend and occasional collaborator Ian McKellen, with whom Stewart starred in two Broadway productions in 2013, officiated his final wedding after a rehearsal.“I think I’ve been in denial about my life for a very long time,” he said to the Guardian ina 2023 interview. “I never really took on board how successful I had become. Even today I sometimes think, ‘You’re a lucky son of a bitch, Patrick,’ when something unexpected or good happens to me.”Explore more on these topicsPatrick StewartStar TrekTelevisionUS televisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Healey backs away from cutting welfare cost amid warnings of public finance shortfall | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Experts round on chancellor over ‘scattergun’ budget, saying he ducked big tax and spending decisions
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Experts round on chancellor over ‘scattergun’ budget, saying he ducked big tax and spending decisions
Content: Disabled people and supporters protest against cuts to welfare benefits in Westminster in June.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDisabled people and supporters protest against cuts to welfare benefits in Westminster in June.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesBudget 2026Healey backs away from cutting welfare cost amid warnings of public finance shortfallExperts round on chancellor over ‘scattergun’ budget, saying he ducked big tax and spending decisionsHeather Stewart,Rowena Mason,Richard PartingtonandPhillip InmanThu 29 Oct 2026 16.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 18.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.Experts rounded on Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget on Thursday, with the Institute for Fiscal Studies saying he hadleft himself a mountain to climbby ducking big tax and spending decisions.In a damning analysis, the IFS said Healey would need to have set aside an additional £28bn a year, to offset the impact of inflation on future spending plans and hit the target of spending 3% of GDP in defence by 2030.Instead Helen Miller, the IFS director, said Healey had opened the way to “a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments” – including real-term budget cuts.“Public service spending plans look extremely tight. They don’t look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver,” she said, adding that meant Healey could face “another season of damaging speculation about tax rises”.The welfare bill will not be part of the spending review, which focuses on departmental budgets. But in a bid to underline his determination to balance the books, the chancellor pointed to plans for reform, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We have to bring the benefits bill down.”He had earlier appeared to say cuts would be made in this parliament, when asked if there would be a reduction in the bill before the next election. “There will be. There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Healey. “We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progress to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.”Budget 2026: what it means for your wallet, your mortgage and your payRead moreHowever, Treasury officials clarified that he had not meant to give a timeline and Healey later told Channel 4: “It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.”Instead, he pointed to forthcoming reviews from Alan Milburn on employment support for young people, and from Stephen Timms on disability benefits.Milburn is expected to recommend additional spending upfront, aimed at bringing down costs over the longer term by helping more young people into employment.The Office forBudgetResponsibility has said total welfare spending will grow from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030 – with about half of that being spent on pensioners and a quarter on sickness and disability benefits. The overall forecast spending has risen by £8bn since March.With a tough global economic backdrop, Healey has said the single biggest driver of better prospects for the UK would be an end to the Iran and Ukraine wars.But in his interviews, Healey appeared to take a more cautious view than the prime minister on the potential for growth from rejoining Europe or the single market. Asked by LBC if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU or the single market, Healey replied: “Well, I don’t actually accept that. Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union. The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient.”Asked later by Channel 4 if he, like Andy Burnham, hoped for the UK to re-enter the bloc in his lifetime, Healey said: “I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.”The chancellor put measures to ease the cost of living at the heart of his first budget, including a £100 winter cost of living payment for most households. However, critics lined up on Thursday to accuse him of taking a “scattergun” approach – and of not hitting Britain’s banks hard enough to fund the package.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Resolution Foundation thinktank said Healey had failed to target energy support to the households that need it most ahead of a difficult winter, with bills expected to rise sharply in January and the Bank of England to raise interest rates next week.Ruth Curtice, Resolution’s chief executive, said: “Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain.“Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.”John Healey faces questions over budget leak that moved bank share pricesRead morePaul Nowak, the TUC’s general secretary, has strongly advocated for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support. He said he welcomed Healey’s approach, but would be pushing for him to go further.The chancellor has doubled the surcharge banks pay on their profits from 3% to 6% for 15 months. Novak said: “It was right to tax banks to help people with their energy bills, but I think banks could have been asked to pay a fairer share. He’s going to review it in 15 months. We’re going to be looking as part of that review – if banks are still making windfall profits – for him to extend and increase the bank tax.”As well as casting doubt on whether Healey’s future spending plans are realistic, the IFS said the £15bn headroom, or buffer, he has left himself against Labour’s fiscal rules could easily be eroded by higher than expected energy costs.The chancellor allowed the buffer to absorb some of the impact of the Iran war, which has driven up the government’s cost of borrowing. At the time of the spring statement, Rachel Reeves had built up headroom of £24bn.Miller said that was a “reasonable” decision to make, but “a lower buffer leaves the chancellor more exposed to future bad news”.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyInstitute for Fiscal StudiesThinktanksBudgetTax and spendingWelfarenewsShareReuse this content

title: Met refers itself to police watchdog over Meghan warning letter | Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex | The Guardian
description: Move comes as Philippines police investigate alleged child sexual abuse images reportedly found at Thomas Markle Sr’s former home
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Move comes as Philippines police investigate alleged child sexual abuse images reportedly found at Thomas Markle Sr’s former home
Content: A letter was sent to the Met ‘to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex’.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA/APView image in fullscreenA letter was sent to the Met ‘to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex’.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA/APMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMet refers itself to police watchdog over Meghan warning letterMove comes as Philippines police investigate alleged child sexual abuse images reportedly found at Thomas Markle Sr’s former homeVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentThu 29 Oct 2026 15.55 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheMetropolitan policehas referred itself to the police watchdog over potential errors in its handling of a 2019 letter warning of dangers to the security of the Duchess of Sussex posed by her father.The letter made allegations about Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, who is facing claims of child sexual abuse images offending linked to thePhilippines, which he denies.It was allegedly written by his former wife and the Met says the letter was passed seven years ago to the private office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who were then both working royals.The Guardian understands that the long letter made claims about Markle’s activities in the US, the Philippines and Thailand.The Met said it did not investigate as the allegations related to potential unlawful activity overseas.The key problem for the Met is its admission that it did not share the letter with law enforcement agencies overseas, and that issue has been referred to the police watchdog, the Independent Office forPoliceConduct.The Guardian understands the Met is now sending details of the letter to the FBI in the US and law enforcement in the Philippines, where Markle lived until May, as well as Thai counterparts.Markle, now in the US, has admitted paying for sex but denies possessing material that would be illegal.On Saturday Jonvic Remulla, the Philippine interior minister,told the Guardian that all signs point to Marklebeing a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” and that a full forensic investigation will give a “definitive picture”.Officials and investigators in the Philippines are examining digital images alleged to belong to the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, and alleged to have been found at his former home in the south-east Asian country.Meghan’s half-brother, also called Thomas, reported to Philippine authorities last week the alleged discovery of child sexual abuse images.The allegations about the letter and alleged Met failings surfaced publicly a week ago. The Met has been unable to find its own copy of the letter making the claims, alleged to have been written by Markle’s former wife.Met Commander Adam Slonecki, who leads its Protection Command, said the letter had been sent in 2019 to the Fixated Threats Assessment Centre: “The author of the letter suggested they were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.“The letter was assessed and subsequently passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”Slonecki added: “A voluntary referral has been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.”The Met cannot find a copy of the 2019 warning letter in its systems, and asked the Duchess of Sussex to send the copy she had to assist Britain’s biggest force to better understand its decision making seven years ago, which she did.An IOPC spokesperson said: “We have received a voluntary conduct referral from the Met police, which relates to the handling of a letter it received in 2019 involving allegations of offending. We are now assessing the referral before deciding what further action may be required.”Possible options include the police watchdog independently investigating or sending the matter back for the Met to investigate.The scale of embarrassment for the Met will depend on whether investigators in the Philippines assess that the allegations relating to child sexual abuse images have any credence.Explore more on these topicsMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMetropolitan policePolicePhilippinesMonarchyLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hegseth reportedly fires high-ranking army strategist over alleged leaks | US military | The Guardian
description: Pentagon says it has referred leak case to justice department for criminal investigation
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Pentagon says it has referred leak case to justice department for criminal investigation
Content: Brett Sylvia, then a brigadier general, speaks at a combined arms rehearsal at Konotop, Poland, in 2020.Photograph: Spc. Javan Johnson/Training Support Activity EuropeView image in fullscreenBrett Sylvia, then a brigadier general, speaks at a combined arms rehearsal at Konotop, Poland, in 2020.Photograph: Spc. Javan Johnson/Training Support Activity EuropeUS militaryHegseth reportedly fires high-ranking army strategist over alleged leaksPentagon says it has referred leak case to justice department for criminal investigationMarina DunbarThu 29 Oct 2026 18.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US defense secretary,Pete Hegseth, has reportedly dismissed Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, a high-ranking army strategist serving on the Pentagon’s joint staff, following allegations that he disclosed classified information to the public.The Pentagon announced on Thursday that it had referred an alleged information leak case for criminal investigation, maintaining that the removal of the senior general was essential “to protect sensitive information”, theWashington Postreported.Sylvia had served as the director for strategy, plans and policy on the joint staff.Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell acknowledged the dismissal in astatementon social media, though he did not mention Sylvia by name.Democratic senator says Hegseth trying to hide costs of Iran war from US publicRead more“Following an extensive Air Force OSI investigation, the Department took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information,” Parnell wrote. “To protect the integrity of the investigation, no further comment will be made regarding the individual or the circumstances of this action.”“This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action,” he added.A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said in a statement that it “has ongoing investigations related to possible leaks of classified information”.“We work closely with our government partners, which includes the Department of War,” the spokesperson added, using the Trump administration’s name for the Pentagon.Sylvia’s removal represents one of the most significant actions so far in Hegseth’s extensive campaign to identify officials suspected of sharing information with journalists, as theunpopularUS war on Iran moves into its ninth month.In July, Hegseth ​announced that the Pentagon and the US Department of Justice hadcreated a joint taskforce“​to identify and ​prosecute” what he called the “unauthorized disclosure ​of sensitive” information to the press.Last year, Hegseth implemented new restrictions governing media access that prompted legal concerns from press organizations.Dozens of journalists surrendered their press badges rather than agree to the new media policies, which have been subject to legal challenges.A senior Pentagon official toldReutersthat Sylvia failed three separate polygraph tests, in which he was asked whether he had disclosed classified material.“The extent of his leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security. Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second,” the official said, according to Reuters.However, a colleague of Sylvia told the Washington Post that the general had consistently rejected accusations that he leaked classified information, while also acknowledging that he had previously communicated with members of the press.In August, three journalistsfiredby the Pentagon from the US government-funded news outlet Stars and Stripes sued the department in federal court, arguing their dismissals were illegal and violated their first amendment rights to free speech.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryPete HegsethnewsShareReuse this content

title: DHS cites risk to more than 40,000 personnel in effort to take leaked data offline | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: The Department of Homeland Security asked an Icelandic hosting company to take down data obtained through hack
Author: Maanvi Singh
Headline: The Department of Homeland Security asked an Icelandic hosting company to take down data obtained through hack
Content: A federal agent stands guard at Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility, in Newark, New Jersey, on 30 May 2026.Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA federal agent stands guard at Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility, in Newark, New Jersey, on 30 May 2026.Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The GuardianTrump administrationDHS cites risk to more than 40,000 personnel in effort to take leaked data offlineThe Department of Homeland Security asked an Icelandic hosting company to take down data obtained through hackMaanvi Singhand agenciesThu 29 Oct 2026 16.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) asked ⁠an Icelandic hosting company on Thursday to take down or limit access to data related to thousands ⁠of agency personnel, saying ⁠the content ​put them at risk, according to the request posted online by hosting company FlokiNET.The database “places more than ⁠40,000 identifiable individuals at risk of harassment, stalking and physical harm”, the request said.ZeroFox, a company authorized by the US ⁠Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)agency to pursue content removal actions, cited the figure in ​an email to FlokiNET.Non-profit group leaks data of more than 40,000 homeland security workersRead moreFlokiNET’s ‌CEO, Kolja Weber, told ‌Reuters that his company would not remove the DHS data because it ‌included government employee work addresses and work phone numbers, not personal phone numbers and addresses.A DHS spokesperson said the agency “is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously ‌and will work to ensure all are properly protected.”The non-profit data transparency group DDoSecrets released data on more than 40,000 DHS personnel ​on its website on Wednesday, alongside a separate, searchable database developed by hacker and journalist “maia arson crimew”. The database was briefly inaccessible on Thursday but was soon republished at a different domain.A group calling itself “the Department of Peace” claimed responsibility ⁠for obtaining the data, and said in a statement on Wednesday ​that DHS ​employees “have our information, so it’s only ​fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped ​the data “can be ‌used to limit ​further harm ​by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”.Privacy advocates have criticized the DHS’s use of personal data from other agencies, including Medicaid records and taxpayer data, for immigration enforcement.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationIcelandHackingICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Was Ralph Nader right about (almost) everything? His challenge to Democrats ahead of the midterm elections | Ralph Nader | The Guardian
description: The ex-presidential candidate tells Democrats to prosecute corruption and bring real change for the working class
Author: Heather Timmons
Headline: The ex-presidential candidate tells Democrats to prosecute corruption and bring real change for the working class
Content: Ralph Nader listens during a news conference on 2 July 2012 at Public Citizen in Washington DC.Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRalph Nader listens during a news conference on 2 July 2012 at Public Citizen in Washington DC.Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty ImagesConsumedRalph NaderInterviewWas Ralph Nader right about (almost) everything? His challenge to Democrats ahead of the midterm electionsHeather Timmonsin WashingtonThe ex-presidential candidate tells Democrats to prosecute corruption and bring real change for the working classThu 29 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA corporate plutocracy. A broken healthcare system. Massive and widening inequality. Cash-soaked elections. Angry people struggling to pay their bills and disgusted with lawmakers inWashington DC.Nearly everything that pushed famed consumer-rights advocate Ralph Nader to launchthe 2000 presidential runthat made him a political pariah in Washington is front and center as the US gears up for the 2026 midterm elections. But this time, things are much, much worse.Nader, now 92, has been seething from his home in north-west Washington as the Trump administrationrips the gutsout of the hard-fought consumer and safety protections he built in the 1960s and 1970s. He’s once again calling for a revolution in a Democratic party that still wants nothing to do with him.“The best thing that could happen for the Democrats is for [Senator Chuck] Schumer and [Hakeem] Jeffries to be voted out in January,” Nader told the Guardian during one of several long phone calls, speaking of the Democratic leaders in both houses of Congress.If Democrats win next week, they need to be bold to fix the country, Nader said: prosecute corruption, restore the federal agencies that have been destroyed, and really change things for the working class. He doubts Schumer and Jeffries will do it.“You think they’re going to have that kind of energy and courage?” Nader said. “They have no stomach for that. They’re going to drag the Democratic party down. People want justice.”As Democrats and their allies seek to defeat Trumpism and restore the US’s teetering democracy, it would be easy to dismiss Nader as a tragic footnote amid the current chaos: the man, although he and his allies vehemently disagree, whose run as a Green party presidential candidate cost Al Gore the presidency and left George W Bush in control.View image in fullscreenRalph Nader addresses supporters as his mother Rose Nader looks on after his arrival at the National Press Club in Washington DC on 7 November 2000.Photograph: Rick Bowmer/APBut the ideas he’s preached for decades, rooted in the New Deal ideals that built the US into an economic powerhouse, are front and center in the midterms and beyond, after a failure to address the woes of working-class Americans opened the door to Trumpism.For Nader, and many others, the central question is: does anyone inUS politicshave the fight to fix what’s wrong?A series of progressive wins in the Democratic primaries and a flood of cash to Republicans has puteverything on the table, from taxing billionaires to raising minimum wage to “Medicare for All” to campaign finance reform. Even the left’s most moderating voices and a few Republicans agree it’s time to rein in the power and influence of big business.Democrats “believe in regulated capitalism, and that we have overdone the capitalism and underdone the regulation”, said Matt Bennett, whose Third Way thinktank pushes moderate ideas. “The fact that we have a trillionaire who is trying to control American politics is pretty good evidence of that,” he added, speaking of Elon Musk’s Republican donations – nowover $442mfor the midterm elections.Tinkering around the edges won’t be enough, many believe.“There’s a prairie fire rebellion taking place across America today,” said Barry Lynn, director of the Open Markets Institute, an anti-monopoly thinktank in Washington. “Tax policy is not enough,” he said. “People want revolutionary change.”The last pro-regulation eraView image in fullscreenRalph Nader, speaking as an auto safety critic, appears in 1966 before the Senate commerce subcommittee, which is investigating charges by Nader that he was harassed and intimidated by General Motors because of a book he had written critical of the automobile makers. Earlier, the GM president, James M Roche, apologized for his firm’s investigation of Nader.Photograph: Bettmann ArchiveAs a lawyer in his 30s working with political heavyweight Daniel Patrick Moynihan, then a labor department official, on auto safety, Nader was thrust into the national spotlight after he wrote Unsafe At Any Speed, which blamed car design instead of what the industry used to call “the nut behind the wheel” for the high rate of US auto deaths.After he appeared before a congressional hearing in 1966 to testify about his findings, General Motors hired private investigators to, as Nader later said, “obtain lurid details” about his private life.When the sting was reported, GM’s then president, James Roche,publicly apologizedand Nader sued. He used the $425,000 invasion of privacy settlement as seed money to build a team of hundreds of lawyers, dubbed “Nader’s Raiders” who investigated everything from airline safety to air quality to the radiation being emitted from television sets, and left a trail of new laws and federal agencies in their wake.Big business hasn’t faced as much pushback in the United States since, with the notable exception of the Consumer Finance Protection Bureau (CFPB) created by the Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren after Wall Street created the 2008 financial crisis.Republicans, led by theTrump administration, have beentrying to destroythe CFPB for a decade and appear to beclose to succeeding. After Joe Biden’s administration stepped up enforcement of predatory practices, re-examined monopolies and championed labor rights, Trump’s White House has gone the opposite direction.What Nader was able to do during the 1960s and 1970s isn’t going to work today. New rules for how businesses should act happened because of the energy in Congress then and Nader’s ability “to create an advocacy model and push through a lot of legislation and policy where business wasn’t ready for it and the times were demanding it”, explains Robert Weissman, the co-president of Public Citizen, one of groups Nader founded.“The problem now is the times demand it and people want it but business is organized against it,” Weissman said. “It’s not that we’re not trying hard enough. There’s a different kind of pushback.”Federal lobbying, or money businesses and other groups spend trying to influence policy set in Washington hit a record of$5.13bn in 2025, a 250% increase from 1998. Trade groups representing industry, realtors and drug companies aretop donors.At the same time, “we’re dealing with an administration that’s both carrying water for corporations and wrecking regulatory agencies, against the backdrop of a hostile court system,” Weissman said.The Vermont senator Bernie Sanders ran presidential campaigns on these issues in 2016 and Sanders and Warren in 2020. But no one has become an effective national champion for them in the way Nader did at his zenith. He was plastered on magazine covers and topped most-trusted polls, appeared on Saturday Night Live and Phil Donahue’s talkshow, and had the ear of presidents, Congress and major news organizations.View image in fullscreenBill Murray and Ralph Nader during the Weekend Update sketch on 15 March 1980.Photograph: NBC via Getty Images“It’s almost infuriating that we don’t have somebody helming a consumer movement in this country given how central these issues are to the national conversation,” said Lindsay Owens, the president of Groundwork Collaborative, a Washington research and policy grouppushing new lawsto curb algorithmic pricing and other pro-consumer moves.And no, Sanders, 85, doesn’t want to talk to him either. “Bernie hasn’t called me back in 25 years,” Nader said.Nader once cornered Sanders in the Senate barbershop while the senator was getting a shave. “He couldn’t run away,” Nader recalled, so he grilled him about why the senator wasn’t meeting with him or other public advocates and organizers. “Look, he doesn’t want to be associated with me because of the way they tainted me on 2000,” he said.Nader remains undeterred. He backed animpeachment seminarin July andpredicted Trump could step downthis month. Recently, he has been dialing progressive candidates including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Maine’s Troy Jackson directly, to present hispolicy planhe thinks would guarantee their midterm success even as money pours into Republican opponents. On the agenda: higher wages, universal health insurance, putting “corporate crooks” in jail and impeaching Trump. “The better their agenda, the less money they need” to win, he said.Nader’s not optimistic about big changes if Democrats win both houses of Congress, however. “They’ll break open the champagne and go back to business as normal and start raising more money for 2028,” he predicts. “I can predict ’em like you predict the sun coming up every morning,” he added.Things go awryThe 2000 presidential election that unexpectedly put Bush into power catapulted the country into a fresh round of corporate tax cuts and deregulation, as well as the disastrous Iraq war. Some liberals point to it as a turning point, marking the death of bipartisanship and politicalization of the supreme court.Nader was first recruited to run for president in 1996 by a Green party dismayed by, among other things, Democratic president Bill Clinton’s welfare reform. The goal was to capture enough of the popular vote to cross the5% thresholdfor a public funding grant in the next election, ushering in a new era of three-party politics in a country dominated by two for over 130 years.Republicans and Democrats had cozied up to corporate power so completely that citizens and citizens groups like the ones he founded couldn’t do much any more, Nader said. “King Corporation rules in Washington DC,” he said in aMay 2000 speech. “We have a government of the Exxon’s, by the General Motors, for the DuPonts.”“He wanted to get his message out but he also wanted to help the Green party get 5% of the vote so they could build as an organization,” said two-time former campaign manager Theresa Amato, a lawyer and public advocate.A precursor to Sanders’ presidential campaign, Nader drew thousands of young people in massive rallies. He was joined onstage by celebrities including Susan Sarandon, Patti Smith, Ani DiFranco and Eddie Vedder.He started his run promising not to campaign in swing states that could have cost Gore the election, but changed his mind after he was blocked from the presidential debate, film-maker Michael Moore, a Nader supporter, recalled in a2020 podcast. “That’s when things went awry for Ralph,” he believes.Stepping aside wasn’t an option. “There was an immense amount of pressure” to exit the race in late 2000, Amato said. “Nader’s view was that we could not abandon our supporters, all the volunteers and donors, and the embryonic US Green party, that had mobilized for the campaign and just drop out at the last minute.”While 2000 was its most successful year, the Green party eked out less than 3% of the popular vote. In Florida, Nader got nearly 100,000 votes. When a5-4 supreme court decisionhalted a recount in the state, Bush had 537 more votes, giving him Florida’s 25 electoral college votes and the presidency.View image in fullscreenActors Susan Sarandon and Tim Robbins lead a Nader 2000 Citizens Committee rally in support of Green party presidential candidate Ralph Nader on 25 September 2000 on the steps of city hall in New York City.Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesGoredidn’t even win his home state, Tennessee (Bill Clinton won there twice). Other third-party candidates and a faulty ballot probably played a role. Pat Buchanan’s “Reform party” got nearly 17,500 in Florida; Stanford Universityresearchers foundPalm Beach county’s confusingly designed “butterfly ballot” caused more than 2,000 Gore voters to vote by mistake for Buchanan there alone.At one point, Gore sent him a letter, Nader recalls, absolving him of responsibility.Gore declined several requests for an interview. He is “overbooked”, a spokesperson said.Nader was suddenly an outcast. “He was no longer invited on to talkshows, he wasn’t invited to anything. He was a pariah,” Moore explained.That hasn’t changed as the economic red flags he warned about proved true. Nader “played a very steep reputational price for being the Cassandra” of the situation the US is in now, said Steve Skrovan, producer of An Unreasonable Man, a 2006 documentary about Nader and the 2000 presidential election.Today’s corporate overreach “would not have happened had the so-called ‘opposition party’ not ceded the ground for this through their own neglect and corporatization”, Skrovan said.Nader remains unapologetic. “The Democrats are scapegoaters on steroids,” he said. “They never look at themselves in the mirror and say ‘How can we not have landslided this bumbling governor from Texas with a horrible record who couldn’t string three sentences together?’” he said, referring to Bush.They did it again in 2016, he added, when Donald Trump beat Hillary Clinton. “Imagine blaming Jill Stein, who got a few votes in Pennsylvania,” he added, speaking of the Green party candidate who got 1% of the vote, running ona $15 minimum wageand guaranteed healthcare. “What if you picked up her agenda? You would have won in a landslide, you idiots.”None of the aboveThe 2000 election was a pivotal moment for the Democratic party’s finances too. That’s when Tony Coelho “revolutionized the party, placing fundraising above ideology as the Democratic credo”, the New York Timeswrote in 1999, as he was placed at the head of Gore’s campaign.In the years since, the amount of corporate donations for both Democrats and Republicans has soared. They got an extra boost from the2010 Citizens United supreme court decisionthat allowed big business to openly back candidates.Multiple line charts comparing donations across Presidential elections grouped by business, labor, ideological and other. Business eclipses donations at $6 billion by recent election cyclesTaxing the wealthy and making companies treat their workers and customers better are highly popular with voters. Republicans crafted a long-term plan to use non-economic ideas to drive wedges into the coalition that passed reforms supporting these ideas in the first half of the 1900s, Pat Buchanan, a consultant to Republican presidents Richard Nixon, Gerald Ford and Ronald Reagan explained in An Unreasonable Man. “You did this with social, cultural issues. You carve off all their issues which do not conflict with your own …and keep hammering and hammering them,” Buchanan said.To win votes on economic issues, Democrats are going to have to turn against their donors and brave an onslaught of lobbying and campaign cash against them. It’s about time, some progressive strategists believe.“You spent a generation cozying up to these guys, and there’s no middle class any more,” Dan Geldon, Senator Warren’s former chief of staff, who worked on her 2020 campaign.The Democratic party’s infighting and Trump’s recentering of the Republican party around white supremacy, a nationalist foreign policy and more power for companies and the wealthy come as fewer and fewer Americans want either party.The percentage of US voters who consider themselves “independent” hit a record high of 45% in late 2025,Gallup polling shows. For gen Z voters, born between 1997 and 2007, that figure is a record 56%, up from 40% for the same-aged voters in 1992.View image in fullscreenThen Ecology candidate Ralph Nader for the US presidency circa 1999.Photograph: Andrew Lichtenstein/Sygma/Getty Images“Workers need rights and representation in this world,” Dan Osborn, who isrunning for Senate from Nebraskaas an independent, told the Guardian. “Otherwise, they’ll work you to death and not pay hardly anything,” he said. Osborn, a union leader,led a strikeat Kellogg’s Nebraska plant after the company said it would offshore jobs and cut benefits while showering investors with stock buy-backs.“To me, it’s all about standing up for the little guy, and I didn’t see anybody doing that,” he said, explaining why he is running. Osborn lost handily in 2024 to the Republican incumbent, Deb Fischer.Going into the midterm election,he’s trailing Pete Ricketts, a Republican whose father is a billionaire. Ricketts now has a slight lead in the polls.For his part, Nader has some more uncomfortable predictions. “Someone asked me decades ago, ‘What’s going to cause the end of the world?’ And my answer was science and technology in the hands of giant corporations and dictatorships’” Nader said. “We’re right on track.”He hasn’t given up.Citizens still have the power to change everything, Nader said, by organizing themselves to demand Congress pass something revolutionary like universal healthcare. Maybe a popular podcaster like Joe Rogan could jumpstart the movement, he said. He hasn’t been able to get through to Rogan, though.“It’s still ‘We the people’ in the constitution. It’s not ‘We the Congress’ or ‘We the Corporation,’” Nader said. All we need is “the people to just get off their ass”.Explore more on these topicsRalph NaderConsumedUS midterm elections 2026US politicsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: US economy grows faster than expected but inflation rises to 3.7% | US economy | The Guardian
description: Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loom
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loom
Content: A person shops for groceries in New York City on 26 August 2026. There has been a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreenA person shops for groceries in New York City on 26 August 2026. There has been a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersUS economyUS economy grows faster than expected but inflation rises to 3.7%Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loomLauren Arataniand ReutersThu 29 Oct 2026 09.09 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS economygrew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third-quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.Estimates ranged from ⁠a 1% growth rate to a 4.2% pace.The growth comesas resilient consumer spending andAI-driven ⁠business investment hasmore than ⁠offset the impact ​of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in theMiddle East.The change is in stark contrast to ​households’ downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in ‌Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings ‌and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment.Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midtermsRead moreThe economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what someFederal Reserveofficials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of about 2%. New data from the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, showed that prices increased 0.5% for the month in September and the annualized inflation rate rose to 3.6%. In August, the PCE’s inflation rate was 3.4%.Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose to an annualized 3.1%.Theconsumer price index, a separate measure of inflation released by the Department of Labor that was released earlier in October, had also shown inflation rising in September, with the annualized inflation rate going from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September.Despite the rise in prices,the US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”.Increasing interest rates can slow inflation, at the risk of slackening economic activity and the jobs market. Because inflation is still hot,economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December. The Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh, told reporters “economic activity is expanding ‌at a strong pace,” noting that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.”Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the ​strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects, in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect ⁠this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.Consumer spending, ​which accounts for more ​than two-thirds of the economy, increased at ​a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in ​the second quarter. Historically low ‌layoffs and moderate ​hiring are helping ​to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged behind inflation.But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon – about $1 a gallon more than a year ago – as theUS-Israel war on Irandrags on, economists anticipate a slowdown in consumer spending.Multiple polls have shown Donald Trump’sapproval ratingon the economy have plummeted in the weeks before the election, with voters citing frustration over rising gas and grocery prices. Overallconsumer sentiment, measured by the University of Michigan is down 15% from February, before the start of the war with Iran, as consumers expect more inflation to come.Explore more on these topicsUS economyEconomicsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: FTC orders Delta, Uber and others to hand over data on algorithmic pricing | US news | The Guardian
description: Regulator demands companies explain how and why they charge different prices for the same product or service
Author: Heather Timmons
Headline: Regulator demands companies explain how and why they charge different prices for the same product or service
Content: A Delta plane waits to depart at Dulles airport.Photograph: Al Drago/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Delta plane waits to depart at Dulles airport.Photograph: Al Drago/Getty ImagesUS newsFTC orders Delta, Uber and others to hand over data on algorithmic pricingRegulator demands companies explain how and why they charge different prices for the same product or serviceHeather Timmonsin WashingtonThu 29 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is demanding some of the US’s biggest airlines, ride-share companies and retailers divulge how they are using algorithms and loyalty programs to target customers and drivers with different prices and wages.US lawmakers demand action on overcharging at 7-Eleven, Dollar General and other chainsRead moreNine companies – Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart – were named in the inquiry, which comes afterinvestigationsand lawsuits alleging consumers are charged different prices based on their buying histories and driverspaid different faresbased on their personal histories.The FTC will “scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service”, chair Andrew Ferguson said in a statement.US family budgets already burdened by inflation arebeing gouged by opaqueand sometimes deceptive store pricing practices, including surveillance pricing and overcharges by Dollar General andconvenience stores.The FTC is tasked with policing “unfair or deceptive acts or practices” in industries except banking and airlines, which means it can not impose any fines or regulations on the airlines named. While the Trump administration has rolled back corporate regulations, the FTC’s consumer protection division has joined with states in some instances topursue legal actionand penalties against some companies.Companies must “turn over information that will allow the agency to assess whether the pricing for a ticket, ride share, food delivery or other product or service varies from one person to the next based on factors such as participation in loyalty programs or analysis of personal data by super-intelligence algorithms”, the FTC said.Several states have begunintroducing legislationto ban surveillance pricing and electronic shelf labels that could be used to set different prices based on shoppers habits and online information.The investigation follows aJuly 2024 inquiryby the Biden administration into surveillance pricing, which demanded information from McKinsey, JPMorgan Chase and others that offered surveillance pricing products to consumer-facing companies.“Details like a person’s precise location or browser history can be frequently used to target individual consumers with different prices for the same goods and services,” the FTC found in January 2025.Whether the inquiry will result in substantial changes in consumer laws or company practices is unclear.“What we have seen so far is that they have not been using these studies that produce meaningful reports that ultimately lead to any rule-making changes,” said Rohit Chopra, a former FTC commissioner who is now head of California’s new Business and Consumer Protection Agency.Explore more on these topicsUS newsTrump administrationUS politicsUberLyftnewsShareReuse this content

title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17bn in major grocery delivery consolidation | Business | The Guardian
description: Acquisition will supercharge DoorDash’s grocery delivery, ‘one of the hardest things to get right online’, CEO says
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Acquisition will supercharge DoorDash’s grocery delivery, ‘one of the hardest things to get right online’, CEO says
Content: A food delivery rider waits at a traffic light on 30 March 2020 in Lone Tree, Colorado.Photograph: David Zalubowski/APView image in fullscreenA food delivery rider waits at a traffic light on 30 March 2020 in Lone Tree, Colorado.Photograph: David Zalubowski/APBusinessDoorDash to buy Instacart for $17bn in major grocery delivery consolidationAcquisition will supercharge DoorDash’s grocery delivery, ‘one of the hardest things to get right online’, CEO saysAssociated PressThu 29 Oct 2026 09.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17bn acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the US andCanada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” – who are independent contractors – completed 338m orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14bn.DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3bn orders last year using a network of 9m independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73bn.DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 US Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco .Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on US delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.Explore more on these topicsBusinessCanadanewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s central bank chief, Christine Lagarde, steps down for ‘freedom of speech’ | Christine Lagarde | The Guardian
description: Possible candidate to run World Economic Forum departs ECB nine months early, saying she wants to speak her mind about world affairs
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Possible candidate to run World Economic Forum departs ECB nine months early, saying she wants to speak her mind about world affairs
Content: In a video message on social media, Lagarde said it had been a ‘great pride and huge privilege’ to serve at the ECB.Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/ReutersView image in fullscreenIn a video message on social media, Lagarde said it had been a ‘great pride and huge privilege’ to serve at the ECB.Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/ReutersChristine LagardeEurope’s central bank chief, Christine Lagarde, steps down for ‘freedom of speech’Possible candidate to run World Economic Forum departs ECB nine months early, saying she wants to speak her mind about world affairsPhillip InmanandGraeme WeardenThu 29 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 06.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”.Ending months of speculation about her future at theEuropean Central Bank, Lagarde said she would quit her role as president in March rather than October next year because the rules of neutrality that governed her job prevented her from influencing debate about financial and economics affairs.She spoke at the end of a press conference to explain the ECB’s decision to hold interest rates – maintaining its key deposit rate at 2.5% – despite inflation climbing to 3.8% last month, its highest since September 2023.Lagarde said: “I ‌want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom ‌to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters.”The former managing director of the International Monetary Fund has been tipped as a candidate to take over the running of the World Economic Forum, which holds its annual meeting in Davos each January. The WEF founder, Klaus Schwab,stepped down last yearafter being accused of financial and ethical misconduct, which he denies.Lagarde’s early departure fires the starting gun on the race to replace her as ECB chief, at a time when the eurozone is struggling with weak growth and above-target inflation. Potential candidates include the former Dutch central bank president Klaas Knot, the Spanish banker Pablo Hernández de Cos, the German central bank president, Joachim Nagel, and Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank.The European Council made up of EU heads of stateappoints the head of the ECB, which sets monetary policy across the eurozone.There has been speculation that Lagarde, a former finance minister ofFrance, has been encouraged to quit early by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, so her successor can be appointed before the possibility of a far-right or far-left presidential candidate being elected to the Élysée Palace. Lagarde will also be able to participate in next April’s elections.She noted that ECB officials were bound by strict rules on not appearing partisan. “We have an obligation of neutrality; we comment on the situation with the focus on monetary policy,” Lagarde said, adding that the mandate was “the price we pay for being independent”.Lagarde said she no longer ‌felt comfortable staying silent on broader global issues. “I’m interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation,” she ​said, without elaborating.Drawing on more than two decades in international economic and financial roles, she said she had more to contribute. “There are things that I can say – whether people will listen or not is another story. But I feel that I ⁠should say those things and I cannot do so in my current ​position.”To reassure markets and staff ​that her early departure would not disrupt the central bank’s operations, she added: “A process ​has already started ‌to identify my ​successor.” She said ​there were “plenty of excellent candidates.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMacron said on Thursday ⁠that the ​succession at the ECB must ⁠be prepared in “an orderly ​and ‌balanced way” ‌with European partners, and also expressed his deep gratitude to Lagarde for her action ‌during her tenure.Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank, said: “TheEuropean Unionis trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that rightwing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027.“Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Élysée Palace. He is a long-term political adversary of Le Pen.”Lagardejoined the ECBin late 2019, shortly beforethe start of the Covid pandemic. During her tenure the central bank has also faced the economic consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war, Donald Trump’s trade war and his war in the Middle East.Lagarde was wearing two plasters on her face in her video message, which she said was because of “a small surgery earlier in the week”. She added: “Follow doctors’ orders and get your skin checked regularly.”Explore more on these topicsChristine LagardeEuropean Central BankEuropeEuropean UnionEuropean monetary unionEconomicsEurozonenewsShareReuse this content

title: Hello Kitty company cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China outcry | China | The Guardian
description: Sanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Sanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’
Content: The company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after backlash from China.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after backlash from China.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersChinaHello Kitty company cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China outcrySanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’Justin McCurryin TokyoThu 29 Oct 2026 04.03 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 02.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe company behind the successfulHello Kittyfranchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media and netizens condemned the show’s “deliberate smears” against China.Sanrio, a Japanese firm whose characters are popular around the world, said in a post on the Chinese social media site Weibo that it had decided to end its association with the TV drama Vivant after concluding that it “contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio’s core values”.In the second season of the popular spy thriller, produced by the Japanese TBS network, Masato Sakai plays a salaryman who is drawn into a web of international crime and espionage.Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains | Rebecca BaileyRead moreThe backlash began this week when Chinese state media blasted the portrayal of Chinese agents using “ruthless violence” to torture members of a secret unit ofJapan’s self-defence forces, calling it a “deliberate smear” against Beijing.Chinese media said that some of the torture methods were similar to those Japanese troops used against Chinese civilians during the second world war.The state-run tabloid Global Times said the acts shown in the episode “bear striking similarities to the torture inflicted on Chinese nationals by invading Japanese troops” during the war, adding that the drama “distorts the truth by attributing these atrocities to modern Chinese characters”.In the 4 October episode, a Chinese agent is seen cutting off the fingers of the Japanese intelligence officer and stabbing him in the abdomen.Sanrio said in a statement: “Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people.“We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects.”The drama’s first season, set in a fictional central Asian country, avoided controversy, but its latest season is being shown at a time of increasingly fractious relations between Beijing and Tokyo.Japan’s conservative prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, set off adiplomatic rowin November last year when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan.Takaichi said earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and hoped to watch them over the year-end and new year holidays.Chinais a crucial overseas market for Sanrio, whose cast of characters includes My Melody and Cinnamoroll – both featured in Vivant-themed merchandise.The Tokyo-based company racked up 781m yuan ($117m) in revenue from the Chinese market in the first half of this year, according to Chinese media, up more than 40% from the same period last year.The backlash against Sanrio comes days after the French international footballer Kylian Mbappé wasdroppedby several Chinese brands after he jokingly referred toMao Zedongas a “dictator”. The Real Madrid forward, who is nicknamed the “dictator” for his influence on the game, later apologised for his “ill-judged” remarks.Explore more on these topicsChinaJapanTelevision industryAsia PacificTV merchandisingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dream serve up lunchtime rout of Valkyries to force historic WNBA finals Game 7 | WNBA | The Guardian
description: Atlanta shook off two straight defeats with a commanding Game 6 win over Golden State to take the WNBA finals to a decider on Saturday
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Atlanta shook off two straight defeats with a commanding Game 6 win over Golden State to take the WNBA finals to a decider on Saturday
Content: Angel Reese celebrates a fourth-quarter three-pointer during Atlanta’s Game 6 win on Thursday. She finished with 15 points, 14 rebounds and six assists as the Dream forced a WNBA finals decider.Photograph: Kevin C Cox/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAngel Reese celebrates a fourth-quarter three-pointer during Atlanta’s Game 6 win on Thursday. She finished with 15 points, 14 rebounds and six assists as the Dream forced a WNBA finals decider.Photograph: Kevin C Cox/Getty ImagesWNBADream serve up lunchtime rout of Valkyries to force historic WNBA finals Game 7Dream win 80-69 to level best-of-seven series at 3-3First Game 7 in WNBA history set for Saturday nightElla Brockway’s minute-by-minute report of Game 6Bryan Armen GrahamThu 29 Oct 2026 14.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 19.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheAtlanta Dreamhad no intention of letting a matinee become their curtain call.Facing elimination at a lunchtime tipoff, the Dream overwhelmed theGolden State Valkyries80-69 on Thursday afternoon to force a decisive seventh game in the WNBA finals, rediscovering their offensive touch just as their title hopes were threatening to slip away.Golden State Valkyries 69-80 Atlanta Dream: WNBA finals 2026 Game 6 – as it happenedRead moreAtlanta buried six three-pointers and shot 73.3% from the floor in a blistering opening quarter at State Farm Arena, built a lead that ballooned to 25 points before half-time and held on to send a series that had swung sharply towards Golden State back to San Francisco’s Chase Center for Saturday night’s winner-take-all finale. Both teams are seeking their first championship.Quick GuideWNBA finals 2026ShowScheduleBest-of-seven series. All times US Eastern Daylight Time (EDT).Sat 17 OctGame 1:Golden State 68, Atlanta 64Mon 19 OctGame 2:Atlanta 79, Golden State 65Wed 21 OctGame 3:Atlanta 97, Golden State 71Sat 24 OctGame 4:Golden State 67, Atlanta 62Mon 26 OctGame 5:Golden State 64, Atlanta 55Thu 29 OctGame 6:Atlanta 80, Golden State 69Sat 31 OctGame 7: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm (USA/CNBC)How to watchIn the US, the series will air on NBC, USA Network and CNBC, with all games streaming on Peacock. In the UK, it will be carried by Sky Sports. In Australia, fans can watch through WNBA League Pass, with selected coverage also available through ESPN.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Allisha Gray scored a team-high 23 points including five threes, Rhyne Howard added 21 whileAngel Reesenotched her fourth double-double of the series with 15 points and 14 rebounds to go with six assists.Gabby Williams finished with a game-high 26 points for the Valkyries after being held to four in the first half. Tiffany Hayes chipped in 15, but Golden State shot just 31.4% from the field and 25.9% from three-point range. Veronica Burton endured a particularly frigid afternoon, making just two of her 13 shots from the floor and missing all six three-point attempts.“It’s do or die. It’s win or go home,” Howard said. “I knew that coming in, we had to be aggressive from the jump, and that starts with me. You know, I have to be a good leader for this team. I have to set the tone early, and I feel like that’s what I did today.”The Dream had managed only 62 and 55 points in back-to-back defeats that erased their 2-1 series lead. On Thursday, they scored 32 in the first quarter alone, making 11 of their first 15 shots and moving the ball with a fluidity Golden State had largely disrupted over the previous two contests.Reese said a players-only meeting before a film session had helped restore Atlanta’s confidence, with Dream forward Naz Hillmon urging her teammates to remember who they were.“All of us have been superstars on a team at some point,” Reese said. “We needed the best out of every single person tonight.”View image in fullscreenAtlanta’s Angel Reese drives to the rim as Golden State’s Kiah Stokes defends during the second half of Thursday’s Game 6.Photograph: Brynn Anderson/APIt wasn’t quite a first-round knockout, but the Dream were never seriously threatened even when the Valkyries found their footing after the intermission. Golden State trimmed the deficit to 13 early in the fourth quarter, only for Gray hit a three-pointer followed by another from Reese to restore a 74-55 advantage with 5min 43sec remaining.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWelcome to the trap: swaggering Atlanta Dream turn WNBA finals into a hometown spectacle | Andrew LawrenceRead moreThe Valkyries made one final push, getting as close as 77-69 on Williams’s three-point play with 1min 15sec to go, which fouled out Howard. But Gray, compromised by an injury to her shooting hand for most of the postseason, answered with her fifth three-pointer off a Reese assist to remove all doubt with 56sec left. Golden State opted not to extend the contest by fouling in the closing seconds, leaving a final margin that barely hinted at the scale of the hosts’ dominance.“We needed the opportunity. That’s all we needed, and we maximized it today,” Reese said. “I’m just really proud of this group. The job is not done, and I’m looking forward to it. One more. Job’s not done.”The performance cameamid the controversysurrounding a 12.30pm tipoff, a scheduling compromise that placed the biggest home game of Atlanta’s season in the middle of a work day. The Dream nevertheless announced a sellout crowd of 17,099.“I had no doubt that they would show up,” Howard said. “Everybody kept asking me about 12.30, 12.30. Now they can leave with a better taste in their mouths, go get the bottomless mimosas, you know, enjoy the rest of the day, ‘cause I know nobody’s going back to work.”For Golden State, the start was equivalent to 9.30am on their normal California clock, but their coach, Natalie Nakase, refused to blame the unusual start time.View image in fullscreenAtlanta’s Allisha Gray celebrates after hitting a three-pointer against the Valkyries during the first quarter.Photograph: Kevin C Cox/Getty Images“No. That had nothing to do with it,” she said. “We played at one o’clock last week.”She added: “We knew they were going to play desperate. We knew they were going to play like their life depends on it. For us not to match that is disappointing and frustrating.”The WNBA adopted a best-of-seven finals last year, only for the seriesto end in a four-game sweep. This time, the extended format has delivered the ultimate decider. After six games have left nothing to separate the Dream and Valkyries, the first Game 7 in league history on Halloween night will settle everything.“Both teams want it, and so the mindset is a sense of urgency,” Burton said. “It is do or die, officially.”Explore more on these topicsWNBAAtlanta DreamGolden State ValkyriesUS sportsAngel ReeseShareReuse this content

title: The low-budget Brewers won the World Series – and exposed baseball’s biggest lie | World Series | The Guardian
description: Milwaukee’s first World Series championship is a rebuke to baseball’s owners, whose insistence that small-market teams cannot compete has been laid bare as fiction
Author: Howard Bryant
Headline: Milwaukee’s first World Series championship is a rebuke to baseball’s owners, whose insistence that small-market teams cannot compete has been laid bare as fiction
Content: Cooper Pratt celebrates with the Commissioner’s Trophy after the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 of the World Series to clinch the first championship in club history.Photograph: Elsa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCooper Pratt celebrates with the Commissioner’s Trophy after the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 of the World Series to clinch the first championship in club history.Photograph: Elsa/Getty ImagesWorld SeriesThe low-budget Brewers won the World Series – and exposed baseball’s biggest lieHoward BryantMilwaukee’sfirst World Series championshipis a rebuke to baseball’s oligarch class, whose insistence that small-market teams cannot compete has been laid bare as fictionThu 29 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTShareFor the entirety of the 2026 baseball season, the overlords of the game have stood on the single position thatwhat has now happenedcould not happen, and the result was a year that has been treated like an appetizer for the main course of the offseason: the shutting down of the game until the players, after 40 years of resistance, finally agree to a salary cap. The insistence that the game had been predetermined undermined the Milwaukee Brewers, who spent 149 days this season atop the standings.Milwaukee Brewers close out Tampa Bay Rays to end 57-year wait for first World Series titleRead moreBaseball dismissedMilwaukee’s 22-0 demolition of Seattleon 18 August, the 20-0 waxing of Cincinnati a month later, and the comprehensive dusting of their division – their fourth consecutive National League Central title and fifth in six years – by 14 games. Baseball’s owners, at their persuasive best, would have their paying customers believe that the Brewers’ franchise-record 103 regular-season wins also were an illusion, or worse, the dreaded outlier, even though Milwaukee have won 770 games since 2018, the fourth-most in all of baseball. Even when Milwaukee exhaled andmade the Dodgers look oldin a stirring four-game sweep, ESPN’s Jeff Passan reported the owners’ position remained unchanged.The Brewers to that point had not helped dispel the notion. They had sputtered badly in recent postseasons, giving life to the thought that maybe their summer wins really were empty. Only one thing could ever change that perception: winning in the playoffs.Quick GuideWorld Series 2026ShowScheduleBest-of-seven series. Milwaukee won, 4-1.Fri 23 OctGame 1:Milwaukee 3, Tampa Bay 2Sat 24 OctGame 2:Milwaukee 5, Tampa Bay 4Mon 26 OctGame 3:Milwaukee 10, Tampa Bay 1Tue 27 OctGame 4:Tampa Bay 4, Milwaukee 3 (12 innings)Wed 28 OctGame 5:Milwaukee 4, Tampa Bay 1How to watchIn the US, all World Series games will air on Fox and Fox Deportes, with streaming available through Fox One. In the UK, the series will be carried by TNT Sports. In Australia, fans can watch on ESPN, with streaming available through Disney+ and Kayo Sports.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Surrounded by so many friends that a Wednesday evening at Tropicana Field in St Petersburg felt like a home game – the good folks of Milwaukee and points beyond will remember the date specifically as 28 October 2026 – the Brewers rejected the notion they could not win both because of the economic forces against them and the intangibles champions possess but seemed to go missing from their group when the clocks fall back. They did so by winning the World Series for the first time in their 58-year history, and doing so resoundingly, destroying theTampa Bay Raysin five games.The final score was 4-1, ending a month that will be played and replayed in the minds and DVRs of Milwaukeeans. Few teams have ever been better. Few moments have exposed the hypocrisy of baseball’s oligarchs. Few teams so emphatically demanded so much of themselves.View image in fullscreenCooper Pratt and Brice Turang embrace after Milwaukee defeated Tampa Bay in Game 5 of the World Series on Wednesday night.Photograph: Carmen Mandato/Getty ImagesWhat had been accepted as fact has always been decidedly fiction – but fiction can live as truth until it is exposed, killed once and for all on the ballfield. No matter the argument to concede the season to the inevitability of money and not having it, the truth is the Brewers have been an elite team for the better part of the decade, and the signature joy of thisWorld Seriesrun has been the joyous, ruthless attention this team paid to the task of not merely believing they were championship level, but proving it, to every team that opposed them this season, but more thrillingly, to themselves.double quotation markFew teams have ever been better. Few moments have exposed the hypocrisy of baseball’s oligarchsNothing else mattered but emerging from this month as champions – not the payroll or the labor battles that will almost certainly shut the game down over the coming weeks and quite likely wipe out spring training and at least a portion of the 2027 season and the Brewers’ title defense, or the mystique and riches of the two-time defending champion Dodgers; not the twin histories of having never won the whole thing since that long-ago day near the end of spring training in 1970 when the Seattle Pilots’ equipment truck loaded in Tempe, Arizona, but the team didn’t know where home would be as a court order determined if the truck was headed back to Seattle or to a new home in Milwaukee, or the Dodgers’ long record of torturing Milwaukee baseball. That torture dated back to losses to Brooklyn in 1956, Los Angeles in 1959 before the Braves left town for Atlanta, and to the recent postseason defeats to the Dodgers in 2018, 2020 and 2025, when the Brewers began their second decade in the National League by being as good as the franchise had been since the big American League years of Yount and Cooper, Molitor and Fingers, only to suffer the familiar NL fate of being good, but not good enough to beat the Dodgers when it counted.The Brewers were nowhere men – only the World Series would heal the past wounds that have stayed with them, highlighted bylast year’s humiliating four-game sweepin the NLCS by the Dodgers – and they played with a buoyant and calm desperation, a gorgeous certainty that could not last, but did. The Brewers won the requisite 11 games to claim the trophy and needed only 13 games to do it, but trailed in eight of them. Yet, as an example of their belief, none of their series this postseason was tied after two games. Both Brewers losses in these playoffs were by one run.When they faltered, they did not panic as desperate teams too close to the prize do; they got tougher. Jake Bauers’ soul-snatching at-bats against the Dodgers offered a sign, the youthful charges of Series MVP catcher William Contreras, Jackson Chourio, and the too-young-to-care stardom of Cooper Pratt was another, coming back from down 4-0 against the Dodgers and Rays was still another, and the two-out, eight-run fifth in Game 3 seemed to end the Series – except that it didn’t. Most impressively, responding to losing Game 4 three outs from the title in the bottom of the 12thnot with the doubts that create suspense and pave the way to epic collapse, but by returning the next night unfazed and champagne-ready, demanding they be taken not as a cute story but a hard-edged team ready, at long last, for its close-up.View image in fullscreenTrevor Megill, Christian Yelich and Abner Uribe embrace after Wednesday night’s final out at Tropicana Field.Photograph: Elsa/Getty ImagesNeither the doomsday rhetoric of an unnecessary work stoppage or the fearsome reputation of the former champions, nor the feisty underdog spirit of an admirable Tampa Bay could block the sunlight, too long in arriving, of this Brewers team. They played pure, determined baseball and responded to the insult – and it is an insult – that the decimal points on the balance sheet meant more than winning 103 games and 90-plus so many times before that, meant that once it was time to deal the cards they couldn’t win. The Brewers won 114 games in 2026, finished the regular season 15-3, and then went 11-2 in the playoffs for a grand total of 26-5 since 7 September.Baseball’s finances need addressing, but they don’t require shuttering the place. Even with the game the owners are playing in their quest to increase franchise values, their words speak an untruth – Brewers owner Mark Attanasio purchased the team from Bud Selig in 2005 for $223m and the team that supposedly cannot win (but did) has avaluation by Forbes at $1.9bn. The game that matters, however, is the one on the field, the one that belongs to the players, and this October, there was absolutely nobody better.Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America.He also writes on SubstackExplore more on these topicsWorld SeriesMilwaukee BrewersTampa Bay RaysLos Angeles DodgersBaseballUS sportsMLBcommentShareReuse this content

title: Everton ease past Newcastle to set up Fleetwood trip after Grealish is dropped | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Everton beat Newcastle 3-1 with goals by James Garner, Hayden Hackney and Thierno Barry to set up a Carabao Cup quarter-final with Fleetwood Town
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Everton beat Newcastle 3-1 with goals by James Garner, Hayden Hackney and Thierno Barry to set up a Carabao Cup quarter-final with Fleetwood Town
Content: Thierno Barry enjoys putting the finishing touch to Everton’s win after scoring their third goal.Photograph: Jon Super/ReutersView image in fullscreenThierno Barry enjoys putting the finishing touch to Everton’s win after scoring their third goal.Photograph: Jon Super/ReutersCarabao CupEverton ease past Newcastle to set up Fleetwood trip after Grealish is droppedAndy Hunterat Hill Dickinson StadiumThu 29 Oct 2026 18.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 19.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe biggest night in Everton’s season started with a big call from David Moyes and demanded a big performance from his players.With the exception of Jack Grealish, they did not let him down. A quarter-final at Fleetwood Town is their prize after a clinical, committed display shattered Newcastle’s hopes of lifting the Carabao Cup for a second time in three seasons.Newcastle dominated spells of the fourth round tie and the stats – registering 28 shots to Everton’s 11, although only nine visiting attempts were on target – but individual defensive errors and an ineffective attack proved a ruinous combination. Matthias Jaissle denied his team are a soft touch, despite persuasive evidence to the contrary, yet called Newcastle “naive” and the defeat, in front of almost 8,000 of their fans, “shocking”. Andy Burnham was among the many Evertonians in attendance grateful for Newcastle’s generosity.Everton 3-1 Newcastle: Carabao Cup fourth round – liveRead moreJames Garner, with his first goal of the season, Hayden Hackney, with his first goal for the club, and Thierno Barry were on target to take Everton into the last eight of a competition they have never won. Jordan Pickford was in commanding form against his old adversaries while Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall ran the show from midfield.
