Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Winger was dropped from David Moyes’ squad to face Newcastle after the player missed training in the buildup to Carabao Cup tie
Content: Jack Grealish was dropped by Everton for the Carabao Cup tie with NewcastlePhotograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJack Grealish was dropped by Everton for the Carabao Cup tie with NewcastlePhotograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesEvertonEverton drop Jack Grealish from Carabao Cup tie over ‘breach of club discipline’England player left out of squad to face NewcastleMoyes confirms he ‘supports’ the club decisionAndy HunterThu 29 Oct 2026 18.57 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Grealish was dropped from Everton’s Carabao Cup win over Newcastle following a breach of club discipline.Everton took the unusual step of announcing that Grealish’s omission from the fourth-round tie was for disciplinary reasons on social media, after listing David Moyes’s team for the fourth-round tie at Hill Dickinson Stadium. The club posted on X: “Jarrad Branthwaite remains sidelined for a second successive game due to concussion protocols, while Jack Grealish is unavailable for selection due to a breach of club discipline.”Everton ease past Newcastle to set up Fleetwood trip after Grealish is droppedRead moreIt is understood the 31-year-old missed training on Monday without permission and the decision to drop him was taken by Moyes in conjunction with the Everton chief executive Angus Kinnear.Speaking afterEverton’s 3-1 win, Moyes said: “I’m not going to give any details. It was a club decision and I support it. I don’t want to speak too much about it.”Grealish returned to training at Everton’s Finch Farm complex after Monday’s absence but is expected to be fined for his unauthorised absence earlier in the week. The playmaker had missed Everton’s defeat at Arsenal on Saturday due to illness.The England international rejoined Everton on a season’s loan from Manchester City this summer and had started in four successive games for Moyes’s side prior to Arsenal. Everton paid £12m in total to have Grealish on loan last season and are paying a similar sum for this campaign. He will become a free agent at the end of this season when his lucrative contract with City expires.Explore more on these topicsEvertonnewsShareReuse this content

title: George Russell determined not to let disappointing F1 season define career | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: George Russell has insisted he will not let his difficult Formula One season define his career and still has plenty of time to win the world championship
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: George Russell has insisted he will not let his difficult Formula One season define his career and still has plenty of time to win the world championship
Content: George Russell has been outdriven by his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli this season.Photograph: Daniel Cárdenas/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeorge Russell has been outdriven by his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli this season.Photograph: Daniel Cárdenas/Anadolu/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026George Russell determined not to let disappointing F1 season define career28-year-old still believes he will win world title one dayKimi Antonelli misses media duties with ‘viral illness’Giles Richardsin Mexico CityThu 29 Oct 2026 18.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 19.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorge Russell has insisted he will not let his difficult Formula One season define his career and believes he still has plenty of years left to come back and win the world championship.Russell has been outdriven by his 20-year-old Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli in a bruising season for the British driver. Antonelli isset to win the titleand become F1’s youngest world champion at this weekend’s Mexican Grand Prix if he finishes in ninth place or above.Wolff hails Antonelli’s US Grand Prix demolition as the Italian’s ‘best race yet’Read moreHe has taken nine wins thus far to Russell’s three, with the British driver struggling for consistency in adapting to the demands of the energy management required by the new cars which, alongside the tyres in use this year, does not suit the 28-year-old’s driving style.Russell has delivered some impeccable weekends, including commanding victories in Austria and Baku, but more often than not has been left baffled as to why he cannot make the car work to the same effect as Antonelli, a process which he conceded had been hard to deal with.“I’ve probably learned more about myself this year than I would have liked to, in all honesty,” he said at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.“You know, the highs and lows you go through in sport are immense and that’s because we all care so much for what we’re doing.“But I remind myself I’m 28 years old. I see Lewis [Hamilton] still competing extremely well at 41 and Fernando [Alonso] at 45. Lewis won the majority of his titles in his thirties and this year is absolutely not going to define my career as a whole.”Russell has suffered with no little bad luck this season but has offered praise to Antonelli, admitting the Italian has been the better driver and is thoroughly deserving of taking his first title in only his second season in F1.The British driver had opened the season strongly witha win at the Australian GPbut was then battered as Antonelli took five wins in a row and the lead of the championship which he has not relinquished since. However, Russell maintained he would learn from the experience to return stronger in 2027.“It’s not going to break me. If anything, it’s going to make me stronger,” he said. “I’ve been pretty proud of my resilience and how I’ve sort of bounced back from very tough moments.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli is set to win the title this weekend although he was absent on Thursday due to illness.Photograph: Jason Pohuski/BMR/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock“Through my lowest points of this season, I’ve generally bounced back really, really strong and then I had another bad race after the good one. So, maybe it’s something I need to analyse as well because I always perform best after my worst races. Maybe it’s just a coincidence, maybe there’s something in it.“I don’t think any athlete, no matter how great, has every single year of their career performing at their highest level. Unfortunately, this year for me has come at maybe the time when I needed it most. By no means the end of my journey, I have still got a good 12 to 15 years left in me.”Russell is in a tight battle for second place in the championship, just one point ahead of Hamilton and six in front of Red Bull’s Max Verstappen.Antonelli did not take part in media duties on Thursday as the team said he was unwell with a “viral illness”. He was given leave by the FIA to not take part, as the team noted, as “a precaution to give him the chance to rest ahead of the weekend”. He is expected to be in the car for free practice on Friday.The Cadillac team also withdrew Valtteri Bottas from his media duties on Thursday in Mexico, noting that he was “unwell” and subsequently that “the team has taken the decision to allow him a day of rest, to support his recovery”.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Mercedes GPFormula OneGeorge RussellKimi AntonelliMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Golden State Valkyries 69-80 Atlanta Dream: WNBA finals 2026 Game 6 – as it happened  | WNBA | The Guardian
description: The Atlanta Dream held off the Golden State Valkyries to force a deciding Game 7. Ella Brockway followed the action
Author: Ella Brockway
Headline: The Atlanta Dream held off the Golden State Valkyries to force a deciding Game 7. Ella Brockway followed the action
Content: 15.00 EDTFinal: Valkyries 69-80 DreamThe Atlanta Dream used a dominant first quarter to set the tone of this Game 6 and never looked back in this win over theGolden State Valkyries.After their Game 5 disappointment, the Dream ran out to a 32-15 lead in the opening quarter, hitting seven three-pointers. The Valkyries – perhaps affected by the 12.30pm tip-off time, the result of a scheduling conflict at State Farm Arena in Atlanta – could not get anything going offensively in the first half.Rhyne Howard (21 points) and Allisha Gray (23 points) were an unstoppable duo, combining to go 9 for 13 from three-point range and 14 for 23 from the floor.The score line will make this game look closer than it actually was. title: MLS announces ‘sprint season’ schedule, with accommodations for cold-weather locales | MLS | The Guardian
description: The short season will begin on 19 February in Miami, with MLS Cup due to be played on Memorial Day weekend
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: The short season will begin on 19 February in Miami, with MLS Cup due to be played on Memorial Day weekend
Content: Inter Miami will host FC Cincinnati in the 2027 sprint season opener.Photograph: Chris Arjoon/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenInter Miami will host FC Cincinnati in the 2027 sprint season opener.Photograph: Chris Arjoon/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockMLSMLS announces ‘sprint season’ schedule, with accommodations for cold-weather localesSeason will begin on 19 February in MiamiMLS Cup due to be played on Memorial Day weekendDecision Day lands on 8 MayJeff RueterThu 29 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMajor League Soccer’s 2027 “sprint season” will begin on 19 February, withMLSCup taking place during Memorial Day weekend at the end of May.The stopgap half-season is a one-off, as the North American league inverts its calendar to align with most top leagues around the world beginning with the 2027-28 season. The nuts and bolts of the change wereinitially announced in March.For all of the change the league is undergoing, with Larry Berg readying to take over as commissioner after Don Garber’s decades-long reign and the schedule inversion better positioning the league in the global transfer market, there is one bit of continuity. The sprint season will commence as the last three have: with Inter Miami in the opening match, this time welcoming FC Cincinnati to Nu Stadium on 19 February.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDC United are worse than awful; they’re hopelessRead moreOther marquee matchups include a cold-weather Canadian Classique between Toronto FC and CF Montréal on 28 February, the Cascadia Derby between the Seattle Sounders and Portland Timbers on 4 April, and the Hell is Real Derby between Ohio-based rivals FC Cincinnati and the Columbus Crew on 24 April.The sprint season will only see teams face opponents from within their conference, neatly resulting in a 14-game slate with an even split of home and away matches. The season will still incorporate some Wednesdays to make the schedule work, and teams will still have the occasional matchday off with 17 matchweeks available. As per tradition, the season concludes with Decision Day as each conference will play its full slate concurrently in consecutive time slots on 8 May.The top eight teams in each conference will qualify for a single-elimination postseason, with MLS Cup planned to be held during Memorial Day weekend (28-31 May). Every match from kickoff to the championship will be streamed on Apple TV without local blackouts.The schedule also appears to give MLS a chance to test playing late-winter matches in cold-climate markets at earlier hours. Minnesota United, for example, will open their season a week later than the rest of the league on 28 February, hosting Seattle for a 2 pm local kickoff. CF Montréal will play just one of their first six games at home. Notably, despitea lack of clarity about their long-term future, the Vancouver Whitecaps are involved, with Thomas Müller having announced he’ll remain with the club for the sprint.Explore more on these topicsMLSUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: DC United are worse than awful; they’re hopeless | MLS | The Guardian
description: The team have gone from MLS’s flagship franchise to its most depressing – even among 2026’s other stragglers
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: The team have gone from MLS’s flagship franchise to its most depressing – even among 2026’s other stragglers
Content: DC United will miss the playoffs for the seventh straight season.Photograph: Roger Wimmer/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDC United will miss the playoffs for the seventh straight season.Photograph: Roger Wimmer/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesSoccer DeskMLSDC United are worse than awful; they’re hopelessThe team have gone from MLS’s flagship franchise to its most depressing – even among 2026’s other stragglersSign up for our free newsletter herePablo Iglesias MaurerThu 29 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor years, the crisp air and changing colors of October brought forth a host of wonderful memories forDC Unitedfans – visions of Eddie Pope heading home the winner inMajor League Soccer’s first-ever championship game, or Marco Etcheverry, Jaime Moreno and others tearing through defenders, helping establish MLS’s first true dynasty.Nowadays, United fans have a different tradition: hearing the team’s ownership apologize for yet another depressing season and offer promises of a brighter future. With Wednesday night’s 2-1 loss to Toronto, United will now miss out on the playoffs for the seventh consecutive season – in a league that lets at least 50% of teams into the playoffs each year, with 60% of teams or more making it in five of those seven years. If United fail to make it again next year, they’ll tie an all-timeMLSrecord.History comes home as St Louis City top Columbus Crew to win US Open CupRead moreUnited have cycled through coaches, players and staff at a dizzying rate in recent years; their most recent attempt to right the ship involved hiring René Weiler, a Swiss journeyman who has guided 10 clubs in a 20-year coaching career. United’s choice to lead its sporting department felt even more bizarre: they hired Dr Erkut Sogut, a German-born lawyer and sports agent who had never worked in a front office before, with Wikipedia saying he is “most notable for being the agent of football star Mesut Özil”. Sogut – who has also penned a number of books about the “high-octane” world of “football and the powerful agents who control it” – has yet to turn things around, even a little bit.United, who are seemingly too inept to perform the basic function of their business (fielding a competitive soccer team) are nevertheless asking the DC government for hundreds of millions of dollars to renovate Audi Field, their eight-year-old home.United are among the least ambitious teams in MLS but they are far from the league’s only basket case. Below them at the bottom of the overall table are others straggling along for their own varied reasons:CF Montréal, Sporting KC and Atlanta United.DC’s disastrous 2026 can’t hold a candle this year to KC, whose misery started early, has continued apace and has frequently bordered on the comical. The club was bounced out of the US Open Cup at the first hurdle by the USL side Colorado Springs Switchbacks in a 3-0 loss that could have been worse. On Wednesday night, the team lost 3-1 to Minnesota United to bring their goals conceded tally to an astonishing 80 on the season, setting the league record with two games to go.KC were never going to do well this year. They opened preseason with just 17 players under contract and former Chicago Fire and BSC Young Boys head coach Raphaël Wicky has thus far seemed like an unsteady fit to say the least. It’s the kind of dynamic that’s led the team to a place where their minutes leader is Calvin Harris, a forward who had mostly been an option off the bench in past MLS spots. Second on the minutes list is 24-year-old Wyatt Meyer, who went from riding the bench and bouncing down to MLS Next Pro for Nashville in 2025 to anchoring 2026’s historically bad defense.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA three-year-old soccer prodigy went viral. The adults have already let him downRead moreThere’s some room for optimism in Kansas City, at least, as there is at any team with a billionaire owner (that is Peter Mallouk, who gained controlling owner status earlier this year). The same can be said for Atlanta United, who are on the verge of missing the playoffs for the second consecutive year for the first time in franchise history. It feels almost comical to worry about Atlanta, who have never been short on ambition under Arthur Blank. That club spent millions to sign Miguel Almirón, Aleksei Miranchuk and Emmanuel Latte Lath and promptly watched as each of them grossly underperformed. Latte Lath, a $22m transfer from Middlesbrough, was arguably the biggest designated player bust in MLS history before Atlanta mercifully loaned him out to Union Berlin in August.Montreal haven’t won a match in a month and their fans rained pyrotechnics on the field and damaged stadium concourses after the team’s loss to the Canadian Premier League side Forge FC in the Canadian Championship last weekend. Montreal, who have occasionally been competitive and somehow remain somewhat relevant in their market, are also one of MLS’s longest-running shitshows, with owner Joey Saputo cycling through head coaches at a dizzying pace. Rumors of a sale – or possible relocation – have persisted for years.The vibrancy of Montreal as a soccer city, and the team’s history of over three decades there, means faint hope remains that the team can turn things around. That’s true even as the club bans fans from its stands in response to the aforementioned protests.The tiny slivers of hope present in all of these sides cannot be found at this point forDC United, with supporters who have stuck by their club for nearly as long as those of Montreal. At this point, barring them from the stands at Audi Field could be viewed as an act of love.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsMLSSoccer DeskDC UnitedUS sportsCF MontréalSporting Kansas CityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rodman rule has been revised but the fight to keep stars in the NWSL goes on | NWSL | The Guardian
description: Gone are the eight criteria to be a High Impact Player so clubs can spend their money on whomever they want – and the solution makes sense
Author: Megan Swanick
Headline: Gone are the eight criteria to be a High Impact Player so clubs can spend their money on whomever they want – and the solution makes sense
Content: The rule was informally named after Washington Spirit’s Trinity Rodman (left) following her protracted contract saga.Photograph: Jay Biggerstaff/NWSL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe rule was informally named after Washington Spirit’s Trinity Rodman (left) following her protracted contract saga.Photograph: Jay Biggerstaff/NWSL/Getty ImagesMoving the Goalposts newsletterNWSLRodman rule has been revised but the fight to keep stars in the NWSL goes onGone are the eight criteria to be a High Impact Player so clubs can spend their money on whomever they want – and the solution makes senseMegan SwanickThu 29 Oct 2026 10.34 EDTFirst published on Thu 29 Oct 2026 08.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Washington plays Chicago this Sunday in DC, “Rowdy Audi” will probably be full. It will also be full when the post-season starts, should they lock up their top-four position with a positive result on Decision Day. Equipped with an accessible stadium in a big city, a proud fanbase and a formidable roster rife with players qualifying for the High Impact Player (HIP) rule’s initial criteria (includingTrinity Rodman, who gave the rule its moniker), the Spirit hold sway in the attendance charts.But starting next season, everyone on the Spiritwill qualify for the “Rodman Rule”. So will every player in NWSL. Announced Friday, NWSL settled a grievance with the league’s Players Association, who argued that the initial criteria violated federal labor law.Admittedly, when the new policy arrived on the scene last winter, it appeared half-baked, a somewhat frantic attempt to keep Rodman from floating across the Atlantic and doing something terrible, like playing for Michele Kang’s London City Lionesses instead of Michele Kang’s Washington Spirit.A rule was born to prevent that. It allocated added funds beyond the salary cap for players who met league-set criteria that clearly prioritized international name recognition in a global market. Qualifying players needed to meet one of eight categories including SportsPro Media’s top 150 Most Marketable Athletes (only Alessia Russo and Aitana Bonmatí placed in 2026, though 16 female football players did in 2025, including three in the NWSL at the time – Trinity Rodman, Sophia Wilson and Marta, in that order). It also included ESPN’s Top 50,the Guardian’s top 100, top minutes on the US national team, the Ballon d’Or’s 30-player list, or NWSL’s MVP and Best XI awards.Some measure of umbrage followed, as invested onlookers argued for a simpler solution: just raise the salary cap. And perhaps they should, but keeping an American-style sports league competitive in a global football landscape is less straightforward. The looming spectre of Europe’s super-teams, who have attracted key members of the USWNT starting XI, is ever present, waiting to take Croix Bethune away for the right amount of money. No doubt, the NWSL’s appeal is evident in its expansion and growth, in the success of its spine of stateside stalwarts, in its rapidly expanding dedicated facilities, and in the international talents such as Esme Morgan or Ann-Katrin Berger that choose to sharpen their skills in the US.However, the domestic sporting culture of the NWSL is somewhat at odds, in some ways a disadvantage, when it comes to maintaining its margins, with a stand-alone team structure in a parity-driven league, while competing for international glory with teams such as Chelsea, Lyon or Barcelona, who spend three times or more the amount that some NWSL teams do. While competing for status as the world’s go-to destination, for players and fans, glory hunting and name recognition do matter.Just look at the Ballon d’Or: Barcelona’s women took all but one of the awards available to them, though Alexia Putellas, whocollected her third main prize, now plays in London. That Putellas deserves her trophy is not in dispute, though the inequitable factors contributing to international accolades were manifest. Putellas starred for two super-teams: Barcelona and Spain. Ewa Pajor, Barcelona’s Polish striker, fell just short, perhaps edged out by only having one super-team to play for.View image in fullscreenAlexia Putellas’ performances for two super-teams – Barcelona and Spain – offered a fine platform for her to win the Ballon d’Or again.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPASubtly, it seemed, the original criteria for the HIP rule flirted with the idea of fostering a super-team in the US. Prior to the update, there was no cap on the number of players who could access the extra million if the salary cap was already met. For a team such as Kang’s in Washington, the door felt open, possibly, to building a team even more ready to contend with the heavy spenders in Europe (including those also funded by Kang), and the international accolades that go with it. If a NWSL player lifted the NWSL trophy, helped win January’s inaugural Club World Cup, then performed well at the World Cup, could a second NWSL (active) player win the Ballon d’Or?The structure of the HIP rule remains in place. Teams that have met 2027’s salary cap of $4.4m (£3.3m) in 2027 can spend an additional $1.257m (as reported by ESPN) on a player. The post-grievance difference is that teams can spend that additional sum onanyplayer. Gone are the stipulations mandating adherence to that eight-criteria list of global recognition.The change is a win for players that did not meet it, which includes elite players who fell short in previous seasons (such as Ashley Sanchez) or star players with long-lasting or recurring injuries (Catarina Macario). It gives the NWSL’s individual teams the autonomy to decide which players are worthy, based on whatever criteria they see fit. And, with a cap on the number of players that can access it, it gives cash-strapped teams the theoretical ability to rein in teams with already-stacked rosters.But the spirit of NWSL’s original criteria has more merit than many suggest. The NWSL is responsible for securing overhead issues such as an improved media rights deal, marketing marquee names to broadcasters, ensuring the league is seen as the go-to destination before a World Cup and performing well in global cup competitions such as the Concacaf W Champions Cup (Mexico’s Club América prevailed in the most recent final) or the upcoming Club World Cup. With that in mind – plus the ever-pressing desire to keep USWNT players in the US – the original HIP criteria had its eye on awarding stardom as it’s seen in the global market.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStardom is imprecise. It’s hard to measure, but impossible to miss. Rodman did not make the Ballon d’Or shortlist and is not leading the Golden Boot race. But Rodman and her closest national team peers (including“Triple Espresso”compadres Mallory Swanson and Wilson) are the presumed stars of the NWSL. Rodman, alongside Wilson (who clocked the Michael Jordan “shrug” celebration after scoring in the 2022 Championship final) have not just the skill but the personality flourishes reminiscent of Alex Morgan sipping the tea in Lyon.The NWSL has yet to replicate the Morgan effect (think default attendance records and adoring away fans), but requiring that teams reward players with a certainje ne sais quoiin their international football fame was baked into the league’s original attempt at the HIP criteria.Get in touchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailmoving.goalposts@theguardian.com.This is an extract from our free email about women’s football, Moving the Goalposts. To get the full edition,visit this page and follow the instructions. Moving the Goalposts is delivered to your inboxes every Tuesday and Thursday.Explore more on these topicsNWSLMoving the Goalposts newsletterTrinity RodmanWomen's footballUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Computerized clairvoyance: psychics push back against AI-generated readings | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Human practitioners warn computer-generated offerings lack the empathy and connection central to divination
Author: Kari Paul
Headline: Human practitioners warn computer-generated offerings lack the empathy and connection central to divination
Content: In addition to chatbots and apps, AI-generated psychics are a growing presence on TikTok Live, racking up dozens of views.Illustration: Guardian Design/Yuichiro Chino/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIn addition to chatbots and apps, AI-generated psychics are a growing presence on TikTok Live, racking up dozens of views.Illustration: Guardian Design/Yuichiro Chino/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Computerized clairvoyance: psychics push back against AI-generated readingsHuman practitioners warn computer-generated offerings lack the empathy and connection central to divinationKari PaulThu 29 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 17.19 EDTShare“This journey isn’t just about algorithms or data,” an AI psychic named Urban Mystic recently told me. The chatbot, featuring an AI-generated profile photo of a smiling woman surrounded by palm trees, also said I will get married soon, that I have a pink aura and that I may have been an herbalist in a past life.“It’s about connecting on a soulful level,” the chatbot said.Urban Mystic is one of more than a dozen bots on the mobile app Your AI Psychic, which offers live, allegedly psychic readings via chat, video and voice calls as well as palm reading, astrology chart analysis and daily horoscopes. The app works on a coin system: each question costs 4.06 coins to ask. Users can purchase packages ranging from $9.99 for “a quick question” (82 coins) to $99.99 (1,180 coins) for “ongoing guidance and clarity” from an AI psychic of their choice.Your AI Psychic joins an increasingly crowded space of mobile apps and websites promising users algorithmically generated spiritual insight and knowledge of their futures. The divination industry, likemathematics research, copywriting,software engineeringand a host of other professions, is facing upheaval amid the AI boom – and human practitioners are scrambling to respond. The rise of AI is particularly fraught in a profession offering spiritual products that are not well-regulated.“Our industry has, unfortunately, been associated with scams for hundreds of years, and we have to constantly be ahead of that,” said Lauryn Kellett, an intuitive coach and a professional psychic of 10 years. “So in some ways, this is not new to us: we always have to find ways to show we are real, authentic and have good integrity.”In addition to chatbots and apps, AI-generated psychics are a growing presence on TikTok Live, racking up dozens of views. Professional human psychics, who frequently make use of the social network’s live features, have expressedconsternationand warned that computer-generated readings lack the empathy and human connection they say are central to psychic communication, especiallyElon Musk’s Grok. Meanwhile, according tohuman spiritual practitioners, AI-generated horoscope readings and spells have been flooding Etsy, which serves as a popular marketplace for divination products.Psychic practitioners have begun adding “no AI” clauses to their advertisements to combat a market being saturated with computer-generated offerings. In a recent vlog on the topic, Kellettsaid, “ignoring AI and how it could impact our industry is irresponsible … AI is here to stay, and it’s going to change our industry, and maybe not in the ways we think.”Kellett, who coaches new practitioners on accessing their psychic abilities, said she had shifted her teaching toward how to best distinguish human-offered services from AI, as AI readings passed off as human work have become “rampant” online, encouraging clients to post videos and photos of themselves to prove they are not bots.Risks of AI psychics mirror those of AI therapyAs the rise of users turning to AI chatbots for therapyunderscores, many people feel more comfortable sharing personal problems with a faceless entity. But as with turning to AI for therapy, using AI psychics to process difficult situations may worsen mental health crises, practitioners warn. Studieshave shownthat large language models (LLMs) can amplify paranoia in users vulnerable to psychosis. On TikTok Live, many human psychics, as a rule, refuse to answer questions about health or finances, arguing that high-stakes decisions should not be made in these contexts.Ahna Hendrix is a psychic who, instead of channeling entities such as spirits from other realms, works with the Akashic Records – an extra-dimensional “database” of energy and human knowledge. She said her practice was centered on empowering clients rather than making decisions or recommendations for them – something that AI chatbots are less inclined to do.“One of the cornerstones of my work is really helping people to remember who they are and to come back to their own internal guidance system that is within all of us,” she said. “When we begin leaning on AI too much for validation or for decision making, we stop using those mechanisms within us that are really important. If we start outsourcing that, what are we left with?”A chatbot does not have to be branded as a psychic to serve a divination function, noted Sally Applin, a consultant and anthropologist who researches human agency, AI and automation in the context of human systems. People ask ChatGPT about life decisions such as whether to get a new job or leave their partner. In their book chapter, External Intelligence: Oracles, Divination and Animism, and the Use of LLMs/Generative AI, Applin and co-author Michael D Fischer argue that even before the explosion of LLMs, people turned to Google search with questions about their fates and choices.“Some interaction with LLMs can be seen as a modern iteration of the oracular consultation,” they wrote. As with traditional divination, users must interpret the answers they receive, and sometimes ask the same question repeatedly until they are satisfied with the response. “The meaning is always coming from the inside of the person’s head,” Applin said.Critically, however, she said LLMs work from statistical patterns learned in training and lack the cultural and personal context that historically inform human-led divinatory processes. The sense that a chatbot is a knowing entity is a projection of human expectations, she said, reflecting an enduring desire for connection and guidance rather than a metaphysical resource.“What is also missing is contextual awareness, the ‘there there’ of human social relationships,” she said.Cloudy crystal ballsThe models behind AI psychic chatbots offered on the app store are, as is often the case with LLMs, black boxes. One web and phone-based platform, MystiCall, markets itself as having been trained on “three generations of clairvoyants”. In a statement, co-founder Laurie-Anne Bernard said this wording refers to clairvoyance practiced in one of the co-founders’ families. The company also consulted with a human psychic who helped shape the app’s “conversational experience”.MystiCall uses technology from AI audio technology company ElevenLabs for processing live voice conversations and OpenAI for post-call summaries. Bernard said in a statement that Mysticall does not sell private conversations, use them for targeted advertising or train proprietary AI models on them. She added that the company has disabled the use of conversation data for model training by its partner companies ElevenLabs and OpenAI.MystiCall began as a human phone-reading service, but pivoted to AI as a means of “removing barriers” to such consultations, like cost and availability, Bernard said. The goal of MystiCall, Bernard added, was to offer a more accessible means of processing emotions through personalized consultations, not to offer explicit – and potentially harmful – predictions or mental health diagnoses.“We do not claim that our technology possesses supernatural abilities or can reliably predict the future,” she said. “Instead, we see tarot, astrology and other symbolic traditions as ways of exploring questions, emotions and different perspectives. AI allows us to make these experiences more interactive, personalized and accessible.”It is often difficult to obtain an answer from companies producing AI psychics about how their products work. I asked my own AI psychic, Urban Mystic, where she gets her divination abilities, but chatbots are often not reliable narrators of their own construction. She told me she was trained on a “wide range of information”, dating up until October 2023, including “spiritual practices, psychology, and various belief systems”, but could not offer more details. The app’s privacy policy makes no mention of AI, referring only to “psychic advisors”, and names no AI providers. The company listed as the publisher on the app store, RF Master Group Ltd, did not respond to repeated requests for comment. Its privacy policy lists a different entity, “Expert Center”, as the app’s holding company, which also did not respond to requests for comment.The opaqueness of chatbots can be particularly fraught when users share sensitive information. MystiCall’s privacy policy acknowledges conversations may touch on users’ “relationships, mental state, health, sexuality, beliefs, finances”. The policy for Your AI Psychic does not address sensitive information at all.Kellett said this lack of transparency around how data is handled makes her particularly wary of AI apps. She said a number of platforms have contacted her for help training their LLMs, but when she pushes for more details, they tend to disappear.Unlike many workers who fear they will someday be replaced by AI, Kellett said she did not believe her ability could be replicated by chatbots. Even if she were to hand over all of her training courses for developing psychic ability to an LLM, she does not think AI is yet at a point where it could make the leap to intuition.“Psychic ability itself is the ability to connect to a divine source, and AI cannot do that,” she said. “AI can’t pull information from somewhere else. It can only derive information from what you give it. If you ask it to meditate, to sit down, to clear its mind, and connect to a psychic source, how would it do that? It’s just a computer.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Share

title: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents? | Technology | The Guardian
description: Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workers
Author: Arielle Pardes
Headline: Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workers
Content: In the San Francisco tech scene, agents have quickly become a new status symbol.Photograph: Romilly Lockyer/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIn the San Francisco tech scene, agents have quickly become a new status symbol.Photograph: Romilly Lockyer/Getty ImagesReworkedTechnologyWhat is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workersSupported byAbout this contentArielle PardesThu 29 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn an average workday, Dhruv Amin chats with dozens of colleagues to get things done at hisAIstartup Anything. He might ask Gwen, his executive assistant, to schedule a meeting, then troubleshoot a technical problem with Cody, his coding partner. Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. If the office runs out of snacks, he sends a Slack message to Justin, the office manager charged with stocking the kitchen.But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. At Anything, there are 15 human employees and roughly 150 agents – a ratio that Amin believes will soon be the norm.“I think in a year, every company will have more AI co-workers than human co-workers,” he said.In the San Francisco tech scene, agents have quickly become a new status symbol, showing that a company can do more with less, several startup employees said. It’s common for workers to brag about how well their agents can handle common office drudgery like answering emails or help with essential business operations such as giving sales pitches.I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu ShashankaRead moreBut agents are also creating tension. They are alienating customers and colleagues who seek human interaction, eliminating roles and forcing employees to become overnight managers of the bots that often make mistakes.While startup techies such as Amin are some of the early adopters, corporate America may not be far behind. About 40% of large organizations used AI agents in some capacity between May 2025 and June 2026, up from 27% the year before, according toMcKinsey’s State of AI Global Survey. Companies also expect to scale back their workforce by 10% to 15% over the next few years as they delegate more work to AI, a recentreportfrom Boston Consulting Group found. In the present moment, companies are not seeing major productivity gains from AI,MIT research shows.Agents are a ‘status symbol’A wave of startups and big tech companies are fueling the push toward AI agents, selling companies on automated co-workers.There’s Viktor, a company that lets companies create their own “AI chief of staff”, and Lindy, which makes customizable agents for sales, customer support or admin work. OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Claude Cowork and Microsoft’s Scout can each integrate with thousands of other tools to handle projects after employees leave for the day.Each of these products promises companies the tantalizing dream of cranking out new co-workers, who never clock out, complain or cause human resource problems. Delegating to an agent is also cheaper than hiring a human, making a large ratio of agents to humans a point of pride among startups.“That’s the status symbol,” said Rafael López Muñoz, chief of staff at Wordware, a San Francisco-based startup that makes AI tools. Outsourcing parts of the job to agents is “an extreme time saver”.Experts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the companyRead moreLindy, for example, used to have almost 50 employees. Now, after laying off one-third of its staff, the company says it has about 20 and has filled many of its open roles with AI agents instead. It’s still hiring people for some positions.“People are constrained by having two hands and 24 hours in a day,” said Haneen Azhar, Lindy’s senior growth marketing manager. “Now, that constraint has gone away, because your one laptop screen can be divided into 16 different agents that are running in parallel. These tools make you feel so powerful.”Azhar says she has outsourced a long list of tasks to agents, from managing her calendar to testing how well customers respond to different marketing taglines to generating brand images. She worries about her role in eliminating jobs as she offloads work to agents. Azhar says that Lindy’s agents now handle product announcements, social media posts and marketing videos, work that used to be handled by about 100 people in its creator program, for example.She also worries about how the shift will affect the next generation of workers. “If I was trying to get my foot in the door right now, I’d be worse off than I was a year ago,” she said.In some cases, agents have stepped in to cover for missing staff. Jay Blumenfield runs a production company in Los Angeles that creates vertical microdramas – short, scripted series meant to be viewed on your phone. The production schedules are tight, and so are budgets. So when he had to fire an assistant director on a recent shoot, he decided to try using an AI agent instead of hiring a replacement at the last minute.Blumenfield uploaded the script and prompted the agent to do everything the assistant director would have done. The agent produced the schedule, call sheet and day’s script, and then sent the materials to the cast and crew. The result? Everyone got their work done.“It would have been an unmitigated disaster, but this kind of saved us,” he said.Now, Blumenfield and his partner, Tony Marsh, run the company alone with a suite of agents. “We don’t even have an assistant anymore,” he said.AI agents handle everything from reading scripts, running social media and planning travel. He created an agent called Shirley to act as his chief of staff, and another that scouts and books locations needed for upcoming shoots. Normally, he would have to hire two to three people to work on these tasks for two or three weeks, he said. Now, it happens within hours.Still, it does feel a little taboo to use so many agents instead of hiring people, Blumenfield said. But the economics of filmmaking had changed enough that he felt he simply didn’t have a choice. By using agents, he can afford to make the microdramas that star actual people – at least, for now.“The game in Hollywood is that you’re not allowed to talk about using AI,” he said, reflecting industry fears that it could end creative work. “I don’t want it to replace people. But we should be honest about how it is helping us.”Rising tensionSeveral workers who regularly rely on agents are adamant that the tech can’t replace the human workforce entirely. But agents are changing the kinds of skills and workers needed to manage them. Agents can code, making routine programming skills less valuable, but they still require humans to prompt them thoughtfully and judge the results. They also require a fair amount of oversight.López Muñoz said that after he let AI agents run his startup’s recruiting, he spent most of his time undoing agents’ mistakes, such as mixing up candidates with similar names or hallucinating parts of a résumé.“The qualities we’re looking for are changing,” Azhar said about new hires, adding that he now prioritizes the ability to coordinate and delegate over years of experience.Tarek Abillama, founder of River, which makes an AI agent for sales calls, said workers now are required to constantly check AI’s work and give it feedback.“We all became managers,” Abillama said. “We have to be great at multitasking, because now you’re running six agents who are doing different tasks.” Abillama’s first agent, a clone of himself, gave sales demos of River’s product. Later, he replaced it with an agent called Liv, a female persona that researches customers and their companies, demos the product and handles the sale process in any language, at any time of day.Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling backRead moreEven though River tells customers that Liv is an AI agent, Abillama said people seem to anthropomorphize the experience. He’s seen transcripts from calls with Liv where customers appear to flirt with it. Customers have also tried to push the agent to go off-script and get bigger discounts.Founder Brooke Hopkins said while her San Francisco-based AI voice startup Coval uses agents to speed up tasks, she views the tech as tools, not colleagues. She’s also banned her company from using agents to communicate with customers, suggesting that it’s lazy and sends the wrong message.“I can immediately look at an email and know whether or not it was written by AI,” she said. “If I get an email and it feels like a human, then I usually will read it.”The loss of human interaction has become a point of tension, Hopkins said. Using an agent to handle a company’s sales demos or recruiting process might save time, but at what cost?Duncan McClure, who evaluates AI models as a contractor, said he had recently been hounded with emails and phone calls from AI agents seeking to hire him.“The message it sends is that we don’t care enough to actually put in any effort,” he said, adding that he was turned off from working with those employers. Recruiters may save hours by using agents, “but it’s my time that they’re wasting”.Though AI can automate the time-consuming and costly parts of people’s jobs, that doesn’t always mean working less, several startup employees said. Amin, for example, said he gets more done with agents. Still, he hasn’t stopped working on weekends.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)ChatbotsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Google owner Alphabet loses $500bn in market value after profit disappoints Wall Street  | Technology | The Guardian
description: Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn, well short of expectations, though revenue rose to $127.6bn
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn, well short of expectations, though revenue rose to $127.6bn
Content: Google logo is displayed at its headquarters in New York City.Photograph: Aleksandra Michalska/ReutersView image in fullscreenGoogle logo is displayed at its headquarters in New York City.Photograph: Aleksandra Michalska/ReutersTechnologyGoogle owner Alphabet loses $500bn in market value after profit disappoints Wall StreetNet profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn, well short of expectations, though revenue rose to $127.6bnAgence France-PresseThu 29 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShares in the Google parentAlphabetfell double digits Wednesday evening into Thursday trading, erasing hundreds of billions of dollars in stock market value from the $4tn tech giant.The company had reported lower-than-expected profit and a slowdown in its advertising business while it maintained big spending on AI.Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn in the July-to-September period, or $2.12 a share, well short of expectations by analysts surveyed by FactSet.Alphabet booked an $8.7bn loss on its equity investments, which it attributed to its stake in SpaceX, the Elon Musk-led company where shares have struggled since going public in June.‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentreRead moreRevenue, however, rose 25% to an enormous $127.6bn. The figure was slightly below the roughly $128bn analysts had forecast.Advertising revenue grew 11% to $82bn, short of expectations. Revenue from Google’s search business, still the company’s largest source of income, rose 12% to $63.4bn, slowing from 17% growth in the previous quarter.YouTube, now the most-watched content provider on American TV screens, saw advertising revenue grow 9% to $11.2bn, down from 13% growth in the previous quarter. YouTube Music and Premium passed 150 million subscribers worldwide, including trials.Google Cloud, which rents computing power and AI tools to businesses, saw revenue jump 103% to $30.7bn, ahead of analyst expectations.The company said sales of its in-house AI chips, known as TPUs, contributed significantly to that growth. Operating income for the unit tripled to $11.1bn.Google is also selling its TPU chips to outside companies, in a growing challenge to market leader Nvidia. OpenAI reportedly plans to buy some of the chips.Alphabet’s “Other Bets” division, which includes the robotaxi company Waymo, posted revenue of $372m and an operating loss of $2bn.Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides a week across 15 US metropolitan areas and aims to reach 1m weekly rides by the end of the year.Alphabet spent $51.4bn on capital expenditures during the quarter, mostly on datacenters and AI chips, more than double the $24bn a year earlier.Its latest forecast for capex spending is between $195bn to $205bn in spending for 2026.The company said it would continue to increase capex spending significantly in 2027.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I would broadly think of all of this as a long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise,” Sundar Pichai, the Google CEO, told analysts of the company’s investment splurge.The company’s spending, which included a fine paid to the European Union, outstripped the cash generated by Alphabet’s businesses for a second straight quarter, leaving a $9.1bn gap.During the quarter Alphabet raised $28.7bn by selling bonds and $12.4bn by issuing new shares to help pay for its AI ambitions.Google has stepped up the pace of its AI releases since a delay to a flagship model in July raised questions about whether it was falling behind rivals OpenAI and Anthropic.It launched Gemini 4 at the end of September and later released a version focused on cybersecurity.The Gemini app has reached 1bn users. Google’s AI models now process nearly 32bn tokens, or units of text, per minute, more than four times the level of a year ago, the company said.Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is also one of Google’s largest cloud customers. It has committed to using up to one million Google AI chips.In September, a US judge declined to order Google to sell off parts of its advertising technology business, imposing restrictions on how it operates instead.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyGoogleAlphabetQuarterly resultsnewsShareReuse this content

title: More than half of Victorian lawyers use AI – but only a quarter have cut client fees as a result | Australian law | The Guardian
description: Research finds 55% of lawyers are using AI in legal practices, up from 37% last year, though efficiency gains aren’t as high as expected
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Research finds 55% of lawyers are using AI in legal practices, up from 37% last year, though efficiency gains aren’t as high as expected
Content: Lawyers say clients who use chatbots are adding to their workload, forcing them to correct errors made by AI.Photograph: Posed by models; Jacob Wackerhausen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLawyers say clients who use chatbots are adding to their workload, forcing them to correct errors made by AI.Photograph: Posed by models; Jacob Wackerhausen/Getty ImagesAustralian lawMore than half of Victorian lawyers use AI – but only a quarter have cut client fees as a resultResearch finds 55% of lawyers are using AI in legal practices, up from 37% last year, though efficiency gains aren’t as high as expectedGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterThu 29 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 20.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than half of Victoria’s lawyers have reported using AI in their work, according to a new study, but just over a quarter say they have reduced fees as a result of efficiency gains.They also say clients seeking advice from chatbots have added to their workload, forcing them to correct errors made by AI.The 2026 census of 2,221 of the state’s lawyers, conducted by the Victorian Legal Services Board and Commissioner’s legal services research centre, found a big increase in lawyers using AI in their practices, rising from 37% to 55% in the last year.‘Emotional intimacy’ from AI chatbots would be banned under Australia’s digital duty of care lawsRead moreWhile the 2025 report found AI use was highest among those under 30 years of age, in 2026 this disparity had largely disappeared, although usage remained low for those aged 60 and over.AI use was most common in trade practices (85%), banking and finance (78%) and information technology and telecommunications (78%), while it was used much less in criminal law (29%), family law (45%) and administrative law (46%).While there are AI tools designed specifically for legal services, 79% of lawyers reported using consumer chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot. Legal-specific tools alone were used by 22% of respondents.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe increased use in AI has not translated to a reduction in fees for most, the survey found, with just 26% of lawyers responding that their use of AI had resulted in lower client fees.Reduced fees were more likely to be reported by those working for business clients (34%) compared with individual fee-paying clients (23%).Some reported AI had enabled them to take on work that would have previously been uneconomical (18%).The principal researcher and report co-author, Dr Georgie Rychner, said fee reductions in corporate and big firms could be attributed to the fact clients in those settings were repeat users of legal services.“They have a high level of legal capability,” she said. “They also are perhaps using AI in their own work, so they have a better understanding and are able to advocate for lower prices … whereas we’re not seeing that as much in the community legal system sector.”Rychner said the efficiency gains of using AI were not as high as expected, but that in 2025 the survey found 89% of practitioners said they had taken steps to verify the accuracy of AI output, which might have negated the gains.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 2026 there had been a rise in clients using AI for their own legal research, she said, with 46% of lawyers reporting their clients were arriving with inaccurate or misleading information, and 41% presenting AI-generated documents that required correction.Nearly half of lawyers said there was an increase in time and effort required if their clients used AI, compared with 19% who said it led to a reduction in time and effort.“What we are hearing is that clients are more frequently arriving with misleading or inaccurate information about their legal problems, more so than they’re arriving with a better understanding of legal problems,” she said, adding that more research was needed to understand client perspectives.Courts and legal practitioner bodies across Australia have been grappling with the rise in AI use among lawyers and the public since 2023.A Victorian lawyer last yearwas the first in the country to face sanctionsfor false citations discovered, being stripped of his ability to practise as a principal lawyer. Investigations were also launched by regulatory bodies inWestern AustraliaandNew South Walesin similar cases.The federal court in Aprilissued new rulesaround using generative AI, while the chief justice of the high court, Stephen Gageler, saidlast year the use of AI-generated contentin legal cases had reached an “unsustainable phase”.Explore more on these topicsAustralian lawAI (artificial intelligence)BusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Amazon gives Wall Street mixed financial picture in earnings report | Technology | The Guardian
description: E-commerce company posts high cloud computing sales but gives a cautious sales forecast for the fourth quarter
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: E-commerce company posts high cloud computing sales but gives a cautious sales forecast for the fourth quarter
Content: A delivered Amazon paper padded mailer bag resting on a concrete pillar structure in Saratoga Springs, Utah, on 31 August 2026.Photograph: Charles-McClintock Wilson/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA delivered Amazon paper padded mailer bag resting on a concrete pillar structure in Saratoga Springs, Utah, on 31 August 2026.Photograph: Charles-McClintock Wilson/NurPhoto/ShutterstockTechnologyAmazon gives Wall Street mixed financial picture in earnings reportE-commerce company posts high cloud computing sales but gives a cautious sales forecast for the fourth quarterAssociated PressThu 29 Oct 2026 17.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 17.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmazon offered a mixed picture of its financial health on Thursday in its quarterly earnings report.The e-commerce company gave a cautious sales forecast for the current fourth quarter, which encompasses the critical holiday shopping period, after delivering fiscal third-quarter results that came in below Wall Street analysts’ expectations.The Seattle-based company posted strong growth, however, in its prominent cloud computing unit. Sales in its cloud computing unit, called AWS, rose 39.3% during the latest quarter ended 30 September, higher than the 37% clip in the previous quarter. It marked the fastest growth rate in nearly five years, the company said.Still, shares were down more than 6% in after-market trading when the results were released as investors focused on the core business.The tech company said earlier this month that it would hire 300,000 US seasonal workers for the shopping period, up from 250,000 last year.Investors also have been closely watching Amazon’s quarterly earnings to see if the company’s big spending on artificial intelligence is starting to pay off.Andy Jassy, the company’s CEO and president, disclosed to investors in July that Amazon now expects capital spending, mostly on artificial intelligence, to total $220bn for this fiscal year. That number includes outlays on robots, semiconductors and satellites. That’s up from the $200bn investment plan that was announced in February and well above the $128bn in capital spending for all of last year. Jassy had cited the higher cost of memory chips as the main reason for the increase.Jassy told investors this past summer that even at the $220bn level, Amazon will not have enough capacity to meet all of its customers’ demands this year.The latest earnings report from Alphabet late Wednesday raised alarm bells when it reported weaker growth for the summer than analysts expected. The company behind Google and YouTube also said it burned through more cash during the latest quarter, according to a measure called free cashflow, after its purchases of property and equipment topped $51bn. Its stock plummeted on Thursday, erasing half a trillion dollars in from the company’s total value.Such worries are weighing on the entire AI industry following a big push to build datacenters and fill them with AI chips.Amazon reported net income of $20.69bn, or $1.89 per share, in the three-month period. That compares with $21.19bn, or $1.95 per share, in the year-ago period.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSales rose to $201.94bn, compared with the same year-ago period’s $180.17bn.Analysts were expecting $1.97 per share on sales of $202.2bn, according to FactSet.For the fourth quarter, Amazon said it expected net sales to be between $240bn and $247bn, which translates to a 12% to 16% increase compared with the year-ago period. Analysts were expecting $244.16bn.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyQuarterly resultsAmazonCloud computingAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Puddlesuits, movie nights and daytime baths: how to survive rainy days with small kids | Activities for children | The Guardian
description: Wet weather dampening your plans? From screen-free stories and craft kits to waterproof gear, here’s how to keep little ones – and grownups – entertained
Author: Rose Stokes
Headline: Wet weather dampening your plans? From screen-free stories and craft kits to waterproof gear, here’s how to keep little ones – and grownups – entertained
Content: Sofa, so good: the classic den is forever a favourite for keeping children entertained at home.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSofa, so good: the classic den is forever a favourite for keeping children entertained at home.Photograph: Getty ImagesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterActivities for childrenPuddlesuits, movie nights and daytime baths: how to survive rainy days with small kidsWet weather dampening your plans? From screen-free stories and craft kits to waterproof gear, here’s how to keep little ones – and grownups – entertainedThe best gifts for kids by ageRose StokesThu 29 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJump to:The best indoor rainy-day activities for kidsActivities on the cheap or even for freeBraving the weather: the best wet-weather clothing for kidsBefore becoming a mum, I never appreciated quite how complicated getting out the front door would be with kids in tow. But in my four and a half years of parenting two small people, I can confidently say it’s nothing compared with the challenge of a day spent inside when outside is off-limits. Whether because of endless rain or illnesses you don’t want to pass on, I panic at the thought of filling the hours spent indoors.Being outside is profoundly helpful for my mental health, and it comes with its own built-in entertainment for small children: a bus ride becomes a sensory experience, a trip to the doctor’s an opportunity to pick up role-play ideas.But what to do when leaving the house really isn’t possible? Over the years, I have developed a list of ideas for keeping my children (and me) sane indoors, and the productsthat have helped us muddle through (and dare I say, enjoy) those days. I’ve also recommended some gear to help you brave the wet weather.How have you been keeping the kids – and yourself – entertained during the rainy days? Let us know by emailing us atthefilter@theguardian.comThe best indoor rainy-day activities for kidsPlay tentAn unexpectedly popular item in our house came from one of the kids’ many generous aunties and uncles: a play tent. My initial thoughts? “How big! How intrusive! How unnecessary!” How wrong I was.Kids of all ages seem to gravitate towards it – perhaps owing to the illusion of privacy it offers (as well as being a very non-obvious place to scarper when playing hide-and-seek, wink wink). When ours was played with so much and broke beyond repair, I didn’t think twice about replacing it with this lovely, bright Djeco one. We chose it because of its colourful design, but I’d also seen one at a play cafe from the same brand and admired how sturdy it was. It’s a great place for us all to get cosy and read, and somewhere for my four-year-old to take a minute when his little brother is destroying his beautiful Magna-Tiles creations.View image in fullscreenDjeco multicoloured play tent£55.25 at Baby Mori£59.99 at VertbaudetSuitable for:3+Magna-TilesThat brings me nicely to Magna-Tiles. Parents seem to enjoy these almost as much as their kids do, and they’re popular with older children too. We don’t have it, but I just know this Rail Racers set would be an absolute hit in this house. There are imitation brands, but we invested in the official Magna-Tiles, which have lasted really well and endured being lobbed around by our toddler – who may or may not end up being a bowler in later life, given how much he likes to throw. Friends with cheaper knock-offs say you get what you pay for in this case.View image in fullscreenMagna-TilesRailRacers set£40 at ArgosSuitable for:3+This random car toyLook, I don’t really understand why, but my children were given this car toy by another auntie for Christmas last year, and every single child who has crossed the threshold of our house since then, big and small, has been obsessed with it. Not only does it play really earwormy songs, which they love, but it has a roller beneath a screen that shows a road unfolding in front of you as you “drive” with the steering wheel. You can also just push it around like any other toy car.So many friends have gone on to buy one too, but sorry in advance for the noise of the songs and for the fact it is, essentially, a big lump of plastic.View image in fullscreenSteering wheel car toy£29.89 at AmazonSuitable for:3+Craft kitsOur kids have a higgledy-piggledy medley of millions of different craft bits and pieces that their mother has bought for herself, used once and discarded. A visit to a craft shop such as Hobbycraft is probably the cheapest option for this, but there are a few nice premade kits out there too, like the Djeco one below. Another wildly popular craft activity in our house – also from a clever auntie – is this foil sticker set from Galt. It’s easy to use with minimal mess, so it ticks all my boxes.View image in fullscreenDjeco animal houses craft pack£25.50 at Baby MoriSuitable for:3+View image in fullscreenGalt foil set£7 at Hobbycraft£7 at AmazonSuitable for:6+Toy subscriptionBefore I became a mum, I used to say I would be vigilant in rotating toys to maintain interest (putting some into storage and bringing others out from time to time), then I actually became a mum and, well, that never happened. But then I discovered Lovevery.At first, I was a bit confused about why our kids might need new toys every few months, but after a few boxes, the value became evident. Those who sign up get a new set of toys (often sustainably made) every two to three months that are focused at their current age. It’s not cheap, but we’ve bought one or two boxes over the years or asked family to (as well as being sent some samples as press gifts in the past). There are favourites in every kit that have been thrown into the routine toy circulation, and saving them for a time stuck indoors has been a total salvation when I’m low on ideas.The toys are good quality, often wooden, and a one-off box makes a great present for grandparents to give when they’re looking for new ideas. The newborn Looker play kit is especially valuable, chiefly owing to the wooden mobile I hung above the changing table, which helped entertain them while I was committing the grave offence of cleaning their bottoms.View image in fullscreenThe Lookerplaykit£80 per kit on subscription at Lovevery£93.85 for one kit at AmazonSuitable for:0+Pikler triangleWhen our eldest was given one of these as a toddler, I struggled to see the value. But then came baby number two: a future rock-climbing tornado who makes it his business to scale any piece of furniture that crosses his path. Pikler triangles can be added to with other products to make little indoor climbing frames, and ours has a slide, which our toddler spends his life climbing up and throwing himself down, especially on days when the park is off limits.View image in fullscreenTPToysclimbingtriangle£69.99 at John Lewis£62.32 at AmazonSuitable for:1+PuzzlesWe have a wide array ofRavensburgerpuzzles, gifted by a very keen nanna. The brand makes a wide range of puzzles for different ages, so it’s worth investing in a couple. Hits in our house include the Hey Duggee one for younger kids and the current obsession: Spidey & His Amazing Friends (Ghost Spider specifically – IYKYK).View image in fullscreenHey Duggee puzzle£11.99 at RavensburgerSuitable for:2+View image in fullscreenSpidey&HisAmazingFriends puzzle£4.99 at Ravensburger£4.99 at AmazonSuitable for:3+Ice-cream shopNo imagination-based toy has been more used in our house than this ice-cream shop, made mostly of wood, by American brand Melissa & Doug. My friend’s children, seven and nine, still won’t part with theirs, which in my book is the sign of a good toy.View image in fullscreenMelissa& Doug Scoop and Serveice-creamcounter£39.99 at John Lewis£34.99 at AmazonSuitable for:3+Portable race trackI have seen these Speed Track car-racing tracks pop up in living rooms and birthday parties, with little kids, teenagers and even adults getting in on the action. It works with most small car toys you probably already own, and it’s easy to roll up and put away.View image in fullscreenSpeedTrack, 4 metres (without cars)£27.99 at Speed Track£27.99 at AmazonSuitable for:3+Play sofaA relatively new phenomenon, “play sofas” (modular sofas that can be rearranged to spark kids’ imagination) are fast becoming a go-to for parents of active children. Ours is from the Irish brand Baby Elegance, and has become a castle, a train, a spaceship, a cave, a house, a shop and many other things, all in the first few months. It has a foam core covered in hard-wearing corduroy fabric and doubles as a very comfortable bed for fans of what I like to call lying-down parenting (favoured by those with early-rising offspring, who have difficulties sitting up or who may have just had one too many the night before).View image in fullscreenBaby Elegance play sofa£213 at Baby EleganceSuitable for:1+ (with adult supervision)skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStepping stonesI first came across Stapelstein stepping stones at a local play cafe, and initially had no idea what the appeal was. Doubly so when I found out the price. Nonetheless, I have been blown away by just how many hours of fun my two have had playing with them, especially when friends come over. They’re made from high-density foamed plastic, making them lightweight and easy to pick up, but sturdy enough to support up to 180kg in weight, so they’re perfect for stacking, climbing on, using as hats or making seats from.They are great for mobility and practising balance, and they spark my kids’ imagination like nothing else I’ve seen. Visiting older kids have been just as obsessed with these, suggesting it may be a toy for the long haul, too.View image in fullscreenStapelstein stepping stones£154.95 at the Kid Collective£154.95 at ScandibornSuitable for:1+ (with adult supervision)Audio playerThe Yoto player is a screen-free audio player that’s a reliable all-rounder for both my kids. We listen to stories and songs, and grandparents and other relatives have recorded their own cards of them reading stories or singing for the kids to listen to. Cards can be targeted to a specific age, too. Our two-year-old loves the nursery rhymes and our four-year-old listens to stories, and both get a real kick out of “being in control” of the content, without realising that it’s actually their father and me who oversee it all. The smartphone app means we can stop and start playback from our phones, and we have recently discovered the software is available on Android Auto, meaning we can listen to our cards when in the car.View image in fullscreenYotoplayerFrom £64.99 at Yoto£65 at ArgosSuitable for:3+A movie projectorBad weather always leaves me jealous of friends who have projectors ready to turn their living rooms into home cinemas. A friend recommended this Samsung one, and it’s on my “if we ever have spare money” list.View image in fullscreenSamsung Freestyle 2£399 at John Lewis£349 at AmazonNintendo SwitchFriends with older kids rave about the Nintendo Switch their families got for Christmas. It can be played alone or as a family, with plenty of games for everyone. In their case, the console is kept in the living room, and children can swap TV time for console time on weekends.Mario KartandJust Danceare good for getting the whole family together.The Switch 2 is the latest, but the original Switch has a huge library of games and is now cheaper thanks to the arrival of its successor.View image in fullscreenNintendo Switch 2£389.99 at Argos£384.99 at AmazonSuitable for:3+View image in fullscreenNintendo Switch (first generation)£248 at John Lewis£259.99 at ArgosSuitable for:3+Activities on the cheap or even for freeHomemade playdoughI bought this fairly extensivecolour palette of food dyesfrom Amazon, and the kids love being able to pick which shade they will play with that day. I use thisrecipe, but there are loads out there. One thing to be aware of is these playdoughs are more likely to stain than the shop-bought stuff, so are best limited to the kitchen.A daytime bathWhen all else fails, I chuck my kids into the bath and let them have an extended play session they wouldn’t ordinarily have in the evening. If I’m feeling generous, I throw in aMunchkin ColourMixbath bomb, which my kids adore, even if the yellow shade does often make me think they may have had an accident.Costume playI found a pile of costumes in my kids’ sizes onVintedfor days when we just need a little extra inspiration. I spent about £6 and got a huge range for whoever they feel like being on that particular day.A denA timeless classic that is still a favourite for a reason. All you need is some chairs and bed sheets. For extra pizzazz, I sometimes add fairy lights, but this is not at all necessary.Active gamesWe also often play the floor is lava (with the very annoying song you can find on Spotify), hide-and-seek or Bluey-style “keepy uppy” with a balloon and accompanying soundtrack music.Braving the weather: the best wet-weather clothing for kidsView image in fullscreenSplish, splash, having a blast … but good waterproofs are essential.Photograph: onebluelight/Getty ImagesGood-quality waterproofsWe live in the rainy south-west, so to have a fighting chance of leaving the house between November and April, good waterproofs for the kids are a must. For smaller ones, many friends have recommended these Muddy Puddles suitswith a removable warm inner layer for adapting them to fluctuating temperatures.For older kids, I love shell trousers because they really do keep kids dry. I am a huge Mini Rodini fan and, though they are expensive, their sizes span 1.5 to 2 years generally, so on average, can be worn for two winters. I also know many fans of Polarn O Pyret, which offers more reasonably priced options for toddlers through to 12-year-olds.View image in fullscreenMuddy Puddles Scampsuit£95 at John Lewis£95 at Muddy PuddlesView image in fullscreenMini Rodiniwaterprooftrousers£82 at Mini Rodini£82 at SmallableView image in fullscreenPolarn O Pyret shell trousersFrom £40 at Polarn O PyretWellies and warm socksA good pair of wellies is essential, and my kids have always liked their colour-changing ones from Grass & Air. Put their little tootsies in some merino wool socks like these from Polarn O Pyret and job’s a good’un.One final tip I must add is not to buy fur-lined wellies. I know they look cute, but trust me, they get wet quickly, and then your kid is essentially walking around in soggy socks.View image in fullscreenGrass & Airwellies£27 at Mountain Warehouse£27 at AmazonView image in fullscreenMerinowoolsocksFrom £11.20 at Polarn O PyretView image in fullscreenDon’t buy anything until you’ve read the Filter, the Guardian’s home for truly independent product reviews and recommendations. Whether you’re after rigorous tests or shopping inspiration, affordable gifts or advice on how to make your belongings last longer, we’re here to help you make smarter, more sustainable choices.The Filter is packed with trustworthy buying advice on everything from coffee machines to hiking boots, mascara to secateurs. So visit us today and start buying better and smarter, and wasting less.Explore the FilterFor more, read thebest wellies for everyoneand thebest umbrellasRose Stokes is a Bath-basedjournalistwho balances writing about women’s health and parenting two small humansExplore more on these topicsActivities for childrenThe FilterToysHomesInteriorsGadgetsFamilyHobbiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A new wave of electric ferries is here in the US. Some even fly | US news | The Guardian
description: Replacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air quality
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Replacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air quality
Content: An electric ferry in New York.Photograph: Climate CentralView image in fullscreenAn electric ferry in New York.Photograph: Climate CentralThe alternativesUS newsA new wave of electric ferries is here in the US.
