Some even flyReplacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air qualityBen Tracy of Climate CentralThu 29 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCutting through New York Harbor in the shadow of the Statue of Liberty, the small white boat we were riding on caught the attention of passengers aboard a nearby sightseeing ferry.“It’s quite a curiosity at the moment,” Eric Laakmann, the chief executive and co-founder of Vessev, said.His company builds fully electric hydrofoil boats. These vessels use underwater “wings” to lift their hulls above the surface as they pick up speed. By raising the boat out of the water, the design dramatically reduces drag, one of the biggest obstacles to making boats more energy-efficient.“We’re picking up speed. We’re going for a takeoff,” Laakmann said as the boat rapidly accelerated.The hydrofoils lifted the hull about a foot and a half above the water. Almost immediately, the ride transformed. The familiar slap of the boat pushing through waves became a smooth, almost airborne glide.How hydrofoils make electric boats ‘viable’The hydrofoil effect is more than a novelty. Water creates significant resistance, and overcoming it takes energy. Electrifying boats is a challenge because batteries are heavy, and that extra weight increases the power needed to move the vessel. Hydrofoils may offer a solution. By lifting much of the hull out of the water, they reduce drag, allowing a vessel to move more efficiently.“We substantially reduce the drag that you feel and that’s really what makes electrification viable,” Laakmann said.Vessev says its hydrofoil design cuts drag by about 66%. That greater efficiency allows the boats to carry smaller battery packs, reducing both weight and cost.But efficiency is only part of the equation. Making a boat electric is not simply a matter of replacing a diesel engine with a motor and battery. Operators must also consider how far a vessel needs to travel, how many passengers it carries, how quickly it must recharge, and how much weight it can accommodate.From novelty to everyday transportVessev operates passenger services in New Zealand and is expanding to Australia. In the US, its first service is planned for Lake Tahoe. Laakmann sees a future in which electric vessels become a routine part of public transportation, rather than a niche attraction.“More like subways, more like buses, more like Ubers, more like taxis but on the water,” he said.Waterways can connect communities and move passengers without adding more vehicles to crowded roads. When powered by increasingly clean electricity, electric ferries can also cut the pollution associated with diesel engines.Transportation remains the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States, according to federal environmental data. Road vehicles account for much of that pollution, but ships and other watercraft also burn fossil fuels. Replacing diesel-powered ferries with electric vessels could reduce emissions and improve air quality around busy waterfronts.Vessev is not alone in pursuing the technology. In Stockholm, commuters are already riding electric hydrofoil ferries built by the Swedish company Candela. The company says its design can reduce energy use by as much as 80% compared with conventional vessels of a similar type. Norway has ordered 20 of its electric hydrofoil boats for coastal service.For ferry operators, the attraction is not simply environmental. More efficient designs and advances in battery technology are opening up routes for electric boats that might once have been impractical. There is also the potential for lower operating costs as fuel prices soar.“I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Laakmann said.San Francisco prepares to plug inIn San Francisco, the city’s largest ferry operator carries about 3.5 million passengers a year, according to Seamus Murphy, who leads the agency. The network serves a region shaped by water, with commuters relying on boats to cross the bay and reach the city.“We have a lot of waterfront,” Murphy said.Yet the fleet runs entirely on fossil fuels. All 18 vessels in the system are powered by diesel. That is set to change as the agency prepares to add four battery-powered ferries over the next two years. It is part of an electric overhaul worth about half a billion dollars that also includes charging infrastructure at docks.Unlike a car that can be plugged in at home overnight, a ferry may need to complete repeated trips on a fixed timetable. Its batteries must provide enough energy for the route, while shore-side chargers deliver enough power during the time the vessel spends at the terminal.Making that work requires more than the right boat. Operators must coordinate vessel range, timetables and charging capacity to keep passengers moving without disrupting service. San Francisco won’t initially be using hydrofoil boats, but the agency says its new vessels will make it the first ferry operator in the United States to run high-speed, all-electric ferries.The economics of going electricFor transit agencies, climate goals alone rarely justify a major fleet overhaul. The numbers have to add up.Battery-powered ferries generally require a larger initial investment in vessels and charging equipment. But electric motors can be more efficient than diesel engines, and operators may save money over time on fuel and maintenance. Murphy said rising diesel costs and improvements in battery technology strengthened the case for making the switch.“You make the upfront investment at the beginning and then you save over time and at the end of the day you’re going to have lower costs in the long term,” he said.The financial case depends a lot on the route. Batteries remain heavy and expensive, charging infrastructure can be costly, and not every route is suited to a fully electric vessel. Long distances, tight schedules and limited opportunities to recharge can all complicate the transition.The shift could create opportunities well beyond the water. For San Francisco’s expansion, the boats and their batteries are being built in the United States. This could create opportunities for domestic manufacturing jobs.For Murphy, the transition is a chance to cut pollution while helping develop new business for shipbuilders and battery manufacturers.“These jobs are going to get created in other countries and we have an ability to create them here if we manage this in the right way,” Murphy said. “We don’t want to be left behind,” he added.Climate Centralis an independent group of scientists and communicators who research and report the facts about our changing climate and how it affects people’s lives.Explore more on these topicsUS newsThe alternativesElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsGreenhouse gas emissionsFerry travelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Despite the teething issues, Dyson’s Camerajet toothbrush packs in a lot of clever tech – but is it worth £420? | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: Dyson’s first electric toothbrush watches you brush and flosses for you, but there are far cheaper ways to get an effective clean
Author: Alan Martin
Headline: Dyson’s first electric toothbrush watches you brush and flosses for you, but there are far cheaper ways to get an effective clean
Content: Camera ready: Dyson’s pricey brush peeks inside your mouth and fires water jets between your teeth.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCamera ready: Dyson’s pricey brush peeks inside your mouth and fires water jets between your teeth.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterHealth & wellbeingReviewDespite the teething issues, Dyson’s Camerajet toothbrush packs in a lot of clever tech – but is it worth £420?Dyson’s first electric toothbrush watches you brush and flosses for you, but there are far cheaper ways to get an effective cleanThe best electric toothbrushes for every budgetAlan MartinThu 29 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenDyson announced it was entering the toothbrush market, the world responded almost as one: “Four hundred and twenty pounds? For a toothbrush!?”No, it wasn’t a stray decimal point – or if it was, Dyson is doubling down and leaning into the mistake. Unlike high-end brushes from Oral-B or Philips Sonicare, where the “recommended” in “recommended retail price” is doing a heroic amount of heavy lifting given the frequent discounts, the Dyson CameraJet will actually set you back £419.99.The CameraJet is an electric toothbrushanda water flosser, so if you were being charitable – or merely looking for a way to justify the cost to yourself – you could call this two for the price of one on thebest electric toothbrushesandwater flossers.There’s a lot of clever technology here, and Dyson’s commitment to doing something different should be applauded, even if it’s just to give your hands something to do besides reaching for your credit card.Note that the brush has had some bad post-launch publicity with multiple online accounts of the pricey purchase failing within weeks. This led to the CameraJet vanishing from virtual store shelves for a time, withDyson blaminga “single component issue affecting a small number of early batches”.I had no such issues with my review unit, and the brush is now back in stock everywhere. Nonetheless, it’s worth remembering that the more intricate moving parts in a product, the more opportunities for breakage.View at DysonView at John LewisHow I testedView image in fullscreenGood vibrations? Reviewer Alan testing the hand and mouth feel of the Dyson CameraJet.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianI’ve become something of a pro toothbrusher in the past two years, having tested dozens of models for our list of thebest electric toothbrushes. Theprocess isn’t a big secret: it just involves brushing to an obsessive degree while observing several factors, including how it feels in the hand and mouth, how easy it is to use, how portable it is and how clean your teeth feel afterwards. It’s a similar story for flossers, with the water tank capacity measured too.There are also objective details you can assess, such as power and battery life. Because the last thing you want is to wait for your brush to charge when you just want to go to bed.Dyson CameraJet: what you need to knowView image in fullscreen‘The camera means you can watch a live stream from the inside of your mouth on the Dyson app.’Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianView at DysonView at John LewisDyson isn’t the first manufacturer to combine an electric toothbrush and water flosser into one product – Irecently testedthe Soocas Neos II, which I deemed a “a jack of two trades, but a master of none” – but this is the first one I’ve used that does both jobs well enough to warrant a recommendation.There are a few reasons for this. The handle is a normal width for an electric toothbrush, rather than distended to hold the water. Unlike regular cordless flossers, where you have to awkwardly refill the reservoir by hand, here a dock tops it up with a single button press.The main advantage, though, is the camera. The 100,000-pixel macro-lens camera sits inside a hollowed-out section of the brush head and captures 28 images of your mouth every second, which Dyson’s machine-learning algorithm uses to identify gaps between teeth. When it finds one, a blast of water or mouthwash is automatically fired into the gap. This camera also means you can watch a live stream from the inside of your mouth on the Dyson app, should you have exhausted the contents of Netflix.The 12.5ml tank is described as “anti-gravity”, meaning the diaphragm pump and pressure chamber adapt to how you’re holding the brush, ensuring that it always has liquid to dispense. This is a big plus over other water flossers, where the “straw in a cup” system often misses the dregs when holding it at the angle required for hard-to-reach places.The jet, Dyson says, is also different from those fired by other water flossers. Working with the National University of Singapore, which helped develop a proxy plaque (a lab stand-in for real dental plaque), the company claims to have found that traditional “needle-type” jets merely punctured a hole in the sticky surface, rather than removing it. Dyson instead opts for a conical shape that it says “sweeps and removes plaque at once”, while being gentler to gums and enamel.So the expense is justified via R&D and clever technology. Note that the high price of entry doesn’t end with the brush itself, as you need bespokereplacement headsto work with the camera, and these cost £25 for two (though your first pair come in the box). The brush heads have an RFID (radio-frequency identification) tag that enables the toothbrush to monitor how often the head has been used and let you know when it needs replacing.Dyson CameraJet specificationsType:variable sonic oscillationModes:three cleaning modes and three brushing intensities (plus water jet)Power:58,000 movements a minutePressure sensor:yesBattery life:up to 10 daysApp:yesWarranty:two years, with 12 months for the brush head cover (registration required if you buy at a third-party retailer)Replacement head cost:£25 for twoWhat we loveView image in fullscreenPlaque, camera, action: the toothbrush’s camera is designed for closeup work.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianWhile the words “camera” and “bathroom” usually shouldn’t be found in proximity to one another, it’s pretty harmless here. It can’t be manually turned off, but no images or video are saved.According to Dyson, “the camera is only active during live viewing or auto-jetting. No images are recorded or stored on the product or in the cloud”. And, even if they could be, the lens isn’t designed for selfies; it only works up close. I mean, can you really tell much about my house from this picture?When used on your teeth, it’s an eye-opening experience, giving you the kind of private screening usually reserved for dental professionals. And, while the dentist has given my teeth a professional signoff in recent trips, seeing a closeup of the discoloration that comes from 40-plus years of chewing is an incentive not to cut any more dental hygiene corners.Intentions are one thing, and actions are quite another. We all know that we’re supposed to floss daily, but how many of us do? Even with water flossers for convenience, it’s too easy to skip it when you’re at the sink.The beauty of the Dyson CameraJet is that it makes that choice for you, and my teeth and gums undoubtedly felt the benefit. Because the jets fire automatically, flossing becomes a part of the brushing process. The result? My smile felt and looked healthier without any extra effort.That’s in part down to the dock, which is a marvellous innovation. As well as charging the toothbrush, the 200ml tank at the back offers a one-touch refill of the CameraJet’s 12.5ml reservoir –put your toothbrush in the dock, hold the button and the reservoir will refill. While you’ll still need to top up the main tank every few weeks, the refill system is significantly more convenient than all other cordless flossers I’ve tested, which either require you to unscrew a tank or awkwardly pour mouthwash or water through a small refilling hole. Crucially, this ensures flossing isn’t an easily skippable step. Dysonrecommendsusing its own low-foaming mouthwash to fill the tank, but you don’t have to.View image in fullscreenPort of call: the CameraJet in its dock, which charges it, and features a 200ml tank.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianThe battery life of 10 days may sound low to some, but it’s important to remember it’s powering a light and camera, as well as the usual motor, even if it is still disappointing to see the battery life dropping 5% as you explore your mouth with the camera. Ultimately, it’s a non-issue with the aforementioned dock: you’re unlikely to ever find yourself out of battery if using it as intended.The performance itself is good too, leaving my mouth feeling squeaky clean. Whether that’s down to the added jets or the fact that it defaults to three minutes rather than the usual two is open to debate, but the cleanliness factor puts it close to the top of the list of thebest electric toothbrushesI’ve tried (though I still find theLaifen Wave Proslightly more effective at defuzzing stickier areas after an evening on the cider). The brush rotates 58,000 times a minute, and the mouthwash distribution via the jet leaves a dentist-fresh feeling when everything works as planned …What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenHole again? Could a blocked camera beneath the bristles be causing the auto-firing issues?Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianThat cliffhanger of a last sentence was a giveaway to my first criticism: the jets don’t always automatically fire (though you can activate one manually at the press of a button if you feel an area is neglected). Through trial and error, I’ve concluded that the most common reason for the jets to take an unwelcome breather is that the camera is blocked, so it can’t see teeth.I believe this is because of toothpaste foaming up in use. When I’ve connected to the live-stream camera, the experience reminds me of trying to see out of the window when going through a carwash. And when it gets too foamy, the jets stop working until you spit out some toothpaste or have your tongue moonlight as a kind of windscreen wiper for the camera. It’s a messy experience, and your bathroom mirror won’t thank you.For this reason, it’s recommended you’re choosier with your toothpaste.Dyson sells its own recommended low-foam paste and mouthwashthat I was able to try, and this significantly improves the experience. With my regular foamy toothpaste, the app reported the jets were usually firing between 25 and 50 times per three-minute session (and on some occasions dropping to single digits). With non-foaming toothpaste and regular spitting, it settled on a fairly reliable 70 to 80.A cynic would point out that this is convenient for Dyson, diverting users from cheaper brands to its own consumables (from £8.49 for 75ml toothpaste; £8.49 for 400ml mouth rinse) for the long haul – you can even subscribe on the website. You can buy non-foaming toothpaste that isn’t Dyson-branded, but it’s not easily found in supermarkets, taking away a little of the hard-won convenience. I also tried Suri’slow-foam toothpastewith it, which worked reasonably well.View image in fullscreenRead all about it: the CameraJet’s manual is essential for decoding its operation.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianThe CameraJet is confusing to use at first, too, which somewhat eats into those convenience credentials. Having reviewed a lot of toothbrushes, I can usually get away with skipping the instructions and getting straight into testing. I quickly learned that wasn’t an option here, and I’ve found myself constantly revisiting the manual to remind myself of the buttons and decode the occasional sounds it makes.One such sound is a warning that you’re brushing incorrectly. Typically with electric toothbrushes, you hover over the tooth and move slowly along, but the Dyson CameraJet requires you to make small oval shapes as you progress. But even when I’ve been following this advice, I’ve been told off for overscrubbing. This makes me think the CameraJet’s either overzealous, or its instructions aren’t clear enough.The good news is that this can be overcome with the use of Dyson’s app to guide you through proceedings. This will tell you when the camera is blocked, and also keep a tally of its water jets, warning you if you’re moving too fast. The app is optional and can be ignored once you’ve got the swing of things, but what can’t be so easily brushed away is the size of the kit. The brush is already on the tall side at 273mm, but the dock takes this even further with a height of 315mm.Nominally, this can be used as a travel case by slipping on a clear plastic cover, but it’s pushing the definition of portable, and will not easily slip into carry-on luggage without clever organisation. Yes, you can take it without the dock and just use the bundled pogo-pin charging cable, but it’s a less elegant solution than the Suri Pro 2.0’s charging travel case, which by my measure is a svelte 241.3 x 31.75 x 31.75mm.More philosophically, while the Dyson CameraJet has made my mouth feel very clean, I wonder if it could lead buyers into a false sense of security with their dental health. The convenience is great, but it leaves you to rely on the camera to detect every gap and fire accurately and at the right time, which isn’t guaranteed. The jets fire so fast that I’d defy anybody to tell the difference between mouthwash hitting the target between teeth and misfiring nearby. With a regular water flosser, the nozzle forces you to hit every gap, even if it is an added hassle, and while there’s a manual flossing mode, without the camera AI, it feels hit and miss.Beyond that, from speaking to dental professionals in the past, the jury is still out on whether water flossing is as effective as using interdental brushes. Sam Jethwa, president of the British Academy of Cosmetic Dentistry, compares flossing to cleaning an algae-covered boat. “Get a hosepipe to try to get it off, it’s not going to do anything,” he told me, arguing that you need “mechanical movement” alongside water to make an impact. So, while my teeth did feel far better than just using an electric toothbrush alone, I’m not sure this is quite the one-stop solution Dyson would like it to be.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenIt’s a brush head-to-head: the Dyson CameraJet and our highly rated flosser, the Waterpik Ultra Professional.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianAll of which brings us to the price: £419.99. Without wanting to state the obvious, that’s a huge amount of money, even taking into account that this is a 2-in-1 device. You could buy our top-rated toothbrush (theLaifen Wave Pro) and flosser (theWaterpik Ultra Professional) for under £200, or both our bargain picks (theOdonta PowerPlusandOperan Cordless Oral Irrigator) for just over £50. And that’s probably what you should do.SustainabilityWhileDyson publishes its own sustainability magazine, there’s as yet nothing about toothbrushes in it. Nor is there any mention on the product page of the Dyson CameraJet’s green credentials.Perhaps this is doing the company a minor disservice, because as well as the RFID tag in the brush heads informing you when they need changing, the company also does more than most in terms of spare parts. Although currently all listed as out of stock, you can buy areplacement battery,dock and reservoir cap, andanti-gravity tank, should any of yours give up on you outside the two-year warranty period. Awhole new refill dock can also be bought.All that’s good, but notably Dyson doesn’t currently offer a recycling programme for its brush heads, as rivals such as Suri and Ordo do.Dyson CameraJet: should I buy it?View image in fullscreen‘It offers a solid clean, and … makes flossing something you can virtually forget about.’Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianDespite its eventful launch, you can’t deny that the Dyson CameraJet is an impressive bit of tech, proving that there’s a surprising amount of room to innovate in the world of toothbrushing. In my weeks of testing, I found that it offers a solid clean, and the fact it makes flossing something you can virtually forget about is a godsend to those of us who often find ourselves skipping that all-important step. While it’s easy to be cynical about the price, it’s doing a lot of clever things, and I would be surprised if we didn’t see a range of imitators launching over the next few years.But clearly, it’s far from perfect, given how easy it is to block the camera, and its substantial travel-unfriendliness.More importantly, considering you can buy our top-rated toothbrush and flosser for a combined £182.10, is paying more than double what you need for some added convenience sensible? Unless your money-to-sense ratio is extremely off-kilter, probably not.View at DysonView at John LewisDyson CameraJet vs …Waterpik Ultra ProfessionalView image in fullscreen£89.99 at Waterpik£82.11 at AmazonYour brush doesn’t need to contain built-in water flossing, with plenty of stand-alone models to choose from. They’re mostly wireless, but if you’ve got the counter space and a bathroom shaver socket, you can’t beat the Waterpik Ultra Professional corded model, my favourite overall from testing.You don’t have to worry about keeping a battery charged, nor are you constantly topping up the water tank because of the built-in 650ml reservoir. On top of that, the nozzle is easier to aim and manoeuvre as it doesn’t have the bulky reservoir built into the handle. The only downside is you can’t easily take it on your travels, where floss or disposable interdental picks will have to sub in.For more, read our guide to thebest water flossersSoocas Neos IIView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£99.99 at Soocas£84.99 at AmazonIf you’re dead set on a two-in-one device but don’t have Dyson money, the Soocas Neos II fits the bill. It also has a built-in water tank, with water-flossing jets fired manually via a small hole in the toothbrush head. It does, however, feel like a jack of all trades and master of none, and I feel you’re better off buying independent devices instead.Lining up the water flosser between teeth is tricky as it doesn’t have tapered tips to direct the jet, nor a camera system like Dyson’s to identify the gaps for you. As a toothbrush, it falls short of the best, in part because the water tank makes the handle bulky. Nonetheless, it does save space overall, and at just under a third of the price of the Dyson CameraJet, it’s worth a look.Laifen Wave ProView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£119.99 at Currys£99.99 at AmazonOur current favourite electric toothbrush is the Laifen Wave Pro. While most brushes make you choose between sonic vibration and physically oscillating heads, the Laifen Wave Pro includes both, with speeds of up to 66,000 vibrations per minute for the former, and a neck that twists left and right up to 60 degrees for the latter.The result is not only an impeccable clean, but something that can truly be customised to your tastes. The accompanying app lets you adjust vibration intensity, oscillation range and speed from scores between 1 and 10, giving you more than 1,000 possible combinations to ensure it’s just right. There’s no water flossing as there is with the Dyson, but for pure brushing, it can’t be beaten – and it’s about a quarter of the price.Suri Pro 2.0View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£105 at Suri£109 at BootsThe need to change the heads on electric toothbrushes makes them environmentally problematic. But Suri has put sustainability at the centre of its design, and while it’s not perfect, it’s one of the strongest options on the market, thanks to its use of plant-based heads (made from cornstarch, with castor oil bristles) that can be sent back to Suri free of charge for recycling.The Suri Pro 2.0 is a big improvement over the original, with less fragile chargers and a pressure sensor built in. It’s not the most powerful brush in town, but if sustainability is your number-one priority, it’s one of the best options (there’s also the cheaperSuri Core 1.0, of course).Read my fullSuri Pro 2.0 reviewFor more:The best electric toothbrushes for every budgetHow to make your toothbrush last longer – and keep it out of landfillSuri Core 1.0 electric toothbrush review: this new budget model is still sustainable – and the one I’d buyExplore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingThe FilterGadgetsBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Night Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head trip | Games | The Guardian
description: You take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbing
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: You take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbing
Content: Unsettling … Night Plane.Photograph: Liquid StaticView image in fullscreenUnsettling … Night Plane.Photograph: Liquid StaticGamesReviewNight Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head tripLiquid Static Studio; PCYou take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbingKeith StuartThu 29 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 07.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was always something creepy about the job-simulator genre. All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop.Now, we have Night Plane, in which you take on the role of a flight attendant on a jumbo jet to hell. It all starts kind of normally. You turn up for the first day of your new job, meet your colleagues, then take your spot at the departure gate, checking in customers and being careful to root out anyone with invalid tickets. Once on the plane, you roll your trolley down the aisle, serving booze and inedible meals, and occasionally dealing with passenger complaints. Then the plane crashes and, frankly, it all goes downhill from there.View image in fullscreenWeird existential horror … Night Plane.Photograph: Liquid StaticAre you dead? Are you in purgatory? And what was that weird creature someone spotted on the wing just before the engines blew up? All you know is, you’re back at the airport, checking in customers again, only this time, some of them are demons disguised as humans and you’re the one who has to sort the people from the people-eaters.Rendered in glitchy low poly visuals, Night Plane is another indie horror game that mimics the technical limits of the original PlayStation era to unsettle the player (see also Crow Country and Fear the Spotlight). The passengers already scare you with their boxy heads and expressionless faces, so when ghostly figures start walking across the aisle and disappearing, you’re already drowning in the uncanny valley. As the game goes on, the dialogue gets weirder, and then just turns into stutters and noises, the lights in the cabin flicker, luggage lockers open and close and rattle, and weird noises follow you. There are elements of the backrooms as well as Japanese onryō movies, as you warp between the plane and the airport, finding yourself trapped in endless passenger lounges and baggage claim areas, being pursued by heaven knows what.It’s all overlaid with a droll sense of humour, so you tend to be laughing to yourself moments before a jump scare jolts you out of your seat. At the outset, New Zealand-based developer Liquid Static Studio cleverly lures you into thinking this is a daft horror spoof, and it kind of is, but its use of nightmarish imagery – from piles of dead rats in the janitor’s room to a recurring image of your burning plane’s wreckage strewn across a remote wilderness – is genuinely disturbing and rife with sick imaginative details.Horror is increasingly the genre through which games dissect and examine themselves and their conventions, and Night Plane is a clever, absorbing example. You can “complete” the game in four or five hours, but subsequent playthroughs will reveal new sub-quests and endings, and priced at less than a tenner, it’s a steal. Even if you never set foot onboard this plane again, it gives you a fascinating budget flight into weird existential horror – and you’ll never take your cabin crew for granted again.Night Plane is available nowExplore more on these topicsGamesPCRetro gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them? | Soccer | The Guardian
description: It makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: It makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma
Content: Dortmund fans were incentivized to keep their phones away for a recent home match against Eintracht.Photograph: Leon Kuegeler/ReutersView image in fullscreenDortmund fans were incentivized to keep their phones away for a recent home match against Eintracht.Photograph: Leon Kuegeler/ReutersSoccerA phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?Leander SchaerlaeckensIt makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemmaThu 29 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTShareBy all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. Dozens of black and yellow flags waved over Europe’s largest standing terrace, a mass of faces fixed on the field beneath them.And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop theBundesligastandings.Yet, apparently, a crisis of a sort has been churning just below the surface of what is, by broad consensus, Europe’s best home support.On Friday, Dortmund hadannounceda kind of bribery scheme. A rewards program is probably a kinder way of putting it. Fans who stayed off their phones during the bout with Eintracht had the chance to win signed jerseys and earn gift cards to the club’s merchandise store. If they activated a so-called “fan mode” on the club’s app – a name so phenomenally passive-aggressive you can only applaud whoever came up with it – the club could count who unlocked their phones the fewest times during the game. For every minute the fans left their phones alone, they got points.Dortmund are not the only German team to pick a fight with phones.Trump’s Fifa peace prize was a sham. A reimagined award can still have meaning | Leander SchaerlaeckensRead moreSecond-division clubs Hertha Berlin and Dynamo Dresden have banned commercial influencer-style videos in their stadiums altogether, fearing for both the integrity of the TV rights they sell and the experience of their fans. Dortmund, likewise, appear motivated by the incursion of influencers, who are siphoning off and monetizing footage of the famous match-day experience and growing into a nuisance for regulars.This problem has also afflicted the tennis majors. The US Open now resemblesan influencer conventionmore than it does a tennis tournament. When the US Tennis Association credentialed more than 100 content creators this year, the influencers grew so disruptive that a match was stopped when a chair umpire had to ask them to turn off a ring light. Wimbledon hasrefusedto credential influencers for just this reason, which doesn’t stop them from getting in with regular tickets or through sponsors.Dortmund’s attempt at shaping fan behavior, however, goes further than warding off the cultural content parasites. Thisplease-stop-holding-up-your-phones-and-just-live-in-the-presentplea raises quasi-existential questions about sport and its consumption.“Over 81,000 people in the stadium, singing, cheering, and holding their breath together: this here and now is irreplaceable,” Dortmund chief executive Carsten Cramersaid. “And that’s exactly what we’re putting front and center together.”“Anyone at a soccer game should experience the moment and the emotions – not just a cell phone screen,” added Marcel de Groot, the chief executive of Vodafone Germany, both a cellphone service provider and a Dortmund sponsor. “Let’s leave our smartphones in our pockets more often at the stadium and instead focus on what’s happening on the field and in the stands.”These were statements delivered with unshakeable confidence in their righteousness, yet there is evidence to suggest this simply isn’t how some fans want to behave at stadiums.Which begs the question: can, and should, professional sports teams get to dictatehowtheir ticket-buying fans experience their games? It’s surely a question that’s crossed the mind of all the musicians who now perform to a sea of cell phones, their flashlights on, obscuring the faces in the crowd. Did their fans buy the right to experience the concert as they please? Or does this objectify the musicians and diminish the performance, somehow?View image in fullscreenThe incentives didn’t keep all Dortmund fans from using their phones at the match.Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPAIt goes back to the question of whether sport is entertainment, and whether its consumers get to sit back and let the proceedings and the attendant stimuli wash over them. Or whether they are something else entirely: active participants in the games they attend. If that is so, then fandom amounts to a parasocial relationship conferring membership to a community with attendant behavioral expectations.What are the responsibilities of the ticketholder? Do teams get to purity-test their supporters? What do fans owe their teams? Is live soccer just content? A day out, not unlike going to the movies or a museum, where nobody expects total focus and for you to cheer on the thing you’re looking at? Is it heresy to even suggest this?The latter tends to be the view, or at least the vibe, in most American sports leagues where fans are often less engaged, told by an announcer and a jumbo screen when and what to clap or stomp or chant. This has always contrasted with the feel of global football, where the folklore is usually organic, sparked and dictated by the fans themselves. It’s why all of those pre-game andhalf-time concertsat the World Cup final rankled, drowning out the thrum of the throaty Argentina fans.It feels both instructive and fitting that this debate broke out at Dortmund. The Bundesliga’s rules on safeguarding fan majority ownership of very nearly every club have preserved the league as a kind of supporters’ paradise, with relatively cheap tickets and policies that put fans first. Dortmund, for their part, have been held up for years as a paradigm for their following – thus attracting the influencers, of course.The latter will be dealt with, it seems. In an age when soccer clubs are essentially production houses who also field company teams, it always seemed inevitable that these interlopers would be expelled from the premises. The fans, however, are not so easily corrected on behavior their teams have deemed undesirable. And they will vote with their credit cards.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.Explore more on these topicsFootballBundesligaEuropean club footballUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: The low-budget Brewers won the World Series – and exposed baseball’s biggest lie | World Series | The Guardian
description: Milwaukee’s first World Series championship is a rebuke to baseball’s owners, whose insistence that small-market teams cannot compete has been laid bare as fiction
Author: Howard Bryant
Headline: Milwaukee’s first World Series championship is a rebuke to baseball’s owners, whose insistence that small-market teams cannot compete has been laid bare as fiction
Content: Cooper Pratt celebrates with the Commissioner’s Trophy after the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 of the World Series to clinch the first championship in club history.Photograph: Elsa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCooper Pratt celebrates with the Commissioner’s Trophy after the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 of the World Series to clinch the first championship in club history.Photograph: Elsa/Getty ImagesWorld SeriesThe low-budget Brewers won the World Series – and exposed baseball’s biggest lieHoward BryantMilwaukee’sfirst World Series championshipis a rebuke to baseball’s oligarch class, whose insistence that small-market teams cannot compete has been laid bare as fictionThu 29 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTShareFor the entirety of the 2026 baseball season, the overlords of the game have stood on the single position thatwhat has now happenedcould not happen, and the result was a year that has been treated like an appetizer for the main course of the offseason: the shutting down of the game until the players, after 40 years of resistance, finally agree to a salary cap. The insistence that the game had been predetermined undermined the Milwaukee Brewers, who spent 149 days this season atop the standings.Milwaukee Brewers close out Tampa Bay Rays to end 57-year wait for first World Series titleRead moreBaseball dismissedMilwaukee’s 22-0 demolition of Seattleon 18 August, the 20-0 waxing of Cincinnati a month later, and the comprehensive dusting of their division – their fourth consecutive National League Central title and fifth in six years – by 14 games. Baseball’s owners, at their persuasive best, would have their paying customers believe that the Brewers’ franchise-record 103 regular-season wins also were an illusion, or worse, the dreaded outlier, even though Milwaukee have won 770 games since 2018, the fourth-most in all of baseball. Even when Milwaukee exhaled andmade the Dodgers look oldin a stirring four-game sweep, ESPN’s Jeff Passan reported the owners’ position remained unchanged.The Brewers to that point had not helped dispel the notion. They had sputtered badly in recent postseasons, giving life to the thought that maybe their summer wins really were empty. Only one thing could ever change that perception: winning in the playoffs.Quick GuideWorld Series 2026ShowScheduleBest-of-seven series. Milwaukee won, 4-1.Fri 23 OctGame 1:Milwaukee 3, Tampa Bay 2Sat 24 OctGame 2:Milwaukee 5, Tampa Bay 4Mon 26 OctGame 3:Milwaukee 10, Tampa Bay 1Tue 27 OctGame 4:Tampa Bay 4, Milwaukee 3 (12 innings)Wed 28 OctGame 5:Milwaukee 4, Tampa Bay 1How to watchIn the US, all World Series games will air on Fox and Fox Deportes, with streaming available through Fox One. In the UK, the series will be carried by TNT Sports. In Australia, fans can watch on ESPN, with streaming available through Disney+ and Kayo Sports.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Surrounded by so many friends that a Wednesday evening at Tropicana Field in St Petersburg felt like a home game – the good folks of Milwaukee and points beyond will remember the date specifically as 28 October 2026 – the Brewers rejected the notion they could not win both because of the economic forces against them and the intangibles champions possess but seemed to go missing from their group when the clocks fall back. They did so by winning the World Series for the first time in their 58-year history, and doing so resoundingly, destroying theTampa Bay Raysin five games.The final score was 4-1, ending a month that will be played and replayed in the minds and DVRs of Milwaukeeans. Few teams have ever been better. Few moments have exposed the hypocrisy of baseball’s oligarchs. Few teams so emphatically demanded so much of themselves.View image in fullscreenCooper Pratt and Brice Turang embrace after Milwaukee defeated Tampa Bay in Game 5 of the World Series on Wednesday night.Photograph: Carmen Mandato/Getty ImagesWhat had been accepted as fact has always been decidedly fiction – but fiction can live as truth until it is exposed, killed once and for all on the ballfield. No matter the argument to concede the season to the inevitability of money and not having it, the truth is the Brewers have been an elite team for the better part of the decade, and the signature joy of thisWorld Seriesrun has been the joyous, ruthless attention this team paid to the task of not merely believing they were championship level, but proving it, to every team that opposed them this season, but more thrillingly, to themselves.double quotation markFew teams have ever been better. Few moments have exposed the hypocrisy of baseball’s oligarchsNothing else mattered but emerging from this month as champions – not the payroll or the labor battles that will almost certainly shut the game down over the coming weeks and quite likely wipe out spring training and at least a portion of the 2027 season and the Brewers’ title defense, or the mystique and riches of the two-time defending champion Dodgers; not the twin histories of having never won the whole thing since that long-ago day near the end of spring training in 1970 when the Seattle Pilots’ equipment truck loaded in Tempe, Arizona, but the team didn’t know where home would be as a court order determined if the truck was headed back to Seattle or to a new home in Milwaukee, or the Dodgers’ long record of torturing Milwaukee baseball. That torture dated back to losses to Brooklyn in 1956, Los Angeles in 1959 before the Braves left town for Atlanta, and to the recent postseason defeats to the Dodgers in 2018, 2020 and 2025, when the Brewers began their second decade in the National League by being as good as the franchise had been since the big American League years of Yount and Cooper, Molitor and Fingers, only to suffer the familiar NL fate of being good, but not good enough to beat the Dodgers when it counted.The Brewers were nowhere men – only the World Series would heal the past wounds that have stayed with them, highlighted bylast year’s humiliating four-game sweepin the NLCS by the Dodgers – and they played with a buoyant and calm desperation, a gorgeous certainty that could not last, but did. The Brewers won the requisite 11 games to claim the trophy and needed only 13 games to do it, but trailed in eight of them. Yet, as an example of their belief, none of their series this postseason was tied after two games. Both Brewers losses in these playoffs were by one run.When they faltered, they did not panic as desperate teams too close to the prize do; they got tougher. Jake Bauers’ soul-snatching at-bats against the Dodgers offered a sign, the youthful charges of Series MVP catcher William Contreras, Jackson Chourio, and the too-young-to-care stardom of Cooper Pratt was another, coming back from down 4-0 against the Dodgers and Rays was still another, and the two-out, eight-run fifth in Game 3 seemed to end the Series – except that it didn’t. Most impressively, responding to losing Game 4 three outs from the title in the bottom of the 12thnot with the doubts that create suspense and pave the way to epic collapse, but by returning the next night unfazed and champagne-ready, demanding they be taken not as a cute story but a hard-edged team ready, at long last, for its close-up.View image in fullscreenTrevor Megill, Christian Yelich and Abner Uribe embrace after Wednesday night’s final out at Tropicana Field.Photograph: Elsa/Getty ImagesNeither the doomsday rhetoric of an unnecessary work stoppage or the fearsome reputation of the former champions, nor the feisty underdog spirit of an admirable Tampa Bay could block the sunlight, too long in arriving, of this Brewers team. They played pure, determined baseball and responded to the insult – and it is an insult – that the decimal points on the balance sheet meant more than winning 103 games and 90-plus so many times before that, meant that once it was time to deal the cards they couldn’t win. The Brewers won 114 games in 2026, finished the regular season 15-3, and then went 11-2 in the playoffs for a grand total of 26-5 since 7 September.Baseball’s finances need addressing, but they don’t require shuttering the place. Even with the game the owners are playing in their quest to increase franchise values, their words speak an untruth – Brewers owner Mark Attanasio purchased the team from Bud Selig in 2005 for $223m and the team that supposedly cannot win (but did) has avaluation by Forbes at $1.9bn. The game that matters, however, is the one on the field, the one that belongs to the players, and this October, there was absolutely nobody better.Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America.He also writes on SubstackExplore more on these topicsWorld SeriesMilwaukee BrewersTampa Bay RaysLos Angeles DodgersBaseballUS sportsMLBcommentShareReuse this content

title: Could Abdul El-Sayed’s plan for AI companies stave off catastrophe? | Jerel Ezell | The Guardian
description: The Michigan Senate candidate is calling for public ownership and other reforms, offering a potential antidote to ideological gridlock
Author: Jerel Ezell
Headline: The Michigan Senate candidate is calling for public ownership and other reforms, offering a potential antidote to ideological gridlock
Content: ‘As we approach the midterms, feverish debates are now erupting over how – or even whether – AI’s soaring risks can now be tempered via federal policy.’Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘As we approach the midterms, feverish debates are now erupting over how – or even whether – AI’s soaring risks can now be tempered via federal policy.’Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Could Abdul El-Sayed’s plan for AI companies stave off catastrophe?Jerel EzellThe Michigan Senate candidate is calling for public ownership and other reforms, offering a potential antidote to ideological gridlockThu 29 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.17 EDTShareTheMichigansenatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, occupies a strange but increasingly common place in modern American politics. He’s praised by progressives, begrudgingly tolerated by moderate Democrats and largely demonized by Republicans.He’s also uniquely positioned to forge an all-too-elusive thread of political kinship between these perpetually-at-odds groups with his bold but contentious plan for reining in AI, calledAI Under Democracy.And it couldn’t come at a better time.According to a pollconducted this summer by NBC News, 70% of Americans said that they were more worried than excited about AI, a shocking reversal from just a couple of years ago.Another poll from Quinnipiacseveral weeks ago found that 73% of Americans are concerned about AI posing a threat to human existence.AI Under Democracy was revealed several weeks before the Michigan Democratic primary. At the time, El-Sayed was still a relative underdog, a physician with threadbare political credentials and views that – it seemed – were woefully misaligned with the moderate, blue-collar sensibilities of Michiganders.Will it be AI or the climate crisis that ends humanity? We can make it neither | Adam McKay and Philip EubanksRead moreWhen it comes to his AI plan, and a companion proposal calledAI Under Controlthat he released this month, that may no longer be the case. In fact, it could be a potential antidote to our ideological gridlock over the promise and peril of AI.Back in 2023, I wasinvited to be a gueston Abdul El-Sayed’s podcast, America Dissected. Both Michigan natives with backgrounds in public health, El-Sayed and I commiserated over global leaders’ glaring lack of relatability and, by extension, the grating way they dismiss – and often increase –the struggles of everyday people. It all seems quite prescient now.Barack Obama recentlyurged Democrats to rally around AI regulationin the midterms, but El-Sayed and many progressive Democrats have already been leading the charge.El-Sayed’s AI ethos is deeply shaped by his history as a healthcare provider – not as a politician. His maxim for AI development is “first, do no harm,” a transposition of the Hippocratic oath into this new wild west of technology, as AI companies face pressure to balance profit against the public interest.To this end, El-Sayed’s proposal calls for corporate divestiture from AI’s largest companies, recognizing that legacy companies such as Google, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon simply have too much controlling interest in frontier AI ventures like OpenAI and Anthropic, creating untenable friction between their revenue-generation prerogatives and our public safety.For example, Microsoft has an estimated27%stakein OpenAI, and Google owns14% of Anthropic, giving each a sizable say in how the companies operate. Under El-Sayed’s proposal, the tech giants would have to divest or abandon those investments within a defined transitional period.The plan also calls for theregulation of datacenters: slowing the volume of developments, facilitating local job creation, freezing residential utility costs, and addressing thepublic health and quality of life issuesthat datacenters produce in terms of noise and pollution. He has been especially vocal about the colossalOpenAI-Oracle datacenterbeing erected just outside Ann Arbor, Michigan, where he attended the University of Michigan.Today, there’s a groundswell of resistance towards datacenters.An August pollfound that only one in nine Americans would support the construction of a datacenter in their local community. El-Sayed’s plan dovetails with the public’s clear and growing opposition: keep AI’s footprint and its environmental and socioeconomic consequences – those known and as yet unknown – contained.double quotation markWhile both Democrats and Republicans may come to support heavier regulation and moratoriums on AI, public control may be an entirely different can of wormsFar and away the most controversial – but essential – part of El-Sayed’s plan to thwart an AI-fueled catastrophe is his call for 50% + one of board seats (a simple majority) at influential AI companies to be publicly appointed or democratically elected. This would in theory foster transparency around AI companies’ plans and give Americans the power to veto decisions – on matters like datacenter development and biological weapons manufacturing – that could undermine the public interest.While both Democrats and Republicans may come to support heavier regulation and moratoriums on AI, public control may be an entirely different can of worms. For many, the idea of transferring ownership of a private enterprise to a public trust smacks of socialism. And this narrative certainly feeds into the common Republican critique of El-Sayed, as well as his Republican challenger Mike Rogers’ even more aggressive attempt totar him as a feckless communist.However, communities across the US have long embraced public ownership of essential resources such as water, natural gas and electricity. And according to a June report,roughly 69% of American adultssupport AI companies transferring 50% of their stock to public sovereign wealth fund, a pot of money used to support public interests.This is a paradigm which Bernie Sanders, El-Sayed’s most prominent booster on Capitol Hill,has legislatively proposed. There’s a good chance that Americans will continue warming up to this idea.It’s not a coincidence that, as we approach the midterms, feverish debates are now erupting over how – or even whether – AI’s soaring risks can now be tempered via federal policy.The Guardian view on AI safety: the push for global regulation must advance | EditorialRead moreNaturally, in the US, people are looking to their political leaders for answers – even though a whopping78% of Americans disapproveof how congressional members are handling their job and Donald Trump’sapproval ratings areunderwater.Many of these politicians seemunawareof or ambivalent about the state of AI and its mushrooming perils. That’s where younger, tech-savvy candidates like El-Sayed – who has called for a pause on AI’s most potent releases, a ban on artificial superintelligence, and an AI kill switch – shine and can provide leadership and restraint as we confront a future where AI is ubiquitous.Exhibit A of the opposite: Trump and other administration officials who have been aggressively pooh-poohing demands to slow AI’s rapid ascension, saying the uproar isa “hoax”while continuing to insist on the US’s AI dominanceat essentially any cost.To be sure, some – including leaders in the White House and Silicon Valley investors beholden to the sunk cost principle – will remain bullish on AI.But calls for regulation fromeveryday people on both sides of the aisleshould be the ultimate shot across the bow. And AI’s top plutocrats, such as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, rallying around the idea of “pacing the frontier” are a big, red flag being waved right in society’s face.All this can be addressed through a deliberate, balanced public ownership policy.Jerel Ezell is executive director of the Center for AI and Everybody and an assistant professor at the University of ChicagoExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionUS midterm elections 2026MichigancommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s easy to see through Trump’s Ukraine ploy | Kenneth Roth | The Guardian
description: In advance of the midterms, Trump is blaming Kyiv for high gas prices while making clear moves to support Russia
Author: Kenneth Roth
Headline: In advance of the midterms, Trump is blaming Kyiv for high gas prices while making clear moves to support Russia
Content: ‘The naive American president, with his inattention to detail, craving for flattery, and disturbing admiration for autocrats, was easily won over.’Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The naive American president, with his inattention to detail, craving for flattery, and disturbing admiration for autocrats, was easily won over.’Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersOpinionUS foreign policyIt’s easy to see through Trump’s Ukraine ployKenneth RothIn advance of the midterms, Trump is blaming Kyiv for high gas prices while making clear moves to support RussiaThu 29 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.47 EDTShareAs the US midterms approach,Donald Trumpis abandoning Ukraine’s democracy in a desperate effort to deny responsibility for worsening inflation. Yet this past weekend’s dramatic elections in Brazil and Serbia show that voters can see through such subterfuge.There is nothing like a political party’scorruptindifferenceto the plight of ordinary people to galvanize voter turnout. If US voters follow in the footsteps of their Brazilian and Serbian counterparts, a Democraticlandslideis likely.If that happens, Democrats in Congress must act quickly to rein in Trump before he does more damage to the US’s economy and global stature.Any objective observer would see that Trump’s war of choice against Iran has inflated energy prices, because Iran predictably responded by restricting shipments in the strait of Hormuz, through which much of the Middle East’s oil and gas flows. But Trump, never one to admit error, needed a scapegoat. EnterVolodymyr Zelenskyy.While holding off Russian troops on the frontlines in the Donbas region of eastern Ukraine, Zelenskyy’s forces have been damaging the Russian economy byattackingits oil refineries. That has finally brought the war home to ordinary Russians in the form oflong linesat gasoline stations. It has also disrupted oil production, puttingpressureon a major source of revenue for Putin to fund his invasion.The Trump-Putin love story’s next chapter: selling out Ukraine | Sidney BlumenthalRead moreTrump is trying to blame the inflationary surge in US gasoline and diesel prices on these attacks, even though their effect on the global market issmallcompared with the diminished flow through the strait of Hormuz.Meanwhile, with Russia making onlylimitedprogress in eastern Ukraine despite losing hundreds of thousands of troops, Putin has taken, as is his wont, to attacking Ukrainian civilians. He has bombed theircitiesand attacked theirenergy infrastructureto deprive them of heat for their homes this coming winter.He seems to hope that a freezing populace will pressure Zelensky to capitulate. Yet many Ukrainians remaindeterminedto defend their country’s democracy from Putin’s dictatorship.So Putin hasturnedto his ace-in-the-hole, Trump. The naive American president, with his inattention to detail, craving for flattery, and disturbing admiration for autocrats, was easily won over.Trump has now openly sided with Russia. He has authorized thepurchaseof diesel fuel from Russia, financing Putin’s attacks on Ukrainian cities. The gesture will not noticeably reduce market prices before the midterms, but it allows Trump to make a nod of acknowledgment toward the affordability crisis that he normallyderides.He haswaivednew sanctions on Russia which had just been adopted by overwhelming congressional majorities in the name of the late senator Lindsey Graham, a purported friend of Trump whose devotion to Ukraine’s democracy Trump now betrays.The Trump administrationsuspendeddelivery of defensive missiles to Ukraine and early-warningintelligenceof Russian attacks just as Putin was intensifying his bombing of Ukrainian cities, leaving civilian residents to their fate.And itreportedly greenlitadecisionby Trump’s buddy Elon Musk toslowStarshield, the version of theStarlinksatellite internet service that Ukraine’s military depends on for its drones to defend the frontline against a vastly larger Russian military.Finally, Trump called for an “energy ceasefire”, by which he effectivelymeantonly anendto Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries (Ukraine has only one badly damaged refinery), not an end of Putin’s efforts to force Ukrainians to freeze this winter. Ukraine is attacking what are arguably legitimate military targets. Putin is committingwar crimes. Yet Trump condemned only Ukraine’s attacks, not Russia’s.The Ukrainian government would havewelcomeda real energy ceasefire but rejected this selective one.Trump claims his embrace of Putin is an effort tobuild a relationshipwith him so he will negotiate peace. But offering him enormous benefits in return fornothingwon’t force him to the bargaining table. The former German chancellor Angela Merkel believed that tying Russia to Europe economically wouldpreserve peacewith Russia. Instead, Putin acquired the means to invade Ukraine.Trump’s amateur diplomats – Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – are hardly primed to do better. Witkoff embarrassingly dubbed Putin a “humanitarian” for releasing one elderly American held in prison on concocted charges while Putin kept up the indiscriminate attacks on Ukrainian cities.The envoys still seem to think that Putinaspiresfor only a chunk of Ukrainian territory rather than the destruction of Ukraine’s democracy.Donald Trump has sold out Ukraine. He makes appeaser Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle | Simon TisdallRead moreTrump hopes his blame-Ukraine campaign will prevent a Republican midterm debacle. It should only reinforce voter sentiment that Trump is indifferent to their plight, that he would rather deploy smoke and mirrors than alter his corrupt, self-serving reign.Will a Democratic midterm victory make a difference? The American presidency largely runs foreign policy, with little input from Congress. However, there are some things that the Democrats might do if they take the reins in January.I would begin with sanctions on Russia. The latest round of sanctions won overwhelming bipartisan support, yet the legislation contained the traditional national-interest waiver that Trumpinvokedto ignore them.The Democrats should re-enact the legislation without the waiver. They might even name the bill again after Graham. Outrage against Trump’s betrayal of Ukraine iswidespreadamong congressional members of both parties in Washington. If the legislation can secure a veto-proof two-thirds majority, Trump would be stuck with it.That might also break his aura of being beyond restraint. A successful rectification of US policy toward Ukraine might be followed by bills that limit Trump’s tariff authority or curtail the funds he needs to keep fighting Iran – as he isconsideringdoingafter the midterms.There is nothing normal about the current Republican Congress’s abdication of its foreign policy role to Trump’s self-promoting priorities. Ukraine is on the frontline of the global defense of democracy. The American people see that. So does Congress. Trump may be oblivious, but under Democratic leadership, Congress should take matters into its own hands.Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author ofRighting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive GovernmentsExplore more on these topicsUS foreign policyOpinionUkraineUS midterm elections 2026Donald TrumpRussiaVladimir PutinEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s plea – ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’ – deserves to backfire | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: With his poll numbers tanking and his behavior getting odder, the remark seems more appealing to himself than to voters
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: With his poll numbers tanking and his behavior getting odder, the remark seems more appealing to himself than to voters
Content: ‘“Pretend I’m on the ballot” has become a regular rallying cry as Trump tries to fend off a Democratic “blue wave” in Congress.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘“Pretend I’m on the ballot” has become a regular rallying cry as Trump tries to fend off a Democratic “blue wave” in Congress.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Trump’s plea – ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’ – deserves to backfireMargaret SullivanWith his poll numbers tanking and his behavior getting odder, the remark seems more appealing to himself than to votersThu 29 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTShareAs he criss-crosses the nation, stumping for Republican candidates,Donald Trumpkeeps asking voters to use their imaginations.“In this election, I’m asking you to pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just pretend,” heurgedat a Kansas rally as he campaigned for the incumbent senator Roger Marshall and gubernatorial challenger Ty Masterson last month.“Pretend I’m on the ballot” has become a regular rallying cry as Trump tries to fend off a Democratic “blue wave” in Congress.But will it work? That seems increasingly unlikely.Given his own lack of popularity and weird behavior, it’s an egotistical notion – more appealing to himself than to voters.After all, his approval ratings are in the basement. Gas pricesare higher, on average, than at any time during the Biden years. People feel like they need to float a loan before heading to the supermarket.Donald Trump has been a disaster for rural America | Steven GreenhouseRead moreIn that Kansas rally, he referred to the opposition as “Dumocrats”, which is typical of the level of presidential discourse to which the nation has become accustomed.In his rallies, he appears “increasingly detached from reality”, as one campaignanalysisin the Independent put it, as he “vacillates between topics to the point where his remarks border on the nonsensical and he ends every appearance by awkwardly dancing to the Village People’s well-known gay anthem YMCA”.Stranger still, as the Guardian’s Adam Gabbattreportedrecently, Trumphas been offering “unsolicited and increasingly unhinged assessments of men’s bodies” over the past few weeks.“I examined his ass,” the president said in Kentucky, speaking about Republican senator Jon Husted. “And then I looked at his shoulders … I looked at his jawline … I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I’m still recovering.”Trump has also been – to put it mildly – stretching the truth on the campaign trail, sometimes merely misleading in his remarks, sometimes straight-up lying.For example, he promised a North Carolina rally that gas and oil prices would tumble soon and he claimed: “I had it down to the lowest level in years,” apparently speaking about the price of filling up a gas tank at the pump. APolitiFact examinationdisputed this, noting that when Trump took office at the beginning of last year, the average gas price was $3.23 a gallon, but by late September of this year, it was $4.61.But it’s not just what he says at rallies that may backfire on the candidates he hopes to help.Much of what’s happened in Trump’s second term is working against Republican candidates. That includes the widespread self-dealing that, as the historian Garrett Graffwroterecently, “is so endemic and so obvious that it has broken through to voters”.It’s also his misguided war, his rants on social media, his disparagement of longtime allies, including Canada. It’s also his obvious plan to declare the election rigged should it not go his way.If Democrats win big, will they learn the right lessons from their victory? | Jan-Werner MuellerRead more“Even Maga die-hards and GOP allies in Congress have grown weary of his erratic behavior,” as the Wall Street Journal’s Jason Rileynoted.And Democrats, including Barack Obama, are only too happy to campaign by associating Republican candidates with Trump.These midterm elections, Obama told a crowd in Ohio, “is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration. It’s the circuit breaker in the system.”That blast of sanity and good sense seems far more likely to resonate with potential voters than Trump’s unhinged rants and dangerous threats.Pretend he’s on the ballot?Maybe that’s effective with Trump’s remaining cult-like base. And maybe itwillbring some of those loyalists out to vote next week if they had been thinking of sitting out this election.But more likely, the imagined association with Trump will serve to remind most voters that Trump’s malfeasance must be rebuked and rejected. Certainly not encouraged.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionDonald TrumpUS politicsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: How Hobart, Sydney and Melbourne are reckoning with statues of colonial-era white men in an age of truth-telling | Paul Daley | The Guardian
description: These misty-eyed monuments often paper over atrocities against Indigenous peoples – something that is finally being officially recognised
Author: Paul Daley
Headline: These misty-eyed monuments often paper over atrocities against Indigenous peoples – something that is finally being officially recognised
Content: In 2022, Hobart city council voted to remove a statue of William Crowther, a surgeon who traded in Indigenous people’s body parts, but the statue was cut down at the ankles by a vandal before it could be officially taken down.Photograph: Ethan James/AAPView image in fullscreenIn 2022, Hobart city council voted to remove a statue of William Crowther, a surgeon who traded in Indigenous people’s body parts, but the statue was cut down at the ankles by a vandal before it could be officially taken down.Photograph: Ethan James/AAPOpinionIndigenous AustraliansHow Hobart, Sydney and Melbourne are reckoning with statues of colonial-era white men in an age of truth-tellingPaul DaleyThese misty-eyed monuments often paper over atrocities against Indigenous peoples – something that is finally being officially recognisedGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastThu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 19.25 EDTShareThis is the tale of three cities and the same number of statues, two of them colonial era and one from early this century.All were erected to celebrate the experiences of prominent white men who lived in colonial Australian times and who respectively treated the Indigenous people of their realms barbarously, murderously and contemptuously.I’m talking about: the 1889 Hobart statue of former Tasmanian premier and thief/trader in Indigenous body partsWilliam Crowther;the 2013 Sydney statue of the fifth governor of New South Wales,Lachlan Macquarie, a massacre commander who used “terror’’ tactics against Aboriginal people; and the statue dedicated in Melbourne in 1865 to the ill-fated explorersBurke and Willsand their expedition, who First Nations people might have been able to save had the explorers more readily accepted help instead of shooting at them.Political hate speech can have real-world fallout. After the alleged attack on Helen Haines, our leaders must act | Paul DaleyRead moreThe cities that respectively stage each of these problematic statues have responded with varying alacrity to the ethical, white-washing and historical dilemmas each has posed to modern Australia (there are many others besides that need dealing with).In 2022 Hobart city councilvoted to removethe statue of Crowther, a surgeon who stole the skull of the deceased Tasmanian Aboriginal man William Lanne in pursuit of the racially charged Darwinian pseudoscience ofphrenology.Across Australia, countless heads of Indigenous people – and other body parts – were stolen to meet the market of (mostly British) adherents of this voodoo pursuit, which adhered to the fallacious view that head shape determined human temperament and intelligence and different races’ rung on the ladder of civilisation.View image in fullscreenThe new project at the former site of the statue of William Crowther in Hobart. An inscription nearby reads: ‘Monuments perish, but deeds – good or bad – never die.’Photograph: Ethan James/AAPCrowther was among them. Not surprisingly, his bronze statue in Franklin Square was frequently vandalised (red paint was a favourite), most notably in 2024 when it wascut down at the anklesand its plinth spray painted with the words WHAT GOES AROUND. Crowther was toppled just hours before the Tasmanian civil and administrative tribunal upheld the council’s decision to remove him.While not condoning vandalism,Hobart– in the most progressive approach so far taken in Australia to the challenges posed by colonial statues – saw this as an opportunity for reformist truth-telling. And so, on Tuesday, a new memorial (based around that vacant plinth) was dedicated to a far broader take on vexed, bloody Tasmanian history than Crowther’s likeness could ever afford.It incorporates a native garden and a circle of bronze inscribed with words from three commissioned writers. The bronze-inscribed sentiments include “monuments perish, but deeds – good or bad – never die”.Indeed. It’s hard to argue against that.One of the writers, Nunami Sculthorpe-Green, of Tasmanian Aboriginal and Warlpiri heritage, said: “It was important to me to re-centre the life of William Lanne in this story. After decades of calling for change, the Aboriginal community can now see our experience and humanity reflected in this space.’’AsI’ve writtennumerous times previously, colonial – and evidently some 21st century – statues are rarely accurate embodiments of history. Indeed, unless they aim to tell historical truths, they are little more than propaganda portals – misty-eyed memorials to bad men that paper over their known deficiencies and, in the case of too many, their atrocities.Which brings us to the statue of Macquarie that stands on the edge of Sydney’s Hyde Park and which in my view – and that of many others – should never have been dedicated to him in 2013, given all that was known about his violent conduct against the colony’s Indigenous people.View image in fullscreenPolice surround a statue of Governor Lachlan Macquarie during an Invasion Day rally in 2026.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianAbsurdly, when the statue was unveiled by various dignitaries who lauded the murderous Macquarie as, among other things, a “hero’’, it also came with an inscription that he was a “perfect gentleman’’.This is wholly inconsistent with his infamous orders to his redcoat soldiers in 1816 ahead of his Appin massacre: “On any occasion of seeing or falling in with the Natives, either in Bodies or Singly, they are to be called upon, by your friendly Native Guides, to surrender themselves to you as Prisoners of War. If they refuse to do so, make the least show of resistance, or attempt to run away from you, you will fire upon and compel them to surrender, breaking and destroying the Spears, Clubs and Waddies of all those you take Prisoners.“Such natives as happen to be killed on such occasions, if grown up men, are to be hanged up on Trees in Conspicuous Situations, to Strike the Survivors with the greater terror.”Australian town defends its ‘long-valued and admired’ statue of an enslaved African American childRead moreIn 2017, amid numerous complaints to Sydney city council, the Macquarie statue was referred for considerationby an advisory panel. Then in 2023 the council supported a motion by Yvonne Weldon (the council’s first Indigenous member in its 180 years), committing to truth-telling in the public domain by incorporating First Nations perspectives on plaques associated with statues of colonial figures.Perhaps Hobart’s progressive action regarding the Crowther statue will give Sydney the impetus – or courage – to finally reckon with its big historically in-your-face Macquarie mistake.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailMeanwhile one activist, Stephen Langford, has maderepeated court appearancesin Sydney after literally adhering to this white elephant of a statue printed copies of Macquarie’s orders to his troops before the Appin massacre.When we met at the statue recently, he said: “I haven’t paid the fines and I intend to keep doing this until something regarding this statue changes.’’The call for change brings us to Victoria and the Burke and Wills statue – the state’s oldest colonial monument. Despite conservative reservations about moving – or “meddling’’ with in any way – such monuments, Burke and Wills have been moved five times, most recently in 2017. It has been in storage ever since.Burke and Wills and theirill-fated – or hapless – 1860 expeditionto traverse the continent by foot – 3,250km from Melbourne to the Gulf of Carpentaria and almost back again – was a foundation myth to Victoria on par with what that other great and hopeless tragedy, Gallipoli, became to the fledgling Australian nation.View image in fullscreenThe Burke and Wills monument in Melbourne when it was still being displayed publicly.Photograph: City of Melbourne Art and Heritage CollectionHow we love a (white) heroically tragic failure.
