I’ve never quite understood why.Anyway, despite the statue’s many moves, it has never reflected the significant parallel Indigenous story of the expedition. Despite setting out with at least 24 camels and several horses, six tons of firewood (wasn’t it everywhere in the bush?), 57 buckets, many skeins of green gossamer for veils, 50 gallons of rum (supposedly for the camels), a cedar-topped oak table and chairs, a piano and a Chinese gong, Burke apparently shunned offers of help from numerous First Nations peoples (a constant occurrence in white continental exploration).The sole survivor, John King, was saved by South Australia’s Yandruwandha people, a critical – if overlooked – part of the expedition narrative that will now be told when the statue is repositioned and unveiled for a sixth time inMelbournenext year.According toMelbourne city council: “The city hasn’t just changed physically. Our understanding of the expedition has changed too. The monument’s return to the public eye is a chance to share a broader story, with new signage recognising the critical role of the Yandruwandha people and their support for the expedition’s sole survivor, John King.’’It’s tempting to say “about time’’. But credit must be paid where it’s due when it comes to colonial statues and truth-telling. Hobart and Melbourne city councils deserve applause given all the controversy, the heat and the light that comes with merely suggesting any change to these monuments.Meanwhile, in the words of one of my old editors, Sydney really should “get an effing wriggle-on’’ and deal with that Macquarie statue.Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsIndigenous AustraliansOpinionStatuesHobartMelbourneSydneycommentShareReuse this content

title: My phone thinks my boyfriend is my ‘best friend’. It’s not alone | Patrick Lenton | The Guardian
description: Being in a same-sex relationship can make you weirdly invisible. Queer identity shouldn’t be treated as abnormal
Author: Patrick Lenton
Headline: Being in a same-sex relationship can make you weirdly invisible. Queer identity shouldn’t be treated as abnormal
Content: ‘It seems as though we have a Goldilocks problem with queer relationship visibility: there’s too much visibility or there’s not enough.’Photograph: Vanessa Nunes/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It seems as though we have a Goldilocks problem with queer relationship visibility: there’s too much visibility or there’s not enough.’Photograph: Vanessa Nunes/AlamyOpinionLGBTQ+ rightsMy phone thinks my boyfriend is my ‘best friend’. It’s not alonePatrick LentonBeing in a same-sex relationship can make you weirdly invisible. Queer identity shouldn’t be treated as abnormalThu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 20.15 EDTShareMy boyfriend and I invented a game on our recent trip toItaly. We called it “invisible gays”, which might have been an attempt at some kind of word play around “gays” and “gaze” – but I was on holiday and feeling lazy, so I didn’t push it.The game began when one night he took me out to a little trattoria to celebrate my birthday. It was a warm night, and fairy lights were entangled in the fragrant blooming flowers over our heads, and we drank good wine and ate bowls of perfect pasta, and there was candlelight, and it was so romantic I wouldn’t have blinked if two dogs had started smooching over a strand of spaghetti. Che bello!We were one of four tables, all couples of various ages looking at each other with disgusting wet amorous eyes. During the evening a man selling roses approached the other tables. One young guy even bought one, presenting the blossom with a flourish to his girlfriend, earning applause from other patrons and a round of toothy photos. Caught up in the moment, my partner pulled out his wallet to buy a rose for me too, despite my wildly insincere protestations – but the rose man didn’t even clock us as a couple and wandered off into the night.Puppy love: why asking my boyfriend to coparent Basil the greyhound was the most important proposal of all | Patrick LentonRead moreI briefly wondered if it was because my outfit wasn’t chic enough for Rome. Then I realised we were the only couple who weren’t the societal default setting of a man and a woman, having instead made the dire mistake of being two beautiful men dining together. I wonder if he thought we were some kind of complicated interracial brothers?This continued all around Italy, with more than seven episodes of being passed over at romantic tourist traps marked on our scorecard. When I organised a fancy dinner for my boyfriend’s birthday weeks later, one of the servers said I was a “good friend” for doing so.I’m used to the way that being in a same-sex couple can make you hyper visible or put a homophobic spotlight on you, so that it feels like every time you kiss in public it’s like Frodo putting on the One Ring, drawing the attention of the Dark Lord and his screeching Nazgûl. I’m used to muttered comments from people you walk by on the streets when you’re holding hands, or of making out with a tall guy outside a bar after our first date only for a car full of men to stop and yell slurs at us. I’m used to holding the hand of a boyfriend as we were chased down the backstreets of Newtown late at night by three silent men.I’ve also dated enough women to know that there’s a contrast – no woman I’ve ever dated has flinched away from a kiss on the cheek and whispered: “Maybe not in public.” I’ve had men I’ve dated comment on how “openly affectionate” I am, because I haven’t had to learn to self-censor my public love languages. Women I date usually just comment on how clean my legs are and how many Gilmore Girls references I make.Obviously being hyper visible and therefore at risk of overt and violent homophobia is worse than not being able to buy an overpriced street flower. Over the past year in Australia,hate crimes against gay and bisexual menhave been making headlines. As someone who has suffered a hate crime or two, I can confirm that dealing with this should be the authorities’ priority instead of cracking down on the rose men of Rome.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Patrick LentonBut with the 10-year anniversary of the marriage equality win coming up next year, it’s worth looking at all the ways being in a same-sex relationship can still make you weirdly invisible. It’s another argument for why Mardi Gras, pride flags andIdahobit daysin schools are still so necessary – because, when love between queer people goes unseen, it makes it seem as though it isn’t “normal”. And when queer identity is treated as abnormal, it fertilises the ground necessary to justify violence against queer people.We all know the little “collections” of photos and videos our smartphones occasionally create. This can be anything from “Your trip in Italy 2026” to “Furry pals throughout the years”. It’s been a source of constant amusement to me that it sorts all the photos of my boyfriend and me into a collection called “best friends”. These are photos of two men kissing and, without oversharing, sometimes photos of two men doing things even more intimate than kissing (kayaking).It shows you that homosexual invisibility is so hardwired into aspects of society that a phone short-circuits and decides that two men in love are just good bros. I’ve never had any of the women I’ve dated put into a folder called “best friends”. In fact, none of the women who are my actual best friends have made it into those folders either. My dog does get filed there, which, when its alongside my boyfriend, feels a little like one of those slippery slope arguments made by the Australian Christian Lobby during the plebiscite.It seems as though we have a Goldilocks problem with queer relationship visibility: there’s too much visibility or there’s not enough. Make up your mind!Not only do I simply want to express my love for my boyfriend publicly and without risk of violence, and for it to be recognised for what it is; I also don’t want my sexuality to be the only thing that people notice me for. I want to be noticed for my abnormally good looks and sex appeal.Patrick Lenton is a writer. His latest novel isIn Spite of YouExplore more on these topicsLGBTQ+ rightsOpinionRelationshipsItaly holidaysItalyMarriage equalitycommentShareReuse this content

title: Is this play-safe budget a sign that the prime minister is planning an early election? | Larry Elliott | The Guardian
description: There’s no real strategy behind this hotchpotch of measures. Andy Burnham may be parking the big decisions until he has a true mandate, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Author: Larry Elliott
Headline: There’s no real strategy behind this hotchpotch of measures. Andy Burnham may be parking the big decisions until he has a true mandate, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Content: John Healey and Andy Burnham visit the Abbey community centre in Westminster following the budget announcement on Wednesday.Photograph: Richard Pohle/ReutersView image in fullscreenJohn Healey and Andy Burnham visit the Abbey community centre in Westminster following the budget announcement on Wednesday.Photograph: Richard Pohle/ReutersOpinionBudget 2026Is this play-safe budget a sign that the prime minister is planning an early election?Larry ElliottThere’s no real strategy behind this hotchpotch of measures. Andy Burnham may be parking the big decisions until he has a true mandateThu 29 Oct 2026 08.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTShareGreat hopes were invested in Andy Burnham when he became prime minister in July. Hewent bigon the failings of 40 years of neoliberalism, emphasised the need for Britain to start making things again and promisedgrowth in every postcode.Back in the summer, John Healey’s first budget was seen as an opportunity to start delivering on these ambitions, but it has been clear for some time that it wouldn’t do so. The road to the New Jerusalem – judging by the chancellor’s “breathing space” package – will be a slow and arduous one. Healey has taken what he inherited from Rachel Reeves and performed some minor tweaks. Not so much a revolution as continuity Keir Starmer.As has been the hallmark of Burnham’s first 100 days in Downing Street, there was plenty of activity in the budget but the slew of measures – almost 100 in all – was a hotchpotch and had no real semblance of a strategy being fleshed out. Not many budgets linger long in the memory and it is unlikely that Healey’s will break with this tradition.In essence, it has bought Healey and Burnham some time. For the moment they can argue that the budget was just part one of a three-stage process, to be followed by the government’s 10-year-plan and next year’s spending review. They need to use that time wisely or the glitzy PR will cease to impress.There are, of course, reasons why the chancellor played it safe. Energy prices have rocketed since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February. Theconsequent higher inflationhas resulted in higher interest rates for mortgages, business loans and government borrowing.Optimism about an early resolution to the war is fast fading. Indeed, the prospect of anintensification of the conflictafter next week’s US midterm elections has led to a fresh surge in the cost of crude oil and gas in the past couple of weeks. The modest help provided in the budget to reduce energy bills will be dwarfed by the expected price increases in January. A tough winter lies ahead.As the dust settles, a number of conclusions can be drawn. One is that Britain remains – as Burnhamonce put it– in hock to the bond markets. Healey may well have wanted to come up with a more generous energy support package, but was constrained by the fear that the financial markets would cut up rough. Ever since Liz Truss’s mini budget in 2022, governments have lived in fear of another sell off in government bonds. Healey is like a contestant in Strictly Come Dancing – he knows that the markets always have the casting vote.To be fair to the chancellor, he borrowed £20bn more to invest ininfrastructure spending, using the flexibility in meeting the government’s rules for the public finances provided by Reeves. That was welcome and – at first glance – didn’t appear to unsettle the markets.Whether Healey’s array of minor fixes to help with cost of living pressures is enough to keep voters sweet is another matter. The economy has so far showed impressive resilience in the face of the energy shock caused by events in the Middle East, but that strength has been concentrated in the financial and business sectors of the economy, with growth in artificial intelligence particularly striking. Consumer-facing sectors – such as hospitality and housing – have been much weaker, with the mostrecent reporton consumer confidence showing the sharpest monthly fall since the Brexit referendum in 2016.That’s hardly surprising given the fact that taxes as a share of national income are on course next year to be at their highest ever level, and that spending power is being eroded by rising fuel and energy costs. In itslatest reporton the economy, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimates that living standards will fall next year and by 2030-31 will be only 2% higher than they were before the Covid pandemic. A lost decade in other words.It is against this unpropitious backdrop that many pundits – particularly in the City – have seen the lack of meat in the budget not as an indication that the government is dithering, but as a sign that Burnham is preparing the groundfor an early general election. On this reading, all the big decisions – on social care, relations with the EU, and defence – have been parked until the prime minister has his own mandate.The case for holding a snap poll is not just that voters seem to have taken to Burnham, although he is certainly enjoying a honeymoon period. It is also that Labour is currently benefiting from the lack of a single challenger on the right as the Conservatives and Reform slug it out, and from the problems facing both the Greens and the Liberal Democrats on the left. The polls show Labourin the lead.Even so, an early election would be a colossal risk for a party with a commanding majority and two and a half years of the current parliament still to run. The OBR thinks the economy will grow more slowly in 2027 than in 2026, while living standards will actually fall before picking up in 2028 as the energy shock abates. Next week’s anticipated rise in interest rates from the Bank of England may not be the last. The prime minister is arguably at the peak of his popularity.Burnham has repeatedly said that he has no plans to go to the country early, which if true will be a relief to the many Labour MPs who would almost certainly lose their seats, even now that the polls are looking more favourable. But if that is his intention, he will need to get a move on – because now is as good as it is going to get.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLarry Elliott is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBudget 2026OpinionBudgetAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyEnergy billsHousehold billsEconomic growth (GDP)commentShareReuse this content

title: If British Library reading rooms become ‘co-working spaces’, what, exactly, is a national library for? | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: The plan to generate revenue from areas currently used by the public is causing bitter dispute, and raises fundamental questions, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: The plan to generate revenue from areas currently used by the public is causing bitter dispute, and raises fundamental questions, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesOpinionBritish LibraryIf British Library reading rooms become ‘co-working spaces’, what, exactly, is a national library for?Andy BeckettThe plan to generate revenue from areas currently used by the public is causing bitter dispute, and raises fundamental questionsThu 29 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTShareIn a crowded country that is short of public money, any expansive public building that seems underused in any way is vulnerable. Professional critics of state spending can claim taxpayers’ money is being wasted. Managers of the building who are under financial pressure can argue it needs to be used more intensely, perhaps that some spaces should be commercialised and offered for rent. The original open, uncommodified, egalitarian quality of the building can be steadily sliced away.The British Library in London is in danger of that fate. A huge brick battleship moored on the Euston Road since 1997, itclaims to bethe largest public building constructed in the UK in the 20th century. Its both forbidding and exhilarating exterior conceals 11 unusually elegant and comfortable reading rooms and one of the world’s most extensive print and digital collections, free to use for anyone who is over 18. Last week, these readers received an email with the subject line, “Transforming your Library”. Next summer, the library would “begin work on repurposing our [three] Science and Social Sciences Reading Rooms to become a flexible workspace … available for hire by workers and businesses for co-working, collaboration and meetings”. The reason given for removing more than a quarter of the library’s much-loved research space was “ensuring we generate the necessary revenue to keep our core services free”.The library has a currentannual budgetof about £170m – a third the size of my local London hospital’s – 84% of which comes from the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. The rest is from donations, investments and “charitable and other trading activities”, such as the private parties and ticketed exhibitions already frequently held in the sweeping interior connecting its reading rooms. Even with these multiple income streams, the library’s financial reserves are perilously low – according to its latest accounts – thanks to inflation and austerity, which meanits state fundinghas in real terms declined to two-thirds of what it was in 2010, and also adevastating cyber-attackin 2023, from which the library has still not fully recovered.Despite this troubled context, and in some ways because of it, the library’s drastic reading room reduction plan has provoked “outrage” from staff, say the Prospect and Public and Commercial Services (PCS) unions that represent them. Reading room staff understandably fear for their jobs, but also for the building’s fundamental purpose, which wasset out by lawin 1972 – an indication of how hard the complex was to conceive and build – as “the establishment for the United Kingdom of a national library”. Staff are now “the most furious I’ve ever seen them about anything”, says a union source. A strike over the reading room plan, followingone last yearover low pay, could begin as soon as December.Behind this potentially explosive dispute – not least because many well-connected authors, academics and journalists use the library – lurks a big question. In a digital age of decentralised study and dispersed online resources, what is a national library for?During the quarter of a century I’ve been regularly using the library, usually the reading rooms that are now under threat, its hierarchy has been trying to answer that existential question by steadily, not always harmoniously, widening the building’s user base and functions. Reading room passes have been transformed from a rationed credential for a few thousand people with supposedly serious research intentions – though some always ended up snoring at their desks – to something provided in minutes to everyone from elderly amateur family historians to undergraduates, particularly when dissertation deadlines pile up in early summer.Meanwhile, the library’s lobbies, landings, hallways and outdoor terraces have been lined with hundreds of chairs and tables and turned into study areas, meeting places, cafes and locations for loud laptop video conversations. These are all heavily used: a sign of good, free spaces lacking elsewhere. A “family station” inside the entrance offers play materials, art supplies and reading corners for young children. What Karl Marx, who researched for years in the reading room of the British Museum, precursor to theBritish Library, would have made of the latter’s invitation this Halloween to “pop in for spooky crafts” and “enjoy a fang-tastic time” is an intriguing question.I generally like the contrast between the library’s studious and boisterous sides: an antidote to the solitary obsessiveness of research and writing. But there are also tensions between the library’s diverging uses, which its management prefers not to acknowledge – and which the proposed changes would almost certainly worsen. Modern life is noisy, especially in London, and the semi-silence of the long, wood-lined reading rooms, with pages softly turning, keyboards pattering, books being slid on and off shelves, and the odd murmured conversation, is precious and addictive, as the constant influx of new young readers makes obvious. First thing in the morning and last thing in the evening, the rooms are half empty. That will probably be used to argue that fewer are needed. But a half-empty place can be an aid to crucial thinking and concentration. And if the reading rooms become fewer and therefore fuller, then users from outside London, whose taxes also pay for this national library, are less likely to be able to get there in time to grab a desk. In the busiest periods, they already sometimes run out.The library is straining to cope with its daily crowds. On bad mornings, the entrance queue lasts over half an hour. The toilets are increasingly often out of order. The free lockers are wearing out, partly because of use by travellers from the many stations nearby. And across the reading rooms, a mysterious hissing has been spreading for months, like a kettle that never boils. The library says it is coming from a failing pneumatic ventilation system, and “there is no quick solution”. The library is starting to get old.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 2032, a towering extension, blander than the original building, is due to open. It is already noisily under construction. Last year, Rebecca Lawrence, then the library’s chief executive, who resigned during the strike, said the extension would “open up the Library even further … [for] future generations of visitors, learners, researchers and budding entrepreneurs”. It will not contain new reading rooms. If you find that ominous, you are not alone.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBritish LibraryOpinionLibrariescommentShareReuse this content

title: Liz Truss has brought our divided nation together – in mockery of her | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: Though times are hard and days are dark, the former PM’s latest book reminds us of the fun to be had when a figure is so ridiculous but cannot see it, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Though times are hard and days are dark, the former PM’s latest book reminds us of the fun to be had when a figure is so ridiculous but cannot see it, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: Liz Truss at the US embassy in London, 10 September 2026.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenLiz Truss at the US embassy in London, 10 September 2026.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAOpinionLiz TrussLiz Truss has brought our divided nation together – in mockery of herEmma BrockesThough times are hard and days are dark, the former PM’s latest book reminds us of the fun to be had when a figure is so ridiculous but cannot see itThu 29 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 09.47 EDTShareIn these times of social and political division, it’s worth doing a quick audit of what keeps us together. Where, as we fight overwhat constitutes “wealth”and whether or not to goback in on Brexit, are the key sites of consensus? The Celebrity Traitors and the gloriousness ofNigella on Bake Offmay offer one area of unity; you can say the words “David Attenborough” to any sample of the population and elicit exactly the same murmur of approval. But, as the recent history of the internet shows, the most forceful bonds are those forged against, rather than in favour of, something. With that in mind, let’s turn to our old friend Liz Truss.It’s an unusual position, isn’t it, wondering if we might owe a debt of gratitude to the former prime minister who, aftertanking the value of the poundin 2022 and otherwise carrying on with the efficacy of someone stopped at random in the street and given the keys to government, is widely regarded as the worst ever to have held office. Truss has a book out this week, her second since leaving office, entitled Bank Job: A Short Book on How the Bank of England Broke the Bond Market and Brought Down the Government, and on the evidence of its early reception, it seems likely to prove even more successful in uniting disparate communities of Britain than her previous volume,Ten Years to Save the West.The government to which she refers in the subtitle is, of course, Truss’s own, which faltered in the wake of her mini-budget four years ago, when she sought to put through£45bn of unfunded tax cuts. Blaming the crash that followed on the Bank of England and the Treasury, the author admits no error, rekindling in observers powerful feelings of fury, mockery, incredulity and shame, plus a release of energy so intense that, like someone kicking in an old TV in a rage room, it might be mistaken for joy.The Independent’s reviewercalled the book“dense, paranoid and peevish”. The Telegraph gave itzero starsand also called it “deranged”. Scottish tabloid the Nationalcalled it“unhinged”. The Daily Star, whichfocused onthe book’s failure to give an adequate account of the role played by theiceberg lettuce that outlastedTruss’s 49-day tenure, called it “loopy”. Writing on X, Truss’s own former trade minister Conor Burnscalled her“an international embarrassment with zero self-awareness”, and “financially illiterate”. And so on.None of these opinions of Truss are new, but condensed as they are into a week of terrible reviews, they perhaps offer us an opportunity to come together to warm our hands around a single point of scorn. Even in a world dominated by horrible characters, this is a rare talent. President Donald Trump, for example, whom Truss has been unsuccessfullytrying to suck up tofor years, even going so far as to colour-scheme the cover of her last book red (for Republican) rather than blue (for Tory), can do no wrong in certain sections of the US electorate because of what he represents – white supremacy.But Truss doesn’t represent anything. She is relieved of all political associations. She stands for chaos unrelieved by charm, deepened by the impression she gives of someone receiving orders at a frequency no one else can hear. As an experiment, I tried just now to see if, with a bit of effort, I could drum up some sympathy for Truss, as I have on occasion managed for Theresa May; then I tried to find her funny, as I can sometimes do with Boris Johnson. But no; with Truss it is simply impossible to summon anything but rage and derision.In light of which, we might say this woman has become a national hero, achieving the seemingly impossible without even trying. In the first weeks after 9/11, Americans in large US cities enjoyed a brief improvement in civic behaviour as reported crime went down. I don’t mean to compare Truss’s premiership to the worst act of terrorism this century, but there is evidence to suggest that when people pull together in the wake of a universally recognised disaster, society briefly improves.The question, given the damage done by Truss to this country’s standing in the world and to our own sense of political and financial security, is: was it worth it? Obviously not. Still, at the time of writing, as Bank Job sits in the Amazon top 20 and Truss’s belligerent expression stares out, across all media, provoking howls of laughter and explosive diatribes from everyone who looks on her, there are really only two words to say: thank you.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLiz TrussOpinionConservativesEconomic policyPolitics bookscommentShareReuse this content

title: Serbia’s students achieved the impossible. Europe must not fail them now | Srđjan Cvijić | The Guardian
description: Some EU leaders courted the authoritarian Vučić regime – they must offer this reborn democracy a future within the union, says Srđjan Cvijić of the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy
Author: Srđjan Cvijić
Headline: Some EU leaders courted the authoritarian Vučić regime – they must offer this reborn democracy a future within the union, says Srđjan Cvijić of the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy
Content: Supporters of the student movement celebrate in the streets of central Belgrade.Photograph: Marko Dimic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSupporters of the student movement celebrate in the streets of central Belgrade.Photograph: Marko Dimic/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionSerbiaSerbia’s students achieved the impossible. Europe must not fail them nowSrđjan CvijićSome EU leaders courted the authoritarian Vučić regime – they must offer this reborn democracy a future within the unionThu 29 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 07.41 EDTShareAs polling stations closed acrossSerbiaon Sunday evening, riot police were deploying around the presidency in Belgrade. Many of us feared the worst: massive electoral fraud, a refusal to recognise defeat or outright violence. After nearly 15 years of Aleksandar Vučić’s increasingly authoritarian rule, a peaceful transfer of power seemed implausible.I had good reason to feel afraid. I am co-founder of an annual conference on the security and foreign policy challenges shaping the western Balkans, and sit on the international advisory committee of a civil society thinktank, theBelgrade Centre for Security Policy. Such work would be uncontroversial in most countries seeking European Union membership. Under Vučić’s regime, it was anything but.Over the past two years, our organisationhas faced cyber-attacksby actors suspected of links to Russian intelligence, spyware attempts and relentless vilification by pro-regime media. After one attack, investigators documented 28,000 email exchanges that had been hacked. At the same time, Serbian regime propagandists portrayed us as foreign conspirators, while the threat of Russian-styleforeign agents legislationcast a long shadow over all of Serbian civil society. Had Vučić won another mandate, exile might have become a reality for many of us.Othersendured far worse.Journalistsandactivistshad theirhomes set on fire. Students who were detained reported being beaten, femalesstripped nakedandhumiliated in police stationswhile activists were imprisoned for exercising their democratic rights. Among them werethe Novi Sad 12– students and activists prosecuted on politically motivated charges during the protests that followed the November 2024 railway station canopy collapsethat killed 16 people. Six were driven into exile; the other six endured imprisonment and house arrest.All this happened in a country negotiating EU membership.And then, on Sunday evening, something extraordinary happened.Vučić conceded defeat. The student-backed list’s margin of victory was so overwhelming that overturning the result might have proved more dangerous than accepting it.‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumphRead moreWhat convinced a man who had spent nearly 15 years concentrating power in his hands to relinquish it? Fear of popular resistance? International pressure, and if it was this, from where?Uncertainty over the loyalty of Vučić’s security apparatus may have been a decisive factor. Days before the election, hundreds of serving and former police and intelligence officials, including former security leaders,signed an appealurging their colleagues to uphold the constitution rather than obey unlawful political orders. It was a reminder that Vučić could not necessarily count on the entire security establishment to keep him in power.An incumbent accepting electoral defeat is ordinary in an established democracy. In Serbia, it felt almost miraculous.The students had achieved what many thought impossible. They had forced a system built around the impossibility of losing to accept that it had lost.Their victory belonged equally to hundreds of thousands who marched, organised and endured intimidation. What began as grief over 16 lives lost in Novi Sad became a movement challenging the foundations of state capture.For nearly two years, the students dismantled the regime’s most powerful weapon: the belief that resistance was futile, everyone had a price and political change was impossible.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs students we never sought power – here’s how we reclaimed Serbia | Novak SiminRead moreBut the significance of their victory is measured not only in votes. It is measured in lives.I think of Mila, Anja, Doroteja, Branislav, Jovan and Dejan, the six Novi Sad activists forced into exile formore than a year and a half. They may finally be able to come home. Six of their comrades in Serbia are now free from detention and house arrest. But I have friends who have confronted authoritarianism in their countries withequal courageand have no prospect of achieving the same breakthrough. I am thinking of Marika from Georgia, Gökçe from Turkey and Andrei from Belarus. For them, exile remains a condition of life.Their fate reminds us that Serbia’s peaceful breakthrough was not inevitable.Geography, too, played its part. Serbia lies at the heart ofEurope, beyond Russia’s immediate reach and too close to the EU for its democratic struggle to remain Europe’s distant concern.Serbia’s students deserve the credit, but what happens next also depends on Europe. For years, some European leaders tolerated, and sometimes effectively supported, Vučić’s authoritarian rule, preferring a predictable strongman to democratic uncertainty. Serbia’s breakthrough happened largely despite Brussels, not because of it.Here lies the irony: while European leaders courted Vučić, much of Serbia’s genuinely pro-European constituency opposed him.Our research foundthat two-thirds of Serbians who supported EU membership also opposed his government. Brussels was looking for stability in the wrong place.Serbia’s ability to consolidate its democracy relies on a future in Europe. And Europe now has an opportunity to regain the trust of those who fought for the very democratic values it professes to uphold.Defeating an autocrat is an event, but dismantling authoritarian institutions is a process. Serbia must restore the rule of law, free its media and ensure that its police and security services serve citizens rather than a political party.The students have won the right to change their government but the harder task lies ahead. And that means building a country where doing so will never again require such extraordinary courage.Srđjan Cvijić is a writer, president of the international advisory committee of the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy and co-founder of the Belgrade Security ConferenceExplore more on these topicsSerbiaOpinionEuropeActivismEuropean UnionStudentsProtestcommentShareReuse this content

title: Exploding heads, mutant aliens and bursting chests: horror’s greatest special effects – ranked! | Movies | The Guardian
description: From the beheading in The Omen to the attic scene in The Birds, here’s a countdown of the genre’s most iconic moments – in glorious, old-school pre-CGI style
Author: Anne Billson
Headline: From the beheading in The Omen to the attic scene in The Birds, here’s a countdown of the genre’s most iconic moments – in glorious, old-school pre-CGI style
Content: Legendary … The ExorcistPhotograph: Warner Bros./AllstarView image in fullscreenLegendary … The ExorcistPhotograph: Warner Bros./AllstarRankedMoviesExploding heads, mutant aliens and bursting chests: horror’s greatest special effects – ranked!From the beheading in The Omen to the attic scene in The Birds, here’s a countdown of the genre’s most iconic moments – in glorious, old-school pre-CGI styleAnne BillsonThu 29 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 18.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Ring (1998)Towards the end of the 20th century, when film-makers’ overreliance on CGI was increasingly making special effects less special, it took the old-school practical approach of Japanese film-maker Hideo Nakata to make one’s hair stand on end. Just when you think the cursed VHS tape has claimed its last victim, Sadako’s vengeful ghost emerges from the well, comes closer … and climbs out of the television screen.19. The Phantom Carriage (1921)The Swedish director Victor Sjöström makes extensive use of double exposure – all done in-camera because optical printing had yet to be developed – to depict Death’s soul-collecting carriage in this folk-horror classic. Sjöström also plays the dissolute antihero, condemned to be the spectral vehicle’s driver unless he can mend his ways.18. The Student of Prague (1926)Henrik Galeen’s expressionist variation on the Faust legend reunites the stars of The Cabinet of Dr Caligari: Conrad Veidt plays the student who makes a deal with the devil (Werner Krauss), who steals his reflection. This evil doppelganger runs amok until Veidt confronts it in a split-screen climax.View image in fullscreenVampire Count Orlok (Max Schreck) being destroyed by sunlight.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty Images17. Nosferatu (1922)FW Murnau commandeers a variety of in-camera effects for this vampire masterpiece. Flipped negatives, sped-up action and stop-motion add to theunheimlichambience until, exposed to the sun’s rays, cadaverous Count Orlok (Max Schreck) vanishes in a puff of smoke.16. Dawn of the Dead (1978)Raise a glass to Jim Krut, who died in August but who will forever be remembered as “Helicopter Zombie” in George A Romero’s undead classic. Thanks to the magic of splatter makeup maestro Tom Savini, he shambles into frame – and gets the top of his head sliced off by a spinning rotor.15. Tetsuo: The Iron Man (1989)Shinya Tsukamoto burst on to the body horror scene with a no-budget semi-experimental cyberpunk nightmare in which a Japanese salaryman’s body parts gradually turn to metal through a combination of juddery time-lapse, stop motion and jump-cutting, all set to a clanging soundtrack. Finally, his penis turns into a giant drill and destroys a coffee table.View image in fullscreenOld school … RingPhotograph: TCD/Prod.DB/Alamy14. The Invisible Man (1933)James Whale’s adaptation of HG Wells’s novel owes much to the sardonic tones of Claude Rains, whose face is only briefly glimpsed in his Hollywood debut. John P Fulton’s special effects show the actor unwrapping bandages from his head to reveal – nothing!13. Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1931)Fredric March won the best actor Oscar for his performance in this violent, sexy pre-code adaptation of Robert Louis Stevenson’s novella. It would be 38 years before the director, Rouben Mamoulian, revealed how they achieved the groundbreaking onscreen transformation of Jekyll into Hyde: Wally Westmore’s makeup combined with coloured filters over the lens.12. Eyes Without a Face (1960)A surgeon kidnaps young women and – in explicit black and white – slices their faces off with a scalpel in an attempt to restore the beauty of his disfigured daughter. Georges Franju’s eerie arthouse horror was dismissed on its release, but is now hailed as an influential masterpiece.View image in fullscreenInfluential … Eyes Without a FacePhotograph: Cinetext/Allstar Collection/The Criterion Collection/Allstar11. The Exorcist (1973)The pea-coloured puke popularised the term “projectile vomiting”, and the deleted “spider-walk” became legendary before its restitution. But the signature effect in William Friedkin’s film is Linda Blair’s 360-degree head rotation, an effect at once ludicrous and horrifying, thanks to Dick Smith and Marcel Vercoutere’s lifesize animatronic dummy.10. The Birds (1963)The climbing frame, the schoolchildren, the gas station are impeccable set pieces, but the attack on Tippi Hedren in the attic is particularly terrifying. Much of the impact was achieved by editing, but some birds were attached to her clothes by nylon threads, and one of the beaks nearly took her eye out. The scene took seven days to shoot; Hedren described it as “the worst week of my life”.9. Eraserhead (1977)David Lynch’s first full-length feature is set in an industrial hellscape, where Jack Nance, he of the tumbleweed hair-do, ends up having to look after a chittering mutant baby. The creature, designed by Lynch himself, was reportedly made from an embalmed calf foetus with added working parts, and was ceremonially buried in a secret location after production wrapped.8. The Omen (1976)Graphic decapitation goes mainstream in a special effect supervised by John Richardson. Photographer Keith Jennings (David Warner) stoops to retrieve the Daggers of Megiddo, the only weapons effective against Damien the Antichrist – and is beheaded by a sheet of glass sliding off a runaway truck. Warner reportedly kept the severed head until his divorce, when his ex-wife claimed custody of it.View image in fullscreenPosh partygoers meld into each other in Society.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/Alamy7. The Howling (1981)Joe Dante’s werewolf satire, co-written by John Sayles, shows Robert Picardo (AKA Star Trek’s holographic doctor) saying “I’m gonna give you a piece of my mind” and offering a bit of his own brain to a horrified Dee Wallace before pulsating air bladders transform him into a beast before our very eyes. Take a bow, Rob Bottin, making his solo special effects debut.6. The Fury (1978)John Cassavetes, darling of American indie cinema, found Brian De Palma’s film “degrading”, but his villain’s comeuppance is so satisfying you wish Rick Baker’s effects could have been retroactively applied to the same actor’s character in Rosemary’s Baby as well. One of the psychic teenagers the scumbag has been trying to control zaps him with her full telekinetic force and kaboom! He explodes!5. Society (1989)Brian Yuzna’s body-horror satire unmasks the upper classes as shapeshifting entities who literally feed off the proletariat. The film climaxes with an orgiastic “shunt” in which posh partygoers merge into an orifice-invading mass not unlikeSalvador Dalí’s Great Masturbator, surreal effects courtesy of Screaming Mad George.4. Scanners (1981)There is no shortage of mind-boggling effects in the early films of David Cronenberg, but his sci-fi thriller about warring psychics provides one of the most memorable. One telepath’s demonstration of his ability is hijacked by a more powerful scanner (Michael Ironside) who makes his head explode. Dick Smith and Chris Walas packed a plaster skull with “leftover burgers”, then blasted it with an out-of-frame shotgun.3. An American Werewolf in London (1981)Rick Baker won the inaugural best makeup Oscar for his work on John Landis’s horror-comedy (with a budget three times that of The Howling). As Sam Cooke’s Blue Moon plays on the radio, David Naughton stares aghast at his hand turning into a werewolf’s paw. As his skeleton painfully reconfigures itself, his shrieks of agony turn into a howl.View image in fullscreenShocking … the cast didn’t know a critter would emerge from John Hurt’s chest.Photograph: Collection Christophel/Alamy2. Alien (1979)The rest of the cast knew something was about to happen, but didn’t know precisely what, so when a critter erupts out of John Hurt’s chest, their shock is almost as extreme as the audience’s. For the money shot, Hurt’s torso was replaced by a mechanical one packed with compressed air and animal entrails, with puppeteers hiding beneath the table. Director Ridley Scott designed the creature, Roger Dicken constructed it and sci-fi cinema would never be the same again.1. The Thing (1982)View image in fullscreenHorrifying .. The Thing.Photograph: Universal Pictures/AllstarA shapeshifting alien infiltrates a US research station in the Antarctic, sporadically erupting into displays of special effects that have yet to be equalled. Take another bow, Rob Bottin, who riffs on elements of human and animal anatomy in surreal sculptures that are simultaneously repulsive and beautiful. In one of the highlights, a geologist’s head separates from his body, sprouts spider-legs and tries to scuttle away. Palmer the pothead (David Clennon) says what we’ve all been thinking: “You’ve gotta be fucking kidding.”Explore more on these topicsFilmRankedHorror filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ​‘He buckled. I could hear his bass ringing out ...’ The luminous rise and tragic end of US alt heroes Morphine | Music | The Guardian
description: ​Fronted by Mark Sandman​,​ the group brought enigmatic, elegant rock to post-grunge America. As lost demos surface, those closest to Sandman remember a man who grabbed on to life’s joys
Author: Stevie Chick
Headline: ​Fronted by Mark Sandman​,​ the group brought enigmatic, elegant rock to post-grunge America. As lost demos surface, those closest to Sandman remember a man who grabbed on to life’s joys
Content: ‘A guy who lived nine lives.’ … Mark Sandman in Morphine.Photograph: Martin Beddall/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A guy who lived nine lives.’ … Mark Sandman in Morphine.Photograph: Martin Beddall/AlamyMusic​‘He buckled. I could hear his bass ringing out ...’ The luminous rise and tragic end of US alt heroes Morphine​Fronted by Mark Sandman​,​ the group brought enigmatic, elegant rock to post-grunge America. As lost demos surface, those closest to Sandman remember a man who grabbed on to life’s joysStevie ChickThu 29 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s early 1998, and at Fort Apache recording studio in Massachusetts, Mark Sandman, the suave frontman of Morphine, is nearing breaking point. Morphine’s four enigmatic and blackly humorous albums have won critical acclaim and, lately, unexpected commercial success considering their uncompromising creative vision. After the excesses of grunge, Sandman considered their idiosyncratic blend of sophisticated storytelling, prowling slide-bass and Dana Colley’s atmospheric saxophone a kind of “palate cleanser”.In 1997 Morphine had signed to DreamWorks Records, founded by industry bigwigs David Geffen and Mo Ostin. Now, working on Morphine’s first LP for his new paymasters – a batch of songs finally seeing release almost three decades later – Sandman was consumed by doubt over their direction. “For the first time, Morphine were trying to please someone other than just ourselves,” remembers Colley.View image in fullscreenRootsy … The pre-Morphine band Treat Her Right in 1989, from left: Jim Fitting, Dave Champagne, Billy Conway and Mark Sandman.Photograph: Jim Steinfeldt/Getty Images“DreamWorks wanted to make the ‘big Morphine record’,” says Paul Q Kolderie, who had produced all of Morphine’s albums and was overseeing the sessions. “But the label didn’t know what they wanted. And Mark didn’t know what he wanted. He wasn’t happy.”The pressure built until DreamWorks ho-hummed over the latest demos, and Sandman had “a particularly bad fight” with Kolderie, ditching the producer and Fort Apache. Soon, he would write and self-produce a whole new batch of songs, later released as Morphine’s fifth album, The Night. But by the time it hit the shelves in February 2000, Sandman was dead.Though only 46 when he died, Sandman was “a guy who lived nine lives”, says Kolderie. “This wasnothis first go-round – he was an old soul.” His partner, Sabine Hrechdakian, says Sandman “was not someone who liked to dwell on the past”.No Reason, a 1989 track by his rootsy pre-Morphine vehicle Treat Her Right, saw him indulge in uncharacteristic autobiography. Describing foundational real-life losses and near-death experiences, Sandman concluded: “There’s no reason in this life / someone lives and someone dies.”View image in fullscreenA rebel … Sandman live in 1994.Photograph: Marie Le MaufRaised in a middle-class home in Massachusetts, Sandman was a rebel whose parents were “lovely people, but they just didn’t understand their bohemian, rule-breaking son”, says Hrechdakian. At 18 he left for Alaska where he worked as a fisher. His travels ended after an early brush with death: having contracted kidney-damaging intestinal problems, Sandman flew home for urgent treatment and recuperation.He returned at a dark time for his family. His youngest brother Roger, who had cerebral palsy, had died in 1978; 16 months later, his brother Jon died after falling from a window at a party. Sandman was distraught, and while he would rarely discuss it, Hrechdakian says these losses acted as “a call to action, to live the life he wanted and pursue it with determination. Mark knew how temporary life was.”double quotation markMy theory is, somewhere inside he knew he was not wellKolderie met Sandman in the early 80s, on Boston’s music scene. “Mark had agreattime. He was completely nocturnal – all he wanted was to hang out and make music with friends.” Sandman also worked in construction and catering, and drove a cab, until – in another near-death experience – he was stabbed in the chest by muggers and left for dead.His next close shave set Morphine in motion. Treat Her Right were splitting up, Sandman having realised he needed to “be the leader and have a band that followedhisvision”, Kolderie says. As Sandman drove home after a farewell show, a car crashed into his Chevrolet Corvair. He ended up in hospital but won a $20,000 settlement and quit work to focus on his next project. “His material suddenly got much better,” says Kolderie, “marrying introspective, thoughtful songwriting to these cool grooves.”Colley had befriended Sandman when his previous band supported Treat Her Right. “Mark invited me to his loft because he had this one-string bass he’d been working with,” says Colley. “We jammed, and it was like a lightbulb went on for Mark. We got a drummer, Jerome Deupree, and immediately started recording Morphine’s debut album.”View image in fullscreenIneffable cool … Morphine’s Sandman (left), Conway and Colley (right) in 1995.Photograph: Bob Berg/Getty ImagesMorphine arrived fully formed on their debut, 1992’s Good, calling their sound “low rock”. Sandman’s murmured voice injected his beat poetics, noirish intrigue and blackly comedic stories with ineffable cool. It seduced everyone who heard it – like Rykodisc president Don Rose, who signed Morphine for their second album, 1993’s Cure for Pain. Aftertheir debut appearance on Late Night with Conan O’Brien, Colley says, “every show we played sold out, until our very last gig,” while Morphine’s music added sulphurous mystery to movies including Get Shorty and Wild Things, plusan early episode of Sex and the City. Being some years older than the typical indie-rocker – Sandman was 40 when Cure for Pain dropped – the success hardly went to their heads. “We weren’t throwing televisions out of hotel windows,” says Colley. “We loved what we were doing, and didn’t take it for granted.”Sandman, meanwhile, had just met the love of his life. “He saw me one night and Cupid drew his arrow,” Hrechdakian laughs. Fourteen years younger than Sandman, she bartended at Boston venue the Middle East, where he “would make puppy-dog eyes at me. He was lovestruck,verydriven; he pursued me for months. I wasn’t playing hard to get, I just didn’t feel an immediate … ” She tails off. But one night Hrechdakian heard Sandman singing No Reason in her living room. “I don’t know if it was hearing his vulnerability, but I was like, ‘Oh myGod– I think I’m in love with this man.’”Much of their early relationship would be conducted via fax machine: Sandman was always touring, Hrechdakian pursuing her master’s in environmental studies. “We could not have lived more opposite lives. But in 1997 I decided, ‘this sucks’, and moved in with him.” They shared Sandman’s loft, where he had built his studio, Hi-N-Dry. “That was his cocoon.”He began work on Morphine’s fifth album in an experimental mood. Deupree, who had left during the Cure for Pain sessions due to an injury, returned to play alongside his replacement, Billy Conway. The new material was strong, but the label’s lack of enthusiasm got under Sandman’s skin. His mood continued to plummet after they relocated to Fort Apache, where Kolderie had recorded Radiohead’s Pablo Honey and Hole’s Live Through This. “He would zone out during sessions,” says Kolderie. “His health did not seem good. People would ask me, ‘Is Mark OK? He looks grey.’ He was the heaviest smoker I ever knew. And it took its toll.”After splitting from Fort Apache, Sandman returned to the loft and self-produced The Night, Morphine’s fifth album, expanding the lineup to include more bass, violin and cello. “My theory is, somewhere inside he knew he was not well,” says Hrechdakian. “The Night is an album of him saying goodbye.”View image in fullscreen‘Oh myGod– I think I’m in love with this man.’ … Hrechdakian on Sandman.Photograph: Mark SandmanSandman signed off The Night in summer 1999 and Morphine readied for dates in Europe. Two weeks before the tour, however, Sandman suffered what Hrechdakian realises now was “the warning”: a minor heart attack. “His arm went numb. The colour drained from his face. I said, ‘Please let’s go to the emergency room’. He refused. So what did I do? I went to fucking Blockbuster to get videos and a pint of ice-cream.”Morphine arrived in Europe in July during a debilitating heatwave. At the first show in Lisbon, Colley remembers “the air coming through my instrument into my lungs felt like a furnace”. The second date was at a festival near Rome. The heat remained intense, but Colley remembers “a beautiful evening, shining faces looking back at us. Seven songs in, we were playing Super Sex and Mark buckled at the knee and fell down. I could hear his bass ringing out, and put my horns down and ran to him. They took him to the emergency room down the street, but he was already gone.”View image in fullscreenSandman in 1994 in his native Massachusetts.Photograph: MediaMedium/AlamyAfter Sandman’s death, Colley “wasn’t sure I’d ever play again”. Over the years since, however, he’s kept Sandman’s music alive via various live projects. Sandman’s estate fell into the control of his father, who “didn’t have any idea what to do with it,” says Kolderie. “He was an ornery cuss. Nike would try to license Morphine songs for an ad and he’d say, ‘Nah, that’s not enough money.’” A posthumous box set of unreleased material, Sandbox, was stymied by an ultimately unsuccessful lawsuit from Rykodisc that nonetheless smothered momentum.Hrechdakian and Morphine’s manager, Deborah Klein, took over the estate after Sandman’s father died, and Hrechdakian began sorting through a huge storage space of Sandman’s artwork, music and correspondence. She contacted Kolderie for help preserving the tapes and realised that the 1998 loft demos that preceded the Fort Apache sessions were a goldmine. “There’s a looseness,” Hrechdakian says. Those excellent recordings are now set to be released (with new sax parts from Colley) as Cocoon. “You can hear him laughing, his fingers on the strings … I sobbed for a while, listening to it.”Everyone involved with the project calls it a “healing” experience. Hrechdakian says she “didn’t fully understand the depth of his love for me until after he was gone. Putting Cocoon together feels like a love story, like we’re communicating across time and space. It’s like Mark has come back to life for everyone who hears it, and he has for me as well.”Cocoon is released via Partisan on 4 DecemberThis article was updated on 29 October to correct details in Sandman’s biography: his brand of car, where he worked as a fisher, and where Hrechdakian heard him play No Reason.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mega mega mega, going back to Romford! How an outer London suburb became a metropolis for 90s dance music | Dance music | The Guardian
description: When 17-year-0ld Danny Donelly got a bank loan to open a record shop and sell dancefloor-filling electronic music, he little knew how he would help revolutionise his town and dance music at large
Author: Tim Burrows
Headline: When 17-year-0ld Danny Donelly got a bank loan to open a record shop and sell dancefloor-filling electronic music, he little knew how he would help revolutionise his town and dance music at large
Content: ‘It was like a youth club’ … Boogie Times Records in Romford.Photograph: Danny DonnellyView image in fullscreen‘It was like a youth club’ … Boogie Times Records in Romford.Photograph: Danny DonnellyDance musicMega mega mega, going back to Romford! How an outer London suburb became a metropolis for 90s dance musicWhen 17-year-0ld Danny Donelly got a bank loan to open a record shop and sell dancefloor-filling electronic music, he little knew how he would help revolutionise his town and dance music at largeTim BurrowsThu 29 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 07.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early 1990s, the suburban town of Romford was known for three things. It was the home of the world’s best snooker player, Steve Davis. It was where people placed bets at Romford dog track, over a dinner of chicken in a basket. And for those in the know, it was where the UK’s best underground dance music was bought and sold.That pedigree was immortalised by Romford’s most famous musical act, Underworld, with frontman Karl Hyde shouting the words “mega mega mega, going back to Romford” at the climax of 1995’s Born Slippy. Those words now form the title of a new exhibition in the town,Mega Mega: Romford’s Suburban Sound Revolution, which charts how this unglamorous but party-spirited backwater became an upstart rival to great dance music cities such as Manchester or Detroit.View image in fullscreenBought with a bank loan … Boogie Times Records, pictured in the 90s.Photograph: westhamdan/Danny BreaksThe scene’s key hub was the record shop Boogie Times, opened in 1989 by Danny Donnelly with a bank loan secured shortly before his 18th birthday. He was born in Stratford, east London, but when he was five his parents moved out to Romford, an oldEssexmarket town that had effectively become a suburb of London as the capital sprawled outwards after the second world war.View image in fullscreenThe Donnellys’ old shop at 18 Abbey Lane, Stratford in 2006.Photograph: © Vici MacDonaldDonnelly’s dad commuted back to Stratford to run the family corner shop, while young Danny inherited his entrepreneurial streak. “I was already buying and selling records at school,” he says. He loved rare groove, where hard-to-find jazz, funk and R&B records were selected for the quality of their breakbeats. At 14, he bought huge speakers for his bedroom, which he later used to put on parties around east London: “You’d hire someone’s flat, charge at the door and it would be treated like a club for the event.”Boogie Times opened just as house music and ecstasy found their way into post-industrial spaces and farmers’ fields, building demand for rave tunes on vinyl. The location of Donnelly’s dad’s shop in Stratford was similarly fortuitous: east London pirate station Fantasy FM launched in the block next door in 1989. “They would come downstairs and get a cup of tea and a sandwich after they had done their show,” says Donnelly. His dad got chatting to future drum’n’bass legend DJ Hype, who soon paid a visit to Boogie Times with another artist, DJ Krome. “Krome said: ‘Your mum makes the best cheese and onion sandwich.’” After being switched on to hardcore rave, Donnelly endeavoured to supply some of the freshest vinyl to a burgeoning local clientele.View image in fullscreenA visiting legend … DJ Hype in Boogie Times Records 1990s dance music record shop in Romford, Essex,Photograph: Danny DonnellyRomford and the wider borough of Havering already housed parties by people such as the polymath producer and promoter Mark Ryder – who later became a star in the UK garage era as Mark “Ruff” Ryder – but Romford was still best known for dancing to pop music on a Saturday night with your glad rags on.Tony Grimley, another local DJ inspired by his first rave, was asked to run a night at Romford’s biggest nightclub, Hollywood. He named it Culture Shock to describe the way the music landed there. “It was a party venue: a very Sharon and Tracy, 80s place,” says Grimley. Instead of tame disco and “erection section” slow dances, suddenly there were exciting new electronic DJs such as Andrew Weatherall, Danny Rampling and Underworld’s Darren Emerson. The local crowd didn’t like hard techno, Grimley says, “but that happy, high-energy sort of house music [such as] Danny Rampling … every time we booked Danny, we reached capacity.”View image in fullscreenMaking music themselves … Danny Donnelly leans on his Jeep with Boogie Times manager and Suburban Base Records artist Winston Run Tings.Photograph: Danny DonnellySimon Duggins AKA Uncle Dugs, DJ and former station manager of pirate-turned-legit radio station Rinse FM, went to his first rave after he noticed a circus big top on the side of the A13 when his dad was driving him to football training at Leyton Orient. “I walked into that rave a budding professional footballer,” says Duggins. “I walked out wanting to be [rave DJ] Slipmatt.” Duggins had already been nervously stepping into Boogie Times on a packed Saturday when he was still at school. “Someone would walk in, and then the whisper would go round the shop:That’s DJ Hype. You can’t even believe that you’re in the same space as these people.”View image in fullscreenGarage music? … Suburban Base’s first recording studio, built in Danny Donnelly’s parents’ garage.Photograph: westhamdan/Danny BreaksRomford was also surrounded by pirate radio stations such as Conflict FM in Rainham, and Force FM, which operated above a nearby sweet shop. “Pirate radio, the community around record stores and flyering was the analogue version of the internet,” says Donnelly. He broadened that community by creating his own record label, Suburban Base, brainstorming its name in the office above the shop on the day of the Rumbelows Football League cup final on 21 April 1991. It was a canny way to surpass dance music’s supply-chain gatekeepers by making the music themselves. “We were trying to compete with more established dance music shops in central London that were getting exclusives, stuff that we couldn’t get hold of,” says Donnelly. So he used Suburban Base to press small runs of records, “that we could keep exclusive to our shop for at least the first few weeks. People had to come to us.”The name Suburban Base accurately described Romford’s outsider status in a scene defined by the inner city: away from more credible tracks in London, sometimes Essex artists veered into full-on cheese such as the kids-TV-samplingSesame’s Treetby Loughton locals Smart E’s. Released by Suburban Base, it reached No 2 in the UK singles chart in July 1992. Donnelly says the track was seen by some on the scene as selling out, but adds: “It was hugely popular amongst rave DJs before it crossed over.” And it does have an innocence that chimed with the family vibe of the Boogie Times shop, which was “like a youth club in a way, with loads of people hanging around listening to music”, says Rachel Wallace, a key member of the Boogie Times tribe. She dated Donnelly and recorded her first tracks for the label in a studio in his parents’ garage, including the relentless and evocatively 90s tuneTell Me Why.View image in fullscreenKey member of the Boogie Times tribe … Rachel Wallace in 1992.Photograph: Suburban Bass RecordsSuburban Base helped to propel the dance scene as breakbeats got faster and more intricate, the bass got bigger and rounder, and ragga MCs became more prevalent. This new sound became known as jungle, showcased on hot Suburban Base dancefloor fillers such as RIP by Remarc. DJ Rap, AKA Charissa Saverio, was living in nearby Walthamstow and put jungle tracks out on Suburban Base, and found the scene unusually welcoming. “You saw Black people and white people together for the first time,” she says. “You walked in [to a jungle night] as a girl, and you weren’t harassed by a bunch of men; you could wear what you want, you didn’t have to look sexy, you could just be you.”Suburban Base Brazil … DJ Marky Mark enters the roster.Photograph: Courtesy Danny DonnellyAs the 90s progressed, Suburban Base became the first independent UK rave label to open up an office in the US, on the corner of Hollywood and Vine in Los Angeles in 1994. It expanded into Brazil, wheredrum’n’bass took off in a big way. Donnelly discovered a DJ working in a São Paulo record shop called Marky Mark, who became DJ Marky, and whose track LK became one of drum’n’bass’s biggest UK hits. “If you travel to Brazil now, particularly São Paulo, and you’re wearing a Suburban Base shirt, someone will come up to you,” Donnelly says.Boogie Times carried on into the 2000s after a record seller from the other side of the river in Gravesend decided to buy it off Donnelly, who had already stepped back from Suburban Base to focus on compiling huge-selling CD compilation series such as Pure Garage and Euphoria.View image in fullscreenSuburban Base on tour … Danny Breaks, MC Special A and Dave Nodz on stage in Orlando Florida 1992.Photograph: Danny DonnellyDuggins, meanwhile, had soundproofed an old primary school building in nearby Dagenham to house Rinse FM, and was putting on nights in Romford to showcase garage-era acts that pre-empted the incoming grime explosion, such as DJ EZ, Masterstepz and Pay as U Go Cartel. EZ would return to Romford to put on what might be the town’s most famous clubbing event:Todd Edwards at Time & Envy on New Year’s Day 2003, in which the US DJ and producer, whose style had so influenced UK garage, stared out at his adoring (and very male) crowd with a mixture of shock, fear and delight – scenes that still frequently go viral on social media.Murder on the dancefloor: are phones, drugs and chatter killing off dancing?Read moreTime & Envy was rebranded a few times before it closed for good in 2024, and the empty venue will now host the Mega Mega exhibition, including a replica of a 90s recording studio with original equipment from Suburban Base, and a pirate station recreated using original transmitters, aerials and the turntables from Boogie Times. “Young people now are so interested in those kind of analogue and early digital forms of music making,” says Katherine Green, the show’s curator.Like his old man might have done on a quiet day in the shop, Donnelly is finally taking stock. “I definitely played my part in the global expansion of the scene,” he reflects, but adds a warning that it wasn’t all parties and glamour. “It just comes from the ethos of doing things in a professional way,” he says. “Creating a label identity – and putting barcodes on the records.”Mega Mega: Romford’s Suburban Sound Revolutionruns from 29 October to 20 December at Atik, Romford. See You Down Raquels: Clubbing and Commune-ing in Essex, edited by Tim Burrows, isavailable to buy here.Explore more on these topicsDance musicClub cultureElectronic musicEssexfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Middlemarch review – World’s Greatest Novel hurtles from deathbed panto to jolting marital tragedy | Stage | The Guardian
description: This RSC staging of the sprawling middle England masterpiece has humour, compassion – and even George Eliot herself as a character
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: This RSC staging of the sprawling middle England masterpiece has humour, compassion – and even George Eliot herself as a character
Content: Each scene shakes you … Rory Alexander as Will Ladislaw and Nia Towle as Dorothea in Middlemarch.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenEach scene shakes you … Rory Alexander as Will Ladislaw and Nia Towle as Dorothea in Middlemarch.Photograph: Johan PerssonStageReviewMiddlemarch review – World’s Greatest Novel hurtles from deathbed panto to jolting marital tragedySwan theatre, Stratford-Upon-AvonThis RSC staging of the sprawling middle England masterpiece has humour, compassion – and even George Eliot herself as a characterArifa AkbarThu 29 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 18.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs there a literary achievement greater than George Eliot’s stonking masterpiece?Not according to a Guardian poll,toppedby this sprawling, contemplative and profound book about marriage, moral goodness, debt, death, God and everything in between. So how do you adapt its nonpareil greatness for the stage without flattening the moral, philosophical and psychological complexities?Andrew Davies had a go at it with his watchable enough 1994 television costume drama, retelling Eliot’s story about provincial life, in six parts. Ameresix-parts, you might say, for a novel that is about 900 pages. While its timeline only spans three years in the life of a fictional Midlands town, it juggles multiple storylines and perspectives, weaves the local with the big socio-political backdrops of its age and follows the trajectories of characters with such detail that it becomes hard to replicate in another form.Now theRoyal Shakespeare Companyhas had a go at a stage adaptation, divided into two parts and totalling almost six hours of viewing (including the intervals). Again, you might say, a mere six hours, particularly in relation to the compressions of Part One. Jeremy Herrin’s production at first seems to sacrifice character study and emotional connection for plot and pace, although it hits all the beats of a pleasing costume drama, is easy on the eye, full of incident and with an understated visual beauty that suits the town of Middlemarch perfectly. Grace Smart’s supple set design contains ecclesiastical touches in the vaulted ceiling and back window, alluding to Eliot’s exploration of divinity. The stage is often lit by candles, perhaps to gesture at Eliot’s famed passage about the candle and pier-glass, which is quoted at the outset of the show. But there is so much incident to get through that you do not get much more than momentary philosophical reflection or inner outpourings before the next flick of the proverbial page.View image in fullscreenPantomime entertainment … Peter Forbes and John Hodgkinson.Photograph: Johan PerssonLike the book, the beginning focuses on the marriage of the young, devout Dorothea (Nia Towle), who sees wedlock as a means of higher learning, but does not quite make you feel enough. Her failed suitor, Sir James Chettam (Gunnar Cauthery), remains featureless, as does her sister, Celia (Lizzie Annis; why is she dressed in the same shockingly unfashionable frock throughout?). Outsider-artist Will Ladislaw (Rory Alexander), meanwhile, is barely there, appearing in brief spotlight as little more than a motif. Beyond the parish of Lowick, the drama of the Vincy family ticks over: Fred’s (Ebenezer Gyau) feckless ways with money, his tenderness for Mary Garth (also Annis), along with the budding romance between Rosamond (Emma McDonald) and the town’s ambitious new doctor, Tertius Lydgate (Andrew Richardson). It is Dorothea’s scholarly and sour husband, Casaubon (Ian Drysdale), who serves as the highlight in Part One, happy to marry a much younger woman but disdainful in the face of marital intimacy.Eliot’s book has sometimes been seen as a satire of middle England, and Nina Raine’s script leans into humour, tipping into a bumptious broadness, which verges on pantomime entertainment in scenes featuring Peter Featherstone (Peter Forbes) on his deathbed, his hands gripped around his money box. He is played like a provincial Scrooge, his greedy family comprising a tableaux of other Dickensian types around him in the inheritance wrangles.Raine treads a fine line between faithfulness and invention, keeping many of Eliot’s lines but turning the omniscient narrator into a character (Amanda Root). It becomes clear that this is Eliot herself, not only watching over her story but listening to characters divulge anxieties or yearning, and sometimes interrupting them, mid-scene. It is a very inventive way to get around delivering a backstory without clumsy exposition, but it feels too much like a device.View image in fullscreenTreading a fine line between faithfulness and invention … Middlemarch.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe author Tom McCarthy recently argued that Middlemarch has been middlebrowed and “heritage-industried to death,” in a podcast for London Review of Books, and this production runs the risk of doing the same by the end of this first half. But then the heavens open and it seems, for a book so preoccupied with divinity, that Eliot herself has descended to touch it with her greatness. Part Two finds its footing and doesn’t take one wrong step: the humour working brilliantly in occasional flecks, the drama leading with emotion, thought and the everyday tragedy of marital disappointment. The piano music, by Nathan Feeney, which sounded so mannered, now seems emotionally integrated. Characters come fiercely, painfully, to life. Dorothea, now a widow, carries great depths. The marriage between debt-worn Lydgate and his starkly withdrawn wife, Rosamond, is heartbreaking. Take away the 19th-century costumes and their marital friction would feel utterly contemporary. Each scene shakes you, each performer excels.The interaction between these characters and the narrator takes on a lovely, tender texture, too. She challenges or soothes them in their worst moments, like a mother would. Eliot’s narration excels in its sustained compassion for the most fallen of characters and Raine’s script does the same. You feel for Casaubon with his writerly paralysis over his unwritten magnum opus, The Key to All Mythologies (the narrator, Eliot, voices her own sympathies), and you even feel for the rapacious Nicholas Bulstrode (John Hodgkinson), for his inability to do good.Marriage is a “noose,” warns Dorothea’s uncle at the start, but there is a return to the “marriage plot” in Eliot’s work, however much she is said to have upturned it. The romance between Ladislaw and Dorothea is heady, intense and also – to invoke the words of Virginia Woolf – very “grownup”. You want happiness for them, for her. You believe in this second go at it.AtSwan theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, until 16 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreGeorge EliotRoyal Shakespeare CompanyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bram Stoker’s Dracula audiobook review – cinematic horror with an A-list cast | Bram Stoker | The Guardian
description: Jonathan Bailey, Ella Purnell, Aimee-Lou Wood, Maggie Gyllenhaal and more bring shock and gore to an immersive retelling with real bite
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: Jonathan Bailey, Ella Purnell, Aimee-Lou Wood, Maggie Gyllenhaal and more bring shock and gore to an immersive retelling with real bite
Content: Gothic garlic-wielding … Maggie Gyllenhaal.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/Getty Images for NetflixView image in fullscreenGothic garlic-wielding … Maggie Gyllenhaal.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/Getty Images for NetflixAudiobook of the weekBram StokerReviewBram Stoker’s Dracula audiobook review – cinematic horror with an A-list castJonathan Bailey, Ella Purnell, Aimee-Lou Wood, Maggie Gyllenhaal and more bring shock and gore to an immersive retelling with real biteFiona SturgesThu 29 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo we really need another retelling of Bram Stoker’s fabled horror novel, which has already yielded multiple films, plays and radio dramas? Perhaps not, but this new audio version of Dracula, directed by Mary Lambert and adapted by Robyn Aherne, justifies its existence with an unusually star-studded cast, a streamlined story and an immersive and frequently nightmarish sound palette.Bridgerton’s Jonathan Bailey is smooth and charismatic as the eponymous count who invites a young solicitor, Jonathan Harker (Louis Partridge), to his castle in Transylvania to assist him with the sale of a property. There, Harker becomes increasingly uneasy as he glimpses the count’s diabolical powers and realises that he is, in fact, a prisoner.Meanwhile, there are strange goings-on in Whitby, England, where Jonathan’s fiancee Mina (Ella Purnell) is visiting her friend Lucy (Aimee Lou Wood). Shortly after a Russian ship is found wrecked on the shore with its captain murdered and its crew nowhere to be seen, Lucy has an unusual encounter in a graveyard that leaves her with puncture wounds on her throat and prone to night terrors. David Jonsson plays the doctor who tends to Lucy, while Maggie Gyllenhaal is brilliantly cast as garlic-wielding vampire hunter Van Helsing.This adaptation comes with a haunting score by Ilan Eshkeri and cinematic sound that plunges the listener into Dracula’s castle with its disembodied voices and echoing corridors (this is a series best heard via headphones). It doesn’t shrink from the shock and gore, either, even though the blood-sucking scenes are done sparingly and without a hint of camp.Available via Audible Originals, 5hr 57minFurther listeningA Rebel and a TraitorRory Carroll, HarperCollins, 11hr 24minThe Killing Thatcher author trawls through letters, police reports and declassified government documents to tell the story of Sir Roger Casement, the British diplomat who became an Irish nationalist and fierce critic of British imperialism.
