title: The Big Moon: Forever review – the hell of hearing loss inspires a defiantly hopeful pop-disco marvel | Music | The Guardian
description: After frontperson Juliette Jackson lost half her hearing, she wrote sad songs and felt frustrated. So she pivoted, writing herself a happy ending. The results are joyfully convincing
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: After frontperson Juliette Jackson lost half her hearing, she wrote sad songs and felt frustrated. So she pivoted, writing herself a happy ending. The results are joyfully convincing
Content: ‘An extra frisson’ … Celia Archer, Juliette Jackson (in red), Soph Nathan and Fern Ford of the Big Moon.Photograph: Melanie LehmannView image in fullscreen‘An extra frisson’ … Celia Archer, Juliette Jackson (in red), Soph Nathan and Fern Ford of the Big Moon.Photograph: Melanie LehmannMusicReviewThe Big Moon: Forever review – the hell of hearing loss inspires a defiantly hopeful pop-disco marvel(Fiction)After frontperson Juliette Jackson lost half her hearing, she wrote sad songs and felt frustrated. So she pivoted, writing herself a happy ending. The results are joyfully convincingDave SimpsonThu 29 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the outside, it looks as if things have gone swimmingly for the Big Moon. Fronted by Juliette Jackson, a former waitress who dreamed big, they have been active for 12 years, a success in itself in these days, notching up four albums including this latest. They have enjoyed a Mercury nomination (for 2017 debut Love in the 4th Dimension), decent chart positions, good-sized gigs and streaming figures in the hundreds of thousands, or millions in the case of 2019 single Your Light.View image in fullscreenThe Big Moon: Forever.Delve beneath the surface, however, and things haven’t always been so sunny. After their debut’s ramshackle wide-eyed pop, second album Walking Like We Do detailed the travails of contemporary womanhood, and Your Light found Jackson bemoaning her generation’s lot with a weary resignation: “We were promised the world, but so was everyone else”. 2022’s Here Is Everything was conceived during Covid and processed Jackson’s life-changing experience of becoming a mother, including the disorienting experience of lack of sleep. Tricky stuff, if nothing that made Jackson’s concerns much different from vast swathes of the population.Forever, though, has a much more troubling backdrop. In 2024, the singer was diagnosed with a cholesteatoma – a destructive cyst inside the middle ear that requires surgical removal. It caused her to lose most of her hearing on one side, which would be an alarming and unbalancing experience for anyone, never mind someone whose life and livelihood centres so much on sound. As she admits: “It was pretty much existential, because writing songs is my job and my identity.” When she was even able to think about writing songs, she understandably found herself writing material so throughly miserable she didn’t like it. At which point she did a complete volte face, and began writing songs not just to cheer herself up but actively imagining “a happy ending that didn’t exist yet”.The Big Moon: Gravity – videoThere are historical precedents for such a sudden pivot from agony to ecstasy. One thinks of New Order throwing off the bleakness of Ian Curtis’s death, and their grand but morose debut Movement, to blissfully reconfigure for Temptation and Power, Corruption and Lies; the Cure’s mid-80s pop rush after years of magnificently anguished albums, or Bon Iver’s move from the melancholy For Emma, Forever Ago, recorded in an isolated log cabin, to the lush, more celebratory Bon Iver, Bon Iver. Here, Jackson’s personal shift results in a collection of joyous, uplifting, ethereally classy pop-disco tunes that have an extra frisson because they have come about through sadness. Shimmery opener Gravity clings to the simple joy of picking up your child from nursery, an unlikely but effective launchpad for a rapturous pop song with shades of Dreaming-era Blondie.Three Things celebrates youth and pop (“My whole life imminent / I remember living inside the songs on the radio”), the wistful undercurrent carefully smothered in bouncy, MGMT-style keyboard riffs and juddering sequencers straight out of new wave and disco. The universally relatable Fun imagines a life beyond constraints – “I’ll slip away and take my brain on holiday” – the dreamily summery sounds recalling Haim and, appropriately, Madonna circa Holiday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I’d rather live through something publicly than escape it privately’: Jack Antonoff on survivor’s guilt and still singing love songs after his breakupRead moreIf Jackson’s lyrics have a recurring theme, it’s of relishing – rather than fearing – life’s transience. Delicate harmonies, Fleetwood Mac production gloss and Soph Nathan’s big guitar twangs power recent single F.O.R.E.V.E.R, a rather poetic song about grabbing moments and milestones while we can, because “some day the ocean will include the drinks that we spill / And rain that used to be red wine will fall on this hill”. The yearning, classic 60s pop-tinged Can I Get a Reading Please picks up the theme: “Life’s not long, regret is though / Can you tell me something I don’t know?” The slightly country Sounds gets even darker – “I’m going to lose something very dear to me, if not now eventually” – but such shadows are more than banished by the overall musical sunniness and loveliness.The Bananarama-ish I See You, Honey seems to celebrate the comfort of being loved (“There’s no need to say ‘I love you’, it’s everywhere to me”). Other songs celebrate the power of determination as Jackson is “pushing through” obstacles in Speed Bump or insisting “I can give a good life / As long as I’m still on my feet” during Sounds. The album’s sense of finding joy in sometimes difficult circumstances crystallises on the wonderfully titled You Remind Me That I’m Dying (And That It’s Good to Be Alive), those words providing what may well be this year’s most bittersweet euphoric chorus. “Happy endings that don’t exist yet” or not, the song is an absolute banger, which suggests Jackson and her band really do have a lot to smile about.This week Dave listened toNell Davies – Never Ever EverI caught this Penzance-based DIY singer-guitarist’s ace set in Leeds. She tours by train and sounds, wonderfully, like an effervescent, witty, one-woman Buzzcocks.Alexis Petridis is awayExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sarah Howe wins Forward poetry prize for best collection | Poetry | The Guardian
description: Howe’s ‘exceptional’ Foretokens took the main £10,000 award, while Nur Turkmani, Tara Bergin and Biff Smith swept up the remaining categories
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Howe’s ‘exceptional’ Foretokens took the main £10,000 award, while Nur Turkmani, Tara Bergin and Biff Smith swept up the remaining categories
Content: ‘A quite brilliant return’ … Sarah Howe.Photograph: Marc LixenbergView image in fullscreen‘A quite brilliant return’ … Sarah Howe.Photograph: Marc LixenbergPoetrySarah Howe wins Forward poetry prize for best collectionHowe’s ‘exceptional’ Foretokens took the main £10,000 award, while Nur Turkmani, Tara Bergin and Biff Smith swept up the remaining categoriesEmma LoffhagenThu 29 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarah Howe has won the Forward prize for best collection, one of the UK’s most prestigious poetry awards, for Foretokens, a collection that explores new parenthood, the death of her father and her mother’s early life in Hong Kong.Howe was announced as the winner during a ceremony hosted by Joelle Taylor at London’s Southbank Centre on Saturday evening, and will receive £10,000.Howe was born in Hong Kong to an English father and a Chinese mother. Foretokens, her second collection, comes a decade afterLoop of Jadebecame thefirst debut to win the TS Eliot prize. Foretokens was also shortlisted for the 2025 TS Eliot prize.Reviewing Foretokensfor the Guardian,Rishi Dastidar called it “a quite brilliant return”, praising Howe’s “keen, probing intelligence”. “Taking on the biggest of subjects – genetics, time’s relativity, becoming a parent – as well as re-examining her mother’s occluded history in Hong Kong, there is now an anger in Howe’s tonal range, which brings a pleasing sharpness to her investigations,” he wrote.View image in fullscreenThe 2026 Forward prize winners, Nur Turkmani, Sarah Howe, Biff Smith and Tara Bergin.Photograph: Forward prizeThe Forward prizes’ co-executive director, Mónica Parle, described Foretokens as “an exceptional collection” that “can emerge after 10 years in the making and still bear distinct relevance to our time”.The prize also recognised three other winners. Nur Turkmani, a Lisbon-based poet who grew up in Beirut, won the £5,000 Jerwood prize for best first collection for October, which was also shortlisted for this year’s PEN Heaney prize. The poems were mostly written in Beirut during a period when “there were protests, wildfires, economic collapse, a port explosion and an ongoing war”, Turkmani said, “and writing became a way of seeing, understanding and continuing”. It is the first nomination and first win for her publisher, the independent Hajar Press.The Dublin-born poet Tara Bergin, who teaches creative writing at Newcastle University, won the Forward prize for best single poem in written form for The Fear, first published in the Irish literary magazine the Stinging Fly. “Many years ago I devised a poetry writing class called ‘Fear Poetry’,” she said. “I got so interested in the whole idea I had to try it myself.”The Scottish singer-songwriter Biff Smith, who won both the Scottish and World Poetry Slam Championships last year, received the prize for best single poem in the performance category for Dumbarton East, recorded at the Scottish performance night Loud Poets. Smith wrote the poem on a train: “So much of life is spent in transit, I feel an urge to make that time count – do some knitting, learn Italian or whatever (maybe even write a poem).” Bergin and Smith each received £1,000.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis year’s judges were the novelist Sarah Moss, who chaired the panel, alongside Romalyn Ante, WN Herbert, Michael Mullen and Yomi Ṣode. “In months when the world could easily seem darker every week, it was consoling to be called back into poems and collections and performances day after day,” said Moss, “not because poetry is any kind of panacea but because poets give us words, images and metaphors for what matters in interesting times.”The Forward prizes were established in 1992 and have recognised some of the biggest names in poetry, including Seamus Heaney, Ted Hughes and Claudia Rankine. Last year,the best collection prize was sharedfor the first time in its history, between Vidyan Ravinthiran for Avidyā and Karen Solie for Wellwater.Explore more on these topicsPoetryForward prize for poetryAwards and prizesSarah HowenewsShareReuse this content

title: Elke Sommer, prolific German star of A Shot in the Dark and And Then There Were None, dies aged 85 | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Berlin-born performer had a gift for languages that took her to Hollywood, landing roles alongside Peter Sellers, Dick Van Dyke and Paul Newman
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The Berlin-born performer had a gift for languages that took her to Hollywood, landing roles alongside Peter Sellers, Dick Van Dyke and Paul Newman
Content: Bombshell image … Elke Sommer.Photograph: Kobal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBombshell image … Elke Sommer.Photograph: Kobal/ShutterstockMoviesElke Sommer, prolific German star of A Shot in the Dark and And Then There Were None, dies aged 85The Berlin-born performer had a gift for languages that took her to Hollywood, landing roles alongside Peter Sellers, Dick Van Dyke and Paul NewmanAndrew PulverThu 29 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElke Sommer, the prolific German star of the Pink Panther film A Shot in the Dark, early 70s Agatha Christie adaptation And Then there Were None, and British sex comedy Carry on Behind, has died aged 85.Bild magazine reportedthat Sommer died in Los Angeles of heart failure.German-born Sommer, whose best-known film roles were in the 1960s and 70s, was one of the wave of European performers who crossed over to Hollywood and English-language cinema with considerable success, following the postwar emergence of European new wave cinema. Sommer was one of the few German actors to make waves at the time, as Hollywood made much of her bombshell image.View image in fullscreenHollywood breakthrough … Elke Sommer with Paul Newman in The Prize.Photograph: Moviestore/ShutterstockBorn Elke Schletz in 1940 in Berlin, the daughter of a Protestant pastor, she was evacuated with her family to Bavaria during the war. Intending to work as an interpreter, she was spotted by celebrated Italian director Vittorio De Sica after winning a beauty contest on a trip to Italy in 1958, and subsequently offered roles in a string of Italian comedy films. She crossed back into more serious work with the West German drama The Death Ship, opposite Horst Buchholz (who would go on to appear in cowboy classic The Magnificent Seven).With her gift for languages, Sommer made her first film in English, the 1961 British comedy Don’t Bother to Knock, opposite Richard Todd, and was billed as one of the “six most exciting women in the world” alongside Melina Mercouri, Jeanne Moreau and Romy Schneider in Carl Foreman’s 1963 war fable, The Victors. Sommer’s Hollywood breakthrough arrived in the same year, with The Prize; she was cast as Paul Newman’s lover in an adaptation of Irving Wallace’s hit novel, for which she was a joint winner of a most promising newcomer Golden Globe.View image in fullscreenLeaning into her ‘sexpot’ image … with Peter Sellers in A Shot in the Dark.Photograph: Moviestore/ShutterstockSommer’s Hollywood career then took off with A Shot in the Dark, in which she leaned heavily into her “sexpot” image as a maid suspected of a series of murders in the sequel to The Pink Panther, starring Peter Sellers. Following its success, Sommer appeared in a string of high profile Hollywood films, including The Art of Love with James Garner and Dick Van Dyke, The Oscar with Stephen Boyd, and the Bob Hope comedy Boy, Did I Get a Wrong Number! In 1968, she achieved leading actor status with The Wicked Dreams of Paula Schultz, a comedy about an East German athlete who pole-vaults over the Berlin Wall.In the 1970s, Sommer appeared in two cult horror films by Mario Bava, Baron Blood and Lisa and the Devil, and sex comedies Percy and Percy’s Progress for British director Ralph Thomas. She followed these with two high-profile British films: as secretary Vera Clyde in And Then There Were None in 1974, adapted from Christie’s hit novel, and a year later, Carry on Behind, the 27th in the Carry On series.View image in fullscreenIn Mario Bava’s cult horror Lisa and the Devil.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockAfter another Sellers film, The Prisoner of Zenda, and Ralph Thomas’s heist film A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square, Sommer scaled back her screen appearances and concentrated on painting. In the mid-1980s, she also became embroiled in a long-running feud with Zsa Zsa Gabor after they appeared together on TV show Circus of the Stars;Sommer was ultimately awarded $3.3min damages for defamation.Sommer was married twice, to writer Joe Hyams from 1964 until 1981, and hotelier Wolf Walther from 1993 until his death in 2026.Explore more on these topicsFilmGermanyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Dónal Lunny obituary | Folk music | The Guardian
description: Producer and musician who played with the influential Irish folk bands Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts
Author: Derek Schofield
Headline: Producer and musician who played with the influential Irish folk bands Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts
Content: Dónal Lunny played a vital role as arranger, ‘instinctively drawn to developing new harmonic and rhythmic structures’.Photograph: Dave Peabody/RedfernsView image in fullscreenDónal Lunny played a vital role as arranger, ‘instinctively drawn to developing new harmonic and rhythmic structures’.Photograph: Dave Peabody/RedfernsFolk musicObituaryDónal Lunny obituaryProducer and musician who played with the influential Irish folk bands Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving HeartsDerek SchofieldThu 29 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDónal Lunny, who has died of cancer aged 79, was a multi-instrumentalist in three of the most influential folk bands of the late 20th century: Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts. He played the guitar, keyboards and bodhrán, but he is best remembered for popularising the bouzouki in Irish traditional music. The round-bodied bouzouki from Greece was adapted by Lunny, resulting in a flat-backed instrument with a shorter neck known as the Irish bouzouki.Lunny often worked in collaboration with the singer and songwriter Christy Moore and the musician Andy Irvine. In all the bands with which he was associated, Lunny played a vital role in arranging the music, being instinctively drawn to developing new harmonic and rhythmic structures. He produced many Irish music albums, also working with artists including Elvis Costello, Kate Bush, Sinéad O’Connor and Mark Knopfler. As a composer, he wrote and arranged the music for films, documentaries and television programmes. In 1991, he was the musical director of the joint BBC and RTÉ television series Bringing It All Back Home, which won an Emmy.Born in Tullamore, County Offaly, Dónal was the fifth of nine children of Mary (nee Rogers), a teacher, and Frank Lunny, an engineer. The family moved to Newbridge, County Kildare, when Dónal was five and he attended Newbridge college before studying at the National College of Art and Design in Dublin. He played drums in a pop band, the Cyclones, at school, and then, alongside his brother Frank and schoolfriend Moore, Dónal played the guitar in a band called Rakes of Kildare. In Dublin he played in the Parnell Folk; with the band Emmet Spiceland he even had a No 1 hit, Mary from Dungloe, in 1968.Lunny was introduced to the bouzouki by Irvine, who brought one back from his European travels in 1970. Together they formed a duo in Dublin but were soon recruited, along with the uilleann piper Liam O’Flynn, by Moore to play on his groundbreaking album Prosperous (1971). The four musicians soon decided to form Planxty.View image in fullscreenLunny, second from right, in London in 1973, with fellow members of Planxty: from left, Andy Irvine, Liam O’Flynn and Christy Moore.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesPlanxty took the Chieftains’ concept of group instrumental playing to a new level with different instrumentation, combining it with traditional and new songs, in contrast to the ballad groups, such as the Clancy Brothers, who relied mainly on guitar and banjo. Planxty’s first gigs were as support for Donovan. An eponymous album in 1973 was followed by The Well Below the Valley in the same year. Moore recently reflected that Planxty would not have succeeded without “the genius and creativity of Dónal”.Despite Planxty’s immediate success, Lunny left the band in 1973, only to return for a reunion of the four original members in 1979. Extensive touring, both inIrelandand internationally, followed. In 1981 they played the interval music at the Eurovision song contest in Dublin, as composed by Bill Whelan and Lunny. Called Timedance, this was the original idea behind Whelan’s later hit show Riverdance, though this was composed without Lunny. Planxty albums included After the Break (1979) and Words and Music (1983), after which the band split up.Wishing to develop his music in new directions, Lunny joined the Bothy Band in 1975. The band had a rock music vibe, in part created by the clavinet, a type of electric keyboard, played by Tríona Ní Dhomhnaill. The solid traditional music sound came from Paddy Keenan on pipes,Tommy Peopleson fiddle and Matt Molloy on flute. The band’s distinctive percussive, rhythmic sound was created by Lunny on bouzouki and Triona’s brotherMícheál Ó Domhnaillon guitar. They recorded on the Mulligan record label, newly created by Lunny who, by this time, was becoming well known as a record producer. The Bothy Band enjoyed great success but, as Lunny said, they “ran out of energy”; they split up in 1979.After the Planxty reunion, Moore and Lunny formed Moving Hearts in 1981. Lunny wanted to further explore the use of bass and percussion alongside his rhythmic and percussive style on the bouzouki, and Moore had songs that did not suit the Planxty sound. Moving Hearts featured a rock/jazz drummer, a rock guitarist and a saxophonist as well as the uilleann piper Davy Spillane. The combination of contemporary sounds and styles plus Moore’s political songs about Northern Ireland and the hunger strikes further pushed the boundaries. After several changes of personnel, the band split up in 1984.View image in fullscreenLunny performing with Moving Hearts in 2008 in Lorient, France.Photograph: Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty ImagesMozaik was Lunny’s next band: an ambitious collaboration between Lunny, Irvine, the Hungarian singer Márta Sebestyén, the Scots singer Dougie MacLean and the uilleann piper Declan Masterson. The band went into abeyance after several tours but returned in 2002 with different musicians alongside Lunny and Irvine, including the Bulgarian-born Nikola Parov. They toured internationally and made three albums, the most recent in 2019.There were other collaborations, many short-lived because of the difficulties of scheduling busy musicians. There were tours with Irvine and Paul Brady, a 1998 album and tour titled Coolfin, and the Atlantic Arc Orchestra, an ensemble of European artists from countries touching the Atlantic. The band Usher’s Island involved two generations of musicians, and there was a trio with Zoë Conway and Máirtín O’Connor, with whom Lunny performed in August this year.In 1996, Lunny produced an album, Common Ground, for EMI, which featured mainly Irish traditional songs sung by himself and a range of performers including Bono,Sinéad O’Connor, Costello and Bush, the last of whom sang a song in Gaelic that she learned phonetically. In the same year, Lunny played on Knopfler’s album Golden Heart.In 2018, Lunny received a lifetime achievement award at the BBC Radio 2 folk awards, and in 2025 a similar award at the RTÉ Radio 1 folk awards, presented by Moore, who also read the citation. In August this year, RTÉ broadcast a biographical documentary film,In Time: Dónal Lunny.Lunny was first married to Judy Slott, with whom he had a son, Oisin. With Julia Buthe he had a daughter, Cora Venus, and with Sinéad O’Connor he had a son,Shane, who died in 2022. With his second wife, Hideko Itami, Dónal had a daughter, Sora. Both marriages ended in divorce. He is survived by his partner Una O’Boyle, and by Oisin, Cora Venus and Sora.Dónal Lunny, folk musician, born 10 March 1947; died 23 October 2026Explore more on these topicsFolk musicIrelandobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Nocturne review – Stephen Graham is TV’s most evil serial killer … and it’s impossible to stop watching him  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The star plays a sadistic murderer still pulling the strings from behind bars. With his high-pitched giggles and fatal whispers, it is a perfectly terrifying show for Halloween
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The star plays a sadistic murderer still pulling the strings from behind bars. With his high-pitched giggles and fatal whispers, it is a perfectly terrifying show for Halloween
Content: Stephen Graham in a scene from Nocturne.Photograph: Dennis P Mong Jr/Apple TVView image in fullscreenStephen Graham in a scene from Nocturne.Photograph: Dennis P Mong Jr/Apple TVTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewNocturne review – Stephen Graham is TV’s most evil serial killer … and it’s impossible to stop watching himThe star plays a sadistic murderer still pulling the strings from behind bars.  With his high-pitched giggles and fatal whispers, it is a perfectly terrifying show for HalloweenLucy ManganThu 29 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has taken a while, but I think the torch may finally have passed from Anthony Hopkins as the screen’s most profoundly unsettling and instantly-absorbed-by-the-cultural-imagination serial killer. From Hannibal’s hitherto unfailing hands it has been thrown toStephen Graham, who plays multiple murderer Jurek Walter in the new 10-part psychological thriller Nocturne.Walter, who draws out the deaths of his victims in order to torture their families as much as the individuals themselves, is incarcerated for life in the bowels of Riverside psychiatric hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He passes the time by doing push-ups, stashing contraband behind his toilet bowl for as-yet-unspecified purposes, and driving fellow inmates to suicide by whispering to them through the pipes. Graham – muscle-bound, preternaturally still and occasionally emitting a high-pitched giggle – is mesmerising and utterly terrifying.He soon has his hooks into his new nurse, Karl (Rory Culkin), who is too young, inexperienced and tender-hearted to heed the staff’s warnings about the manipulative monster in the basement. Walter has a way, as one former nurse notes, of making you feel sorry for him – “a man who buried people alive”. Soon Walter has Karl offering up personal information and carrying illicit messages to his supposed lawyer.View image in fullscreenHoodwinked … Rory Culkin in Nocturne.Photograph: Apple TVIn addition to the murders he was convicted for, Walter is also suspected of abducting and killing two children, Michael and Felicia Frost, though their bodies were never found. When Michael (Landon Valentin) stumbles out of the woods after three years, the man who was in charge of the Frost case, Jonah Lynn, comes out of voluntary retirement to work out if and how he was wrong, and where Felicia might be. Lynn (Liev Schreiber) is still grieving for the wife and son he lost in an accident and the partner who killed himself. The question of whether these many sorrows threaten to make him reckless in pursuit of the truth or merely relentless is one of the many uncertainties that will come to infuse the story.His late partner’s child, Saga (Zazie Beetz), is an FBI agent who has become a surrogate daughter to Lynn. Which is why he is not best pleased when, as the police begin to suspect that Walter has smuggled out a note telling an accomplice to release Michael, she insists that the best way for them to find out more is for her to go undercover as a patient at the facility.In she goes, parlaying her experience with a long-institutionalised mother into something useful – palming pills, fighting off assaults from other staff members and behaving badly enough to get herself sent down to the basement and become Walter’s neighbour. Can you pretend to be criminally insane without jeopardising your own sanity? Can you instigate a relationship with someone who lives to unearth weaknesses in others and exploit them without getting suckered in? Can you exist within a dehumanising system and keep your sense of self, let alone a professional self, intact? More uncertainties and ambiguities gather.‘I felt like I was a made man’: Stephen Graham on working with his childhood heroesRead moreNocturne is adapted, by Rowan Joffé, from two volumes of the Joona Linna series by Lars Kepler (the nom de plume of husband-and-wife team Alexander Ahndoril and Alexandra Coelho Ahndoril). As with most Scandi noir, their books are slow burns, and so too is Nocturne, though the series’ focus is narrower – there is less space given to the impact of Walter’s crimes on the community and more to his present influence on those around him.This means that certain roles are underdeveloped, despite some beautiful work from the cast (particularly veteran character actors Bill Camp as the harrowed police chief and Chrissy Metz as the children’s mother). They do, however, give glimpses of how the series might have been strengthened by a little more emphasis on the trail of suffering caused rather than just its execution; if perhaps a few twists and revelations had been cleared for emotional delineation and investment instead. There is a slight but growing sense as the series wears on that it is just a bit less impressive than it was shaping up to be, a little more hollow than it thinks.Then Graham appears again and the adrenaline that floods your system in the presence of his radiant evil pushes all rational thoughts from your mind, and you are captivated once more. It is the perfect watch for Halloween, especially for those of us who are always more horrified by the menace that stalks the earth in all-too-human form than by anything they say the supernatural can throw at us.Nocturne streams on Apple TV from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionStephen GrahamThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: South Park turns to America’s beef shortage – and explodes in diarrhea | South Park | The Guardian
description: The 29th season has begun to slightly spin its wheels, but this poo-splattered episode suggests an imminent story arc: the release of Grand Theft Auto VI
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: The 29th season has begun to slightly spin its wheels, but this poo-splattered episode suggests an imminent story arc: the release of Grand Theft Auto VI
Content: Check the label for any side effects of consuming South Park beef.Photograph: ParamountView image in fullscreenCheck the label for any side effects of consuming South Park beef.Photograph: ParamountSouth ParkSouth Park turns to America’s beef shortage – and explodes in diarrheaThe 29th season has begun to slightly spin its wheels, but this poo-splattered episode suggests an imminent story arc: the release of Grand Theft Auto VIJesse HassengerThu 29 Oct 2026 00.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 08.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAre record beef shortages simply not that rich a topic forSouth Parkto riff off? The show’s 29th season had its first outright middling episode this week with a zigzaggy outing that gestured vaguely toward the performative eating of particular foods, nodded slightly at a father-son story development, and wound it all up by repeating and amplifying a funny season-long running gag that increasingly seems like it will actually serve as a makeshift story arc.But let’s jump back to the beginning, perhaps the most laugh-out-loud moment of the episode: Cartman in a fugue of delight over the impending meal of sloppy joes at the school cafeteria, to which he forms a tribute in the form of a sloppy-joe-themed version of Gary Glitter’s Rock and Roll Part Two – a music clearance reaffirming that Trey Parker and Matt Stone don’t care if a song choice might make people tut-tut (because the singer is a serial sex offender) or just annoyed (because that song sucks). Cartman’s infectious glee is short-lived, however, when he’s informed that the lunch special for the day isn’t a sloppy joe after all, or anything beef-related, butcuy– Guinea Pig on a stick.South Park takes on looksmaxxing, aura-farming and influencer nonsense with grotesque gleeRead moreThis is anactual Peruvian dish, to match with South Park’s season-long rechristening as South America. And thanks to its patriotic (if confusingly so) bona fides, beef farmed in South, uh, America is in higher demand than ever in the rest of the country. So while it’s a beef town, no one who lives there can actually get a reasonably priced cut of meat. This despite the fact that frequent cutaways, usually to Ruth’s Chris Steakhouse, reveal that South Park beef, rich and buttery as it is, gives people who eat it literally explosive diarrhea after one bite (and yes, obviously this is shown in great cartoonish detail.) This side-effect does not sate demand for the beef; consuming it is seen as a patriotic act.This seems like both a commentary on the actual beef shortage in the United States, as well as theMAHA-driven desirefor stuff like beef tallow. This week’s South Park – “Guinea Pig on a Stick” is the episode title – doesn’t get into all that, but there are certainly undertones in the way it depicts demand for larded-up beef from faraway elites. The steakhouse clientele are all drawn to look like the show’s celebrity caricatures, even though none of them are quite an exact match for any real figure that I could recognize. It’s a metaphor for the episode at large, which perpetually feels like it’s satirizing something bigger and more direct but doesn’t quite come into focus.Part of the problem is that the beef shortage dilemma only lightly dovetails with the episode’s wispy kid plot, which is that Stan’s dad Randy, still in a miniaturized child’s body afterthe previous episode’s Sephora looksmaxxing mishap, wants to be one of the gang. Kyle and Cartman both seem willing to shrug him off, but Stan keeps snapping at him. It’s understandable; it’s annoying that Randy oscillates between off-trend kid obsessions (laughing about Italian brainrot) and his own dad-aged references (he simply refuses to shut up about the Goonies). But he does sincerely want to connect with Stan, and eventually everyone kinda tells Stan he’s being a jerk. Stan softens in the face of his dad’s sincerity.View image in fullscreenStan’s dad Randy, still in a miniaturized child’s body after a Sephora looksmaxxing mishap, wants to be one of the gang.Photograph: ParamountThe kids do come up with a solution to the beef shortage after a violent showdown between Ruth Chris herself (not her actual name; that would be Ruth Fertel, the founder of the confoundingly named chain) and the fake cowboys who run the Sizzler. Sizzler runs away with all of the cows in town, even the ones that might have been consigned to the cattle farm’s champagne room (a funny idea that turns out to be a momentary gag), and like everyone else in the South Park universe this season, Ruth Chris says issues like this will be massively affected by a big change that’s on deck for November.As before, she means the release ofGrand Theft Auto VI.Unlike in previous episodes, this joke is finally elaborated upon: Ruth Chris shows a top-secret video of GTA gameplay, opening the kids’ (and Randy’s) eyes to just how much things could indeed change in November. Maybe this will remain a running gag, but the way it’s brought to the foreground now, almost in lieu of an actual resolution, makes it seem like it will figure into the season finale (which does, after all, air not too long after the game’s release). So, wait, is this a piece-moving episode? Of South Park?! It sounds absurd, like a recapper reading an irreverent animated comedy like it’s a self-serious serialized show – but it does feel like the endgame.In the meantime, the kids do figure out what to do about the beef shortage. They rebrand Guinea Pig on a stick as a particularly patriotic delicacy; it turns out the steakhouse customers don’t care what they’re eating so long as it’s got that American branding and is larded up with plenty of rich butter. With the right preparation, Guinea Pig on a stick can provide the exact same explosive diarrhea – and so we’re treated to the episode-closing sight of diners exploding into fecal matter, now with an extra hue of red and blue fireworks in accompaniment. Again, a pretty funny gross-out sight gag, but no moreso than the first dozen times. Weirdly, this episode of South Park made me look forward to Grand Theft Auto VI, too, assuming there’s now a fun storyline building up to it.South Park is streaming on Paramount+ in the US, UK and Australia.Explore more on these topicsSouth ParkTelevisionAnimation on TVUS televisionTV comedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Are You With Me Now? by Hanif Kureishi review – a novelist unleashed | Hanif Kureishi | The Guardian
description: The constraints of Kureishi’s life after a devastating accident infuse his writing with a new and thrilling immediacy
Author: Melissa Denes
Headline: The constraints of Kureishi’s life after a devastating accident infuse his writing with a new and thrilling immediacy
Content: Hanif Kureshi.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHanif Kureshi.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianBook of the dayHanif KureishiAre You With Me Now? by Hanif Kureishi review – a novelist unleashedThe constraints of Kureishi’s life after a devastating accident infuse his writing with a new and thrilling immediacyMelissa DenesThu 29 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome months after returning home, after a grim year in hospitals in Rome and London,Hanif Kureishibegins to rebel. Not against his family, or the physical reality of beingtetraplegic(and how could he?), but the liberal homogeneity of Shepherd’s Bush. He gets a diamond stud in his left ear at Westfield shopping centre, a piercing that enraged his father when he was 17. He sends off for a Maga cap and wears both to the farmers’ market, hoping for vitriol but getting nothing. “These quiescent scumbags only cared about themselves and their shopping,” he grumbles. “Being a fascist is far less thrilling than I imagined.”Kureishi’s “re-punking” after decades in the metropolitan elite remains an ongoing project, just one response to his paralysis after a fall on Boxing Day 2022. His memoirShatteredwas written in the long shock of that severance from a former life, which left him with no movement in his hands or legs, “a Beckettian chattering mouth”.But Kureishi’s mind remains intact, even unleashed: free from the pull of a phone (he can’t scroll), he is funny, nostalgic, profound, petty and never sentimental, not even about the family he relies on. His latest collection of essays, co-written with his son Carlo, takes its title from a song he used to listen to while driving in Italy, his partner Isabella at the wheel while he smoked a fat joint. (It’s also a question his iPad asks him in Shattered – “Are you still there?” – when paralysis leaves him unable to hit refresh.) Now, Carlo is always with him as he dictates, each chapter the product of a conversation between 10am and 1pm. The book has a more outward-looking feel – less stunned, less homesick, sometimes transcribed as a dialogue.double quotation markThere are great, gossipy digressions on taking acid with Billy Idol, a schoolmate, and his friendship with David BowieThese back-and-forths have a distinctive energy. An argument over what to write becomes a disquisition on art versus politics, Kureishi wanting to reflect on beauty, Carlo insisting that the only subject is Gaza. An experiment with a sex chatbot hits a wall of shared embarrassment. Carlo convinces his father of AI’s usefulness – but their collaboration is the perfect illustration of its limits: here are two humans with a long history of navigating each other’s weaknesses with love.Where to start with: Hanif KureishiRead moreThere are great, gossipy digressions on taking acid with Billy Idol, a schoolmate, and Kureishi’sfriendship with David Bowie. Bowie would call at 2am with an urgent question about serial killers, when Kureishi was “a new father of twins, dressed in only my underpants”. Dennis Hopper, Kureishi’s co-juror at the 1992 Venice film festival, was a disappointing square. Isabelle Huppert was a “sweet and intelligent” ally as jury president at Cannes 2009, “a frantic, crazy party that you could never leave”. He misses it all, but these memories push the horrors of the spinal injuries ward – the patient crawling across the floor at 2am, the bodies removed at dawn – that bit further away.Meanwhile, Kureishi has a house full of strangers, a drama he plays as comedy and farce. There are the carers fighting in the kitchen, and the nice woman who tells him “I really don’t like penises” as she washes his. Someone always has a finger up his arse. He and Carlo are working on a movie about his accident: who will play them, they wonder? But life is mostly a thousand small humiliations: in the park, an acquaintance pats him on the head.Kureishi revels in a new kind of writing – the essays were originally drafted as Substack posts – discursive, energised by a readership that writes back. His best novels have a clear-eyed quality that can border on cruelty – the famous “fucks for which a person would have their partner and children drown” in the autobiographical novel Intimacy. Here, that deep attention to his own ego expands to the world around him and becomes fiercely illuminating. What a thrill it is to be here, he writes from the edge of the abyss, as well as frustrating and often boring.The book ends with his marriage to Isabella, Elton John pulling up in a cherry-red Bentley. Kureishi is rawdogging life, he tells his son Sachin, in the gen Z sense of doing it without distraction: “I am compelled to be present”. Sex is difficult, but desire – for everything – remains. This exhilarating book looks death and decay in the face and asks: is that all you’ve got?Are You With Me Now? by Hanif Kureishi with Carlo Kureishi is published by Hamish Hamilton (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
