title: How did a fishmonger who starred in an adult movie make Rocky? The film about Sylvester Stallone’s amazing triumph | Movies | The Guardian
description: Belittled for his speech and looks, and so short of cash he had to sell his dog, Stallone managed to write and star in one of the greatest boxing movies ever. How does Anthony Ippolito feel about playing his hero?
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: Belittled for his speech and looks, and so short of cash he had to sell his dog, Stallone managed to write and star in one of the greatest boxing movies ever. How does Anthony Ippolito feel about playing his hero?
Content: ‘I ate a lot of protein’ … Ippolito re-enacts a famous scene in Rocky.Photograph: Claire Folger/Amazon MGM Studios/APView image in fullscreen‘I ate a lot of protein’ … Ippolito re-enacts a famous scene in Rocky.Photograph: Claire Folger/Amazon MGM Studios/APMoviesInterviewHow did a fishmonger who starred in an adult movie make Rocky? The film about Sylvester Stallone’s amazing triumphGwilym MumfordBelittled for his speech and looks, and so short of cash he had to sell his dog, Stallone managed to write and star in one of the greatest boxing movies ever. How does Anthony Ippolito feel about playing his hero?Thu 29 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 09.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifty years ago this December, cinema’s greatest underdog story hit the screen, a tale about a Philadelphia ham-and-egger who takes the world heavyweight boxing champ all the way to the final bell, losing the fight on a judge’s decision but winning the hearts of a nation. That film, of course, was Rocky. Its creation, famously, was no less remarkable an underdog story – one about an out-of-work character actor with the curious name ofSylvester Stallonewho wrote his own boxing movie then managed to convince a studio not only to finance it, but also to cast him in the title role. He then went one further than the character he was playing by earning the top prize: a best picture Oscar.If you thought, half a century on, Rocky’s punching power – its unerring ability to make heroes out of zeroes – has faded, think again. This, after all, is a movie franchise whose stirring qualities are enough to make thousands of people hurtle up all 72 of the Philadelphia Museum of Art’s steps every yearin homage to its plucky pugilist.View image in fullscreen‘They told me not to get my hopes up’ …Anthony Ippolito.Photograph: Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty ImagesAnd now Rocky has birthed a third great underdog story. This one is about a 27-year-old New Yorker who, through grit, persistence and a never-ending stream of unsolicited audition tapes, bags the role of a lifetime and propels himself into the Oscar running, alongside the likes of Tom Cruise, Matt Damon and John Malkovich. His name is Anthony Ippolito and he’s playing Sly Stallone himself in Peter Farrelly’s rousing, making-of movieI Play Rocky.The role, which follows Stallone from his early struggles in New York to movie greatness in LA, is one Ippolito has been circling – like Ali or Tyson rounding their prey – for years, before the project even had a script. Such was his desperation to play Stallone, he started sending in self-taped performances of what he thought those making the film might be after, an experience that felt like “sending your work into the abyss – even more so when no one’s asking for your audition in the first place”.It’s a process, Ippolito remembers with a wry smile, that could feel “a little discouraging”, particularly when film websites were tipping big names for the role – Superman David Corenswet, Jacob Elordi, even Timothée Chalamet. Ippolito recalls: “People around me said, ‘Don’t get your hopes up, they’re probably looking at bigger names. That’s Hollywood.’”He would not be deterred, though, and his self-confidence was justified: according to Farrelly, Ippolito was the first person he and the film’s producers looked at for the part. And once they saw him there was no point in auditioning anyone else.Speaking to Ippolito by video call from a hotel room in Rome, it’s not easy to discern immediately what made those producers so convinced of his Sly-ness. Granted, he doesn’t look dissimilar to Rocky-era Stallone – the square jaw and mop of dark hair are present and correct – but his features are softer, more boyband, and his voice is noticeably higher than Stallone’s bassy drawl. You’d be more likely to compare him to a young Al Pacino – fitting, as Ippolito played Pacino in another making-of project,The Offer, a TV series about the protracted creation of The Godfather.View image in fullscreenCan you beat up a frozen side of beef? … Ippolito as Stallone in I Play Rocky.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyYet the moment the opening credits of I PlayRockyroll, a remarkable transformation occurs. Ippolito’s voice drops an octave, and he affects that stuffy sinus-heavy delivery of Stallone’s. His eyes droop, his chin juts, his shoulders seem to grow rounder and he starts to move in that loping shuffle. He looks broader and more imposing, too – the result, Ippolito says, of a bulking-up regime that involved “a lot of eating, a lot of protein … it required an entire lifestyle shift”.It’s a performance that could so easily lapse into lazy caricature – or even worse, punching down, given that Stallone’s drooping features and slurred speech are the result of a forceps injury at birth. But Ippolito is so note perfect that even Stallone has been in touch to offer his approval. “He had a positive reaction and I’m very grateful – because this is, in a lot of ways, a love letter to what he persevered through.”The film, Ippolito says, covers a “very dark, lonely time” in Stallone’s life, when he worked in a fishmonger’s and appeared in an adult movie to scrape together rent. What serious roles he did get tended to be bit parts as tough guys, cops or thugs. He was routinely belittled for his speech and looks – particularly by his domineering father, played by Matt Dillon in the film. But Stallone had a remarkable raw talent hidden under the surface. “There’s this incongruence,” Ippolito says. “People would mistake him for being, um, maybe not smart – just a strong, burly guy with this slur. And then he’s actually a brilliant writer. Burt Young [his Rocky co-star] called him ‘an orphan in life’ with ‘a big fire burning and no place to put it’. You can feel this great depth and intensity.”View image in fullscreen‘Raw talent’ … Stallone as the plucky pugilist in Rocky (1976).Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyI Play Rocky doesn’t seem terribly preoccupied with these roiling internal dynamics – though that isn’t to its detriment. It’s not hard to see why crowds have chimed with the film, which turns Stallone’s story into part inspirational sports movie, part comedy caper. Farrelly has great fun in depicting the scrappy, seat-of-its-pants production of the original film, which couldn’t go a day over for risk of its studio shutting the whole thing down: scenes are rattled off in single, frenzied takes; Stallone limps through filming with a strained leg tendon, then a broken hand from punching a frozen side of beef in the film’s famous meat-locker scene; at one point, cast and crew have to squeeze into a walk-in freezer with their equipment to hide from a union rep threatening to take their filming permit away.The most entertaining section, though, comes before Rocky has even been greenlit, when the film’s producers are trying desperately to convince Stallone to give up the title role in return for a life-changing sum of money. No matter how many zeroes are added, Sly stands firm: no starring role, no deal. This despite him having few career prospects and a heavily pregnant wife. It’s a remarkable act of brinkmanship – at one point, Stallone is forced to sell his own dog to make ends meet – but it proves successful.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markThe film is being talked up for a best actor nominationStallone turned down $300,000, the equivalent of almost $2m today. Would Ippolito have gone to such extremes? “I don’t know, it’s a lot of money,” he laughs “I don’t want to make myself sound spineless! But it’s certainly tempting. I guess that’s what makes it so incredible, maddening almost. I think there’s a certain naive quality. Like he was able to just, at a young age, almost not know the rules so he could break them.”In another life, rather than playing an actor playing a boxer, Ippolito might have been a baseball player. At three years old, he was a pitching prodigy able to throw a ball at “40 miles per hour or something”, a talent that led him to appear on an episode of Ripley’s Believe it or Not!. For much of his childhood, playing baseball professionally was “the main goal”, and he carried on at a high level at college. “I learned a lot about acting inadvertently,” he says, “because there’s a ton of failure in that sport.”By his late teens, he had started to take acting seriously. He began picking up walk-on parts in films: David Chase’s coming of age movie Not Fade Away, where he got to watch James Gandolfini from afar; Julianne Moore comedy-drama The English Teacher; and Adam Sandler vehicle Pixels, where he first understood the appeal of doing this thing full-time. “I was like, ‘Wow, these guys look like they’re really having fun at work.’ That stuck out.”View image in fullscreenIppolito as Al Pacino in The Offer.Photograph: Nicole Wilder/Paramount+After college, his career moved up a gear: there was a main role in edgy Netflix high-school dramaGrand Army, then his appearance as Pacino in The Offer. How does it feel to play not one but two of the most famous actors alive? “It’ll throw you, for sure. But it’s also an incredible opportunity to explore stuff. There’s almost a voyeuristic quality to it – like an infinity staircase.”Now, with the success of I Play Rocky, Ippolito is finding himself among the big names, rather than impersonating them. He recently met Andrew Garfield and “is still recovering”. More encounters will surely come in awards season: his Stallone performance is being talked up for a best actor nomination, which would put him up against “people I’ve looked up to for the last 20 years”. Don’t count Anthony Ippolito out yet.I Play Rocky is in UK and US cinemas from 6 November and Australian cinemas from 1 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsFilmRockySylvester StalloneDrama filmsBiopicsSport filmsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wicker review – Olivia Colman finds the perfect lover in intriguing folk-horror romance | Movies | The Guardian
description: Colman stars as a depressed and bullied fisherwoman in medieval England. Fortunately, Peter Dinklage’s basketmaker delivers the answer to her dreams – an Alexander Skarsgård made of wicker
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Colman stars as a depressed and bullied fisherwoman in medieval England. Fortunately, Peter Dinklage’s basketmaker delivers the answer to her dreams – an Alexander Skarsgård made of wicker
Content: True love … Olivia Colman as the fisherwoman and Alexander Skarsgård as her wicker husband in Wicker.Photograph: Black Bear/PAView image in fullscreenTrue love … Olivia Colman as the fisherwoman and Alexander Skarsgård as her wicker husband in Wicker.Photograph: Black Bear/PAMoviesReviewWicker review – Olivia Colman finds the perfect lover in intriguing folk-horror romanceColman stars as a depressed and bullied fisherwoman in medieval England. Fortunately, Peter Dinklage’s basketmaker delivers the answer to her dreams – an Alexander Skarsgård made of wickerPeter BradshawThu 29 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe spirit of mystery author Shirley Jackson is interestingly revived in this peculiar folk-horror romance, adapted from a 2006 story called The Wicker Husband by British writer Ursula Wills. It’s almost funny but not exactly, and almost disturbing but not exactly, occupying a strange and intriguing Venn-diagram overlap between macabre horror and sentimentality. Yet devotees of bucolic British screen-scariness will note that it is, after all, about a wicker man.The scene is a fabular medieval-effect village that could be in central Europe or England, where there are bizarre patriarchal rituals, like the placing of metal collars on new brides. A depressed middle-aged fisherwoman (fiercely and naturalistically played by Olivia Colman) lives alone in a remote cottage and regularly brings her unappetising tench and gudgeon to market, where she is mocked and bullied by the nasty, closed-minded locals, including Richard E Grant as a lazy and incompetent doctor. Chief among her tormentors is the spiteful tailor’s wife, an elegant, sharp-faced woman played byElizabeth Debicki.But the fisherwoman, showing a good deal more imagination than everyone else, boldly approaches the Basketmaker (a droll performance from Peter Dinklage) and commissions him to make a wicker husband for her; this wicker hunk, magicked up in a secret workshop, is played byAlexander Skarsgård. His soulful eyes look out attractively from that weird wicker face.This new husband turns out to be an amazing catch: attentive, sensitive, non-toxically masculine, a wicker man of few words, great at fixing things in the cottage as he creaks self-effacingly around the place. (This is just as well as it’s still Colman who is earning a living for them both.) And above all, he is a wonderful lover; we don’t see his wicker genitals but there is evidently no problem with abrasion discomfort. (A movie more conventionally aware of comedy might have felt the need to explain this away a little more.)Instantly, the fisherwoman’s domestic bliss triggers poisonous envy among the sex-starved villagers, especially that noisome tailor’s wife. And it leads to an almost disquieting (and certainly amusing) climax of dismay.Wicker is out on 23 October in the US, on 30 October in the UK and 5 November in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmPeriod and historical filmsDrama filmsOlivia ColmanAlexander SkarsgårdScience fiction and fantasy filmsRomance filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: I Love Boosters review – supercool outlaw women go shoplifting in Boots Riley’s frantic and funny caper | Movies | The Guardian
description: Demi Moore’s haute-couture maven attracts the attention of a gang of contemporary Robin Hood type clothes robbers in Riley’s fashion biz satire
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Demi Moore’s haute-couture maven attracts the attention of a gang of contemporary Robin Hood type clothes robbers in Riley’s fashion biz satire
Content: Clothes encounter … I Love Boosters.Photograph: Courtesty of NeonView image in fullscreenClothes encounter … I Love Boosters.Photograph: Courtesty of NeonMoviesReviewI Love Boosters review – supercool outlaw women go shoplifting in Boots Riley’s frantic and funny caperDemi Moore’s haute-couture maven attracts the attention of a gang of contemporary Robin Hood type clothes robbers in Riley’s fashion biz satirePeter BradshawThu 29 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 11.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is an entertaining, if very exhausting fantasy-caper about the fashion biz from Boots Riley, a madcap mile-a-minute melee of unadulterated ker-aziness. You might need a couple of ibuprofen and a lie-down afterwards. Demi Moore perhaps thought she was here getting a gamey starring role, comparable to her Oscar-nominated turn in thebeauty-industry satire The Substance. In fact, the way the film is structured and edited, Moore is hardly more than a returning cameo, though a potent one.View image in fullscreenPotent … Demi Moore as Christie Smith in I Love Boosters.Photograph: Neon/PAShe plays Christie Smith, a billionaire couture designer who has an office in a trendily designed city block which leans over at an experimental angle. Christie is the object of obsessive attention from “boosters”: supercool young outlaw women who, nettled by her arrogance, shoplift her clothes from upscale stores and sell them on at knockdown Robin Hood prices. They are Corvette (Keke Palmer), Sade (Naomi Ackie) and Mariah (Taylour Paige), the latter having the ability to, by holding her breath, turning herself into a white woman who is less likely to be challenged in a store; an interesting metaphor for what Frantz Fanon might have called black skin, white masks.For all their savvy, the boosters have a soft spot for certain men in their lives, notably a charismatic community leader called Dr Jack (Don Cheadle), who is running a friendship self-help scheme that is actually a fraudulent pyramid scam. And Corvette is entranced by a laidback charmer and oral sex enthusiast played by LaKeith Stansfield, who turns out to be a demonic male succubus.The boosters’ chaotic way of life becomes even more problematic when they realise they are up against what appears to be a rival thief from China; this is Jianhu (Poppy Liu), who wields a magic portal ring the size of a toilet seat which sucks all the clothes out of a store and teleports them back to China, where underpaid workers have been making them under scandalously bad conditions. Jianhu is protesting against Christie Smith’s exploitative employment practices – and by being forced to make common cause with her, the boosters find themselves in unexpected territory: the moral high ground.This is a cacophonous, chaotic film which delivers a sensory overload of almost incoherently frantic onscreen activity, and it can be hard to take, though it is often funny. There’s enough material here for a 12-episode streaming show, and that may be where Riley may wish to take it – although it’s quite an experience at feature-film length, a compressed spectacle of hellzapoppin’ uproar.I Love Boosters is out on 30 October in the UK, and on 12 November in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsCrime filmsFashion industryBoots RileyDemi MooreKeke PalmerreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Sea review – Jennifer Saunders takes fussing over buying curtains to Shakespearean levels | Stage | The Guardian
description: Edward Bond’s play about consumerism and the strength of humans in dark times is hugely enlivened by Saunders and her tight-lipped pomposity
Author: Holly O'Mahony
Headline: Edward Bond’s play about consumerism and the strength of humans in dark times is hugely enlivened by Saunders and her tight-lipped pomposity
Content: ‘Consumerism as a distraction from the pain and absurdity of life’ … Jennifer Saunders and Lucy Briers in the draper’s shop.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreen‘Consumerism as a distraction from the pain and absurdity of life’ … Jennifer Saunders and Lucy Briers in the draper’s shop.Photograph: Marc BrennerStageReviewThe Sea review – Jennifer Saunders takes fussing over buying curtains to Shakespearean levelsTheatre Royal BathEdward Bond’s play about consumerism and the strength of humans in dark times is hugely enlivened by Saunders and her tight-lipped pomposityHolly O'MahonyThu 29 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen describing his own play, the late playwright Edward Bond said he wanted The Sea to deal with tragedy, be a comedy and end with people being as honest and open as they could. Jonathan Munby’s production – the first major revival in almost 20 years – begins by offering its audience a view that would ordinarily be obscured: we’re plunged underwater to where the seafaring Colin (Elliot Goodhill) hangs suspended from a rope, fighting for his life, as the waves of Luke Halls’ impressive videography engulf him.It’s a fitting opening sequence for a play that subsequently demands its audience look beneath the surface to find meaning in seemingly trivial interactions. It’s jarring when, come the following scene, we’re flung into a draper’s shop, where Jennifer Saunders’ avaricious, egotistical Mrs Rafi is fussing over curtain material. But Bond understood consumerism as a distraction from the pain and absurdity of life. Similarly, his characters sing their hymns ever louder when there’s gunfire in the distance. They also stage an annual play to raise money for their seaside village’s coastguards, while maintaining distance from any trouble their beneficiaries face on the ground.View image in fullscreenDressed in black … Saunders and the rest of the cast in the Bond revival.Photograph: Marc BrennerSaunders brings tight-lipped pomposity to the imperious Mrs Rafi, though her early snobbishness mellows into something more mischievous towards the end. Her character’s late speech on her disappointment in, but dependency on, others rivals Shakespeare’s Jaques in its melancholy wisdom. Meanwhile, the reclusive Evens (an enigmatic Lloyd Hutchinson) seems like a stray Beckett character with his musing on striving to find faith amid the seeming meaninglessness of it all. The play’s setting in 1907 affords these characters a listlessness that, we imagine, could well give way to a carpe diem spirit were they to live through the first world war.Bond also wanted his play to capture the strength of human beings. Though the death of Colin – “for whom the future seemed all brightness” – initially leaves his fellow sailor Willy (Sean Delaney) and fiancee Rose (Holly Godliman) with a loss of purpose, in closing on a half-spoken thought between them, it ultimately ends on a note of hope.AtTheatre Royal Bath, until 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreJennifer SaundersTheatre Royal BathreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Pop prodigy Underscores: ‘I don’t think Gen Z is a loveless generation’ | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: With a sound inspired by the San Francisco tech boom, the hyperpop musician is entering the big leagues, and has a slot on Charli xcx’s tour. First she needs to get over her own shyness – not to mention a fear of love songs
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: With a sound inspired by the San Francisco tech boom, the hyperpop musician is entering the big leagues, and has a slot on Charli xcx’s tour. First she needs to get over her own shyness – not to mention a fear of love songs
Content: Live wire … Underscores AKA April Grey.Photograph: Bailey KrawczykView image in fullscreenLive wire … Underscores AKA April Grey.Photograph: Bailey KrawczykPop and rockInterviewPop prodigy Underscores: ‘I don’t think Gen Z is a loveless generation’Shaad D'SouzaWith a sound inspired by the San Francisco tech boom, the hyperpop musician is entering the big leagues, and has a slot on Charli xcx’s tour. First she needs to get over her own shyness – not to mention a fear of love songsThu 29 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 05.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe life of a rising pop star: One day, you’re performingyour own songwithCharli xcx, her dancers emulating your choreography, an arena’s worth of fans screaming along. The next, you’re on a surgery table, with a healthcare professional yanking four superfluous teeth out of your mouth. Even pop stars need emergency dental work sometimes.It’s all par for the course for April Grey, the San Francisco-born, Chicago-based musician who records as Underscores. Her 2026 has been, plainly, wild: her third album, U, released in March, was met with acclaim and attracted a small army of new fans. Many of the shows on her tour in support of U, earlier this year, were upgraded due to demand, and one expects the bump she’ll get from her current run supporting Charli xcx’s Music, Fashion, Film tour will push her into even bigger rooms. It’s a blow-up befitting the level of ambition Grey put into U, which is a taut, compulsively listenable pop record that sounds like a mid-2000s Now That’s What I Call Music! compilation as recreated by Aphex Twin. “As I was making it, it felt like a very big swing for the fences,” she says. “I wanted it to be big.”Grey is video-calling from her tour bus a week after her wisdom tooth surgery. (“The swelling wasn’t too bad,” she says. “I don’t even think I got too chipmunky.”) She knew that this year would be crazy – any album release year is, given how much touring and promotion is required to sell a record – but getting the call to join the Charli tour kicked things up a notch. “On my headline tour, many of the shows were upgraded to larger venues, but some weren’t, so there was this whiplash of playing to 4,000 people and then 400 the next night. The main struggle has been trying to figure out how to adapt the show,” she says. “After getting the Charli call, it’s like: ‘How does this look in an arena?’ It definitely is chasing a moving target.”Grey was born in the year 2000 and grew up amid the San Francisco tech boom. Her father is a musician who was “discovered by Elton John in a bar” but by the time Grey was born, he was “deep in startup world”. Her mother was a teacher, but now has a “crazy job selling jewellery to like, princes and stuff”. Grey “had a very vibrant childhood, and [San Francisco is] a really insane place to grow up … I think there’s an era before the tech boom that people romanticise a lot, but I can look at it now post-Covid and be like, wow, the tech boom, when it was first happening, was the glory days,” she says.Grey started making music at a young age, but really began taking things seriously when she was about 12, she says. It was hearing the American dubstep producer Skrillex that really changed things. “After discovering Skrillex, I was like: ‘All right, I’m gonna start taking this shit seriously,’” she recalls. From there, she was very “one-track minded” in that she didn’t really do anything else: “I didn’t have other friends, so I was obsessed. Now, I think I have a better work-life balance, but I’m a pretty shy person. But if I’m being honest, I was always very confident about music. There wasn’t really a plan B.”Away from Silicon Valley, a rowdier group of revolutionaries were congregating in the city, which was quickly becoming a hub for future bass producers such as Shawn Wasabi and the Nest HQ label in the mid-2010s. Grey was a teenager and fledgling producer around that time, and relished the opportunity to see stars of the scene so close to home. “I was like: ‘These people are legends’, and it was such a trip to be able to go to those [events]. I was trying to immerse myself in it, and then everyone left because they got priced out,” she says.double quotation markI haven’t really resonated with love songs in ways other people haveDuring high school, Grey realised that maybe she should have been spending more time cultivating a social life, as she saw people “going to parties and doing all these crazy things”. “I was like, ‘Damn! I haven’t done any of that shit,’” she recalls. But within a few years, it was clear she was on the right path. After spending a few years releasing brazenly avant garde music online, Grey released her debut album, Fishmonger, in 2021. It was an underground sensation and turned her into a critical darling.Fishmonger and its follow-up, 2023’s Wallsocket, felt hugely accomplished, but they didn’t have the intense laser focus of U. Wallsocket was a sprawling, rock-adjacent concept album about three young women coming of age, and Grey says its reception made her feel “misunderstood”. “I was almost embarrassed that I had accidentally made a rock opera or something – I’m not a theatre kid, I’m a jazz band kid,” she says with a laugh. “Afterwards, I thought if I was going to try my hand at a pop record, now would be the time to do it.”On U, Grey tried to write nine love songs, because she hadn’t written many previously. Before, she hadn’t thought that she was even able to. “I just don’t think I’ve really resonated with many love songs in ways that other people have, and growing up, I had issues with showing affection or intimacy. It was something I had to work at,” she says. Even so, she doesn’t buy the idea that gen z is a loveless generation. “I feel like there’s a lot of love to be had. Maybe we’re having less sex because it’s scary or something.Thatmight be true.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionU, with its Britney-meets-Oneohtrix Point Never production, vaulted Grey out of the underground into a more mainstream arena. But it wasn’t until about a month ago – when she met her childhood hero Skrillex at a dinner – that she realised she was in a new echelon. “I was sitting next to him, and he was just really nice, trying to include me as much as possible, asking questions,” she recalls. “I think people like that are just so willing to talk to people, and I’m not as much like that. It’s hard for me to initiate, and I’m kind of realising like, damn, I’m 26. I can’t be shy any more. We gotta cut that out.”Underscores: U review – ultra-imaginative auteur has pop’s most brilliant brainRead moreSpending time on tour with Charli, too, has shown her a different side of celebrity and pop stardom. “She is one of the nicest people I’ve ever met. She pops in and checks on us, and she’s very supportive,” she says. “At a level like hers, you worry that anybody under that scrutiny will turn into some kind of diva, and she’s not like that at all. It reminds me to check myself when I get diva-y. Like: Charli doesn’t do that, so I shouldn’t.”Whatever move Grey makes next, it seems likely that she’ll keep graduating to bigger and bigger stages. “If I think about it too long, it starts to make less and less sense,” she says. “But I gotta be ready for anything.”Underscorestours the UK and Ireland, 9 to 16 November; tour starts Dublin.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockCharli xcxinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comeback  | Music | The Guardian
description: As John Lewis reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players, music fans share their reasons for ditching streaming
Author: Alfie Packham
Headline: As John Lewis reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players, music fans share their reasons for ditching streaming
Content: Young people select and listen to CDs in a music shop in Munich.Photograph: Sueddeutsche Zeitung Photo/AlamyView image in fullscreenYoung people select and listen to CDs in a music shop in Munich.Photograph: Sueddeutsche Zeitung Photo/AlamyMusic‘Algorithms make everything predictable’: why the CD is making a comebackAs John Lewis reports a 96% rise in searches for CD players, music fans share their reasons for ditching streamingAlfie PackhamThu 29 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCDs appear to behaving a resurgence. John Lewis said searches for CD players are up 96% since July, whileanother reporton trends in music and film this year found that CD sales are up 16%.With this in mind, we asked music fans why they favour discs over other formats, and if it is a new preference or a lifetime habit.‘I have well over 10,000 CDs’View image in fullscreenAndrew Wales says his wife is very considerate about his CD collection.View image in fullscreenMore of Wales’s CD collection.Andrew Wales, 67, from London, owns “well over 10,000” CDs. “My wife’s very considerate,” he says over the phone. “There’s quite a few in this room where I’m speaking.” They have also spilt into the next bedroom and into the corridor.“I don’t need Spotify,” says Wales. “The fact is, I like listening to music and I have always preferred owning it in a physical form. The [size of the] CD format allows me to own the number I own despite living in a two-bedroom flat and not a country mansion, so that’s another bonus.”Much of the classical music Wales buys and listens to is available only on CD. “I bought my first CD in 1991 – John Scofield, Meant to Be – around the same time that I bought my first CD player. LPs were becoming increasingly shoddy, both in terms of pressing and presentation, and their limitations meant that often or not songs or tracks were included on the CD release, but not on LP. There are still cases where that happens today.”That said, Wales also owns “about 2,000 LPs”, “a few hundred cassettes” and an increasing number of Blu-rays. “I’m not always wedded to a single format.”‘After having a baby, our records were too bulky and inconvenient’View image in fullscreenGabriela Crowley with her daughter and her CD player.Unlike Wales, Gabriela Crowley, 32, from San Jose, California, started listening to CDs only over the last year. “Growing up, my parents had a tonne of them,” she says. “My dad played them in the car and everywhere. And then he got an iPod. By the time I was like 18, everything had started to shift away from physical media.”‘I don’t give a damn what people think any more!’ Jimmy Webb on his wild days – and writing hits for Dolly, Glen and FrankRead moreHer return to physical records started with the vinyl trend a few years ago. “I met my husband, who also had a large record collection, and we enjoyed that hobby together for a while. But after having a baby, we found we really weren’t listening to our records much any more – they were too bulky and inconvenient. My father-in-law gave us one of his old CD players and now we use that every day.”A CD collection helps with the “paradox of choice” that streaming brings, she says. “Instead of being paralysed by the endless options, you become more intimately familiar with what you have. I find it a much more satisfying way to engage with music. Plus, no autoplay or AI-generated playlists are being forced on me.”‘I buy CDs directly from the bands’View image in fullscreenNeil Cumming has several hundred CDs from classical to folk, rock and blues.“I bought my first CD in 1988 and have been collecting ever since,” says Neil Cumming, 53, from Gloucester. “I have several hundred of them. Everything from classical, folk, rock, blues …”Cumming buys CDs mostly to support musicians. “I like a lot of small indie and folk bands, who are not making a lot of money. I buy CDs directly from them when I can, which means they get a bigger share of my money than they would if I streamed their music.“And it means I own the CD for ever,” he says. “Streaming means you are basically renting the music, and it can disappear from the streaming sites. I enjoy the ritual of selecting a CD and putting it in the machine – it is a nicer experience than just pressing play on an app.”Not that he’s anti-streaming. “It’s quite good for trying music before you buy CDs or finding new acts. But in the evening, with a mug of tea or a glass of whisky, I find the experience of a CD more satisfying.”‘The antithesis of scrolling’View image in fullscreenAsha Varadharajan says the patience required in listening to a whole CD makes songs memorable.“I am drawn to the narrative and aesthetic arc of an album,” says Asha Varadharajan, 65, from Toronto. “It’s the antithesis of scrolling. I’ve never been a fan of music as white noise in the background, unless I’m boogying while vacuuming.”Varadharajan has owned her CD player since 1999, “which allows me to listen to five CDs at a time in any order I choose, building my own narrative arc as I listen.“I’m grateful to friends who introduced me to artists I may never have listened to,” she says. “The patience and persistence required in listening to a CD makes songs memorable. Streaming makes music ephemeral. I think algorithms make everything predictable, but everybody’s taste is kind of random.”It helps that CDs are hard to damage, she says. “I’m a klutz and was terrified of scratching albums as a child because I never could place the needle accurately without my hand shaking.”View image in fullscreenVaradharajan’s CD player allows her to listen to five CDs at a time ‘in any order I choose’.‘They give me something tactile and tangible’Ed, 63, from London, bought his first CDs in 1986 – “Genesis, Invisible Touch, and Level 42, World Machine, if you must know” – and has “never stopped”, he says. “But my interest in the format has waxed and waned.“When they first came out, CDs were very much positioned as: they’ll last for ever, you can drill holes in them, you can put jam on them and they still play. But I got put off CDs because they sounded too bright and shiny compared to vinyl.”But over the past two years, Ed has bought more CDs owing to their “almost throwaway prices against the excessive costs of vinyl”. Having music on CD “gives me something tactile and tangible”, Ed says. “A good digital source is now every bit as engaging as a good record player.”Explore more on these topicsMusicRetail industryMusic industryPop and rockMusic streamingCollectingVinylfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Mad Lover review – eccentric charm and baroque brilliance as duo move from Eccles to Indiana Jones | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Part of the London Festival of Baroque Music, lutenist Thomas Dunford and violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte’s concert struck a balance between freewheeling music-making and precise virtuosity
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Part of the London Festival of Baroque Music, lutenist Thomas Dunford and violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte’s concert struck a balance between freewheeling music-making and precise virtuosity
Content: ‘Freewheeling’ … violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte and lutenist Thomas Dunford.Photograph: Sophie OliverView image in fullscreen‘Freewheeling’ … violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte and lutenist Thomas Dunford.Photograph: Sophie OliverClassical musicReviewThe Mad Lover review – eccentric charm and baroque brilliance as duo move from Eccles to Indiana JonesSmith Square Hall, LondonPart of the London Festival of Baroque Music, lutenist Thomas Dunford and violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte’s concert struck a balance between freewheeling music-making and precise virtuosityErica JealThu 29 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 12.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Mad Lover was a 1616 play with incidental music by the English composer John Eccles. But, as the lutenist Thomas Dunford explained, we didn’t really need to know that: he and the violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte just liked the title. You can imagine it fitting many more programmes this duo might play together in the future – as they surely should, judging by the amount of fun they were having here.The two recorded this 75-minute programme of music by Eccles and his 17th-century contemporaries back in 2020, but this performance of it was their first in London. It was part of the week-long London Festival of Baroque Music – the last before a two-year break while the festival’s venue, Smith Square Hall, is refurbished – and struck a balance between freewheeling music-making and precise virtuosity.The hall was set up with a low platform in the centre, the audience on all four sides. The musicians walked in playing, the neck of Dunford’s lute swinging over our heads, Langlois de Swarte’s violin tone muscular yet sweet. An Eccles Aire gave way to a sonata by Daniel Purcell, then to an improvisation from Dunford, one of many: sometimes authentically baroque, sometimes expressing a more modern melancholy. Dunford also played the troll, throwing in snippets of Indiana Jones or Radiohead to make his colleague laugh.One of Dunford’s reveries morphed into the familiar repeating harmonies of La Folia, the 12-bar blues of the baroque period, here in a piece by the obscure London composer Nicola Matteis. The Fantasia in A minor by his son, Nicola Matteis Jr, was a web of chords delicately seesawing back and forth across the strings, and should be every violinist’s next encore. In Matteis Sr’s C Major Suite, one of Dunford’s lute strings unfurled, but he worked around it so skilfully that you could barely tell.Finally, Dunford persuaded an unusually willing audience to sing, thus providing harmonies first for a Henry Eccles piece drawing on a tavern song, then for a mystery encore based on JS Bach: the Beatles’ Blackbird, a song that can’t help being beautiful, and a fitting sign off given this concert’s eccentric charm.TheLondon Festival of Baroque Musiccontinues until Saturday. The Mad Lover is available onHarmonia Mundi.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Britten: Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings album review – Wilson explores British music’s highway and byways | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The Sinfonia and John Wilson bring warmth and sparkle to works by Ireland, Walton and Goosens; rising star tenor Laurence Kilsby and Christopher Parkes are expressive soloists in the Britten Serenade
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The Sinfonia and John Wilson bring warmth and sparkle to works by Ireland, Walton and Goosens; rising star tenor Laurence Kilsby and Christopher Parkes are expressive soloists in the Britten Serenade
Content: Seriously impressive … tenor Laurence Kilsby.Photograph: Benjamin ReasonView image in fullscreenSeriously impressive … tenor Laurence Kilsby.Photograph: Benjamin ReasonClassical musicReviewBritten: Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings album review – Wilson explores British music’s highway and bywaysSinfonia of London/Wilson/Kilsby/Parkes(Chandos)The Sinfonia and John Wilson bring warmth and sparkle to works by Ireland, Walton and Goosens; rising star tenor Laurence Kilsby and Christopher Parkes are expressive soloists in the Britten SerenadeClive PagetThu 29 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 10.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is John Wilson and the Sinfonia of London’s third album exploring British music for strings and, like its predecessors, showcases lesser-known repertoire alongside an acknowledged masterpiece. In this case, the byways include music by Ireland, Walton and Goossens with Britten’s Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings as centrepiece.View image in fullscreenBritten: Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings album cover.Written with the country on the brink of war, Ireland’s Concertino Pastorale comes with a baked-in nostalgia for an imagined rural idyll. Wilson gets to the troubled heart of the matter with a brooding Eclogue and poignant Threnody before finding release in the upbeat Toccata. The Sinfonia of London string sound displays a tremendous warmth in Chandos’ spacious recording, especially evident in Goossens’ lyrical nature poem, By the Tarn.Walton’s Sonata for String Orchestra, a late work from 1971, is a mix of honey and vinegar with an affecting central Lento. The counterpoint comes up polished and gleaming in the sparkling Presto and a syncopated finale.Laurence Kilsby and Christopher Parkes are the soloists in an expressive performance of the Britten. Like the young Peter Pears, Kilsby has a light, supple tenor that floats through Cotton’s dusk-infused Pastoral and Keats’ Sonnet and lends brilliance to Tennyson’s Nocturne and Jonson’s Hymn. Parkes, for his part, is sure-footed and sonorous. Horn and orchestra slightly overpower the voice at the terrifying climax of the Lyke-Wake Dirge. Nevertheless, this is a seriously impressive and subtly inflected account by Kilsby, a rapidly rising star.Listen onSpotifyExplore more on these topicsClassical musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Night Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head trip | Games | The Guardian
description: You take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbing
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: You take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbing
Content: Unsettling … Night Plane.Photograph: Liquid StaticView image in fullscreenUnsettling … Night Plane.Photograph: Liquid StaticGamesReviewNight Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head tripLiquid Static Studio; PCYou take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbingKeith StuartThu 29 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 07.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was always something creepy about the job-simulator genre. All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop.Now, we have Night Plane, in which you take on the role of a flight attendant on a jumbo jet to hell. It all starts kind of normally. You turn up for the first day of your new job, meet your colleagues, then take your spot at the departure gate, checking in customers and being careful to root out anyone with invalid tickets. Once on the plane, you roll your trolley down the aisle, serving booze and inedible meals, and occasionally dealing with passenger complaints. Then the plane crashes and, frankly, it all goes downhill from there.View image in fullscreenWeird existential horror … Night Plane.Photograph: Liquid StaticAre you dead? Are you in purgatory? And what was that weird creature someone spotted on the wing just before the engines blew up? All you know is, you’re back at the airport, checking in customers again, only this time, some of them are demons disguised as humans and you’re the one who has to sort the people from the people-eaters.Rendered in glitchy low poly visuals, Night Plane is another indie horror game that mimics the technical limits of the original PlayStation era to unsettle the player (see also Crow Country and Fear the Spotlight). The passengers already scare you with their boxy heads and expressionless faces, so when ghostly figures start walking across the aisle and disappearing, you’re already drowning in the uncanny valley. As the game goes on, the dialogue gets weirder, and then just turns into stutters and noises, the lights in the cabin flicker, luggage lockers open and close and rattle, and weird noises follow you. There are elements of the backrooms as well as Japanese onryō movies, as you warp between the plane and the airport, finding yourself trapped in endless passenger lounges and baggage claim areas, being pursued by heaven knows what.It’s all overlaid with a droll sense of humour, so you tend to be laughing to yourself moments before a jump scare jolts you out of your seat. At the outset, New Zealand-based developer Liquid Static Studio cleverly lures you into thinking this is a daft horror spoof, and it kind of is, but its use of nightmarish imagery – from piles of dead rats in the janitor’s room to a recurring image of your burning plane’s wreckage strewn across a remote wilderness – is genuinely disturbing and rife with sick imaginative details.Horror is increasingly the genre through which games dissect and examine themselves and their conventions, and Night Plane is a clever, absorbing example. You can “complete” the game in four or five hours, but subsequent playthroughs will reveal new sub-quests and endings, and priced at less than a tenner, it’s a steal. Even if you never set foot onboard this plane again, it gives you a fascinating budget flight into weird existential horror – and you’ll never take your cabin crew for granted again.Night Plane is available nowExplore more on these topicsGamesPCRetro gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Looming stone towers like Maya temples’: a hike through Snowdonia’s slate country | Snowdonia holidays | The Guardian
description: A new trail in the national park traces the legacy of Welsh industry, while offering some of the UK’s finest riverside and mountain walks
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: A new trail in the national park traces the legacy of Welsh industry, while offering some of the UK’s finest riverside and mountain walks
Content: The abandoned Cwmorthin quarry and lake on the 83-mile Snowdonia Slate Trail.Photograph: robertharding/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe abandoned Cwmorthin quarry and lake on the 83-mile Snowdonia Slate Trail.Photograph: robertharding/AlamySnowdonia holidays‘Looming stone towers like Maya temples’: a hike through Snowdonia’s slate countryA new trail in the national park traces the legacy of Welsh industry, while offering some of the UK’s finest riverside and mountain walksKevin RushbyThu 29 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 03.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe vital moment comes a couple of hours into the walk. I drop down from a tussocky hill towards the village of Y Fron. There’s an abandoned slate-quarrying machine and a grassy track that suddenly emerges on the rim of a deep lake-filled crater. The water is the colour of an old bruise. Around the rim is a fence of lichen-crusty slates like gravestones. It’s a dark, brooding spectacle and totally unexpected. At that moment, I know that whoever designed this route knew what they were doing.This is theLlwybr Llechi Eryri(Snowdonia Slate Trail), an 83-mile hike that follows a great loop around the national park, starting in Bangor and ending in Bethesda. It strings together a series of abandoned slate quarries with some of the finest riverside and mountain walking in the UK. I’m doing just three days, starting in Llanberis and heading to Betws-y-Coed via stops in Beddgelert and Llan Ffestiniog.Beyond Y Fron village, I descend into my first quarry, and it proves to be a classic. This was once the Dorothea slate quarry, a vast abandoned complex of railways, cottages and chasms. I start exploring: tunnels, cuttings, huge looming stone towers like Maya temples, all overgrown with ash, birch and oak. What strikes me is the craftsmanship and precision in construction, each stone hand-fitted without mortar, all for workaday industrial buildings.View image in fullscreenThe mountain village of Beddgelert makes a good pitstop for those hiking the trail.Photograph: Alex Manders/Getty ImagesThe quality of this slate was known from early times. Edward I is thought to have had his Welsh castles roofed with it, but industrial production began in the 1820s and peaked in the 1870s. Soon, there was a railway to Caernarfon and the area bristled with steam pumps, aerial cables and chains. The last-ever Cornish beam engine was installed to pump water from the deep pits, sucking up 10 gallons a second from 500ft down.From here, the trail burrows eastwards into the Welsh mountains, until Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) appears on the horizon when it turns south, occasionally following the line of theWelsh Highland Railwayall the way into Beddgelert, my first overnight stop. Named after a dog or a saint, depending on who you believe, this is a good base for hikers, having pubs, cafes, restaurants and outdoor gear shops.double quotation markThe water is the colour of an old bruise. Around the rim is a fence of lichen-crusty slates like gravestones. It’s a dark, brooding spectacleThe second day begins along a path combining the Slate Trail and theCambrian Way, one of the grandees of the long-distance genre at 298 miles. I follow the route as it heads south along the River Glaslyn, with some spectacular sections on crags with the torrent below. We are getting along very nicely – so well, in fact, that I start to get footpath envy. When the Cambrian Way turns east, heading up the Matterhorn-shaped peak of Cnicht, I cannot resist. The weather forecast is bad, but the sun is out. If I pop over the peak, I can see how the two paths cross each other later.View image in fullscreenCwmorthin quarry was once known as ‘the slaughterhouse’ due to the number of fatal accidents.Photograph: Digital-Fotofusion Gallery/AlamyViews of the Irish Sea open up as I climb, but there is an ominous black cloud approaching. As I reach the summit, a howling wind threatens to blow me off course. I face down the hailstones and get back to the Slate Trail, which now descends into Cwmorthin quarry. Not on the scale of Dorothea, Cwmorthin still seems epic today, dominated by vast heaps of spoiled stone – it took 10 tons to make 1 ton of marketable material. In the late 19th century, Cwmorthin was known locally as “the slaughterhouse” for its propensity to slay workers in fatal accidents. From here, the path runs down a desolate valley before dropping into Blaenau Ffestiniog, where I find a good cafe,Burrito Blasus, to fire me up the last miles into Llan Ffestiniog.I stay in theY Pengwern, a community-owned pub that has an excellent, friendly bar and basic rooms and food. Outside, a storm is buffeting the building, but the next day the rain has stopped and I begin with a rare treat: a magical trail beside the tumbling River Cynfal. Here, thunderous white spumes of water and dark powerful currents punch their way through a deep mossy gorge overhung by ancient fern-decked oaks. One of the midstream rock towers is said to have once been the “pulpit” of a magician called Huw Llwyd and, according to the 18th-century traveller and naturalistThomas Pennant, his voice could be heard at night, ringing down the enchanted chasms.double quotation markWhat strikes me is the craftsmanship and precision in construction, each stone hand-fitted without mortar, all for workaday industrial buildingsAs I climb higher, the forest dwindles and I emerge on a remote, wind-scoured upland of crags and bog. Even here, you can come across fragments of old quarry workings. In one abandoned cottage, a jacket still hangs on a nail behind the door, as if the occupant had just flounced out: “I’ve had enough. I’m off to America.” Many Welsh slate workers did head to the US, fed up with the poor pay and the repeated failure of strikes. In 1901, sympathetic workers in England sent a two-and-a-half ton Christmas pudding, which briefly lifted morale, but after violent clashes the landowner won, and many quarrymen emigrated.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe high street in the ancient village of Betws-y-Coed, another place of respite for hikers.Photograph: David Chapman/AlamyI stop and brew some tea on my stove. I have not seen another soul all day, yet Yr Wyddfa, with all its crowds, is less than 10 miles away. This remote walk takes me to the top of the old tramway incline down to Rhiwbach quarry – an epic approach, descending to the old engine house. This place peaked in the 1860s, and being so isolated, the miners lived in barracks, some of which remain.Scrambling, walking and swimming in splendid isolation: 75 years of the UK’s national parksRead moreFarther down the valley, I spot peregrine falcons nesting close to a tumbling waterfall, above the little village of Cwm Penmachno. A few miles on, thechurch of St Tudcludcontains an astonishing collection of inscribed stones, including the Carausius Stone. This is thought to be the gravestone of a commander of the Roman empire, who pulled off a coup d’etat in AD286, making himself emperor of Britain and northern Gaul for seven years before his assassination.Approaching Betws-y-Coed, the path joins the River Conwy, first singled out as a beauty spot in the 17th century, long before the Romantic poets seized on the idea. For me, it’s the finale to this fine route, but the path continues and I’ll be back soon for more mountains of slate and spectacular riverside walking.The trip was provided byWalkers’ Britain & Europe, which offersHiking the Snowdonia Slate Trailas aseven-dayself-guided83-milewalk, includingsix nights’ accommodation, breakfast, luggage transfers, digital app with tour information and navigations, andemergency hotlinefrom £890pp,departing dailyfromApril to OctoberExplore more on these topicsSnowdonia holidaysWalking holidaysWales holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysWalkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The high drama of volcanic wines | Wine | The Guardian
description: Is it a taste or just a feeling? Not to get woo-woo, but ashy landscapes give wines an energy
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Is it a taste or just a feeling? Not to get woo-woo, but ashy landscapes give wines an energy
Content: Volcanic landscapes impose particular demands on vines.Photograph: Dirk Renckhoff/AlamyView image in fullscreenVolcanic landscapes impose particular demands on vines.Photograph: Dirk Renckhoff/AlamyWineThe high drama of volcanic winesVines on volcanic soil are hard to grow and their grapes are hard-won, but it all combines to produce wines with a very particular sense of placeMina HollandThu 29 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGood stories need jeopardy. TakeThe Princess Bride, one of my favourite films, which I recently introduced to my mildly terrified children. It’s a cult love story of high peril: Westley, believed dead, sets out to win back Buttercup (forced into marriage with another) on a quest involving pirates, duels, torture, a miracle and a battle of wits over a goblet of poisoned wine. There is struggle, magic and, ultimately, emotional reward. You’ll need to stay with me here: volcanic vines, too, tend to have a rocky journey, albeit with happy results for the drinker.My ears perk up at the term “volcanic wine”, despite being less a style than a geological category. Volcanic soils take many forms – ash, basalt, obsidian, pumice, tuff – and interact with climate, altitude, water availability, grape variety and farming to produce wines with a very particular sense of place. Often, they have little in common with each other; a deep, rich nerello mascalese from Mount Etna’s north side bears little comparison to a light, leathery listán negro from Tenerife, say. And yet I’m sure thereissomething – perhaps it’s more a feeling than a taste – that I get from wines from volcanic terroirs. “It’s a hard thing to get across,” agrees importer Nic Rizzi ofModal Wines, “but they do have an extra tension.”Tension is the word. Volcanic landscapes impose particular demands: on Etna, for instance, the vines’ roots have to negotiate thin, stony soil formed from lava flows and ashfall; on Santorini, vines grow in loose pumice, ash and volcanic sand, with little rainfall and fierce winds; while in the Canary Islands, the vines can grow in deep layers of black ash. These are difficult landscapes to farm, but, as we know, a rocky journey does make for a good story.Rizzi imports wines made byVictoria Torres Pecisfrom La Palma in the Canaries, a place with “a majestic and wild energy”. There are black ash soils, vineyards above the cloud layer at 1,200m and ancient vines trained low to the ground to protect them from high winds. Farming here is labour-intensive; there are heatwaves and drought, and in 2021 a volcano erupted during harvest. “It takes a certain kind of person to put themselves through that pain and graft,” Rizzi says, “and that struggle comes through in the wine.” (Torres’ Las Machuqueras in today’s pick is a unicorn wine that sings deliciously of struggle.)Not to get too woo-woo about it, but, for me, volcanic wines share an energy. Legends have been built around volcanoes; they hold a mystical place in our imaginations. But, in very real terms, wines from these terroirs are deeply complex – saline, herbal, savoury and mineral – with a sense of tension that keeps you coming back. Like all interesting characters, their charisma is hard won.Volcanic wines that give you bang for your buckM&S Etna Rosato£14 Ocado, 12%. From high, lava-terraced vineyards comes this deeply hued, mineral rosé that goes with everythingBodega Volcanes Carménère 2024£12.50 Majestic, 14%. Energetic autumn red from one of Chile’s 3,000 volcanoes – expect dark fruit and umami.De Falco Fiordilava Falanghina del Vesuvio 2024£16 The Wine Society, 13%. The name means “flower of lava”, though it’s not floral, but rather a softly mineral falanghina from the slopes of Vesuvius.Rampazzi Bianco Andrea Occhipinti 2025£23.50 Sip Wines, 12%. Savoury and subtly smoky Tuscan beauty from above Europe’s oldest volcanic lake.Cave Verdier-LogelVolcanique Gamay Rouge 2024£20 Sourcing Table, 13.5%. At once juicy and peppery, this great-value Loire gamay hails from the volcanic basalt soils of the Massif Central foothills.Victoria Torres Pecis Las Machuqueras 2016/19£55 Modal Wines, 12.5%. Pricey, yes, but black ash soils, very old vines, harsh conditions and tiny yields combine to create a deeply textured and salty wineExplore more on these topicsWineFoodItalian food and drinkFrench food and drinkSpanish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu – recipe | Italian food and drink | The Guardian
description: A historical adventure deep in the very heart of pasta country in southern Italy unexpectedly unearths a sauce dish with roots in Senegal
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: A historical adventure deep in the very heart of pasta country in southern Italy unexpectedly unearths a sauce dish with roots in Senegal
Content: Rachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkRachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu – recipeA historical adventure deep in the very heart of pasta country in southern Italy unexpectedly unearths a sauce with roots in SenegalRachel RoddyThu 29 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 30 kilometres south of Naples, the town of Gragnano is surrounded by the Monti Lattari mountain range – the limestone backbone of the Sorrento peninsula. Historically, a series of natural springs fed into a larger stream called Vernotico, which flowed down the mountainside, passing through what was at the time the small village of Gragnano.The natural slope of the terrain was fortuitous, because it allowed for the construction of a sequence of mills, which started in around 1263. During a visit to Gragnano last month, local historian Giuseppe Di Massa explained how it all worked; how gravity drove the flow of water from one mill to the next, in order to power vertical millstones – a system created for the inconsistent flow. The valley, with its clever water system, became known as the valley of the mills; its role milling grain, which arrived at the nearby port of Castellammare di Stabia, a vital operation to Naples and surrounding towns.The activity of the 30 mills peaked during the 18th century, but another industry was growing, one that harnessed another natural aspect of the town: its climate. The temperature, humidity and sea breeze were ideal conditions for drying pasta.Often in strings hung over wooden frames, pasta was dried in the streets of Gragnano, then moved inside when necessary; the skill of the pasta makers and their ability to harness the weather every bit as important as the weather itself. And the industry grew. According to the city of Gragnano website, by 1859 there were 81 pasta factories, requiring ever increasing amounts of hard durum wheat for their pasta, while the mills produced soft wheat. The mills ceased operations in the 1950s, and were largely abandoned until renovation projects turned some of them into small museums.What has continued to grow in Gragnano, though, is the tradition and art of pasta making; now with its own Indicazione Geografica Protetta, which protects its quality (provenance of wheat, how it is extruded, how long it is dried) and connection with the region. These days, 23 producers – from tiny to vast, 15 of which make up a consortium – make more than 100,000 tonnes of pasta annually in carefully controlled conditions – conditions very different from the open streets, but requiring just as much skill. I returned to Rome with bags of pasta from seven different makers – Di Martino, Faella, Garofolo, Liguori, Afeltra, Antiche Tradizioni di Gragnano, Ducato di alfalfi – all of which pleased me with their nutty scent, porous texture and resilience in the pan.I also came back from Gragnano with a recipe devised for the town’s Mondopasta festival this year by chef Astou Ndiaye. Born in Dakar and now living with her family in Milan, Ndiaye’s cooking draws both on her heritage and her home. For her beautiful Senegalese ragu, the meat (I used lamb) is marinated in an aromatic blend of vegetables, coriander and cloves before being braised for a stew soft enough to be pasta sauce. I usedcandele(hollow tubes) made by Garfalo, which I broke into short lengths. It’s a dish that sums up the spirit of pasta di Gragnano, I think; rooted in both Gragnano and Dakar, and at home anywhere.Pasta with Senegalese-inspired lamb raguServes41 stickcelery,trimmed1 small red pepper,trimmed, deseeded and cut into strips1 shallot,peeled1 small bunchcoriander2garlic cloves,peeled3 clovesSalt600g boned lamb shoulder,cubedOlive oil1 large onion,peeled and diced1 tsp paprika1 tsp garam masala400-500g pasta(broken candele, maccheroni, mezze maniche)Working in a food processor, pulse the celery, red pepper, shallot, coriander, garlic, cloves and a pinch of salt into a rough mixture. Put half the mixture into a bowl, add the meat, then toss so all the chunks are coated.
